11205015.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11205015.value: This project aims at investigating the methodology in multi-dimensional imaging for infrared motion detection and tracking by integrating mobile reference structures with pyroelectric infrared (PIR) sensor arrays. A divide-and-conquer based hierarchical model for multi-dimensional imaging will be developed for mobile reference structure enhanced infrared motion sensing. The mobility of reference structures will be explored to perform a sensing task, and a closed-feedback paradigm will be investigated to coordinate the hierarchical reference structure tomography (RST) procedures in an optimal fashion. The goal in developing the hierarchical sensing model is to facilitate the high-dimensional imaging for RST enhanced infrared motion sensing under reference structure complexity constraints, where the mobile mechanism introduced plays an important role in limiting the amount of reference structures involved. Studying the structural redundancy in high-dimensional tomographic images will be useful for reducing the complexity and amount of reference structures involved, which calls for an adaptive sensing framework for coordinating the mobile PIR sensor arrays to perform hierarchical RST tasks. The output of the project will be a novel yet practical solution for the use of RST enhanced PIR sensor arrays in high-dimensional infrared motion sensing. The results of the project will contribute to the development of RST techniques. The study will have significant impact on the theoretical development in motion tracking and the practical applications in the related fields including smart environments, human-robot interactions and advanced surveillance. 本项目旨在研究一种多维成像的新方法及探索热释电红外传感的新模式,结合自主移动与参考结构层析成像以实现对运动的探测和跟踪。通过探究实现分治的复用设计方法，研究参考结构层析成像的分治模型理论，以加强此类红外传感的运动测量.并运用闭合反馈法以自主移动机制集成的自主复用实现技术，实现优化分层结构设计.通过限制多维成像对参考结构复杂多样性的过度需求,进而实现复用分治过程的自主优化.通过建立可实现参考结构设计相匹配的成像模型，找到调节参考结构复杂多样性的实现技术和设计方法.将多维影像信号的结构约束和冗余度转化为限制参考结构设计复杂度.这将需要具有自适应能力的感应模式以在执行此多层任务中去协调各传感阵列.本项目对参考结构层析成像方法在多维成像技术方面的研究将对用此方法的运动探测有重要意义. 通过对多维压缩传感成像理论的研究及拓展，其探讨结果将对相关领域有重要的学术意义，并将在智能环境、人机交互和监控等领域中得到广泛应用.

11205015.label: Realisation of objectives
11205015.value: In this project, extensive studies were conducted on motion sensing and tracking in relation to the project objectives. On infrared imaging and sensing, we proposed a novel Gabor transform-based infrared spectrum restoration method. A total variation regularized descriptor is designed and incorporated into the restoration model. The proposed model is inferred via an efficient optimization approach. Experiments show significant and consistent improvements of the developed model over state-of-the-art approaches. This method can be utilized to have a new feature for target detection for use in robot visual tracking systems [J12]. Related to imaging model studies for motion sensing, an active imaging method is proposed with fringe pattern projections [J1]. Based on this, the problem is studied on how the uncertainty of the relevant parameters would affect the 3D measurement accuracy, with relative error and sensitivity analysis provided. We also propose a joint optimization technique to combine the merits of both the intensity and phase-based optimization, which includes a pre-intensity optimization and a further optimization based on the synthesized error function. These are related to Objective 1 which is studied to the depth. In studying visual sensing and object detection, a cross-level feedback fusion approach is taken with RGB-D vision sensor [J6,J9,J16]. We propose a hierarchical cross-modal distillation scheme, in which the side outputs from the well-learned source modality serve as supervisory signals to facilitate the learning of the new unlabeled paired modality. We also design a top-down cross-modal cross-level fusion pattern, which allows sufficient cross-modal interactions and cross-level transmissions. In an effort to design hierarchical approach for the motion sensing task, a Rotation and Relative Velocity (RRV) descriptor is proposed for motion tracking and motion trajectory description. The RRV descriptor can be applied to characterize motions of an articulated structure with interconnections of multiple rigid bodies [J5]. This will enable hierarchical representation for motion. These are related to Objective 2 and 4 which are extensively addressed. To achieve enhanced motion sensing, some new sensing and motion tracking methods are explored. In studying new sensing approach, we have explored the use and feedback of prior knowledge of depth data on saliency perception for feature sensing. We focus on probing the spatial structure and layout in a depth image and inferring some saliency prior knowledge on the depth distribution. We studied motion tracking with a binocular vision system to precisely record the target motion trajectories in Cartesian space. Two fundamental problems are solved. The first problem arises from the limited depth of field (DOF) of microscope. Considering the motion of the objects, the existing autofocusing methods requiring sequential images either in focus or defocus are not workable. Therefore, a one-shot prior autofocusing approach is desired, which needs to take the motion tendency of objects into account. Besides, the autofocusing process always lags behind the motion of objects, and there inevitably will be prediction deviation on the motion tendency of objects. This leads to the second problem to estimate the 3D motion states from defocused images. In this work, we develop a method to estimate the depth from defocus from a single image. Then the motion states including both the position and velocity estimation approach is developed within the Kalman filter framework. The above two aspects mutually supply the necessary information for each other to be functional to accurately realize the DOF tracking and motion tracking of moving objects in feedback manner. In this way, a precision visual sensing-control feedback loop with motion tracking is achieved [J10,J11,J13]. In another case study, precise on gaze is achieved by feeding back the visual sensing and estimation for a mobile gaze tracking system [J8]. Towards optimal sensing, information fusion is explored in RGB-D visual sensing for target detection [J6]. Here multi-scale multi-path with cross-modal interactions is attempted progressively and adaptively in the learning method implemented [J16]. With the visual sensing information acquired, effective motion tracking and recognition is achieved. Towards optimal approach to information acquisition, we propose an optimization technique to combine the merits of both the intensity and phase-based optimization in our active imaging method, which includes a pre-intensity optimization and a further optimization based on the synthesized error function. This technique is implemented in two frameworks, the whole-fringe optimization and the best-patch optimization in the imaging framework. These are related to Objective 3 and 4 which are fully addressed.

11205015.label: Major findings and research outcome
11205015.value: In this project, we studied the issues in advanced motion sensing. In developing new sensing approach, we have explored the application of knowledge of depth data on saliency perception for feature sensing. We focus on probing the spatial structure and layout in a depth image and inferring some saliency prior knowledge on the depth distribution. Based on the saliency cues, we propose an effective RGB-D saliency detection framework with easy implementation, in which the saliency values of each region are measured by comparing the background and foreground queries sorted out by the proposed saliency cues. Optimal sensing is achieved by information fusion in RGB-D visual sensing and target detection. Here multi-scale multi-path with cross-modal interactions is attempted progressively and adaptively in the learning method implemented. In an effort to design hierarchical approach for the motion sensing task, a Rotation and Relative Velocity (RRV) descriptor is proposed for tracking and describing motion trajectories. The motion behaviors of a rigid body can be characterized by a six degree of freedom (DOF) motion trajectory, which contains the 3D position vectors of a reference point on the rigid body and 3D rotations of this rigid body over time. The proposed method explores the local translational and rotational invariants of rigid body motion trajectories, which is insensitive to noise, invariant to rigid transformation and scale. This method can be applied to characterize motions of a human body model for its tracking. This approach has its potentials and applications in different rigid body motion sensing and recognition tasks. The research show that the proposed approach can achieve superior results for various motion sensing and recognition tasks. Related to infrared sensing, some special imaging approach is studied and a novel restoration method is developed that can be useful for robot sensing and visual tracking. At the same time, an active visual sensing system is built for 3D measurement with a novel preprocessing method developed to generate high-quality binary fringes in DFP. In this work, we propose a joint optimization technique to combine the merits of both the intensity and phase-based optimization, which includes a pre-intensity optimization and a further optimization based on the synthesized error function. This technique can generate binary fringe patterns with high phase quality and robustness to projector defocus levels. Such a 3D imaging method will be useful for accurate motion sensing. A case study is conducted on using precision vision on a sensing-control feedback loop with accurate motion sensing and tracking achieved. These different methods developed will benefit effective motion tracking for theoretical analysis and practical applications.

11205015.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11205015.value: In this project, we studied the issues in advanced motion sensing to provide efficient way for complex motion tracking. The optimal sensing method is achieved by information fusion in RGB-D visual sensing. The learning approach studied here will invite more explorations with high potential for applications in AI and robotics. The active visual sensing system built with special fringe projection provides a way for high accuracy 3D measurement and motion sensing. This technique can generate binary fringe patterns with high phase quality. Such a 3D imaging method will be useful for accurate motion. The hierarchical method developed can be for full motion description and tracking with six degree of freedom (DOF) motion trajectories. This method can be useful for tracking complex motions like human actions, showing its potential in activity recognition and behavior monitoring in many tasks like security surveillance. The enhanced motion tracking and description method will be useful for human-robot interactions. We have planned to propose a following up project in this regard. Using information from gaze tracking, we can guide a robot and achieve interactions between a robot and human operator.

11205015.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11205015.value: This project investigates new imaging methods and system method for motion detection and tracking. In this work, the new motion sensing method developed can overcome the limitation of the current sensing system and approach and it will enhance the tracking performance with the sensing as well. The methods and system will be useful in practical applications including security surveillance and robotics. The motion tracking and description method is useful for behavior monitoring in security surveillance and activity recognition in motion reproduction in advanced robotics. These will be useful for raising the level of automation in robotic applications. This will in turn promote the theoretical development in motion tracking, to have its impact on the practical applications in the related fields including smart environments, human-robot interactions as well as advanced surveillance.

11205115.value: 高功率可調色LED照明系統之研究

11205115.label: Project Objectives
11205115.value: Investigate into a dimming and current-balancing structure with soft-switched dimming modules and derive mathematical models to describe the static and transient characteristics of the structure. Investigate into a power processing unit that delivers high-frequency AC current, and a synchronization strategy for operating with the dimming and current-balancing structure.

11205115.label: Realisation of objectives
11205115.value: An inductive power transfer system for driving multiple organic light-emitting diode (OLED) light panels is presented. Each light panel is driven by an output in a daisy-chained transformer (DCT) structure through a detachable transformer. The DCT structure allows using a single switching network to drive multiple light panels with good current balancing. A primary-side freewheeling (FW) circuit and an open-load protection network are introduced to maintain the current-balancing function of the DCT structure upon abnormal power transfer from the primary side to the secondary side of the detachable transformer. Apart from easy and safe operation, the proposed system also offers a modular, scalable, maintenance-free, and hot-swappable platform for large-area illumination. Modeling, design, and analysis of the system under normal and faulty operating conditions and misalignment of the detachable transformer have been done. A prototype system with four OLED light panels has been built and evaluated. The experimental results show that the circuit has a robust current balancing ability and fault condition tolerance. In addition, a comparison on the cost effectiveness between DCT structure and “one-drive-to-one-load” structure has been investigated. An investigation into the use of single inductor for driving N series-connected LED channels has been developed. Each channel has a parallel-connected switch for controlling the LED channel current, as well as charging the inductor. Compared with the conventional structure having all LED channels connected in parallel and (N + 1) switches, the proposed structure has the merits of 1) requiring N switches, 2) allowing all channels to be driven concurrently in every switching cycle, and 3) being insensitive to the duration of the transition switching from one channel to another. Detailed mathematical analysis on the topological operations have been done. The proposed concept has been successfully demonstrated on a two-channel structure. A prototype with two 7 W LED modules has been built and evaluated. A control mechanism that can regulate the output luminous flux and correlated color temperature without sensing the inductor current and channel currents has been be discussed. Experimental results have been favorably compared with theoretical predictions. It is sometimes unavoidable to place light sources and drivers far apart in large-scale LED lighting installation, where a long cable is used to connect the light source to the LED driver. LED drivers typically deliver pulse width-modulated pulses. The long cable inductance will delay the rate of rise of the current pulses and will also cause negative off-state voltage across the light source. Apart from reducing luminous output, such phenomenon also causes an impact on the life expectancy of the light source. A simple passive current compensator, which is connected between the driver and the light source to mitigate the distortion of the current pulses caused by the cable inductance, has been developed. The concept is based on recycling the energy stored in the cable after the end of a current pulse to drive the light source synchronously with the driver at the beginning of the next current pulse, so as to modify the rise time of the current pulses. The topological states and operations of the compensator will be discussed. Simplified design procedure for the compensator has been given. A prototype for a 12 V LED driver to drive LED strips of rated current 4.5 A has been built and evaluated. Experimental results are compared with theoretical predictions. The light-emitting diode (LED) has become a very promising alternative lighting source with the advantages of longer lifetime and higher efficiency than traditional ones. The lifetime prediction of LEDs is important to guide the LED system designers to fulfill the design specifications and to benchmark the cost-competitiveness of different lighting technologies. However, the existing lifetime data released by LED manufacturers or standard organizations are usually applicable only for some specific temperature and current levels. Significant lifetime discrepancies may be seen in the field operations due to the varying operational and environmental conditions during the entire service time (i.e., mission profiles). To overcome the challenge, an advanced lifetime prediction method, which takes into account the field operation mission profiles and also the statistical properties of the life data available from accelerated degradation testing have been developed. The electrical and thermal characteristics of LEDs are measured by a T3Ster system, used for the electrothermal modeling. It also identifies key variables (e.g., heat sink parameters) that can be designed to achieve a specified lifetime and reliability level. Two case studies of an indoor residential lighting and an outdoor street lighting application are presented to demonstrate the prediction procedures and the impact of different mission profiles on the lifetime of LEDs. The application of a solid-state input current harmonic filtering technique, named as power semiconductor filter (PSF), for boost-type power factor corrector (PFC) has been attempted. The filtering technique is based on connecting an active device, namely, series pass device (SPD), in series with the input of the boost converter. By adjusting the control signal to the SPD, the input current of the PFC is profiled to be in phase with the supply voltage and regulate the output voltage. The power dissipation of the SPD is maintained at a low level by operating the SPD at the boundary between the linear and saturation regions. Modeling of the static and dynamical characteristics, design, and analysis of the entire system will be given. A 100W, 85–265 Vac/400 Vdc PFC with the boost converter operating in discontinuous conduction mode has been built and evaluated. Experimental results reveal that the PSF can reduce the input current harmonics and improve the input power factor. They are in close agreement with the theoretical predictions. Finally, the conducted electromagnetic interference under different supply voltages has also been reported. A novel color control method for multicolor light emitting-diode (LED) systems has been proposed. The proposed control method can achieve high color rendering indexes by approximating the spectral power distributions (SPDs) of black bodies. The SPD control of the LED system is accomplished by combining a sensory module and a control module. The sensory module implements a linear function that merges readouts from multiple color sensors and maps the data into the optical powers of the LED channels, while the control module utilizes such data in a feedback loop to control the optical power of each channel. Compared with conventional control methods, the proposed method has the merits of 1) not requiring an accurate electrical-optical system model, 2) requiring only a few spectra data for offline calibration, 3) requiring only red-green-blue (RGB) color sensors for online operations of tetracolor and pentacolor LED systems, 4) providing consistent color with high color rendering index, and 5) being applicable to all multicolour LEDsystems. The proposed control method has been evaluated by applying it to an example of an RGB-amber LED system driven by a buck-type single-inductor-multiple-output LED driver with the LED channels connected in series. Experimental results have verified the effectiveness and robustness with ambient temperature of the proposed control method.

11205115.label: Major findings and research outcome
11205115.value: An inductive power transfer system for driving multiple organic light-emitting diode light panels has been developed [J1]. Each light panel is driven by an output in a daisy-chained transformer structure through a detachable transformer. The structure allows using a single switching network to drive multiple light panels with good current balancing. An investigation into the use of single inductor for driving N series-connected LED channels has been developed [J2], [C1]. Compared with the conventional structure having all LED channels connected in parallel and (N + 1) switches, the proposed structure has the merits of 1) requiring N switches, 2) allowing all channels to be driven concurrently in every switching cycle, and 3) being insensitive to the duration of the transition switching from one channel to another. A simple passive current compensator, which is connected between the driver and the light source to mitigate the distortion of the current pulses caused by the cable inductance, has been developed [J3], [J6], [C2]. The concept is based on recycling the energy stored in the cable after the end of a current pulse to drive the light source synchronously with the driver at the beginning of the next current pulse, so as to modify the rise time of the current pulses. An advanced lifetime prediction method, which takes into account the field operation mission profiles and also the statistical properties of the life data available from accelerated degradation testing has been developed [J4]. An application of a solid-state input current harmonic filtering technique, named as power semiconductor filter (PSF), for boost-type power factor corrector has been developed [J5]. The filtering technique is based on connecting an active device, namely, series pass device (SPD), in series with the input of the boost converter. It was developed for the front-stage AC/DC converter for the LED driver. Based on the architecture in [J2], a novel color control method for multicolor light emitting- diode (LED) systems has been developed [J6], [C4]. The developed control method can achieve high color rendering indexes by approximating the spectral power distributions (SPDs) of black bodies. A dimming module that can generate current pulses of variable pulse width, frequency, and amplitude supplying to LEDs from a DC source with high voltage ripple has been developed [C3]. It is connected in series with the LEDs and acts as a buffer between the DC source and LED.

11205115.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11205115.value: Further research can be conducted for control methods that can achieve color control with high color rendering indexes even when there is ambient light. Since the spectral peak control could provide data points with high color rendering indexes, those data points could be updated and utilized for the training of neural networks on microcontroller. The trained neural networks could achieve the color control of multi-color LED systems with or without ambient light. Compared with previous color control methods, the proposed method could 1) achieve color control with high color rendering index with or without ambient light, 2) be operated without an accurate electrical-optical system model, 3) be applicable to all multi-color LED systems, and 4) improve the performance without modifying any hardware. It could provide the color control for professional lighting.

11205115.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11205115.value: High-brightness light-emitting-diodes (LEDs) continue to reform the lighting industry with the increased efficacy, reduced cost, and added versatility and intelligence they bring to general illumination for both white-light and colored-light designs. The light is synthesized by mixing appropriate proportion of multiple primary colors. Each primary color is produced by a channel having multiple LED strings connected. The luminance of each channel is adjusted by a dimming controller that controls the magnitude of the electric current through it. However, different colors of LEDs have different forward voltages to operate. During the transition from one color to another, the output voltage of the LED driver cannot react instantly due to the output capacitor. It will cause a transient current spike through the LED of low forward voltage. Such spike will give rise to undesired electromagnetic interference, heating, and reliability concern. It will adversely affect the lifetime and quality of the LED. Although there are several remedial approaches to tackle such issue, they each have their own merits and limitations. This project aims to investigate an architecture that does not exhibit such problem, produces highly accurate colored light, and has high operational reliability. Extensive theoretical and experimental work have been conducted.

11205415.label: Project Objectives
11205415.value: Demonstrate an automated optically-induced electrohydrodynamic kinetics (OEHK) platform that is capable of controlling electrohydrodynamic instability of thin fluidic layer by optically-induced electrical stresses and thermocapillary flow. Using the OEHK platform, perform parametric experimental studies to find optimal optically-induced electrokinetics (OEK) conditions that allow rapid fabrication of microscale and nanoscale lens arrays with suitable morphology and refractive index (i.e., different optically transparent polymers) for near-field super-resolution imaging. Demonstrate a nanolens-array-based scanning near-field optical system (NASOS) using the nanolens arrays fabricated by the OEHK platform for large area (i.e., at least 1 order of magnitude larger scanning area than AFM system) super-resolution imaging (i.e., having optical resolution of 200 nm or below). Perform parametric experimental studies to find optimal scanning conditions such as the distance between nanolens array and sample, and the fastest scanning velocity without distortion. Explore theoretical models to elucidate the underlining principles of the capability of the nanolens in breaking the diffraction limit.

11205415.label: Realisation of objectives
11205415.value: We have achieved all objectives as stated in 5.1 above. Discussed below are methodologies used to achieve these project goals. A high-precision OEHK system was built in this project, which is automated with computer controllable micron-precision-movements in x, y, and z coordinates. The system was used to control the lens geometric parameters. The system consists of a controllable digital micro mirror projection kit to optimize the resolution and optical spectrum of the images projected onto the OEHK chips. A Nikon AF NIKKOR 50-mm f/1.8D lens was used as a microscopy component of the OEHK system. The OEHK system has an image resolution of ~ 2 μm, the micro-precision actuators allows spatial movements in 2 μm increments in the x and y directions, and submicron increments in the z direction. We have also built a device which contains two five-axis translational/tilting stages to precisely control the lens array and sample area to be parallel over as large a space as possible. The Newport 8082-M, which is a motorized wide XYZθxθy tilt aligner with minimal incremental linear motion smaller than 30 nm and angular resolution smaller than 0.7 µrad, was used to hold the lens array to allow a high-precision position control. Then, another five-axis translational/tilting stage was used to adjust sample surface to be as parallel to the lens array plane as possible. Between this stage and the sample, a high resolution five axis piezo positioning system (Power Integrations) was used to keep the distance between the NLA chip and sample constant during scanning. Four capacitor electrodes was fabricated and distributed on the four corners of the lens array. To control the gap between the NLA chip and the sample, a high accuracy capacitance meter was used to detect the capacitances of the capacitors, and the signal was used as the feedback signal to control the piezo actuator. In short, we have demonstrated an automated optically-induced electrohydrodynamic kinetics (OEHK) platform that is capable of controlling electrohydrodynamic instability of thin fluidic layer by optically-induced electrical stresses and thermocapillary flow. Essentially, it is a “muti-nozzle virtual dispenser” which draws femtolitre droplets from a dielectric fluidic thin film using pulse-voltage-triggered optically induced electrohydrodynamic instability (PVTOEHI). The “virtual dispenser” generates instability nucleation sites by controlling the optically induced lateral electrical stress and thermocapillary flow inside an OEK (optoelectrokinetics) chip. Physically, an electrohydrodynamic (EHD) instability is induced across the upper and lower electrodes of an OEK chip. We observed two droplet dispensing mechanisms which correspond to different EHD states: Taylor cone formation and optically induced EHD jet. The EHD states transition could be realized by adjusting the pulse voltage parameters to alter the morphology of dispensed micron-scale polymer droplets, which could then be formed into organized arrays of microlenses with controllable diameter and curvature based on surface tension effect. Parametric experimental studies were also performed to find optimal OEK conditions that allowed rapid fabrication of microscale and nanoscale lens arrays with suitable geometrical and optical properties. We have studied the relationship between microlens height, contact angle, diameter, volume, and parameters of pulse voltage. For example, typically a pulse voltage of 340V (3s duration) was required to produce a microlens of ~24 um diameter (hemispherical lens). It is interesting to note that, during the microlens fabrication process, micro-pillars were observed in areas that were not projected by light patterns in the OEK chip. We conjecture that these micro-pillars are due to uneven film or impurities induced nucleation sites, which are governed by EHD instability. When the upper and lower electrodes were separated, spherical drops appeared, and their contact angles were obtained by analyzing AFM; the contact angle analyses proved that EHD states transition induces the differences in morphology of the microlenses. The results also indicate that the diameter of the microlens shows a negative correlation to applied voltage; moreover, as voltage decreases and pulse duration increases, stable liquid bridges were generated. In addition, we have explored alternative methods to fabricate microlens arrays. Described below is another fabrication process developed which could provide microlens arrays using commercially available microspheres. Small pieces of blank Blu-ray disc (TDK BD-R 25 GB) samples were prepared with their surface protection layer removed. Two groups of dry BTG microspheres with diameters ranging from 27 to 32 μm and from 60 to 65 μm were purchased form Cospheric. The refractive index of the BTG microsphere is 1.9. Milli-Q water (resistivity: 18.2 MΩ, Millipore Systems) was used to wet the dry microspheres for dispersion. Standard coverslips as substrates were rinsed using dehydrated ethanol and dried under nitrogen flow, followed by O2 plasma treatment using a commercial Plasma Surface Modification System (Femto A, Diener electronic Inc., Germany) to enhance hydrophilicity. The BTG microsphere dispersion solution was dropped onto the coverslip surface for assembly. SYLGARD 184 silicone elastomer base and curing agent were acquired and used at a base/agent mass ratio of 10:1 for preparing the flexible polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) elastomer. A commercial spin coater (WS-650_BT, Laurell Technology, USA) was used to cast thin layers of the PDMS film onto the BTG-attached coverslip substrate. The PDMS films were cured in an oven at 65 ℃ for 2 h. The micro-sphere array (MSA) films were peeled off from the coverslip substrates using scalpels and tweezers with their freshly exposed surface marked as positive side for subsequent experiments. The thickness of the MSA film was determined using an upright optical microscope equipped with a high-precision tri-axial PZT translational stage by calculating the focal position shift from the upper surface and bottom. Using the developed lens-arrays, we have performed near-field optical scanning of samples with surface features smaller the diffraction limit. Two imaging modes were developed: the lens array-based dynamic scanning imaging mode and the stochastic lens-array region imaging overlay reconstruction mode. A large area surface image of 900 um^2 was acquired by stitching 210 images together. The image processing and analysis were conducted using the ImageJ software (Fiji). As an example, an 100×image (in air, without microlens/nanolens) with a calibrated pixel size of 0.065 μm/px was used as the reference image in determining the magnification factors of the microlens/nanolens images. SEM images with pixel sizes of equal or less than 0.014 μm/px were used as reference images in analyzing the subdiffraction-limited features. The grid/collection stitch plugin in ImageJ was used for reconstructing the meta-images. We have also used theoretical models to investigate the underlining principles of the capability of the nanolens in breaking the diffraction limit. For example, we used the FDTD method (Lumerical FDTD Solutions) and ran the simulation in 2D TE mode. By tracing and connecting the Poynting vectors, we obtained the vector magnitudes and directions as colors and streamlines, respectively, or different combination of refractive index and the size of nanosphers. Finally, we envision the fast scanning near-field optical system developed in this project could potentially offer a technology for observing large-area real-time manipulation events in the nanoscale.

11205415.label: Major findings and research outcome
11205415.value: Our team has explored several methods to fabricate nanolens arrays in this project and then applied these arrays for large area nano-scale imaging experiments. We have investigated the fundamental mechanisms behind using optical wavelength-scale lenses to resolve objects smaller than Abbe’s diffraction limit. We have successfully fabricated nanolens and microlens arrays using an optically-induced electrohydrodynamic kinetics (OEHK) platform and then integrated them into a parallel scanning system for near-field nano-scale imaging in large area. The key research outcome of this project include: i) successful development of simulation models to understand more in-depth the mechanisms of super-resolution capability of wavelength scale lenses; ii) demonstration of a high-resolution and high-precision computer controllable OEHK platforms for rapid fabrication of nanolens arrays; iii) development of a fast scanning near-field optical system for large area nano-scale imaging. We have published 6 journal papers (including 1 accepted paper, but excluding 1 more still under revision after first-round of review), 2 conferences papers, and trained 2 PhD students using the project funding. In terms of major findings from our research activities, we significantly enhanced the fundamental understanding of super-resolution imaging using microlenses by matching modelling and experimental results; we also explored the applications of microlens-array imaging in biological research. For example, we introduced a probe-lens device for scanning supper-resolution microscopy, under both real or virtual imaging modes. We characterized BTG-based microlens’s virtual image resolution and studied dependency of magnification factors on the focus positions. The observed correlation is consistent with theoretical modelling predictions. Most importantly, we have demonstrated a universal method for quantitative measurement and definition of magnification factor and resolution of a microsphere virtual image for any feature pattern. This work is described in the IEEE Open J. on Nanotechnology paper listed in Part C. We have also demonstrated that parallel microlens imaging and dynamic large-scale scan-imaging could be combined to achieve super-resolution imaging under visible light. In static imaging mode, we realized parallel multi-area block super-resolution imaging using a microlens array, which reduced imaging duration and improved imaging efficiency. In dynamic large-area imaging mode, we revealed nano-scale details of the samples (breaking the diffraction limit) while realizing high-speed large-area imaging. In summary, our method provides a potential tool to study multi-scale samples, such as mouse brain slices and nano-scale features in IC chips, under visible light. Details of the above results were reported in our paper published in Applied Surface Science listed in Part C.

11205415.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11205415.value: Our team will continue to push for the limit of using micro/nano lenses to observe nano-scale features smaller than the diffraction limit using visible light. We intend to explore different fabrication processes to create nanoparticle-based metalenses (NPMs) for super-resolution imaging -- NPMs have been shown theoretically to have higher magnification than homogeneous microlenses. Currently, no technology exists to reliably and accurately fabricate hemispherical metalenses with controllable morphsoology. For example, we will develop a three-dimensional microfluidic device where nanoparticle colloidal solutions can be delivered into it, which then could convert the nanoparticles into NPMs via a pervaporation process. These NPMs could potentially have two major advantages over exiting microsphere-based superlenses: a) improvement of collection efficiency of the evanescent waves from sample surfaces by increasing the imaging ‘spot’ from point-contact to surface-contact; b) elimination of the requirement that the refractive index ratio between microsphere and its immersion medium should be less than two, which has confined the magnification factor and resolution of microsphere-based imaging. We also perform numerical analyses to further elucidate the mechanisms behind evanescent waves propagation tightly-packed nanoparticles in a metalens. We intend to apply for grants from the HKRGC and the NSFC to continue our research activities.

11205415.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11205415.value: Optical microscope is one of the most significant inventions in human history. Its development has revolutionized biological sciences among many other fields. However, its resolution is confined by Abbe’s diffraction limit to about half of the visible-light wavelength. In this project, our team has extended the capability of super-resolution microscopy, which is a relatively new technology that uses micro-scale lenses to collect evanescent waves close to the surface of samples and allows the observation of features smaller than the diffraction limit. Compared to methods such as confocal microscopy and scanning near-field optical microscopy (SNOM), micro-lens based super-resolution imaging (1) allows imaging in real-time, (2) eliminates the requirement of fluorescent samples, and (3) provides significantly larger field-of-view than SNOM. To further promote this imaging principle for acquiring optical images of nano-scale features in large areas with fast speed, we introduced parallel scanning using an array of micro-lenses. A key research goal of this project was to explore various fabrication processes to realize organized arrays of micro-lenses for super-resolution image scanning. We envision the fast scanning near-field optical system developed in this project could potentially offer a new paradigm for fast real-time imaging of biological and physical events in the nano-scale domain.

11205515.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11205515.value: High-strength structural materials are highly desirable for a wide range of lightweighting applications. Nanoparticle strengthening is one of the most effective approaches to improve material strength without significant reduction of ductility. Basically, the stregnthening efficiency depends highly upon the intrinsic mechanical properties of the nanoparticles. However, due to their extreme small size which is too small for most conventional mechanical techniques, the nano-mechanical properties of the nanoparticles are poorly understood, and many interesting and important areas remain to be clarified. With Cu nanoparticles in the high-strength Fe-based alloys as a model, this proposed research aims at three aspects for a fundamental understanding of nanoscale mechanics: (1) the intrinsic mechanical properties of the Cu nanoparticles with different crystalline structures and structural features; (2) the interaction of dislocations with the Cu nanoparticles; and (3) the correlation between bulk mechanical properties and the Cu nanoparticles. First, we intend to determine the intrinsic mechanical properties of the Cu nanoparticles with different crystalline structures and structural features, such as nano-twins. We will first attempt to experimentally determine the mechanical properties of the Cu nanoparticles using peak-force tapping atomic force microscope (PFT-AFM). In parallel, first-principles (FP) calculations will be employed to calculate the elastic properties of the Cu nanoparticles with different crystalline structures, aiming to correlate the nanoscale mechanical properties with their nanostructures. Second, we plan to understand the dislocation interaction with the Cu nanoparticles. Transmission electron microscope (TEM) characterization will be conducted to determine the critical size of the Cu nanoparticles for the interaction transition from cutting to looping models. In addition, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations will be performed to elucidate the effect of the Ni interface on the deformation-induced shear transformation of the Cu nanoparticles. Finally, we aim at correlating the bulk mechanical properties with the Cu nanoscale particles. The strengthening mechanism will be critically evaluated by considering all strengthening contributions, including modulus strengthening, transformation strengthening and coherency strengthening, while the work hardening behavior will be correlated with the dislocation interaction of the Cu nanoparticles, with the aim at predicting the macroscale stress-strain behavior from the nanoparticles. The successful implementation of this proposed research will lead to an unprecedented understanding of the nano-mechanics of the Cu nanoparticles and their correlation with the bulk mechanical properties. 11205515.label: Realisation of objectives
11205515.value: 1. To characterize the intrinsic mechanical properties of Cu nanoparticles with different crystalline structures and structural features in the high-strength Fe-based alloys. It is known that Cu nanoparticles exhibit unique structural evolution with aging time, i.e., from BCC to 9R and finally to FCC structure. The intrinsic nano-mechanical properties of the FCC structured Cu nanoparticles with sizes of ~30 to 50 nm in the high-strength Fe-based alloys were successfully characterized with the high-resolution atomic microscopy (HR-AFM). The effects of deformation on the mechanical behaviours of these FCC structured Cu nanoparticles were also studied. A series of heat treatments at temperatures between 550 and 640 °C for various periods of time were conducted to get Cu nanoparticles with different structures. 3D atom probe tomography (3D-APT) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) were used to characterize the microstructure, composition, size, and number density of the Cu nanoparticles. This serial of Cu nanoparticles with different sizes and crystal structures provide a good model for further characterization of the intrinsic nano-mechanical properties of Cu nanoparticles. Besides, the interesting solute segregation behavior and nucleation mechanism of Cu nanoparticles in multi-component alloys were studied. Two types of Cu precipitation pathways were identified. In alloys with high Cu concentrations, the Cu nanoparticles can nucleate independently from the supersaturated solid solution due to the low solubility of Cu in bcc Fe-based matrix. In comparison, in Fe-Cu-Ni-Al-based alloys with low Cu concentrations, NiAl nanoparticles enriched with a significant amount of Cu first nucleate from the supersaturated solid solution. The formation of NiAl nanoparticles leads to the rejection of Cu solutes toward the nanoparticle surface, resulting in the heterogeneous precipitation of Cu nanoparticles on the outer surface of NiAl nanoparticles. After determining the size and composition of the nanoparticles in the steels using APT and TEM, the intrinsic nano-mechanical properties of the nanoparticles were characterized using HR-AFM with a cantilever of carbon nanotube of radius ~1 nm after careful calibration. Standard mechanical polishing was performed to obtain scratch-free flat surfaces for HR-AFM characterization. The intrinsic nano-mechanical properties of individual Cu nanoparticles can be probed by measuring the energy dissipation due to the phase shift of a vibrating cantilever as it taps the surface of the steel specimens. For the FCC structured Cu nanoparticles after annealing for 10 h at 640 ℃, our HR-AFM measurements show an average particle size of ~30 to 50 nm, in consistent with the TEM results. Besides, we also found that the FCC Cu nanoparticles with sizes of ~50 nm are soft and have an average energy dissipation 24 % higher than the surrounding steel matrix. To study the effects of deformation on the nano-mechanical behaviours of the FCC Cu nanoparticles, HR-AFM measurements were performed on the tensile deformed specimens. The results reveal that the FCC Cu nanoparticles turn hard and have an average energy dissipation of 7% lower than the steel matrix after tensile deformation. The results about the intrinsic nano-mechanical properties of Cu nanoparticles have been published in Scientific Reports, 6: 21364, 2016 and Materials Today, 20(3): 142–154, 2017. 2. To correlate the bulk mechanical properties of the high-strength Fe-based alloys with the Cu nanoscale particles. It is our aim to correlate the precipitate microstructure with the bulk alloy mechanical properties. Steel samples strengthened by Cu nanoparticles with different sizes and crystal structures were produced by different heat treatments. For example, finely dispersed Cu nanoparticles of ~3 to 4 nm were obtained after aging at 550 °C for 2 h. The Cu nanoparticles grew to ~5 to 6 mm after aging at 640 °C for 10 min. With prolonged aging at 640 °C for 10 h, the nanoparticles were overaged to ~30 to 50 nm. Tensile tests were performed on these steel samples to obtain the bulk mechanical properties, such as the tensile strengths and elongation. Our results show that for small and weak particles (<50 nm), the particle strengthening effects can be modelled through the Russel-Brown model. The model was developed based on the pinning of dislocations as a result of the attractive dislocation-precipitate interaction due to the difference in elastic modulus between the soft Cu nanoparticles and the α-Fe matrix. The model operates by assuming dislocations cut through the soft Cu nanoparticles. The strength increment due to the 3-4 nm, 5-6 nm, and 30-50 nm Cu nanoparticles were calculated to be approximately 400, 318, and 80 MPa, respectively. Moreover, we also studied the toughening mechanism of Cu-nanoparticle-strengthened steels at low temperatures. We found that the high-strength Fe-based alloys containing low levels of carbon, copper, and nickel additions possess multiple strengthening and toughening mechanisms depending on the cooling rate and heat treatment conditions. These elements stabilize the austenite phase at high temperatures (~900 °C) and induce martensite strengthening when cooling rapidly to room temperature. The formation of tempered martensite along with Cu nanoparticles give rise to the strengthening after annealing at a low temperature (~500 to 640 °C). This multiple strengthening and toughening mechanisms are of technological importance as it allows for annealing at temperatures (>600 °C) above the dangerous 300-600 °C temper embrittlement regime which is important in producing steels with both superior strength and toughness. The results about the phase-property relationship have been published in Acta Materialia 110: 31-43, 2016, Acta Materialia 120: 216-227, 2016, and Acta Materialia 172: 150-160, 2019).

11205515.label: Major findings and research outcome
11205515.value: Through the ultrafine dispersion of high number densities of Cu nanoparticles, we developed high-strength (> 1 GPa) Fe-based alloys with satisfactory tensile ductility of over 10 % and reduction in area of ~60 %. With the aid of the HR-AFM, we have made some impressive achievements on the micro-mechanical characterization of nanoscale precipitates, which put new insights into the intrinsic nano-mechanical behaviours of these Cu nanoparticles. We found that the FCC structured Cu nanoparticles with sizes of ~30 to 50 nm are soft as compared with the bcc-Fe matrix. However, these nanoparticles turn hard after tensile deformation, indicating that the nanoparticle-dislocation interaction hardens the Cu nanoparticles. Besides, the bulk mechanical properties of the high-strength Fe-based alloys were correlated with the Cu nanoparticles. The strengthening due to the Cu nanoparticles (up to 50 nm) were well predicted through the Russel Brown model by considering that the Cu nanoparticles are softer than the steel matrix, in agreement with the HR-AFM results. Apart from the strengthening due to the Cu nanoparticles, we also revealed the toughening mechanism of Cu-nanoparticle-strengthened steels at low temperatures. We found that the high-strength Fe-based alloys with additions of Cu, Ni, and C show multiple strengthening and toughening mechanisms depending on the cooling rate and heat treatment conditions. Gigapascal-grade steels with the yield and ultimate tensile strengths of over 1000 MPa, a ductility of more than 10%, and a reduction in area of >60% can be obtained by water quenching after a 900˚C solution treatment followed by a 10 min aging at 640˚C. The realization of the GPa-grade high-strength Fe-based alloys without the temper-embrittlement at 300–600˚C is achieved through multiple strengthening and toughening mechanisms.

11205515.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11205515.value: Due to the extreme small sizes, complex crystal structures and structural features of the Cu nanoparticles, the nano-mechanical properties and interaction with dislocations are not completely understood, and many interesting and important areas are worthy of further exploring. The dislocation interaction with the Cu nanoparticles is central to understanding the fundamental strengthening mechanism and obtaining a clear scenario of the Cu nanoparticle-dislocation interaction is essential. Apart from this, the thermal stability of nanoparticles is an important factor that has to be taken into consideration for high-temperature applications, such as turbine blades for aircraft engines and power plants. Most of the high-strength Fe-based steel alloys loss their particle strengthening to less than 200 MPa after exposing at elevated temperatures of 500–600 °C for 50–500-h due probably to the coarsening of the nanoparticles. For this reason, more research efforts have to be made to improve the thermal stability of nanoparticles in the future work.

11205515.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11205515.value: High-strength steels strengthened by Cu nanoparticles are highly desirable for a wide range of light weighting applications. Basically, the strengthening depends highly upon the mechanical properties of Cu nanoparticles. However, the intrinsic nano-mechanical properties of Cu nanoparticles have been an unsolved mystery due to their small sizes and complicated structure features. In this project, we experimentally characterized the intrinsic nano-mechanical properties of Cu nanoparticles by using high-resolution atomic force microscopy (HR-AFM). Our results indicate that the face-centered cubic structured Cu nanoparticles with sizes of 30-50 nm are soft as compared with the bcc-Fe matrix, and they turn hard after tensile deformation. These innovative efforts are essential for a fundamental understanding of the strengthening mechanism of Cu nanoparticles in the advanced high-strength steels. Besides, we studied the toughening mechanism of Cu-nanoparticle-strengthened steels at low temperatures. We found that the impact toughness at low temperatures can be significantly improved by control of annealing treatments outside the temper embrittlement regime. The discovery of multiple strengthening and toughening mechanisms through control of heat treatments opens up a new window for the development of advanced steels with superior strength and toughness.

11205615.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11205615.value: 有效的温度管理系统对于保持电池处于最佳运行状态至关重要。由于电池温度分布的多尺度和时空动态特性以及电池单元内部无法安装传感器，电池的内部温度分布的估计变得非常困难。而且由于缺乏直接的空间控制方程，对电池组有效的温度管理也变得十分困难。 该项目针对电池/包的内部温度分布旨在设计一个多尺度时空建模方法和基于时空模型的管理方案；提出了通过实时实验，物理模拟和分析模型集成建模与控制的多阶段方法。 • 首先，针对电池的温度分布，进行多尺度下的模拟，从粒子反应到热量产生。首次提出基于迭代优化的近似模型方法，通过实验数据对模型参数进行迭代估计。 • 其次，在时空分离下构建电池温度分布的解析模型，并利用物理仿真所得的数据对其加以训练。通过数据学习减少传感器的使用，通过在线学习不断更新解析模型，逐步生成一个可行状态预测模型用于电池的健康监测。 • 最后，在适当的位置和气流控制机构中添加半导体制冷片，在此基础上，设计时空模糊控制方案，将电池温度场维持在理想状态中。

11205615.label: Major findings and research outcome
11205615.value: The physical model, including electrical model and thermal model, of the battery, has been developed in terms of distributed parameter systems (DPS), and simulated using the commercial software package COMSOL [1, 3, 4]. Two useful multi-scale approaches are developed for tuning multiple parameters of the physical model. 1) Sensitivity based group-wise parameter identification [3] - All parameters will be identified based their sensitivity (importance), and then tuned from the most important (sensitive) group, and then to the least important group. 2) Multi-scale (coarse/fine) parameter optimization [4], with the particle swarm optimization algorithm for the coarse-scale identification, and the Levenberg-Marquardt (LM) algorithm for the fine-scale parameter identification. The analytical model is critical to online estimate temperature distribution of the battery, however, it is difficult due to the spatiotemporal dynamics of DPS. Important achievements are obtained under the framework of space/time separation, including the first incremental spatiotemporal modeling [22] for online estimating temperature distribution based on small batch of data, the first sliding-window based approach [19] for modeling of DPS with non-smonth dynamics, and the first “deep learning” approach for digging complex dynamics of DPS [2]. Besides, many different kinds of intelligent methods and computational intelligence methods are developed for improving the above online modeling approaches [5, 14, 16, 18]. Model based fuzzy management of DPS is a difficult task that include knowledge discovery for decision making and state detection for health monitoring. 1) Knowledge extraction for decision making requires the capability to handle both vagueness and stochastic variations. The probabilistic fuzzy system [10] is developed to possess such a kind of ability for knowledge discovery. The Dempster-Shafer (D-S) theory of evidence is also applied for the situation under small samples [9]. 2) DPS control can be viewed as the low-level management. Several novel control approaches are developed for DPS. An iterative learning control law has been designed for the first time for the parabolic DPS system under the periodic disturbances [6]. Disturbance rejection approaches are also studied for the system under different kinds of periodic frequencies [7, 13]. As fuzzy system is effective under nonlinear uncertainties, various fuzzy control methods are developed for DPS under spatially discrete actuators [11], coupled PDE-ODE dynamics [12], and for exponential stability under sampled-data [15]. 3) It is the first time to detect the spatiotemporal abnormality for the DPS using the spatiotemporal model developed above [20].

11205615.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11205615.value: Analytical modeling of DPS under limited sensors is till not mature. Lots of constraints are needed, either lots of sensors or the homogeneous boundary conditions are required. Developing an effective modeling without such constraints is very important for real applications. Detection and spatial localization of the abnormality in DPS is still in the beginning phase. Similar to the spatiotemporal modeling, detection of spatiotemporal faults or abnormality are much more difficult compared to the traditional fault diagnosis for ODE system. Significant efforts are needed to improve both theoretical developments for more methods and practical implementation of these methods.

11205615.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11205615.value: Many of industrial processes, including the battery system, are distributed parameter systems (DPS) that exhibit strong space/time coupled dynamics. Modeling, control and health management of these kind of systems are extremely difficult, especially for online performance prediction and detection of any spatial abnormality for the health maintenance. The feasible solutions will come from the space/time separation based approach for modeling, control and detection, with assistance from other intelligent areas, like machine learning, fuzzy system and computational intelligence, etc. Success of this project will have good theoretical development for online estimation of DPS performance, DPS control and management. These theoretical work will lead to a better management system of battery operation.

11205715.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11205715.value: The continuous growth in the Internet traffic coupled with the rapid developments in big data, cloud computing, and Internet of things is putting much pressure on the bandwidth that can be provided by the existing wavelength-division multiplexing (WDM) technology, where a single-mode optical fiber is allowed to carry many close wavelength channels. Simply increasing the fiber count without increasing the transmission capacity of each fiber is not economical. There is intense world-wide research effort in the pursuit of new technologies to increase the transmission capacities of optical fibers. Mode-division multiplexing (MDM) that allows different modes in a multimode fiber to carry different channels is a particularly promising technology. This proposal aims at developing key photonic components to advance the MDM technology. Like the existing WDM networks, the future MDM networks will need to be reconfigurable, where different modes in a fiber can be switched or routed into different fibers. However, there are no effective active mode-controlling devices like mode switches and reconfigurable mode multiplexers available for MDM applications at this time. The goal of the project is to develop new mode-controlling devices based on lithium-niobate (LN) three-mode waveguides, where fast electrical mode switching is achieved by exploiting the electro-optic (EO) effect in LN. The project will investigate two types of EO mode-controlling devices: (1) mode switch that can switch any mode into any other mode along the same waveguide, and (2) mode (de)multiplexer that can switch a selected mode between two waveguides. The mode switch is based on the generation of an EO grating in an LN waveguide. Because of the mode symmetry, two different designs of mode switches are needed to achieve switching among the three modes. The mode (de)multiplexer is based on the configuration of two parallel LN waveguides with EO controlled coupling between the two waveguides. Only one design of the EO mode (de)multiplexer for a specific mode is needed, as the device can be used in conjunction with the mode switches to achieve space switching for the other modes. The project will also study the integration of these mode-controlling devices to achieve more advanced switching functions. The PI has over 30 year experience in the development of waveguide (including LN) devices. CityU is equipped with the necessary facility for the fabrication of LN waveguides and EO gratings. The project will lead to experimental demonstration of new mode-controlling devices with potential applications in reconfigurable MDM networks.

11205715.label: Realisation of objectives
11205715.value: All the project objectives have been addressed and achieved. The studies involved can be grouped into the following topics: (1) Development of EO mode switches with lithium-niobate (LN) three-mode waveguides (Objectives 1 and 2) We first studied two types of EO mode switches individually, namely the LP01-LP11a mode switch (Type A) and the LP01-LP11b mode switch (Type B). The LN waveguides used for realizing these switches were fabricated on Z-cut LN substrates with the anneal proton exchange (APE) process. We spent much effort in tuning the fabrication parameters to produce the refractive-index profiles of the waveguides for supporting three modes. In our early devices, we used metal grating electrodes to achieve EO switching, which required a sufficiently thick buffer (SiO2) layer placed between the metal electrodes and the waveguide to reduce the metal-induced loss. The presence of the buffer layer, however, significantly reduced the switching efficiency. To solve this problem, we replaced the metal electrodes and the buffer layer with graphene electrodes (graphene electrodes can be placed directly on the waveguide surface without inducing significant loss to the guided TM waves, so there is no need to use any buffer layer). With the graphene electrodes, we were able to reduce the switching voltage from 70 V to 24 V. The mode-conversion ratios of our gratings were higher than 20 dB (or 99%) at the resonance wavelengths. The first objective of the project has been fully achieved. With the success of realizing the two types of mode switches, we next demonstrated a three-mode switch by integrating three cascaded EO mode switches along an LN waveguide, where the first and the last grating were identical Type A mode switches and the middle grating was a Type B mode switch. The device was capable of providing all the six mode-switching functions available with the three modes (the LP01, LP11a, and LP11b modes). The main challenge in this study was the matching of the resonance wavelengths of the cascaded gratings. Our experimental device fabricated by APE with Z-cut LN had a total length of 26 mm, which employed patterned graphene electrodes to drive the grating switches and a metal electrode heater to compensate for the wavelength mismatch between the gratings. The switching voltages of the three EO gratings were 48, 37, and 43 V, respectively, and the maximum mode-conversion ratios of the gratings at ~1545 nm were higher than 20 dB. The second objective of the project has been fully achieved. (2) Development of EO mode (de)multiplexers based on parallel LN waveguides (Objectives 3 and 4) In collaboration with the University of Electronic Science and Technology of China (UESTC), we performed a series of studies on EO mode (de)multiplexers based on the configuration of an asymmetric directional coupler (DC) formed with a few-mode waveguide and a parallel single-mode waveguide. We successfully demonstrated an EO mode (de)multiplexer with an asymmetric DC formed with X-cut LN waveguides designed for switching between the LP11a mode in the few-mode waveguide and the LP01 mode in the single-mode waveguide. Our experimental device operated over a broad tunable range of wavelengths (~240 nm) with a switching efficiency higher than 10 dB at a driving voltage varying in the range from –23 V to +20 V. The modal crosstalk was lower than –12.5 dB (or 5%) in the C-band. In the realization of an LN asymmetric DC by the APE process, we found that the two waveguides of the DC had different heights, which made possible strong coupling between the LP11b mode of a few-mode waveguide to the LP01 mode of a single-mode waveguide. Because the LP11b mode has an antisymmetric field distribution along the vertical direction, such coupling is not allowed in a conventional asymmetric DC made of other materials (such as polymer and silicon) where the cores of the two parallel waveguides have the same height. Our finding opens up new possibilities for the realization of EO mode-controlling devices for high-order modes. By taking advantage of this property of an LN asymmetric DC, we also demonstrated EO mode (de)multiplexers for the LP11b and the LP02 mode. The third objective of the project has been fully achieved. The main challenge in the fabrication of an LN asymmetric DC is the production of matching waveguides by the APE process. The two waveguides that formed the DC must be precisely made, so that the modes in the two waveguides are phase-matched. Perfect matching of the two waveguides is difficult to achieve, as the APE process is sensitive to environmental disturbances, such as fluctuations in temperature and humidity. To overcome this problem, we developed a post-tuning technique, where a layer of high-index TiO2 layer was deposited onto one of the waveguides after the DC had been made to improve phase matching. With the help of this post-tuning technique, we demonstrated a reconfigurable EO mode (de)multiplexer (or mode-selective spatial switch) for the LP01, LP11a, and LP11b modes by integrating two EO asymmetric DCs. The device could switch the LP11a mode with an efficiency higher than 75% from 1530 nm to 1612 nm with a driving voltage varying between –9 V and +30 V, and switch the LP11b with an efficiency higher than 90% from 1534 nm to 1577 nm with a driving voltage varying between –21 V and 0 V. The fourth objective of the project has been fully achieved. (3) Other relevant studies The LN waveguide produced by the conventional APE or Ti-diffusion process has a highly asymmetric refractive-index profiles, which makes it difficult to achieve low crosstalk connection to a few-mode fiber. To solve this problem, we collaborated with the University of Electronic Science and Technology of China (UESTC) and fabricated a radially symmetric buried LN waveguide that supported six fiber-compatible spatial modes (the LP01, LP11a, LP11b, LP02, LP21a, and LP21b modes) by a bonding process. In addition, we demonstrated a vertical DC formed with this waveguide and another single-mode waveguide placed on top to achieve mode-selective coupling between the two waveguides. We made two DCs, one for coupling to the LP21b mode with a maximum coupling efficiency of 56% and the other for coupling to the LP02 mode with a maximum coupling efficiency of 18%. This 3D LN structure could be further developed into a platform for future development of fiber-compatible EO mode multiplexers. Before we realized the possibility of using only LN asymmetric DCs for implementing mode-selective spatial switches, we studied a more complex configuration to implement the same function, which consists of an LP11b-to-LP11a mode converter integrated with two identical asymmetric DCs designed for the LP11a mode. We successfully demonstrated such a configuration for passive three-mode (de)multiplexing with polymer waveguides. After we realized the possibility of using only LN asymmetric DCs to achieve the same function, we no longer worked on this configuration, and turned to the study of LN asymmetric DCs, as described in (2) above.

11205715.label: Major findings and research outcome
11205715.value: The major findings and research outcome are listed below: (1) We have proposed and demonstrated two types of EO mode switches based on electrically generated long-period gratings formed along lithium-niobate (LN) waveguides fabricated by the anneal proton exchange (APE) process [J1], [J4]. These switches allow fast switching between the LP01 mode and the LP11a mode (Type A) or between the LP01 mode and the LP11b mode (Type B) and can serve as building blocks for implementing advanced mode-controlling devices. (2) We have proposed and demonstrated a reconfigurable three-mode converter by integrating three cascaded EO mode switches along an LN waveguide, where the first and last switches are identical Type A switches and the middle one is a Type B switch [J4], [C2]. This device provides all the six mode-switching functions available with the LP01, LP11a, and LP11b modes. The results of the study have been accepted for publication in a special issue (Programmable Photonics) of IEEE Journal of Selected Topics in Quantum Electronics [J4]. (3) We have demonstrated the idea of replacing conventional metal electrodes with graphene electrodes to significantly reduce the driving voltage of an EO mode switch [J1]. All the EO mode switches in the reconfigurable three-mode converter described above employ graphene electrodes [J4], [J2]. (4) We have proposed and demonstrated mode-selective spatial switches based on LN asymmetric directional couplers (DCs) fabricated by the APE process [J3], [J5]. These spatial switches can serve as building blocks for implementing advanced mode-routing devices. (5) We have demonstrated a three-mode spatial switches by integrating two LN asymmetric DCs designed for different modes [J5], [C3]. We have also proposed a post-tuning technique to improve the performance of the asymmetric DC [J5], [C3]. (6) We have demonstrated a six-mode buried LN waveguide by a bonding process [C1]. Such a waveguide supports fiber-compatible modes and allows direct connection to an optical fiber with low modal crosstalk. We have also made attempt to form DCs on such a waveguide to show the feasibility of coupling light from a surface LN waveguide to a buried LN waveguide [C1]. This 3D LN waveguide structure could be further developed into a platform for future development of advanced switching devices for fiber-based mode-division-multiplexing applications. (7) We have demonstrated a three-mode (de)multiplexer with a grating-type mode converter and two identical asymmetric DCs with polymer material [J2]. This structure can serve a general platform for implementing more sophisticated mode-controlling devices.

11205715.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11205715.value: We have demonstrated two platforms for the realization of mode-controlling devices based on the electro-optic (EO) effect of lithium niobite (LN): mode switches with EO gratings and spatial switches with asymmetric directional couplers. Our studies have proved the feasibility of the LN waveguide technology in realizing few-mode devices, yet revealed some difficulties in this technology. The main difficulty lies in the control of the effective indices of LN waveguides fabricated with the APE process. Small fluctuations in the effective indices can significantly degrade the device performances, as our devices relies on precise matching of the effective indices in different waveguides or gratings. By incorporating the compensation methods that we have developed, the LN waveguide technology can be a practical technology for the implementation of few-mode switching devices. Recently, a new LN waveguide technology based on LN thin films has emerged and been proved to be highly successful in the implementation of single-mode EO devices. Given our experience gained in this project, our next step will be to explore the LN thin-film technology for the realization of integrated mode-controlling devices with more powerful switching functions for application in mode-division-multiplexing fiber communication.

11205715.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11205715.value: There is intense world-wide research effort in the pursuit of new technologies to increase the transmission capacities of optical fibers to meet the rapid growth in the demand for communication bandwidth. A promising technology is mode-division multiplexing (MDM), which allows different modes in a few-mode fiber to carry different channels. The goal of the project is to develop fast mode-switching devices based on lithium-niobate (LN) waveguides by exploiting the large electro-optic effect in LN. On completion of the project, we have successfully developed two types of switching devices with LN waveguides: mode switches and mode-selective spatial switches. A mode switch is a device that can switch any mode into any other mode along a waveguide, while a mode-selective spatial switch is a device that can switch a selected mode of a few-mode waveguide to a single-mode waveguide. These devices can find applications in reconfigurable MDM systems where different modes in a fiber can be switched or routed into different fibers. We have performed detailed studies on these devices and solved many difficult problems in the fabrication process. Our research work has led to a solid technology basis for further development of LN-based mode-controlling devices for application in MDM networks.
