11606715.label: Realisation of objectives
11606715.value: The project has fulfilled all of the following major objectives described in the proposal. 5.3.1. Sample size and Procedures. We have promised to recruit at least 100 students from Grade 7 to Grade 10 in Hong Kong. A total sample size of 155 secondary school students – 80 girls (51.6%) and 75 boys (48.4%) – were recruited to participate in this study. Thirteen of these 155 participants reported that they had either heard about the procedures or known about the details of the experiment before they attended the assessment session. Because prior knowledge of the directed forgetting procedures would affect the responses in the experiment, these 13 participants were excluded in the final analysis. The sample size is above the target number and the sample profile is similar to our proposed sample characteristics. We had followed the procedures outlined in our proposal closely. In brief, (1) the participants read the instructions on the computer screen; (2) the research assistant repeated the instructions aloud to ensure that all the participants understood the instructions; (3) the participants completed the DF task; and (4) the participants completed a set of questionnaires. 5.3.2. The Directed-forgetting (DF) test. We have mentioned in the proposal that we will refine the stimuli (words) of the DF test used in our previous study to make it more age and culturally appropriate. In the current project, we have selected 144 adjectives, with 48 positive, 48 neutral, and 48 negative words from the Chinese Affective Word System (CAWS) (Wang, Zhou, & Luo, 2008) which is a validated database among Chinese university students. Two members of the research team including the PI first selected the words and grouped them into positive, negative, or neutral categories according to the valence scores of the CAWS. Another research team member, who is an educational psychologist at the participating secondary school, reviewed all of the words to ensure that they were suitable for the reading level of the students. These 144 words were matched in terms of arousal and word frequency score on the CAWS, and they differed in terms of valence score only. These 144 adjectives in both English and Chinese were published as an Appendix in one of the papers related to this project (re first paper in Part C). We have used these 144 words to run the DF test with success. The procedures are described clearly in one of the published papers from this project (re Figures 1 and 2 of the first paper in Part C). The results of the DF test provided support to the validity of our apparatus and procedures. We found that the participants correctly recognized more To-be-Remember words than To-be-Forget words. Furthermore, negative words were better recognized than either positive words or neutral words irrespective of anxiety and depression levels. The above results are consistent with theoretical expectations as well as most of the current findings. We consider that we have achieved this objective of the project. 5.3.3. Research Questions There are two main research questions (re Part 5.1). We will discuss each of them below. Objective 1. The effect of age on DF of negatively valence words and positively valence words. We have mentioned in the original proposal that intentional-forgetting is a late-emerging memory capability that reaches maturity after certain age. According to some researchers, DF is either not observable among young children or it is irrelevant to their anxiety symptoms. We have mentioned in the original proposal that the current project will investigate if there are age differences in DF of negatively and positively valence words among our participants. We did not find significant relationships between age and any of the DF scores in our study (re Table 2 of the first paper in Part C). We concluded that participants across all ages in our study exhibited the same level of positive and negative memory biases. Age showed a relationship with psychological symptoms in this project which is consistent with existing findings. We consider that we have addressed this research question in the current project. Future longitudinal studies could be conducted to investigate the trajectory development of direct-forgetting and memory biases in order to investigate this research question further. Objective 2. The relationship between intentional forgetting (and memory bias) and anxiety symptoms among young people. The core research question of the current project is to examine if intentional forgetting (i.e. memory bias) is related to anxiety symptoms among our participants. Depression is included in the current project because of the high co-morbidity between anxiety and depression. Accordingly, we use moderation analysis to examine the anxiety x depression interaction effect on DF of positive and negative words. The results are reported in a paper published by the Journal of Clinical Psychology (re first paper in Section C). The main results are described below (see also Table 3 of the first paper in Part C). Regarding negatively-valence words, a higher anxiety score was related to a lower DF index for the negatively-valence words. In other words, anxious individuals exhibited an impaired ability to forget negative memories irrespective of their depression level. Regarding positively-valence words, we found a significant anxiety x depression interaction effect on DF of positive words. Our findings showed that anxiety level showed a positive relationship with DF of positive words only among individuals with high levels of depression. In other words, individuals with both high anxiety and depression levels are more prone to forgetting the positively-valence words. When the depression level was low, anxiety has no relationship with DF of positive words. In summary, our project shows that negative memory bias is a cognitive processing error exhibited by anxious adolescents, irrespective of their level of depression. The effect of positive memory bias on anxiety was moderated by severity of depression symptoms: only individuals with high level of depression showed a negative relationship between anxiety level and positive memory bias (i.e. positive relationship with DF of positively-valence words). We are the first research team to report the interaction effect of anxiety and depression on memory bias, to our best knowledge. Our results suggested that conventional intervention to reduce negative cognitive bias may be effective in reducing anxiety symptoms irrespective of the depression level. Interventions to increase positive memory sensitivity may be effective in reducing anxiety symptoms only among those with concurrent high depression levels. We consider that we have adequately addressed the research questions of this project as stated in our proposal.

11606715.label: Major findings and research outcome
11606715.value: Regarding objective 1, our results showed that age had no significant relationships with direct forgetting of positive, negative, and neutral words (re Table 2 of the first paper in Part C). In order to examine the development of anxiety and depression symptoms further, we have conducted an additional longitudinal study and assessed the participants one year later. Our results showed that memory bias did not predict future development of anxiety and depression symptoms. The results have been published the International Journal of Clinical and Health Psychology (2017 JCR IF = 3.90) (re second journal paper in Part C of this report). Since the wave 1 data of this study are from the current funded project, we have acknowledged RGC in this paper. Regarding objective 2 above, the most important findings is that anxiety level was negatively related to the directed forgetting of negatively-valence words. Regression-based moderation analysis revealed a significant anxiety × depression interaction effect on the directed forgetting of positively-valence words (p = .02, LLCI = .00, and ULCI = .01). Greater anxiety was associated with more directed forgetting of positively-valance words only among participants with high depression scores. With negatively-valence words, the anxiety × depression interaction effect was not significant (p = .15, LLCI=−.00, and ULCI = .01). The results have been published in Journal of Clinical Psychology (2017 JCR IF = 2.33) (re Paper 1 of Part C). The findings have been presented in two invited keynote addresses in Spain and Singapore as described in Part C of this report. It should be noted that for the keynote address at the International Congress of Clinical Psychology in Spain, the PI has reported the findings of this study amidst a series of studies conducted by him, and RCG was not acknowledge in the address. One undergraduate student has participated in this GRF project and developed a final year project under my supervision on working memory bias. This student is now furthering his study in UK. One Master student from Mainland China had conducted a preliminary study of the current project for her final year project under my supervision. She has graduated and returned to Mainland China. In sum, this project has generated two papers published in peer-reviewed international clinical psychology journals, two invited keynote addresses in international conferences, and trained two students at CityU.

11606715.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11606715.value: As mentioned in Part 5, a longitudinal study could be conducted to investigate the relationship between age and DF. Future studies could include younger students in primary school as well. Based on the results of this study, the PI has developed another experimental study on working memory updating, and conducted a pilot study to examine the relationship between anxiety and working memory updating of positive, negative, and neutral stimuli. We have submitted a journal paper which is under review at present.

11606715.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11606715.value: The current project investigates if secondary school students with higher anxiety are more prone to forget positive events as well as more incline to remember negative events. This project also aims to examine if the above relationship would change with age. We find that anxious students exhibit more difficulty to forget negative things, especially when they are instructed to forget them. This tendency applies irrespective of their depression level. On the other hand, anxious students tend to forget positive things easier only when they are also depressed. When depression is low, both anxious and non-anxious students show the same level of inclination in forgetting positive things. We are the first research team to report such findings, to our best knowledge. The implications are: (1) helping individuals to disengage from negative memory may reduce anxiety level, irrespective of whether they are depressed or not. Strategies to improve recollection of positive memory may reduce anxiety level only among those individual who are also depressed.

11606815.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11606815.value: This research addresses the legitimacy of mandatory chemical castration as a response to pedophile offenses. Should states compel men convicted of sexual offenses against children to undergo (reversible) chemical castration as part of their punishment and rehabilitation programs? Is chemical castration an effective method to control pedophile offenders and provide the greatest protection to society? Does chemical castration as mandatory state policy comply with generally recognized norms of international human rights law? The effectiveness of mandatory chemical castration turns on the issue of public safety, considered use of scarce state funds and ease of subverting the effects of the drugs. Many sex offenders are motivated out of a deviant need to exert dominance over their victims, something chemical castration does not address. Moreover, certain drugs can be used to counter-act the effects of chemical castration such as the steroid testosterone. States that adopt mandatory chemical castration run the risk of relying on it as a panacea at the cost of other more effective means of curbing pedophile behavior. Additionally, mandatory chemical castration may violate widely accepted principles of international human rights law. These objections are grounded in theories of cruel and unusual punishment, violation of the right to privacy, right to procreation, and that it is a form of torture or cruel, inhumane and degrading treatment or punishment. Arguably, mandatory chemical castration is unnecessary in relation to the gravity of the problem and the existence of other treatment/punishment modalities and it disproportionatly impacts the human rights of the offender. Additionally, non-compulsory chemical (or physical) castration may violate the human rights of the offenders as the accused may lack the requisite voluntariness for true consent. The importance of this research is manifest as a number of countries have already enacted mandatory chemical castration (e.g., Moldavia, Russia, South Korea, etc.) and a far larger number are contemplating it. Mandatory chemical castration represents a major departure from previous practices and will greatly impact criminal and human rights law as well as the study of criminology. Yet, there is scarcely any literature on this point, creating a lacuna in the scholarship. The value of this work is that it can assist policy-makers and stake holders in the criminal justice system to realistically appraise whether mandatory chemical castration is a legitimate response to pedophile offenses.

11608115.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11608115.value: This research proposal is concerned with the experience and impact of rapid urbanisation in China. It is concerned with processes of migration to, and adaptation in, cities and with the everyday life of the urban residents of these fast changing places. How do people feel about city life in contemporary China? To what extent do they have a strong sense of belonging, community or neighbourhood? Is the city experienced as a place of unity or division, integration or segregation? Are people concerned about these issues-do they matter and in what ways? What do the attitudes and practices of residents indicate about policy development with regard to governance and social participation? Rural-urban migration and urban social cohesion have always been important research issues for social scientists. Until recently, however, much of the academic research in this field had a strong western focus. This research aims to make an important contribution to the expanding urban studies literature on Chinese urbanism and urbanization and to inform wider policy and popular interest about what is happening in Chinese cities. The research will focus on Shenzhen. Its particularly rapid emergence as a new, major city makes it a highly appropriate site for this investigation. It has also been at the forefront of policy and political experimentation and was the first and most important Special Economic Zone. There has also been surprisingly little research on the city when compared to Guangzhou, Shanghai or Beijing. The research will involve a mixed methodology of secondary data analysis, social survey, focus group and in depth interviews. Face to face interviews with 1000 Shenzhen residents will form the empirical core of the study. 本研究關注快速城市化在中國的經驗及對它的影響。其中農村人口往城市移居的過程與與適應，及城市居民在這急劇轉變城市裡的日常生活，將是研究的重點。人們對當代中國城市生活有怎樣的感受？他們對社區或鄰里有著甚麼程度的歸屬感？城市究竟被感受為團結，凝聚或是分化，隔離的地方？ 人們是否關心這些議題－他們是否覺得議題重要，他們又怎樣關心？直到最近，大部分這方面的學術研究都從很強烈的西方觀點出發，這研究希望為中國的城市化與城市研究做出貢獻，及對政策制定及一般民眾提供參考材料。深圳將是這研究的個案城市。它迅速崛起成為一個新的重要城市讓這研究提供合適而重要的研究素材。深圳一直站在政策與政治創新的前沿，也是中國第一個，同時是最重要的經濟特區。但與廣州，北京，上海比較，對深圳的研究卻十分少。這研究將以包括次级数据分析，問卷調查，深度訪談的混合的方法進行研究；其中面對1000深圳居民的面談將會為研究提供重點數據。

11608115.label: Realisation of objectives
11608115.value: Project management and revisions to work plan All the original objectives for this project have been addressed and most will be fully realised over the coming months as more papers emerge and further data analysis is completed. Some objectives, however, may not be fully realised because of the revised funding originally allocated for this project which necessitated some revisions to the overall work programme. The original proposal was costed at $HKD1,208,075. However, the approved budget was reduced by some $HKD360000. This reduced funding did not require any alteration to the key objectives but it did mean that the main empirical work for the project revolved around the face to face survey. It was not possible to undertake most of the follow-on qualitative work originally envisaged. Thus, some of the additional depth of analysis which would have been achieved though follow up qualitative work with particular subgroups was not undertaken. This is the reason why the report the extent to which objectives were achieved have been achieved is less than 100% in most cases. However, it should be highlighted that the core survey was a significant success in terms of response rates, the quality of the responses and the coverage of the key issues of the research. The project was also affected by two other factors. First the PI moved institution after the first year of the project. This had been anticipated for some time and limited progress on the research in the first year for a variety of reasons. Some preliminary work was possible in the first year but the budget remained intact and was transferred in its entirely from City University to Lingnan University and research staff were appointed after the PI took up his post in August, 2017.. This involved inevitable delays and meant that the work on the survey design and planning did not get underway till well into the second year of the project. A second and more serious issue concerned the difficulties of undertaking this kind of research in the Mainland. Social surveys in Mainland China must be carried out by officially approved agents. In addition, face to face household surveys in the home are particularly challenging in terms of access and permissions. Overcoming these challenges was time consuming and ultimately involved some compromises in terms of survey strategy and questionnaire content. For example, some minor changes had to be made to questions deemed to be sensitive but the overall integrity of the questionnaire, and our ability to make robust comparisons with previous related studies, was not compromised. Different regulatory regimes between Hong Kong and the Mainland added some additional complications in terms of financial reporting. After the tendering process, which involved three approved agents and further negotiations, we were very fortunate to be able to employ Dataway Horizon, one of the most respected and professional social survey organisations in Mainland China. In close consultation with Dataway we agreed a strategy for the face to face survey in the home. A pilot survey was undertaken and one of the project researchers accompanied the interviewers to check on the quality of the interviews, the viability of the fieldwork strategy and whether the questions needed further adjustment. In line with the original project proposal the main stage survey achieved a total of 1007 completed interviews across the four districts of Nanshan (310) , Futian (360), Luohu (270) and Yantian District (60). This sample distribution is consistent with the population in each district. Respondents were adult household members aged between 18 and 75 who had lived in the local area for more than half a year. The sampling method involved multi-stage random sampling in which the number of neighbourhood committees was calculated on the principle that the sample size of each neighbourhood committee should be more than 35. The target respondents were selected according to neighbourhood committee. After entering the household, an interview was held with a household member who had lived there for at least 5 days a week. Where there was more than one eligible household member, the target was the person whose birthday was closest to the date of the interview. Consistent with the project objectives,the survey ranged across a number of areas including housing histories prior to arriving in Shenzhen, the reasons for moving to the city, aspects of neighbourhood use and local belonging, the use of and feelings about Shenzhen and future intentions. Activities Over the course of the project a number of outputs have been produced and various talks and conference papers have been, or are scheduled. Two working papers were produced as background work in the first phase-a scoping study on Segregation Research on Urban China (WP1) (attached to previous report) and an Update on Neighbourhood Research (WP2). Various pieces of background work were carried out on Shenzhen`s policy, development history and its so-called immigrant culture. Of particular interest was the evolving discourse on the ‘identity’ of Shenzhen residents and the changing official visions for the city. In doing so, we looked at official urban plans, newspaper reports and internet platforms. Prior to moving the project from City to Lingnan University, the PI raised funding to organise an international seminar which involved a number of eminent urban scholars from Europe, China and North America. The aim was to use this workshop, titled From Chicago to Shenzhen: The City One Hundred Years On to explore and test some of the ideas for the empirical work and also to ensure that the research engaged with the broader canvas of work on the contemporary Chinese city. The PI, with two co-editors, continued with this project after the move to Lingnan and the book from Bristol University Press (The City in China) was finally published in January, 2019 (the PI has a chapter in this and there are various other papers focused on Shenzhen in the volume). Apart from the published and under review papers listed, other dissemination activity by the PI includes: Keynote paper, ‘Neighbourhood, Cohesion and Urban Life in Shenzhen’, to the Conference on Global Governance in the Greater Bay Area (Lingnan University, October 22/23); ‘ City of Renters or City of Owners: Shenzhen in China`s Home Owning Society’, invited paper to workshop on Between Property Accumulation and Private Renting, European Network of Housing Researchers, Technical University of Vienna, May 16-17,2019; Guest speaker, Faculty of Global Human Sciences, Kobe University, ‘Does Neighbourhood Still Matter? New evidence from China’, December 6th,2019; ‘The Neighbourhood in the Chinese City’ (one of the talks as visiting invited speaker, Luxembourg Institute for Social and Economic Research, May 19-22, 2020). When the outstanding planned papers have been completed and submitted, the intention as per the original proposal, is to seek a publishing contract for a book focused on Shenzhen. The most likely appropriate series is The Contemporary City, Palgrave.

11608115.label: Major findings and research outcome
11608115.value: The analysis is ongoing, particularly in relation to the second section of the survey data which focuses on Shenzhen urbanism and attitudes towards city life. The keynote conference paper, Neighbourhood Cohesion and Urban Life in Shenzhen (Forrest ) is being written for Cities; one on Social Class , Belonging and Neighbourhood is planned for Sociological Review and, “If you come, you are a Shenzhener”: migration, hukou, and city attachment in Shenzhen. a paper by one of the project postdocs (Du,2019), has just been submitted to Population, Space and Place. Some of the main project findings so far are: • Shenzhen is the quintessential high-speed city with a relatively young, highly educated population- the kinds of people much of the existing research evidence suggests are more likely to be extra than intra neighbourhood oriented. However, this new urban fluidity and dynamism sits comfortably with traditional attitudes towards neighbourhoods and neighbouring. • People generally value their neighbourly relations and have positive feelings towards their residential environment. They enjoy meeting neighbours, strolling around their neighbourhoods and have a strong sense of community. Contrary to ‘the neighbourhood lost’ thesis, in Shenzhen it remains resilient as foundation for community, sense of belonging and social solidarity. • Shenzhen may now be a relatively mature new town now but it is still a major city in which most residents have migrated from somewhere else. Like all new towns, there may thus be less of a sense of locals and newcomers, the kinds of divisions which often act to erode neighbourhood cohesion. • Its dynamic image obscures an underlying stability. People like living there and want to stay. For example, more than two thirds agreed (46.7%) or strongly agreed (21.7%) with the statement “If I had to live anywhere in the world, it would be Shenzhen”. • Feelings of neighbourhood belonging and sense of attachment are higher among higher status groups. In higher status neighbourhoods, this strong sense of neighbourhood belonging may reflect a more Bourdieusian sense of distinction and of being among people of a similarly, high social status. • Comparisons with similar, older studies in Hong Kong and Guangzhou show differences but also striking similarities , continuities rather than the discontinuities over time and space-in different cities at different times and with different dynamics. • Shenzhen is a city of renters whereas home ownership dominates in other major cities. It is observed that this urban renting may be more representative of new urban China in the future.

11608115.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11608115.value: The original proposal envisaged a potential longitudinal development of the survey and this is still worth serious consideration. However, the logistical difficulties of undertaking social surveys in Mainland Chinese cities from a Hong Kong academic base should not be underestimated. Moreover, the present situation in Hong Kong makes social research in Mainland China by Hong Kong based academics extremely problematic. This is likely to remain a problem for the foreseeable future. Another area for further development, which is being taken forward, is to pay more attention to the 'vertical dimension' in research on belonging, cohesion, community etc. Many of the respondents in this study lived in high rise housing but we did not collect information on floor level-a strange omission in retrospect but true of most studies in this area. A GRF has already been submitted which pays closer attention to the increasingly vertical dimension of contemporary urban life in much of Asia.

11608115.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11608115.value: Ideas of community, cohesion and neighbourhood have been always been central concerns of urban sociology and urban studies. They have also been a major concern to policymakers and politicians who often search for ways to 'rebuild' community and neighbourhood, at least in their rhetoric. There is, however, a strong current which runs through much of the popular and academic literature suggesting that the residential neighbourhood is of diminishing relevance to our sense of belonging or social identity in the contemporary city. This research engages directly with these issues and suggests, among other things, that even in such a fast changing, rapidly expanding and economically dynamic city such as Shenzhen, the apparently more traditional role of the residential neighbourhood survives and remains an important site for socialisation and friendship across a wide cross section of residents.The research also suggests, however, that the meaning and role of the residential neighbourhood may vary for different groups in society. Comparisons with similar data from other cities indicates a strong element of continuity over time in relation to responses to questions about belonging, neighbourhood and community.

11608515.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11608515.value: 自从20世纪80年代，出现了一个国际趋势，就是发展一些政策和面向公众的项目，务求大众参与科学 (Fujun 2013; Webster and Dyball 2010; Glinkowski and Bamford 2009; Zhang and Zhang 1993)。这些鼓励公众参与科学并提高科学素养的途径是多方面的，英国的工程和物理科学研究理事会与美国国家科学基金会引入资金进行一系列的研究，从增强科学家沟通技巧 (Webster, 2010)、到开发的科学家对媒体的运用能力 (Downey, 2006)以及如何让艺术─科学文化活动吸引大量参与人群 (Heath, Hindmarsh and vom Lehn, 2005)。然而，这些方法的有效性还有待商榷，尤其是那些太过偏重于“教育”的办法(Heath et al, 2005)。学者们指出那些科学家们的目的并非出于无私，仅仅是为自己的研究利益而参与(Li, 2008)。随后科普的重心逐渐从狭义的促进公众理解科学转移到鼓励公众参与科学 (Hargreaves and Ferguson, 2000)。随着“参与”科学的理论逐渐深入人心，文化人类学的学术界开始争论文化活动和文化产品是否能有效地“承载”科学知识 (Csikszentmihalyi and Hermanson, 1995)，尤其是基于计算机的智能互动展品Heath et al, 2009)。 自60年代以来香港与中国大陆一直在探讨向大众普及科学的必要性，值得一提的是，在2006年全国科学技术大会，国家主席胡锦涛敦促科学家们“要在全社会广为传播科学知识、科学方法、科学思想、科学精神，使广大人民群众更好地接受科学技术的武装，进一步形成讲科学、爱科学、学科学、用科学的社会风尚” (Qi and Fujun, 2012)。由英国惠康基金会与英国工程物理科学研究委员会共同主导，对结合艺术与科学、意图通过制造和展览文化产品强化公众对科学的参与的项目的利弊进行过报道(Webster and Tyball, 2010; Paterson and Grant, 2011)。然而到目前为止，没有任何针对某一个项目本身的深入评估，或是其交流科学知识和方法的有效性评估，例如模型的运用。我们需要开发一些方法，让我们能够精确地了解经过艺术处理的词汇怎样激发、挑战并增强公众的科学认知。 如果没有有效的检测方法，无法确实证明普通大众中确实有人通过这些途径受益，那么我们无法准确衡量艺术─科学结合的项目能激励公众参与科学这些方法是否有效。 为弥补这一空白，本研究将会 a)完成以上所述的方法 b) 检验并衡量与艺术文化产品的接触是否能够增长其对于科学模型的理解。这项研究将分析：从当代科学中，本地公众如何使用关键的方法和数据的含义。我谨此申请GRF 用于巩固一个现有的研究项目，以协助公众理解模型在当代科学中所扮演的角色及其在科学传播中所起的作用。

11608515.label: Realisation of objectives
11608515.value: 5.3.1 Objectives remaining since the last reporting period In our mid-term report, we reported completion of a working prototype. We had also started to conduct user evaluation. These activities covered objectives 3, 4, 5, and 6. In the following, we will briefly mention these early activities, while focusing on remaining objectives 1, 2, and 7. 5.3.2 Mid-term report summary In the earlier reporting period, we had developed a prototype ready for communication, public engagement, and user evaluation. We had visualized Internet Weather and Air Quality Data (scientific model) and their information sources including temperature (data) (objective 3 completed). We used a basic deterministic 3D L-System to visualize the data as a realistic looking cherry blossom tree (interactive graphics) (objective 4 completed). In the app, users can interact with the model using smartphones (objective 5 completed). From day to day, life -enhancing air quality and weather data will grow the tree, while air quality and weather data detrimental to health will inhibit growth (objective 6 completed). We started the process of communicating science and user evaluation by conducting a design workshop with 60 undergraduate students. In this design workshop, we communicated the idea of scientific discovery to students by having them engage with the app for one week, and produce drawings, sketches, and other diagrams to illustrate their understanding of the app, and their ideas to improve the app design (objectives 1, 7). 5.3.3 Communicating science, user evaluation, and public engagement First round: Design workshops To analyze the design ideas suggested by the 60 students, we performed iterative coding during and after the participants’ presentations. This process extracted knowledge from each presentation. We used a collaborative mind mapping web tool, Coogle (coogle.it) that enables multiple users to construct a mind map together. The two mind maps captured key points from all the presentations. Both researchers accessed the same mind map document, each from their own laptops, and simultaneously added categories as the presentations took place. No categories were discussed or developed by the researchers beforehand - all were determined, openly and inductively, in response to the presentations. Research team members’ iterative coding and analysis made it clear that certain virtual items are mediating social interactions - a salient theme found in many of the presentations. We identified a set of design features to help improve the app. (Objective 7) Since completing the participatory design workshops we have implemented the following ideas that were the most salient from the participants’ evaluation, as evidenced in their illustrated presentations: firstly, to increase gamification and provide more visual feedback when users take actions. Participant designers wanted the addition of more international air quality index stations and we have added five. Our co-designers in the workshops suggested tapping icons was boring and more dynamic graphic representations were needed to promote more engagement by users, to show the tree’s changes in health instead of it always looking perky. We have therefore developed 1) a wider range of leaf and blossom textures to express health, for example brown dry leaves signifying ill-health, and 2) an animated particle system watering can feature that emphasised the user’s intervention (watering) that then impacted the underlying data and the results of that data on the tree’s health as displayed in the health status bar. (Objective 7) Second round: Wizard Of Oz Evaluation In July 2017, we prototyped features identified through design workshop for use in a Wizard of Oz evaluation. “Wizard of Oz” is a method for prototyping complex interactivity quickly and realistically. The “wizard” refers to an unseen human operator who manipulates reactions on the computer screen to create the illusion that the device is functional. In this demonstration, the researcher pretended that she was interacting with a functional version of Pocket Penjing, with her mobile phone screen projected for all participants to see. In fact, the projection was a recorded video that correlated to the scripted words and gestures used, live, by the researcher. We conducted a total of three such five-minute demonstrations, each followed by a 30-minute focus group discussion. The study brought together 20 participants who had not seen the app before. (Objective 1 and 7) Based on the outcome of the Wizard of Oz evaluation, our team developed an improved prototype with features of an in-app currency and gardening tools, also usable enough for participants to engage independently for a period of time. For example, we included “seeds” as the primary currency,, which can be earned daily as long as the participants kept their trees healthy the previous day. This was part of a further gamification of the app. To encourage their participation, we also rewarded users via these seeds for a daily login to the app. As such, a healthy tree was rewarded with 80 seeds, while a login rewarded an additional 20 seeds. These seeds can be used to buy tools, including “greenhouse,” and “watering can.” For example, when the temperature is high and rainfall is low, a user can apply “watering can” to resolve this problem. But each tool has limited use; for example, each “watering can” contains “10ml” of water. When a tool is used up, the user has to buy a new one using her “seeds.” Each tool costs 10 “seeds.” The need for costing creates dependencies between tree health, seeds, tools, and environmental conditions—challenging the user to balance these variables. (Objective 7) Third round: Field study With a final prototype embodying the first two rounds of user evaluation, we recruited 18 college students to participate in a one-month field test. Of these 18 participants, nine were male, and nine were female; there were 15 undergraduate students, and three master students. Between October 9 and October 16, 2018, we scheduled five different time slots, each an hour long, for our participants to attend a briefing. In this briefing, we focused on two aspects of the study. First, we ensured that each participant was able to download Pocket Penjing and install it in their Android devices. Following the demonstration, each participant was instructed to use Pocket Penjing for a one-month period, after which they would return to us individually for a post-test interview. (Objective 1) Between November 13 and November 20, 2018, we invited each participant to attend a one-to-one interview. (Objectives 1, 7 completed) We discuss research outcomes in Section 6.1. Public engagement through “The Best Gardeners” competition We engaged the public with the app through an activity, “The Best Gardeners” competition, held at our university. This activity was open to any student outside of participants from our user evaluation. Any students who downloaded the app online could participate. During a one-month period, each student’s goal was to collect the most number of seeds from one virtual tree—which entailed keeping them alive and as healthy as possible across the whole period. Students needed to examine and analyze how the data affected tree growth to achieve the highest possible score. The app was available for download on January 21, 2019, and the competition ended on February 19, 2019. 67 students took part in this competition. The Pocket Penjing app is also available freely for download at Pocket Penjing website (pocketpenjing.com) (Objective 2 completed)

11608515.label: Major findings and research outcome
11608515.value: Pocket Penjing’s cherry tree is a locally-relevant icon, reflecting, firstly, regional visual aesthetics of Chinese cherry blossom paintings and, secondly, the ancient and popular Chinese folk art of paper cutting (Prophet, et al., 2018). Pocket Penjing’s localized design contrasting with other environment’s apps’ uses of grand meanings such as “saving our planet” or “saving the polar bears” to motivate citizens, whom may not feel a sense of connection with these environmental motifs (Prophet and Kow, 2018). Our participants, from the Wizard of Oz demonstration to field-test interviews, suggested the importance of feeling “being there” when using the app. Our participants pointed out how the AR, as well as localized, live, and figurative representations of data, mediated a sense of realism when they interacted with the app. They wanted more quantitative data to be represented figuratively—such as the AR model showing yellowing of leaves and “bright and attractive colors” (Prophet, et al., 2018b). Thus, beyond an AR tree and virtual tools, the inclusion of more figurative representations could make the in-situ experience (“being there”) more seamless. Our findings point to the importance of mediating participants’ sense-making with scientific data, by means of places they are affiliated with. Nearly all participants opted to grow trees in these places. “What is the fun?” said a participant when we asked him about choosing other localities. If science refers to a process of taking abstract relationships out of nuanced practices, citizens’ meaning-making of scientific data comprises a reverse process—of putting abstract data back in places and to re-establish their meaningful connection to people (Kow, et al., under review). By embodying scientific data within localized, live, and polyaesthetic expressions, the data becomes externalized in a form that perhaps could bridge the distance between citizens and scientists in their understanding of environmental concerns. For example, even though we were unable to develop social features for the field test, some participants reported engaging in discussion with their friends and family members (Kow, et al., under review). In sum, live data and local, blended offline/online spaces of AR conveyed localized, live, and figurative expressions of quantitative data, which helps situate abstract science, and may re-establish science’s meaningful connection to citizens. This is a part of what has been termed the “civic turn”— the use of technology in civic action, engagement and participation in civic life (Prophet, et al., 2018; Prophet and Kow, 2018).

11608515.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11608515.value: The app can be further developed and more widely distributed by 1) developing an iOS version as well as the existing Android version; 2) implementing more enhancements that increase the visual expression of data to make the app even more appealing; 3) developing teaching packs for school teachers to enable the app to be used as part of STEM education classes; 4) developing a version for informal STEM learning in non-school settings. For example, a larger GPS locative media version for science museums where users move around a space on an AR treasure hunt and access interactive stickers that trigger in-game tokens to learn more about air quality, weather and health.

11608515.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11608515.value: In Hong Kong, many citizens did not make use of scientific data from weather stations when determining air quality. Pocket Penjing is a smartphone app that teaches its users, thus changing their mindset, about the importance of reading scientific data. The app allows users to grow a 3D computer-generated cherry tree. Using the smartphone camera, this virtual tree can be position in real-world locations. As users grow this tree, they will discover that whether the tree grows or stagnants depend on a range of data including air quality, temperature, and humidity. We spent two years developing this app by working alongside and testing it with more than 90 college students. We found that the Pocket Penjing’s choice of a local symbol (i.e., cherry tree) allows users to feel the tree “being there,” to immerse in the play, and to share this experience with family members and friends. This contrasted with other designs using more globalized symbols like “saving the polar bears,” which may not connect with Hong Kong people. With many people seeing science as cryptic, complex, and mysterious, we found that a design like Pocket Penjing can reconnect science back to forms they can comprehend.

11609515.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11609515.value: Consistent with theories of lifelong psychosocial growth and human development, older adults generally possess rich and valuable wisdom concerning many important aspects of life. However, whether this wisdom, can be fully conveyed to benefit them and future generations, remains uncertain due to inevitable physiological decline and increasing ageist attitudes in society. Narrative therapy (NT), as a solution to this challenge, views people as experts in their own lives who possess abilities, knowledge, and beliefs that assist them in coping with difficult life situations. Through this paradigm, NT offers an effective means for wisdom rediscovery and recollection, both for personal life management and sharing with others. A new practice to recognize the life wisdom of Hong Kong Chinese older adults, using a strength- and meaning-based NT in group practice is developed. Through this practice, their wealth of wisdom would be sustained and transferred to others to achieve a higher common good. The objectives of the study are three-fold: to analyze whether wisdom is more strongly related to well-being, for HK Chinese older adults ranging from their 50s to 80s randomly assigned to an immediate NT group, compared to a waitlist control group at baseline (T1); to examine the effectiveness of NT practice in enhancing wisdom, improving a sense of mastery, hope, meaning of life, and well-being among those older adults randomly assigned to the NT group, as compared to the waitlist control group after the NT group has completed the intervention (T2); and to test the longer-term effects at two months (T3) and eight months (T4). Through utilizing a randomized waitlist controlled trial, the effects of this group-based intervention will be tested utilizing qualitative data. A total of 144 older adults will be recruited for the study, 72 of which will be randomly assigned to nine intervention groups. There will be eight participants in each group, each of whom will receive four two-hour NT sessions using a “Tree of Life” metaphor. The findings have significant theoretical contributions for professional social work practice to develop a positive approach to late life development, and ground a new theory in understanding wisdom in older adulthood. This study is a pioneer in developing a new paradigm of clinical practice that facilitates a better understanding and appreciation of wisdom. The study will also produce, along with a variety of scholarly outputs, a practice guide to be disseminated among health and social care practitioners in Hong Kong. 正如終身心理發展理論和人類發展理論所講 ，長者在生活的很多重要方面擁有很豐富 、很有價值的智慧。 然而，由於自身生理上不可避免的衰退和社會上日益增加的年齡歧視，長者自身擁有的智慧是否可以為他們帶來好處以及傳遞給子孫依然無法確定。作為解決這類問題的一種方法，敘事治療認為人們是自身生活的專家，擁有能力、知識、信念去説明解決自身生活中的困難。 通過這種範式，敘事治療能提供有效的方法來重新發掘和重新收集智慧，以有效管理個人生活並學會與他人分享。 為了發掘在港華裔長者的生活智慧，一種以長處和意義為基礎的新的敘事治療小組實踐得到發展，通過這項實踐，他們的智慧財富得到維持，並可以傳遞給他人，以達到更高的公共利益。 此項研究目標分為三步：第一步是通過比較被隨機分配到敘事治療實驗組和被分配作為基準的等待對照組的 50歲到80歲的在港華裔長者，分析智慧是否與健康有很強的關聯性；第二步是等被隨機分配到敘事治療小組的長者們完成敘事治療後，通過與等待對照組的長者進行比較，來檢測敘事治療在增強智慧，提高自我控制感、希望感、生命意義感和健康水準方面的效果；第三步是二個月和八個月後，分別測試敘事治療的長期效果。 通過運用隨機等待對照試驗，這項小組治療效果會使用量化資料來分析。 共有144位長者加入到此項研究中，其中72位長者被隨機分配到九組介入小組中，每個小組共有8名成員，每位成員會參與用「生命樹」作為隱喻的四次課程，每節課為 2個小時。 研究結果為專業社會工作實踐提供了重要的理論指導，為人生晚年發展探索一種積極的路徑，並形成一種有關理解長者智慧的新理論。 此項研究是一次探索，旨在發展一種新的臨床實踐範式，以説明更好地理解和欣賞智慧。 隨著不斷產出的學術成果，此項研究還會為在健康和社會照顧領域的香港從業者提供一套實踐指導。

11609515.label: Realisation of objectives
11609515.value: Background: Consistent with theories of life course and development change, older adults generally possess rich and valuable wisdom concerning many important aspects of life. However, whether this wisdom, can be fully acknowledged by the persons, families and society, and conveyed to benefit the persons and their future generations, remains uncertain due to physiological decline and increasing ageist attitudes in society. Narrative therapy (NT), as an alternative solution to this challenge, views people as experts in their own lives, who possess abilities, knowledge, and beliefs that assist them in coping with difficult life situations. Through this practice, NT offers an effective means for rediscovering, recollecting, and sustaining a wealth of life wisdom for personal life management, and transferring to others to achieve a higher common good. Objectives: The study aimed to examine the effectiveness of NT practice in rediscovering life wisdom, improving a sense of mastery, hope, meaning of life and well-being among those older adults randomly assigned to the NT group, as compared to the waitlist control group, after the NT group has completed the intervention (T1), and two months after intervention (T2), and eight months after intervention (T3). Other than adopting a randomised waitlist controlled trial, the effects of this group-based intervention were also confirmed through in depth interviews. Methods: A total of 157 Hong Kong Chinese community-dwelling older adults aged 60 to 90 were recruited for the study, 78 of which had been randomly assigned to thirteen intervention groups. In collaboration with 19 community-based District Elderly Community Centres across Hong Kong, Kowloon, and New Territories regions, 26 “Life Wisdom” narrative groups were conducted from 2016 to 2018. 352 life episodes over a 4-week period were collected, recording difficult life circumstances, which made them stronger. Two researchers involved in analysing the transcripts independently using thematic analysis. Findings: Participants in the NT group showed significant improvements in the various outcome measures: sense of mastery (F = 3.54, p<.03), hope (F = 3.15, p < .03), meaning in life (F = 3.28, p < .02), wisdom (F = 7.21, p<.001) and wellbeing (F = 6.67, p<.001). Most improvements were sustained 2 and 8 months post intervention. No adverse reaction was recorded in any of the cases mentioned at all study sites. Six themes related to rediscovering wisdom were identified: 1) Insights about their abilities, intentions, and problem-solving capabilities, 2) a sense of purpose and commitment to their preferred identities, 3) Realisation of personal values and beliefs, 4) Increasing sense of agency and level of acceptance, 5) Maintaining hope in times of challenges, 6) Cherishing life as a journey to consolidate their wealth of wisdom for common good. NT offers an effective means for wisdom rediscovery and recollection, both for personal life management, and for reconstructing their meaning of life to overcome life transitions with others. Use of a “Tree of Life” metaphor and narrative conversations was effective. Implications: Wisdom has been associated to increased self-knowledge in the context of reviewing life-lessons for personal growth and common good. The participants reconnected their core values of personal inner resources, such as beliefs, hopes, loves, competence, commitments, in line of one’s preferred identities to reconstruct their sense of self and recollect their life wisdom through narrative conversations. These findings have significant theoretical and practice contributions for both health and social care professions to develop a constructive perspective to late life development, and ground a new theory in understanding wisdom in older adulthood.

11609515.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11609515.value: Future research is valuable in elaborating knowledge and practice in advancing social constructionism and narrative practice. Such research can notably fill gaps between the availability and activation of life wisdom as inner human resources and capital and using or investing this capital in production. This would mean the identification of capital as useful and fungible resources as such, and the deliberate investment and transformation of capital to benefit others for common good. Meanwhile, future research can also examine the effectiveness of narrative practice on various disadvantaged populations in overcoming life challenges in older age, such as confronting chronic and terminal illnesses, taking up caregiving and advance care duties, and recovering from bereavement.

11610215.value: 男人為何要承擔照顧責任? 香港男性照顧者的經驗

11610215.label: Co - Investigator(s)
11610215.value: Dr CHAN, Kam Wah Dr Tam, Kin Yuen

11610215.label: Project Objectives
11610215.value: To review the effectiveness of the child care and family-friendly policies of selected European and East Asian countries in supporting men as caregivers; To examine how Hong Kong people perceive the role of male caregivers and the factors that lead men decide to take on caring and domestic work in the family; To understand the needs and problems of male caregivers in the family; To explore the roles of social policies and social services in enhancing gender-sensitive interventions in assisting male caregivers.

11610215.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11610215.value: In Hong Kong, the majority of men are reluctant to partake in family affairs such as caregiving because these affairs fall outside of the roles accorded by the traditional gendered division of labour. However, in recent years, the changing social and economic environment has led to greater numbers of men assuming the major caring role in the family. However, although this shift towards more males becoming caregivers is in line with Hong Kong’s policies on gender equality and the gender division in other developed economies, the prevailing gender bias has meant that the challenges faced by male caregivers are not well addressed in Chinese society. In addition, the majority of the literature on the role of men as caregivers is based in Western contexts, and there is little available research applicable to Hong Kong. The proposed study will thus focus on the experiences of men who have shouldered a major role as caregivers in the family. The aims will be to 1) review the effectiveness of child care and family-friendly policies of European and East Asian countries in supporting men as caregivers; 2) examine the perceptions of Hong Kong people about the role of a male caregiver and the factors affecting their decisions on caring and domestic work in the family; 3) understand the needs and problems of male caregivers in the family; and 4) explore the possibility of developing a gender-sensitive policy and practice for male caregivers. Both quantitative and qualitative methods will be used in the study. Work will begin with a review of the policies in Singapore, the United Kingdom and Sweden that support men taking the role of caregivers. A telephone survey will then be conducted to obtain an overview of how Hong Kong people perceive the role of men as caregivers and their decisions on caring in their families. In addition, 20 men who are the main caregivers in their families will be recruited to participate in in-depth interviews so we can understand their views on caring and experiences as caregivers. Overall, this study will provide valuable information and insights on the challenges and problems that men experience in relation to the changing family and gender roles that are emerging as result of the ongoing socio-economic changes in today’s post-industrial society. The results will also help to develop a new understanding of the relationship between men and caring in a Chinese social context 香港的男士大部份都基於傳統的性別分工觀念而不願意參與家事。然而，近年因社會及經濟環境的變遷而有所改變，不少男性承擔主要照顧者的角色。雖然男性成為照顧者與香港鼓吹男女平等的政策相配合，然而，男性承擔照顧的責任所面對的挑戰在華人社會則備受忽略。況且，有關男性作為照顧者的討論主要來自西方的文獻，未必符合香港的社會環境。 研究的重點主要是探討男性在家庭中承擔主要照顧者的經驗。目的是: 1) 參閱歐洲及東亞不同國家的兒童照顧和家庭友善政策如何為男性照顧者提供支援; 2) 探討香港市民大眾如何理解男性照顧者的角色以及影響他們承擔照顧責任的因素; 3) 了解男性照顧者的需要和面對的問題; 4) 研究發展具性別敏感度的男性照顧者政策及措施的可行性。 是次研究採用量性和質性的方法。首先，檢視新加坡、英國和瑞典的照顧者支援政策。我們採用電話訪問的方法去搜集香港市民大眾如何理解男性照顧者的角色以及影響他們承擔照顧的因素。與此同時，我們會以深入訪談方式訪問20位男性照顧者以了解他們的照顧經驗。 總的來說，是次研究的資料有助我們理解男性在後工業時代，在家庭及性別角色轉變的過程中所面對的困難和挑戰。研究亦有助我們重新理解男性，特別在中國家庭的照顧關係。

11610215.label: Realisation of objectives
11610215.value: The objective 1 was achieved. To achieve this objective, we documented the childcare, elderly care and family-friendly policies of three Western and Asian countries including Sweden, the UK and Singapore. We could not find any policies in particular for supporting male carers but carers in general. However, Sweden has introduced some policy measures to encourage men to take up the role as carers in their families. The care support policies and services in these countries are found to be much better than that of in Hong Kong, which Hong Kong can be learnt from their experiences. The objective 2 was achieved. To achieve this objective, we conducted telephone survey to 514 respondents to understand their perceptions on men as carers. The study was commissioned to the Centre for Communication and Public Opinion Survey of the Chinese University of Hong Kong was commissioned to conduct a telephone survey based on random sampling. Among the respondents, 36.6% were men and 63.4% were women. The largest group of respondents were middle-aged (40-49 years old) and the percentage was 41.8%. The second largest group were 60 years old or above. Only 27.6% of the respondents were in the young age group (18-39 years old). In terms of educational level, the distribution of respondents was quite even. 32.7% of the respondents had a low educational level (Form 3 or below), 31.6% had a middle educational level (higher secondary education and pre-university), and 35.7% had a high educational level (college or above). In terms of family income, 33.2% of the respondents belonged to the low family income group (monthly income: $19,999 or less), 47.9% belonged to middle family income group (monthly income: $20,000-$59,000), and 19% belonged to high family income group (monthly income: $60,000 or above). The survey had covered four main areas: (1) the perception of respondents on men as carers; (2) the caring experiences of respondents; (3) the willingness of respondents in taking up a carer’s role; and (4) the views on social support for carers. The objective 3 was achieved. To achieve this objective, we conducted in-depth interviews to 20 male carers about their experiences in caregiving. Availability sampling methods were used. We had contacted respondents through elderly centres, personal network and internet. Seven of the respondents cared for their children, 2 cared for their children and spouses, 6 cared for their spouses and 5 cared for their parents. In terms of income level, 9 respondents belonged to high income group and had a middle-class background. Eleven respondents belonged to low income group. The objective 4 was achieved. To achieve this objective, we explored the views and expectations of respondents on social service support for carers. Based on the views that we had collected from the interviews, we had made some suggestions to improve the existing policy measures and service provisions to support male carers in Hong Kong. Apart from the interviews to carers, we thought that it is better include the voice of other stakeholders such as social service providers. Therefore, we conducted a focus group to 4 social workers to understand their views and experiences in working with male carers. The focus group is an additional work which had not planned in the proposal. The findings show that men had problems in caring commonly faced by female carers, but they had special needs due to their gender. Therefore it is suggested that the social policy and social service interventions should adopt a gender-sensitive approach to address the special needs of men in caring.

11610215.label: Major findings and research outcome
11610215.value: The major findings of this study are as the following: 1. Gender of caregivers According to the findings of the telephone study, female respondents regarded themselves as full-time carers more than their male counterparts, which is consistent to the official data. Among the 188 male respondents in the survey, 16.0% had ever been full time caregivers. The figure is noteworthy. This shows that men are getting more involved in caregiving due to social changes such as changing employment pattern, family structure and gender role concepts. The caregiving experience of men and the problems they face may not be the same as women. The society should pay attention to the gender difference in caring and re-examine the current support measures for male carers. 2. The decision of men become caregivers The quantitative findings show that men’s decisions to take up the caregiving role were mostly influenced by economic factors. They thought that it is more economical to provide care themselves than employing someone to take up the duties. Male respondents from low family income group and with low educational level were more willing to be full time caregivers compared to middle-income group. However, qualitative data of this study provide more dynamic explanation on the decision of male carers. Quite a few young middle-class male caregivers were willing to become stay-at-home fathers because of the following reasons: (1) they accepted non-traditional gender role concept; (2) they engaged in flexible work; and (3) they have a high-income spouse. This study shows that gender role perception and class background are the two important factors that interact to influence the decision of men to become full-time carers. 3. Pressure on male caregivers In this study, most caregivers cared for their children, some cared for their spouses or parents. Most caregivers reported that they experienced heavy burden in caregiving. The average number of hours that caregivers spent on caregiving per day was 13 hours. Some caregivers reported that they spent 24 hours every day to take care of their families. Although the number of hours were only the subjective perception of respondents not statistical data collected in a systematical way, this shows that carers experienced enormous pressure both physically and mentally, and had impacts on the personal development and employment opportunity of the person who take up the duties. 4. Reconstructing men’s role in the family The caring experience for men is not totally negative. Some male carers reported positive experiences in caring, such as developing intimate relationship with children, improving spousal relationship, more space for personal development and have become a caring person. The caring experiences of men challenged the traditional concept of gendered division of labour, i.e. men as breadwinners and women as homemakers, which will bring positive impact on promoting gender equality in society. 5. Support for full time caregivers This study shows that very few caregivers had received social service support in caring, for example, cash allowances, social services and work benefits. Respondents of different socio-economic background expressed different needs in caregiving. For example, caregivers from high and middle income families agreed that family-friendly employment policy in Hong Kong is more important for them to balance the need in family and work, while caregivers from low-income families expected cash allowances and affordable social services provisions. There is no single support service that can meet the needs of all caregivers. Different social groups need different types of social service. At the same time, men had more interest in acquiring knowledge and skills in caring rather than emotional support, which is different from most female carers. The social support services should adopt a gender-sensitive approach in service provision.

11610215.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11610215.value: This study provides valuable information and insights on the challenges and problems that men experienced in relation to the changing family and gender roles that are emerging as result of the ongoing socio-economic changes in a post-industrial society. The result helps to develop a new understanding of men’s caring experiences in a Chinese social context. However, this study has limitations such as small sample size and have not covered ethnic background of respondents. This study has potential to further develop in two aspects: first, to include respondents of diverse ethnic background so that we can understand men’s experiences in caring not only in relation to gender and class but also ethnicity. Second, it is also interesting to examine more depth on the coping strategies and the time-use of male carers in caregiving. The future study will provide useful indicators to develop social service strategic plan to support carers. The findings of this study had disseminated in a press conference and presented in three international conference, that would help to arouse public attention on the care support services and attract more policy debate on this issue. This part of work will be continued.

11610215.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11610215.value: The study aimed to examine the perceptions of Hong Kong people about the role of a male caregivers and their experiences and challenges in caregiving. This study adopted both quantitative and qualitative methods including telephone survey, in-depth interviews and documentation. The findings of telephone survey show that respondents who were less educated and unemployed were more likely to become full time caregivers than those who had high-income jobs. Respondents who had been full time caregivers reported that they spent long hours to care for their family members. Respondents who had been full time caregivers reported that they spent long hours to care for their family members, and experienced very heavy burden and pressure in caring. The findings of in-depth interviews show that the decision for men to become carers was not merely economic consideration. The decision were closely related to three interconnected factors such as gender role concepts, the concept of filial piety and the work identity of male carers. The involvement of men in caring may lead to social change for men and transform gender relations. Learning from the experiences of other countries, this study suggested that the government should improve the family-friendly measures and provide support to voluntary agencies or social enterprises to encourage them to provide support services for male caregivers. At the same time, it is also important to build a caregiving-friendly community to reduce the barriers faced by male caregivers in caring.

11610715.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11610715.value: The future of art criticism is in jeopardy. There have been numerous public discussions (ICA, 2011; Witte de With, 2012; AIAC, 2013) and publications on the crisis of art criticism (Elkins, 2003; Rubinstein, 2006; Plagens, 2007; Elkins and Newman, 2008). The internet is often blamed as widespread access to instant self-publishing allows anyone to be a critic (Gat, 2013; Myers, 2013) and devalues the role of the educated, professional art critic (Heartney, 2006; Westbury, 2010). In the West, the critic’s fall from power appears compounded by the increasing exclusivity of high culture (McEvilley 2006; Plagens, 2007) and the rise of the international curator (Allen, J. 2008; Vidokle, 2010). Yet art critical practice remains an essential component of any philosophically and financially successful art ecosystem (McDonald, 2007; Strauss, 2012; Thomas, 2012). Without art criticism, emerging art scenes in the East, like Hong Kong’s, cannot compete on a world stage (Yao, 2008; Lee, 2013). However, there have been no comprehensive studies of art criticism after the internet. Art criticism is difficult to research. It is transient and archives are rare. Online art criticism is particularly difficult to store and navigate. Many early email-based art discussion lists are no longer online and searching through old Facebook posts is a laborious task. Yet without understanding the way art criticism has been practiced online since the early 1980s, we cannot assess the true scope of the global art critical crisis or what new forms of art criticism are emerging. To remedy this situation, this research aims to analyse, historicise and archive the products of art critics operating within online (internet-based or digital and networked) communities. It will produce the first ever: 1) conceptual framework for identifying and analysing forms of online art criticism, 2) historical account of online art criticism, 3) public educational database of examples of online art criticism (in partnership with pioneering online forum for art criticism: Rhizome). The research will use networked art projects, early Bulletin Board Systems, email discussion lists, blogs and social media platforms like Facebook, YouTube and Twitter as case studies to determine the ways that art criticism has been generated online. It will develop a typology of the various forms (platforms, genres, formats) of online art criticism, expand the definition of art criticism and support the ways art critical culture can be fostered in the future. 藝術評論界的未來正面對未知的風險。各公開討論媒介 (ICA, 2011; Witte de With, 2012; AIAC, 2013) 和岀版刊物等多處已有所覆蓋有關藝評界的危機 (Elkins, 2003; Rubinstein, 2006; Plagens, 2007; Elkins and Newman, 2008)。很多時候，互聯網所帶給任何人即時及廣泛地發表言論的方便 (Gat, 2013; Myers, 2013) 令互聯網被指影響到受過專業訓練和正規教育的藝評家，令他們的藝評工作貶值 (Heartney, 2006; Westbury, 2010)。在西方國家中，藝評家影響力的下降因傳統「高級文化」的排他性 (McEvilley 2006; Plagens, 2007) 和策展人國際化的增長而給複雜化 (Allen, J. 2008; Vidokle, 2010)。然而，藝術評論的實踐仍舊是任何哲理上和經濟上成功的藝術界生態系統中不可或缺的要素 (McDonald, 2007; Strauss, 2012; Thomas, 2012)。沒有了藝術評論，東方的新興藝術產業，如香港的藝術界，是不能夠在世界藝術舞台上作有力的競爭的 (Yao, 2008; Lee, 2013)。可是，現階段是未有全面地對互聯網普及化後藝術評論界的廣泛研究。 藝術評論自身的短暫性和稀有的歸檔儲存令它成為了一門難以研究的科目。網上的藝術評論更是特別難以儲存備份，搜索和了解。很多早期以電子郵件為本的藝術討論錄已不再在線，而從臉書(Facebook)上搜索資料也是有它的難度。可是，沒有清楚了解到從1980年代初開始的網上藝術評論，我們是不可能準確地評估和預測全球藝評界面對着那前所未有的危機，和從此以後新增的各種藝術評論模式。有見及此，本研究旨在分析，歷史化，和歸檔化各式各樣線上藝術評論家的產物，包括互聯網絡上，電子化，和其他聯網化的各種群體社區。這研究會產生及發表有史以來初次的：（一）辨認和分析網上藝術評論時概念上的研究骨架；（二）有關網上藝術評論歷史性的描述報告；和（三）由網上藝術評論例子組成，與前瞻性網上藝評平台Rhizome合作而成，以教育為本的公開資料庫。 本研究將以各種不同的聯網藝術項目、早期的佈告欄式系統、電子郵件討論區、部落格與各社交媒體平台（如Facebook, YouTube, 和Twitter）等等為實例探討和說明各式網上藝術評論產生的過程和現象。同時，本研究將會創建岀在網上藝術評論中不同形式的平台、類別、模式等類型學上的規範界別，擴展藝術評論的定義，和支持及孕育藝術評論文化界未來的發展。

11610715.label: Major findings and research outcome
11610715.value: A major part of this research is presented in the 339-page book Art Criticism Online: a History (Charlotte Frost, 2019) following a series of conference attendance, presentations and pedagogic activities. This book takes the readers through the three main phases of development in the history of online criticism in the west. The prevalence of art discussions on social media that we are familiar with was preceded by networked art projects, art critical Bulletin Board Systems, email discussion lists and blogs. Next to the question of software and platform, changes in content, form and style of art criticism were connected to the evolution of the contemporary art world. The book also considers the shape of things to come in terms of a critical agenda for online art criticism, such as new experimental writing practices triggered by online platforms, including non-textual forms like Web TV and Internet meme. As for Hong Kong, there has not been any systematic or formal research in the history or development of art criticism. The remaining 20% of the research therefore was planned to lay the ground work for focused research for online art criticism in future. This objective is fulfilled by extensive literature research. As a result, I have compiled several fact lists to cover as many types of stakeholders and catalyst activities as possible. These include active and representative art critics since the 1960s, art and media organizations involved in art criticism, bibliographies of writings discussing the status quo and objectives of art criticism as well as collection of art reviews by individual critics, and major events to explore the actual practices of art criticism with a training component from 2001-2018. Online art criticism in Hong Kong occurs mainly in on-line magazines, newspaper and newsletters. Whereas they are appreciated for immediacy of dissemination and broader coverage, there is not much innovation and experiments with writing forms, as evident as well in the 5 focus interviews conducted in the last two months of the research period. The collected data should lead to more systematic analysis whereas immediate findings should better be published as short monographs.

11610715.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11610715.value: The collected data on Hong Kong should lead to more systematic analysis through the preparation of a full manuscript. This would take two more years of work to complete. In the immediate near future, the list and interviews should better be published as short monographs. See 5.3 and 6.1.

11610715.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11610715.value: There are three phases of historical development in online criticism in the west. The first, driven by the culture of Conceptual art and independent grassroots arts organizations, sees artists experimenting with new technologies to create networked and collaborative art projects and online arts publication spaces. Following this line of experimentation, the second phase centred around listserv software. New activities emerged, such as posting art critical writing to the listserv community, participating in group identities, staging critical or satirical projects and so on. The Third phase saw a shift away from listserv software to participative platforms made possible by Web 2.0, from blogsphere to social media from Facebook to Instagram. Changes in content, form and style of art criticism were closely connected to the evolution of the contemporary art world. Online platforms have triggered new experimental writing practices, including non-textual forms like Web TV and Internet meme. All this implies the need to innovate the teaching of art criticism, especially to develop a critical literacy in using online platforms. Online art criticism in Hong Kong, in on-line magazines, newspaper and newsletters, has been appreciated for immediate dissemination and broader coverage, but there is not much innovation with writing forms.
