11610915.label: Project Title(Chinese)
11610915.value: 香港女導演和女性電影：1950-1997

11610915.label: Project Objectives
11610915.value: To examine how HK women directors established and sustained their role as directors in the city’s film industry; To investigate the major historical or social themes treated by women directors: are they offering different understanding of these themes; and if yes, how? To highlight how female directors incorporate their diasporic experiences into the filmic narrative and how such incorporation helped to define Hong Kong cinema’s transnational and transcultural tendencies; To provide a framework for adapting Western feminist film theories into our study, while redefining concepts of woman’s film and women’s cinema by analyzing a significant body of works produced in a specific locale; To provide the first comprehensive filmography of female directors in Hong Kong.
rows: To examine how HK women directors established and sustained their role as directors in the city’s film industry;
To investigate the major historical or social themes treated by women directors: are they offering different understanding of these themes; and if yes, how?

To highlight how female directors incorporate their diasporic experiences into the filmic narrative and how such incorporation helped to define Hong Kong cinema’s transnational and transcultural tendencies;

To provide a framework for adapting Western feminist film theories into our study, while redefining concepts of woman’s film and women’s cinema by analyzing a significant body of works produced in a specific locale;
To provide the first comprehensive filmography of female directors in Hong Kong.

11610915.label: Realisation of objectives
11610915.value: Through this research project, we aim to produce the first primary historical overview of Hong Kong female directors and women’s cinema between 1950 and 1997. The year 1950 marked the beginning point where Chinese language cinema began to develop in three separated territories—Mainland China, Hong Kong, and Taiwan. 1997 saw the end of HK’s colonial rule and created uncertainty within its film industry. During this crucial period, the city was a major center for global filmmaking while HK cinema competed Hollywood cinema in its local and Southeast Asian markets. The year 1997, however, did not mark the end to the peak of Hong Kong’s film industry that enjoyed a new boost towards 1997. The low point came in the early 2000s. Before conducting the research, we noted that despite the extensive academic work on Hong Kong cinema, only a small number of writings are devoted to female directors. This does not seem to be justified as Hong Kong’s is one of the few film industries in the world to cherish a continuous trajectory of women directors. Within the period of our research (from 2016 to 2018 officially), we conducted web and archive searches. We listed 35 female directors and 5 significant writers and producers who emerged before 1997, who have produced a total of 296 films by 1997 and 569 films to present. We have met all project objectives and been working on more publications and sharing of the data. Here is a summary of the research process. Objective 1: Hong Kong women directors’ career We have conducted and collected many in-depth interviews with directors like Ann Hui, Angie Chen, Mabel Cheung, Ivy Ho, Rachel Zen, Aubrey Lam, Barbara Wong, Jessey Tsang, and Heiward Mak. These names, in fact, belong to three generations of Hong Kong filmmakers. Through the interviews, we understand how they entered the film industry, established their directing career, and sustained their creative works at intermissions of filmmaking by making either documentaries or TV films. Objective 2: Historical/social themes treated by women directors We have confirmed that nearly all major historical events that happened in Hong Kong and Greater China since the Sino-Japanese War (1931-1945) have been reflected or documented by female directors. For instance, Esther Eng reflected China’s fundraising campaign—the Bowl of Rice Movement—for the Sino-Japanese War in Golden Gate Girl (1941). Wan Hoi Ling depicts the trauma and aftermath of WWII in South East Asia. Mabel Chang portrays “the most powerful woman in the world” during WWII—Soong Mei-ling and her sisters in The Soong Sisters (1996). Ann Hui made three features about Vietnamese refugees in Hong Kong in the 1970s and into the 1980s in her Vietnam trilogy. She also reflects upon the social upheavals around the 1967 riot in Ordinary Heroes (2000). The memory of 1984 and 1989 are reflected in many films focusing on the lives of Chinese immigrants in the 1980s and 1990s. We definitely see women dealing with history in different lights in comparison to their male peers. A more in-depth analysis of this theme will be included in our monograph on female directors in Hong Kong. Objective 3: Incorporating their diasporic experiences? Since the 1930s and 1940s, films by Esther Eng already address the issues encountered by Chinese immigrants living in the Pacific diaspora. Wan Hoi Ling moved from Hong Kong to Singapore to escape the war in 1940 and made Malaysian language films for the local audience. After Ren Yizhi and Chu Feng joined the film business in the 1950s, HK female directors have produced a persistent stream of films that paralleled and interacted with the city’s highly commercial mainstream cinema. Ren and Chu made films about women who migrated to Hong Kong from Shanghai and elsewhere, who experienced the process of modernization in Hong Kong. Cecile Tang came back to Hong Kong from the US and made a film about young people escape from China during the Cultural Revolution. Ann Hui made three films in her earlier years about Vietnamese refugees in Hong Kong, while Mabel Cheung and Clara Law both began their filmmaking with works about Chinese immigrants. All these female directors have migration experiences in life and are very sensitive in dealing with migration themes. Their films, while following the earlier tradition of transnational cinema in Hong Kong, show more sensitivity over gender issues. Objective 4: Adapting Western feminist film theories We are well versed in Western feminist film theories and found many concepts very useful. Our framework of discussion will mainly involve three aspects of Hong Kong women’s cinema. At the narrative level, we will examine if female directors involve a different film language. This will be done through a close reading/analysis of visual and audio motifs. We find, for instance, that women directors often use emotion to push forward the narrative, which lends their films a great emotional fluidity. As their perceptions of space are also different from men, they would select different spaces in Hong Kong, which lend signatures to their films as well. At the thematic level, as we also mentioned earlier, women directors work out of the mainstream and focus more on the daily life of women, children, and the disadvantaged years before the independent filmmakers turned to them. The deal with historical subjects differently, and often use daily-life scenarios to construct political events. At the reflective level, as women directors in Hong Kong all highly educated, the self-reflexivity in their works is much higher, which we think is also a key factor for film work to appeal to younger audiences. Objective 5: Filmography of female directors in Hong Kong We have compiled a filmography dealing 35 Hong Kong female directors and 5 producers and writers. It includes 296 films they made before 1997, and 569 films they made in total. This filmography includes information including the production year and company, the director, writer, producer, cinematographer, and original score (if available). We will find a sustainable way to publish this filmography so it can be updated annual and serve other researchers. Objective 6: Important/prolific female producers and screenwriters; While constructing the filmography, we found that Hong Kong has super-power female producers. The most prolific is Mona Fong, who produced 134 films and directed a couple for the Shaw Studios. She helped Mabel Chueng and Angie Chen with their directorial debut, and also produced films made by Ann Hui. Jacky Pang directed 3 films and produced a total of 23 films, including most Wong Kar Wai films. Janet Chun also produced 9 films by 1997 and a total of 28 films to date. We included all the films they produced into the filmography as well. Meanwhile, since Hong Kong women screenwriters actively involved in filmmaking, we also include the most prolific writers who work closely with women directors. Objective 7: Extending research after 1997 Many of our selected women directors are still working today. We have also included their films in the filmography and in later writings, we do not want to be limited by the year of 1997.

11610915.label: Major findings and research outcome
11610915.value: The history of female directors in Hong Kong, as both professional women and cinematic authors, began with Chinese American director Esther Eng, when she directed National Heroine (1937) and became the first woman to direct a feature film in Hong Kong. In retrospect, we can see Eng shared many aspects in common with women directors coming after her. In the 1930s and 1940s, there was Wan Hoi Ling, who directed two films and co-directed several films in Hong Kong before moving to South East Asia to became the first woman director there. In the 1950s and 1960s, Ren Yizhi and Chu Feng, who moved to Hong Kong from Shanghai and began their film career as actresses, directed feature films reflecting the modern and traditional life of Hong Kong. From 1969 to 1978, Cecile Tang, who grew up in both Hong Kong and Taiwan and studied in the US, came to Hong Kong and directed four feature films that were too advanced for the audiences at the time. Meanwhile, the actress turned director-producer Ko Pao Shu directed ten features for her own production company with controversial social issues. Even though these names are not familiar to today’s audience, their films contribute to the collective memory of Hong Kong. Growing up before, during, and after WWII, their lives all involved migration experiences that allow them to gain a better understanding of gender, culture, and race issues. From 1979 to around 1997, along with the first and the second Hong Kong New Wave emerged many prominent female directors like Ann Hui, Angie Chen, Mabel Chang, Clara Law, and Casey Chan, who are still directing films. These women have all studied abroad, joined the film industry without a long apprenticeship, showed their capability in handling a variety of themes, dealt with themes of women and migration very well, and configured unforgettable screen images of Hong Kong (or Chinese) women. These directors have a significant influence on two younger generations of female directors emerging after 1997 by being a role model for younger women, producing some of their works, and continuing directing and maintaining the lineage and legacy of Hong Kong female directors and women in general.

11610915.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11610915.value: The current research sets its time period between 1950 and 1997. Most female directors in our studies made their directorial debut with 35mm films. Technology-wise, the Hong Kong film industry produced commercial films on 35mm well into the 2000s, but many women directors were more adventurous and already tried out the digital form. In future research, we would like to take three aspects into consideration. First, we will explore female authorship in film and video works by women who cross over from the film industry to outside the core industry. Second, we would like to do more research on the lineage of female screenwriters and especially those who have an influence as a literary writer. Third, we will study female filmmakers, no matter in what position, but sustained their career for more than 30 years in order to document their version of the film's transformation in Hong Kong.

11610915.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11610915.value: History is only complete when both men and women tell their stories. Unfortunately, in existing film histories, women directors are often left out for all kinds of reasons, but mainly because the film industry has always been dominated by men, and the leadership role like “director” has not been handed easily to women. This phenomenon is worldwide, but in the past decade, studies about female directors and women’s cinema became the new frontier of both film studies and women’s studies. Comparing to many film industries, Hong Kong has kept a continuous lineage of female directors with important names in each decade since 1937. However, the number of female directors is far less than that of male ones, which resulted in inequality in their working conditions in the industry. More writings on the achievement of veteran female directors and more discussions on their recent films would help to change the attitudes towards them in the industry. The recognition of older and working directors will also encourage younger women to pursue their dreams to direct their movies. When more women are directing films, the younger generation will see more independent and realist women on screen as they grow up.

11611215.label: Project Title(Chinese)
11611215.value: 去除對性工作者的歧視化: 中國性工作者與客人親密關係的研究

11611215.label: Co - Investigator(s)
11611215.value: Prof Ho, Sik Ying, Petula Dr Ho, Wing Chung

11611215.label: Project Objectives
11611215.value: To improve knowledge about the sociology of sex work by exploring the intimate relationships between sex workers and their clients in urban China. To describe and explain the connection between money and intimate relationships in China’s urban sex service. To explore the wider implications of the connection between money and intimacy in Chinese society.
rows: To improve knowledge about the sociology of sex work by exploring the intimate relationships between sex workers and their clients in urban China.
To describe and explain the connection between money and intimate relationships in China’s urban sex service.
To explore the wider implications of the connection between money and intimacy in Chinese society.

11611215.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11611215.value: Conventional wisdom has it that relationships between sex workers and their clients are based entirely on direct exchanges of sexual favours and money. The proposed study will consider whether sex workers and their clients can generate intimate relationships that go beyond pecuniary transactions. It will examine emotional labour of sex workers, their quest for cultural capital and technologies of embodiment, and the connection between money and intimacy. Emotional labour is the commodification of private emotions, intended to be sold for a profit in a capitalist economy. Technologies of embodiment refer to the processes by which women produce, transform or manipulate their bodies through particular kinds of body-related work that signify beauty and make their bodies look more attractive and appealing. Intimacy is the personal relations within which the interactions are built on knowledge and attention that are not widely available to third parties, and if the knowledge and attention are made widely available, they would likely endanger the social status of one of them. Building on these sociological concepts, the proposed study will ethnographically analyse both sides of the female sex worker/client relationship in karaoke lounges and bars in Dongguan, southern China, comparing the low-end sector (such as streetwalkers) with the high-end sector (such as women working in upscale hotels) of the industry. The hypothesis of the study is that as a result of social changes, the relationships shared between sex workers in the high-end sector and their clients (both local Chinese men and foreigners) may involve not only pecuniary transactions but also genuinely intimate and non-remunerative feelings. The relationships can best be explored by examining the complex connection between money and intimacy. Workers in the high-end sex industry make use of their earned economic capital to acquire cultural capital, and use technology as a marketing tool to forge longer-term intimate relationships while male clients in more commercialised, post-industrial cities in China begin to seek diverse types of sexual experiences. The study will aim to make a major contribution to the current literature on the sociology of sex work in China, which has thus far focused narrowly on sex workers and largely ignored the dynamics of worker/client relationships.

11611215.label: Realisation of objectives
11611215.value: 1. To improve knowledge about the sociology of sex work by exploring the intimate relationships between sex workers and their clients in urban China This project brings together many sociological concepts and theories such as cultural capital, economic capital, technologies of embodiments, emotional labour, intimacy, east Asian femininity, displaced masculinity, edgework, and criminal justice to enrich the literature on sociology of sex work. One of most important findings emerging from this project was the application of Biopolitics (Michel Foucault) and homo sacer (Giorgio Agamben) to the field of Criminal Justice. Some mid-tier and low-end sex workers are unable to extricate themselves from their situation due to overriding contextual and environmental factors; These individuals cannot ‘break the loop’ whereby they go into sex work because they have few skills and low status; But since sex work is illegal and carries social stigma, they become homo sacer, that is, figures stripped of political status and societal recognition. The findings suggest needed changes regarding rehabilitation and the criminal justice system in China. 2. To describe and explain the connection between money and intimate relationships in China’s urban sex service. The relationships shared between sex workers in the high-end sector and their clients (both local Chinese and non-Chinese men) involve not only pecuniary transactions but also genuinely intimate and non-remunerative feelings. The relationships can best be explored by examining the complex connection between money and intimacy. High-end sex workers use their earned economic capital to acquire cultural capital and use technology as a marketing tool to forge longer-term intimate relationships. The male clients in the more commercialised, post-industrial cities in China seek diverse sexual experiences. Both high-end sex workers and their clients are considered ‘active social agents’ who seek intimacy. Sex work is used not only for sexual purposes, but also to establish relational intimacy. However, among street walkers and sex workers in mid-tier and low-end bars, sexual activity is exclusively sex-for-money. Low-end workers agree to provide services in exchange for money from their clients who seek only sexual satisfaction. The relational ties between the workers and clients are weak or non-existent. The clients focus exclusively on physical sexual services rendered. In addition, low-end sex workers must contend with environmental risks associated with this illegal activity, such as offering bribes to police and triads. 3. To explore the wider implications of the connection between money and intimacy in Chinese society. The connection between economic transactions and relational intimacy are not equal across China’s bars and lounges. High-end sex workers have more opportunity to establish intimate relationships than their low-end counterparts because they have more economic and cultural capital and use technologies of embodiment to provide greater emotional labour and thereby develop intimacy with their clients. It is also clear that some high-end sex workers and their clients engage in both pecuniary transactions as well as genuinely intimate and nonremunerative exchanges. Male customers of high-end sex workers seek to buy both authentic-emotional and physical-sexual encounters. Both high-end sex workers and their clients are considered ‘active social agents’ who seek intimacy. Sex work is used not only for sexual purposes, but also to establish relational intimacy. Some of them transition from paid intimacy to authentic intimacy, taking the form of boyfriend-girlfriend relationship or even spouses.

11611215.label: Major findings and research outcome
11611215.value: 1. This project provides the background and foundation for an ethnographic journey. It covers the inspiration, the methodological design, the qualitative perspective, and how ethnographic data was collected and analyzed regarding the three niche markets in Dongguan. 2. This project examines the life of the streetwalkers, as well as workers in the low- and mid-tier bars where sex services are offered. 3. This project looks at the low- and mid-tier business from the perspective of clients; specifically, the single-adult migrant men who buy sex. This particular group has a number of conflicts regarding their masculinity and the expectations placed upon them by Chinese society. Together these chapters book-end the sociocultural space inhabited by the sex industry in China for low-end men and women. 4. This project shifts to the different worlds of opportunity that exist in high-end sex work, where money and connections lead to economic capital and the creation of intimacy. It examines how Chinese and foreign clients overcome social barriers to develop and consummate long-term relationships with sex workers. It also looks at how high-end girls and their clients reciprocate sexual intimacy. 5. This project focuses on social policy implications and criminal justice. It presents the theoretical argument that selling sex is edgework for female sex workers. Edgework is voluntary risky activity that leads to new adaptive behaviours enabling the individual to continue that activity. The concept of edgework captures the perspective of a number of the women interviewed and offers a powerful explanation for why many will not leave. It also closes the loop, bringing us back to the sweatshop factory life that many sex workers left in the first place. Once arrested, female sex workers (almost exclusively mid- and low-tier) and streetwalkers are sent to custody education centres for “re-education through labour camp” (RTLC) programs. The sex workers say the centres fail at retraining because the women are instead humiliated, exploited, and abused. In fact, the women say the centres operate like the factory sweatshops. In conclusion, the sex work industry in modern China needs rethinking in terms of intimacy, masculinity, and criminal justice.

11611215.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11611215.value: 200 words) The project suggests extending this project to male sex workers in north China. The plight of male sex workers (hereafter money boys, MBs or MB) remain under-researched, needing sociological investigation. The rising numbers of MBs in China raises questions of relevance to readers from backgrounds in social and public policy, migration studies, geography, demography and public health. In particular, research is needed to identify the major concerns of MBs and how NGOs help them transition out of the trade. In China, NGOs work with MBs to help them test and combat the spread of HIV and other STIs. Also, NGOs work with MBs, their wives (homowives), their clients, and medical doctors who treat them. The medical system in today’s China should enhance the occupational safety of the frontline medical doctors.

11611215.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11611215.value: This project explores the experiences of both male clients and female sex workers, this project expands upon the complex dynamics of sex worker and client relationships, and places them within the wider implications of expanding globalization and capitalism. The purchasing of commercial sex by single, young-adult males is increasingly viewed as a socially acceptable way for men to pay for the opportunity to perform and experience heteronormative masculinity. Investigating human rights, social policy, and the criminal justice system in China, this project applies the concept of ‘edgework’ in Dongguan, studying how men and women interact within the post-financial-crisis economy that emerged after 2008 in China.

11611815.label: Project Title(Chinese)
11611815.value: 香港黑社會有組織犯罪以及社會資本之研究

11611815.label: Project Objectives
11611815.value: To investigate the role of triad societies and functions of triad activities in facilitating the development of social capital of triad members. To investigate how triad members utilize their social capital in the operation of organized crime. To investigate the role of bonding, bridging and linking social capital in criminal organizations and organized crime.
rows: To investigate the role of triad societies and functions of triad activities in facilitating the development of social capital of triad members.
To investigate how triad members utilize their social capital in the operation of organized crime.
To investigate the role of bonding, bridging and linking social capital in criminal organizations and organized crime.

11611815.label: Realisation of objectives
11611815.value: The present study was conducted using qualitative research method and purposive sampling. In-depth and semi-structured interviews were conducted after ethical review was approved by the university ethics committee. Informed consent was sought from the interviewees. The duration of each interview was about 1.5 to 2 hours. Some participants were interviewed a couple of times if additional information was required. The main source of interviewees came from a Christian church which specializes in providing outreach religious services for the triad community. As a regular church attendant, the P.I. gained approval from the chief pastor and pastors of the church for conducting triad research. The pastors referred church members with triad backgrounds to the P.I. for interviews. The pastors also invited the P.I. to represent the church to attend birthday parties and festive events of current triad figures. Through the weekly church meetings and other activities, the P.I. established a social network with about 60 triad church members, who covered different triad ranks and positions and from different triad societies. Other sources of samples were referred by a number of NGOs specialized in providing services for ex-offenders, such as The Society of Rehabilitation and Crime Prevention. To select the right triad members, a legal definition was used for screening suitable interviewees. The screening questions were: (A) What is your triad rank and what triad society do you belong to? (B) Have you attended a triad initiation ceremony? Supplementary questions were asked about the basic triad structure in triad society and the process of the initiation ceremony, in order to check their triad knowledge and reconfirm their triad membership. Only adults of over 18 years of age were interviewed to ensure their maturity to understand the purpose and nature of the research. As being, or claiming to be, a triad member is a criminal offence in Hong Kong, it is unlikely that an adult interviewee would mimic being a triad member for interview. Moreover, only ex-offenders were selected to ensure that the interviewees were more willing to share their triad experiences, since they had less to lose by disclosing information about their relationships with other collaborators in organized crime. During the interviews, the P.I. emphasized the role of academic who is interested in triad subculture and inter-relations between triads. The P.I. also emphasized the outreach social worker’s role in the past decades to secure their confidence in releasing sensitive information. By emphasizing the researchers’ scholar and social worker identity, the interviewees were provided with a sense of security that enhanced their openness in revealing truthful information while protecting their privacy and interests. As the interviewees were referred by trusted staff of the church and various NGOs, the trust established between the interviewees and the staff, together with the P.I.’s trustful relationships with the staff, acted to enhance the level of trust between the researcher and the interviewees. The P.I. advised the interviewees not to disclose any names, including theirs and their triad title, during interviews. Details of their rank, name of triad society, and clarification of the initiation ceremony process undertaken, were asked. In terms of crime operations, the interviewees were invited to mention only the crime for which they had already been convicted in court, and provide a general description on the crime involved. The P.I. explained to the interviewees how the collected data would be handled after the interviews, and promised to keep their identity in strict confidence. Where names were accidentally disclosed during the interviews, they were removed in the verbatim records and replaced with a fake name. The P.I asked similar questions at different phases of an interview and, where possible, over the course of the research if multiple interviews were conducted, to assure the accuracy of information. After the interviews, findings were transcribed into Chinese verbatim and then translated from Chinese into English if they were selected for publication. During transcription, names of interviewees were changed to codes. All the translation was read and approved by the researcher who conducted the interviews. Occasional grammatical corrections were conducted without sacrificing content and triad idiosyncrasies. The translated transcripts were saved in WORD format and imported into the qualitative analysis software, NVivo 10, whereupon the data were organized to facilitate the identification of themes and sub-themes. After coding the data in NVivo 10, all passages assigned to specific codes were viewed and analyzed so as to facilitate the search of information and comparison of data. The collection and analysis of data were organized in such a way that can fully address the following three objectives of the present study: (1) to investigate the role of triad societies and functions of triad activities in facilitating the development of social capital of triad members; (2) to investigate how triad members utilize their social capital in the operation of organized crime; (3) to investigate the role of bonding, bridging and linking social capital in criminal organizations and organized crime. The data collected are very rich and provide fruitful information for the investigation of the role and formation of social capital in triad societies and triad organized crime.

11611815.label: Major findings and research outcome
11611815.value: The present study examined the hierarchical structure and organized crime operations of triad groups in Hong Kong and the process of collaboration in the organized crime operation. From interviewing a diverse group of triad members, it was found that the triad societies were made up of factions connected together, each having their own hierarchical and decentralized structure. Seniority and financial power determines the Dai Lo-Lang Chai (leader-follower) relationship, making up the hierarchy within the faction. Access to triad resources, which has a direct effect on the success of criminal collaboration, was restricted based on the triad structure and the rankings of the members. Aside from such limitations, personal factors such as Dor (reputation) and face (status) were keys to establishing social capital for the purpose of running illicit businesses. Gang members commit criminal activities to build Dor and face and establish a greater criminal network, which in turn grants them greater access to the resources in the triad underworld. This makes Dor and face to be one of the essential assets for triad members to build on as it represents a form of power within the triad underworld. The system of triad hierarchical structure allows the triad members to pool together the resources within its network to accomplish tasks for the individual members. Within the underworld network, having seniority and money works in favour of Dor and face, improving the chances of criminal collaboration because of the resources and triad networks one has access to, which in turn, further brings more money, social capital and power back to the triad faction in a perpetuating cycle. This underground network also serves as a platform to share information among triad members, and promote opportunities for criminal collaboration. The results of the present study also show that the hierarchical network of the triad factions gives restrictive access to resources for their own members, thus making the triad identity and status one of the most valuable assets to the members. These are valuable factors when the triad members attempt to achieve success in the criminal underworld.

11611815.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11611815.value: China proposed the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) in 2013 to further connect countries in the region and encourage factors of collaboration, including policy, trade, and financing between them, while increasing the speed of each country’s economic development. However, this ambitious project is not without consequences, as the intensifying connections between these countries may facilitate the movement of illegal goods and services, and create a new network of criminals. The recent fight against triads by President Xi in China is a warning to triad leaders. If China is no longer a safe haven for triads, triads will become another form of excess capacity in BRI. When the demand for triad services slows down in China because of the series of crackdowns, the triads’ excess capacity will be transferred and utilized in BRI nations. The research question that arises is whether or not the launch of BRI and its potential to attract international criminogenic flows of capital will contribute to a heightened amount of triad organized crimes in newly linked regions and how law enforcement agencies respond to them in a collective manner. All these issues are potential topics worthy of rigorous research.

11611815.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11611815.value: There are various approaches in studying organized crime, such as hierarchical approach, patron-client relations approach, entrepreneurial/market approach, and social network approach. In the literature of triad organized crime, the hierarchical approach has been often adopted. From the “structural perspective”, triad societies are regarded as cohesive criminal organizations with a hierarchical structure and strict control mechanisms for enforcing norms, such as punishments and rewards for undesirable and desirable behaviors of members and the approval of senior members for organizational decisions, in order to maintain cohesiveness and to commit organized crime in systematic ways. Through this structure, triad members come to know many triad brothers and criminal collaborators, acquire knowledge of specific crime techniques, illegal marketing information and strategies, and sponsors and protectors of illegal triad businesses. These are different forms of social capital that the triad members can obtain through the triad organizational structure. Based on these results, this study advocates a structural-social capital perspective in understanding triad organized crime. It would strengthen existing triad literature and provide theoretical insight into how triad societies develop social capital, and how triad-related social capital functions in organized crime. The findings would help law enforcement agencies develop intervention strategies against triads and organized crime.

11612215.label: Project Title(Chinese)
11612215.value: 自治搏奕: 麥理治年代(1971-1982)与殖民管治本貭

11612215.label: Project Objectives
11612215.value: To enhance understanding of the nature of colonial governance by identifying the strategies and leverage adopted, and opportunities and constraints faced, by Hong Kong’s colonial government during crises with London. To develop a nuanced narrative of autonomy under imperial rule through case studies of the failures and successes of the colonial government in defying the demands of London. To contribute in theoretical terms a fresh perspective for understanding central-local relationships beyond a formalistic analytical approach.

To develop a nuanced narrative of autonomy under imperial rule through case studies of the failures and successes of the colonial government in defying the demands of London.
To contribute in theoretical terms a fresh perspective for understanding central-local relationships beyond a formalistic analytical approach.

11612215.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11612215.value: 麥理浩的年代 (1971-1982) 一般被人視為殖民統治的黃金時期。他在位內，港英政府推動了廣泛的社會改革，包括十年建屋計劃、九年免費教育、設立廉政公署等，大大改善了社會面貌。傳統智慧把這一連串的德政歸功於麥理浩本人，或視之為倫敦對六七暴動的反思成果。但這些觀點忽略了殖民地政府的本質﹕殖民地的政治秩序，建基於宗主國與本地社會之間的互動。而身處其中的殖民地政府，便必須從中取得平衡，而箇中關鍵往往是如何在英國利益和憲制框架下取得某種形式的自治。這項研究，集中分析港英政府在三個爭議中如何尋找自治空間，這包括﹕越南船民問題、政制改革和跨越九七的土地契約。這三個爭議牽涉不同的英國戰略考慮和本土利益，是了解殖民地政府尋求自治的策略、手段和局限的絕佳個案。

11612215.label: Realisation of objectives
11612215.value: The project started with several key questions: How autonomous is colonial Hong Kong government? What are the leverages available for the colonial administration and what are the limitations? How should we define the central-local relationship before 1997? The project tried to evaluate these questions with analysis of three carefully chosen cases under Murray MacLehose governorship (1971-1982): Vietnamese refugee crisis, political reform and land lease beyond 1997. These episodes constituted major challenge to colonial governance, and even more importantly, involved intensive exchange and negotiation between the Hong Kong and London. Each case represents distinct constellation of interest and tension between the colony and the sovereign state and together they offer a window to evaluate the logic and pattern of central-local interaction in colonial era. The Vietnamese refugee case represents an episode of intense conflict as each side was determined to pursue and defend its own interest. On the contrary, the debate on constitutional reform in MacLehose years is a lukewarm affair as neither Hong Kong nor London was motivated to go beyond the option of inclusion of a few new faces into Legislative Council. The case of land lease is an interesting case as while MacLehose was anxious to offer some kind of certainty to investors with his audacious and creative idea of separating the land lease issue from the bigger issue of the future of Hong Kong, London appeared to be insensible to the local anxiety and was not yet ready to start the conversation with Beijing. Over the 36 months of research, hundreds of files and records deposited in National Archives in Britain (Kew), and National Administration of Records and Archives in the United States (College Park/Maryland) were studied. These include files of US State Department, CIA, Defense Department, British Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Home Office and Cabinet Office. Meticulous reading of these materials allow us to answer the research questions raised above. The general consensus among extant scholarship recognizes the substantial degree of autonomy enjoyed by the colonial administration despite the extensive formal constitutional restraints on the power of the Hong Kong government as stipulated in the Letters Patent and Royal Instructions. The major narratives can be categorized into two major lines of inquiry. Firstly, it is attributable to the general indifference of the sovereign to colonial affairs. Leo Goodstadt has phrased it elegantly as “informal devolution”. Likewise, Robert Bickers has reiterated the British imperial tradition of “ruling the empire on the cheap”. In short, the colonial autonomy is a result of the sovereign’s lack of interest in Hong Kong, and as long as the colony could manage its own business without financial assistance from the homeland, she would be left alone. The alternative explanation is down to the distinctive nature of the British Empire. John Darwin, for example, argues that its character as a mercantile empire with its primary concern on trade accounts for her limited desires in muddling in the domestic affairs of colony. Particularly, London found little motivation to invest and involve in the development in overseas possession like Hong Kong, which possessed no valuable natural resources. As a result, there emerged a tradition for respecting “man on the spot”. Our findings offer us a more nuanced perspective in understanding the relationship. The relationship between Hong Kong and London is much more contentious than the depictions mentioned above. Three variables are central to the determining the outcome of the bargaining. First, public opinion in the colony matters and the Governor’s skill in mobilizing the public sentiment can make a difference in the bargaining with the sovereign. In spite of the undemocratic character of the colonial state, views of the local community, particularly those of the business elites, did exert influence on the policies of the Hong Kong government. On the one hand, it can prompt the government into action. For example, the anxiety of local business about the future of Hong Kong had pushed MacLehose to test the water with Beijing with his creative idea of granting land lease beyond 1997, even when full support of London for such audacious move was not secured. On the other hand, local the economic elites’ reluctance to embark fundamental change that may disturb their privileged position had accounted for MacLehose’s half-baked attempt in political reform in the aftermath of 1967, though London was aware of the importance of creating a new form of state-society relationship that could restore public confidence in the colonial rule. The general resentment of the population against the unceasing inflow of refugees from Vietnam and the growing burden in accommodating such unabated influx had emboldened the Governor in making a “draconian” turn in handling the crisis (closed camp policy, repatriation etc.) vis-à-vis the British officials as well as international opinion. Global politics also has a major impact on the Hong Kong-London interaction, of which the strategic calculation of the United States and the People’s Republic of China’s is most relevant. In the three cases studied in this project, their position can restrict the room for Hong Kong’s pursuit on the one hand, and may empower the colony to take more drastic measure in defending its claim on the other. The deterioration of Indo-China crisis in the 1980s for example, had shifted American attention from Vietnam to the wider concerns in Cambodia, Laos and Thailand. For the US, the moral responsibility in accommodating refugees from Vietnam had become a secondary concern since then and rendered Hong Kong’s effort in lobbying for international assistance more difficult. Yet, the colony’s position in pushing for more proactive measures in alleviating her predicament was strengthened when China become more concerned with the prospect of the lingering of a huge refugee leftover in Hong Kong beyond 1997. The salience of the factor of global politics however hinges upon the prospect of its translation into the strategic thinking of London and this is in turn determined by a number of variables. For example, a change of leadership may make a big difference. Thatcher’s desire to make use of the refugee crisis as part of her global anti-communist plot, for example, accounted for London’s enthusiasm in pushing the United Nations towards the Geneva Conference in the late 1970s. This provided an opening for Hong Kong’s assertion. However, London’s priority in appeasing the American and the imperative of reducing her own burden in refugee intake only ended up in a worst case scenario for Hong Kong: the colony was designated as the port of first asylum, an option MacLehose had tried very hard to avoid since the mid-1970s. Overall speaking, the project was implemented smoothly with most of objectives achieved. Nevertheless, the writing up process was seriously disrupted by the protests in Hong Kong since mid-2019. As Associate Head of the Department, the PI has been heavily involved in the contingency planning, student counselling or even legal support for students. The total disruption of university operation and sudden termination of class in October simply make any writing impossible. A paper on the land lease issue and another one on political reform are in advanced stage of writing though and expected to be ready for submission in the 1st quarter of 2020.

11612215.label: Major findings and research outcome
11612215.value: The single most important finding of the research is the confirmation of the high degree of autonomy enjoyed by the colony before 1997. Despite the formal position of subordination, there were always room and possibility for the Hong Kong colonial administration to defend the local interest. The success of such efforts however depends on the “diplomatic skills” of local leaders, the Governor in particular. The “diplomacy” worked on two fronts. Firstly, lobbying politicians and public opinion in Britain could help mobilize support for the cause of Hong Kong, and exert pressure on London. Both the democratic nature of the British polity and personal connection between the colonial governor and senior officials in Whitehall worked in the favour of Hong Kong. Secondly, Hong Kong also enjoyed the privilege of pursuing its “foreign affairs” in reality—meeting with foreign dignitaries (e.g. MacLehose’ visit to Washington meeting with Deng Xiaopeng in the late 1970s), participation in international conference (e.g. Hong Kong presence in Geneva Conference in UN in 1979) or other initiatives in making her case in global scene, all helped to pile pressure on London and facilitate her negotiation with Britain. Outcomes so far Some of the findings have been disseminated into various form. A background paper on the overall analysis of the autonomy of the colony is included in the newly released book, Hong Kong 20 Years after the Handover, co-edited by Brian Fong and Tai-Lok Lui (2018). A paper on the historical background of the colony’s anti-corruption efforts and MacLehose campaign London was presented in the Association of Asian Studies in Asia Conference (Kyoto) in 2016. A full paper was drafted and ready for submission for the Journal of Commonwealth and Imperial History. A presentation on the Vietnamese Boat People Crisis in the 1970s and 1980s was made in the Hong Kong History Project Conference, co-organized by Bristol University and University of Hong Kong (Hong Kong, 2019).

11612215.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11612215.value: Further research effort can be made on the study of the Vietnamese Refugees crisis. While the MacLehose era witnessed the beginning of the crisis and the confirmation of Hong Kong as the port of First Asylum after the United Nation Conference in Geneva in 1979, there were major twists in the handling of the issue in the following decades. Contrary to the general compliance with the principle of humanitarianism as expected of the global community, Hong Kong had adopted a more “draconian” regime in addressing the Boat People crisis in the 1980s and 1990s. The renewed inflow of Vietnamese since the mid-1980s, the declining enthusiasm of the United States in taking refugees from Hong Kong and the consequent political and financial implications for the colony had led to policies like closed-camp policy and voluntary repatriation. In short, Hong Kong became more determined to defend its own interests and the tension between the colony and London escalated as a result. The situation was further complicated by the 1997 issue as Beijing was desperate to sort this out before the handover. This is a good window for understanding the dynamics of central-local relationship in colonial time. Another GRF application is planned.

11612215.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11612215.value: The findings of the research offer important insights for understanding the autonomy of Hong Kong in the past as well as in the future. The freedom of Hong Kong colonial administration in pursuing its own agenda and defending its local interests, in short, was not preordained by its formal constitutional position of subordination under the imperial framework. Instead, it was determined by several factors including strategic concern of Britain, development in global politics, and the political skills of Hong Kong officials in mobilizing domestic and international support. Two contextual conditions are however particularly important for Hong Kong: the democratic nature of the British political system, and the leeway for global engagement. The former implies London’s vulnerability to public opinion, home and abroad, whereas the later allows the colony to solicit sympathy for its causes across the globe. Whether these two prerequisites are still present after the handover is debatable. The authoritarian character of the People’s Republic of China may denote a different response to public opinion and international pressure, and the room for Hong Kong’s effort in asserting its own agenda in global scale may also be circumscribed by the imperative to entertain Beijing’s diplomatic priorities.

11612315.label: Project Objectives
11612315.value: National (macro) level. Given the status of foreign OEMs, to what extent can state institutions and regulations protect labor rights? Under the pressure of global competition for growth, how would changes to state regulations, including liberalization, affect labor conditions? We will document the changing configurations of labor laws in both countries and examine the extent of employer implementation over time at the national, local, and factory levels. Local state/provincial government (individual policy) level. We will investigate any local state modifications or enforcement issues on labor laws and their effects on the variations of labor conditions within the country by comparing the two domestic OEMs. Ownership. How does ownership matter in these relations? Will joint ventures (JVs) with government-owned firms affect labor conditions? If foreign OEMs are dominant as predicted by GVC, we expect to see little difference between the ER outcomes of wholly owned foreign OEM and the JVs.nd the JVs. Management level. To what extent do state institutions affect factories’ lean production? If state institutions can affect the foreign OEMs’ operations in another country, then the countries with more effective labor institutions will have better ERs than the assembly factories of the same foreign OEMs in these two countries. We will examine the work plans such as shifts, work schedules, as well as team work/production cycle organizations and utilizations. We will also investigate labor flexibility in each factory, such as the use of migrant workers, dispatched workers, temporary contract workers, and student interns. Labor unions. Similar to the argument in point 4, we aim to explore relations between labor unions, such as the official union in China (e.g., All-China Federation of Trade Unions, ACFTU) and unofficial unions, as well as their functions and relations with ER.

11612315.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11612315.value: Global value chains (GVC) represent a large, cross-disciplinary area of research. However, employment relations (ER) and labor conditions have been downplayed in the literature. GVCs refer to commodity chains across multiple countries that are dominated by “lead firms,” which are often powerful transnational corporations. Some scholars contend that the global production network (GPN) approach is better suited to the study of ER than GVC because of its focus on the links between these commodity chains and economic development in different countries and regions. We will conduct a comparative case study of the automotive industry in China and India to explore the debates on GVCs, GPNs, and their implications on ER. We focus on the operations and ER practices of three rising stars of global automotive production: German carmaker Volkswagen (VW), Chinese firm Geely Holding Group, and Indian firm Tata Motors. This study is the first international comparative study of automotive industry workers in China and India. The auto industry has been crucial to the development of “modern” industrial and consumer societies in the West and Japan, where workers are historically regarded as benefiting from good wages and employment conditions. Using the GVC/GPN framework, our project will explore whether or not auto industry ER in China and India will follow a similar path. The auto industry represents a specific type of “value chain” and is now shifting to these emerging economic giants, where global carmakers are keen to take advantage of huge domestic markets and relatively low-cost production. VW, one of the world’s leading auto firms, is one such company that has substantial investments in China and India. In each country, VW has had to adapt its distinctively “German” ER practices to local conditions. By documenting and analyzing VW’s practices and comparing them to those of Geely in China and Tata in India, we intend to contribute significantly to the literature on value chains as well as to assess whether the GVC or the GPN approach is more effective in incorporating and explaining the role of ER in industrial development. We will also outline the possible direction of ER practices in Chinese and Indian auto firms as the industry continues to expand. We will survey workers, interview managers and trade union representatives, and generate reports and articles of interest for scholars and practitioners alike. 全球價值鏈（GVC）研究是一個大的，跨學科的領域。但是，僱傭關係（ER）和勞動條件的研究在這領域裡一直被忽略或低估了。全球價值鏈是指在多個國家商品鏈通過“龍頭企業” ，往往是強大的跨國公司，所主導。一些學者爭辯說，因全球生產網絡（GPN）方法關注到這些商品鏈之間的在不同經濟發展程度國家和地區的聯繫，所以它更比GVC適合於研究ER。我們會進行一個汽車行業在中國和印度的比較案例研究，探討在辯論全球價值鏈，GPNs，並在ER及其影響。我們專注於全球汽車產量的三個新星的運營和ER實踐：德國汽車製造商大眾汽車公（VW），中國公司吉利控股集團和印度公司塔塔（TaTa）汽車公司。這項研究是第一個比較中國和印度汽車行業工人的國際研究。 在西方和日本，汽車工業一直是至關重要的“現代”工業與發展社會消費，那裡的工人被歷史視為受益於良好的工資和就業條件。使用GVC / GPN框架下，我們的項目將探索在中國和印度的汽車工業行業的ER會否將遵循類似的路徑。汽車行業代表了“價值鏈”的一個特定的類型，而現在轉向這些新興的經濟巨人，在那裡，全球汽車製造商都熱衷這些新興的經濟體的巨大國內市場和相對低成本生產的優勢。大眾是一個全球領先的汽車公司，就是這樣一個公司，擁有大量投資在中國和印度。在每一個國家，大眾要因地制宜，不得不調整其獨特的“德國”ER實踐。通過記錄和分析大眾的做法，再比較中國的吉利在和印度的塔塔的ER實踐，我們打算對價值鏈的文獻做顯著的貢獻，以及評估是否GVC或所述GPN方法是更有效地摻入和解釋工業的發展中ER的作用。我們也將概述，隨著行業的不斷擴大，中國和印度的汽車企業的ER實踐的可能方向。為同樣的學者和實踐者的興趣，我們將調查工人，採訪管理人員和工會代表，並生成報告，文章。

11612315.label: Realisation of objectives
11612315.value: The project was headed by Dr. Vincent Chen (PI), with Prof. Anita Chan and Dr. Thomas Barnes as Co-Is, when it was applied and granted. Dr. Vincent Chen's employment was ended at City University of Hong Kong from September 2017, and then Chris Chan was invited by Vincent Chen to hold the project as the PI, as the topic is close to Chris Chan's research area, and also Chris Chan has collaborated with Anita Chan (Co-I) in another GRF project. Since September 2017, Vincent Chen has continued to be the main researcher and operate the project as the main Co-I while Chris Chan has advised on the administration and finance aspects of the project. Chris Chan moved to the Chinese University of Hong Kong in December 2019. The employment status of Vincent Chen has affected the progress of the project, as he has to move around different part-time and visiting appointments after he left CityU. The data collection work has been continued with the assistance of collaborators in China and India, and the research objectives are generally achieved. While the Chinese collaborator is able to complete the survey in time, the Indian part has been delayed. Drawing from the Chinese part of the data, one paper has been published in China Quarterly, the leading China studies journal by Vincent Chen and Anita Chan. Vincent Chen has published two other papers in World Development and Regional Studies, both are top journals in social development and urban studies. He has also completed two more articles to be submitted to journals. Other papers, especially on the part of India and comparing China with India, will be prepared in the next step. With funding support from CityU, Chris Chan organised an international conference on "Labour in Rising Powers" (including China and India) in September 2017. Some team members of this project were invited to attend in the conference. Based on this conference, Chris Chan has edited a special issue for China Review. The special issue will published in February 2020 and cover topics that this project aims to investigate.

11612315.label: Major findings and research outcome
11612315.value: The aim of this project is to conduct a comparative study on automobile workers in the two biggest developing countries in the world. The levels of comparison are multiple, such as national and local governments, ownership and management, and labour institutions. In particular, we look at the pairwise comparisons of major car producers and the local producers in each of the two countries. We have comparable data on China: Volkswagen (shanghai and Changchun), Honda (Guangzhou), Toyota (Guangzhou), General Motors (Shanghai), and local car producers, such as BYD (Shenzhen). In India, we have surveyed workers at Honda Siel (Greater Noida), Hyundai (Chennai), Volkswagen (Pune) and General Motors (Pune); we have also local companies, such as, Tata (Pune), Maruti Suzuki (Delhi), and Mahindra and Mahindra (Pune), as a reference. We found that employment strategies in China and India are very similar; they both use a large number of precarious workers, and a much smaller size of regular workers in the same production unit. However, due to the difference in survey initiation and process timing, our research outputs are mainly focused on the Chinese survey. The paper, entitled “Comparing Regular and Agency Workers’ Working Conditions, Attitudes and Resistance: A Case Study of Chinese Auto Joint Ventures” , was published in a top area studies journal, China Quarterly, in 2018, by Vincent Chen and Anita Chan. This paper was based on a questionnaire survey of regular workers and agency workers at major auto joint ventures in China and compare their work conditions, job satisfaction, and willingness to take collective actions. Resource in the project has allowed Vincent Chen to study the state policies, labour market and wage mechanism beyond the automobile industry. He has published two papers in top development and urban studies journals, World Development and Regional Studies, on these topics. Vincent Chen have also produced two working papers that are relevant to this project, entitled: "How does corporate social responsibility code of conduct impact on labor conditions? Evidence from American MNCs’ suppliers in Southern China"; and "Cream-Skimmer or Underdog? A case study of labor type selectivity in a rural labor training program in China". As the Indian survey has just been finished recently, its analysis is undergoing and will be presented to the 61st Annual Conference of Indian Society of Labour Economics in December 2019. Papers on the case of India and comparing China with India will then be sent to journals.

11612315.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11612315.value: This project is a comparative study on labour relations between the two biggest countries. It has laid the foundation for future similar studies. The further development of the research could be on other comparable industries concerning both countries, such as the electronic industry.

11612315.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11612315.value: Significance: China and India are the two biggest developing countries that absorb large amounts of foreign investments. However, few studies have rigorously compared the labour problems in these two countries and examined the possible causes of these problems. As a comparative study, we can compare the same companies’ subsidiaries and find out the possible driving forces of the differences in labor conditions outcomes. Value of the research project: this project is valuable because currently there are only a few comparative labour study research between the two biggest developing countries, partly due to the difficulty in coordinating the comparable project on two countries with very different institutions, cultural, and languages limitations.

11612615.label: Project Objectives
11612615.value: To develop a database of neighborhood physical environments and socio-economic statuses of 160+ public housing estates in Hong Kong based on objective measures derived from geographic information systems (GISs). •A combined detailed GIS database for a 1-km street network buffer around each residential estate will be created. •The neighborhood of each public housing estate will be assessed with a single composite walkability index. •The average family income at each public housing estate will be determined. To select the study area and sample •Twenty-four public housing estates will be selected based on neighborhood walkability and average family income. •Eight hundred forty participants will be enrolled via stratified random sampling. To assess site-level physical environments •Measures of site-level environmental characteristics will be developed. The measures will be operationalized from the concept of proximity and accessibility. •The site-level environmental characteristics of the study area will be assessed according to the proposed site-level measures. To collect demographic and health information on the individual participants •Individual health characteristics will be identified through a validated health survey. •Demographics, including age, gender, education level, marital status, and household income, will be collected via a self-report survey. To objectively assess the physical activity of participants •The duration and level of physical activity will be assessed with an accelerometer, and the location of the physical activity will be identified with a Global Position System (GPS) unit. •Data from the accelerometer and GPS units will be merged using timestamps. •The levels of physical activity occurring in different spatial spheres (building site, neighborhood, and beyond the neighborhood) will be identified through the merged data. To identify physical neighborhood and site-level characteristics which are associated with increased physical activity. •To identify environmental factors with multilevel linear regression models. •Disseminating of research findings.

11612615.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11612615.value: Hong Kong and many other developed societies are facing the challenges of aging populations, with one being an increased demand for healthcare services and expenditures. There is compelling evidence that physical activity can improve the health of older adults. In turn, physical activity can lower annual direct medical costs by US$695 per person (2014 price). However, roughly two-thirds of old adults in Hong Kong fail to achieve the recommended 30 minutes per day of moderate physical activity. The physical environment is believed to be an important factor that can hinder or facilitate daily physical activity, such as walking or jogging. Numerous studies have found that residents walk more in neighborhoods with certain environmental characteristics, such as high density and high street connectivity. However, most previous studies have been cross-sectional studies, which are limited in establishing causality between the environment and physical activity. Many Hong Kong residents live in high-density large-scale residential properties that have large open spaces built for physical activity within the property site. Making use of those property sites to promote physical activity of older adults seems to be a reasonable approach, because older adults spend an average of 19 hours per day around home. However, little is known about the effect of site environment on physical activity. This study will address those gaps in the literature by comparing the differences in physical activity of residents who have been randomly assigned to different public residential estates. The study will include 840 older adults in 24 public housing estates. Guided by the social ecological model, comprehensive data collection methods will be used to measure (1) the neighborhood and site-level environmental characteristics; (2) individual demographic and health data; and (3) individual walking and other physical activity data. Multilevel linear regression model will be used to investigate association of neighborhood and site-level characteristics with walking and other physical activities, after adjustment for individual-level characteristics. This study is significant for several reasons. Theoretically, the natural experiment design will address the limitations of prior cross-sectional studies. The study will also identify site-level physical environmental factors that support walking among older adults. Practically, the results of this study will help designers and developers of large residential building complex create activity-friendly residential sites. This work will also promote the physical activity and quality of life of older adults and thereby reduce the healthcare costs imposed on society. 香港和其他許多發達社會都面臨著人口老齡化帶來的種種挑戰，其中之一是日益增長的醫療需求和醫療開支。有大量證據表明身體活動包括步行可提高老年人的健康水平。適當的體力活動可以為每個老人每年減少695美元的直接醫療費用。然而，大約三分之二的香港老年人未能達到推薦的每日30分鐘的適當身體活動。 建成環境被認為是能夠阻礙或促進日常的身體活動的一個重要因素。許多研究發現，居民在特定的社區，如高密度和高連通性的社區中步行得更多。然而，大多數的研究採用了橫斷面研究方法，它們在建立環境和身體活動的因果關係時有一定的局限性。 許多香港居民住在高密度大規模的屋苑中，其屋苑場地往往有大型活動空間和多條步行道。利用屋苑場地設計，以促進老年人身體活動似乎是一個合理的方法，因為老年人平均每天有19小時停留在家附近。然而，幾乎沒有研究調查屋苑現場環境對身體活動的影響。 這項研究將比較被隨機分配到不同的公共屋苑居民的身體活動的差異。此項研究將調研居住在24個公共屋苑的840老年人。在社會生態模型的指導下，採用比較全面的數據收集方法來測量：（1）社區和場地的建成環境特徵；（2）個人人口和健康數據;及（3）個人步行和其他身體活動數據。將採用多元線性回歸模型來研究社區和場地的建成環境特徵與步行和其他身體活動的關係。 這項研究有重要意義。理論上，自然實驗設計將突破現有橫斷面研究的限制。這項研究也將甄別出有助與老年人步行的建築環境因素。研究結果將幫助設計師和大型住宅管理者創建具有活力的居住環境。這項研究也將促進老年人的身體活動和提高其生活質量，從而減少社會的醫療成本。

11612615.label: Realisation of objectives
11612615.value: Realization of Objective 1: There are more than 160 public housing projects with 2 million residents across Hong Kong. We purchased geo-coded GIS data from Lands Department, and developed a detailed GIS database for all residential estates in Hong Kong. This database includes street centerline, building footprint, outdoor amenities, recreational facilities, and block and block group census data. We also collect social-demographic data for each housing estate, such as average family income, age composition, education level, unemployment rate. A composite walkability index is derived from GIS. Realization of Objective 2: We select 36 public housing estates based on neighborhood walkability and average family income. The selected public housing estates is equally stratified into four groups: high walkability/high income, high walkability/low income, low walkability/high income, and low walkability/low income groups. The study assessed 29–30 participants from each housing estate, with a total of 1078 participants. The research team selected the participants from a stratified random sample. Realization of Objective 3: A comprehensive set of built environment variables are derived from our GIS database, including residential density, land use mix, and intersection density, urban greenness, number of bus stops and retail stores, and distance to the closest Mass Transit Rail (MTR) station. Realization of Objective 4 & 5: The participants’ personal characteristics and physical activity data are collected through self-report questionnaires and travel diary. For a subset of participants, their physical activity data is concurrently collected by means of two complementary measurement devices: an accelerometer (Actigraph GT1M) and a GPS unit (Garmin Forerunner 205). In addition, we obtained travel behavior data, mainly walking behaviors and commuting trip mode choice, from Hong Kong Travel Characteristics Survey (HKTCS) of 2011. The main travel survey had a large sample size, comprising 101,385 residents of 35,401 households spatially distributed throughout the territory of Hong Kong. Realization of Objective 6: Several multilevel regression models are used to explore the associations of built environment and individual physical activity and walking behaviors. Multilevel modeling can account for the clustering in the walking behaviors of a neighborhood’s participants. Individual participants (level 1) were clustered within street blocks (level 2), which are census-defined aggregates in Hong Kong delineated for town planning purposes. There are four findings. 1) The results showed that street greenery and the number of parks were associated with higher odds of walking. Street greenery was also associated with total walking time. Our results suggest that walking behavior is strongly affected by eye-level street greenery. 2) For older adults in public housing estates, transportation walking was positively associated with the number of bus stops and the presence of Mass Transit Railway (MTR) stations. Recreational physical activity was positively related to the number of recreational facilities. 3) New town residents walked less for transportation purpose than urban residents. 4) For commuting mode choice, design and destination accessibility had greater effects on the choices to walk and take public transport. Density and diversity had only marginal effects on mode choice. The above findings are disseminated in six journal articles and three conference papers.

11612615.label: Major findings and research outcome
11612615.value: The physical environment is believed to be an important factor that can hinder or facilitate daily physical activity, such as walking or jogging. This research addressed an important issue that what kind of built environment characteristics affect physical activity of urban residents of Hong Kong. Four major findings were developed from this project. 1) The results showed that urban greenness, especially that measured from eye-level perspective, is positively associated with walking and physical activity (Part C Journal Publications No. 1 & 2). In this project, novel methods for exacting urban greenness from Google Street View images are developed and validated (Conference No. 1 & Journal No. 2). Furthermore, the Google Street View method is more time- and cost-effective than field audits, which involve the difficulty of transporting observers to sites (Conference No. 2). 2) For older adults in public housing estates, we confirmed that easy access to public transit and pedestrian destinations were associated with increased walking and physical activity for older adults (Journal No. 3). The original ‘3Ds’ variables—density (Conference No. 3), land-use mix, design—however, were largely negative or not associated with any specific domains of physical activity. The mixed results from this study and others show a threshold effect in the built environment-physical activity associations. 3) We compared the residents’ walking behaviors in both new towns and traditional urban neighborhoods of Hong Kong (Journal No. 4). The results showed that new town residents who reside far from transit stations walked less compared with urban residents. The spatial disparity of pedestrian destinations, jobs and infrastructures may account for the observed difference in walking behavior. The findings challenge the commonly accepted concept that Transit-Oriented Development neighborhoods and old traditional urban neighborhoods had similar impacts on residents’ walking behavior. 4) We examined the association between commuting mode choice and built environment characteristics in Hong Kong (Journal No. 5). We found that commuting travel choice was reasonably sustainable in Hong Kong; on average, residents tend to use public transport (66%) for commuting trips more often than driving (24%) or walking (10%). In a high-density urban setting, density and diversity may be ineffective at curbing automobile use in the already extremely compact development. In addition, we suggest that built environment interventions such as pedestrian infrastructure or job−housing balance policies should be implemented together.

11612615.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11612615.value: There is one major potential further development from this research. Further study should be devoted to establishing causal relationship between built environment physical activity behaviors. Our studies of this relationship have been cross-sectional; thus, whether there is a causal relationship between the built environment and behavior is uncertain. Residential self-selection may confound any association between the built environment and observed physical activity. For example, residents with advanced knowledge of the beneﬁts of physical activity and positive attitudes toward walking may choose to live in high walkable neighborhoods. The observed environment-behavior association may be spurious explained by underlying personal factors. In simple words, we observe an association because the individuals who prefer to walk also like to live in walking-supporting places. Two research design options can be implemented to mitigate this limitation. First, researchers may measure personal preferences and attitudes and then control those personal factors as confounders during data analysis. Second, researchers may use longitudinal research design to study change in physical activity before and after residential relocations or built environment interventions.

11612615.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11612615.value: Population aging is a global phenomenon. Older adults require increased healthcare services and healthcare expenditures. Physical activity has preventive effects against many chronic diseases. For example, it can reduce the risk of heart disease by 40%. However, roughly two-thirds of older adults in Hong Kong remain inactive. Researchers are exploring the role of the physical environment in physical activity. Numerous studies have found that residents walk more in neighborhoods with certain environmental characteristics. However, most evidence came from Western countries. A recent review calls for studies from diverse regions to understand the complex patterns in built environment-physical activity associations. Hong Kong and other high-density cities in China are different from cities in Western countries in many respects, having larger populations, higher population densities, lower crime rates, a lower socioeconomic status, and different family structures and other cultural affinities. Hence, replicating policies based on Western contexts in Hong Kong may prove to be ineffective or misleading. This project provides evidence that certain built environment characteristics, such as urban greenness, accessibility to destinations, have significant impact on physical activity in Hong Kong. The findings can help urban planner and government agencies to create walking-friendly urban environment to improve physical activity and health of urban residents.
