12601715.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12601715.value: This project will investigate the implications of social media for media policy and regulation. The research will address two sets of issues: first, the development of the Chinese national communication and information technology regulatory policy amid the lack of effectiveness and accountability of state and legal regulation in the social media environment; secondly, the network form of governance of social media in China. Instead of seeing regulation solely as a top-down imposition of law and control by the state, this research project proposes to approach the subject of social media regulation critically, and adopts the theory of network governance (NG) in analysing the complex regulation of social media in China. This is because NG reflects a changing relationship between state and society in which social problems are solved through multisectional collaboration between the state and private actors and states increasingly rely on the cooperation of stakeholders to mobilize fragmented resources to realise favourable outcomes. NG is pertinent to Chinese governance since the incremental change from government control (guanzhi) to public management (guanli) and to network governance (zhili) in China. It is pertinent to Chinese social media governance because legal and state regulation have been either poorly enforced or lacking in accountability, and self-regulation and collaboration between state, non-state organisations and industry in governing social media have been called. And NG provides one possible way of connecting state institutions with civil society organisations (CSOs). This research study will use a case study method, and locating its study on the CSO actor, namely the Beijing Internet Association (BIA). It will examine the networks BIA has established with other institutional actors in Chinese social media network governance. The BIA was founded in 2004 as a government-recognised CSO. It was the first local internet CSO with the aim of establishing a self-regulatory system and of connecting the Internet companies with government departments. The research aims to explore the questions of the nature of networks between private and state actors; the patterns of private-state collaborations; and the distributions of benefits and power in the network governance of social media in China. 本项目研究社交媒体对媒体政策和规制的影响。這項研究將解決兩個方面的問題: 首先，在社交媒體的国家和法律規制缺乏有效性和問責制的情况下，中國传播和信息技術政策的發展; 其次，中國对社交媒體的網絡治理的形式。這一研究採用網絡治理框架来分析中国社交媒體的複雜规制，而不是僅僅视规制為國家自上而下強加的法律和控制。網絡治理反映了不斷變化的國家和社會的關係: 社會問題通過國家和社會的多种協作来解決, 國家越來越多地依賴於利益相關者的合作来調動分散的資源解決社會問題。在中国，因为社交媒體的国家和法律規制實施不力或缺乏問責，学界和政府呼吁以國家，非國家組織和行業間的自律和協作方式来管理社交媒體。網絡治理提供了連接政府機構與民間社會組織的一種可能途徑。這項研究將採用案例分析的方法，研究社會組織-北京互聯網協會（BIA）- 的網絡治理角色，它會研究BIA與其它機構參與者建立的社交媒體治理的網絡。BIA成立於2004年，是政府認可的民間組織， 它是第一個以建立自我規管制度为目, 連接互聯網企業與政府部門的本地互聯網民間組織。這項研究旨在探索民間和國家行為體之間的合作模式; 及中國社交媒體的網絡治理的利益和權力的分佈。

12601715.label: Realisation of objectives
12601715.value: This project addressed four sets of objectives: 1) the responses of Chinese national communication and information technology regulatory policy to the lack of effectiveness and accountability of state and legal regulation in the social media environment; 2) the roles of private institutions (including both social media companies and Beijing Internet Association) in social media governance in China 3) the patterns of private-state collaborations in the network governance of social media 4) the distributions of benefits and power of the network governance of social media in China. All four objectives have been fully achieved. Methods In order to achieve the first research objective, a qualitative documentary analysis has been used to examine how national communication and information technology regulatory policy has developed in responding to the ineffectiveness and lack of accountability of state and legal regulation over the time period 1994-2016, since China first formally accessed the Internet in 1994, and subsequently, the government began to promulgate a series of regulatory policies. Policy and regulatory documents have been collected from the official websites of various government administrative departments and organs overseeing social media such as the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT), The State Administration of Press, Publication, Radio, Film and Television (SAPPRFT), the Ministry of Culture (MOC), the State Council’s office of Information (SCOI), the State Internet Information Office (SIIO), and the China Internet Network Information Centre (CNNIC); from official websites of self-regulatory organization e.g. Beijing Internet Association (BIA); and also from social media companies like Tencent and Sina; as well as from open and semi-open academic and governmental publications, policy websites, and legal databases. To achieve the research objectives two to four, a multitude of methods including case study, documentary analysis, semi-structured interviews, observation and international workshop have been utilized. First, instead of exhausting all governance networks, this research used a case study method and took a key civil society organization, the Beijing Internet Association (BIA) as the subject of the case study to examine the network governance of social media in China. The case study method allows us to systematically investigate the key network actors in a comprehensive fashion. Second, documentary analysis was used by collecting and studying three categories of documents: a) organisational charters, service agreements, self-regulatory agreements and big events published by the BIA, government agencies and social media companies, such as the Charter of the BIA, and the Beijing Internet Industry Self-Regulation Agreement; b) meeting reports/minutes, reports, rulings and documents published by the BIA, Online News and Information Council, Anti-Online Rumour website py.qianlong.com and other network actors; c) secondary academic and media publications. Most of the documents are available to the public. Additional documents were given by some of the interviewees during the fieldwork. Third, semi-structured interviews were conducted with policymakers, senior management members of Internet companies, and scholars. A purposive sampling method was used first to identify key figures in the field, and the snowball sampling method was applied later to expand the pool of interviewees. Nine interviews were conducted with two policymakers (respectively from the Beijing Internet Association and Beijing Internet Information Office), three scholars (respectively from Tsinghua University, Renmin University and Chinese Academy of Social Sciences), and interviewees from four Internet companies (respectively from Qianlong.com, Sina, YNET.com and ChinaCache) during the first fieldwork in Beijing from 4 August to 23 August 2016. More than one interviewee participated in some of the interviews, for example, altogether 7 interviewees participated in the interview with Qianlong.com on 10 August 2016 and 15 August 2016. Follow-up interviews with some of the previous interviewees, e.g. policymaker from Beijing Internet Information Office, and interviews with senior management members from Tencent and China Internet Network Information Center (CNNIC) were conducted during the second fieldwork in Beijing from 28 November to 2 December 2016. Fourth, a participatory observation was done in the py.qianlong.com media organization during the first fieldwork in Beijing from 4 August to 23 August 2016. By closely observing, recording and engaging in the daily operation of the py.qianlong.com, rich first-hand data in the natural setting were generated. Data are collected and recorded according to categories of a) type of networks; b) prerequisite of networks; b) steering mechanism; c) network management; d) social capital building strategies. Comparisons were also made between the observed behaviors and proclaimed operational process and networks established. Fifth, an international workshop with the theme “Social Media, Policy and Regulation: A Network Governance Perspective” was held in Tsinghua University, Beijing on 3 December and 4 December 2016 not only to present some of the preliminary research findings and enlarge the impact, but also to further investigate some of the research questions as the workshop has invited professionals at new media companies, regulators, NOGs, and academics inside and outside China to share their experiences and knowledge in regulation especially network governance of social media. Speakers invited include the director of China Internet Network Information Center (CNNIC), the deputy director of Beijing Internet Information Office (BIIO), director of WeChat Security Risk Control Center, deputy director of Sina Weibo Social Forum Management, executive and assistant director of Advertising Standards Authority of Singapore (ASAS), managers from Privacy Commissioner for Personal Data (PCPD) Hong Kong, former head of BBC Chinese, and scholars from China, US, South Korea, Malaysia and Indonesia. Issues such as online rumor, privacy and data protection, online bullying, intermediary liability, and network neutrality were discussed at the workshop. Thus having these professionals to present and discuss at the workshop is a way to further investigate the research questions, and can be used as first-hand resources of the study. After the workshop, a half-day visit to Sina – one of the largest Internet companies in China has also been arranged to gain more insights into the research questions.

12601715.label: Major findings and research outcome
12601715.value: The major findings of this research include four parts: 1) The concept of network governance/social governance has been applied in China's social media governance. The Chinese government has delegated some social media governance functions social media companies, and “licensed” nonprofit organisation, i.e. Beijing Internet Association (BIA) . And also, a class of people like technocrats, scholars, bureaucrats and more recently entrepreneurs has influenced Chinese leaders’ decision-making in information technology policy. 2) The nonprofit organization, i.e. BIA, is not entirely independent from the Party-state, but they cooperate with each other. The power of semi-dependent nonprofit organization BIA and its members should not be underestimated. The BIA has played a role in communication and capacity-building, training, knowledge, and skills sharing. The Party-state needs it to reach and communicate with a much wider range of active Internet industry actors; to access the latest development of the industry and technology; to realize the diversity and effectiveness of Internet governance in form and in essence. While the BIA also represents its members to communicate their issues, problems, demands and industry development with government agencies. Social media companies, which are more capable than the government in understanding significant issues especially issues, could influence the social media policy agenda. 3) The nonprofit organization BIA is not entirely independent from the Party-state, but rather they cooperate with each other i.e. the state’s partnership with civil society organizations in governance. The BIA and Beijing Internet Information Office (BIIO) share the top leadership. Financially, BIA partially relies on the purchase of its service by the government. BIA and BIIO share other resources like internal human resources. The Chinese government still sees social actor such as BIA as a subordinate and supplement unit rather than an actor in its own right and can independently operate. 4) The power inequality exists among the actors. Brokerage, type of relations, and capacity are powerful explaining measurements. BIA's secretariat occupies the central position of the network, it acts as the broker. Commercial web companies occupied more powerful positions than other types of actors (research institutions, technology companies and traditional media). Secretariat has special capacities of information control, funding, accessing to key personnel in both network and government, and setting up key agenda. 60 of BIA's 106 members are core because of their roles in news and information communication and dissemination. Commercial web companies occupied more powerful positions than other actors (research institutions, technology companies, and traditional media).

12601715.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12601715.value: This research used a case study method in exploring the pattern and power relationship in the network governance of Chinese social media. The case studied is the Beijing Internet Association (BIA). The findings demonstrated the complex network governance and power relationships between the BIA network and government agencies, and between the members of the BIA network. The project also developed an analytical model to explore the power of the governance network. In other words, brokerage, type of relations, and capacity are powerful explaining measurements in the BIA case. Based on the findings and outcomes of this project, the research questions, concepts and analytical models can be further used to study other cases such as China Internet Association in network governance so that the conceptualisation and understandings of the roles of semi-independent non-profit organisation and private social media companies in China’s internet governance can be further tested and enhanced.

12601715.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12601715.value: This project investigated the implications of social media for media regulation. It explored the development of Internet regulatory model in China amid the lack of effectiveness and accountability of state and legal regulation in the social media environment; it studied the network form of governance of social media in China. Instead of seeing regulation solely as a top down imposition of law and control by the state, this research project approached the subject of social media regulation critically, and adopts the theory of network governance in analysing the complex regulation of social media in China. This research used a case study method in exploring the pattern and power relationship in the network governance (the state’s partnership with civil society organizations, private companies in governance). The research outcome of the project not only affirmed the complex governance relations between the semi-independent non-profit organisation, private social media companies and government agencies, but also developed an analytical model to study the power relations in network governance, i.e. brokerage, type of relations, and capacity are powerful explaining measurements.

12602115.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12602115.value: This project will identify and synthesise ethical best practices in Asian journalism, through an analysis of leading news organisations’ internal policies and codes of practice. The study will be based on interviews with senior editors and/or publishers, analysis of written guidelines where available, and case studies of ethically challenging situations that illustrate how the organisations’ principles are applied in practice. Twelve news organisations will be selected from 9-10 Asian markets (including mainland China and Hong Kong SAR). The project fills a gap in both media scholarship and professional development. Comparative studies of non-Western journalism have investigated norms and practices that typify different societies. These illuminate the general landscape. But they do not highlight outcrops of professional excellence, which are invariably confined to a minority of organisations. Another limitation of such studies is that the unit of analysis is the individual journalist, whereas organisational settings are known to be the major influences on journalists’ ethical conduct. This study will overcome these limitations by focusing on organisations that are regarded as exemplary – even if by no means perfect – in their pursuit of ethical, high-quality journalism. It will allow us to arrive at empirically grounded normative statements about professional practice in Asia. It will also help us identify challenges – political, economic and organisational – that stand in the way of ethical practice for quality media that aspire to high standards. The comparative approach – covering different types of media organisation as well as diverse political systems and markets – will allow us to distinguish norms that are relatively universal, from those that depend on context, such as the organisation’s political environment. The study will focus on pertinent ethical dilemmas that the profession faces today: (1) how to deal with conflicts of interest, involving owners, advertisers or individual journalists; (2) hybrid, disguised forms of advertising, which are integrated seamlessly into the editorial mix at the risk of deceiving audiences; (3) audience metrics that allow media organisations to respond to audience tastes, but which may dilute the role of editorial judgment; and (4) how to handle hate speech and other forms of extreme expression, which have proliferated on online forums. In addition to providing a unique contribution to our scholarly understanding of Asian journalism, the project will generate knowledge that is immediately transferable to industry, both directly, through sharing of best practices, and indirectly, by arming journalism educators with compelling examples from the region. 摘要 本項目會識別出亞洲新聞業最佳職業道德操守的實例。研究將檢視新聞機構如何處理不同的情境。 研究員會訪問出版人，編輯和記者並考查新聞機構面對道德考驗時的情況。這研究會在亞洲， 包括中國大陸和香港特別行政區，選出十至十二個新聞機構作調查為對象。

12602115.label: Realisation of objectives
12602115.value: The project succeeded in shedding light on leading Asian news organisations’ internal policies toward contemporary ethical challenges. The target of 12 organisations was met, though only 7 societies were covered, short of the 9–10 initially proposed, due to the fact that the grant was less than the sum applied for. Nevertheless, the number of societies covered far exceeds what is normal for qualitative studies. As planned, face-to-face interviews were conducted with senior leaders of the news organisations, usually chief editors or other senior editors with the knowledge and authority to speak on behalf of their organisations. The ethical issues originally identified for study were (1) conflicts of interest, especially involving owners and advertisers; (2) hybrid, disguised forms of advertising; (3) audience metrics; and (4) hate speech on media outlets’ online platforms. Although information was gathered pertaining to all four questions, the final question, on hate speech, was eventually dropped from the analysis. This was because the information gathered was too thin, for a mix of reasons. In several cases, the media organisations were not greatly affected by the problem, because their more upmarket and loyal readership was less prone to the kind of hateful comments that inflict that outlets with a more broadbased readership. However, the material obtained from one organisation was substantive enough to generate one conference presentation about online harassment of media in the Philippines. All the media included in the study acknowledged that they were under commercial pressures that could compromise their professional journalistic missions. However, in keeping with their reputations for high professional standards, all were consciously trying to mitigate the negative effects of these pressures. In some cases, the steps taken were far in excess of what is widely considered to be the norm. There were clear cases of media that were prepared to sacrifice short-term profitability for the sake of professional principles. The premise of the project was thus confirmed, that despite the financial crisis facing the news media industry, there remain exemplary cases of professional integrity that the industry can learn from. The project found that commitments to protect editorial integrity are often not written into company policy but are rather a part of their tradition and culture. This culture of independence is consciously promoted organisation-wide. This observation resonates with research on ethical discourse within journalism as a community of practice. It appears that exemplars feed on one another, drawing inspiration from other news organisations that they consider to be members of the same community of practice, or to whose standards they aspire. Although the normative thrust of the project is to encourage media to pick up best practices from others, the findings suggest that there may be limitations to the diffusion of positive professional habits and traits. Several organisations cited their founding visions as playing a critical factor. They were launched by journalist-publishers that set the tone for public service journalism and editorial independence from the start. Indeed, not one of the outlets started life in the more commercially-oriented corporate sector or as a government propaganda mouthpiece. This raises the sobering question of whether such reform is even possible. Research findings were presented at three major communication studies conferences and one international professional conference. An article has been published in a leading journalism studies journal. As planned, the project’s findings were also made freely available on a custom-made website, in the form of articles written for a lay audience. Three PhD students were involved in the research. They assisted with interviews and authored reports. Two students are currently PhD candidates at HK Baptist U. The third was at City U of HK, who has since graduated with a PhD, and was engaged as a Research Associate for the project.

12602115.label: Major findings and research outcome
12602115.value: The organisations covered were conscious of the ethical risks that are at the heart of the study. Many had instituted formal checks or cultivated organisational cultures to protect their editorial processes from non-professional interventions by owners. In several cases, that sensitivity was present from the moment of inception: they were founded by journalists and not businessmen. Several were family-owned, or had ownership structures deliberately designed to minimise conflicts of interest. Pressure from advertisers was minimised by, in one case, opting for a non-commercial, donor-driven business model; in most cases, organisations depended on maintaining a strict separation between marketing and editorial functions. Commercial organisations acknowledged that this separation is getting harder to maintain due to financial pressures. More than in the past, editors need to be aware of marketing considerations and to try to find ways to accommodate business priorities. However, they claim that do not give in to pressures that would corrupt their missions to put the public first or harm their organisation’s reputation for independence. In some cases, the marketing departments themselves understood that the brand would suffer if editorial compromised its principles. In dealing with hybrid formats of advertising, such as sponsored content and advertorials, the organisations apply a combination of disclosure (through labelling and distinct design) and containment (ghettoising hybrid formats in “lighter” sections such as lifestyle) to keep advertising and promotional content separate from their journalism. Some editors have come around to accepting partnership deals with corporations as a way to boost their capacity to handle a special project, such as international sports events that require costly travel for their reporters and photographers. Organising events is another emerging revenue stream. The organisations studied recognised the value of events, while remaining wary of the risk that partnerships would compromise their editorial integrity. They resolve this tension in different ways. All of them, though, said that they would not give these events more coverage than they were due. The organisations’ policies regarding these newer ethical challenges tend not to be codified and are still evolving. Best practices emerge from an organisational culture rather than written codes of ethics.

12602115.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12602115.value: There is scope to expand the scope of this research, to add more news organisations to the reports that are now available publicly at the project’s website. This can be achieved with new research funding or with the help of overseas collaborators. The main new theoretical insight that is worthy of further research is that professional exemplars may include media that have died; their best practices may be emulated after they die by other organisations. A professional journalistic ethos may thus be regarded as a movement, connecting various media over time and space. This idea will be pursued in a separate journal article or book chapter.

12602115.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12602115.value: News media are prone to a conflict of interest between the commercial needs of advertisers and owners and the public service objectives of professional journalism. However, there are still principled news organisations that try to protect their editorial integrity. This project studied twelve respected outlets in seven Asian markets, to identify best practices. Through interviews with their editors and publishers, the study examined their policies with regard to important contemporary challenges. In particular: how they deal with pressures from owners and advertisers who want favourable news coverage; and how they respond to the demand for commercial deals that blur the boundaries between editorial and advertising, such as “native” ads and event sponsorships. The organisations were found to have policies aimed at preserving their editorial integrity even as they become more accommodating to the market. Our interviewees point to the importance of organisational culture, more than written policies, in maintaining professionalism: most of the organisations were founded by journalist-publishers whose ethos continues to exert a strong influence. The project responds to recent calls in media ethics scholarship for studies on actually existing—even if imperfect—exemplars rather than abstract ideals. The findings can feed into professional training and education of journalists.

12602515.label: Realisation of objectives
12602515.value: Firstly, I have extended the research scope of artists works until 2017. We have delayed the prolonged the research period so that latest artists works can be also included in the analysis. Different than documentary makers, artists may rework various installation versions in different exhibition settings. Hence, it is important to extend the scope of years of artwork from 2015 to 2017. In particular, the major research subject Tang Kowk Hin, had documentary-based works with new installation settings in 2017, e.g. Grandpa Tang and Nancy. In terms of scale of research and number of artists/artworks, we have searched, collected and studied 220 artworks from 31 artists for textual analysis and basic information analysis. Then, we chose 11 artists/artgroups for focus studies and semi-structure in-depth interview. The artworks information, artists information and an edited short version (around 10mins) of the interviews with English translation, are posted on a web-based platform for free public assess. It is open to all future researchers, educators, artists and people who are interested in the topic to use. We have promoted it on social media. I also have sent it to most local art critics and researchers and related colleagues in various universities. If they would like to get the full transcript of the interview, we are more than happy to share, with artists’ consent. Also, in the video short interviews, artworks are also shown visually, so audience can understand more when artists explaining the artworks. (artworks shown in video with artists permission). The web stie: https://docuarthk.wixsite.com/research Secondly, there are several practices that both documentary makers and contemporary artists both apply. One major finding is the research method of autoethnography. I have written a journal article and will do a conference to present it. Autoethnography, originally from qualitative research methods in the field of anthropology and sociology has been further developed in the field of experimental ethnography, diary film, personal cinema that practiced cross-disciplinarily by contemporary artists. Thirdly, since Documenta has become the big hit every 5 years, and more and more moving image works shown in galley space and exhibitions, there are quite some literatures on documentary-based works by contemporary artists in the field of contemporary art. However, most of the theoretical inquiry is not very strong. Many books mainly show artists practices and records of artworks/exhibitions only. Hence, I have chosen to use theories on experimental ethnography, personal cinema and reflexive documentary especially regarding issues of (inter-)subjectivity as the theoretical framework on one hand, and autoethnography practice, as research method as well as visual ethnographic representation in qualitative research one the other hand. Fourthly, there are quite some artists doing experimental documentary-based works in Hong Kong, out of my expectation. One reason why most people could not realize is that, artists use various media and for most of the time, they do mixed media and moving image for conceptual works. However, they may have done a few (sometimes only 1-2 works) that are documentary-based. As we have gone through full list of artworks (textual analysis) of the artists chosen, hence we could spot the few works out. Last two interesting notes about research findings: -- artists may not be very aware of documentary theories as they are not from film background, except 6 subjects. They (e.g Leung Mee-peng) consider video footage, similar to other materials e.g. found objects which carry traces of real people. And they organize them and consider the spatial visual representation similar with the ways they deal with other materials. it is very different from video-maker ways of work. -- artists take shooting as bodily interaction with the environment and as performance, these are totally different practice from capturing-images-oriented approach of regular documentary maker. Besides the external qualities -- people and environment being shot, artists also rethink a lot internally regarding their own bodily and mental response with the environment, and these responses are not mere research but also as part of the artwork. The difficulties of the research has two fold, external and internal: External difficulties: there is no previous research on similar topic, so we have to start from zero. We had to go to various organizations and institutions to search for all catalogs that might have information about artworks in our radar. Fortunately, artists are all very collaborative on offering artworks for us to view, as well as doing in-depth interview and observation of their ways of practices. I am very grateful to the artists friends and the helpful community. Internal difficulties is my health, I was in hospital both in 2017 and 2018. And my health condition was critical last year that had put the research stopped and resumed a few times. I am grateful that it can be finished at the end. The fund could not be spent fully, especially on the part for international conference. I was seriously ill and was in hospital in April 2017 and Feb-March 2018. I did submit an abstract and got accepted to The Asian conference on Arts & Humanities, late March 2018, at Kobe Japan. But my health could not afford to attend the conference after one month out of the hospital, though I had already paid for conference registration. I have coronary heart disease and thickening of heart wall, plus meningioma (brain tumour) in the front left brain. It has taken me a long time to stabilize the condition. Hence, I am trying to make it up and do it out of my own fund, though fall behind the time-frame of the research. I have submitted an abstract and also accepted by International Convention of Asian Scholars, ICAS 11 at Leiden University, Netherlands that will happen in July 2019. The presentation is titled: The Notion of Home: auto-ethnographic artworks of Law Yuk Mui and Tang Kwok Hin in Hong Kong. As it is after the research period, thus, I will pay by my own fund and try my best to release research findings as much as I can.

12602515.value: In terms of scale of research and number of artists/artworks, we have searched and collected and studied 220 artworks from 31 artists for textual analysis and basic information analysis. Then, we did focus studies and semi-structure interview on 11 artists/art groups. The artworks information, artists information and an edited short version (around 10mins) of the interview with English translation, are posted on a web-based platform for free public assess. It is open to all future researchers, educators, artists and people who are interested in the topic to use. There are artworks that go with the video interview for audience to understand the artworks while the artists explaining. Artworks used on video with artists' permission. The web stie: https://docuarthk.wixsite.com/research Two conferences. First conference (at Chinese University of Hong Kong), I focus on the Chan Tze Woon’s works. The presentation explores ways documentary works that share poetic nature of contemporary art, and the auto-ethnographic practice at fieldwork (Umbrella revolution). It also looks at Chan's ways of work -- selection of footage and editing of the fieldwork materials after 2-3 years of the event. This presentation examines the gap of time and distancing of one-self (the artist) with the same self at the field years before, that is actually, a re-visit of inter-subjectivity both to the artist himself as well as people being studied and represented in the ethnographic presentation. Second conference (at 11st Asian Studies Conference this year at Leiden University, Netherlands), I try to work the other way round (not from the practices of documentary film artists but contemporary artists) to study the ways contemporary artists work on documentary-based works. Super interesting findings include de-colonoalization tactics via exploration of the notion of home, the ways artists use cameras, the performative qualities of shooting, and the debates about psychology truth in domestic ethnography as well as artists' research methods at the field including participant observation and wandering tactics. The conference presentation is an oral presentation together with artworks screening. I think this is important to let overseas scholars/participants of Asian studies (of various fields) view the artworks themselves, hence to also promote Hong Kong contemporary art works regarding autoethnography. Artwork screening with artists' permission. The presentation of the conference is a summary of a journal article, sent to Visual Ethnography, titled, Convergence of the practices of documentary and contemporary art in Hong Kong: Autoethnographic works of Tang Kwok Hin and Law Yuk Mui. It is sent and undergoing peer review.

12602515.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12602515.value: The public free assess website https://docuarthk.wixsite.com/research has provided much room for further development, not only by myself but also other researchers. This website is promoted on social media and has got over 5000 posts reach. It is also sent to related professors and teachers I know in Hong Kong, and also to art critics and researchers. I have also mentioned in the mail that, I shall be more than happy to share full transcription if they need them for their researches. One experienced researcher Phoebe Wong, is working on an article on the same topic (as her keen interest). She has used the web site information for her writing. Yeung Yang also an experienced researcher/critic is working on an article about Tang Kwok Hin and I have mentioned to her I could share full transcription of Tang's interview with her. One last note, I am working on a Chinese version of the journal article, and I am now discussing with editor of p-articles (虛詞), and they are very interested in. I hope besides academic publication, and free assess of research information/data on website, there is also Chinese publication for local readers and the general cultural field in Hong Kong.

12602515.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12602515.value: Since the last three decades there are more and more documentary moving image works shown in exhibitions and gallery spaces in the field of contemporary arts. Studies of the convergence practices at the field of documentary and contemporary arts in Hong Kong are essential and important. This research is particularly interested in the poetic aesthetic quality and issues of inter-subjectivity of autoethnography. Some documentary makers and contemporary artists though of different backgrounds, share autoethnographic practices (as research method and ways of visual presentation) and also topics of interests regarding the notion of home, cityscape, community history, identity, familial relations. By studying and presenting the artists themselves, together with their families and communities, they re-consider the notion of identity and home and share with audience the cultural and social knowledge of Hong Kong. There are 220 artworks from 31 artists collected and studied. 11 artists/art groups were selected for focus studies. Research data and an edited short version (around 10mins) of the interviews with English subtitles, are posted on a web-based platform open for free public assess. 12602915.label: Project Title(Chinese)
12602915.value: 丹青中教誨兒女的母親：清代課子圖解隱

12602915.label: Project Objectives
12602915.value: No change No change No change To compare and contrast, selectively, the representation of teaching mothers in paintings and other forms of art To conduct a preliminary cross-cultural comparison of the representation of teaching mothers in artistic forms
rows: To compare and contrast, selectively, the representation of teaching mothers in paintings and other forms of art

12602915.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12602915.value: The major objective of this project is to conduct a thorough study of the representation of teaching mothers in a particular category of painting, kezi tu 課子圖 , which became fashionable in Qing China (1644-1912). Efforts will be made to collect and investigate existing works, plus a historical survey of works that are no longer available or would have to be rediscovered from libraries, museums, and private collections. Kezi tu has not previously been the subject of systematical and thorough scholarship. This is the first project-length study on kezi tu. Blessed by the flourishing gender and childhood studies, the historical role of mothers in different civilizations has recently gained more scholarly attention. However, investigation on Chinese motherhood as seen in paintings is still rather limited. Recognizing the fact that mothers are always respected in Chinese culture, this study will employ kezi tu as well as related textual and visual materials to reflect on a substantial fact in late imperial Chinese society: elite women were honored with power to teach their sons. Hundreds of didactic texts encourage women to perform their simultaneous roles of kind mothers and strict teachers. It is wrong to think that all women were uneducated in pre-modern China, or to generalize that women were victims in Chinese history. Those are notions that have been declined by mainstream scholars in the field of gender history over the past two to three decades. In fact, learned mothers did their best to cultivate their sons, and some of them could finally enjoy living within the success of their children. The production of kezi tu vividly illustrates the common expectation of mothers as teachers, especially in the literary class. 本研究計劃旨在對清代課子圖中母親教誨兒女行為的藝術呈現作一歷史分析。明代中期，士人家庭中的母親課子圖創作，已有明確記載，而以課子圖為主題的青花瓷器，亦已十分流行。到了清代，在社會安定、經濟繁榮、文化興盛的背景下，由於閨秀母親群體積極地透過教育下一代、立德立言等行為，努力締建她們的身份認同，課子圖的繪製更是蔚然成風。 清代課子圖也有表揚父教的，但以表揚母教者較多。雖然能保留到今天的課子圖恐怕只佔總數相當少的一部分，幸而古代文人雅士以互相題詠為尚，為課子圖留下不少信息，而許多已佚課子圖的原貌或可借助題詠文字得以推敲一二。本計劃打算從歷代畫目、圖錄中稽查傳世作品以及有目無圖者；又準備從詩文集中蒐集極其豐富的課子圖題詠文本，進而探討清代女性在課教行為上呈現的主體性。她們如何透過自寫課子圖作形象化的劬勞自述，怎樣通過彼此題贈來互相標榜，她們的下一代又怎樣藉著自行或僱人繪畫課子圖來彰顯母教恩德，以至社會上對母親教誨子女的普遍認同和期待等，均在論述之列。

12603615.label: Project Title(Chinese)
12603615.value: 二十一世紀中國城市的住宅搬遷：住房歷程及社鄰管治的含義

12603615.label: Project Objectives
12603615.value: To depict the trend of residential mobility and housing career building in Guangzhou, especially since the 1998 housing reform for different age cohorts and across hukou and migratory status categories. To analyse how the effects of variables usually identified as major causes for residential mobility change over time and vary across age cohorts, hukou categories and work-unit affiliation by way of a life-course approach. To examine the interrelation between residential mobility and neighbourly relations and neighbourhood governance, particularly the role played by HOAs, estate management firms and residents' committees. To hold a workshop/conference with participation of leading international scholars to exchange views and research findings on residential mobility and neighbourhood governance and change from a comparative perspective. To present the findings in international conferences and to publish three to four articles based on the research findings.

12603615.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12603615.value: The proposed study tries to address a relatively neglected and yet important process underlying China’s unprecedented urban transformation, specifically residential mobility or intra-urban migration, which has major implications for housing career and well-being of individual urbanites and also for neighbourhood sustainability and governance. The focus of the study is on residential relocation since the ending of the welfare allocation of housing in 1998, which has fundamentally changed the meaning of housing to Chinese people, both as a consumption item and as an investment. To unravel the residential mobility trends and the factors underlying residential move or lack of it, and to examine the extent to which residential mobility is related to neighbourhood governance and neighbourly relationships, two interrelated strands of analysis will be undertaken. First, based on two large-scale household surveys conducted in Guangzhou respectively in 2005 and 2010, the trends of residential mobility and the outcomes of residential move for cohorts of population grown up in pre- and post-reform times and across population groups of different hukou status and migration histories will be studied. The adoption of a life-course approach helps shed light on such issues as: how people brought up in different periods of China’s recent history of unprecedented political, economic and social changes progress along the housing career; the validity of the thesis of residential mobility as a spatial adjustment process for individuals and households of different socioeconomic background, especially hukou status, and age cohorts, and how China’s persistent socialist legacies affect residential relocation; the extent to which specific events particularly those related to housing and financial reforms trigger or inhibit residential mobility. Homeownership has become as much a Chinese dream as it is an American dream. The rate of homeownership in urban China today tops 70 per cent. Homeowners’ associations, initially emerged more or less spontaneously and lately also formed with local government support, together with estate management firms, have become instrumental in managing community affairs, with the view to protecting if not enhancing the home values. A survey of 1800 Guangzhou households was conducted in late 2012 to elicit the role of homeowners’ associations in residential neighbourhoods of various kinds and located in different parts of the city. The second part of the proposed work will employ this set of newly collected data to examine how neighbourly relations and participation in community affairs, particularly in homeowners’ associations, affect and are conditioned upon residential movements. 此項研究針對城市內部的遷移 — 一個相對受到忽略但卻對理解中國當前的城市化和城市結構轉變的過程。居所的流動性不單影響到個人和家庭的住房歷程的進程，也跟社區的可持續發展與治理有密切的關係。自1998年停止福利分房以後，自置居所成為新常態，業主委員會、發展商、物業管理公司、居民委員會、地方政府等構成一個縱錯複雜的社區管治混合體；同時，住房的交易價值往往高於使用價值，搬家除了為了改善住房環境，切合轉變中的個人和家庭需要外，更往往伴隨著物業投資、財富積累的考慮。因此，本研究集中1998年、特別是踏進本世紀以來的住宅搬遷和社區管治間的互動過程，研究資料，主要基於項目的主持者於2005和2010年在廣州作的大型入戶住房調查，以及主持者和共同主持者於2012年為了社區管治和業委會扮演的角色在廣州進行的1800戶入戶調查。透過被訪者提供的回顧歷史，本研究將以生命歷程探求法作為主要的理論和方法論基礎，並在這個基礎上檢驗下列假設：居所流動性為個人和住戶減低住房需求和住房實況之間的差異的最重要的空間行為；居所流動性密切地影響到包括業主委員會在內的社區管治模式的形態和可持續性。

12603615.label: Realisation of objectives
12603615.value: For objectives 1 and 2, we explicitly incorporate cohort or generation differences in an event-history analysis of residential mobility in Guangzhou over the period 2000-2012 based on sample survey data. The results reveal substantially higher mobility propensities for young adults than middle-aged individuals and senior citizens. Also, there exist significant differential effects of major determinants on housing consumption and residential relocation across age cohorts; e.g. education attainment is significant only for middle-age persons, who are also more responsive to triggers such as child birth on house move. In respect to flow patterns, while outward shifts during recent years mainly involve local hukou holders, families with socio-economic status or working for state institutions are more likely to settle in high-rise commodity housing in the inner core. As for non-hukou migrants, moves are typically within the same street or between adjacent streets in the suburban area, where their jobs tend to locate. The relatively balanced jobs-housing relationship among non-hukou migrants is reflective of the spatially restricted job opportunities available to them. Regarding Objective 3, based on the same set of data, multi-level models are employed to explore the extent to which residential mobility affect three different dimensions of neighbourhood attachment. The findings show that mobility experience and neighbourhood-related factors including the performance of the Homeownership Association significantly influence attitudes towards the neighbourhood. Specifically, while people staying in reform/work-unit housing compounds have better acquaintance of their neighbours, those moving from reform/work-unit compounds to commodity housing estates exhibits higher emotional attachment to the new neighbourhood. The built environment, homeownership rate, and frequency of population turnovers in the neighbourhood underpin residents’ attachment to it. With respect to Objective 4, a two-day conference entitled "Polarisation, Fragmentation and Resilience: Four Urban Contexts" compared was successfully held at Hong Kong Baptist University on 29 November - 1 December 2017, in which some 50 delegates from Hong Kong, mainland China, USA, South Africa, UK and Canada gave presentations and discussed aspects of population mobility, including residential relocation and interrelation and international migration, residential segregation and polarisation in Hong Kong, and cities on the mainland and in South Africa and USA. As for Objective 5, we have presented different parts of our findings in various international conferences. Moreover, four papers based on the project have been published in premier journals in Urban Studies and Urban Geography; two others are under review.

12603915.label: Project Title(Chinese)
12603915.value: 二十世紀上半葉中國天主教在華的高等教育發展史

12603915.label: Project Objectives
12603915.value: This project is expected to lead to three articles in international refereed journals or book chapters with distinguished international publishers. Together, these articles/chapters will investigate the glocalization of the Catholic Church in the context of higher education in China. The first article/chapter will compare the educational philosophies, modernization objectives and global perspectives of three Chinese intellectuals. The second article/chapter will investigate Zhendan University and Furen University with regard to educational provision, curriculum design and contribution to society. The third article/chapter will address the cross-cultural relations between the Catholic missionaries and the Chinese intellectuals. After completing this project, the principal investigator (PI) will pursue further research to produce a monograph comparing Zhendan and Furen. The project will investigate the overall position of the worldwide Roman Catholic Church/the Vatican with respect to China in the first half of the 20th century. The Pope’s understanding of matters in China, and the Vatican’s overseas missionary agenda and the priority given to China in this agenda, will be assessed. The Vatican’s relations with the Chinese Nationalist Government will also be considered. The PI will examine the implementation of the Vatican’s China mission with particular attention to the operation of three Catholic missionary societies in Chinese cities: the French Jesuits (Society of Jesus) in Shanghai, the Beijing-based American Benedictine Monks of Saint Vincent Archabbey, and the German Society of the Divine Word, also stationed in Beijing. These societies pledged loyalty to the Roman Catholic Church. The PI will examine the perceptions held by these Catholic societies and missionaries of their role in China and their undertakings on the mainland. Attention will be paid to important individuals such as Rev. François Perrin, S.J., Rev. George Barry O’Toole, O.S.B. and Rev. Aurelius Stehle, Archabbot of Saint Vincent Archabbey. Also of significance were Celso Costantini (the Apostolic Delegate to China) and the Belgian priests Vincent Lebbe and Joseph Rutten, C.I.C.M. The project will investigate the collaboration and interaction of three key Chinese Christian intellectuals with the three missionary societies listed above. Ma Xiangbo (馬相伯, 1840-1939) and Ying Lianzhi (英斂之, 1867-1926) were Catholic scholars, and Chen Yuan (陳垣, 1880-1971) was a Protestant historian. Their cooperation and conflict with the foreign missionaries during the modernization of higher education in China will be considered. The project will investigate the establishment and development of Zhendan University (Aurora University, 震旦大學, 1903-1952) in Shanghai and Furen University (輔仁大學, 1925-1952) in Beijing. The mission and vision of each university in providing higher education for the youth of China will be examined. The founders of the two universities sought to cultivate a Chinese elite capable of contributing to China’s modernization and upholding Catholic beliefs and values.

12603915.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12603915.value: The proposed project will investigate the glocalization of the Catholic Church in the context of higher education in China in the first half of the 20th century. The research objective is to gain insight into the possibility of future Chinese-Western ventures in elite higher education in Chinese society. Although glocalization is a modern neologism, which refers to the enactment of global concerns in a local context, the term applies equally to the adaptation of foreign missionaries in China, the indigenization of the Chinese Catholic Church and the cultivation of the Chinese Christian elite in the first half of the 20th century. The proposed project will address the expansion of the Catholic Church through the dispersal of foreign missionaries worldwide, especially in China in the early 20th century. It will investigate the very significant contribution of the Catholic Church to China’s development, specifically in founding two institutions of elite higher education, namely Zhendan University (Aurora University, 震旦大學, 1903-1952) in Shanghai and Furen University (輔仁大學, 1925-1952) in Beijing. The principal investigator (PI) hopes to conduct an in-depth study of these two universities in the coming years, after which she will examine a third Catholic tertiary institute: the Higher Institute of Industrial and Commercial Education in Tianjin (1921-1952). The project will be groundbreaking in three respects. First, the PI will take an unprecedentedly detailed and multi-archival approach to the glocalization of the Catholic Church in China. Second, the focus of the project will be limited to two Catholic universities in China. Although previous research has been conducted on these two universities, no scholars have to date compared Zhendan University and Furen University (not to mention the Tianjin Institute) in a single monograph. Third, the project will highlight three prominent Christian intellectuals who worked with the foreign Catholic missionaries to provide higher education, namely Ma Xiangbo (馬相伯, 1840-1939), Ying Lianzhi (英斂之, 1867-1926) and Chen Yuan (陳垣, 1880-1971). Although scholars have discussed these intellectuals individually, the proposed project will be the first to compare and contrast their philosophical approaches to modernization, education and Westernization. The activities of the Chinese elite who worked with the foreign missionaries will be assessed to determine how both Chinese Christian intellectuals and foreign missionaries contributed to the glocalization of the Catholic Church through their devotion to elite higher education. 此研究計劃探討上海震旦大學(1903-1952)及北京輔仁大學(1925-1952)在中國的發展史。同時，此計劃亦就馬相伯(1840-1939)丶英歛之(1867-1926)及陳垣(1880-1971)的教育理念及他們與傳教士的關係作深入的考証。

12603915.label: Realisation of objectives
12603915.value: Traditionally, the history of Christianity in China was largely described as that of conflicts owing to the social, cultural, and ethnic differences between the Chinese and foreign missioners. THIS PROJECT critically evaluated Sino-foreign relations in the development of Christianity in Republican China. It addressed the Catholic Church; and both the cooperative nature of Sino-foreign relations, which casual viewers were prone to overlook, and the co-existing disputes, which bothered the Chinese people and the foreign missioners. This project studied the interactions between the Chinese intellectuals and foreign missioners in the establishment and progression of Zhendan University in Shanghai (Aurora University震旦大學 1903-1952) and Furen University in Beijing (輔仁大學 1925-1952). It showed that the history of Chinese Christianity was that of cross-cultural relations and mutual exchange as mentioned in recent scholarly works, such as Daniel H. Bays’ edited volume Christianity in China. Another example is Stephen Uhalley Jr. and Xiaoxin Wu’s edited book China and Christianity: Burden Past, Hopeful Future. The subtitle well illustrates the coexistence of attachment and animosity in the account of Chinese Christianity. Uhalley says, “This grand story of such an exceptional and historic intercultural encounter, featuring as it does such a provocative religious cutting edge, remains one of epic proportions.” He states that scholars have been focusing on “a longstanding and continuing drama” of remarkable dimensions. Naturally, there were cases of cooperation as well as conflicts in Chinese Catholic mission history. Most important, the Chinese intellectuals working with the missioners were the cream of society, well-bred in both Chinese and Western learning. This project (1) critically evaluated the Chinese response to the presence of foreign Catholic missioners and vice versa; (2) assessed the impact of the Catholic Church on China; and (3) understood the Chinese assimilation of foreign teachings on the basis of their traditional heritage. It emphasizes the indigenization of the Catholic Church in China and recognizes the associated problems. Essentially, this project explored the cross-cultural relations between the Chinese Christian intellectuals Ma Xiangbo (馬相伯1840-1939), Ying Lianzhi (英斂之1867-1926) and Chen Yuan (陳垣1880-1971) and the foreign Catholic missioners. It traced the cultural interactions between the Chinese and the Westerners. At the same time, it stressed that China was facing huge difficulties, unprecedented challenges and rapidly changing situations. This project is about cross-cultural studies in the context of modernization, the development of higher education, and the indigenization of Christianity in early 20th-century China. This project addressed the international trends of the first half of the 20th century. Foreign missioners, Catholics and Protestants alike, took much pride in establishing mission fields overseas. Foreign Catholic missioners had been lagging behind their Protestant counterparts and tried to catch up in the endeavor. There had been the trend of evangelization abroad and China had been the focus of foreign missioners. The spread of Christianity was the world trend. If this trend could be considered a cultural evolution, the Chinese themselves were also engaging in their intellectual renaissance. There was the urge to learn from the West in the New Cultural Movement and the May Fourth Movement, exerting tremendous impact on the mentality of the educated and elite of Chinese society. The May Fourth Movement also witnessed the upsurge of nationalism in China. Chinese intellectuals were highly concerned about their country’s wellbeing in the world community. Westernization, modernization, and evangelization had great influence on Chinese society. This project attempted to use the history of Zhendan University and Furen University to reflect on modern and even contemporary Chinese history. First, it assesses the collaboration efforts of the foreigners and the Chinese elite in the modernization of China. It discusses the advantages as well as the difficulties of such cooperation. What were the similarities and differences between the foreigners and the Chinese in their objectives, management style, and vision for the future? The first half of the 20th century was a period of rapid change and the import of Western ideas, witnessing the rise of modern China. Therefore, the outcomes of this research can throw light on the Four Modernizations through comparing the first half of the 20th century with the period that was of slightly more than three decades from 1979 to the present. The rise of modern China could be compared with the rise of contemporary China.

12603915.label: Major findings and research outcome
12603915.value: In 1903, Zhendan University was founded in Shanghai and was under the guidance of the French Jesuits. During this time, the famous Belgium priest Frederic Vincent Lebbe was pronouncing the slogan of “China to Chinese, the Chinese to Christ.” This meant modernizing the society and establishing the Catholic Church for the Chinese people. Modernization and indigenization were serious issues that the Catholic Church had to consider. Established in 1923, the Higher Institute of Industrial and Commercial Education was under the patronage of the Jesuits in Tianjin. In 1925, Furen University was founded in Beijing under the auspices of the American Benedictines. Later on, the German Society of the Divine Word took over the management of Furen. In an era of change and transition, Zhendan University, Furen University and the Higher Institute of Industrial and Commercial Education became the respectable Catholic institutions offering much sought-after higher education in China. Zhendan University was a superb amalgam of Chinese and Western styles of education. It became a model for other Christian institutions. Zhendan University was an institute of advanced learning. It specialized in the training of translators for Western books, which were crucial for China’s modernization efforts, and for textbooks in arts and sciences, which Chinese universities urgently needed. Therefore, Zhendan played a key role in China’s modernization, which was made possible through the cooperation between the Chinese and the Westerners in the first half of the 20th century. In 1925, Furen University was established and signified the collaboration between the Chinese Catholic educators (or reformers) and the American Catholic clergy. Furen University was another example to illustrate the cooperation between the Chinese and American Catholic educators during the Republican period.

12603915.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12603915.value: This project assessed “whole person education” in tertiary institutions of the Catholic Church in China in the first half of the 20th century. While we often talk about “whole person education” in contemporary settings, Chinese Catholic elite and foreign missionaries already devoted much effort in the pursuit of this area. Therefore, this project l investigated the very significant contribution of the Catholic Church to China’s development, in founding two institutions of elite higher education, namely Zhendan University (Aurora University, 1903-1952) in Shanghai and Furen University (1925-1952) in Beijing. First, this project investigated Zhendan University and Furen University with regard to educational provision, curriculum design and contribution to society. Second, it highlighted the prominent Christian intellectuals who worked with the foreign Catholic missionaries to provide higher education, namely Ma Xiangbo (1840-1939), Ying Lianzhi (1867-1926) and Chen Yuan (1880-1971). Third, it discussed these intellectuals individually; and fourth, it compared and contrasted their philosophical approaches to modernization and “whole person education.”

12603915.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12603915.value: This project examined the mission and vision of each university in providing higher education for the youth of China. The founders of Furen and Zhendan universities sought to cultivate a Chinese elite capable of contributing to China’s modernization and upholding Catholic beliefs and values. In the first half of the 20th century, Catholic educators provided Chinese students with all round education stressing on whole person development. Therefore, this project addressed the contemporary discussion of “whole person education” from a historical and Catholic perspective.

12605115.label: Project Objectives
12605115.value: To determine the optimal stimulation frequencies for discriminating emotional and familiar faces from neutral faces in the SSVEP paradigm To evaluate the impact of countermeasures on the effectiveness of the present protocol to detect people’s emotional reactions to and knowledge about faces
rows: To determine the optimal stimulation frequencies for discriminating emotional and familiar faces from neutral faces in the SSVEP paradigm
To evaluate the impact of countermeasures on the effectiveness of the present protocol to detect people’s emotional reactions to and knowledge about faces

12605115.label: Realisation of objectives
12605115.value: The two objectives have been fully achieved via the completion of 4 experiments with 137 participants’ behavioral and neural (EEG) data recorded. To achieve objective 1 “to determine the optimal stimulation frequencies for discriminating emotional and familiar faces from neutral faces in the SSVEP paradigm”, we conducted Experiment 1-4 which studied the processing of familiarity, arousal, and attractiveness of face stimuli by analyzing the steady-state visually evoked potentials (SSVEP) triggered by visual oscillations of emotional and familiar faces as compared to neutral and unfamiliar faces. In Experiment 4, we compared the 3-Hz and 6-Hz visual presentation to determine which frequency is the optimal stimulation frequency for discriminating familiar faces from unfamiliar faces in the SSVEP paradigm. We have presented different types of faces in the four experiments: familiar vs unfamiliar faces in Experiment 1 and 4; faces that triggered highly or lowly aroused emotions (in either positive or negative valence) and neural faces in Experiment 2; and faces with different levels of attractiveness in Experiment 3. To ensure participants’ attention on the faces, they were required to count the number of color changes of a dot appeared at the nasal ridge of faces within a 10-s period of time in all the experiments. Six posterior channels (O1, Oz, O2, PO3, POz, and PO4) were selected to be the region-of-interest (ROI) based on past findings. Results of Experiment 1 suggested that 6-Hz visual presentation of faces triggered SSVEPs at scalp which revealed significant differences between familiar and unfamiliar face conditions at the second-harmonic (12-Hz) SSVEP responses. This significant difference can be found in 78% of the participants, suggesting the potential application on criminal investigation setting given the high detection rate. In Experiment 4, the SSVEPs triggered by 3-Hz and 6-Hz oscillations of familiar and unfamiliar faces were compared. We also analyzed both the first-harmonic and second-harmonic EEG responses at the left, middle and right regions of interest (ROI). No significant differences were found between familiar and unfamiliar faces for all the conditions with 3-Hz visual stimulus presentation at all 3 ROIs. Significant effect of face familiarity was found for the right ROI first-harmonic EEG response (i.e. 6-Hz SSVEP) to the 6-Hz visual presentation condition. We therefore conclude that 6-Hz is the optimal frequency of visual stimulation to detect the neural processing differences in response to familiar vs unfamiliar faces. Objective 1 was achieved. To achieve objective 2 “to evaluate the impact of countermeasures on the effectiveness of the present protocol to detect people’s emotional reactions to and knowledge about faces”, we have conducted Experiment 4. There were two sessions (Baseline and Cheating session) that all participants went through in the experiment. In the Baseline session, participants saw flickers of familiar and unfamiliar faces which were selected based on their ratings of familiarity on over 300 photos of faces sought from internet. The flicker frequencies of visual presentation of faces were either 3-Hz or 6-Hz. To ensure their attention on the faces, participants were required to count the number of color changes of a dot appeared at the nasal ridge of faces within a 10-s period of time. Participants then completed the Cheating session, in which they were instructed to perform countermeasures so that their emotional reactions and knowledge about familiar faces would not be detected by our protocol. We have taken reference to a memory suppression paradigm used in a past study (Hu et al., 2015). Participants were instructed to imagine that they were a terrorist and some police agents tried to investigate their relationship with or feelings towards certain people. The police agents would show them some photos on the computer screen. Some of them were people they don’t like, and some were people they don’t know. In order to pass the test and avoid continual investigations and prosecution, they should try their best to control their mind and treat every face as strangers or unfamiliar persons. To achieve this goal, they should try to avoid recalling anything related to the familiar persons, including his/her name, identity, things happened, what he/she did, and so on. If at any moment things related to the familiar persons come up in their minds, they should erase their thoughts immediately. If they could control their mind and not to think of anything related to the familiar persons, they would gain $80 bonus in addition to the $80/hour payment. In the suppression session, the participants were again instructed to pay attention to the faces and count the number of color changes to ensure visual attention to the faces, while they were supposed to suppress their thoughts and control their minds in order to obtain the bonus monetary reward. Results of EEG analysis showed that the 6-Hz (but not 3-Hz) visual presentations of familiar and unfamiliar faces triggered 6-Hz SSVEP with different amplitudes in both Baseline and Cheating session. The amplitudes of 6-Hz SSVEPs were significantly smaller in response to familiar face than to unfamiliar faces in both Baseline and Cheating session. The larger amplitude of 6-Hz SSVEP in response to unfamiliar than familiar faces is consistent with the literature and past findings showing that synchronization in the theta band EEG activity reflects the encoding of new information (Klimesch, 1999), as 6-Hz falls into the range of theta band (4 - 7.5 Hz). To conclude, objective 2 was achieved with the results of Experiment 4. Our findings support that the present protocol is effective to detect people’s recognition of familiar faces and countermeasure does not have any impact on its effectiveness, since significant SSVEP amplitude differences between familiar and unfamiliar faces were detected in both the Baseline (without countermeasure) and the Cheating session (with countermeasure).

12605115.label: Major findings and research outcome
12605115.value: Our project is innovative to investigate the effect of face familiarity on SSVEP recorded from occipital sites at scalp, and whether countermeasures affect detection by such physiological measures. One major finding is that the 12-Hz event-related spectral perturbations (ERSPs in decibel) at parietal-occipital electrodes were significantly lower when viewing familiar faces compared to unfamiliar faces. The 12-Hz activity falls into the alpha-band activity, which is related to inhibition of attention allocation (Klimesch, 2012) and cortical deactivation (Pfurtscheller, 1989). Our results suggest that the processing of familiar faces (as compared to unfamiliar faces) requires more attentional resources and cortical activation, possibly because of the retrieval of autobiographical information and emotional processing. In individual subject analysis, 78% participants had significantly lower 12-Hz ERSPs at left parietal-occipital ROI in familiar than unfamiliar face trials. This results have an implication that individual subject analysis may potentially be applied in criminal investigation setting for detection of suspects’ recognition of faces in time of denial. These findings were published in the International Journal of Psychophysiology (IF = 2.87; ranking 5th in Biological Psychology). Another novel finding is that human recognition of familiar faces could be detected by analyzing the SSVEP responses even in people who apply thought-suppression as a countermeasure to detection. Results showed that although the 6-Hz SSVEP amplitudes were smaller in the Cheating session than in the Baseline session, the difference between familiar and unfamiliar faces was significant in both sessions. Specifically, the amplitudes of 6-Hz SSVEPs were significantly smaller in response to familiar faces than to unfamiliar faces in both sessions. It is noted that the 6-Hz EEG oscillation fall onto the range of theta activity (4 – 7.5 Hz), which is related to the encoding of new information and formation of episodic memory as found in the literature (Klimesch, 1999). We believe that the larger 6-Hz amplitude responses to unfamiliar faces reflect the automatic encoding of novel faces which is an important cognitive mechanism facilitating human social interactions and communications. Importantly, this automatic encoding mechanisms cannot be overridden by higher-level cognitive control, in other words, the countermeasures applied in an attempt to minimize the processing differences between familiar and unfamiliar faces among our research participants. These findings have both theoretical and practical significance and a manuscript is under preparation to be submitted to the Psychophysiology journal (IF = 3.12; ranking 3rd in Biological Psychology).

12605115.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12605115.value: Although our study’s results are of high practical value for use in real-life forensic contexts, one concern is the technical knowledge and expertise required to perform the analysis of SSVEP data, as most frontline crime investigators do not have such expertise. To facilitate the usage by frontline investigators, future projects could develop a user-friendly GUI interface for laymen to acquire EEG data and to analyse the EEG data in an easy and convenient way. Furthermore, further studies could investigate the application of machine learning and AI in analyzing the brain wave data to detect the levels of familiarity, emotional arousal, valence of faces and objects as perceived by human beings. Finally, the present study tested the effect of one type of countermeasure which is by suppressing the responses when the lying-related (or salient) information is presented. Further studies may investigate the impact of other kinds of countermeasures on the effectiveness of using SSVEP as an index of face recognition, such as instructing participants to enhance their responses to irrelevant control stimulus to minimize the differences between lying-related information and control information.

12605115.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12605115.value: The global rapid growth of terrorists and crimes has called for the search for effective lie detection methods to assist criminal investigation. The polygraph test has been used by the authorities to distinguish liars from truth-tellers. There are however concerns because of high false alarms and low sensitivity for certain populations (e.g. agents trained to perform countermeasures). Our study developed an innovative paradigm to detect human face recognition while minimizing the effects of countermeasures. Face recognition by criminal suspects is often an important information for investigation. We attempted to decode mental processes by examining the early visual processing of faces with measurement of brain waves measured from scalp, and examined the impact of mental countermeasure on the effectiveness of our protocol. Results of brain wave analysis showed significant differences in brain responses to familiar and unfamiliar faces and 78% participants demonstrated such pattern. Importantly, significant effect of face familiarity on brain waves was found even in people who have applied a thought-suppression technique as a countermeasure. The results are of high practical value for use in real-life forensic contexts to discriminate guilty people from innocent ones by analyzing the brain’s responses when processing crime-related information.
