12607815.label: Major findings and research outcome
12607815.value: Repeated measures ANOVA showed that there were significant Group x Time interaction effects on psychological distress (F(1, 72) = 4.08, p = .047, η2 = .054), acculturative stress (F(1, 72) = 11.25, p = .001, η2 = .135), positive emotions(F(1, 72) = 5.17, p = .026, η2 = .068), negative emotions(F(1, 72) = 6.08, p = .026, η2 = .078), positive thoughts(F(1, 72) = 7.54, p = .008, η2 = .095), negative thoughts (F(1, 72) = 4.17, p = .045, η2 = .055), sense-making coping (F(1, 72) = 13.23, p = .001, η2 = .155), and post-migration growth (F(1, 72) = 8.06, p = .006, η2 = .101). The effect size of partial η2 ranged from 0.055 to 0.155, indicating medium to large effect sizes. This indicates that the effect of time was dependent on the groups. The decrease in psychological distress from the pre-test (M = 5.34, SD = 3.05) to the post-test (M = 2.07, SD = 2.14) was significant for the CBT group (t = 4.37, p = .000) with a very large effect size (Cohen’s d = 1.24), but not for the waitlist control (WLC) group (t = 1.27, p = .216). Although the CBT group experienced a higher level of acculturative stress than the WLC group at the pre-test, acculturative stress dropped significantly from the pre-test (M = 1.26, SD = 0.37) to the post-test (M = 0.97, SD = 0.36) for the CBT group (t = 5.66, p = .000) with a large effect size (Cohen’s d = 0.79), but not for the WLC group (t = 0.76, p = .455). Paired sample t tests indicated that the CBT group showed a significant increase between the pre-test and the post-test in positive emotions (t = -3.69, p = .001), positive thoughts (t = -3.59, p = .001), and post-migration growth (t = -4.29, p = .000), and a significant decrease in negative emotions (t = 4.95, p = .000) and negative thoughts (t = 3.09, p = .004). In contrast, the WLC group showed insignificant increases or decreases in these variables (t = -1.35-1.47, p = 0.155-0.537). This indicates that the intervention was more effective in decreasing psychological distress, acculturative stress, negative emotions and negative thoughts, and increase positive emotions, positive thoughts and post-migration growth for Mainland Chinese university students in Hong Kong. At post-intervention, about 46% and 30% of the participants in the CBT group and WLC group, respectively, were classified as non-at-risk cases for development mental health problems.

12607815.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12607815.value: (1) Though the sample size of this study was small (n = 74), the study has demonstrated the positive effect of CBT group intervention in reducing psychological distress of Mainland Chinese university students in Hong Kong. However, future research should test the effectiveness of group CBT for Chinese international students using a larger sample. (2) The study was conducted within a relatively short time frame with limited resources, follow-up test could be conducted to evaluate the long-term effect of the intervention. (3) With limited resources, the research was conducted with waiting-list control (WLC) group. The long waiting time of students in the control group to receive intervention might cause some students, particularly those in the WLC group, to quit the study, which led to difficulties related to the RCT design of the study. With more resources, future research should reduce the waiting time for the waiting list control group and to arrange the experimental group and control group be implemented at the same time. (4) The CBT group intervention developed in this study is specific to Mainland Chinese students in Hong Kong, future studies should extend this version of adapted CBT to Chinese international students in other countries, such as US or Australia, and test its effectiveness. (5) Possible mechanisms of change were not investigated in this study. Future research should explore the predictive effects of the therapeutic factors used in the intervention.

12607815.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12607815.value: Mainland Chinese university students responded well to cognitive behavior group therapy, which significantly reduced their psychological distress and acculturative stress and improve their mental health during their study in Hong Kong. Almost one of every two Mainland Chinese university students in Hong Kong who joined cognitive behavior therapy group became non-at-risk cases at post-intervention compared with their counterparts who did not received the service. The study has confirmed the positive effect of a 8-session culturally adapted cognitive behavioral group intervention programme for reducing acculturation stress of Mainland Chinese university students. The study has demonstrated strong implications for acculturation of Chinese students in other countries/regions to facilitate their psychological adaptation in the host institutions.

12607915.label: Project Objectives
12607915.value: To provide the first in-depth, holistic study of collaborative translation practices in a specifically religious context, one which combines more traditional modes of interaction with online collaboration. To produce a critically informed delineation of the participatory mechanisms and discursive practices through which stakeholders in the translation process interact and negotiate meaning to produce the final product. To examine at the textual level the intertextual changes in "edit chains" -- the various versions and revisions of the translated text produced by each participant in the production network -- and to assess the scope for individual flexibility and agency in relation to the project conventions and regulations that aim to impose discursive stability on the project. To understand how learning and translation-related expertise-acquisition operate in communities of practice, particularly those involving volunteer translators. To suggest ways in which strategies of community-based learning seen in volunteer translator communities can be applied to tertiary-level translation training. To open up possibilities for exchange and knowledge transfer activities with the communities in question, in both research and pedagogical areas, for instance by the development of inter-community workshops on issues such as workplace collaboration for translators and the collective solution of terminology problems. To contribute to the research literature in a fast-emerging but hitherto little studied area of the translation studies field, and to the theorization and application of the “communities of practice” concept in translation studies.

12607915.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12607915.value: This project examines the work of volunteer translators in Buddhist translation communities, focusing on how translators work collaboratively to produce a final translated text. The notion of collaborative translation is one that has only recently begun to gain importance in translation research: whilst it has long been recognized that certain translation activities have been undertaken collaboratively, the image of the lone translator working in relative isolation has continued to inform perceptions of how translations are produced and what it means to translate. The growth of online “wiki”-style translation communities that allow multiple inputs to a given translation in progress has led to a scholarly reappraisal of these perceptions. Key issues include the blurring of boundaries between professional and non-professional practice, authority and community organization, learning and expertise acquisition, and participant motivation. Despite the importance of these issues, still relatively little is understood about translator behaviour and text production in collaborative contexts. Translation communities that do not rely exclusively on online collaborative platforms have been under-researched, and this is especially true of religious translation communities, notwithstanding the fact that large amounts of volunteer translation take place in such communities on a regular basis. Buddhist translation communities are particularly interesting both because of their importance in the East Asian region and their link with historical traditions of Buddhist sutra translation, which still sometimes explicitly informs their collaborative practices. The present project will consider two different communities that each involve a mixture of lay volunteer translators and Buddhist monastics (both with different levels of translation experience). Both of the chosen communities have complex networks of text production that include translators, revisers, accuracy checkers and quality controllers, working both on-site in the same workspace and online in a worldwide virtual community. In each case, this project will conduct an in-depth study to examine modes of text production, mechanisms of collaboration, community organization and member identity, and issues of learning and expertise acquisition within the community. The project takes as its theoretical framework Wenger’s “communities of practice” theory, whilst its methodology combines ethnographic approaches such as interview surveys and participant observation with textual analysis of “edit chains” – drafts of previous versions of the translation that show editing decisions by different participants in the translation and revision process. The project expects to make a significant contribution to expanding existing conceptions of collaborative translation and understandings of translator expertise acquisition in a community-based interactive context.

12607915.label: Realisation of objectives
12607915.value: The various project objectives have generally been achieved, with Objectives 1, 4, 5 and 6 having been 100% achieved. In realizing Objective 1 and key related objectives such as Objective 2 and Objective 4, a combination of approaches has been used. These include textual analysis of community materials such as guidelines and reflective reports in community members’ publications, translation drafts (where available), and interviews with community members. In achieving these objectives, the project team has also found it necessary to undertake broader analysis in two areas. Firstly, it has collected and examined a large amount of online materials that map the landscape of Buddhist collaborative translation communities more generally and clarify how the online presence of such communities relates to broader religious activity in the Buddhist cyberspace as a whole. Secondly, it has conducted a review of historical research on Buddhist traditions of translation, as a means to better understand how contemporary practices relate to past precedents. This has been particularly important in the case of the Buddhist Text Translation Society, whose guidelines relate directly to sixth century Chinese Buddhist discourses of translation and cannot be adequately understood without such knowledge. The realization of Objectives 4 and 5 has further been aided by the involvement of a PhD student (now graduated), whose own work on Community of Practice theory in non-religious online contexts has illuminated the workings of communities in the religious sector, in respect of questions such as the negotiation of authority between more experienced community members and novice members, and the conceptualization of materials (such as guidelines) as key components of the community’s shared repertoire. In the course of her involvement with the project, her own training has in turn been enriched by this exposure to an area of collaborative practice previously not considered in her studies. With regard to Objective 6, the project has succeeded in opening up possibilities for collaboration. In particular, the team has been involved in the joint establishment of a collaborative translation project with the Hong Kong Buddhist Education Foundation (HKBEF), an organization affiliated with the Pure Land school of Master Chin Kong, whom the team have also met personally. As included in the project output, the team has recently formalized this as a signed collaborative agreement. The collaboration involves the translation of a major Pure Land sutra, and aims through the collaborative translation process, to both model and further research the kinds of practices investigated by the present project. In this regard, it also feeds into Objective 5, particularly since several participants are from the tertiary translation education sector and have direct interest in exploring the application of collaborative methods to translation training. Objectives 2 and 3 have not yet been fully achieved. As detailed in an earlier report, a problem encountered by the project team has been the difficulty of gaining access to internal community information, in particular translation drafts. Thus while the team has interviewed various members from different communities, it has not been possible to gain more than limited access to certain written materials. Therefore, a full delineation of discursive practices and participant interaction, of the kind that examination of these textual materials would specifically shed light on, has not been possible. This is particularly true for Objective 3, which focused specifically on analysis of “edit-chains” in the production of translations. Only a limited amount of information of this nature could be collected. The project team has sought to mitigate this situation, which arises from the reluctance of communities to share internal documents, through the establishment of its own collaborative enterprise with the HKBEF, referred to above, in which the team is directly involved in the translation production process and thus has direct and mutually approved research access to the translation drafts and meetings. Clearly, this process is ongoing, but it is believed that it will lead to a fuller achievement of Objectives 2 and 3 in the period of its operation beyond the project’s official completion. Objective 7 is listed as 80% met. The project has certainly made contributions to the research literature, and has generated strong interest, through a significant number of conference and invited lecture presentations at various international venues. However, the Objective is not fully achieved at this present stage, as some publication outputs are still either under review or in preparation. The team had hoped that these would have been brought to publication sooner, however the process has taken longer, owing to factors referred to above including (a) the methodological difficulties of community engagement – particularly the access to internal documents; (b) the large amount of online material to deal with, including the fact that little previous research exists in regard to such documentation; and (c) the inclusion of a historical dimension to the research. The project team is confident that the project will generate at least two more papers beyond the publications listed in the outputs section of this report.

12607915.label: Major findings and research outcome
12607915.value: The project has a number of findings and outcomes. At a macro level, it has established that collaborative translation occurs extensively in contemporary Buddhist translation activities, both offline and online, and that such communities employ a whole range of different collaborative modes according to the particular needs and aims of the community in question, as well as the type of source text material being translated. While this means that particular micro-level strategies and participatory mechanisms must necessarily be understood in terms of specific cases, certain broader themes are also discernible. Firstly, contemporary translation activities, particularly where they concern the translation of Buddhist sutras, tend to be grounded, often explicitly, in past collaborative practices, which link to the translation tradition in question. Thus, while major Tibetan translation projects tend to invoke the classical Tibetan mode of the monk-translator working with a single collaborator on a given text, Chinese projects such as those of the BTTS reference the collaborative assemblies of classical China. These references not only provide models for practice that are then recontextualized for modern usage, for example in Western contexts, but also provide authenticity for the resulting translation output: the textual encoding (as formal guidelines) and practical performance of classically proven modes of translation validates output as having religious reliability. Secondly, communities place strong emphasis on the importance of sharing and the idea that no one member has the given expertise required. At the same time, considerable stress is laid on the expertise of particular members, usually those from the monastic community. Such dynamics are seen not only in the communities studied in the project, but also in the collaborative translation group established by the project with the Hong Kong Buddhist Education Foundation, outlined above: democratic mechanisms to ensure the realization of the community’s joint enterprise are at the same time balanced by a deference to a central member recognized as having doctrinal authority, who acts as the community’s gatekeeper in the production of the final output. Thirdly, translation is seen as a form both of spiritual cultivation – sometimes even of meditative practice – and of religious learning, and this approach is also incorporated into the particular forms of collaboration seen, for instance where collaborative sessions are led by ordained monastics who lead participants in the understanding of the sutra. These are insights which have received little attention so far in the field of religious translation research.

12607915.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12607915.value: The team sees several ways forward for the research. Firstly, the ongoing translation group collaboration with the Hong Kong Buddhist Education Foundation is seen as having long-term significance, since it provides a unique opportunity for participant observation by the PI in a group that contains academics, non-academics, lay Buddhists and ordained Buddhist clergy. This is a very valuable opportunity which has not previously been possible with other groups. This will enable a more fully immersive ethnography that can develop further the understanding of these groups as Communities of Practice. In addition, this collaboration represents an important outreach initiative with significant impact potential. Secondly, the project has collected a large amount of online material from a number of communities, which needs to be further analysed to give a more complete account of the online presence of Buddhist collaborative translation communities. Finally, it has become clear during the course of the project, that while much has been said regarding Buddhist translation in the classical period, more historical research is needed to understand the precise relationship of past traditions to particular contemporary practices. In addition to these strands, the team is finalizing articles in preparation from the existing data for submission for publication.

12607915.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12607915.value: This project has examined collaborative translation practices in contemporary Buddhist communities. Using a variety of data, it has sought to gain insights into the nature of such practices, the experiences and interactions of the participants, and the ways in which invocation of historical translation approaches informs communities’ claims to be producing doctrinally reliable and authentic content. The findings are of particular importance to our understanding of translation, which has tended to be seen – at least in modern times – as a single-translator activity. The continuance of traditional modes of collaboration in modified form also affords insights into the nature of continuity and change in both translation practice and religious translation discourse. The project has also established a collaborative initiative with a Hong Kong-based Buddhist foundation that has links to one of the key Buddhist masters of the modern age. This provides crucial material for further, participative research, as well as forging a link between the academic translation studies community and an external religious community with an extensive network. In all, the project opens up an area of research – Buddhist collaborative translation – that has been very little researched outside the classical context.

12608815.label: Project Objectives
12608815.value: To document the whole process of publication: from the negotiation of translation rights to the marketing or dissemination of the finished e-book. This will enable a better understanding of the way in which digital literary translations are produced, contributing both to sociological research in Translation Studies and translator training. To propose a detailed account of the possibilities offered by the hypertext in the publication of literary translations based on concrete examples drawn both from the translation and the paratext, and to contrast these possibilities to the constraints often found by translators in traditional publishing systems (Buzelin, 2007a). To compare the findings with previous research on the publication of print literary translations of Chinese literature in Spain (see the work of the PI in this field under “Background of research”). To study the agency of the translator in two different ways: a) In the textual dimension, by examining “points of visibility” both in the translation, the hypertext and the paratext (the website, the blog, social media). This involves identifying “either traces of the translator’s presence or of the foreign” (Coldiron, 2012: 198). b) In the organisational structure, by examining changes in hierarchy, power dynamics, role definition, interactions between the actors, translation proposals and the management of the translation. To inform larger-scale reflections on normative practices (Toury, 1995; Chesterman, 1993; Hermans, 1996) and sociologies of translation. To examine whether digital translations offer possibilities to strengthen the status and identity of the literary translator. • To contribute to socially situated Translation Studies research through the publication of journal articles. • To disseminate Hong Kong literature to a global readership, creating cross-cultural links between Hong Kong and Spanish readers. It is worth mentioning that this will be the first translation of Hong Kong literature in Spanish. The e-book will include a preface on the author and her work, introducing the Spanish readership (both in Spain and Latin America) to Hong Kong contemporary fiction. • To organise two international workshops, one in Hong Kong and one in Barcelona, to discuss issues related to translation and new media bringing together international researchers, and translation and publishing professionals.

12608815.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12608815.value: Whilst considerable scholarship has been devoted to documenting the publishing of print translations, scant attention has been paid to emerging practices related to digital translations. The publishing of literary translations in digital format is transforming two interdependent realities: translation practice, and the interactions and roles of the actors involved in the publication. These two realities are part of the “making” of translations that the research team will analyse. This project starts from the assumption that the materiality impinges on the making of the translation in different ways. Special attention will be paid to two key issues in translation theory: the agency and the visibility of the translator. The project will focus on examining the making of Dorothy Tse’s 《頭》 (Head) translation into Spanish, which will be published by ¡Hjckrrh!. Translations published by ¡Hjckrrh! are designed to be published as e-books, which means that they do not necessarily imitate the print book. All the actors involved are translators, the traditional hierarchy of the publishing company disappears and actors that share the same professional expertise assume different roles. A pilot project involving the Spanish translation of Shanghai modernist fiction for the same publishing company is currently underway, paving the way for a fruitful participant observation research. Three types of data will be gathered to analyse both the transformation of the translation and the interactions between the actors: 1) discursive data to analyse the practices themselves (based on interviews with the participants); 2) written data related to the management of the translation (email correspondence, contracts); 3) written data connected to the translation and its paratext (translation drafts, the website, the blog, social media). The visibility of the translator will be examined by identifying traces of the translator or of the foreign in the translation and the paratext. The agency of the translator will be the key issue when looking at the organisation and management of the translation. The outcomes of the project will include: three to four papers on translators’ agency and visibility in the making of digital translations; and two workshops (in Hong Kong and Barcelona) bringing together researchers in the field, and professional translators and publishers. By offering a detailed ethnography of the making of a translation in digital format, the results of this project will be beneficial for the training of translation professionals. The outcomes generated in this project will also contribute larger-scale sociologies in Translation Studies. 目前已有相當數量的學術研究專門記錄印刷翻譯的出版過程，但與數碼翻譯相關的新興作法卻甚少受到關注。以數碼形式出版文學翻譯作品，使兩個相互依存的現實出現重大改變：一是翻譯實踐，二是參與出版過程的行動者之間的互動和扮演的角色。研究團隊將對包括以上兩者在內的翻譯「製作」流程加以分析。本研究項目假設物質性會以不同方式影響翻譯的製作，以此展開研究，並特別關注翻譯理論中的兩大議題：譯者的能動性（agency）和可見性（visibility）。 是項研究將集中探討謝曉虹《頭》譯成西班牙語的製作過程，成果將由 ¡Hjckrrh! 出版。¡Hjckrrh! 經手的翻譯作品一般設計成電子書出版，換言之毋須仿傚印刷書的做法。由於所有參與的行動者本身都是譯者，傳統出版社的層級體系不復存在，擁有共同專業知識的行動者擔當不同角色。有一項先導項目正在展開，研究對象涉及同一出版社的當代海派小說西語譯本，為將來創獲可觀的參與觀察研究鋪路。 本研究將收集三類資料，藉以分析翻譯本身和行動者之間的互動有何轉變：1) 用來分析翻譯實踐的論述資料（根據參與者的訪談資料）；2) 與管理翻譯相關的書面資料（電郵通信、合約）；3) 有關譯文及附文本（paratext）的書面資料（譯稿、網站、博客、社交媒體）。通過識別譯文及附文本內譯者或異質（foreign）的痕跡，審視譯者的可見性；而在探討翻譯的組識和管理時，譯者的能動性將成為關鍵議題。 是項研究的成果將包括：三至四篇論文，探討數碼翻譯的製作過程中譯者的能動性和可見性，以及兩場工作坊（在香港及巴塞隆納舉行），讓翻譯學研究者、專業譯者和出版人互相交流。通過對數碼形式翻譯的製作流程作出詳細的民族誌描述，本項目的研究成果將有益於翻譯專業人員的培訓，並對翻譯研究中較大規模的社會學研究帶來貢獻。

12608815.label: Realisation of objectives
12608815.value: 1. We have been able to document the whole process of publication of two translations: three stories by Liu Na'ou, Mu Shiying and Du Heng, translated into Spanish by Maialen Marin-Lacarta and published by the digital publishing initiative ¡Hjckrrh! (this was the pilot); and 'Tou', by Dorothy Tse, translated into Spanish by Juanjo Ciruela, and published by ¡Hjckrrh!. Documenting the whole process has included: collecting e-mails (from first e-mails to the author to obtain the translation rights to e-mails announcing the release of the e-book in online retailers such as Kobo), interviewing key actors in the process (the editors, the translator, proofreaders, and the designer of the e-book cover) and comparing various drafts of the translation. The results of this objective have been mainly disseminated in two publications: Marin-Lacarta (2018) and Marin-Lacarta and Vargas-Urpi (2019). 2. Concerning the second objective, Marin-Lacarta's (2018) article focuses on the the possibilities offered by the hypertext in the publication of literary translations, and uses concrete examples drawn from the translation, the paratext, and interviews to translators and editors. The project results reflect that translators do not really experience differences when translating for print or for electronic versions. However, they feel empowered by the possibilities of publishing translations in digital platforms; they have a major sense of freedom to choose what to translate and how to translated, as well as more flexible deadlines. The revision process is much more detailed (since there are no commercial deadlines) and various drafts are revised before reaching the final version (see Marin-Lacarta and Vargas-Urpi, 2019). Comparing our results with Bourdieu's (1999) description of the French publishing field, our results showed that many of Bourdieu’s observations remain relevant, and the characteristics he defined are useful for understanding many of the changes that have taken place in the last two decades. New categories were created to describe specific features of our case study and to show how digital advances have created possibilities for new forms of publishing. We have seen that the materiality affects some of the features and that new possibilities have emerged, such as self-publishing without being legally established as a publisher. The distribution of books, a key step in print publishing, has also changed with the development of digital publishing; it is now possible to upload e-books directly without any intermediaries. However, this means platforms often place more obstacles to the smaller publisher, as we have seen in the section about copyright issues. Thus, the trend of the field, even in digital publishing, remains commercial. Bourdieu considered “love of art” and “love of money” incompatible from a sociological standpoint. However, he also acknowledged that only those publishers who combine literary competence and economic realism can survive (Bourdieu 1999:19). The existence of publishing as a non-profit activity, as in ¡Hjckrrh!’s case, contradicts this; although it still remains to be seen how long this initiative will survive. 3. The round table held in Barcelona was used to compare findings with previous experiences in the field of print literary translations of Chinese literature in Spain. Previous research conducted by the PI in relation to the reception of Chinese literature in Spain was fundamental in achieving this objective. The reason why this objective was only achieved to a certain extent (50%) is that the case study focused on the publication of two stories and further research on digital translations is necessary to be able to generalise the results and compare the situation with that of print translations of Chinese literature. 4 + 6. Translators' agency has been explored by means of fourteen interviews with participants who have collaborated with ¡Hjckrrh!, comprising eleven translators (including the three founding members of ¡Hjckrrh!), two proofreaders and a graphic designer. The article by Marin-Lacarta and Vargas-Urpi (2018) discusses translators’ roles, production teams and relationships, and pays special attention to the agency and visibility of translators, mainly using data from the interviews, but also including information from the "points of visibility" found in the translation, the hypertext and the paratext. Our findings show that technology has had a positive impact on translator agency, status and identity among the founding members and collaborators of ¡Hjckrrh!. These translators have used the shifting professional boundaries and technological advances to develop their roles as cultural mediators. The article describes the work of the translators who collaborate in this digital initiative and discusses the ways they relate to each other, the roles they play and how they cross professional boundaries. Translators take on new roles: as initiators, when they suggest the text to translate; as editors or commissioners, when they monitor the whole publishing process; as revisers, when they review other translator's translations; as testers, when they test the final e-book in their devices. 5. Other scholars have recently considered the integration of ethnographic approaches as a viable and necessary form of data collection in Translation Studies and a way of enriching sociologies of translation (Wolf 2002; Koskinen 2006; Buzelin 2004, 2005, 2007a, 2007b). The use of an ethnographic approach (involving participant observation, field notes, reflective diaries, semi-structured interviews, and the collection of translation drafts, correspondence and paratexts. Book reviews and blog posts were also collected to study the dissemination of the translations) in the study of how translators work and learn to work in new (and challenging) environments has certainly contributed to sociologies of translation, and, by extension, to larger-scale reflections on normative practices (Toury, 1995; Chesterman, 1993; Hermans, 1996) as is also explained in Marin-Lacarta and Vargas-Urpi (2018). 7. Three articles have been published in international journals: - Marin-Lacarta, Maialen (2018) Characteristics of a digital literary translation publisher: revisiting Bourdieu’s mapping of the publishing field. The Translator, Doi: 10.1080/13556509.2018.1543566 - Marin-Lacarta, Maialen; Vargas-Urpi, Mireia (2018). When the Translator Does More than Translate: A Case Study of Translator Roles in a Digital Publishing Initiative. Hermes, n. 58, 117-137. - Marin-Lacarta, Maialen; Vargas-Urpi, Mireia (2019). Marin-Lacarta, Maialen; Vargas-Urpi, Mireia (2018). Translators Revising Translators: A Fruitful Alliance. Perspectives, n. 27 (3), 404-418. A fourth article on translators' motivation is under review in a top-rank international journal. The publication of 'La cabeza', by Dorothy Tse, has meant the first publication of a direct translation of Hong Kong literature from Chinese into Spanish. Two round tables were organised during the project, one in Hong Kong, with the participation of Tammy Ho, editor of Cha, Yau Wai-Ping literary translator and Sherlon Ip, translator and copy editor and one in Universitat Pompeu Fabra (Barcelona), with the participation of Juan Gabriel López Guix translator and founding member of the digital publishing initiative ¡Hjckrrh!; Celia Filipetto, translator and collaborator of ¡Hjckrrh!; Manuel Pavón Belizón, translator; and editor of 'China traducida y por traducir'; and Jordi Ainaud, translator and editor. This second round table is available in the following link: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WjTz_MUsmO4&feature=youtu.be

12608815.label: Major findings and research outcome
12608815.value: 1. The ebook has become a form of empowerment for translators. In the case of ¡Hjckrrh!, the ebook has become a form of empowerment that has allowed the three founding members to create a different kind of production team. When comparing this production team to traditional publishing houses, certain differences become evident. Here, translators can choose what they want to translate and publish, and can even re-edit translations they have previously published and give them new life. Translators can thus exert agency to act as initiators and cultural mediators at virtual zero risk; however, revenue is also minimal. The translator acting as ‘chief editor’ or leader of the production team contributes to the larger visibility of the translator by encouraging translators to write prologues and epilogues about the translation process. The translator is also included in the e-book cover, credits and retailers’ platforms. 2. Materiality makes self-publishing possible, though not easy New possibilities have emerged, such as the self-publishing of e-books without being legally established as a publisher. Distribution, a key step in print publishing, has also changed with the development of digital publishing; it is now possible to upload e-books directly without any intermediaries. However, platforms often place more obstacles in the way of smaller publishers; for example, informants recall many problems related to copyright issues. Thus, the trend of the field, even in digital publishing, remains commercial. 3. Translators appreciate getting involved in the revision process, when possible Most translators in our sample appreciate the opportunity to supervise the revisions of their translations and some even explicitly mention this desire to control what is changed, even if this part of work is not usually included in the reimbursement received for a translation. This reflects translators’ sense of responsibility for the quality of translation as a final product. The possibility of discussing changes between the reviser/editor and the translator is also regarded as a fruitful activity: translators are usually eager to engage in lively discussions while jointly looking for the best solution. 4. Translating for pleasure Most translators participate in ¡Hjckrrh! (which is a non-lucrative publishing initiative) on a voluntary basis, without expecting any kind of reimbursement. There are various reasons that explain their motivations to translate for ¡Hjckrrh!: friendship, excitement, freedom, creativity or cultural mediation are just some of these reasons.

12608815.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12608815.value: The study of other similar digital-publishing initiatives (such as "Asymptote" journal, which publishes world literature in English translation; "Paper Republic", which publishes short stories translated from Chinese into English; "China traducida y por traducir", a Spanish non-profit initiative led by three translators who publish Chinese literature translated into Spanish; and "Paper de vidre", a Catalan online literary initiative that publishes short stories, some originally written in Catalan and some translated from other languages, would certainly be very interesting in order to compare results and reach more general conclusions. In terms of translators' motivations, which is one of the main results obtained, the recent interest in organisational culture in translation studies might lead to more research in this direction and comparing our findings with participants’ motivations in traditional publishing practices would open new avenues of research.

12608815.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12608815.value: The project has analysed the making of two translations: three short stories by Liu Na'ou, Mu Shiying and Du Heng, translated into Spanish by Maialen Marin-Lacarta and 'Tou', by Dorothy Tse, translated into Spanish by Juanjo Ciruela; both published by the digital publishing initiative ¡Hjckrrh!. The analysis has involved collecting data from a great variety of sources (e-mails, interviews, translation drafts, etc.) from the commissioning of translations to the dissemination of their publication as e-books. Previous research in literary translation has mainly focused on print translation, thus, this research is valuable because it sheds light on the differences between digital and print publishing of translations. Interviews with¡Hjckrrh!'s founding members and collaborators have revealed that the possibility of publishing digitally has empowered these translators: they can now decide what to translate (thus, they can act as cultural mediators), how to translate it (they have a greater sense of freedom to experiment in their translations) and when to publish these translations (there are no fixed deadlines). They participate on a voluntary basis, without expecting reimbursement for their translations, but they still feel responsible for the quality of their translations, and most of them actively engage in the revision of translations.

12609015.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12609015.value: China has a long and unique tradition deliberating matters about war and peace. While Confucianism is most well-known today, there were many competing thoughts in the Pre-Qin period and Daoism was a prominent one among them. Although over the last few decades, there has been a growing body of writings on early Daoism offering a wide range of interpretations targeting the hermeneutical interest of contemporary readers, there is hardly anything substantial to connect Daoist thought to contemporary debates on ethics of war, peace, and related controversies due to reasons listed here: (i) As a dialogue partner, Confucianism has been viewed as a more important and influential tradition that represents the moralpolitik of ancient China; (ii) It is relatively difficult to schematize Daoist philosophy in terms of normative ethics since the very effort to do so seems to be contrary to its principles of non-conceptualization and non-dogmatization; and (iii) “Daoism” is a contested and ambivalent term, so much so that any attempt to speak of “Daoist ethics” as a coherent whole would be considered suspicious, if not meaningless. As such this project will focus on early Daoist thoughts, including Laozi’s Daoism and Huang-Lao Daoism, contending that there is much of value in the tradition that can be reconstructed to make it part of the contemporary discourse. The PI’s intention is to look not only backward but also forward by assessing potential contributions of Daoist social, political and ethical thought in contemporary times. Methodologically, the project focuses on textual-hermeneutical analysis of early Chinese texts, ethical inquiries with regard to contemporary debates on war, peace, and global order, and critical dialogue between Chinese versions of pacifism and various pacifist theories in the West. Due to the complexity of ancient Chinese texts and their contexts, some of the findings provided by historians will be used as well to explicate specific historical conditions in which discourses on war and peace are given. The PI aims to map out an ethical contour of a Daoist alternative on particular political and intellectual issues, bringing them into conversation with the current debate. Although contemporary ethics will, to some extent, define the parameters for application of ethical terms regarding just war theories and pacifism, it should not preclude an attempt to explore the Daoist thought within its own context and tradition, and to locate the classical Chinese thinking in the matrix of contemporary explications and comparative discussion. 先秦的戰爭觀與和平觀是先秦政治哲學重要的組成部分。本研究課題以道家思想為重點，探討中國早期的戰爭觀與和平觀。這裡的“道家思想”除了基於馬王堆《老子》帛書以及與戰爭相關的《老子》文本的註釋傳統外，還包括道家中的“黃老”思想。主要研究文本包括《黃帝四經》（黃老帛書）、《鶡冠子》和《呂氏春秋》。研究的內容涉及戰爭的定義和種類，戰爭的目的與手段，戰爭與政治的關係，老子道家與黃老道家在戰爭與和平議題上的異同，以及它們與同時代其他哲學學派和思潮的關係。 另外，研究課題在一定程度上借用當代西方“[積極]和平主義”（pacificism）和“正義戰爭論”（just war theory）的框架。通過論述老子道家的和平哲學以及它與黃老道家有關開戰正義（jus ad bellum）和交戰正義（jus in bello）思想的重疊與矛盾，說明道家倫理思想本身的多元性和複雜性。在全球化的今天，隨著中國的崛起和軍事力量的強大，中國應該在維繫世界和平中扮演什麼樣的角色成為中所關注的問題，道家的積極和平主義思想無疑為此話題的探討提供了一個新的視角。 就研究方法而言，本研究課題以文本-詮釋學分析為基礎，進而帶入哲學和倫理學的探尋。研究者在將中國早期道家思想與當代西方思想進行對談的同時，盡量還原道家文本自身的體系、概念和思想，而非以達到論辯性的共識為最終目的。與此同時，本研究對當代西方正義戰爭論（如R2P）作出回應與質疑。

12609215.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12609215.value: The food system in Hong Kong has shown itself to be inequitable: everyday, we throw away 3300 tonnes of food into landfills while 1.5 million people go hungry. The question of what to do about surplus food, hunger and waste is an ethical issue that has direct impact on the environment, urban health and social justice. Current efforts that address this issue through tackling food waste (recoverable and non-recoverable) are undertaken by different sectors of society which have established separate spheres of information, knowledge, resources, networks and relationships, thus limiting the potential for local or global change. This interdisciplinary project uses the commons as a theoretical and pragmatic framework to extend the scope of understanding by reframing surplus food and its recovery practices as commons (understood as resources accessible to all members of society). This enables the research to focus on conditions necessary for food recovery and redistribution, building capacity for collaborative practices and knowledge building. The project will identify limitations in current models, develop intellectual and technological tools to facilitate networked community practices and establish parameters to evaluate and further the ethical capacities of surplus food rescue. First, data sets from food rescue NGOs will be collected and analysed to establish an overview of the current food surplus situation in Hong Kong. Second, detailed case studies will be built from interviews with stakeholders and participant observation to identify limitations and opportunities of respective operational models. An open source online platform will be developed to investigate the potential of networked community practices by facilitating the effective sharing of surplus food information. This tool will enable collective knowledge building by offering an open, shared database. The empirical material reinforces the social analysis of food waste that in turn informs the theoretical development of an ethics of the commons in the context of food. Conference papers, journal articles, book chapters will contribute to fields of Cultural Studies, Media and Communication, Information Technology, Urban Design and Infrastructure and Policy Studies. Documentation, data analysis and technological tool detailed in the Hong Kong case studies address current gaps in the field, laying the foundation for the researchers, NGOs and government to further streamline their efforts. International collaboration will put Hong Kong on the global scene and take the lead in addressing questions ethical surplus food practices and sustainable urban development in the context of an inextricably linked global/local food system. 目前，香港的食物系統失平: 每天約有3,300噸食物被棄置到堆填區，與此同時卻有1,500,000人缺乏溫飽的保障。剩食、飢餓和浪費所構成的問題無疑是一個直接影響環境、城市健康和社會公義的倫理議題。現時，社會各界處理廚餘(可回收/不可回收)方面，建立了不同領域的資訊、知識、資源、網絡和關係網絡，缺乏了共同參與改變的可能性。 這個跨學科計劃以「共享」這概念(可理解為一個供社會所有成員使用的資源)作為理論和實踐的框架，重新審視剩食和剩食回收工作，從而延伸對公義食物未來的理解。因此，研究放眼於討論食物回收和再分發的必要條件、建立合作機會和知識建構的能力。本計劃亦將識別現有型式的局限，建立知識和科技工具去推動網絡社區實踐和建立指標以評估和推動增進拯救剩食的倫理能力。 首先，收集和分析各NGO(非政府組織)救食數據表以展示香港剩食拯救情況的概覽。其次，從利益關係者和參與者的角度進行詳細的個案研究去找出各自操作型式的局限和機會。建立一個公開的網上平台將有助探討網絡社區合作的可能性。透過提供公開和共享的資料庫，更有效推動剩食資訊的共享。這些實證資加上學術研究分析能就未來公義食物系統發展提供資料。 會議論文、期刊論文和書籍中的章節將為文化、媒體和傳播、資訊科技、城市設計和基礎建設、政策研究領域作出貢獻。香港的個案分析中詳列的文件編制、數據分析和科技工具填補現時的研究空隙，並為日後研究員、各NGO和政府打下基礎和簡化日後的工作。國際合作亦可將香港呈現於全球的舞台上，由難以解決的全球/本地食物系統切入，就剩食回收的倫理和可持續城市發展問題開展討論。

12609215.label: Realisation of objectives
12609215.value: The project set out to provide partial insight into the current recoverable food waste situation in Hong Kong. A general overview of food rescue operations and a detailed analysis of the rescued food have been provided using both quantitative and qualitative data to offer insights into current practices. For the general overview, a list of all current food rescue organisations was compiled and mapped with details of the types of food handled, the service area and the districts covered. The project database documented donors, type and volume of food, location of surpluses from 3 collaborating NGOs over the course of 2 years. The project generated monthly and annual reports for each of the participating NGOs. The data sets were then combined, aggregated, anonymised and a time-series analysis was performed to visualize overall trends and identify recurrent issues. Edge cases were documented to provide insight and identify opportunities and challenges that affect food rescue. Part of the key challenge was the varied quality of NGO data, the data recording practices vary greatly between small, medium and large operations. Local grassroot organisations rely mainly on pen and paper to record food collections , while medium and larger organisations have access to digital tools. There is no standard amongst organisations on what data points should be recorded and in what volumetric units. The lack of comparable data make sharing difficult, resulting in valuable information being locked to individual operations. To this end, the project created an online tool for participating NGOs to input their data, and standards set to reflect their reporting and record needs. This had been valuable to both stakeholders and the project. It allowed NGOs to streamline their recording and reporting processes, capture important information about their work and better communicate impact using analysis and reports the project provided. By creating and implementing a standard, the project was able to create a common platform and language to discuss and share insight into food rescue practices, thus achieving the objective of using technology-based tools to enable collaborative processes and knowledge building. Apart from the data collection tool mentioned above, a proof of concept for the Free Open Source System (FOSS) was designed and built to demonstrate the potential for a crowd-based response system for the collection of surplus food. The design process was collaborative, employing the principals of participatory design. The PI has performed participation observation with all stakeholders – including donors, NGOs and volunteers, as well as interviews in order to fully understand current ground practices and organisational specificities. A user flow was created and functionalities and features have been identified that would solve the specific challenges of collecting surplus bread in this case study. The platform streamlined labour intensive processes and enabled donors, volunteers and NGOs to collaborate more effectively. The platform has been designed specifically using free open source software and open API’s to contribute to the common pool of resources that is shared by the community. This is both a theoretical and technological decision that is in line with the project’s objective of reconfiguring surplus food practices as a common resource. The conceptual framework posits that enclosing resources leads to deterioration and waste (both data and food – see Harvard Design Magazine article). The platform exemplifies how sharing tools as well as material resources (such as food and information) could engage more stakeholders, facilitate collaboration that eventually contribute to the wider goal of sustainability. The development of the tool contributes to a form of practice-led research where crowdsourcing has been tested beyond its conventional use of knowledge gathering. This platform is novel is that is tests the feasibility of orchestrating on-the-ground movements, which extends the power of the crowd. Despite its early stage of development, this feature could be applicable in other circumstances and benefit stakeholders beyond food rescue in Hong Kong. During the course of the research, 2 journal articles have been published, most notably the piece in Theory, Culture and Society. The PI was also invited by the Harvard Design magazine to write on the topic of food waste. 6 papers have been presented at international conferences, most notably the PI has been invited to give a keynote speech on the project in Berlin in 2016. 11 academic workshops have been delivered, most notably MIT (Massachusetts Institute of Technology) in Boston. 11 community talks and events have been delivered, most notably the TedX Wanchai to a live audience of 1400 at the Academy of Performing Arts. 12609215.label: Major findings and research outcome
12609215.value: There is a need to develop food rescue operations more comprehensively and more effectively in Hong Kong in order to reduce waste and improve food security. Food rescue operations are not evenly distributed or equally matched across the city. There are districts with high poverty rates with few to no NGO presence. Food rescue organisations require time to establish operations and demonstrate effectiveness. Data shows exponential increase in the volume of rescued food over time across NGOs. This is due to increased trust from donors as well as having more time to establish a larger donor base. Quantity vs Quality. Volumetric target is used as the primary measure of effectiveness, while this is useful to a certain extent, it is unable to reflect the regularity of donation or quality of food. Manufacturers and suppliers often donate irregular, large volumes of processed and packaged food; while local green grocers in wet markets offer smaller, but more regular donations of nutritious and healthy food. Large vs small operations. Large organisations are better equipped to respond to large donations as well as high-risk foods, while small operations are often unable to handle quantities above a certain limit but they are suited to collecting fresh, perishable produce from local markets. City-wide vs district based operation. Large operations have better access to logistical support to respond to opportunities across the city while district based operations are limited geographically. However, this does offer opportunities for community networks to grow. Volumetric targets could have a negative effect on surplus food donation. One data set showed that a small organisation changed strategy to meet funders demands. Targeting food suppliers instead of local wet markets, the organisation was able to meet its goals, but the regularity of quality of food dropped. This organisation is no longer in operation. Food rescue NGOs could benefit hugely from sharing information and intel. Most of the organisations do not see each other as competitors, but rather, the lack of common ground, tools, language (data) means that it is often difficult to communicate impact to funders and policy makers. Certain programmes such as the bread donation programme is too labour intensive and can benefit from the development of technological tools. Hong Kong has the infrastructure to implement these tools.

12609215.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12609215.value: Compared to other parts of the world, food rescue in Hong Kong is still a very young industry, and there is a huge potential to develop the sector. Comparative case studies of other international cities should be studied to identify a longer term strategy that is suitable for Hong Kong. Surplus food rescue is part of a larger food system that sustains the city of Hong Kong. Better understanding the way the city feeds itself would increase food security and align the gaol of waste reduction with sustainable development. The FOSS platform is a proof of concept that demonstrate the potential power of the crowd. Advancing features on the platform to increase information sharing amongst volunteers, or improve usability for donors would extend the model of “crowd sourcing” to a more dynamic understanding of collective intelligence. The platform could be applied in different cases outside of food rescue. Further collaboration with urban risk/ disaster relief research groups could produce more impactful results.

12609215.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12609215.value: Reducing food waste is key to sustainable urban development. In a city where 3600 tonnes of food is thrown into landfill everyday while 1.3 million people experience hunger, food rescue plays an important role in improving immediate food security for the needy and reducing waste. Food rescue is a young industry in Hong Kong, but lack of research in the area and the wider food system makes it difficult to identify a long term strategy. This research has established a baseline study that provides an overview of current food rescue operations in Hong Kong and detailed insights into the challenges and opportunities in the field. In addition, the project developed an online tool that facilitates pick-up of surplus food for food rescue operations. The design of the tool crowdsources logistical solutions and streamlines work processes for all stakeholders. The platform goes beyond the traditional limits of information gathering to coordinating on-the-ground movements which is innovative and applicable beyond food rescue.

12609615.label: Project Objectives
12609615.value: To investigate the emergent trend of Chinese queer women moving outside China across continents for reasons related to their sexuality and gender. To document new forms of intimate relationship, kinship and family formed by transnational or transcontinental movement through the lived experiences of Chinese queer women in overseas destinations. To generate field knowledge of the lived experiences of Chinese queer women in overseas destinations. To contribute new empirical knowledge to the scholarship of queer migration, Chinese diaspora, queer Asian studies by extending this discussion in ethnic, geographical and theoretical dimensions. To publish a number of journal articles and a monograph. To transfer the knowledge generated in this project to local Chinese queer women community and the general public in Australia. A community-based project in the form of a photo exhibition, life-story archive or a book project will be organized together with the local LGBTQ groups in Australia.

12609615.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12609615.value: Mobility of LGBTQ (lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and queer) people around the globe has been accelerated in the past 30 years due to both structural (migration policy, law governing sexuality and gender) and private factors. Mobility cross national borders, from rural to urban areas, from city to city has accelerated as a result of the globalization of economy, the rise of a global gay culture and cities, the introduction of progressive sexual and gender laws in some countries, the availability of gay tourism, and a hostile environment in one’s home country. The movement can be caused by more intimate reasons. For example, the aspiration to live a life free from family control, to reunite with one’s same-sex partner in another continent, to look for LGBTQ communities in another city for social support, to explore job opportunities in another country where people do not need to hide their non-normative sexualities or genders at work, to move to another state where lesbians can adopt a child or be accessible to reproductive technology. Past studies of sexuality and migration have a heavy focus on North American societies and the movement of queer people from the so-called global south to the global north. This research project will explore an entirely new path of movement of queer mobility— the movement of Chinese queer women (lesbian, bisexual, transgender and queer identified women) from China to Australia. The choice of destinations is based on the findings from the PI’s previous ethnographic research of queer women in China (2005-2011). Australia is one of the most popular destinations of work, study and emigration for queer women in China. The research project will be a pioneer one in the field to study the queer mobility of women from China. PI uses the term “queer mobility” to refer to the transnational or trans-continental movement of queer Chinese women from China to have temporary or permanent stay in the host countries. It is queer because the cause of the movement is mainly or partly related to one’s sexual or gender nonconformity. Extensive field studies such as participant observation and in-depth interviews will be conducted in the chosen cities to document personal lives and community development. The project intends to generate community-based field knowledge of the lived experiences of Chinese queer women in their overseas destination, and therefore enriches the existing scholarship of queer migration in ethnic, geographical and theoretical dimensions.

12609615.label: Realisation of objectives
12609615.value: PI interviewed about 30 “mobile queer women” in China and Australia, and a few from Hong Kong who are now residing in Europe during 2015 and 2018. Among them, there are international students in western countries, working holiday goers, recently arrived immigrants in Australia, transcontinental commuters between China/ Hong Kong and Australia/ North America, young urban women in China who are planning to go abroad, and women who are having frequent internal and international travels. These women belong to an emergent urban mobile population in China. Mobility forms a significant part of their everyday life and long-term life course planning. Objective 1-3: During the funded period, PI has conducted 4 field trips to Australia (Melbourne and Sydney) and 2 field trips to Beijing. PI has conducted 3 more field trips than originally proposed. The 6 field trips have allowed PI to accomplish objectives 1-3. PI has conducted in-depth interview to 30 informants in Australia and China and collected rich ethnographic data. The interviews were recorded and transcribed into text. Objective 4-5: PI has presented at 6 local and international conferences about the project. The 6 conferences are: 1. The Inter-Asia Cultural Studies Conference 2017 (Seoul, Korea) 2. International Communication Association Annual Conference 2017 (San Diego, USA) 3. Symposium on “Movements of Desires: Identity Politics, Consumption and Citizen-making in China and Hong Kong” 2017 (Hong Kong) 4. Crossroads Conference 2016 (Sydney, Australia) 5. Symposium on Mobilities and Borders 2016 (Hong Kong) 6. Sexing the City: HERA SINGLE Final Conference 2016 (Leiden, the Netherlands). The presentations and conference papers have allowed PI to accomplish objective 4, to contribute new empirical knowledge to existing scholarship. Through those conferences and other networks, PI has been invited to submit journal paper and book chapter. Published and forthcoming articles of this project include: 1. A journal article to be published in the special issue of “Mobilities, Borders and Precarities in Asia’s New Millennium (Cultural Studies); 2. A book chapter to be included in the edited anthology titled Being Single in Urban Asia: Spaces and Mobilities, Pleasures and Precarities (Heidelberg University Press); 3. Lucetta Y. L. Kam “Going Abroad: A New Mobility of Queer Women.” CPI Analysis, October 3, 2017. In the coming year, PI will proactively approach academic publishers to submit a manuscript in the form of a monograph. Objective 6: PI has successfully built up rapport with local queer women organizations and leading activists in Australia and China during field trips. After knowing the local communities better, PI found that it will be more relevant and effective to accomplish objective 6 by speaking directly to the general public in some established official and NGO platforms in Australia, and by using social media such as WeChat to reach out to local Chinese mobile queer women community in and out of China. During the funded period, PI has already connected with transnational mobile Chinese queer women from China via WeChat and participated in group communication and networking. In the coming year, PI will continue to work on objective 6 by the following means, 1. PI has been invited by the Australian Glbtiq Multicultural Council (AGMC) as an official guest speaker for the 2018 AGMC National Conference Melbourne (September 2018) to speak about queer Chinese women in Australia. It is an event to transfer knowledge to the general public and local activists in Australia. 2. PI will create a new group on WeChat (the social media used by most Chinese queer women) to connect queer Chinese women in Australia for networking and resource sharing.

12609615.label: Major findings and research outcome
12609615.value: It is found that transnational mobility, whether if it is short-term leisure travel or long-term movement for education, work or migration, is both a personal and national project of embodying a new form of self in post-socialist China, which is usually imagined as global, cosmopolitan and desirable. For women, their position in the Chinese kinship network decides the possibility and the extent of movement. In addition, their familial position and marital status control not only the space factor of their movement (how far and where) but also the time factor of mobility (how long and when). The desire to be global exposes those young women to the dilemma of personal freedom versus social, familial responsibilities. (More in forthcoming article “‘Single’ and Mobile: Transnational Mobility of Chinese Queer Women”.) It is found that to go abroad, for leisure travel or for longer stay, is a general desire in today’s China. But for queer people, mobility can be understood as a moving away from a predictable route or life routine, whether if it is a geographical location or a normative way of existence. Their aspirations of being mobile are partly nurtured in the same socio-economic an political context as other young people in China, and partly resulted from their lived experience as a sexual or gender non-conforming person. Transnational mobility enables them to find possible exits to a new life. The newly available opportunities of mobility allows young women in Chinese cities to find alternative space and extended time to live away from heteronormative gender roles and expectations. Being single or detached from the heteronormative life course and family structure is an exit for queer women to enhance their mobility. ( Published article “Going Abroad: A New Mobility of Queer Women”.) Regarding queer Chinese women’s adaptation in Australia, it is found that there exists a cultural, sometimes linguistic, barrier for them to participate fully in the local Asian queer women communities or the wider LGBTQ community. Their social networks are limited to a close circle of friends who share similar linguistic and cultural backgrounds. (More in forthcoming article “Queer Mobility and Immobility: Mainland Chinese Women Before and After Leaving China”.) It is also discovered that there are many different patterns of transnational mobility of queer Chinese women. The patterns of transnational mobility of them are diverse and flexible. (More in the forthcoming article “Queer Mobility and Immobility: Mainland Chinese Women Before and After Leaving China”.)

12609615.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12609615.value: The long-term development and transnational mobility of queer women informants in Australia and China can be an area that the PI would like to explore further. Proposed action can be to apply for internal funds or other short-term funds to conduct follow-up research. As reported above about Objective 6, PI will continue to transfer academic knowledge generated from this project to the general public and the researched community. Proposed action includes the creation of social media platform for queer Chinese women who have transnational mobility and conduct public seminars and talks in Australia for the general public to understand more of the researched community.

12609615.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12609615.value: Nature: The project is a field research to understand the transnational mobile experiences of queer (non-heterosexual) women from China in Australia and China. The informants include 1) international students and recent immigrants in Australia, 2) those travel regularly between Australia and China; 3) those who are planning to go abroad; 4) those who have returned to China from overseas countries. Significance: It is one of the few projects that explore the relation between sexuality and transnational mobility. It is the first project to investigate the recently arrived queer Chinese women in Australia. We know very little about this group of people. Why do they want to leave China? What are their experiences of mobility? How do they live as a queer Chinese woman in Australia? What is their connection with China? This project intends to explore these questions. Value: The findings can help related parties such as social workers, policy makers, activists to know more about the situation and needs of queer Chinese women in Australia and China. Queer Chinese women can also learn more about the experiences of people with similar backgrounds. Knowing and connecting with each other is the first step to offer support and build up communities.

12610315.label: Project Objectives
12610315.value: To provide a comprehensive and critical survey of Xinjiang Uyghur cinema since the first recorded film screening in 1912. To conduct detailed textual and contextual analyses of representative Uyghur films in order to show the dynamics of the political, economic, cultural, artistic and technological forces that shape Xinjiang cinema. 12610315.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12610315.value: ABSTRACT The proposed research is a critical and comprehensive study of Xinjiang Uyghur cinema. "Xinjiang Uyghur cinema” is defined as cinematic works made by or involving the participation of Uyghur film makers, films made in or involving the use of the Uyghur language, films made on subject matters about Uyghur culture, history and/or people, and films made on location in the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region, China. The first item of output of this research will be a monograph tracing the development of Xinjiang Uyghur cinema since the first recorded cinematic screening in Xinjiang in 1912. The chapters of the monograph will follow a chronological order, each will explore the aesthetic, social, cultural, political and economic functions of the films produced in respective periods. Focus will be placed on the representations of modernity in Xinjiang in these films. The second item of output will be a website listing known Xinjiang Uyghur films with relevant information about them. The third item of output will be a collection of Xinjiang Uyghur films subtitled in Chinese and English housed in the University library for access by the academic community. Data collection and textual analysis supplemented by contextual reading will form the main research methodology. Since there are no comprehensive studies on Xinjiang Uyghur cinema available to date, the data presented in the monograph will mainly constitute primary data resulting from original searches. Three historical and press archives have been identified as the main sources. About 70 films fitting the definition of Xinjiang Uyghur cinema in this research have been collected by the PI. Many of them have not been studied in academic discourses, and some of them have never been circulated beyond the Uyghur communities. About 20 will be used as major case studies. Detailed textual analysis and contextual reading will be conducted on these films. All the analysis in this research will be underpinned by the theoretical principle of historicisation, and by the research intention of discovering the representations and construction of modernity in these films. The Uyghur perspective will be given prominent attention in order for Uyghur cinema to be understood on its own terms in addition to being a genre of Chinese cinema.

12610315.label: Realisation of objectives
12610315.value: Objective 1: To provide a comprehensive and critical survey of Xinjiang Uyghur cinema since the first recorded film screening in 1912. This objective is achieved. In my research I have discovered information to challenge the extant theory that the first film viewing in Xinjiang was an event that took place in the Urumchi Russian Consulate to entertain official dignitaries of the Xinjiang government. There is substantial evidence that points to probable earlier screenings in the northern city of Ghulja. I have made use of lesser known Uyghur research sources in comparative analysis side by side with the better known Chinese sources in order to chart a comprehensive timeline of film viewing activities in Xinjiang in the early twentieth century. This method of comparative referencing, alongside my first-hand search of films, is also adopted in the charting of the subsequent stages of film activities in Xinjiang that extends from before 1912 to 2019. In this timeline I have divided Uyghur film activities into seven stages: 1. First viewings: In or before 1912 - 1930s 2. First filmic images of the Uyghurs on documentaries made by missionaries, diplomats and explorers: 1926-1934 3. Films made in Xinjiang within the national establishment of film-making in the early years of the People’s Republic: 1953-1962 4. Post-Cultural Revolution liberalism within the establishment of Tianshan Film Studio: 1979-1989 5. Production of “harmony main-melody” films within the establishment of the Tianshan Film Studio in the era of the market economy: 1991-2016 6. Independent VCD films produced for an exclusive Uyghur market: 2000-2005 7. Extraterritorial independent productions: 2015-present I have acquired about one hundred fifty films that fall within the scope of this study which are commercially available. To acquire these films, I searched all the internet stores that I could find that stocked Xinjiang films. Then I travelled to Xinjiang and visited as many main and backstreet bookstores and music stores as possible in Urumchi, Kashgar and Kucha. About eighty films were also acquired one by one through my personal contacts in the film-making circles in Xinjiang, and by visiting individual film-makers in Xinjiang and Turkey to ask them for a copy of their films. Having collected these films, a database in the form of an excel sheet of films from stage 3 onward of the above list is constructed. The list is as exhaustive as possible and includes two hundred and thirty films arranged in chronological order. It is attached to this report. In addition, a book manuscript containing a critical analysis of Uyghur film history based on the material in this survey is under preparation. My book proposal, including a detailed chapter summary and a sample chapter is also attached to this report. Objective 2: To conduct detailed textual and contextual analyses of representative Uyhgur films in order to show the dynamics of the political, economic, cultural, artistic and technological forces that shape Xinjiang cinema. This objective has been achieved. After watching the two hundred and thirty films collected for this project, I have worked out a general description of the films of each period, and then selected outstanding examples for detailed case study. Some of the films are in Chinese, while some have versions in Chinese and Uyghur. The majority are only in Uyghur. Very few Uyghur language films have English or Chinese subtitles. I watched those in Chinese without help. The ones in Uyghur language were watched with help from a translator who provided a roughly recorded, but accurately translated, audio recording of every line of conversation in the films. This was the only solution because subtitling would have been too expensive and not financially viable for this project, considering the numbers of films collected. As for the films containing both Chinese and Uyghur audio tracks, I watched it in Chinese, and then asked the Uyghur translator to compare the two audio tracks to spot any possible discrepancies. Since the period dealt with in the research spans over one hundred years, it is inevitable that the political, economic and technological circumstances of film-making in Xinjiang have experienced drastic changes. I have drawn heavily on published research in the disciplines of Xinjiang history, China studies and Central Asian studies. It is most fortuitous that the extremely limited discipline of Xinjiang historical research has seen a vibrant development in recent years. Excellent historical monographs by international experts especially focusing on the late Qing and subsequent periods have been published. These works have fed directly and in timely fashion into my contextual analyses of the films. In my analyses, I have placed specific focus on the following forces which I have discovered to be of vital importance to the shaping of film activities in Xinjiang: the Uyghur aspiration for modernity, the requirements of political propaganda, censorship control, and the possibilities in the new market economy. These factors are intrinsic to in all the film analyses in this project. Objective 3: To study the way the Xinjiang film industry operates, including its modes of production, distribution, promotion and training, in order to understand how the industry has positioned itself in the changing social situations of Xinjiang. This objective has been achieved. When this research project was proposed and accepted for funding, film production in Xinjiang was experiencing a stage of regular production in terms of mode and number in both private sector and within the establishment of Tianshan Film Studio. Therefore, the industrial aspect of Xinjiang film history featured prominently in my initial plan. However, since the project commenced in 2016, the situation in Xinjiang has changed drastically. The ongoing system of ‘vocational training and re-education’ has taken many film professionals out of the production system; and the social, political and economic conditions have been changed beyond recognition. Film production has basically halted in Xinjiang. I have included the industrial details in my analysis of all the films and stages of film activities in Xinjiang. However, with the radical changes that have happened to the profession and the creative conditions for its pursuit, my industrial analyses can only serve as a historical record of former practices To date, there is no indication of how film production might be resumed, and under what conditions the film-makers who could eventually return to film-making will work. It is, at this point, impossible to project the future development of Xinjiang film production. Considering present circumstances, a second focus is being introduced into the research: the study will also explore how Uyghur identity or ‘Uyghurness’ is constructed in Xinjiang cinema throughout its film history. This approach is intended to function both in the historical-critical dimension and as intellectual intervention in response the current situation
