12610315.label: Major findings and research outcome
12610315.value: 1. The arrival of film in Xinjiang in the early 20th century was bound up with the indigenous Turkic people’s attempts to bring modernity to Xinjiang. The first film produced with Uyghur capital was made for the purpose of industrial modernisation; moreover, Uyghur Jadidist intellectuals were highly likely to be among the first Uyghur viewers of films when they travelled abroad. 2. Although a good number of film reviews and popular discussions outside China about creative arts in Xinjiang assume it impossible for indigenous Uyghur voices to assert themselves if they deviate from official discourses on ethnicity and Uyghurness, the textual analyses of the films in this empirical research indicate a more complex reality. While it is true that Uyghur film-makers in Xinjiang have never been able to work without heavy pressure of political censorship, many of them have found artistic idioms for self-expression and self-empowerment even under the most stringent conditions. Throughout the different stages of the modern period, Uyghur film-makers have tended to find favourable factors in their milieu to facilitate both sensible and sensitive ways of opening up creative possibilities. At every historical stage they have been able to develop aesthetic strategies to express and construct their idea of Uyghurness in their films, something that would be impossible to achieve in the non-artistic arena. 3. Two bodies of works neglected in Xinjiang film studies so far are in fact the most representative of the indigenous creative voices. First, about two hundred VCD films were produced between 2000 and 2005 exclusively for the local Uyghur market. Since distribution on VCD allowed them to replace the more stringent process of film censorship with a simpler alternative, these films have displayed more creative liberty. The exclusively Uyghur production and reception conditions also contributed to minimising exoticism in these films. Second, there is an emerging group of films made by Uyghur film-makers in extraterritorial situations. Some of them travelled to Xinjiang for film-shooting but the films were intended only for overseas distribution. Others set Uyghur stories abroad, or were shot in locations that look like Xinjiang. Without the pressure of political censorship, these films have shown greater liberty than any films produced in Xinjiang. In the current situation in Xinjiang where no film production has been possible, extraterritorial modes of production, together with the accompanying extraterritorial aesthetics, will be increasingly important to the short and the long-term future of Uyghur cinema.

12610315.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12610315.value: A database of two hundred and thirty films has been constructed in this project. An accompanying database of the production details of over one hundred VCD films has also been developed. Upon publication of the monograph these two lists will be published online providing free access. To date there is no known database of this kind, and it is intended that, through sharing the database, new research on Xinjiang cinema can be generated and encouraged. Physical copies of all two hundred and thirty films have been collected for the purpose of this research. The original plan was to make them available to other researchers by placing them in the HKBU Library. Unfortunately, with the current situation in Xinjiang, it has been impossible to contact most of the film-makers or copyright holders of the films to solicit their consent for library collection, and only a few who are now residing abroad can be contacted. A few dozens films are available commercially on DVD. Therefore, the second and third categories of films will be housed in the HKBU Library. The first category will be held by the PI who will do her best to entertain requests for viewing from bona fide researchers.

12610315.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12610315.value: Xinjiang comprises one-sixth of the total area of China, and its geopolitics represents one of most complicated situations in the country. Cinema, as probably the most influential cultural form of the modern era, simultaneously reflects and informs the reality of the region. However, to date, there has been no independent and comprehensive study of Xinjiang cinema available to scholars in international academe. The present research study has filled this void. By collecting and critically analysing over two hundred films produced in Xinjiang between 1926 and 2019, this research investigation has provided the first analytical narrative of Xinjiang film history in English. Many of the films studied as part of this research initiative were artistically innovative and cultural representative, but had escaped attention from critics and academics. Among these films many were previously unknown outside the Uyghur community. By bringing Xinjiang cinema into the spotlight of international scholarship, this research has provided a perspective on Xinjiang, facilitating an understanding of its film arts against the backdrop of its geopolitical situation. The monograph resulting from this research will serve as a valuable reference resource for those who want to better understand Xinjiang and ethnic minority cinemas in China.

13200015.label: Realisation of objectives
13200015.value: The base two-stage model constructed for this project allows us to analyze the transshipment decision in stage 2 and the order quantity decision in stage 1. We obtained complete analytical results and also performed some sensitivity analysis numerically. We added a pricing stage to study the pricing issue and also obtained complete analytical results, including coordinating transshipment prices and ex-ante endogenous transshipment prices. When demands are correlated, the model is much more complicated and analytical results are complicated and hence no significant new insights were drawn from the complicated results. Objectives 1-3 are completely reached and we documented the results in a paper (see below in Part C 8) currently under 2nd review with Production and Operations Management (POM). We are confident that this paper will be accepted for publication at POM. We have made significant efforts to study the three-player problem (Obj. 4). The model becomes more complicated with many cases (pair-wise and different parameter ranges) to analyze. We did not find significantly different behavior for the transshipment between any pair of players with a 3rd player on the sideline compared with the case with two players. Although we completed analysis of the three-player model, the results are unlikely publishable in reasonably good journal, and thus, the PI does not consider Obj. 4 is fully reached. The purpose of objective 5 is to understand the future effect of transshipment. However, the two-period model is analytically unsolvable because to obtain any results for period 1 (analytical or numerical), explicit analytical equilibrium results for the period 2 game are required, but it is impossible. We thus study two transshipment modes, inventory transshipment first or customer switching first, to try to understand the future effect from a different angle (and, thus, the PI does not consider Obj. 5 is fully reached). We have obtained interesting results both analytically and numerically. In particular, we find that the combination of customer’s loyalty (opposite to switching) and transshipment price affects the performance of the players significantly. We have documented the results related to Obj. 5 in an initial draft (see the working paper listed in Part C 8). I expect a few rounds of revisions and improvement will get the paper ready for submission to a respectable journal (e.g., EJOR or better).

13200015.label: Major findings and research outcome
13200015.value: Analyzing the two-stage end-of-season transshipment model with customer switching, we find that unconditional full transshipment is no longer optimal. Instead, the optimal transshipment policy consists of no transshipment, partial transshipment, and full transshipment, determined by the interplay of switching probability, transshipment price, and remaining inventory. A unique Nash equilibrium for the stage-1 inventory competition exists, and there exists a threshold such that transshipment dampens (intensiﬁes) the inventory competition when the transshipment price is below (above) it. In addition to its positive inventory pooling eﬀect, transshipment under competition also has a competition eﬀect which is positive when transshipment dampens inventory competition. The competing retailers always have an ex-ante incentive to transship when the competition eﬀect is positive; but even when the competition eﬀect is negative, the retailers may still have an incentive to transship for a wider transshipment price range in which the combined pooling and competition eﬀect is positive. We identify explicitly the necessary and suﬃcient conditions for the existence of a unique pair of coordinating transshipment prices and provide formulas to compute them. We also provide a complete solution for the ex-ante endogenous transshipment prices between symmetric retailers. These findings are documented in a journal paper (Paper 1, Part C) under second review. We build a two-stage model with pre-substitution transshipment (TS) and post-substitution transshipment (ST) modes. When retailer with excess inventory can dictate the transshipment price, a unique equilibrium order quantity exists for both timing scenarios. The equilibrium order quantity in the ST scenario is higher than that in the TS scenario in the symmetric case. When transshipment price is set to retail price, the ST scenario dominates TS scenario in expected proﬁt although inventory competition is mitigated in the TS scenario. This is an interesting new result. We also ﬁnd that when the switching ratio is high and transshipment price is low, TS scenario beneﬁts retailers more; when the ratio is low or transshipment price is high, ST scenario is more preferable. We ﬁnd that the two asymmetric retailers may not prefer the same scenario even though the market parameters are the same and transshipment price is set to the requesters’ retail price. By renegotiating the transshipment price between two asymmetric retailers, the system can be coordinated so that the two asymmetric retailers will both prefer the ST scenario under most of the market parameter combinations. See Paper 2, Part C.

13200015.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
13200015.value: It is difficult to obtain further results that are interesting to readers of good OM journals. The interest of the PI (and his co-authors) has also moved other problems. So, there is no plan to continue working along this direction other than efforts to publish the current results.

13200015.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
13200015.value: Retailers often sell the same or similar products so that their markets are overlapped if not identical. Customers do not usually have complete loyalty to any stores, although they may have preferences. Encountering stock out at a store, a customer may switch to another store to purchase the item. Previous research shows that retailers in such situation engage in a quantity competition and tend to overstock their inventory. This research shows that there exists an alternative for competing retailers to “help” each other, when one retailer has a surplus whereas the other has a shortage, by transshipping one’s surplus to the retailer with a shortage. Our modeling analysis shows that in the above situation, the retailer with surplus can compute, from customer switching probability, transshipment price, and its surplus, an optimal transshipment quantity that will benefit itself while helping its competitor. By transshipping properly, the retailers can avoid damaging competitive overstocking and dampen the competition. We also find that there exist coordination transshipment prices with which the competing retailers act (transshipping and ordering) for the best interest of them as a whole and themselves individually. We also study and find when transshipment should be ahead customer switching and when otherwise.

13500015.label: Project Objectives
13500015.value: We will find the optimal return policy under which an online retailer achieves its maximum profit. We will investigate which policy is the most effective in reducing the wardrobing likelihood. We will examine the impact of the restocking fee on the wardrobing likelihood for each policy involving such a fee. We will address how the product nature influences the wardrobing likelihood for each policy and the online retailer's optimal decisions and policy choice. We will analyze how the retailer's optimal pricing and restocking fee rate decisions vary for different policies. We will discuss the practice under the REP-I policy in Table 2.

13500015.label: Realisation of objectives
13500015.value: We have carefully worked on this project to address six major objectives. For the first objective, we investigated an online retailer’s problem of efficiently managing the returns of consumers’ mismatched products via a strategic choice of return policies. As observed in actual practice, the retailer has three possible return policies: (i) refund, (ii) exchange, and (iii) a combination of refund and exchange (mixed policy). We develop an analytical framework in which consumers strategically behave in their purchase and refund/exchange decisions, and the retailer determines the optimal price and restocking fee(s) to maximize his profit. Our results have been used to propose a paper which is under review with Production and Operations Management (POM, 2018). In addition, as this project is concerned with customer behaviors in eBusiness, we also studied customer reviews-related problem in which a manufacturer controls the product quality/delivery speed in the presence of online customer reviews and thus indirectly influences consumers’ purchases and product returns. The manufacturer sells the product to a market through a retailer who makes her optimal retail pricing decision according to the manufacturer’s quality/delivery and wholesale pricing decisions. For this issue, we have proposed two papers, among which one is under the second-round review with European Journal of Operational Research (EJOR, 2018), and the other joined the 2018 MSOM Data-Driven Research Challenge Competition and was invited for a fast-track review at Manufacturing & Service Operations Management (MSOM 2018). We believe that our results can contribute to the operations management literature, and have drawn a number of managerial insights that are expected to be important to practitioners. For the second objective, we have proposed the paper POM (2018) in which we analyzed a strategic consumer’s purchase and product return decision problem to investigate the impact of a retailer’s different policies on the consumer’s return behavior. Specifically, we start with the consumer’ decisions given a return policy; then, for each policy in terms of the consumer’s optimal decisions, we maximize the retailer’s profit to find the optimal policy. Similarly, in the papers EJOR (2018) and MSOM (2018), we examined the consumer’s return behavior in a supply chain setting. For the third objective, we proposed the paper POM (2018) to analyze a retailer’s three return policies by using the backward induction approach. For each policy, we found the retailer's optimal pricing and restocking fee decisions, and analyzed the impact of the restocking fee on consumers’ return behaviors. For the fourth objective, in the paper POM (2018) we have studied the impact of important product natures (which are represented by some factors such as the match probability, the hassle cost as well as the salvage value for exchanges and that for returns) on the retailer's policy choice, the optimal pricing and restocking fee, and the consumer refunds and exchanges. For the fifth objective, we also compared our results under different policies and observed how the optimal policy decisions change in the policies; see the paper POM (2018). For the sixth objective, we have compared a retailer’s optimal restocking fee rate for the exchanges and that for the refunds, as presented in the paper POM (2018). When we worked on this project, we also identified two important supply chain problems, for which we published two papers in Operations Research Letters and International Journal of Production Economics.

13500015.label: Major findings and research outcome
13500015.value: We have written five quality research papers that were published in Operations Research Letters and International Journal of Production Economics, and are under review with Manufacturing & Service Operations Management (MSOM, 2018), Production and Operations Management (POM, 2018), and European Journal of Operational Research (EJOR, 2018). Next, we focus on POM (2018), MSOM (2018), and EJOR (2018). In our paper POM (2018), we investigated an online retailer's problem of efficiently managing the returns of consumers' mismatched products via a strategic choice of return policies. The retailer can benefit from allowing both consumer refunds and exchanges with a hassle-free service. When the retailer implements a refund policy, he finds it better to keep the retail price unchanged but use the restocking fee solely to control consumer returns. However, the restocking fee is not the only option to influence the levels of consumer refunds and exchanges. For the exchange and mixed policies, it is optimal for the retailer to employ both price and restocking fee(s) to control consumer refunds and exchanges, and higher restocking fee(s) would lead the retailer to set a lower selling price. In addition, for the mixed policy, it is not always beneficial to charge a lower restocking fee for exchanges than that for refunds. When the hassle cost is sufficiently low, the retailer should set a higher restocking fee for exchanges. In MSOM (2018), we considered a supply chain in which an online retailer and a supplier make their pricing and delivery-effort decisions in the presence of delivery-time-based customer ratings. We investigated the effects of these ratings on the supply chain both empirically (using a rich—13 million—Cainiao dataset) and analytically. The relationship between delivery time and delivery ratings is also statistically significant but very inelastic. The low elasticity of customer ratings to delivery time is required for the presence of delivery ratings to increase equilibrium sales and profits. In EJOR (2018), we investigated a two-period problem for a supply chain involving a manufacturer and a retailer. When early customers overrate the actual quality, the manufacturer improves his quality level, the sales in the second period are higher, and the retailer's expected profits in the two periods are increased whereas the manufacturer's expected profits may be decreased. The supply chain benefits from a larger variance of early customers' quality expectations and is also better off from a smaller variance of later customers' quality estimates.

13500015.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
13500015.value: For this project, we have successfully proposed three papers to investigate the pricing and product return problems for a single online retailer or a supply chain, and two publications for supply chain analysis. In POM (2018), we have analyzed a single online retailer’s optimal policy selection problem. In reality, two retailers may compete in a market with their policies. In future, we would address the pricing and return policy problem in a duopoly setting. In MSOM (2018) we used around 13 million Cainiao datasets to explore customers’ responses (their purchases and returns) to delivery service and then studied a supply chain to obtain some implications regarding the optimal pricing decisions in the presence of customer reviews. In this paper, we developed an aggregate demand function in terms of price and customer ratings. In future, we may investigate the customer choice models for this problem. In EJOR (2018) we investigated a two-stage problem in which late customers observe early customers’ ratings and then make purchase and return decisions. We did not involve the restocking fee decision in this paper, which may be considered in future.

13500015.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
13500015.value: In POM (2018), we have found that an online retailer can benefit from implementing a hassle-free mixed (refund/exchange) policy. In a refund policy, the retailer should keep the retail price unchanged but use the restocking fee solely to control consumer returns. However, the restocking fee is not the only option to influence the levels of consumer refunds and exchanges. For the exchange and mixed policies, it is optimal for the retailer to employ both price and restocking fee(s) to control consumer refunds and exchanges, and higher restocking fee(s) would lead the retailer to set a lower selling price. In addition, for the mixed policy, it is not always beneficial to charge a lower restocking fee for exchanges than that for refunds. When the hassle cost is sufficiently low, the retailer should set a higher restocking fee for exchanges. In MSOM (2018), we have concluded that a low elasticity of customer ratings to delivery time is required for supply chains to willingly allow customer reviews. In EJOR (2018), we learnt that supply chains benefit from a larger variance of early customers' quality expectations; but, supply chains can achieve a higher profit if the variance of later customers' quality estimates is smaller.

13500215.label: Project Title(Chinese)
13500215.value: 下調稅率和強化稅收執法對沖減企業因財稅報表不一致之避稅行為的效力

13500215.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
13500215.value: In 1998, China initiated a shift away from its traditional tax-based accounting system to follow closely the International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS). This move significantly reduced book-tax conformity. Chan, Lin and Mo (2010) examine the tax-reporting behaviour of Chinese firms between 1996 and 2003, and find that the firms’ tax noncompliance increases when book-tax conformity decreases, due to the reduction in non-tax costs. In 2007, China issued a new set of accounting standards to converge with the IFRS, which further reduced book-tax conformity. On the other hand, tax reform designed to unify the tax rates for foreign and domestic enterprises were implemented in 2008, reducing the corporate income tax rate from 33 per cent to 25 per cent for listed companies in China. Although this reduction in tax rate was not intended primarily to reduce tax noncompliance, it has nevertheless decreased the incentive for noncompliance. Aggressive tax-reporting practices are costly to society. In particular, tax evasion has made the recent economic crisis worse in many countries. One of the main tasks of policy makers in both developed and developing countries is to combat tax noncompliance by tightening tax enforcement. The proposed project is a follow-up study that extends Chan, Lin and Mo’s (2010) research to examine the tax-noncompliance behaviour of Chinese firms between 2001 and 2012 (i.e., before and after China’s formal adoption of IFRS-equivalent accounting standards in 2007), and the effectiveness of two measures (tax enforcement and tax-rate reduction) implemented to offset the increase in corporate-tax noncompliance caused by the adoption of the IFRS in China. The findings of this project are expected to be of substantial interest to regulators and policy makers in many countries, especially given the widespread adoption of the IFRS to meet the challenges posed by business globalisation.

13501415.label: Realisation of objectives
13501415.value: Our first objective is to explore how firms make operational decisions without information sharing. The retailer possesses some private information about future demand and each firm makes decisions based on its information available. If the retailer does not share information, in the first period, the manufacturer decides the wholesale price based on the prior information and the retailer decides the order quantity based on his private information. At the beginning of period two, the manufacturer knows the retailer’s period-one quantity, which conveys his private information. The manufacturer will try to infer it from the order quantity and decide her period-two wholesale price based on the inferred information. Specifically, in period one, if the retailer observes a high (or low) demand signal, he will decide a high (or low) order quantity. In period two, the manufacturer knows the retailer period-one order quantity. If the order quantity is high, she believes that the retailer observes a high demand signal in period one. Otherwise, he believes the retailer observes a low demand signal in period one. Receiving the manufacturer’s period-two wholesale price, the retailer decides his period-two quantity based on the latest information. The second and third objectives are to study the effect of information sharing on the manufacturer’s profit and the retailer’s expected profit and on the retailer’s incentive to share information. As argued in the literature, information sharing strengths the double marginalization, which benefits the manufacturer but hurts the retailer. However, if the retailer does not share information with the manufacturer, the retailer need to downward distort his quantity to signal an unfavorable market condition to the manufacturer due to the information inference effect. Hence, the retailer’s incentive to share information depends on both the double marginalization of information sharing and the inference effect. We find that the retailer has no incentive to share information with the manufacturer voluntarily. However, different from the literature, we find that the retailer has an incentive to share information with the manufacturer with a side payment when the demand uncertainty is low. The fourth and fifth objective are to explore how the accuracy of downstream information affects the manufacturer’s profit and the retailer’s expected profit, and the retailer’s incentive to acquire more accurate information. We show that the higher the demand correlation between two periods is, the more accurate the past sale information is to forecast the future demand. If information sharing agreement is established between the manufacturer and the retailer, both firms makes their respective decisions based on the same information set and their profits are increasing in the information accuracy. If the retailer does not share information, in single-period model, the manufacturer does not know any information about the demand except the prior information and she makes the wholesale price decision based on the prior information. Then, her profit is independent of the information accuracy. As to the retailer, he makes his quantity decision based on his private information and he benefits from more accurate information. However, different from the single-period model, we find that in multi-period model both the manufacturer and the retailer are better off with more accurate information (higher demand correlation). The reason is that in the multi-period model, though the manufacturer does not know the retailer’s private information, the manufacturer can inferred the retailer period-one information and decides her period-two wholesale price based on the inferred information. If the information is more accurate, it is also more useful to forecast period-two demand. Thus, the manufacturer is also better off with more accurate information. To sum up, both the manufacturer and the retailer are better off with more accurate information regardless of the retailer’s information sharing decision. The retailer has an incentive to improve the information accuracy. The sixth objective is to study how the upstream competition intensity affects the above results. If there exists upstream competition (two competing manufacturers, rather than a single manufacturer), the retailer can share information with both manufacturers, only one manufacturer and neither manufacturer. If information is shared with both manufacturer, both manufacturers strategically use the information to decide the wholesale price, which strengths the double marginalization effect, hurting the retailer. If information is shared only with one manufacturer, the informed manufacturer decides the wholesale price strategically, which hurts the retailer. Besides, the retailer needs to downward distort his quantity to signal an unfavorable market condition to the uninformed manufacturer due to the inference effect, which also hurts the retailer. If the retailer conceals the information, in period two both manufacturers will try to infer the retailer’s private information from the past order quantities and makes quantities decisions based on the inferred information. We show that similar to the literature and the base model, information sharing strengths the double marginalization effect, which benefits the manufacturer but hurts the retailer. Thus, the retailer has no incentive to share information with the manufacturer voluntarily. We consider concurrent information sharing contracting. With concurrent information contracting, the retailer makes concurrent and identical offers to the manufacturers by charging each firm a side payment for the information. The manufacturers then simultaneously decide whether to accept the offers or not. We also find that if the demand uncertainty is less than a threshold, the retailer shares information with both manufacturer with side payment. Otherwise, there is no information sharing. The threshold is increasing in the competition intensity. That is, as competition becomes more intense, the double marginalization effect of information sharing becomes insignificant. Thus, with more intense manufacturer competition, the retailer is more likely to share information with the manufacturers.

13501415.label: Major findings and research outcome
13501415.value: We first consider a two-period supply chain in which one manufacturer supplies to one retailer. The retailer possesses some private information about the uncertain demand and decides whether to share the information with manufacturer. If an information sharing agreement is achieved, the retailer will share the observed demand information truthfully to the manufacturer. Then the selling season with two periods starts. In each period, the manufacturer decides on a wholesale price, which the retailer considers when deciding on the retail price. The manufacturer can observe the retailer's period-1 decision and the realized period-1 demand, and use this information when making the period-2 wholesale price decision. Thus, without information sharing, the two firms are involved in a two-period signaling game. If the demands across periods are positive correlated, the retailer need to downward distort his order quantity to signal an unfavorable market condition to the manufacturer. The quantity distortion hurts the retailer. If the retailer shares information, as argued in the literature, the double marginalization hurts the retailer and supply chain. Considering this trade-off, we study the retailer’s incentives to share information with his manufacturer. We find that voluntary information sharing is not possible because it benefits the manufacturer but hurts the retailer. However, different from single-period model, in which no information is shared even with side payment, the manufacturer can make a side payment to the retailer to induce information sharing when the demand range is small. Both firms benefit from more accurate information regardless whether the retailer shares information. We then extend our two-period model to three-period and infinite-period model, and find that the qualitative results remain intact. As the number of periods increases, the downward quantity distortion becomes more significant and the retailer is more likely to share information with the manufacturer with side payment. We also consider the case of negative demand correlation. If the demand across periods are negative correlated, the retailer needs to upward distort his quantity if there is no information sharing. The quantity distortion also hurts the retailer and we find that the retailer may voluntarily share information with the manufacturer when the demand range is small. We also study the impact of upstream competition of the retailer’s information sharing decision. We find that the retailer has incentive to share information with both manufacturers with side payment when the demand uncertainty is less than a threshold.

13501415.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
13501415.value: There are several possible extensions to this study. It is interesting to extend our single supply chain model to other supply chain structures, such as competing supply chains. In addition, it is interesting to consider firms’operational improvements such as quality enhancement levels. Finally, it is interesting to study how the manufacturer's nonlinear production cost affects the retailer's incentives to share information in a multi-period model.

13501415.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
13501415.value: With the increasing opportunities for customer interactions and the advance of information technology, retailers can acquire rich market data about future product demand. With the information, whether a retailer has an incentive to share it with the manufacturers. The literature shows that information sharing strengths the double marginalization, which benefits the manufacturer, but hurts the retailer, so the retailer has no incentive to share information with the manufacturer even with side payment. In our paper, we study whether the repeated interaction is an important driver of retailer’s information sharing decision, and we find that when the demand uncertainty is low, the retailer can share information with the manufacturer by charging a side payment. This study not only contributes to the vertical information sharing literature but also has significant practical implications. This paper can help a retailer strategically deal with its private demand information, i.e., whether or not to share it with upstream firm when there is repeated firm interactions. This study will help to enhance practitioners’ decisions to selectively share information with competing manufacturers.

13600015.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
13600015.value: Art, in its fundamental sense, is a language written in images. Its intrinsic and expressive nature is valuable for children whose language skills are still developing, and even more so for children who have had traumatic experiences. This project will study the use of art as a language in cases of childhood trauma. Childhood trauma is induced by conditions that shatter a child’s sense of safety and security, such as family violence, abuse (sexual, physical, verbal), neglect, serious illness or intrusive medical procedures. Children growing up under such conditions are constantly stressed by fear, pain and insecurity. It has been shown that childhood trauma can lead to personality and behavioural disorders as the child victim grows older (Bennett et al., 2005; van der Kolk, 2003; Leskela et al., 2002; Andrews et al., 2000). Owing to their limited and still developing cognitive and language abilities, children undergoing traumatic experiences cannot comprehend what is happening to them or make sense of the reality. Their confused and repressed emotions can exert a deep influence over their development of self-regulation, self-concept and interpersonal functioning (Cloitre et al., 2009). A fundamental focus of intervention for childhood trauma is to help children liberate and recognize their inner feelings. Most children, especially younger ones, cannot articulate their experiences and thoughts in words. Art, as a form of play, creates a non-verbal platform for children to disclose their abstract thinking and feelings through images. Their ways of creating as well as their final products are revelations about their perceptions of the world. Through these images, traumatised children can achieve a better understanding of themselves and their reality. In Hong Kong, statistics announced by the Social Welfare Department indicate that there are around 800 to 1000 newly reported child abuse cases annually. This number is just the tip of the iceberg, as most Chinese parents tend to deny abuse and avoid seeking help. This number also excludes those suffering from chronic or terminal illness. Local services for childhood trauma are mostly counseling services reliant mainly on verbal communication. This project will collaborate with relevant organisations or units to use art as a non-verbal platform in their services. Through a series of substantial art facilitation workshops specially designed for these children, the project will scrutinize the effects of creativity and art making among these children to determine whether this means of expression can help to improve their well being. 藝術作為受創傷兒童的語言 藝術的內在本質就是一種用圖像書寫的語言。對於語言能力還在發展的兒童來說，圖像書寫至為重要，尤其是那些心身飽受創傷的孩童如生長在家庭暴力或面對嚴重疾病的兒童。本計劃是研究藝術作為圖像書寫的本質，如何幫助心身受過創傷的孩童去表達他們的內在世界。 有研究顯示成長於不安全和穩定的生活環境如家暴或嚴重急疾的孩子長期生活在惶恐、驚嚇、焦慮、痛苦等情緒當中，長大後容易有病態的人格或行為表現（Bennett et. al., 2005; van der Kolk, 2003; Leskela et.al., 2002; Andrews et. al., 2000）。這是因為孩童的語言和認知能力都尚待發展，沒有能力和辦法理解身邊發生的複雜事件，以致成長過程充斥著昏亂和被抑壓的情報，影響自信、自制自律和與人溝通的能力(Cloitre et.al., 2009)。因此處理孩童創傷的基本要點之一是幫助受創傷的兒童去抒發和認識自己那無以明之的內在感受。藝術作為一種不依賴語言的遊戲平台，很適合兒童利用圖像去表達一些抽象的概念和情緒。他們所畫的圖像往往反映他們如何看待他們的世界，促進他們對自己和外在世界的認識。 根據一項社會福利署的調查報告， 香港每年約有八百至一千名受創傷兒童的新増個案。中國社會一般不會張揚家事，因此這數字只是冰山一角，而且這數字主要針對家暴，並未計算面對長期病患和急疾的兒童。社署現有的服務和支援主要是面談的輔導，這計劃將與相關的機構合作，將藝術倡導引進他們的服務，研究藝術作為語言的功用和成效。

13600015.label: Realisation of objectives
13600015.value: Undertaken in collaboration with the Social Welfare Department (SWD), the project involved two series of specially designed 1-year art therapy programmes, serving 20 child victims of family violence, between September 2016 and July 2018, and a third programme that began in August 2018, involving 14 child victims. Hong Kong has more than 1,000 newly reported cases of family violence annually. As their cognitive and linguistic abilities are still developing, the child victims from these families cannot comprehend or articulate what they have experienced. Social workers at the Family and Children Protection Services Unit (FCPSU) find that conventional counselling often fails to help their young victims. The programmes used art as an intervention for victimised children referred to the project by the FCPSU. They were all serious cases exhibiting psychosomatic symptoms. The youngest was 6 and the eldest was 11 at the time of recruitment. The two completed programmes were unique and pioneering in Hong Kong due to their long duration, interdisciplinary methodology (action research and art therapy) and genuine inter-professional collaboration. Each programme was structured on a child-centred, psycho-educational basis, enabling the design of joyful and imaginative creativity workshops (Obj. 2). For example, negative emotions like anger and fear were explored through the guise of creating a ‘monster’ and associated story telling. The child victims were free to create. No judgments were made on their skill or on the artistic quality of their works. They had full autonomy throughout the art-making process. Direct observation of each child’s performance showed that once they were engaged, their acts of creation became more expressive, involving the forceful pounding of clay, aggressive tearing of paper and splashing of colours (Obj. 2). This indicated that the nonverbal and sensory-based nature of art making had relaxed the child victims’ self-defence mechanism and accessed their repressed emotions (Obj. 1). The spontaneity of creation released the children’s inner feelings (Obj. 2), and their images and stories carried symbolic messages (Obj. 1). Narratives of killing, death, bloodshed and secrets were common in their works. As the programme developed, many started to reveal actual scenes of their past trauma (Obj. 1). The programmes consisted of both individual and group workshops. Whilst the former enhanced a sense of privacy and security; the latter encouraged sharing and support (Obj. 3). With a fixed venue and the same members in each group, sharing their works and stories without judgement allowed the child victims to experience appreciation, trust and respect (Obj. 3). Their full autonomy over their creation induced a sense of self-directedness. The project found that a year’s worth of these experiences had a significant impact on the child victims, as the values of trust, safety, respect and self-directedness had been almost totally absent from their daily lives (Obj. 3). Evaluation of the effectiveness of art as an intervention for these children included direct observation, detailed documentation, analysis of images, semi-structured interviews, pre- and post-questionnaires and feedback from case social workers (Obj. 1). The performance of each child in each workshop was carefully observed, documented and measured on a 5-point scale in three dimensions, namely engagement, expressiveness and teamwork, by the three parties involved (art therapist, social worker and research assistant). The average of a child’s scores for the three dimensions was recorded as the child’s score for that workshop. The distribution of these scores provided an indication of the child’s behavioural changes across the programme. Each child’s own account of their works revealed their perceptions of self and others (Obj. 1). The evaluative findings indicated that the children made significant progress in expressing and articulating themselves, and that their psychosomatic symptoms had significantly reduced, if not totally disappeared, towards the end of the year (Obj. 1). This indicated that the art-making process had released repressed emotions with negative psychosomatic effects on the children. The success of each programme was grounded in the active participation of the various professionals involved. A core work team consisting of an art therapist, four social workers and a research assistant was led by the Chief Investigator (CI). The team held regular meetings, working closely on selecting and recruiting the subjects, planning and implementing the workshops and assessing and evaluating the performance of each child as the programme developed (Obj. 4). Case social workers, when available, were invited to join the meetings to discuss their own cases (Obj. 4). Feedback from social workers indicated that they had a great understanding of how art can serve as a language, and were willing to adopt some of the skills they had acquired in their later services (Obj. 5). Two training seminars and talks attracted more than 130 professionals in the field of child social services (Obj. 5). Feedback revealed a compelling need for training in and research on the skills involved in using art in social services. This was also hinted at by an exclusive presentation given to a government policy committee and another talk for paediatricians of the Tuen Mun Hospital by the CI concerning art as a language for children in need (Obj. 5). Two books and two articles concerning art for traumatised children were published and uploaded to Digital Commons for free download to reach a global audience. A readership report shows that the book and article written in 2016 had received hundreds of downloads worldwide (Obj. 5). Four hundred hard copies of the book (introduction and manual) were distributed to various FCPSUs and nongovernmental organisations (NGOs) (Obj. 5). An archive of the child victims’ artworks with annotations in Chinese was published in November 2019 to demonstrate the use of art as image writing to allow children to express abstract and inner feelings (Obj. 5). Family violence is only one kind of childhood trauma. First, the CI explored the possibility of collaborating with various organisations, such as the paediatric unit of Tuen Mun Hospital, Little Life Warriors Society (LLWS), Harmony House and schools for students with special educational needs. Although all of these organisations were interested in collaborating, the CI noted some adverse factors, such as the following. - Unfavourable hospital setting – no fixed venue and risk of abrupt interruption of the programme due to quarantine concerns. - Exhausted parents – the CI developed a group therapy programme with LLWS social workers for children with cancer, but most of the parents were too exhausted to commit. - Limited manpower in small NGOs, which could not spare staff to participate in all of the group workshops. In contrast, the FCPSU (Tuen Mun) was totally committed and the CI secured collaboration with this unit after obtaining approval from the headquarters of the SWD (the process took some time). The first programme commenced in September 2016, which explains why the progress in the first year was slow. The third programme was structured in the summer, and the CI hoped to extend the project to December 2018, but the application was declined. The study of inter-generational trauma was well-integrated but under-achieving. Child abuse is still a taboo subject in Chinese culture. Although the parents involved were asked to disclose any abuse in their own childhoods, only a few were willing to discuss the issue. As the number of children involved was still relatively small, demographic subdivisions of the data collected were documented for further study.

13600015.label: Major findings and research outcome
13600015.value: The major findings were as follows.  Child victims of family violence have many repressed emotions that limit their developmental growth, leading to various psychosomatic symptoms and behavioural problems. Releasing their repressed emotions is critical to help these children.  Art as a nonverbal platform is effective and powerful in facilitating these children’s inner expression. With its guise of play and joyful nature, art easily allows children to become engaged and absorbed in their own worlds.  Spontaneous creativity connects these children with their inner worlds in the here and now, helping them to vent their hidden emotions through aggressive acts of creation. This gives them a safe platform for the release of their negative emotions.  The images and stories created by these children revealed very complicated and confusing emotions. They often confused feelings of anger and hatred, pain and fear, and sadness and regret. This explains why they found it difficult to articulate their feelings in words.  The artworks, once created, helped the children to visualise their repressed emotions and perceptions of reality. This aids identification of their developmental needs and promotes effective counselling.  A substantial amount of time and joint professional efforts are required to make real changes for these children.  Art as an intervention offers a new tool to improve social services for children.  It is urgently necessary for social workers to learn more about art as a language for children. The main research outcomes were as follows.  Twenty child victims completed and benefited from the year-long art therapy programme accomplished in this project.  Four publications, including two books and two professional journal articles, were published. The two books provide significant insights for social workers into art as a language for children in need. The latter two articles offer medical professionals and art therapists the relevant theoretical support for the use of art with children in need.  An exclusive presentation was given to a high level policy making committee at the SWD headquarters in Feb 2017.  A whole-day training seminar on the uses of art in child services was given to 40 professionals in the field of child services in November 2017.  Another training seminar organised by SWD Wong Tai Sin District Office was delivered for 80 professionals in child services in Jan. 2018.  A conference paper was presented at an international art therapy conference in 2016.

13600015.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
13600015.value: Locally, the impact on our child victims was so positive that social workers in the FCPSU (Tuen Mun) were committed to pursuing the third programme. The substantial collaboration enabled the social workers involved to integrate art as an intervention with their services. The publications and training seminars have led local professionals to focus on the uses of art in social child services. Some NGOs have invited the CI to structure more training seminars for their staff. The two books (manual and archive) provide a point of reference for further development in this area. The vision of art as a language for traumatised children has also attracted private donors’ attention. A private donation was granted to the CI to conduct a 3-year art therapy programme for traumatised teenagers in 2017. Globally, download numbers indicate that the CI’s publications (three in English and one in Chinese) are reaching a fairly large readership across Europe, the USA and China. Having compiled all of the findings, the CI will share her works at upcoming international conferences. The first one will be the PHENND Conference: Trauma + The Arts in April 2019 at the University of Pennsylvania.

13600015.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
13600015.value: In its fundamental sense, art is a language written in images. It is particularly helpful for child victims of family violence in enabling them to express and release their very complicated hidden feelings. With its guise of play and its self-directed nature, art in this project offered a non-verbal, playful and engaging platform enabling these children to liberate their inner emotions. This was pivotal to their developmental growth. In addition, the structure of the two art therapy series allowed the victims to experience a sense of security, sharing, trust, support and respect that were largely, if not entirely, lacking in their daily lives. Evaluation revealed that the year-long experience played a significant role in promoting their expressiveness, self-understanding and confidence. Making any real effort to address a social issue demands joint professional efforts. Family violence is a complex social issue and the children involved are the most helpless. Whilst conventional social services tend to adopt family-based approaches, this project took a child-centred approach. The intensive collaboration of social workers, art therapists and academia actualised in this project not only provides new tools for social child services, but also shows how inter-professional collaboration can make real changes.

13600115.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
13600115.value: Active within the ‘Bohemian Enlightenment’ in early 19th-century Prague, Bernard Bolzano (1741-1848) was a brilliant and popular professor at the Charles University. His promising academic career was cut short, however, in 1819 when the Hapsburg Emperor dismissed him and forbade him to teach publicly. Although Bolzano went on to do an enormous amount of research as a private scholar, his impact on philosophy was diminished as a result of this politically motivated suppression of his teaching. Mathematicians widely acknowledge Bolzano's important contributions to their field. Bolzano is somewhat well known in philosophy for his contributions to logic and the theory of knowledge. Edmund Husserl, the founder of phenomenology, lavishly praised Bolzano’s work in logic. Interest in other aspects of Bolzano's achievement is now increasing, and I hope to contribute to this trend. Bolzano wrote two books on aesthetics. These works have remained largely unknown, which is a pity because Bolzano was way ahead of his times. Bolzano developed a detailed and remarkably inventive definition and classification of the fine arts. He even anticipated art forms that did not yet exist. Bolzano was also a precursor to what is now called ‘everyday aesthetics’, which focuses on the place of beauty and other aesthetic qualities in everyday life. Bolzano also made a significant advance with regard to the clarification of diverse conceptions of beauty. He distinguished between 'pure' and 'mixed' kinds of beauty and described the former in terms of a special kind of cognitive process that only some objects tend to occasion. More specifically, this is a process that involves a mixture of what he called ‘clear’ and ‘dark’, ‘distinct’ and ‘confused’ thoughts--or what contemporary psychologists have called 'processing fluency'. An adequate understanding and appreciation of these and Bolzano’s other claims in aesthetics requires reference to other aspects of his philosophizing, and in particular, his views about meaning, value, and cognition. One of the goals of my research on this topic will be to provide such a contextualization of Bolzano’s books in aesthetics. More generally, my aim will be to explicate Bolzano’s contributions to aesthetics and to demonstrate their relevance and value in relation to contemporary research in this area. That is a worthwhile goal, I believe, because getting the history of the field right is an important part of philosophy, especially when the historical contributions have contemporary significance, which is true in the case of Bolzano’s aesthetics. 《博爾扎諾與美學》撮要 活躍於19世紀初「波希米亞啓蒙」時期的伯納德‧博爾扎諾曾任教於布拉格查理大學，是一位出色及受愛戴的教授。原本一片光明的學術生涯受到哈布斯堡皇帝的干預，博爾扎諾於1819年被免去教職，並被禁止公開講學。雖然遭受免職後的博爾扎諾仍以個人學者的身份從事大量的學術研究，但他對後世哲學的影響亦因此次的政治打壓而大打折扣。 博爾扎諾在數學上的成就受到廣泛的重視。他所從事的邏輯及知識論研究在哲學界也頗具名氣。現象學的始創人埃德蒙特‧胡塞爾對博爾扎諾邏輯學的著作亦賦予很高的評價。現今學界日益關注博爾扎諾其它方面的學術成就，筆者亦有志為此出一分力。 博爾扎諾撰寫了兩冊極具前瞻性的美學著作，可惜它們並未為世人所知。他發展出一個對「純藝術」既詳細又別出機杼的定義及分類，甚至預視了當時一些還未面世的藝術形式。博爾扎諾亦可算是當今所謂「日常美學」的先驅者，重視「美」及其他美感性質在日常生活中的地位。對於釐清「美」此概念的多重意義，博爾扎諾作出了別具意義的推進。他區別了「純粹」及「混雜」的美。對於前者的描述他認為涉及一種特殊的認知過程，而此種過程只由某些對象所引發。進一步而言，他稱此認知過程會混合「清澈」及「暗淡」、「明晰」及「混亂」的思想，以現代心理學的術語來說，即「處理流暢度」。 要對博爾扎諾以上的內容及其美學相關的主張有一公允的理解及評鑑，需參照考究博爾扎諾對其他領域的哲學反思，尤其他對意義、價值及認知的觀點。本研究的一個目的是為博爾扎諾的美學著作提供一個整體的脈絡。 更大的目標是闡釋博爾扎諾對美學的貢獻，論證其思想與現當代美學研究的相關性及價值。筆者相信此研究具重要的學術價值，因為釐清歷史淵源是哲學研究其中一個重要的部分，尤其當某歷史上的貢獻與當代研究依然密切相關。博爾扎諾的美學正好兼有歷史和當代意義。

13600115.label: Realisation of objectives
13600115.value: The promised book is now completed and under review. As promised in objective 1, I have also already published some of the findings in top-ranked scholarly journals in aesthetics. Together these writings realise the philosophical objectives identified in 2-4 above. I believe I have done a good job of realising these objectives. Due to my obligatory retirement on June 30, 2017, the project was shortened; with more time I could have written far more extensively about contemporary work in relation to Bolzano. As it stands, this aspect of my results is highly selective. Here is a brief outline of the book: The introduction establishes conclusively that Bolzano's contributions to aesthetics have largely been overlooked in the literature. I also identify the small number of published discussions of the topic, most of which have been published in German. I think I make a very strong case for my claim that Bolzano's work has not received sufficient attention. The introduction handles various preliminary topics and gives readers a brief overview of his life and works with special attention to issues in aesthetics. Chapter One is designed to give readers unfamiliar with Bolzano’s essay on beauty an overview of his explication of the concept of the beautiful. As Bolzano’s accounts of beauty and ugliness rely heavily on some of the claims he had made about cognition in his Theory of Science, these background assumptions are explored at some length. This is something that has definitely been missing in the small literature on the topic of Bolzano's aesthetics. I also set forth Bolzano’s argument regarding the source of the pleasure that is normally experienced when the beautiful attributes of an object are appropriately contemplated. I am definitely the first commentator to have pinned this down. Chapter Two is devoted to the detailed historical survey of previous accounts of beauty that Bolzano provided in the second half of the essay on beauty. I identify the argumentative goals pursued by Bolzano in this survey, analyse his criticisms of rival approaches, mention some pertinent oversights and omissions, and outline his most important criticisms of Kant’s analysis of beauty. The evidence presented in this chapter runs counter to the thesis that Bolzano’s views about art and beauty were essentially a derivative ‘synthesis’ of notions from Baumgarten, Kant, Herbart, or any other predecessors. Another topic that emerges in Bolzano’s survey of the literature is his explicit rejection of formalist accounts of beauty. As my aim in the book is not simply to present Bolzano’s ideas, but to engage critically with them, in Chapter Three I raise a series of objections to Bolzano’s explication of beauty and consider possible responses to them. One family of objections targets his analysis of beauty as a complex dispositional attribute. An analytic reconstruction of the account is set forth in order to provide a precise identification of possible counterexamples. Relevant passages from Bolzano's masterpiece, Theory of Science, provide an indication of how Bolzano might have responded to such objections. Another objection targets the psychological assumptions figuring within Bolzano’s account of the ‘apt contemplation’ necessary to the recognition and enjoyment of beauty. On this topic I compare Bolzano’s claims to more recent work in empirical psychology. Other objections pertain to the nature of his claims about conceptual analysis or explication, the relations between beauty and morality, and some puzzling aspects of the exposition. Epistemological questions and objections are taken up in Chapter Four, where I propose a reconstruction of Bolzano’s position on the epistemology of judgements of beauty. Here I present some of the elements of his theory of knowledge (including concepts of judgement, propositions, truth), his discussion of scepticism, and his accounts of persuasion and testimony in Theory of Science. I assess his implicit position on several different versions of the acquaintance principle, according to which first-hand experience of the object is a necessary condition on (adequate) aesthetic judgements. This latter section is a matter of bringing Bolzano's views in relation to published work in contemporary aesthetics on a central topic in the field. Chapter Five discusses Bolzano’s understanding of art in general and his explication of the subordinate concept of beautiful art. I also explore the classificatory scheme he proposed. This chapter brings to light Bolzano’s remarkable anticipation of previously unexplored art forms and art-ontological themes. Bolzano's anticipation of changing images accompanied by sound as well as his anticipation of a kind of conceptual art show just how relevant his work is to contemporary aesthetics.

13600115.label: Major findings and research outcome
13600115.value: The main thesis that I have developed and defended in this research runs as follows: writing in Bohemia in the first half of the 19th century, Bernard Bolzano devised some detailed and fascinating positions on central topics in aesthetics--positions and arguments that anticipate some findings of contemporary philosophers and psychologists. Essentially this is a matter of two distinct but related lines of argumentation: (1) his analysis of beauty (and related aesthetic properties) as being complex dispositional qualities that are apt to occasion what contemporary psychologists call 'processing fluency', a kind of pleasurable cognitive success; and (2) his traditional 'skill' based notion of art in general and his aesthetic-based conception of the specificity of the fine arts; his subsequent rigorous elaboration of a classificatory framework for the fine arts, which lead him to anticipate a variety of art forms that were only practically developed many years after Bolzano's death. Furthermore, Bolzano's sophisticated views in epistemology, including his highly informative account of testimony and persuasion, allowed him to advance robust claims on a number of key issues in the epistemology of aesthetic and artistic matters, including a lucid position on what is often called 'the acquaintance principle' in aesthetics.

13600115.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
13600115.value: As the literature of contemporary aesthetics is truly enormous, it was impossible in this research to make comprehensive and systematic reference to the welter of rival views on all of the main topics. There are of course many topics about which Bolzano had little or nothing to say, partly because his illness prevented him from finishing all of his ambitious projects in aesthetics. Yet there are other topics about which he did make some pronouncements and it would be possible to say more about the implications for contemporary debates. One topic that could be developed, for example, is the limitation of the sort of very strong moralism Bolzano apparently defended in his discussion of topics in aesthetics.

13600115.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
13600115.value: According to an old saying, people who ignore history are bound to repeat it. This is true of aesthetics, the sub-field of philosophy that deals with beauty and art. In particular, generations of philosophers have overlooked two very inventive essays that were written by Bernard Bolzano in German in the first half of the 19th century. In this research project, Bolzano's little-known discoveries are presented to readers who have not read his untranslated essays; the relevance of Bolzano's ideas to contemporary debates on these matters is demonstrated. Very briefly, Bolzano devised the idea that beautiful objects are those that make possible a certain kind of pleasurable and 'fluency' cognitive processing. He thought of the 'fine' arts, as opposed to various other useful kinds of arts, as those that are devised to make possible this kind of intrinsically valuable contemplative or observational experience. Surveying the various means or media that fine artists could employ, Bolzano set forth a classification of the fine arts. In so doing he literally discovered art forms that would only come into existence many years after his death.

13600315.label: Project Objectives
13600315.value: To examine the intended meanings of the ancient Chinese references to interpreters and interpreting. To analyze the hidden values associated with these textual references, and their significance. To make links with the approaches taken by Western and other East Asian translation scholars to the archival traces and origins of interpreters. To find out why interpreting captured chroniclers’ attention. Although interpreters are often ‘invisible’ in China’s archives, the act of interpreting is not. To examine if interpreters as portrayed in the archives were diplomatic agents or subordinates to such agents. To determine if the relatively inferior official ranking of interpreters was a result of their frequent contact with the foreigners, Yi 夷. To identify the motives of the imperial Chinese government in emphasising diplomatic and tributary visits facilitated by relay interpreters in its archival records; and to map out the intrinsic connections between interpreting and tributary visits from vassal states in ancient China.

13600315.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
13600315.value: Textual archival references to interpreters and interpreting are crucial sources for a critical examination of the meanings and significance of linguistic mediators and mediation in ancient time. Scarce even in the Chinese archives, these earlier texts throw light on the work nature of the inter-lingual practitioners during a time when written records were flimsy worldwide. The data of this project is culled from classical writings about interpreting in China’s standard histories, political treatises, memorials, literary pieces, annotations, and commentaries up to 600CE. This time frame was characterized by the frequent interaction between the “civilized” Chinese and the “less-civilized” peoples in and surrounding China. Notwithstanding the broad temporal span, the amount of archival texts relating to interpreters and interpreting is limited to 255 entries as identified by Hung in 2005. These entries, however, can be categorized into general and specific references before further analyses are conducted. This project will explore the meanings of these two types of reference in context. It will also examine the nature of interpreting duties. More precisely, the research questions include: Did the earliest Chinese expressions denoting interpreters (‘ji’, 寄; ‘xiang’, 象; ‘Didi’, 狄鞮; and ‘yi’, 譯) have specific meanings, or were they simply phonetic translations of words in foreign tongues? What were the concrete purposes of textual references to these intermediaries in the archives of imperial China? Did such references have primarily symbolic, spatial, ideological or pragmatic value? This subject was recently approached, but the discussions are inconclusive, and most problematically, at times, plagued with fundamental flaws. The definitions of terms relating to interpreters and interpreting were inconsistent and controversial. These unresolved issues need to be addressed. Crucially, this project takes on some new research questions, not previously examined in the literature. Its findings will thus provide a platform from which to undertake further analysis of the documented origins and ideological significance of acts of interpreting between China and its neighboring regions. This project has three objectives. The first objective is to examine the intended meanings of the ancient references to interpreters and interpreting. The second objective is to analyze the hidden values and significance of these textual references. The third objective is to compare the research methodology with approaches taken in Western and other Asian translation studies to the origins and archival traces of interpreting. 史料中有關口譯人員和口譯活動的記載至為重要，有助探索古時口譯人員和口譯的意義及其重要性。中國史料中有關口譯人員和口譯活動的記載雖然匱乏，可是相關記載仍揭示了，在各國文字記錄還沒普及的年代裡，語際轉換工作的關鍵人物。本研究的資料採集自公元600年前，中國正史、政論、奏摺、文學作品、評註和評述中有關口譯的古籍記載。 此時期的特徵是自恃「文化優越」的華夏民族和國內外「文化稍遜」者之間的頻密交流。雖然時間跨度長，但孔慧怡在2005年指出，該時段的史料只記載了255項與口譯人員和口譯活動相關的紀錄。然而，在開展進一步研究前，這些紀錄可歸類為一般的口譯史料和特定的口譯史料。 本研究將探討這兩種口譯史料中的特定語境，也會探索口譯職務的性質。更明確的說，研究問題包括：漢語裡最初對於口譯人員的職稱(寄、象、狄鞮和譯)到底是有特定含義，還是純粹從外語音譯而來？把這些口譯人員錄入中國史料的實質目的是什麼？這些是否具有象徵意義、地緣空間意義、意識形態意義或實質意義？ 有關的課題近年備受關注，但討論還未有一致的定案，最大的問題是，有些論據不盡不實，而口譯人員和口譯活動相關的術語定義既不一致又具爭議性，這些問題必須要處理。本研究著重討論一些文獻裡從沒處理過的課題。這樣，研究結果將會是重要的平台，讓學者進一步分析包括中國和鄰近地區之間有記載的口譯活動和其意義。本研究有三個目的。第一，探索史籍中記載口譯人員和口譯活動的意義；第二，分析這些史料的隱藏價值和重要性；第三，把翻譯研究中，口譯活動在史料裡的起源及發展軌跡和其他中外論著聯繫起來。

13600315.label: Realisation of objectives
13600315.value: The stated objectives were realized. This study succeeded in exploring the underlying cultural and ideological significance of textual references to Yi (interpret / translate) and Chongyi (relay translation). Going beyond the surface meaning, this study taps in the metaphorical, cultural, and political meanings embedded in the expression of terms relating to translation or interpretation in the ancient Chinese text. Based on the consolidated data set of 180 passages containing Yi, the study further categorized the data into several themes or sub-categories, to be discussed in the result section. Such further processing of the data set enables the researcher to approach the intended meanings and the hidden values (objectives 1 and 2) of textual references containing yi. The same translation actions seem to be viewed quite differently by the Chinese host and its visitors. Yi is used to describe the Chinese attempt to explore foreign territories through interpreters, but only chongyi is used for foreign envoys' China visits in my corpus. The distinct usage suggests the Sinocentric mentality embedded in the conscious use of chongyi. Besides, the foreign envoys’ efforts to visit China through interpreters were keenly documented by Chinese chroniclers, officials and literati as the utmost respect shown to the host. This view is a stretch, because these contingent linguistic measures taken by the envoys were communicative moves in essence. Moreover, qualitative analysis suggests that wordings referring to ‘interpreting’ do not actually denote linguistic mediation. After examining their broader contexts, references to ‘interpreting’ are found to function as reference points to inform spatial and cultural dynamics of Sinitic China and its counterparts. Objectives 7 and 4 were also achieved when the researcher noticed the sophisticated and elaborate and yet Sino-centric overtone in the Sinitic Chinese narrative in the description and documentation of visiting envoys' use of interpreters to pay tribute. The chroniclers' approach quite likely reflects the rhetoric of the ancient Chinese governments across centuries in Early China. For example, I identified a rhetorical pattern of the use of "envoys visiting China through chongyi" in ancient China as events to corroborate auspicious signs observed years earlier in eight passages. In these texts, ‘relay interpreting’ is documented not because of its practical communicative function in diplomatic contexts. Instead, the documentation has an unmistakably auspicious connotation, which goes beyond its linguistic purpose. The elevation of an interpreting act to a cultural icon is unique in the Chinese tradition. Objective 3 has not been fully achieved, because data about interpreting in Europe and East Asia before 600AD is scarce. Straight comparison is difficult to undertake. What I can manage in this aspect is simply general comparison at best at this stage. The act of translation triggers imagination across cultures. Notwithstanding our ignorance about its sophisticated cognitive mechanism, the magic wand that transforms a text from one language to another is whimsical all the same. The mystic charm of translation in the western tradition is rooted in, and for centuries often associated with, religion and spirituality. In this tradition, God’s will is portrayed as the central and ultimate force in the creation of biblical translations. For instance, the alleged mystical creation of Joseph Smith’s English translation of the Book of Mormon speaks of the miraculous nature of translating and translation. Besides, the all-mighty wonder over the creation of a perfectly identical translation as in the Septuagint among seventy-two translators is miraculous. Whether these preternatural events did happen is irrelevant. Of importance is simply to be aware of these numinous elements in the western translation tradition. This mystical link with translation, however, is not unique to the western culture. Mystical elements were also found in the diplomatic visits, through interpreters, to Sinitic China. In such descriptions, relay interpreting was often associated with roseate and propitious state of Sinitic China. Besides, diplomatic relay interpreting was often taken as an event to confirm or validate auspicious signs predicting good fortune for Sinitic China. It is intriguing how both the western and Chinese traditions relate inter-lingual communication to some mystic and augury spells. Objective 5 was reasonably achieved even though interpreters were hardly mentioned in the ancient Chinese text pertaining to interpreting, apart from limited information on interpreters in these texts. Terms denoting interpreters across different language cultures could be traced as connected and associated. The borrowing and adoption of terms that refer to ‘translators’ from one language culture to another seems to be quite common as well in ancient languages, although the direction of borrowing is not always clear from existing evidence. Similar linguistic adoption for the meanings of “interpret” or “translate” was found in the Chinese context too. Examining terminologies for ‘interpreters’ would also bear methodology implications. Mairs (2012) was concerned that the semantic ambiguity in the Latin (interpres) and Greek (hermêneus) references for ‘interpreters’ in the Roman empire might have misinformed the archival traces located, given their wide range of connotations, such as ‘commercial go-between’, trade facilitator, or ‘negotiator’. If the researchers end up getting materials mistakenly compiled based on which they then try to explain and theorize, a different sets of conclusions would be falsely drawn. The linguistic references to ‘interpreters’ cannot therefore be taken for granted, but should be finely analyzed, giving due consideration to their historical contexts of usage. Objective 4 is well achieved. While the interpreters are made invisible in these references, the act of interpreting is not. The ancient Chinese emphasis is on the act and the concept of interpreting rather than the agent of interpreting, as evidenced in the passages in the data set. For instance, the practical communicative function of translation was systematically downplayed with the intent to trumpet Sinocentric ideologies. The same translation actions seem to be viewed quite differently by the Chinese host and its visitors. Yi is used to describe the Chinese attempt to explore foreign territories through interpreters, but only chongyi is used for foreign envoys' China visits in my corpus. The distinct usage suggests the Sinocentric mentality embedded in the conscious use of chongyi. Besides, the foreign envoys’ efforts to visit China through interpreters were keenly documented by Chinese chroniclers, officials and literati as the utmost respect shown to the host. Objective 6 was largely achieved. More than a millennium ago before the interpreting official’s subordinate image was first depicted in the Chinese silk painting in early Tang China, however, numerous ritual and political treatises bearing records to interpreters and interpreting can often be found. Lifting the study onto a cultural plane, I managed to ruminate interpreters and the cultural and ideological contexts of the time. Apart from discussing the literal meaning of these texts documenting interpreters and interpreting, I argue that these textual references serve to relate a Sino-centric ideology between the “civilized” Chinese on the central plain and the “less civilized” non-Chinese in the periphery. My observation testifies the use of interpreting concepts in these texts to trumpet for the Sino-centric superiority, which in themselves have little bearings on language mediation. In other word, literally, in the ancient Chinese context, interpreters and interpreting were complimented for their importance in bridging communication in Sinitic China’s encounter with the foreigners. Yet, ironically in their essence, the core values of these Chinese rhetoric were to promote instead the Sino-centric ideology, in which language mediators played no more than a secondary role.
