14500715.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14500715.value: Online peer-to-peer (P2P) lending is the practice of making unsecured microloans to individual borrowers, or “peers”, through online platforms without the mediation of a traditional financial intermediary such as a bank or other traditional financial institution. In the absence of financial intermediaries, the borrowers’ financial background and information cannot be fully and honestly disclosed to the lenders. In addition, borrowers and lenders in the P2P marketplaces are completely anonymous. Hence, information asymmetry exists between lenders and borrowers which could eventually lead to adverse selection and moral hazard problems. The solutions to these information asymmetry problems include signaling and screening. Signaling is the term for the observable actions taken or signals given by the more informed party to the less informed party in an attempt to convey meaningful information about itself to the less informed party. Screening, in contrast, is the action taken by the less informed party to learn as much information as possible from the more informed party. Prior research on online P2P lending focuses mainly on signaling but rarely on screening. Of all signals investigated, trust, friendship, and social network have received the most research interest. In the proposed study, we will develop a model to evaluate how language analysis (as a signal) and imitation (as a screening method) can reduce information asymmetry, and in turn improve bidding performance. We further propose that social media use and lenders’ risk attitudes play critical roles in affecting information asymmetry reduction and bidding performance. Both objective and subjective data will be collected from PpDai to evaluate the proposed research model and hypotheses. Innovative techniques — LIWC for Chinese text analysis and PROCESS for dichotomous data analysis — will also be used to derive our research findings. 在线个人对个人（P2P）借贷是通过网上平台，省卻传统金融机构 (如银行) 作為中介的小额金钱借贷。在没有金融中介机构的仲裁下，借款人的财务背景和资料不能得到充分、如实的披露给贷款人，從而導致贷款人和借款人信息的不对称，最终引發逆向选择和道德风险的问题。要解决信息不对称的问题，借贷雙方可以採用信令或筛选的解決方案。信令是知情較多的一方尝试传达多些有關自身的資訊予知情較少的一方。与此相反，筛选是知情较少的一方盡量學習知情較多一方的有關信息。 在本研究中，我们認為借方的语言使用（作为一種信号）和貸方的模仿（作为一种筛选方法）可以减少信息的不对称和提高競投的成效。我们还認為社会化媒体的使用和贷款人的风险态度亦會影响信息的不对称与競标的成效。要証實這些論點，我們將會從拍拍貸 (PPDai) 網站收集客观和主观数据来评估我們所提出的研究模型和假设。我们亦會使用创新技术 (包括 LIWC文字分析处理和PROCESS二分类数据分析) 來引証我們的研究

14500715.label: Realisation of objectives
14500715.value: The three objectives designed into the project have been fully achieved. Objective one: Signals of imitation and language In achieving this objective, , loan listings containing loan descriptions were processed automatically with the Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC) software. LIWC is a computer-based text analysis program that can analyze more than 70 language dimensions of written or spoken samples on a word-by-word basis. This software, combined with the Chinese LIWC dictionary, was used to determine the scores of internal imagination, dissonance, and negative emotion. With the use of LIWC, Language analysis was measured in three dimensions, internal imagination, dissonance, and negative emotion.. Internal imagination was assessed by counting the number of temporal words (e.g. yesterday, today, now, afternoon) in each loan description to determine the extent of its deceptive information. This measure was based on the assumption of reality monitoring theory, which suggests that events from real, external experience contain more temporal information than information generated from fabricated, internal imagination. Dissonance was measured by the number of disassociating words in a loan description and determined the extent of dissonance. This measure was based on previous studies suggesting that deceivers tend to use more non-first-person pronouns (e.g. you, your, her, she, he, they) to disassociate themselves from their fabricated stories. Negative emotion was assessed by counting the number of negating words in the loan listings. Past research has found that deceivers tend to use more negation words (e.g. hurt, ugly, nasty) due to the guilt they experience when lying. The values of language analysis were obtained by averaging these three dimensions. Objective 2: the integrative effect In testing the integrative effect of imitation, language, and bidder’s characteristics on bidding outcome, logistic regressions were performed using Stata. In addition to these independent variables, this study adopted five moderators (lenders’ bidding experience, lenders’ PPDai membership duration, borrowers’ and lenders’ friendship ties, and risk attitude) to evaluate their effects on the relationship between our independent and dependent variables. Based on these independent and control variables, the following integrative model was investigated: logit(p)=α0+α1 Controls+α2 Imitation+ α3 Language+α4 Credit+ α5 Experience+α6 Experience×Imitation+α7 Membership+ α8 Membership×Imitation+α9 BFriendship+ α10 BFriendship×Language+α11 LFriendship+α12 LFriendship×Language+α13 RiseAverse+α14 RiskAverse×Credit+α15 RiskSeeking + α16 RiskTaking×Credit_i+ α17 Imitation×Credit+ α18 Language×Credit Using this approach, a series of regression analyses were run in a specific order, each with one or more variable(s) than the previous regression analysis. In Model 1, only the control variables were regressed against the dependent variable. In Model 2, the three main predictor variables (imitation behavior, language analysis, and borrower’s credit) were added. Subsequently, the moderators proposed in this study (bidding experience, membership age, borrower’s friendship, lenders’ friendship, risk-aversion, and risk-taking) were added to Model 2, thereby creating Models 3-5. To better interpret the significance levels of the moderators, we added the moderators for each main variable one by one. In Model 6, the interaction effects of the three independent variables were tested for the simultaneous effect of imitation and language analysis on supplementing creditworthiness. Objective 3: Lenders' risk attitude This study assumes P2P lenders approach gains and losses differently, generally acting risk-averse on gains and risk-seeking on losses. In other words, if outcomes are perceived to be better than the reference point, then lenders will be more risk-averse. However, if outcomes are perceived to be worse than the reference point, then lenders will be more risk-seeking. Hence, in classifying lenders to be of risk-averse, neutral, and risk-taking, we find the prospect theory to be applicable. Following the guideline of this theory, risk-averse lenders were considered to be the high performers in the gain domain who avoided risk. Alternatively, risk-taking lenders were the low performers in the loss domain who sought risk. In other words, risk-averse lenders followed a positive risk-return pattern and risk-seeking lenders followed a negative one. Based on this classification, lenders were classified and analysed using logistic regression.

14500715.label: Major findings and research outcome
14500715.value: In this study, we developed a model to evaluate whether imitation and language analysis can complement creditworthiness in improving bidding performance. Data from China’s PPDai were used to evaluate our research model and hypotheses. The results suggest that creditworthiness, imitation, and language analysis were all effective in bidding success. However, the imitation-creditworthiness relationship was found to have a surprising substitutable effect. This study not only proposes that new signals should be implemented but also suggests that these new signals are subject to the influence of a lender’s personal attributes. Among the attributes proposed to moderate imitation behaviors, we found lenders’ bidding experience to be critical. Although lenders’ membership age was not found to be a significant moderator of imitation, its direct effect on bidding success was significant. With respect to the moderator language analysis, lenders’, but not borrowers’, friendship ties were found to be significant. Further, the risk attitude of lenders, both risk-averse and risk-taking, was found to be a critical moderator of borrowers’ creditworthiness. Finally, we found imitation to have a substitution effect on creditworthiness in evaluating listings and bidding success. This finding is thought provoking and deserves further investigation. In summary, a total of seven major hypotheses were postulated in this study, the results of these investigations are stated as follows: H1: Imitation can improve lenders’ bidding success. (supported) H2: Lenders’ experience can moderate the relationship between imitation and bidding success. Specifically, lenders’ bidding experience interacts negatively (a) and membership age interacts positively (b) with imitation to affect bidding success. (H2a supported, H2b not supported) H3: Language analyses of deception can improve lenders’ bidding success. (supported) H4: Friendship ties of lenders and borrowers can moderate the relationship between deception analysis and bidding success. Specifically, borrowers’ friendship ties interact positively (a), but lenders’ friendship ties interact negatively (b) with language analysis for greater bidding success. (H4a: Not supported, H4b supported) H5: Borrowers’ creditworthiness can improve lenders’ bidding success. (supported) H6: The risk attitude of lenders will moderate the relationship between creditworthiness and bidding success. Specifically, risk-averse lenders are more likely to consider higher creditworthy borrowers (a) and risk-seeking lenders are more likely to consider lower creditworthy borrowers (b) for bidding success. (H6a: supported, H6b: supported) H7: Imitation (a) and language analysis (b) can complement, rather than substitute, creditworthiness in bidding performance improvement. (H7a: not supported, H7b: not supported)

14500715.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14500715.value: To the best of our knowledge, this study is the first attempt to evaluate three P2P lending signals (imitation, creditworthiness, and language), and to provide empirical evidence of the complementary or substitutable relationships across them. However, the finding that imitation is substitutionary rather than complementary to creditworthiness is thought provoking. The insignificant yet deceptive cues on whether to complement or substitute creditworthiness also warrant further investigation. With these two unexpected findings, we believe that theories exploring the interplay of bounded rationality and irrational auction behaviors might provide insights into understanding the signals’ coming from complementarity and substitutability in reducing information asymmetry. Would auction fever and its associated phenomena (such as commitment escalation and competitive arousal) play a role in a signaling relationship? When auctions become intense, bounded rational lenders are susceptible to the influence of auction fever due to the win-lose nature of the activity. Past research has confirmed that a consequence of auction fever is “competitive arousal,” which results in anxiety, rivalry, and recognition of scarcity to impair decision-making and influence irrational decisions. This competitive arousal phenomenon and other auction fever phenomena need to be explored further for their direct, indirect, and interactive effects on the interplay between bidding signals and bounded rationality.

14500715.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14500715.value: Online peer-to-peer microloan lending practices are becoming prevalent worldwide. However, information asymmetry between the lenders and borrowers in this market may result in adverse selection and moral hazard problems that can eventually lead to high risk in loan lending. In this study, we propose a holistic approach to evaluating solutions to the information asymmetry problem in P2P lending. We propose new signals of imitation and language analysis, along with credit information and friendship ties, in lending decisions. Our findings suggest that these signals have a direct and significant effect on bidding success, and they are also consistent with the results of most prior studies of online P2P lending. This study makes a few important contributions. First, our findings provide evidence on the effectiveness, both direct and moderated, of linguistic and imitation signals in bidding success. Second, this study provides evidence to confirm the roles of different signals, both individually and jointly, in reducing information asymmetry. Third, our study uses a new methodology, LIWC, for Chinese language data analysis. This technique has seldom been applied in IS research. We hope our use of this technique enhances IS researchers’ understanding of its applicability in empirical IS research.

14500815.label: Project Title(Chinese)
14500815.value: 生育对母亲劳动市场行为和经济福利的生命周期影响：基于生育對母親勞動市場行為和經濟福利的生命週期影響

14500815.label: Project Objectives
14500815.value: To construct a longitudinal individual-level data set of the entire Dutch population (~17 million individuals) combining administrative records on socio-demographics with administrative records on labor force participation, earnings, non-labor income, and pension entitlements. To estimate the causal effect of childbearing on mothers’ market behavior and economic well-being over the life cycle by exploiting the plausibly exogenous variation in childbearing due to sibling-sex composition as well as its interaction with mother’s age at birth. To distinguish between the immediate effects of childbearing (e.g., duration of labor force withdrawal, earnings, non-labor income) and the long-run effects (e.g., retirement age, pension entitlements) and estimate them separately. To explore heterogeneity in the effect of childbearing on the basis of women’s previous labor market history and other characteristics, in order to provide recommendations on which specific population subgroups to target on public policies aimed at assisting maternity and mitigating the adverse impacts of childbearing on mothers’ subsequent labor market outcomes and economic well-being.

14500815.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14500815.value: While substantial research in economics and other social sciences documents a negative relationship between fertility and female labor supply/earnings, the interpretations of these negative correlations remain unclear because fertility and labor market behavior are jointly determined decisions of household utility maximization. A few prior studies that have examined the causal link running from fertility to females’ labor market behavior and outcomes are almost all cross-sectional studies and are restricted to examining the effect of fertility on mothers’ labor market behavior and outcomes at a specific time in the life cycle, usually during or immediately after childbearing. Any inferences concerning the life-cycle effects of childbearing drawn from these cross-sectional evidences are subject to contamination due to cohort differences in the behavioral responses to childbearing, which have been demonstrated to be very important. This project plans to employ rich population-wide administrative records from the Netherlands containing longitudinal information on labor force participation, earnings, non-labor income, the retirement age, and pension receipt after retirement to examine the life-cycle effects of childbearing on mothers’ market behavior and economic well-being. In contrast to the existing literature, this project will be able to estimate duration models that allow drawing the full dynamic labor force response to childbearing rather than the cross-sectional snapshot of labor supply and earnings; with the availability of women’s employment and earnings history prior to childbearing, it will also be able to examine the heterogeneity in such effects by mothers’ prior employment history. Furthermore, it will also expand the scope of the existing literature to investigate the long-run consequences of childbearing on mothers, such as retirement decision and well-being after retirement. In addition to improving our understanding of the causal effect of childbearing on the dynamics of women’s labor market/retirement decisions and earnings/retirement entitlements, the findings of this project can also have important implications on which specific population subgroups to target on public policies that are aimed at assisting maternity and mitigating the adverse impacts of childbearing on mothers’ subsequent market work and economic well-being. 經濟學和其他社會科學都發現女性的勞動供給和收入與生育率的負相關性。但因為生育率和勞動市場行為都是在效用最大化下共同內生決定的家庭行為，對這些負相關性的解釋目前仍不清楚。一些早期的關於生育率對女性的勞動市場行為的因果作用的研究都是基於橫截面數據並侷限於生育率對女性生命週期中某一時期的勞動市場行為和結果的影響，往往是在懷孕和哺乳期間或緊隨其後。由這些橫截面證據推斷得來的有關生育對女性整個生命週期的影響都會被不同代際之間對生育的行為反應的差異所干擾，而此前的研究表明此差異非常明顯。 本項目計劃使用覆蓋全民的荷蘭行政數據庫，包括勞動市場參與、勞動收入、非勞動收入、退休年齡、退休金等時間序列的個體信息，來研究生育對女性市場行為和經濟福利的生命週期影響。不同與已有的文獻，本項目可估計持續時間的模型，從而能到全面的、動態的生育對女性勞動市場行為的影響；利用女性生育前的就業和收入的有關歷史數據，研究生育對女性勞動市場行為的影響與母親生育前的就業歷史的關聯。此外，本項目也會擴展現有文獻所涉及的領域，研究生育對母親的長期影響，例如退休的時間選擇和退休後的福利。除了增進我們關於生育對女性勞動市場/退休決定以及勞動收入/退休金的動態影響的認識，本項目的結果也可以啟發制定相關的公共政策以針對特定女性群體的提供幫助成為母親以及減少生育對她們接下來的勞動參與和經濟福利的負面影響。

14500815.label: Realisation of objectives
14500815.value: 1. We obtained data on demographics, parents-children links, employment status, hours of work, labour earnings, non-labour incomes, tax payments, as well as childcare subsidy receipts for the entire Dutch population from various administrative records. The time spans of these data sets differ substantially. While basic demographics and employment status are available since late 1990s, job and wage registers containing hours of work and labour earnings variables are available only after 2006. The relative short time span of the latter variables imposes some restrictions for taking a look at the long-run or entire life-cycle effects of childbearing. 2. We employed two identification strategies to estimate the causal effect of childbearing on parents’ labour market behaviour: sibling-sex composition and event-study approach. a. The sibling-sex composition strategy is exactly what we proposed in the research proposal. Another idea proposed in the proposal is to interact the sibling-sex composition with mother’s age at birth. However, when we implemented this idea practically, we found a rather weak first stage, raising concerns over the weak-instrument problem for continuing going this direction. b. Since the sibling-sex composition instrument can be only used to estimate the effect of higher-parity births (i.e., having 3 or more children), which becomes less and less common over time, we also searched for alternative identification strategy. We discovered a few studies published very recently (e.g., Angelov et al. 2016; Kleven et al., 2019) that employ the event-study approach to exploit the variation in the timing of first birth for identification of the causal effect of childbirth among parents with children. We followed these studies and employed the event-study approach. This event-study approach has two advantages over the conventional sibling-sex composition instrument. First, it allows estimating the causal effect of the first childbirth on parents’ labour market behaviour. Second, by construction, it allows the effects of childbirth to be dynamic to the child’s lifetime as the estimated event coefficients are child-age specific. However, resorting to the event-study approach also imposes restrictions for estimating the effects of childbearing on women’s later-life labour market outcomes that we initially proposed, which we elaborate in more details below. 3. By construction, the event-study approach estimates separate effects of childbearing on parents when the first child is of different ages. Therefore, all of our estimates distinguish the effects of childbearing by child age. However, since employing the event-study approach requires the construction of a panel data set with mothers who had given their first birth during the panel period and our panel only spans and our panel spans only 12 years (from 2006 to 2017), from which we had to further exclude 2006 and 2007 data for pre-trend testing. Thus, our baseline analysis focuses on estimating the immediate effects of childbearing during preschool years (i.e., before the child reaches age 4) employing a balanced panel two years before and three years after childbirth. Nonetheless, we still explore estimating the longer-term effects of childbearing by employing an unbalanced panel for the event-study estimation. Specifically, for the first cohort of women in our analysis who gave birth in 2008, we are able to estimate the effects of childbearing up to 9 years after child birth. Thus, although we indeed distinguish between the immediate effects of childbearing and the longer-term effects, the estimated longer-term effects are capped at 9 years after birth and are shorter than we initially had in mind when we prepared the proposal. Moreover, since almost no woman in our analysis sample (who gave first birth between 2008 and 2016) had reached retirement age by year 2017, the last year with available data, we are unable to estimate the effects of childbearing on women’s retirement well-being such as pension entitlements. 4. We have explored heterogeneity in the effects of childbearing by conducting some subgroup analysis. Our efforts have focused on testing alternative hypotheses for the existence of child penalty measured by the enlarged gender gap in working behaviour and earnings after childbirth. First, we conduct separate estimates for a subsample of couples where the mother out-earns the father before childbirth to test the hypothesis of whether the existence of child penalty can be explained by optimal specialisation within the family. Second, we conduct separate estimates for a small sample of lesbian couples to test the role of gender norms in determining the child penalty. We admit that there are more rooms to further explore the heterogeneity and shed more insights on better-targeted public policies to mitigate the adverse effects of childbearing on mothers’ subsequent labour market outcomes and economic well-being. (2019) “Children and Gender Inequality: Evidence from Denmark,” American Economic Journal: Applied Economics, 11(4): 181-209.

14500815.label: Major findings and research outcome
14500815.value: In Rellstab, van Kippersluis, and Zhang (2019), we apply an event-study approach to the universe of Dutch parents with a first child born between 2008 and 2014 to first estimate the child penalty for the Netherlands. We find large and persistent child penalty for the Netherlands. Although there are modest differences in hours of work and earnings between fathers and mothers before the birth of a child, we find these differences increase dramatically after childbirth. Three years after childbirth, the gap between fathers and mothers has increased to over 500 hours for yearly hours of work and and over 11,000 Euros for yearly earnings. The gap is still increasing towards the end of our observation period up to 9 years after childbirth. We next exploit the unprecedented policy variation in the generosity of childcare policies in the Netherlands to establish whether childcare policies can reduce the child penalty. In particular, we exploit two measures of the childcare subsidy reforms in the Netherlands taken place in 2012 and 2013 that first restricted and linked the subsidised hours of childcare to the minimum of hours of work of the couple and then drastically reduced the hourly subsidy rate. In exploiting these reforms, we simulate the predicted maximum yearly subsidised hours of childcare for each couple who gave first birth after 2009 by applying the transition probabilities for employment status, hours of work, and joint income of the baseline cohort of couples who had given their first birth in 2008, and then interact this predicted exposure to the reforms with the event time dummies for childbirth to identify the causal effect of childcare policies on child penalty up to three years after childbirth. We find a non-negligible moderating effect of changes in the childcare subsidy policy on the child penalty. In particular, our estimates suggest that childcare reforms over the last decade led to a convergence in the hours of work between fathers and mothers, reducing the child penalty by about 4%. In a technical paper, van Kippersluis and Rietveld (2018) employ the Dutch population registrar data as an example to employ a two-step procedure that tests and relaxes the exclusion restriction of the instrument. Their 2SLS estimates show that that an additional child reduces the probability of working by 2.9 percentage points (4%) and reduces hours of work by 24%.

14500815.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14500815.value: We identify four areas for further development: First, we will further explore mechanisms through which changes in childcare policies affecting the child penalty. Regarding the changes in the Dutch childcare policies during our study period, we would like to distinguish between the effects of the restricted subsidised hours of childcare and reduced hourly subsidy rate. Second, we will conduct welfare analysis and possibly simulate the effects of potential childcare policy reforms on various stakeholders, including the government, families with and without children, etc. Third, we will conduct more heterogeneity analysis across different subgroups to shed more lights on better-targeted policies to mitigate the adverse effects of childbearing on women’s subsequent labour market outcomes and economic well-being. Fourth, we will also explore linking our data to the actual childcare use data to link the effects of childcare policies on parents’ labour market behaviour to the take-ups of childcare use.

14500815.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14500815.value: We apply an event-study approach to estimate the gender gap in labour market outcomes after childbirth using the universe of Dutch parents with a first child born between 2008 and 2014. Although there are modest differences in hours of work and earnings between fathers and mothers before the birth of a child, we find these differences increase dramatically after childbirth. And the gap is still increasing towards the end of our observation period up to 9 years after childbirth. We also exploit the unprecedented policy variation in the generosity of childcare policies in the Netherlands to establish whether childcare policies can reduce the child penalty. In particular, we exploit two measures of the childcare subsidy reforms in the Netherlands taken place in 2012 and 2013 that first restricted and linked the subsidised hours of childcare to the minimum of hours of work of the couple and then drastically reduced the hourly subsidy rate. We find a non-negligible moderating effect of changes in the childcare subsidy policy on the child penalty, resulting in a convergence in the labour market behaviour between fathers and mothers.

14501015.label: Project Title(Chinese)
14501015.value: 對立情緒陰影下的跨國公司:基於產品銷售的研究

14501015.label: Project Objectives
14501015.value: We will investigate the impacts of the anti-Japanese demonstration of 2010 in China on the sales of Japanese-brand automobiles relative to those of brands of other countries. We will examine the channels mediating the impacts of the demonstrations on Japanese automobile sales in China.
rows: We will investigate the impacts of the anti-Japanese demonstration of 2010 in China on the sales of Japanese-brand automobiles relative to those of brands of other countries.
We will examine the channels mediating the impacts of the demonstrations on Japanese automobile sales in China.

14501015.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14501015.value: This proposed project plans to use the three waves of anti-Japanese demonstrations in China in 2005, 2010 and 2012 as shocks of interstate friction and oppositional sentiments to study the impacts of the shift in international relations on multinational enterprises. In the past 15 years, economic interdependence between China and Japan grew rapidly, but at the same time bilateral political relations and non-governmental exchanges and cooperation entered tumultuous waters. Given that China and Japan are the current world’s second and third largest economies, the coexistence of close economic linkage and interstate hostilities provides us with a good setting to study whether oppositional sentiments can create shocks to and cast negative impacts on business operations and expansion strategies of multinational enterprises. We investigate whether product sales and overseas acquisitions of multinationals were affected by the shocks of the three anti-Japanese demonstrations in China. First, we examine the case of Japanese-brand automobile sales in China before and after the anti-Japanese demonstration. Japan is one of the world’s leading automobile manufacturing countries. But at the same time, automobiles are a primary target product of consumer boycott and government regulatory sanctions. By comparing the changes in Japanese-brand automobile sales in the wake of the anti-Japanese protests with the corresponding changes for indigenous brands and other countries’ brands, we can find direct evidence on whether interstate animosity hit multinationals’ product sales. Second, we investigate the case of Japanese acquisitions of Chinese targets. Japan is a leading capital exporter. Japanese multinationals are well known for their merger and acquisition activities around the world. But overseas acquisitions can often meet the resistance from local people and regulatory authorities. We will compare the changes in various aspects of Japanese acquisitions of Chinese targets following anti-Japanese protests with the corresponding changes for acquirers from other countries, from which we can understand whether Chinese nationalism deterred Japanese multinationals’acquisitions. At the same time, the Chinese overseas acquisitions have grown rapidly in recent years. The interstate hostilities, however, may also deter Chinese acquisitions of Japanese targets. We therefore will analyze the situations for Chinese acquisitions too. Third, we will make use of the cross-region and cross-industry variations to shed light on the channels mediating the impacts of oppositional sentiments upon multinationals. We will pay particular attention to the roles played by war memories, nationalism promoted by government propaganda, government's regulatory intervention, the occurrence of strong protests, and local residents’attitude. 14501015.label: Realisation of objectives
14501015.value: Our work on the project mainly consists of two stages so far. In the first stage, we carry out our work according to our research proposal. Based on the data we obtained by that time and consistent with the research plan in the research proposal, we mainly investigate the impacts of the anti-Japanese demonstration of 2010 in China, i.e., the incident of fishing craft collision in September 2010, on the sales of Japanese-brand automobiles relative to those of brands of other countries. Our main findings can be summarized as follows. Firstly, by comparing the changes in Japanese-brand automobile sales in the wake of the anti-Japanese protests with the corresponding changes for Chinese domestic brands and other countries’ brands, we find direct evidence that the boycott following interstate animosity hit multinationals’ product sales. Secondly, it is mainly the individuals rather than corporations or government entities that curtailed saliently their purchases of Japanese-brand autos. Females decreased their purchases more than did males. At the same time, older generations (people born in the 1960s or earlier) reduced their purchases of Japanese-brand cars more than did the younger generations. Thirdly, by employing heterogeneous responses analysis, we find that nationalism is a major factor motivating consumer responses. In particular, war memories and nationalist education played an important role in promoting boycott in the wake of the protests. Meanwhile, the concern about the possible damage to the purchased Japanese-brand cars is also an important reason for the changes in consumer purchasing behavior. In the second stage, we obtained the updated data on nationwide automobile registration records that cover years 2012-13. This allows us to substantially expand the time coverage of our analysis. More importantly, this enables us to incorporate the political incident of the nationalization of Diaoyu/Senkaku Islands into our analysis. This political conflict has aroused widespread protests and deep impacts on the Sino-Japanese relations. Examining the consumer boycott behavior around this political confrontation event could clearly add much value to our study. Moreover, we have collected and obtained data on the national reference prices for different auto models in 2012-13. Although the data are not the individual auto purchase contract prices, they still could help us gauge the price adjustment of different auto country brands in response to the political conflicts. At the same time, we expand our search and reading of the relevant literature in disciplines other than economics such as political science, international relations, marketing, business, psychology, etc., and find that many of the conceptual issues discussed in these disciplines could expand the scope and enrich the content of our investigation. Over the past two years, we have been conducting the research over the Sino-Japanese political conflicts in years 2010-2013, focusing on the two political incidents: the fishing boat collision event and the Diaoyu/Senkaku Island nationalization event. This allows us to achieve much more analysis than what is contained in the original plan. Firstly, we analyze three political incidents: the fishing boat collision event, the event of the preparation for the nationalization of the Diaoyu/Senkaku Islands, and the event of the formal nationalization of the Diaoyu/Senkaku Islands. Secondly, we introduce the nationwide recommended (reference) prices of each auto model in some parts of our analysis so as to control for the effects of price adjustment on consumer boycott behavior. Thirdly, we investigate whether consumers switched to buying Chinese domestic-brand autos after boycotting Japanese-brand autos so as to support Chinese domestic brands. We compare the strong-form boycott, i.e., the substitution of Japanese auto brands with domestic brands, and the weak-form boycott, i.e., the replacement of Japanese auto brands with other foreign countries’ brands. So far, the scope of our analysis and the richness of the issues and the findings are much more than what is expected on the basis of the original research proposal.

14501015.label: Major findings and research outcome
14501015.value: Our study finds that the Japanese-brand car sales experienced a decline relative to those of automobiles of domestic brands or other foreign countries’ brands over a period of approximately three months after the breakout of the Sino-Japanese political conflicts, and then started to rebound. Nonetheless, the market shares or sales volume of Japanese-brand autos typically could not reach the pre-shock level in the sample period, which suggests a relatively long-lasting negative impacts of political confrontations on Japanese-brand auto sales. We investigate the heterogeneity of boycott propensity among buyers with different demographic attributes. Females exhibited a stronger propensity to boycott than males, and individuals boycotted much more saliently than non-individual business or government entity buyers. Younger-generation buyers often boycotted more than did older-generation ones. We explore the mechanisms for oppositional sentiments to affect boycott behavior. Firstly, we find that the boycott activities were more intense in those cities which had more major conventional battles or had biological warfare during the war period, and the effects of the latter were stronger. More importantly, consumers in the cities with historical battle experience exhibited a relatively “persistent” lower propensity to purchase Japanese-brand autos in the whole post-shock period in our analysis, i.e., a relatively long-lasting consumer boycott effect. Secondly, anti-Japanese protests also exerted negative effects on Japanese-brand auto sales, which suggests the roles of both nationalism and buyers’ concern over property damage risks in prompting boycott of Japanese-brand automobiles. Consumers in the cities with protests in 2010 and 2012 generated contemporaneous as well as longer-term effects. We introduce the nationwide recommended (reference) prices of each auto model in some parts of our analysis so as to control for the effects of price adjustment on consumer boycott behavior. It is found that Japanese-brand auto sales dropped even in the presence of their downward price adjustments. On average Chinese consumers switched to the Chinese domestic-brand autos after boycotting Japanese brands. Males and consumers based in the cities with historical battles and protests showed a stronger pattern of switching to domestic brands. Consumers of lower-class automobiles displayed a stronger pattern of switching to domestic brands. Meanwhile, presumably lower-income consumers displayed a stronger inclination to switch toward domestic brands. Consumers in the cities with historical battles or patriotic education bases in the middle and western hinterland areas exhibited a stronger switch toward domestic brands than their counterparts in cities without such war memory in the same megaregion.

14501015.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14501015.value: The major strength of our study is the individual-level auto registration data which can provide valuable information on the basic demographic attributes and automobile characteristics in an actual purchasing environment. Nonetheless, the dataset still has limitations. For instance, the individual-level auto purchase price data are not available. The available information on the characteristics of individual auto buyers is not rich enough to provide more of direct background information like job types, economic status, etc. In the future, the emergence of more detailed datasets can help overcome these weaknesses.

14501015.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14501015.value: The study of consumer boycott is a recurring theme in various disciplines such as economics, political science, marketing, business, psychology, etc. This study employs a unique nationwide individual-level automobile sales dataset in China to study how consumers reacted to the Sino-Japanese political conflicts in the period 2010-13. The political confrontations between China and Japan provide a good setting to examine how the war-based consumer animosity affected the product sales of multinationals from a country at fault. Our analysis finds that consumer animosity prompted consumers to boycott Japanese-brand autos in 2010-13. The prefecture-level cities’ historical war experience and current anti-Japanese protests promoted boycott, and they worked with the characteristics of buyers, autos, etc. to shape the heterogeneous boycott behaviors with varying intensities. The boycott was relatively long-lasting and remained salient after Japanese-brand autos made downward price adjustments. Furthermore, we make a distinction between strong-form and weak-form boycotts. In the former, consumers switched to Chinese domestic brands after boycotting Japanese ones at the risk of lower quality and technology. In the latter, consumers switched to non-Japanese foreign brands after shunning Japanese ones. We find that strong-form boycotts were observed, and they were strengthened by war memory.

14501115.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14501115.value: This proposal explores the effects of product market peer pressure on firms’ engagement in corporate social responsibility (CSR). Using a Regression Discontinuity Design approach (RDD), this project studies the reactions of non-voting peer companies to a firm’s CSR proposal that passes or fails by a small margin. We combine RiskMetrics and Factset SharkRepellent to obtain a sample of CSR-related proposals brought by shareholders. And we use peer firm pairs identified by Hoberg and Philips from a text-based analysis of 10-K product descriptions. An important and under-studied driving force for firms to behave in socially responsible ways is pressure from product market peers. In the long run, firms can gain competitive advantages and “social capital” by being involved in good CSR. Consequently, when a firm observes a (potential) commitment in being socially responsible from its rival firms, it will be threatened. In response, the firm will increase its engagement in social good to be more competitive. At the same time, peer firms operate under similar social norms and institutional environments. If the common stakeholders value corporate social responsibility and observe the passing of CSR-related proposals in peer firms, they can impose pressure on firms that do not invest adequately in the social good. We therefore expect (1) a negative reaction in the stock market to the approval of CSR-related proposals by peer firms, as a potential consequence of losing competitive advantage, and (2) an increase in CSR engagement after peer firms pass a CSR-related proposal. The preliminary empirical results lend strong support to these hypotheses. Our project will contribute to the literature on the determinants of CSR and the importance of being good citizens in product market competition. It will identify the conditions that encourage responsible corporate behavior. It will also enhance our understanding of the effect of peer pressure in shaping corporate policies. This project may also shed light on the underlying economic links between product market peers. 本研究計劃旨在探討產品市場上的同業壓力對企業社會責任(CSR)行為的影響。 基於斷點回歸的分析方法, 本項目探討存在競爭關係的同類公司對於其對手公司于邊緣通過或不通過企業社會責任提議的市場反應。 我們結合RiskMetrics和Factset SharkRepellent兩個數據來源以獲得有關股東發起的關於企業社會責任提議的樣本。 基於Hoberg和Philips從公司在10-K檔中進行產品描述的相似程度資料,我們得以識別在產品市場上存在直接競爭關係的公司。 同業壓力是否影響企業社會責任表現是一個重要的話題,而學術界對其的研究尚不足以得出結論。 長期看來,社會責任表現良好的公司可以獲得競爭優勢與社會資本。 因此,當公司觀察到競爭對手提高或有傾向提高社會責任表現時,其會感到競爭威脅。 與此同時,同行業公司在相似的社會規範以及制度環境下共存。 假設共同利益相關者重視企業社會責任並觀察到行業中某一公司通過了承擔企業社會責任的提議,那麼共同利益相關者可以向其他同業公司施加壓力以迫使其在未來承擔更多的社會責任。 基於以上兩點,我們提出假設1)當同業公司通過企業社會責任相關提議時,其對手公司會因失去競爭優勢而出現負面市場反應;2)當同業公司通過企業社會責任相關提議時,其對手公司會在未來改善企業社會責任表現,以重獲競爭優勢。 我們的初步實證結果證實了以上假設。 本項目將對於有關企業社會責任決定因素的文獻做出貢獻，也有助于理解在產品競爭中做“好公民“的重要性。這會有助於發掘促進企業社會責任的相關條件，同時增進我們對同業壓力如何影響企業決策的理解。本項目或許可以幫助我們更好理解產品市場上同業者之間的經濟關聯。

14501115.label: Realisation of objectives
14501115.value: 1. By empirically testing a sample of more than 3,000 U.S. public nonvoting peer firms over the period of 1997–2011 using the RDD approach, we find strong effects of the passage of close-call CSR proposals on the stock market reaction and the adoption of CSR policies by the voting firm, as well as subsequent adoption of CSR policies by its peer firms. Specifically, if the voting firm marginally passes a close-call CSR proposal, it experiences higher three-day cumulative abnormal returns (CARs) and, subsequently, a higher CSR score. The average CSR score for its competing peer firms in the following year is significantly higher (30% of the standard deviation) than that of the competing peer firms in which the vote fails by a small margin. The effect is even stronger if the close-call CSR proposal was actually implemented in the subsequent year, suggesting that these effects go beyond pure signaling—they can materially influence peer firms. Using global polynomial estimations, different measures of CSR and their subscores, and different competing peer samples, we found these results to be robust. Such effects are absent from non-peer groups and for non-CSR proposals. In addition, the effects are generally concentrated in the same domain in which a competing voting firm passes a specific type of CSR proposal, though industry followers also adopt other types of CSR to some extent. In exploring the channels through which CSR peer effects are transmitted, we find little evidence that they are driven by financial intermediaries’ propagation, as such effects are absent from peer firms, defined by common analyst coverage or common institutional investors. Similarly, we do not find significant differences between two subsamples of product-market peers with and without common analysts or common institutional owners with the voting firm. Instead, the peer effects of CSR policies are concentrated in a subsample where the competitive pressure between voting firm and peer firms is relatively strong, suggesting a channel through which competitive pressure is exerted. In order to better understand the underlying mechanism, we further investigate peer firms’ stock market reaction to the passage of a CSR proposal. The passage of a CSR proposal should be bad news to competing peers if the voting firm’s CSR policy forms a competitive threat to these peers. We find significantly lower three-day CARs for product-market peers around the passage of a close-call CSR proposal. Such negative CARs are more significant in firms with greater financial constraints and more competitive pressures when the voting firm’s CSR proposal is more likely to be implemented (based on ex ante recommendations by the board), and when the gap in CSR between voting and peer firms widens after the vote. Our empirical results confirm that the unfavorable market reaction comes mainly from those who have greater difficulty catching up in CSR; furthermore, they lend additional support to the competition-based explanation, that CSR can enhance a firm’s value by creating a competitive advantage. 2. We find the competitive pressure between the voting firm and its non-voting peer firm to be the most important factor that drives the peer effects of CSR. We define competitive pressure, which captures the similarity of two competing firms’ products by measuring changes in the competing firms’ products relative to the focal firm’s products (Hoberg et al. (2014)). This competitive-pressure variable is constructed according to the way in which competitors change the wording used to describe the product, which overlaps with the focal firm’s vocabulary of the product description section in the 10-Ks. When a firm’s products are more similar to those of its peers, the competitive pressures among its peers is greater; thus, peer firms may have a stronger desire to mimic their competitors’ commitment to CSR. Specifically, we divide the peer firms into two groups according to their associated voting firms’ competitive pressure level in the year before the vote. A high-competitive-pressure group includes peers of the voting firms whose competitive-pressure scores are higher than those of the sample median among all voting firms. We expect that peer firms in the high-competitive-pressure group are subject to more pressures than those in the low-competitive-pressure group. Consistent with the above conjecture, we find that the CSR peer effect is present mainly in the high-competitive-pressure group—namely, peer firms whose products are similar to their competing voting firms’ products and thus face greater pressure to engage in CSR. 3. In addition to the negative market reaction from non-voting peer firms, which shows that CSR is likely to be a competitive advantage in competition, we also explore more details. To be specific, we examine whether the adoption of peer firms’ follow-up CSR is a mimicking strategy or a differentiation strategy. Peer firms may adopt different strategies depending on their position in the product market (i.e., whether they are market leaders or followers). To test these, we further break down the voting firms’ CSR proposals into different types by classifying the proposals as environment-related proposals, workforce diversity–related proposals, or proposals related to employee relationships, since these are the most important aspects of CSR and cover most firms. We then break down the overall adjusted KLD score into a few subdimensions, such as environment, employee relations, and workforce diversity, to match the proposal type and analyze these subsamples with respect to different types of CSR proposals. First, we observe that both mimicking and differentiation in the following adoption of CSR policies. However, mimicking seems to be economically more important than a differentiation strategy. For example, an environmental proposal is more likely to generate the follow-up adoption of environmental policies than other kinds of policies. Second, peer firms that are industry followers will be more likely to adopt a differentiating strategy, besides mimicking the voting firm’s specific CSR practice. For example, non-voting peers, if defined as industry follower (according market share, profitability, or CSR performance), are more likely to adopt workforce diversity policy following an environmental proposal of voting firms. Based on the above mechanism of peer effects of CSR and the role of CSR in product market competition, our study suggests that policy makers should consider the product market competition landscape to promote CSR. Our study also sheds light on the potential ripple effects of other corporate policies generated through product market connection or financial intermediary.

14501115.label: Major findings and research outcome
14501115.value: Cao, Liang, and Zhan (2018) investigate how firms react to their product-market peers’ commitment to and adoption of corporate social responsibility (CSR) using a regression discontinuity design approach. Relying on the passage or failure of CSR proposals by a narrow margin of votes during shareholder meetings, the study finds the passage of a close-call CSR proposal and its implementation are followed by the adoption of similar CSR practices by peer firms. In addition, peers that have greater difficulty in catching up with the voting firm in CSR experience significantly lower stock returns around the passage, consistent with the notion that the spillover effect of the adoption of CSR is a strategic response to competitive threat. Cao, Liang, and Zhan (2018) also documents that the implementation of the passed proposals generates larger peer effects. Such peer effects of CSR contains both mimicking and differentiation strategies in the product market. Product market followers are more likely to adopt differentiation strategies than product market leaders. The study shows the dynamics in a firm’s CSR policy and the interaction with product market competition. Cao, Jie, Hao Liang, and Xintong Zhan, 2018, Peer effects of corporate social responsibility, Management Science, forthcoming

14501115.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14501115.value: 1. Extend the sample to international level. Different countries have different attitude towards CSR, we would expect the peer effects of CSR to be stronger for countries with strong preference for social performance. 2. Further understand the role of corporate governance in the peer effects of CSR. Though on average, our evidence shows the peer effects of CSR is a rational choice of firms in competition, it is still possible that some managers use the shareholders’ money to create a better personal image or simply waste the money as an agency issue.

14501115.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14501115.value: The existence of peer effects on individual and household financial decision making and behavior has been well documented. Recent studies have found substantial externalities and peer effects in corporate policies as well. For example, peer effects are more important for determining capital structure than most previously identified determinants. Despite the vast literature on peer effects in various corporate activities, an important yet largely unexplored aspect of such effects is its social component. Corporate social responsibility (CSR) policies have been widely adopted by companies around the world, and more than 80% of S&P 500 companies regularly publish CSR reports. This movement has fundamentally changed the competitive landscape and industry structures of economies around the world. Our documented evidence suggests that there are an economically large peer effects of corporate social responsibility. Such effects are generated through product market competition, which deepens the understanding of CSR as a product market competition. The detailed evidence about mimicking and differentiation strategies further corroborate the aforementioned argument. Our study adds to the growing literature on CSR and industry organization. The interaction of CSR and product market competition gives a complete picture of how CSR creates value for shareholders.

14501415.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14501415.value: In the past several decades, childhood obesity has increased significantly worldwide. In Hong Kong, according to 2012 statistics from the Student Health Service of the Department of Health, 18.4% of secondary school students are overweight or obese. The identification of modifiable lifestyle risk factors is essential to successfully addressing adolescent obesity. Although numerous studies have independently or concurrently associated regular physical activity and sufficient sleep with reduced risk of adolescent obesity, 91.6% of Hong Kong adolescents are reported to be physically inactive and 72.6% of them get insufficient sleep on school days. However, studies have also found that local adolescents tend to accumulate more minutes of physical activity and longer sleep duration on non-school days than on school days. Thus, weekends and holidays may provide potential opportunities to compensate for insufficient physical activity and sleep, thus alleviating the risk of childhood obesity. Preliminary evidence has shown positive relationships between sleep compensation on weekends or holidays and a reduced risk of obesity in children. However, existing research has been limited in its measurement methods (subjective measures of sleep and obesity). Moreover, no study has examined the combined effects of physical activity and sleep compensation on childhood obesity. Therefore, the proposed study will aim to (1) objectively assess the weekday and weekend physical activity and sleep patterns of adolescents, and (2) investigate the relationships between compensating for insufficient weekday physical activity and sleep on weekends and the risk of obesity in adolescents. A total of 1,100 adolescents aged 12-17 years will be recruited from local secondary schools in different districts with varying socio-economic status. The participants’ physical activity and sleep patterns will be objectively measured by having them wear an ActiGraph accelerometer for eight consecutive days. Body weight and height will be assessed by trained staff and used to calculate the body mass index (BMI). Overweight and obesity will be classified based on the BMI. Potential confounding factors will also be assessed, and include puberty, total sedentary time, screen time, perceived stress, age, gender and parental education. Logistic models adjusting for the confounding factors will be performed to determine the relationships between physical activity and sleep compensation, and obesity risk. The proposed study will be the first in Hong Kong to provide valuable objective data on physical activity and sleep patterns among adolescents. More importantly, it will contribute to efforts to address childhood obesity by identifying potential modifiable lifestyle behaviour. 在過去的幾十年，兒童期肥胖的情況在世界範圍內持續加劇。據香港衛生署學生健康服務2012年的調查顯示，18.4%的中學生為超重或肥胖。確定那些可被改變的生活方式風險因素對於改善青少年肥胖至關重要。雖然已有眾多研究顯示日常體力活動及充足的睡眠可獨立或聯合地降低青少年肥胖的風險，但報告在上學日體力活動不足及睡眠缺乏的香港青少年比例分別高達91.6%和72.6%。與此同時，研究亦顯示與上學日比較，本港青少年會在非上學日參與較多的體力活動及擁有更長時間的睡眠。因此，週末及假日可提供補足體力活動與睡眠時間的潛在機會，并因此降低青少年肥胖的風險。在兒童中的初步證據表明週末日或假日補充睡眠與肥胖風險的降低呈正相關。然而，現有研究在測量方法上有較大局限性，即採用主觀方法測量睡眠和肥胖。此外，目前為止尚未有研究探索體力活動與睡眠補償對於青少年肥胖風險的聯合效應。 因此，本研究將（1）客觀地測量青少年上學日和週末日體力活動與睡眠模式；（2）探索週末日補償上學日缺乏的體力活動和睡眠與青少年肥胖風險的關係。本研究將在香港社會經濟地位不同的行政區內的中學招募1,100名12-17歲的青少年參與研究。參與者將連續佩戴ActiGraph加速度計八天以客觀測量其體力活動和睡眠模式。研究人員還將測量參與者的身高、體重以計算身體質量指數（BMI）。超重及肥胖狀況將依據BMI界定。青春期發育階段、總的靜坐時間、屏幕時間、主觀壓力感受、年齡、性別、父母受教育水平等潛在混雜因素也將被測量。控制了上述混雜因素的Logistic模型將用來分析體力活動和睡眠補償與肥胖風險的關係。 本研究將首次提供香港青少年體力活動與睡眠模式的客觀數據。更重要的是，本研究將確定潛在的可被改變的生活方式因素，從而有助於更好地對抗青少年肥胖。

14501415.label: Realisation of objectives
14501415.value: This project investigated the relationships of physical activity and sleep patterns with obesity risk for adolescents aged 12 to 17 years. The three objectives have been fully achieved. In general, over 2,000 participants were invited from 18 secondary schools (located in 16 out of the 18 districts in Hong Kong) whose principals agreed to be involved. Parental consent forms and adolescents’ assent forms were then obtained from 1,227 youth in grades 1 to 5 (60.8% response rate) from these schools. Eventually, 1,039 participants were present during the scheduled school visit and completed the data collection. Weekly patterns of physical activity, sedentary time and sleep duration were measured via the activPALTM accelerometers (PAL Technologies, Glasgow, UK) (Objective 1). Participants were asked to attach the activPALTM tightly at the midpoint of the anterior aspect of the right thigh. A continuous (24-h) 7-day wear waterproof protocol was used to ensure that the devices could be worn during water activities and showering. The 15-second epoch data were downloaded using the activPALTM software (v7.2.32). The original data were analyzed using the Matlab program. Nonwear time was defined as: 1) a period with ≥ 60 minutes of consecutive unbroken zero accelerometer counts except individual sleep period; 2) time reported in the removal logs of a single day. A day was considered to be valid with all summed nonwear time less than 240 minutes. Participants who provided valid activPALTM data for at least 3 valid weekdays and 1 valid weekend were included in data analyses. Data files from individual participants were manually and visually screened to detect bedtime and rise time for sleep duration. The first non-sedentary epoch after 6:00 a.m. was identified as rise time. This time was chosen because manual prescreening of participants’ rise times identified that no participants woke before 6:00 a.m. The last non-sedentary epoch, following by the uninterrupted sedentary period >2 h, was identified as bed time. Moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA) was defined as ≥ 25 steps per 15 second. Sedentary time was calculated as total time in sitting or lying poster minus sleep duration. Anthropometric assessments were conducted by trained assistants during school visits. Body mass index (BMI) was then calculated and body weight status was classified based on the international standard for children by the use of age- and gender-specific BMI cut-off points (obese including overweight or not). Consequently, the associations of physical activity and sleep duration with BMI or body weight status were determined using linear mixed models while adjusting for other covariates including sex, maternal educational attainment, and puberty stage (Objective 2). To further explore the relationships between weekend physical activity/sleep compensation and obesity risk (Objective 3), weekend catch-up patterns of behaviors were generated for MVPA and sleep (weekend values - weekday values). Linear mixed models were performed, adjusting for other covariates including sex, maternal educational attainment, and puberty stage. In addition, it is the first study in Hong Kong that has used the activPALTM to objectively measure the movement behaviors over 24 hours. The findings of this study led to further investigations including: (1) practical issues of continuous wearing the activPALTM in Hong Kong (a manuscript has been accepted for publication in Pediatric Exercise Science); and (2) associations of weather with physical activity, sedentary behavior, and sleep duration (a manuscript under review).

14501415.label: Major findings and research outcome
14501415.value: Weekly patterns of physical activity, sedentary time, and sleep On average, the adolescents spent 0.7 hours in MVPA, 10.9 hours in sedentary behaviors, and slept for 8.0 hours per day over a week. No gender differences were found. The proportion of meeting recommendations of physical activity (at least 60 minutes of MVPA daily) and sleep duration (13-17 years: 8-10 hours; <13 years: 9-11 hours per day) was 9.9% and 39.2%, respectively. However, weekday-weekend variations were obvious: they accumulated 10 more minutes of MVPA (mean difference: 0.16 h, 95% CI: 0.14 to 0.20), while 111 less minutes of sleep (mean difference: -1.85 h, 95% CI: -1.98 to -1.72) on weekdays than on weekend days. Associations of physical activity and sleep duration with obesity After adjusting for gender, puberty stage, and maternal educational attainment, MVPA was negatively associated with the risk of being overweight (B = -0.998, 95%CI: -1.814 to -0.182), while sleep duration was not associated with the risk of being overweight in both univariate and multivariate regression models. Relationships between weekend compensation/meeting guidelines and obesity Approximately one fourth of the adolescents spent more time in MVPA on weekend days than on weekday. Only 28% of them met the recommended sleep duration on weekday. Majority of the adolescents (87.3%) compensated sleep on weekend days, with 32.7% of them overslept, i.e. longer than the recommended sleep duration. However, weekend compensation of MVPA and sleep duration was not associated with the risk of being overweight. Adolescents who did not meet the physical activity recommendation (B = 1.34; 95% CI: 0.32 to 2.36) and those who did not meet the combination of physical activity and sleep recommendations (B = 2.15; 95% CI: 0.49 to 3.82) had higher BMI than those who met the respective recommendations. Beyond the three objectives Partial data from this study has been analyzed to examine the compliance and practical utility of a continuous wear protocol for the activPALTM in Hong Kong. Nearly three-fourths of the participants provided valid data for at least four days including one weekend day. Higher compliance rates were found when there was less rainfall and when cartoon stickers were used during the attachment phase. Sweating and skin irritation were the two most reasons for device removal during the data collection period. Higher relative humidity in Hong Kong led to a less MVPA time and longer sleep duration, while high temperature contributed to a higher sedentary time.

14501415.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14501415.value: This study is a cross-sectional investigation of physical activity and sleep patterns among adolescents in Hong Kong. It provides the first dataset of the activPAL-assessed movement behaviors across 24-hour period. The data generated from this study enable us to further explore the compliance with the 24-hour movement guidelines (including physical activity, sedentary behavior, and sleep) which was released by various countries in recent two years. A manuscript on this issue is under preparation and will be submitted to refereed journal in the first quarter of 2019. In addition, we have made efforts to follow up the adolescents who participated in the current study in order to investigate the longitudinal patterns of movement behaviors. So far, approximately 200 adolescents have agreed to participate in the follow-up measurement.

14501415.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14501415.value: This study used an objective measure to assess lifestyle physical activity and sleep duration of adolescents in Hong Kong with a focus on weekday-weekend behavior patterns. Only 10% of the participants met the recommended level of physical activity, while nearly 40% of them had sufficient sleep over a week. In particular, the adolescents were less physically active on weekend days than on weekdays. Meanwhile, only one fourth of them had sufficient sleep on weekdays. It was not surprising that adolescents compensated their sleep on weekend days, however, one third of them slept longer than the recommended duration during weekends, i.e., > 10 hours per day for 13-to-17-year-olds and > 11 hours per day for 6-to-12-year-olds. Higher level of physical activity was associated with lower risk of being obese. However, neither sleep duration nor weekend compensation was related to obesity for the participants.

14501515.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14501515.value: Conditional conservatism has long been a popular research topic. Empirically, a positive incremental coefficient of earnings on bad news (proxied by negativereturns) over that on good news (proxied by positive returns) in a piecewise linear regression ("Basu measure" hereafter ), is often interpretated as evidence consistent with the existence of conditional conservatism. Further, many studies document that Basu measure varies with variables capturing economic incentives related to agency issues in the predicted way. Although Basu measure is intuitive and conceptually appealing, it has long been subject to discussion. Detrich et al. (2006) and Patatoukas and Thomas (2011) argue that Basu measure suffers from econometric issues. Lawrence et.al (2013 and 2014) find that Basu measure also capture the non-discretionary conservatism unrelated to economic incentives and capture firm's curtailment decision, which is not an accrual based accounting treatment. Refuting Detrich et al. (2006) and Patatoukas and Thomas (2011), Ball et al. (2013a; b) theoretically derive and econometrically prove that Basu measure is a valid proxy for conditional conservatism under the assumption that the equity market is efficient. In this project, we evaluate whether and how Basu measure biases the estimation of the degree of conditional conservatism when the firm equity is overvalued. Under overvaluation, returns over the year for which earnings are measured will be higher than those would be. Thus, for the good news sample, the coefficient of earnings on returns will be understated. In contrast, for the bad news sample, the coefficient of earnings on returns will be overstated. By definition, Basu measure is the difference in coefficients between the bad news sample and the good news sample. Correspondingly, Basu measure will be overstated with the presence of overvaluation. In the empirical tests, we conjecture and test (1) overvaluation firms have NO more conservatism accounting treatments such as write down, write off and special items than the rest of firms in the sample; (2) overvaluation firms have more equity issuance, debt issuance or engage in more M&A activities than the rest of firms in the sample; and (3) controlling for the overvaluation effect in Basu model can have material impact on some of the prior findings about capital market incentive (consequences) and conditional conservatism. 长期以来，会计研究者依赖Basu（1997）回归方程的系数来度量有条件的会计谨慎性。近期，越来越多的文献讨论了Basu度量的局限性和产生错误结论的各种情况。 在资本市场有效地前提下， Ball（2013）从计量理论上推导了Basu度量的正确性。在这个项目，我们将讨论，当资本市场不是完全有效，公司市值被高估的情况下，Basu度量是否还是一个可靠的会计谨慎性的度量。

14501515.label: Realisation of objectives
14501515.value: The reason we cannot make further progress relative to last report is below. During the research process, we find it is very hard to obtain an reliable empirical proxy for market overvaluation. Among the existing proxies available in the literature, they can only generate marginal statistical results in expected way for our original first objective. They yield insignificant results for our original second objective. However, during the exploration of data, we uncover an very interesting phenomena under the same framework of accounting conditional conservatism, measured as Basu asymmetric coefficients. We find that two important transitions in the U.S. economy, the growth in intangible investments and the younger age when firms go public, reduce the timeliness of earnings in recognizing bad news for newly listed firms relative to seasoned firms. More strikingly, we find an impressive monotonic increase in DELAY ratio, defined as the Basu coefficient on lagged returns divided by the Basu coefficient on current returns, from 1.13 for 1970s listing cohort to 3.68 for the 2000s listing cohort.

14501515.label: Major findings and research outcome
14501515.value: We propose that two important transitions in the U.S. economy, the growth in intangible investments and the younger age when firms go public, reduce the timeliness of earnings in recognizing bad news for newly listed firms relative to seasoned firms. This is because more immediate expensing of intangible investments and startup expenditures under GAAP generate larger accounting slack that preempts the need for future conditional conservatism. Defining listing cohort as the common decade when firms go public, we find that the Basu asymmetric coefficient declines significantly by half from the 1970s listing cohort to the 2000s listing cohort. More strikingly, we find an impressive monotonic increase in DELAY ratio, defined as the Basu coefficient on lagged returns divided by the Basu coefficient on current returns, from 1.13 for 1970s listing cohort to 3.68 for the 2000s listing cohort. The attenuated Basu coefficient and the strengthened DELAY ratio across listing cohorts are from accruals, not cash flows, and are present in both high and low beginning-period book-to-market ratio regimes. Outcome We have finished the first draft of working paper and the paper is accepted by European Accounting Association annual conference of 2019. Due to the time conflict, I have withdrawn the paper from presentation. I will submit the paper to other reputable international conference as well as academic journals. In addition, I invite our current ph.d student, An Ran as the coauthor for this working paper. This project serves also as a effective tool to improve her research skills. It is included in her job application package and help her to find a satisfactory academic job.

14501515.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14501515.value: We have achieved several research objectives in the current version already. To further increase the impact of our paper, we do plan to add a potential section on whether some prior literature findings are confounded by the delayed recognition of bad news. However, our current version of paper can be standalone without this part.

14501515.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14501515.value: Timely recognition of bad news into earnings is an important objective of financial accounting and such accounting practice is referred as "conditional accounting conservatism" Prior literature document all sorts of determinants and consequences of conservatism accounting. Our findings suggest that studies using Basu coefficients to investigate the relation between conditional conservatism and variables of interest should consider controlling for changes in the fundamental factors. One may draw erroneous inference that certain kind of firms are less conservatism due to managerial discretion. But the underlying reason could be such firms are tangible intensity firms and have great buffer of delaying the recognition of bad news. Second, our findings that the DEALY ratio increases dramatically across listing cohorts and in general is bigger than one suggest that examining only the contemporaneous Basu asymmetric coefficient may not be sufficient for the full picture of conditional conservatism, especially for firms listed in recent periods.

14501815.label: Major findings and research outcome
14501815.value: The major findings of this project is the following: "In its recent anti-corruption campaign, China removed the criminal immunity originally enjoyed by its leaders. Absent fundamental changes in the political institution---in which incumbent leaders, instead of citizens at large, select the next leaders---such a partial reform pays off only if (1) it takes place at the `right' time, (2) it goes easy on corrupt low-rank officials, and (3) the government is reasonably centralized. Failing any of these, such a partial reform would lead to rampant corruption throughout the government hierarchy---an outcome far worse than retaining leader immunity." Multiple conference presentations and two refereed journal articles have been generated by this project.

14501815.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14501815.value: In my model, corruption and public goods provision have a very simplistic, monotonic relationship, in which higher levels of public goods always come with lower levels of corruption. In reality, this relationship is not always monotonic. For starters, low levels of public goods drive away businesses, which in turn reduces corruption opportunities. A do-nothing government also generates few corruption opportunities for its officials, who often rely on infrastructure construction to collect kickbacks and on regulations to collect bribes. My welfare analysis may need to be qualified once such nonmonotonicity is taken into account. In my model, bureaucrats are heterogeneous only along one dimension; namely, their civic-mindedness. In reality, they are likely to be heterogeneous along multiple dimensions, including competence and ideology. I do not immediately see how introducing other dimensions of heterogeneity may interfere with my qualitative results, but this is an important issue to explore in the future.
