To examine the contribution of situational correlates of routine activities and social correlates (social bonds, control balance, delinquent peer association, and social strain) to the victimization of left-behind adolescents in rural China.
To compare victimization and its situational-social correlates between left-behind adolescents and those adolescents living in non-migrant families in rural China.

14602115.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14602115.value: As in many other developing countries, China’s substantial internal labor migration has spawned much concern for child development. The longstanding rural-urban divide in China has prompted rural-to-urban migrants to leave their children behind in rural origins. Much of the prevailing migration literature on left-behind adolescents in both China and international contexts, while informative, has tended to focus on their well-being in terms of education and health outcomes, and has not been sensitive to their potential victimization experiences as another facet of well-being. Also, few studies have elaborated and explicitly examined various mechanisms that mediate the influence of parental out-migration on the well-being of left-behind children. In view of these substantive concerns, this study represents one of the first attempts to address the extent of victimization in rural children left behind by migrant parents and to compare the strength of various sociological theories of deviance/victimization in explaining adolescent vulnerability within the migration and rural contexts. The analysis will be informed by a theoretical framework incorporating various mechanisms of situational routine activities/lifestyle, social bonds, control balance, delinquent peer association, and social strain that are presumably protective factors, or risk factors, of victimization in teenagers left behind. The major research design is a cross-sectional school-based survey of rural middle school students in Hunan and Guangdong, two of the provinces with the largest proportions of children left behind in rural China by working migrant parents . A sample of 2,400 rural students of eighth and ninth grades will be drawn by a stratified two-stage cluster sampling based on the socioeconomic levels of counties of each province and the rural schools of sampled counties. Although we target rural left-behind adolescents, the sample will also include their non-left-behind counterparts of non-migrant rural families for comparison to detect the possible pattern of victimization and its situational and social correlates that may be unique to the left-behind. Based on the case of left-behind children in rural China, this study will not only add to the broader migration literature on adolescent well-being, but also extend the substantive study of deviance and victimization beyond its exclusive focus on urban settings.

14602115.label: Realisation of objectives
14602115.value: The major research design of the study was a cross-sectional school-based survey of rural middle school students, which was used to realize the research objectives. The target respondents were rural middle school students in Hunan and Guangdong provinces, China. The sample was proposed to be formed by 1,200 rural middle school students from each province (40 students per class x 2 classes per school x 3 rural middle schools x 5 counties from each province). The Hunan and Guangdong provinces were selected as the field sites for two reasons. First, Hunan and Guangdong are two of the provinces with the largest proportions of children left behind in rural homes by their migrant parents. Second, inter-provincial migration is dominant in Hunan whereas intra-provincial migration is prevalent in Guangdong. Selecting these two provinces enables us to identify the possible variations in left-behind children between inter- and intra-provincial labor outflow. This was the work schedule originally proposed for the research project: Project duration of 36 months from January 1, 2016 to December 31, 2018. 01/2016 - 07/2016: Preparation stage involving questionnaire design, identification of and communication with survey partners in Hunan and Guangdong, pilot study, and finalizing questionnaire 08/2016 - 05/2017: Sample selection and student survey data collection in Hunan province 06/2017 - 07/2017: Data entry for student survey conducted in Hunan 08/2017 - 05/2018: Sample selection and student survey data collection in Guangdong province 06/2018 - 07/2018: Data entry for student survey conducted in Guangdong 08/2018 - 12/2018: Data analysis and preparation of research outputs The research project consistently followed the original plan of the above research schedule. The formulation of the anonymous, self-report survey questionnaire was completed in May 2016. The questionnaire items encompassed parents’ rural-urban migration history and current migration status, various forms of direct and indirect victimization (conventional violent crime victimization, conventional property crime victimization, victimization by child maltreatment, victimization by peers/siblings, sexual victimization, Internet victimization, witnessing domestic violence, and witnessing community violence), fear of victimization, and psychological wellbeing. The questionnaire items pertaining to situational correlates included non-deviant routines (structured non-solitary routine activities with the presence of capable guardians, solitary routine activities, and unstructured socializing with peers in the absence of capable guardians), and delinquent lifestyle. The questionnaire items pertaining to social correlates involved attachment to family caregiver/non-migrant parent/migrant parent, attachment to school, school disorder, delinquent peer association, perpetuation of peer bullying, neighborhood safety and support, control imbalance, confrontation with different forms of social strain, and negative emotions toward social strain. To test the questionnaire and the data collection method, we did a field visit to a rural county, Xiangxiang, in Hunan and conducted a pilot survey on a sample of 61 students from two classes of eighth graders and ninth graders of a rural middle school in Xiangxiang county on June 21-24, 2016. During the field visit, several interviews with teachers and students who participated in the pilot survey were also done in order to collect qualitative feedback on the issue of left-behind children and the suitability of the questionnaire. The questionnaire was finalized in August 2016. In selecting rural middle schools in Hunan and Guangdong provinces, we ensured that left-behind adolescents comprised 30%-50% of the student population, such that there would be ample cases of left-behind students to be compared with their non-left-behind counterparts of non-migrant rural families. Formal data collection of the school-based survey in Hunan province commenced in August 2016 and completed in January 2017. We collaborated with a lecturer at the Department of Sociology of the Central South University, Changsha, Hunan, to conduct the survey. A stratified two-stage cluster sampling was used to obtain a sample of rural students in Hunan. Rural counties in Hunan were classified into five socioeconomic levels based on the GDP per capita. Five rural counties from each socioeconomic level were selected. The five sampled counties in Hunan included Xiangxiang, Changning, Pingjiang, Shuangfeng, and Luxi. We then recruited three rural middle schools from each sampled county. Each participating school was invited to supply one class of eighth graders and one class of ninth graders for data collection. The trained fieldwork assistants, who were hired from the aforementioned Central South University in Changsha with the help of the survey collaborator, administered the anonymous, self-report questionnaires to the participating students in a classroom setting. Altogether, for the Hunan part the school sample comprised 15 rural middle schools from the five sampled counties and we successfully surveyed 1,482 rural students of which at the time of survey 355 were left-behind children by one migrant parent, 718 were left behind by two migrant parents, and 409 were non-left-behind. Respective data input and cleaning were done in March 2017. After the survey completion in Hunan, a research assistant with a doctoral degree was hired to assist the principal investigator of the study to select and liaise with rural middle schools in Guangdong province. Formal data collection of the school-based survey in Guangdong began in September 2017 and completed in February 2018. Similarly, a stratified two-stage cluster sampling was used to obtain a sample of rural students in Guangdong. Rural counties in Guangdong were classified into five socioeconomic levels based on the GDP per capita. Five rural counties from each socioeconomic level were selected. The five sampled counties in Guangdong were Huidong, Xinyi, Lechang, Xuwen, and Dongyuan. Three rural middle schools were then recruited from each sampled county, and each participating school was invited to supply one class of eighth graders and one class of ninth graders for data collection. The research assistant administered the anonymous, self-report questionnaires to the participating students in a classroom setting. For the Guangdong part, we successfully formed a school sample of 15 rural middle schools from the five sampled counties, and surveyed 1,357 rural students of which at the time of survey 346 were left behind by one migrant parent, 252 were left behind by two migrant parents, and 759 were non-left-behind. Data input and cleaning of the survey data from Guangdong was done in July 2018. Collectively speaking, the actual student sample size and the sample proportion of left-behind versus non-left-behind reached our proposed target. The full sample consisted of 2,839 rural students from 30 middle schools in 10 rural counties in Hunan and Guangdong provinces. Among all respondents, 701 (24.7%) were left behind by one migrant parent, 970 (34.2%) were left behind by two migrant parents, and 1,168 (41.1%) were non-left-behind at the time of survey. In other words, 58.9% of the sample were rural left-behind adolescents.

14602115.label: Major findings and research outcome
14602115.value: (1) Multivariate analyses of victimization experiences as the outcomes predicted by the left-behind status at the time of survey: 1.1 Relative to their non-left-behind counterparts, rural left-behind adolescents with one or two parents migrating did not seem to be particularly more vulnerable to direct victimization (conventional violent crime victimization, conventional property crime victimization, victimization by child maltreatment, sexual victimization, victimization by peers/siblings, and Internet victimization), indirect victimization (witnessing community violence), and poly-victimization (cumulative exposure to multiple types of direct and indirect victimization). The left-behind status also was not significantly related to gender differences in victimization. These nonsignificant associations between left-behind status and victimization were found after controlling for the situational and social correlates. 1.2 The nonsignificant associations between left-behind status and victimization did not imply that the left-behind experience is not burdensome for rural adolescents. This is because we found that left-behind tended to affect the odds of victimization through situational and social correlates reported below. (2) Multivariate analyses of victimization experiences as the outcomes predicted by the situational correlates (delinquent lifestyle and non-deviant routines) and the social correlates (social strain, social bonds, and delinquent peer association): 2.1 Compared to the rural non-left-behind, delinquent lifestyle and delinquent peer association put rural adolescents left behind by one or two migrant parents at a higher risk of being victimized. Nonetheless, unstructured socializing with peers (in the absence of capable guardians), structured non-solitary routine activities (with the presence of capable guardians), and solitary routine activities, which indicated non-deviant routines, did not have significant differences in predicting the risk of victimization among left-behind and non-left-behind adolescents. 2.2 Exposure to social strain (in particular the failure to achieve positively valued goals and confrontation with negative stimuli) put rural adolescents left behind by two migrant parents at a higher risk of being victimized than their peers left behind by one migrant parent and the non-left-behind. 2.3 In terms of social guardianship against victimization, social bond with family caregiver was more likely to decrease the odds of victimization in rural adolescents left behind by one or two migrant parents than the non-left-behind. Its guardianship role for rural left-behind adolescents was more pronounced than that of social bond with school. (3) Multivariate analyses of victimization experiences as the independent variables predicting the psychological wellbeing (indicated by psychological distress and happiness) of rural left-behind adolescents: 3.1 Compared to their non-left-behind peers, rural left-behind adolescents with one or two migrant parents were more susceptible to the adverse effects of victimization by peers/siblings, sexual victimization, and poly-victimization on psychological distress. 3.2 Compared to their non-left-behind peers, rural left-behind adolescents with one or two migrant parents were more vulnerable to the adverse effects of victimization by conventional violent crime and child maltreatment on unhappiness.

14602115.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14602115.value: First, our research design only speaks to cross-sectional relationships of left-behind status, situational correlates and social correlates to exposure to victimization among rural adolescents. While delinquent lifestyle, delinquent peer association, social strain, and weak social bond with family caregiver are more strongly associated with victimization among left-behind adolescents in rural China, we cannot rule out the possibilities that victimization experiences may result in delinquent lifestyle, stressful circumstances or disrupted social bond. Hence, a longitudinal panel design would be useful for future research to substantiate the causal effects of those situational and social correlates on victimization among rural left-behind adolescents. Second, our research results suggest that the wellbeing of left-behind adolescents in rural China due to parents’ rural-urban migration can be expressed in terms of situational and social circumstances and exposure to victimization. Service intervention sought to protect the wellbeing of rural left-behind adolescents should address their delinquent lifestyle, delinquent peer association, social stress, family bonding, concomitant victimization experiences and psychological distress or unhappiness. A program evaluation study using a pre-test and post-test design can be used to assess the intervention. It will inform not only the effectiveness of such intervention for the left-behind adolescent populations in rural settings, but also the social impact of the findings of this research project.

14602115.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14602115.value: The longstanding rural-urban divide in China has prompted rural-to-urban migrants to leave their children behind in rural origins. Much of the prevailing rural-to-urban migration literature on left-behind adolescents in China has tended to focus on their well-being in terms of education and health outcomes, and has not been sensitive to their potential victimization experiences as another facet of well-being. This study bridges this gap by examining the extent of victimization in rural children left behind by migrant parents and probing the social correlates of their victimization experiences. Data of this study were collected by a school-based cross-sectional survey of 2,839 rural students from 30 middle schools in 10 rural counties in Hunan and Guangdong provinces. In the sample, 58.9% of the rural respondents were left behind by one or two migrant parents. Three major findings emerged from the study. First, we found that compared to their non-left-behind peers, the risk of victimization in rural left-behind adolescents tends to be higher when they have delinquent lifestyles, delinquent peer association and exposure to social strain. Second, we found the salience of social bond with family caregiver to protect against victimization among left-behind adolescents in rural settings. Third, rural left-behind adolescents were more susceptible to the adverse impact of victimization on psychological distress and unhappiness than their non-left-behind counterparts. Altogether, the study findings highlight that a better understanding of the vulnerability to victimization, and concomitant psychological distress and unhappiness, among rural left-behind adolescents should take account of the social mechanisms underlying the influence of parental out-migration.

14602215.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14602215.value: 運用象徵的能力一直是現代智人的固有特徵，例如語言及裝飾品的使用。西方崇尚黃金，東方則自史前時期已視玉器為最珍貴的象徵性器物。玉器泛指由軟玉及翡翠製作成的器物。近年，在中國東北、貝加爾湖畔及俄羅斯遠東地區的考古遺址中出土了大批新石器至青銅時代的軟玉器物，以環及璧最為普遍。各地區礦物資源、玉石器製作傳統及使用方法等的異同，延伸出東北亞洲各地如何在玉器擴散及演變的過程中使用象徵意義。 本研究計劃旨在分析亞洲東北地區新石器至青銅時代早期玉器遠距離交換及移動。我們將會考察各地的礦物來源、器物的製作工藝、文物出土狀況、社會文化內涵、文物及相關器物的空間分布等資料。 我們將透過第一手考古出土材料，分析礦物的來源、SEM顯微鏡對器物微痕探索等手段，對亞洲東北地區軟玉玉材、成品、製作工藝遠距離交換及移動進行最全面的研究。 本研究計劃的目標包括： 1. 搜集貝加爾湖畔、俄羅斯遠東地區及中國東北地區考古出土軟玉文物及原料，進行文物的局部及顯微拍攝、記錄屬性、硅膠印模及礦物樣本搜集。 2. 對貝加爾湖畔及中國東北部的軟玉進行區分元素及同位素檢定，以探索各地出土玉器的礦物來源。 3. 研究史前出土玉器上的微痕、使用痕、類型學及群組，分析各地區玉器的製作工藝、用玉目的及使用者特性。 4. 進行實驗考古論證學者Semenov及鄧聰對於玉環、玉璧鑽孔技術的理論。比較實驗成品及出土文物之間微痕，將這些異同仔細記錄並製作資料庫，並將各項技術定立標準名稱，以便日後學界廣泛討論。 5. 搜集玉器的考古出土資料，進行遺址地區內及不同地區之間有關玉器生產、消費及遺棄等行為的比較。 6. 繪製玉器及其製作技術的分布地圖，分析各地玉器交換機制不同時空的情況。

14602215.label: Realisation of objectives
14602215.value: During this project, we have systematically collected first-hand data of a wide extent of prehistoric jade objects and raw materials in Eastern Europe, the Altai Mountains, Cis-Baikal, Russian Far East, Northeast China, and Japan. In 2017-2018, I have traveled to Russia six times (Moscow, Saint Petersburg, the Altai Mountains, Novosibirsk, Irkutsk, and Lake Baikal). In Novosibirsk, we visited Academician Derevianko and the Siberian Branch of the Russian Academy of Sciences (SB RAS), and collected data on the earliest personal accessories and lithic tools unearthed at the Upper Paleolithic (UP) site Denisova Cave. The earliest personal accessories in the world, a chlorastrolite bracelet found in Denisova (dated to approximately 40,000BP), was heavily documented during this project. In Moscow and Saint Petersburg, I visited the Moscow State Museum, the State Hermitage Museum, and the Zaraysk Museum. In Moscow State Museum, we documented the earliest nephrite objects, dated to approximately 22,000BP. Furthermore, nephrite rings of Seima-Turbino culture were extensively documented at the State Hermitage Museum. In Ikustsk, Co-I Goriunova and the Irkutsk State University provided significant amount of nephrite collection from the early Neolithic to the Bronze Age in the Cis-Baikal region. Artifacts unearthed from sites including Moty-Novaya-Shamanka, Lokomotiv, Shamanka II, Moty-Novaya-Shamanka, Shamanka II, Elga III, Budun II, Khuzhir-Nuge VI, KypmaXI, Shumilikha, Sarminskii Mys, Ust’ Anga, Uliarba, and Khadarta were documented. Our meticulous documentation and close-up photography have enabled us to observe their physical characteristics and production marks, which aided the comparative analyses of drilling technologies in prehistoric China. Additionally, I have collected important first-hand data of excavated nephrite artifacts in Northeast China and Japan. As stated in previous annual reports, I have systematically collected data across Northeast China in Beijing, Inner Mongolia, Liaoning, and Heilongjiang. In May 2019, I was invited by the Heilongjiang Provincial Institute of Cultural Relics and Archaeology again to document the latest findings of nephrite artifacts from Xiaonanshan site. The jade artifacts of Xiaonanshan are currently the earliest known nephrite artifacts in China, dated to approximately 10,000BP. In the same month, I traveled to Jilin, and documented nephrite artifacts unearthed from Houtaomuga site. Lastly, in May 2018, Co-I Goriunova, Prof. Alexei, Prof. Bazaliiskii, and I visited Hake site in Hailaer, Inner Mongolia, and documented Hake nephrite artifacts. This documentation was especially important, as the Hake artifacts have strong similarities to the artifacts of Cis-Baikal. In April 2019, the RA and I visited Awara, Japan to systematically document 88 artifacts unearthed from Kuwano site. Intriguingly, the Kuwano nephrite rings draw strong resemblance to the nephrite artifacts found in Xinglongwa, Inner Mongolia. As demonstrated, I have systematically and extensively collected firsthand data of excavated nephrite artifacts and raw materials in Northeast China, Cis-Baikal, Russian Far East, European Russia, and Japan. We have documented over 3 TB worth of data with tens of thousands of photographs. Almost all of these artifacts have not been published yet. We have meticulously studied the tool marks, use-wear, typology, associated assemblages to analyze the two major production systems of nephrite objects in prehistoric Northeast Asia. The emergence and subsequent development of jade culture have been published in English, Chinese, Japanese, and Russian. With the data we have collected, it is possible to publish several monographs. With the consent of our collaborators, our enormous data can be organized into a large data bank on prehistoric jade in East Asia for future studies. Furthermore, I have thoroughly conducted archaeological experiments to investigate prehistoric drilling technologies of nephrite objects, and have created a viable data bank that record the characteristics of these techniques with standardized terminology. PhD student Xu Fei and I conducted seven experiments for over 94 hours at the Experimental Archaeology Room at the CUHK. To test my proposed technology, we built a rotary machinery using materials including bamboo, wood, and cement. Raw materials of nephrite and serpentine were used as test subjects. Water and sand were used as abrasives to drill the test subjects. The turning wheel was able to rotate up to 200 RPM using only manpower. Using this technique, we have successfully drilled through nephrite objects with an opening of over 6 cm. Our experimental objects were brought to the University’s Department of Physics to conduct SEM analysis to document the production use-wear. Xu also compared the data with the archaeological samples from Lingjiatan. Additionally, we have performed experiments regarding Semenov’s proposed drilling technology. However, it was extremely difficult to drill through a hard mineral such as nephrite. We have concluded that a greater manpower might be needed in order to reproduce nephrite rings that share identical production wears as the archaeological samples. We have thus put meticulous attention in photographing the use-wear and production marks of unearthed nephrite rings made using Semenov’s drilling technology for future analysis. We have also expanded our research on prehistoric perforation technologies by reproducing the bracelet from Denisova. In just over 25 hours, student helper Liao Yating and I were able to replicate a bracelet stunningly similar to the excavated artifact. The production marks and use-wear found on the experimental bracelet are vital to the future research of UP drilling technologies. In regards to collecting data on the in situ archaeological contexts of excavated nephrite artifacts, I have thoroughly performed intra- and inter-site analyses of the production, consumption, and abandonment contexts of these artifacts by conducting on-site investigations. In August 2018, we had the rare opportunity to investigate important UP sites in the Altai Mountains. Sites of Denisova Cave, Karama, Chagyrskaya, Anui II, Anui III, and Ust Karakol were visited. In July 2018, Co-I Goriunova and Prof. Alexei invited us to travel across Lake Baikal, and visited relevant archaeological sites, including Khuzhir Nige VI & XIV, Sarminskii Mys, Kurma XI, and Khadarta IV. Furthermore, I have conducted extensive intra-site analysis regarding Hamin, Inner Mongolia, a Neolithic site dated to approximately 5,500BP. Archaeologists have found skeletons unceremoniously piled up on the living surfaces of the burned house at Hamin. Studies on the distributions of human bodies and the inheritance system of nephrite objects for the Hamin people were conducted. The analysis was published in the book 《哈民玉器研究》 (2018). With the extensive data I have collected from the UP to the Bronze Age in a wide extent of the region, I have produced the most systematic documentation of geographical and temporal distribution of studied nephrite artifacts and related technologies. The exchange mechanisms at play in the region of Siberia and Northeast China and overall geographical and temporal distribution were published extensively in the aforementioned book 《哈民玉器研究》. Although we have faced difficulties in conducting scientific analyses, we were eventually able to perform disruptive analysis on nephrite artifacts unearthed from the site Houtaomuga. Prof. Wang Lixin of Jilin University provided a total of eight nephrite artifacts to conduct experiments in the laboratory at China University of Geosciences (CUG). A preliminary report has already been published by Co-I Shi. Unfortunately, Co-I Goriunova had regrettably rejected our funding for the disruptive analysis on the excavated artifacts in Cis-Baikal, as it involved complicated foreign policies. However, Co-I Goriunova provided us with raw materials collected in the Baikal region, and these samples are currently being analyzed by the laboratory in CUG.

14602215.label: Major findings and research outcome
14602215.value: The research outcome gained from this project have completely redefined the studies of the origin and dispersal of jade culture in Northeast Asia. The earliest jade culture had likely occurred in the area between Siberia and Northeast China. In approximately 40,000 BP in the Upper Paleolithic, symbolic accessories had emerged in the Altai Mountains. The earliest usage of nephrite was found in Lake Baikal, dated to 20,000 BP. However, other greenstone was still being used along nephrite. In approximately 10,000 BP, nephrite culture began to disperse to northern Heilongjiang at Xiaonanshan site from the east of Baikal. However, both nephrite and other green minerals were found in Xiaonanshan. This infers that in the early Neolithic, people did have a fascination for the color green, however, the ultimate preference for nephrite did not develop until later on. In roughly 8,000 BP, all precious objects found in the sites of Xinglongwa and Chahai cultures in Inner Mongolia and western Liaoning were produced with nephrite. This period was the dawn of the nephrite culture that still continues in China today. Our major research outcome was published extensively in multilingual archaeological reports in English, Russian, Chinese, and Japanese. Additionally, I have collaborated with the Inner Mongolia Institute of Cultural Relics and Archaeology, and published a book titled 《哈民玉器研究》(Hamin Jades). In here, I have published a total of ten new articles regarding the exchange and dispersal of jade culture in Siberia and Northeast China in over 400 color pages. The book has received critical acclaim in academia. PhD student Wen Yadi also successfully graduated with a doctorate degree based on the research outcome of this project (title:“史前環狀玉器研究”). Furthermore, archaeological experiments conducted based on my proposed rotary technology have groundbreaking results. Past scholars stated that drilling of hard materials, such as nephrite, must have required metal. However, our repeated experiments have proven that even plant material (such as bamboo) could drill through nephrite, and the experimental drilled cores and rings were stunningly identical to the archaeological samples. This is a significant breakthrough in our understanding of the prehistoric production technology of perforation of hard materials before the age of metal, completely rewriting the history of drilling technology of jades. Additionally, PhD student Xu Fei graduated with a doctorate degree based on our experiments (title: “中國史前玉工輪軸機械實驗比較研究”). His thesis contains an extensive data bank of our experiments, and will be crucial as a foundation for future experiments.

14602215.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14602215.value: The archaeological experiments we have conducted thus far have created extensive impact in academia, and have greatly expanded our studies on prehistoric drilling technologies of other precious goods. In particular, the studies on the production of Liangzhu cong can benefit greatly from our archaeological experiments. Future analyses should also focus on other greenstone for comparative analysis. In July 2019, Director Chen Xingcan (Institute of Archaeology of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences) visited the Centre for Chinese Archaeology and Art at CUHK to inspect our archaeological experiments. We are planning to hold an international conference on our findings and its application to the studies of woodworking, pottery and metal working. Our studies thus have provided an important groundwork for scholars in the research of prehistoric rotary and perforation technologies. Furthermore, future studies can conduct comparative analysis on the string-sewing techniques found in the jade rings and slit rings in Xiaonanshan, Xinglongwa, and Kuwano sites. The striking similarity between Xinglongwa and Kuwana slit rings suggest that seafaring occurred in the early Neolithic between 8,000 to 7,000 BP. The studies of ancient seafaring and the dispersal of value system and nephrite culture in East Asia will be fascinating topics to explore.

14602215.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14602215.value: Since the early 20th century, the studies on the origins of jade in prehistoric China have been an interest among archaeologists. Although scholars have offered different explanations on this subject, our research outcome this time has completely rewritten the history and production technology of ancient jade in Northeast Asia. In approximately 40,000 BP in the Upper Paleolithic, symbolic accessories (a chlorastrolite bracelet) had emerged in the Altai Mountains. And in 20,000 BP, nephrite was already a desired material in Cis-Baikal. By 10,000 BP, nephrite culture had dispersed to Northeast China. And by 8,000 BP, nephrite had become an enduring symbolic vehicle that we still see in East Asia today. We thus have established the most systematic foundation to the dispersal and exchange of nephrite in prehistory. Furthermore, a major breakthrough in our archaeological experiments have greatly advanced the studies of prehistoric rotary technologies. We have proven that even plant materials (bamboo) could perforate hard minerals such as nephrite. More importantly, our experimental nephrite drilled cores and rings produced identical use-wear and production marks as the archaeological samples. This is an important breakthrough in pushing the studies of the history of science and technology in ancient China.

14602415.label: Project Objectives
14602415.value: To examine what consumers in mainland China and Hong Kong expect from companies engaging in CSR activities relating to “what and how to communicate” about CSR and any differences between the two. To investigate what makes CSR communication effective by identifying significant antecedents of effective CSR communication in China and Hong Kong as well as examining whether there is any significant difference among the significant antecedents in mainland China and Hong Kong compared to the US findings reported in the PI’s previous work. To validate and refine the measurements of effective CSR communication, using culturally different markets of mainland China and Hong Kong. To develop and test the influence model of CSR communication on public responses, such as corporate reputation and organization-public relationships. This will involve the following: (a) testing the impact of CSR communication on public responses, (b) identifying the most salient predictor of effective CSR communication, and (c) investigating the relationships between the effective CSR communication predictors and other possible mediating or moderating factors such as knowledge, CSR skepticism, trust in CSR commitment, and engagement.

14602415.label: Realisation of objectives
14602415.value: Through the first study (Study1) with two surveys conducted in mainland China and Hong Kong, the objectives 1 and 2 were well-achieved. The PI identified what consumers expect from organizations in terms of what and how to communicate CSR, and extracted significant important CSR communication factors that could be used for measuring the practice of effective CSR communication. The PI identified government involvement factor as a salient and unique CSR communication component expected by Chinese consumers. This dimension is considered a unique characteristic of Chinese CSR contexts different from the US. The PI also identified some significant differences between mainland China and Hong Kong in terms of consumer expectations of CSR communication and important CSR communication components. Hong Kong consumers’ expectations are more similar to US consumers than mainland Chinese consumers. Hong Kong consumers expected to know more about CSR beneficiaries just like US consumers and preferred CSR beneficiaries as a credible CSR communication source, but mainland Chinese consumers were not so interested in the information related to CSR beneficiaries and considered CSR beneficiaries as the least preferred CSR communication source. Through the validation of effective CSR communication dimensions, the PI identified five common significant factors of effective CSR communication that can work both mainland China and Hong Kong. Those include dimensions of government involvement, general CSR information, factual tone, transparency, and personal relevance. The differences of identified salient CSR communication factors are also identified. Promotion cost was identified as one of the essential CSR communication factors in Hong Kong, while self-promotional tone was identified as a sixth dimension for mainland China. The most salient factor of government involvement in both mainland China and Hong Kong is considered culturally-specific aspects of Chinese consumers, which is quite different from US consumers for essential CSR communication factors. Through the second study (Study 2) with two surveys conducted in mainland China and Hong Kong, the PI was able to achieve the objectives 3 and 4. By testing the proposed process model of CSR communication in both mainland China and Hong Kong, the PI demonstrated that the identified CSR communication components identified in the Study 1 are indeed positively associated with CSR knowledge, trust, engagement, and in turn with corporate reputation. The identified essential CSR communication antecedents have positive relationships with various cognitive, affective, and behavioral responses of consumers. More specifically, for the objective 3, the PI confirmed the measurements of CSR communication used in the US can work in mainland China and Hong Kong. In addition, the PI also identified culturally-specific aspects of Chinese consumers. In both mainland China and Hong Kong, the presence of government involvement in organizations’ CSR activities is an important CSR communication component, different from the US consumers. The additional measurement items related to government involvement were proposed to be part of effective CSR communication components and further tested that the factor of government involvement is indeed considered important in China and leads to more positive cognitive, affective, and behavioral responses of consumers in CSR communication contexts. The PI also identified cultural differences in the process model of CSR communication between Chinese and US contexts. For Chinese contexts (both mainland China and Hong Kong), CSR engagement was identified as a strong mediator between CSR communication predictor dimensions and corporate reputation along with the other two mediators (CSR knowledge and trust in CSR commitment), indicating when essential CSR communication dimensions were included in an organization’s CSR communication practice, consumers’ CSR engagement improved, and in turn, resulted in more positive corporate reputation. However, in the PI’s previous research with US consumers, CSR engagement was not identified as a significant mediator. Only CSR knowledge and trust in commitment were significant mediators among US consumers. This may suggest that the positive consequences of the identified CSR communication components are more comprehensive in Chinese contexts than in US contexts. Since the PI found the cultural differences between Chinese and Western cultures in the proposed process model, more research should be done in other cultural aspects to further refine the process model of effective CSR communication. Overall, all objectives are well achieved through the two stages of studies (a total of 4 surveys).

14602415.label: Major findings and research outcome
14602415.value: Through two representative surveys (mainland China and Hong Kong) in the first stage of the project, Study 1, the PI investigated what Chinese consumers expect for CSR communication such as communication content, media channels, and sources. One dimension of CSR communication in China that the PI identified as unique is government involvement. Other dimensions include general CSR information, factual tone, transparency, and personal relevance. In Study 1, Chinese consumers are found to prefer non-corporate sources and uncontrolled media channels to corporate sources and controlled media channels. The study also identifies differences between mainland China and Hong Kong consumers regarding their expectations of CSR communication. Mainland Chinese consumers least preferred CSR beneficiary communication source, while Hong Kong consumer considered CSR beneficiaries important communication sources for organizations’ CSR activities. The first study offers a basis for developing a culturally relevant theoretical framework of CSR communication, as it identifies the significant dimensions of such communication from a stakeholder-centric perspective in the context of China. The second stage of this project, Study 2 through two additional surveys in mainland China and Hong Kong, the PI empirically validated an existing U.S.-based model of corporate social responsibility (CSR) communication process proposed by the PI’s previous work. In this study, the PI extended the existing U.S.-based model by adding government trust as a second moderator and government involvement as a unique dimension of CSR communication in Chinese contexts. The perceived presence of CSR communication factors results in increases in consumers’ cognitive, affective, and behavioral responses. In turn, these increases improve favorable corporate reputation perception. Such results demonstrate the significant contributions of CSR communication dimensions to positive consumer outcomes in Chinese contexts. The process of CSR communication has significantly different features in Chinese contexts than in Western ones. Chinese consumers (both mainland China and HK) revealed a very high tolerance and acceptance of CSR communication with a self-promotional tone. The trust levels of HK consumers in the government tended to negatively moderate the effectiveness of CSR communication, while those of mainland Chinese consumers did not.

14602415.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14602415.value: The process model of CSR communication tested and validated in Chinese contexts can be further examined in other cultural aspects. Significant differences exhibited in this study call for a modification and extension of the existing U.S.-based process model of CSR communication when applied to the Chinese contexts. In Hong Kong, the effectiveness of CSR communication factors is smaller among government trusters than distrusters; among Beijing consumers, there was no such moderating effect of government trust despite the enormous role government plays in CSR in mainland China. The role of government trust in the process of CSR communication should be understood from consumers’ expectations of the government role. That is, depending on whether consumers believe the government should possess power and legitimacy to govern the business sector or not, government trust may or may not play a moderating role in the process of the company’s CSR communication. This should be further examined in future research.

14602415.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14602415.value: Through this project, we can better understand what Chinese consumers expect from organizations in terms of CSR communication such as what and how to communicate CSR, their preferences in communication sources and media channels. Chinese consumers prefer non-corporate sources to corporate sources (e.g., CEO, etc.) for CSR communication. They also prefer uncontrolled media channels to corporate-controlled media channels (e.g., websites). In addition, the project demonstrated that meeting consumer expectations in CSR communication can result in more positive consumer perceptions, attitudes, and behaviors. The project also identified a unique aspect of CSR communication in China. Chinese consider the presence of government involvement in organizations’ CSR very much important, which is quite different from Western countries. Chinese consumers also exhibit a high level of tolerance and acceptance toward CSR communication with a self-promotional tone when compared to US consumers. Given consumers’ willingness to reward or punish a company for its practice could be largely affected by the degree of consumer expectation-confirmation, this project demonstrate that organization should strive to continually evaluate their CSR and CSR communication practice in terms of whether consumer expectations are being met.

14602715.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14602715.value: The use of lexical tones is a salient feature of Cantonese but some tone pairs are merging in Hong Kong in recent years, most notably T2 vs. T5, T3 vs. T6 and T4 vs. T6. The tone merging patterns in adults are very similar to those of children’s tone acquisition as they also find these tone pairs difficult and acquire them last. Similarity between adult tone merging and child tone acquisition suggests that language acquisition may have contributed to this sound change, as many children were exposed to non-standard Cantonese in the past sixty years because of refugee influx and cross-border marriages in Hong Kong. However, no study has investigated the effects of family language background on Cantonese tone acquisition. Moreover, previous studies using simple transcription data show that children can produce all six Cantonese tones by age two but perception studies show that they still have difficulty in perceiving the tones until age ten. This stands in stark contrast to the general principle that perception precedes production in child language acquisition. Additionally, no acoustic data of Cantonese tone acquisition has been reported so far. All this demonstrates that more study on Cantonese tone acquisition is needed. This study will re-examine Cantonese tone acquisition by using acoustic methods to assess children’s production and will collect perception data from the same children. Both cross-sectional and longitudinal data will be collected for a more comprehensive evaluation of tone acquisition. Correlation between children’s performance in production and perception will be assessed statistically. Comparison will also be made between children exposed to standard and those exposed to non-standard Cantonese in order to investigate the effects of family language background on tone acquisition. The results not only can shed light on the relationship between language acquisition and sound change on the one hand, but can also reveal children’s actual tone production ability which is likely to be more protracted than previously suggested, on the other. The results can also contribute to the important but unsettled link between production and perception in phonological development. Moreover, a more accurate understanding of children’s tone acquisition resulted from this study can facilitate both assessment and treatment of normal children and children with speech disorders and language impairments in Hong Kong.

14602715.label: Realisation of objectives
14602715.value: All objectives are achieved with concrete data. Objective 1 A previous study examined the effects of several demographic factors on Cantonese speech acquisition, e.g., family income, parental education, the presence of siblings and domestic helpers, but they were found to have minimal effect on speech acquisition. However, they did not include family language background. Using data from 111 children aged between 2;1-6;0, our results demonstrate that the native language of the mother has a significant effect on children's tone production accuracy. Children whose mothers were native speakers of Hong Kong Cantonese produced tones slightly more accurately (~5%) than children whose mothers were not. The native language of the father had no effect. This is consistent with our hypothesis that the native language of the primary caretakers would be the most influential in tone acquisition. This is the first time such an effect of family language background was shown to affect Cantonese tone acquisition. Objective 2 Only some general acoustic data of Cantonese tones produced by 20 children with a mean age of 3;7 (range = 3;1 – 3;11) was published in 2018 during the course of our project. No acoustic data of child Cantonese tones were reported before that. We used production data of 159 children aged between 2;1-6;0 divided into eight 6-month age bands for finer analysis to explore the development of acoustic patterns. Comparisons with reference speakers are included. We focused on the development of phonetic contrasts in Cantonese tone acquisition by comparing important acoustic features of several similar tone pairs to assess if children knew what was important phonologically and phonetically. Acoustic measurements included overall tonal dispersion and specific contrasts between similar tone pairs: ratios of average pitch height for the level tones (T1, T3, T6), magnitude of rise and inflection point for the rising tones (T2, T5), magnitude of fall and H1*-H2* for the low tones (T4, T6). Auditory assessment of creakiness for T4 was also included. Our results show that children, even the youngest age group (2;1-2;6), already had accuracy significantly higher than chance level and were generally producing major acoustic contrasts between tone pairs similarly as adults (although the actual values between tone pairs still varied across age groups). Children differed from reference speakers in three ways. First, the tone space of the youngest children (before 3;0) was more dispersed, i.e., they likely have produced more exaggerated tones. Second, even the eldest children (5;7-6;0) still failed to produce the covert contrast of the inflection points of T2 vs. T5. Third, children produced much fewer T4 tokens with the concomitant feature of auditory creakiness than reference speakers did. Our data give us a wider perspective on how to define successful acquisition by providing layered production accuracy data and acoustic data. Objective 3 Data of 111 children aged between 2;1-6;0 were used to assess the link between tone production and perception. Perception data of children aged 2;1–3;0 was reported for the first time in our study, as previous studies on tone perception all started at 3;0. Our production and perception data demonstrate a general increase of accuracy with age, albeit the pattern being much stronger for the perception data (r = .834) than for the production data (r = .548). A significant positive correlation is found between perception accuracy and production accuracy. In addition, perception accuracy significantly predicts production accuracy. Nevertheless, the R2 is quite small (0.2152), which indicates that perception ability was only one of the factors affecting children’s tone production. Much of the variance in production cannot be explained by perception accuracy alone. Detailed explanation and discussion of how Objectives 1 and 3 were achieved can be found in Mok, Fung & Li (in press). Those for Objective 2 can be found in Mok, Li & Fung (submitted). Both journal manuscripts can be found in Part C of the report. The two groups of children participants reported in the two manuscripts partially overlap: 111 children in Mok, Fung & Li (in press) and 159 children in Mok, Li & Fung (submitted), in which 78 children were the same. It was because of some problems in the perception task during the first batch of data collection. We had to re-collect both production and perception data from some new participants for assessing the link between production and perception. Nonetheless, the production data collected in the first batch had no problem. Thus, we could use more data for the acoustic study in Mok, Li & Fung (submitted). During the course of our project, very similar data on Cantonese tone acquisition were published (Wong, Fu and Cheung, 2017, Wong and Leung, 2018). We took reference of their work, and improved on various methodological aspects and interpretation of the data. This led to an unplanned research outcome of methodological evaluation. See point 6 in Section 6. Research Outcome. Detailed discussion can be found in both of our manuscripts. Wong, P. S., Fu, W. M. & Cheung, E. Y. L. (2017). Cantonese-speaking children do not acquire tone perception before tone production — A perceptual and acoustic study of three-year-olds’ monosyllabic tones. Frontiers in Psychology, 8, 1450. Wong, P. 14602715.label: Major findings and research outcome
14602715.value: 1. Children’s accuracy of production and perception of all the six Cantonese tones was still not adult-like by 6;0. This demonstrates the protracted nature of Cantonese tone acquisition, concurring recent findings. 2. Both production and perception accuracy matured with age. A weak positive link was found between the two types of accuracy in our study. These findings are contrary to the perplexing findings of earlier studies showing large discrepancy between tone production and perception abilities: very early acquisition of production but relatively late acquisition of perception. Our findings reveal a new understanding of the acquisition process with more reliable data. 3. Family language background in terms of mother’s native language contributed to children’s production accuracy. Nevertheless, a large amount of variance (~70%) in children's tone production accuracy still needs to be accounted for by other factors. 4. Tone production of 159 children aged 2;1-6;0 were examined acoustically. They were adult-like in major phonetic contrasts between similar tone pairs, while they differed from reference speakers in covert contrasts and fine phonetic detail. Our data give us a wider perspective on how to define successful acquisition. 5. The age of four was found to be a watershed in tone acquisition for both perception and production. There was a more steady increase in perception accuracy before 4;0 while the perception development had slowed down after 4;0 with reduced improvement. For production, more fluctuation was found before 4;0. There was a consistent and steady increase in accuracy from 4;0 to 6;0. In addition, more creaky tokens of T4 were produced by children from 4;0 onward, with creakiness being a concomitant feature of T4 in adult's production. The possible watershed of tone development was unreported in the literature before. 6. Earlier studies on Cantonese tone acquisition were based on transcription data of children’s natural production by one native transcriber while some recent studies promoted the use of low-pass filtered materials for tone transcription by multiple judges. We revisited the whole issue by having four judgement conditions incorporating the two extremes: unfiltered one judge, unfiltered two judges, filtered one judge, filtered two judges. We demonstrated the problems with using filtered materials and concluded that the unfiltered-two-judges condition would be the most realistic criterion.

14602715.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14602715.value: A natural extension of the project is to investigate Cantonese tone production and perception of older children (>6;0) as our data demonstrated that children at 6;0 were still not adult-like in some aspects. A more interesting further development is to investigate Cantonese tone acquisition of heritage children. For many overseas communities, Cantonese is a heritage language: children learn Cantonese at home as the first language, and English outside as their second language. Heritage bilingualism is a newly recognized form of bilingualism, and has attracted much recent research attention. Previous studies suggested that compared to other linguistic domains, phonological development of heritage speakers appears to be less vulnerable with native-like performance possible. Nevertheless, these studies often focus on certain phonological contrasts only without very in-depth analysis of speech data. Currently there is no study on the acquisition of Cantonese tones by heritage children. Our present data can form the best baseline for comparisons. Pilot data from heritage children in Canada using exactly the same experimental paradigm is now being collected.

14602715.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14602715.value: Our study revisited tone acquisition in Cantonese-speaking children. Previous studies showed an unusual acquisition development of early accurate production by age two preceding late accurate perception over age six. Our study used data from over 100 children with improved research methods. We found that both production and perception matured with age showing a weak positive link between the two, and that Cantonese tones were still not fully acquired at age six in both production and perception. Family language background in the form of the native language of the mother is a factor contributing to children’s tone production accuracy. The dynamic demographic composition and language contact in Hong Kong due to cross-border marriage over the past few decades can explain the above finding. Additionally, our data demonstrate that young children could already produce Cantonese tones much better than chance level and had major acoustic patterns very similar to those of adult already, while maturation in both production and perception abilities would take much longer. Our study provides a new understanding of Cantonese tone acquisition and contributes to the larger theoretical issue of how children acquire their first language by providing specific data on a less researched aspect of lexical tones.

14603015.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14603015.value: This project is a pioneering attempt to develop an evidence-based parent support group and education program for Chinese rural-to-urban migrant mothers of left-behind children. To aid program planning, the first stage of this project will involve a qualitative needs assessment study of migrant mothers’ parenting needs and their views on parent education. Specifically, it will find out (1) how migrant mothers interpret their parenting needs and how these interpretations affect their parenting roles and relationships with children; (2) how they perceive the goals, contents, and delivery modes of parent support groups and parent education for migrant mothers; (3) whether a parent support group and education program specifically designed for migrant mothers would be an effective experience; and (4) which components are essential to the usefulness and feasibility of parent support and education for migrant mothers. This study will proceed in two stages. During the first stage, 30 research participants living in Guangdong Province will be purposively selected and invited to narrate their parenting needs and perceptions of parent education through individual interviews. Each participant has at least one child living in his or her hometown as both parents have relocated to work elsewhere for at least six months. During the second stage, the findings of the needs assessment study will produce four parent support and education groups (two for mothers of preschool children and two for mothers of primary school children) that will be organized for a total of 60 migrant mothers. Each group will meet in six sessions, each with tailored contents and goals. A five-tiered model of evaluation proposed by Jacobs (1988), which includes the needs assessment, process evaluation, client satisfaction evaluation, outcome evaluation, and impact evaluation, will be adopted to examine the program’s effectiveness and the participants’ experiences. Academically, this study’s findings will offer a significant insight into the development of evidence-based parent support and education programs for migrant mothers, as well as facilitate further investigations about the protective factors affecting the well-being of migrant mothers and left-behind children. Findings will also serve as references for both local and overseas evaluative studies on family support programs for itinerant parents. Practically, educators and social service providers will derive knowledge that enables them to design and organize comprehensive parent support and education programs to enhance family resilience. Furthermore, conclusions will yield useful ideas about formulating social policies and generating service strategies that serve the needs of migrant families.

14603015.label: Realisation of objectives
14603015.value: Objective 1 was fully realized. A qualitative interview research and a quantitative survey were undertaken to investigate the parenting needs and experiences of Chinese migrant mothers of left-behind children. Regarding the qualitative interview research, a total of 30 migrant mothers living in Guangzhou and Shenzhen cities were selected as research participants from January 2016 to April 2016. Each participant had at least one child living in his or her hometown with both parents who had relocated to work elsewhere for at least six months at the time of data collection. The sample comprised 15 mothers of children aged 6 or below and 15 mothers of children aged between 7 and 12. All interviews were conducted in private places, each lasting approximately 1.5-2 hours. For the quantitative survey, a total of 203 migrant mothers and 92 migrant fathers were openly recruited in a social service center serving migrant families to complete a structured questionnaire. All of them had relocated from their hometowns to work in Shenzhen for more than 6 months and had at least one child aged 12 or below who was left behind in the respondent’s hometown. Three refereed journal articles have been published/accepted and three conference presentations have been delivered based on these qualitative and quantitative studies. Objectives 2, 3, and 4 were also successfully achieved. By analyzing the data obtained from the aforementioned qualitative and quantitative studies, the findings about migrant mothers’ parenting needs and experiences were identified to provide significant references for the design and planning of a parent support and education program for those mothers. Four parent support and education groups were organized in two rounds of the program. The first round was conducted from June 2016 to October 2016 and recruited 28 migrant mothers to join the immediate and waitlist control groups, whereas the second round was conducted from December 2016 to April 2017 and recruited another 28 migrant mothers to join the immediate and waitlist control groups. In each round of program, both immediate and waitlist control groups administered the pretest assessment simultaneously; the immediate group began meeting right away while the delayed group waited. The immediate group conducted the posttest assessment upon completion of group activities, while the delayed group conducted the assessment a second time before commencing their group activities, and a third time upon the meeting’s completion (i.e., the posttest assessment for the delayed group). The changes in parenting cognitions, parent-child relationships, and parenting practices were used as indicators to assess the program’s effectiveness. Four postintervention focus groups with 28 participants were also arranged after the program. Two refereed journal articles have been published and two conference presentations have been delivered based on the findings of this randomized controlled trial and postintervention focus group research. With regard to Objectives 5 and 6, possible ways of supporting migrant mothers were identified, and recommendations about the objectives, strategies, contents, and delivery modes of parent education for those mothers were made. For instance, the findings of this research underscore the role of mutual aid among those mothers. Moreover, they should be supported to make use of the rapid advancements in communication technologies to connect with their children, as well as synthesize online parenting activities with real parent-child contact via periodic visits. The current findings also help to generate useful ideas regarding the formulation of social policies and services that are more responsive to the needs of migrant parents. For example, they should be given fringe benefits, such as adequate annual leave and emergency leave in carrying out their parental responsibilities. All these recommendations have been articulated clearly in the five refereed journal articles and five conference papers.

14603015.label: Major findings and research outcome
14603015.value: Qualitative Interviews The thematic analysis of migrant mothers’ narratives gathered from qualitative individual interviews indicate that they had relentlessly sought meanings of parenthood amid daunting challenges in childrearing and that meaning-making was particularly important to them in confronting highly stressful mothering experiences induced by their migrant circumstances. Furthermore, four types of maternal self-evaluation were identified. The findings were reported in two journal articles published in Journal of Child and Family Studies and Applied Research in Quality of Life. Quantitative Survey The findings of the survey indicate that both parental self-esteem and parent-child relationships had positive associations with authoritative parenting among migrant mothers; however, the perceived parent-child relationship quality was a more important predictor than parental self-esteem. There was also an interaction effect between parental self-esteem and parent-child relationships on migrant mothers’ authoritative parenting. The findings indicate that migrant mothers’ perception of their encounters with their children has a profound influence on their parenting behaviors. The findings were discussed in a journal article published in Asian Social Work and Policy Review. Randomized Controlled Trial Regarding the waitlisted controlled group randomized trial, while the results revealed no significant difference in parental identity between the intervention group and the waitlist control group at the post-test assessment after ruling out the effects of pretest survey scores, significant differences did emerge in parent–child relationships and parenting practices. The findings were reported in a journal article published in Family Process, which offer insights into developing empirically supported parent education programs for migrant parents. Postintervention Focus Groups Themes of the narratives gathered from postintervention focus groups suggest that the program has helped participants to reconstruct what migrant mothering means to them, reorganize their lived experiences, reflect upon their priorities in life, adjust their parental expectations, deepen their parent–child connectedness by visiting and calling home, express gratitude to their children’s caregivers, reaffirm the role of the children’s fathers in parenting and facilitate learning from other participants. The findings were reported in a journal article published in China Journal of Social Work, which offer insights into developing parenting programs for migrant mothers that focus on meaning-making, storytelling, and mutual learning.

14603015.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14603015.value: The results indicate that the present studied parent support and education program for Chinese migrant mothers is feasible for further development and examination of its impact. First, the high retention rate of participants in this study can be regarded as an indicator of the acceptability of the intervention. Second, positive outcomes of the program on parent-child relationships and parenting practices also serve as indicators for future research. Third, the outline of the intervention and procedures of the RCT can provide materials for replicating the clinical trial in other groups of migrant mothers. Furthermore, as both migrant mothers’ and fathers’ parenting needs were discovered in the quantitative survey, I plan to apply for other funding such as the South China Program of The Chinese University of Hong Kong to develop and evaluate a parent support and education program for migrant fathers. Moreover, an existential–narrative approach to parent support and education can be used to theorize a practical framework for designing parenting programs for other disadvantaged mothers. To this end, I have submitted a research proposal to apply for the General Research Fund 2019/20 to develop an evidence-based, existential–narrative-informed parent support group for mothers who have a substance use problem.

14603115.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14603115.value: This project aims to trace the development of a set of key cultural terms between English and Chinese in order to come to a better understanding of cross-cultural knowledge relating to China in a variety of historical contexts. Centrally, it will address how specific ideas about what constitutes the uniqueness of Chinese culture influence the ways users of these concepts think about China and themselves. Since early contact between China and Europe in the 16th century, there has been a tendency to use key concepts, often translated or adapted from Chinese, to understand Chinese culture. This study focuses on seven such terms: 孝 (filial piety), 面子 (face), 關係 (guanxi /social networks), 風水 (fengshui /geomancy), 陰陽 (yin yang), 山寨 (copycat) and 忽悠 (bamboozle), chosen for variety of length of time of interaction (filial piety in English goes back to 1669; copycat and bamboozle have emerged in the past two decades) and variety of techniques used to translate them (equivalence, transliteration and calquing). “Face” and “guanxi” have been adopted by specific disciplines (sociolinguistics; business and cultural studies) and thus are conceived as universal; the others are generally conceptualized as unique to China. All have made multiple trips back and forth between English and Chinese, and been used by the Chinese to explain their own culture, or, in the case of early 20th-century Chinese anti-tradition campaigns, to criticize ingrained prejudices that the Chinese saw as holding themselves back from ‘modernity’. This project will adopt a historical approach to these seven key cultural concepts that will uncover how translation has allowed a movement back and forth between cultures and languages. Through a combination of archival research and mining of electronic databases, I will trace the history of translation exchanges between Chinese and English, showing how that translation process has been bound up in the production of new meaning, not just the transmission of “old wine in new bottles”. This project thus goes beyond previous accounts of global translation, which simply traced the path of linguistic exports from the West to China. In uncovering how both sides of the translation process stand to be transformed by it, I hope to make evident the dialogic nature of translation and its potential contribution to cross-cultural understanding. I also aim to develop a foundation on which other area studies might build broader scholarship about global knowledge production and exchange. 本項研究計劃的主要目的在於探討某些關於中國的英/漢文化關鍵詞，據以深刻理解跨文化的中國知識如何在不同環境及時代脈絡中形成。這項研究將關注形成中國文化獨特性的特定關鍵詞如何影響詞彙使用者對其自身與中國的想像。 自十六世紀中西文化最早的交流開始，用一些從中文譯為英文的關鍵詞來理解中國文化逐漸成為普遍的現象。本研究以七個關鍵詞為主：孝（filial piety），面子（face），關係（guanxi/social networking），風水（fengshui/geomancy），陰陽（yin and yang），山寨（copycat）以及忽悠（bamboozle）。研究選用這七個詞是因為它們出自不同的時代（孝的英文翻譯早已經在1669年出現，而山寨以及忽悠最近十年才出現），其翻譯與接收也涉及在不同的翻譯技巧（對等、音譯和借譯）。在英語語境裡，“face”以及“guanxi”已然成為社會語言學及文化研究的專用詞，而另五個詞一般認為是中國所特有。這七個詞全都經驗了從中文翻作英文、又從英文譯回中文的歷程；也都在不同時期被華人用來解釋自己文化的優點與弊端。例如二十世紀初五四運動批評傳統中國文化之際，知識分子認為「孝」、「風水」等觀念妨礙中國「現代性」的發展，當代則有人認為中國之所以自外於世界性的系統是因為「關係」、「山寨」與「忽悠」等概念。 本研究計劃會採取歷史的角度來說明這七個文化關鍵詞如何透過翻譯在中英兩種語言間不斷來回。本研究員會採用香港、中國大陸、英國和美國的檔案館館藏以及電子版的相關材料來獲得比較全面的理解，本研究將用這些材料來證明翻譯不只是“新瓶裝舊酒”，而是一種創造新意的過程。 本研究將足以使我們更深刻理解翻譯，因為研究把中西文化交流視為複雜的雙向來回過程，而非僅是單向的過程。研究也希望能夠說明，中西兩方參與文化對話時，雙方會彼此影響，並會被這對話過程改變。

14603115.label: Realisation of objectives
14603115.value: The project was successful in realizing each of the four objectives, although due to delays, the monograph is still in preparation. First, I have been able to trace the development of four cultural concepts relating to China: filial piety, face, fengshui, and guanxi in detail. Filial piety begins as two separate concepts in English and Chinese; after detailing what those were before contact, I follow the way in which they merge together and influence each other right up to the early twenty-first century, when the revival of Confucianism in China brings it back in much-altered form as a part of the social safety net as the state retreats from its earlier cradle-to-grave support. Face begins in China and then spreads to English in the early nineteenth century, after which the concept is modified in English and then, in turn, influences Republican-era China, before becoming a (contested) universal feature of human interaction in the 1950s with the work of Erving Goffman and then the work of Levinson and Brown in the 1970s. Fengshui, or an earlier related concept of 地理 dili is first translated as geomancy, but then in the early nineteenth century the term fengshui is imported into English. These two terms (geomancy and fengshui) then are caught up in a larger discourse relating to religion, belief, and superstition first in English and then in Chinese, leading in the early twentieth century to a radical devaluation of these practices, even as their efficacy as a way of protesting against foreign colonial power in Hong Kong and the treaty ports is demonstrated. Yet after reaching a nadir in the 1940s or early 1950s, fengshui makes a surprising comeback, first among overseas Chinese and then as part of New Age beliefs and the counter-culture in the United States. Finally, I trace the roots of the contemporary controversy over guanxi, or connections, back to nineteenth century British debates about professionalism, patronage, and corruption, and seeing its emergence in modern Chinese as part of the discourse of modernity in China. The resulting mosaic of overlapping issues (for example filial piety, to the extent that it prioritizes the family, is linked to guanxi as ‘nepotism’) gives us a better understanding of cross-cultural knowledge relating to China in various historical contexts, which was the second objective. In particular, I discuss how these terms fared during periods such as the late Qing and early Republican era, when colonial and semi-colonial arrangements in Hong Kong and the treaty ports led to intense interaction and a general devaluation of all things considered traditional in China; how they fared during the Cultural Revolution and the left-wing fascination with China in the 1960s counter-culture in America; and finally how these terms are faring now, after decades of rapid economic growth in China and a more assertive foreign policy. Thus important developments of the concepts are tied to particular historical and social changes, rather than simply being presented in chronological order. The project was also successful in finding evidence of translation as a two-way process between Chinese and English and, in some cases, a multi-directional process among three or more languages. At various times Latin, Spanish, French, Italian, and Japanese were involved; this was not in the original objectives, but emerged as the research proceeded and, in hindsight, it should have been obvious that there was no particular reason that conceptual interchange would be easily limited to two languages. Some of my preliminary ideas on how digital humanities tools can help us to handle the large amount of material necessary to see such patterns were presented at two conferences and one published paper. Chapter one of the monograph deals with more of the conceptual issues relating to how translation studies should approach such issues. These ideas and methods can, in turn, be used to develop a foundation on which other area studies and other reserachers in translation studies can build to broaden our understanding about global knowledge production and exchange, which was the final objective. Two main problems were encountered, which has led to the delay in finishing the monograph, of which I have one chapter finished and one almost finished, plus portions of other chapters, out of a total of six chapters. First, the story of even one concept turned out to be more complicated than I had anticipated and, involving in some cases multiple languages, it was difficult to gather sufficient evidence to construct a coherent narrative. The chapter on filial piety is almost 16,000 words and is still not completed; I estimate that it will be at least 20,000 words, probably longer, whereas I had originally estimated each main chapter would be 12,000 – 14,000 words. My estimates for the remaining chapters, based on my outline and partial drafts, indicates that they will be of similar length. As a result, to keep down the length of the entire monograph, I have decided to fold my discussion of yin-yang into the chapter on fengshui, and to follow the advice of one reviewer to cut the proposed chapter on ‘bamboozle’ and ‘copycat’, since they lack the historical depth of the other terms. I may consider writing a separate article on this topic. Second, as a reviewer of a paper with preliminary findings on filial piety pointed out, it was easy to show that the concept changed over time in the two languages, but it was not always possible to provide direct, hard evidence that translation was the sole or main driver in those changes. To overcome this problem I have had to widen my search of sources and, more importantly, use digital humanities tools more extensively than originally planned. Working with such tools (mainly large corpora of books, newspapers, and magazines in Chinese and English) has given me much more material, but that wealth of material in turn meant that it either had to be processed mechanically, generating large quantitative datasets that then needed to be interpreted statistically, or gone through selectively and read closely. Both processes have turned out to be time-consuming, especially the generation of quantitative datasets from databases that were not designed for the purposes to which I have put them. This resulted in my having to learn to code in Python in order to design programmes in conjunction with my research assistant that could do this, and also resulted in my giving two papers on the use of DH methods in translation research, one in 2017 on large corpora of books (published in 2018; see section C), and one in June 2019 in Venice on periodical databases. After discussion with Zheng Yangwen, the series editor of “Alternative Sinology” at the University of Manchester Press, who expressed great interest, I have submitted a proposal to them and am awaiting their reply. My proposed date to submit the finished manuscript to them is August 2020. Finally, because I did not receive all of the funds I originally requested, I cut back on travel to international conferences. To compensate, I organized an international conference here at CUHK, at which I presented some of my preliminary findings, and I secured funding from my faculty to attend one conference in Venice, June 2019. The postdoctoral fellow also attended two international conferences.
