14606815.label: Major findings and research outcome
14606815.value: Research outcome 1 (as promised in the application): Single-authored monograph, “Taiwan New Cinema as Soft Power: Authorship, Transnationality, Historiography” Major findings: While the notion of soft power has had a mixed reception within academia, it has recently attracted considerable interest from film scholars. An international network on “Soft Power, Cinema and the BRICS” was formed in 2015, and an edited volume, Screening China’s Soft Power, was published in 2018. This project has found soft power a useful conceptual holder for a thorough tracking from agent (institutions of production) to affect (interfacing the encounter between text and audience during consumption) and effect (audience response) so that a fuller picture of a film’s trajectory from inception to reception can be painted. In the cases examined, foreign agents such as European museums and film festival programmers as well as a Hollywood studio have worked with Taiwanese authors and local city government officials to put Taiwan cinema on the global map. Affection for a recent crop of more popular films and cultural products from Taiwan has also been evident among youth consumers in China and Hong Kong, thus manifesting a regional soft power appeal. Taken together, these examples demonstrate that the notion of soft power can be traced from the reverse direction of the cultural transaction, prioritizing the effects Taiwan cinema has had on foreign audiences and institutions rather than actions taken by local agents. Research outcome 2 (additional): Chapter in edited book, “Soft Power and Cinema: A Methodological Reflection and Some Chinese Inflections” Major findings: Until recently, the specific role that cinema has played in the exercise of soft power remains underexplored. This chapter draws out the wider methodological implications for the interrogation of the relationship between soft power and cinema. It has found affect to be a missing but crucial factor in mediating soft power transactions. Via the example of The Great Wall (Zhang Yimou, 2016), it demonstrates how the very making of the film can be perceived as an occasion in which affective resonances towards the emergence of China coalesce to generate an environment that would undermine the film’s reception. It concludes that China’s hard power manoeuvres have rendered the performance of its soft power efforts rather flaccid precisely because affect is intrinsic in, rather than external to, agent, atmosphere, and effect. About half of the chapter has been incorporated into the Introduction and Chapter 5 of “Research Outcome 1”.

14606815.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14606815.value: The Epilogue of the monograph (the main research outcome of this project) points to a younger generation of directors from Southeast Asia and the People’s Republic of China who have demonstrated their affinity with the legacy of Taiwan New Cinema in their filmmaking, generating an afterlife for Taiwan cinema that exists both within and beyond the island’s shores. Among these directors, I am particularly interested in exploring the work of the Burmese-born Midi Z (Zhao Deyin in pinyin). Midi has naturalized as a Taiwan citizen, though his films are mainly set in Myanmar and Thailand. Having published an article (in 2018) on Midi Z’s work, entitled “Towards a Poor Cinema: Ubiquitous Trafficking and Poverty as Problematic in Midi Z’s Films,” I intend to investigate further the notion of a cinema of poverty. My planned course of action includes the following: 1. To apply for a GRF grant to develop this new project, tentatively called “Cinema of Poverty: A Global South Perspective”; 2. To collaborate with international scholars to organize conferences to collectively explore the abovementioned notion. I have held discussions with Professors Catherine Grant (Birkbeck College, London; expert in Latin American cinema) and Will Higbee (Exeter; expert in African cinema).

14606815.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14606815.value: This project investigates the impact of the Taiwan New Cinema movement on global filmmaking since its inception in the 1980s. Focusing on the period after the year 2000, it tracks the transnational careers of Hou Hsiao-hsien, Ang Lee, and Tsai Ming-liang. As their films are increasingly co-produced with foreign funding (from France, Japan, the United States, etc.), and made in non-Chinese-languages, they pose a challenge for the writing of Taiwan film history. Besides the international reach of these authors, films made by a younger generation of directors, such as Wei Te-sheng’s Cape No. 7 (2008), have also become hugely popular in China and Hong Kong, thus demonstrating the regional appeal of Taiwan cinema. This project suggests that a small nation such as Taiwan can also possess considerable soft power through the favourable reception of its films abroad. In the absence of hard power tools such as diplomatic status and economic prowess, cultural products such as film and political values such as democracy have become soft power resources to help Taiwan gain international recognition. The project will enhance our understanding of the role of emotion, affection, and identification in promoting a nation’s values and cultures through the medium of film.

14606915.label: Project Title(Chinese)
14606915.value: 移動的情愛: 中國的性小眾移民及其家庭關係

14606915.label: Project Objectives
14606915.value: By collecting data on and examine the factors related to the migration of LGBT people in post-socialist China this study aims to address the empirical lacuna on migration research, which has thus far focused on economic and family migrants. By focusing on LGBT migrants, this study challenges the heteronormative assumptions of existing migration studies in China, which have mostly focused on the experiences of people who were assumed or regarded to be heterosexual, and addressed the effects of migration within heteronormative institutions. By exploring the social, family and interpersonal factors that are directly and indirectly linked to LGBT people’s decisions to relocate, this study aims to shed light on the specific predicaments and social dilemmas of LGBT people in post-socialist China. It also examines their agency in negotiating the tension between the increasing social visibility of same-sex intimacy and the continued discrimination and stigma that this marginalised group experience. By delineating the intergenerational dynamics that shape how LGBT people decide to move and the strategies they use to fulfil their traditional duties of filial piety towards their parents, this study clarifies the more general processes through which Chinese parents and their adult children resolve the tension between the persistent prominence of marriage and family and the rising tides of individualism ushered in by 30 years of economic reform, modernisation and Westernisation.

14606915.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14606915.value: 中國現在面對可能是人類歷史上最大規模的境內遷移. 過去大部份有關中國的境內遷移研究多關注經濟及家庭移民, 並絕少探討因情感或性取向因素而移民的群體. 本研究有別於過去的研究, 主要探討遷移及性取向如何交織, 並形成中國的性小眾群體一種平衡個人對自由戀愛的追求及來自家庭方面要婚嫁及生兒育女的壓力的策略. 本研究有五個目標. 其一, 搜集及分析性小眾移民成長社區有甚麼因素推動他們的遷移; 其二, 探討遷移後他們是否真的得到較大的空間追尋非異性戀生活, 或是面對另一種的社會邊緣化; 其三, 探討性小眾遷移的歷史及路徑; 其四研究性小眾在遷移後如何與家鄉的父母及其他親人保持關係, 並盡其為人子女的責任; 其五, 研究性小眾在回鄉時如何與父母相處. 我們希望透過回答以上的問題, 補充中國人口遷移研究中缺乏對情感及性移民的一個缺口, 並對國內外的人口遷移, 家庭及性研究討論作出貢獻.

14607415.label: Project Objectives
14607415.value: Explore the multiple meanings of intimacy in the lives of African asylum-seekers and refugees (ASR), with specific focus on love and sex. Understand how love relationships between ASR and non-ASR, in light of their differences in material and social conditions as well as immigration status, constitute a particular discourse of morality and pattern of intimacy. Analyze how intimacy and its dilemma communicates contending values about selfhood, intimacy, and family in processes of modernization and globalization. Identify ASR as desiring subjects, not just suffering subjects, in order to see them as whole persons. Investigate how intimate practices and sexual choices between African ASR and non-ASR constitute sites of creative cultural production and challenge to normative ideals of gender, sexuality, and ethnicity. Examine how the political economy of refugee migration intersects with the cultural logics of love and desire.

14607415.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14607415.value: This study examines what love means to African asylum seekers and refugees (ASR) in interracial relationships in Hong Kong. Romance serves as an important site for negotiating differences, inequalities, and self. This project seeks to identify how the political economy of asylum intersect with cultural logics of desire, the human agency made possible in this convergence, and the transfomative potential of “love.” There are approximately 8,000 asylum and torture claimants in Hong Kong, with over 6,000 of them from South Asia and over 1,000 from Africa. Prohibited from working and studying, ASR have to rely on the meagre assistance from the Hong Kong government while waiting for years for their applications to be processed.Unlike South Asians who have had a history of residence in Hong Kong as a result of British colonial rule, Africans have had little presence in Hong Kong until their recent arrival in the 2000s. Their physiognamy mark their isolation in the city. Struggling between bare survival, discrimination, and illegal work is an everyday reality for most African ASR in Hong Kong. The dominant approach of current research on ASR focuses on exposing the “bare life” that institutional and social discrimination has reduced ASR to, and their resistance against these structures of violence. In this context, the importance of love, sex, and related pursuit of personal happiness is rarely a topic of research in ASR studies. Since 2013, there has been a number of media reports on marriages between Africans and Chinese in mainland China. This cross-cultural intimacy has caused many speculations about whether these are “genuine” relationships or a marriage of convenience. Are African ASR using these relationships to improve their lives? Are non-ASR using their material and economic powers over these ethnic others for their own pleasures? This research understands love as a means of negotiating the effects of and opportunities in globalization. As African ASR battle against the relentless marginalization as unwanted migrants in the public sphere, it seeks to examine how love is central to making relationships and lives meaningful in the personal realm, and how such negotiations overlap. Through ethnographic research and interviews with African asylum-seekers and their non-ASR partners, this study explores love as a means of negotiating differences and selfhood in a transnational site. The analysis will make a critical intervention in current understanding of ASR both in Hong Kong and globally, opening up critical dialogues between theories of emotion, humanitarianism, and immigration. 本研究探討親密關係對在港的非洲籍尋求政治庇護者及難民（ASR[asylum seekesr and refugees]）的意義。親密關係及愛情不只是個人經歷，更對種族差異，社會不平等和自我認同有重要影響。此研究項目旨在探討政治庇護的政治經濟學(political economy of asylum) 與慾望的文化邏輯如何交互影響人類的能動力（human agency )。繼而理解 “愛"的社會及文化特質及從其創造變革的可能性。 香港大約有10,000 申請庇護和酷刑聲請人。其中約8000人來自南亞，約2000人來自非洲。與南亞人相比，非洲人在港居住的歷史很短，他們的外表令他們很容易成為排斥的對象。另外，制度上ASR不能合法地工作及讀書，生活只能靠香港政府微薄的援助。他們的申請經常要耗時多年，令不少人在無奈和無力的窘境下等待多年，生活於如 Agamben 所描述的「裸露生命 (bare life)」 的狀態下。 現存ASR的研究，重點在於針對他們作為「受苦難者」的經驗，揭露法律體制和社會歧視對ASR的影響。在此背景下，愛情和相關追求個人幸福的重要性很少成為研究課題，讓我們對ASR的主體性及生活經驗的理解有顯著的差距。 自2013年，多家媒體報導非洲人和中國人在中國大陸的婚姻。這種相對較新的跨文化親密關係的形成也引起了許多猜測，懷疑這些是不是“貨真價實”的關係或婚姻。 在全球化的影響和機遇下，愛情與友情怎樣成為一種尋求人生意義和安穩的手段呢？對生活於邊緣化的ASR，這些「私人」的關係，又怎樣成為他們尋求認同和肯定的平台呢？ 通過參與研究和採訪，接觸和理解尋求庇護的非洲人與其親密愛人，朋友及家人的關係和挑戰，這項研究的結果和分析將為現有ASR在香港和全球其他地方的理解作出貢獻；並展開對情感，人道主義和移民理論之間的關鍵對話。

14607415.label: Realisation of objectives
14607415.value: The project sets out to challenge two accepted narratives about ASR: 1. that they are suffering subjects who are incapable of having desires for intimacy, love, and marriage, 2. that intimate relationships are just a means for them to access material support and security, as well as to regularize their immigration status if they marry with locals. The research thus seeks to focus on intimacy as a way to consider ASR in their full personhood. Therefore, although the main focus of the research was on heterosexual intimate relationships and marriage, it was important for the PI to locate these intimate bonds in relation to friendship, community-participation as well as community-building efforts – these webs of relations provide the important context in which intimacy was pursued by ASR. The PI conducted ethnographic research and interviews with 17 African ASR men, 2 African ASR women, and 12 of their local partners. The ethnographic component was focused mainly on 6 men and their partners, in which the PI would accompany the ASR, and sometimes their partners, on their visits to immigration offices, NGOs, hospitals, as well as attend weddings and pay family visits. This project has achieved all of its stated objectives to different extent. Objective 4, which proposes to examine ASR as desiring subjects and as whole persons, has been a consistent theme in the entire research project. I will evaluate the achievement of other objectives below. Multiple meanings and Morality in African-Chinese Love (Obj 1 & 2): Why is love so important for ASR? And what does love mean to them? Despite their shared structural vulnerabilities, and no shortage of NGO and church activities for asylum-seekers to meet with each other, friendship is often fraught with suspicion. Faced with the border regime of exclusion and subordination, ASR often locate the source of blame for their suffering within their own community through gossip and rumor, and scorn the prospects of solidarity and collective action. In this context of social isolation and distrust, romantic relationships with non-asylum-seekers become all the more desirable with their modern connotations of affective bonds, intimacy, and self-fulfilment (Giddens 1991; Hirsch 2010; Padilla et al 2008). The perception that marriage for love and marriage for immigration status are incommensurable acts shapes many of the dilemmas that ASR men and their female partners face. In this narrative, “real love” should be unconditional and devoid of pragmatic concerns such as visas; care about securing a residence permit would render any intimacy as “fake” or, at best, “tactical love.” My findings compelled a more critical engagement with the naturalized idea about love and romance. Intimate relationships have never been free from exchanges – material and financial calculation are always embedded in intimate relationships. In fact, being able to detach love and marriage from a secure immigration status is, in fact, a privilege afforded by one’s membership in a particular citizenship regime. Gaining a dependent visa that allows asylum-seekers to stay, work, and live as legal entities in Hong Kong is one, not only, measure of their relational needs. Selfhood, intimacy, and Family (Obj 3, 5): Because of the challenges to their relationships, both the men and the women have to find their own strategies in negotiating with the imbalances within their own relationships, and the resistances from outside. Gender roles and division of labor sometimes become upended as a result, or when they do not, tensions arise. These challenges compel some creative reinterpretations of masculinity and femininity, gender division of labor, and family in the process. The passivity and powerlessness associated with ASR, however, is dehumanizing for all adult men and women, but in particular antithetical to heteronormative masculine ideals of independence, authority, and power. Even for men who may pursue sexual conquests in the first few years of their stay in Hong Kong, their structural vulnerability as ASR soon made them see intimate relationships no longer as just masculine sexual conquests, but as an important source of companionship and support, offering a pathway to respectability and security. Within the relationships, however, there sometimes is a departure from conventional gendered division of labor as the situation dictates that ASR could not work. Overall, my research found that the pursuits of intimacy and marriage for ASR men provide insights into how individuals negotiate their own subjectivity in relation to different sets of gendered expectations, racial hierarchies, and border regimes, pertinent to their meaning-making projects in displacement. Political Economy and Love (Obj 6): The research also demonstrated the importance of taking a political economy approach to such “individual” expressions of love, for three main reasons. These relationships took shape within the broader context of growing China-Africa encounters in the 21st century that coincided with the securitization of borders after 911, as well as Hong Kong’s contested autonomy and identity following its return to China in 1997. The U.S. and European countries tightened their borders following the terrorist attacks in 2001, driving the flows of ASR into various parts of Asia. The arrival of African ASR also needs to be understood within the unprecedented levels of Chinese economic investment in different African nations supported by the Chinese state, based on old socialist ties and in pursuit of new political-economic influence (Siu & McGovern 2017). In Hong Kong, the institutional and social rejection of African (and South Asian) ASR have to be examined within the contestations over Hong Kong’s identity in the poast-1997 era. The highly defensive posture in reclaiming authentic “Hong Kong-ness” (Abbas 1990:98) ethnically, culturally, and politically also means that non-Chinese asylum-seekers and refugees become targets of exclusion and rejection in mainstream society. Taking a longitudinal approach by interviewing ASR who have been in Hong Kong between 16 to 3 years, I discover that the meanings of intimate heterosexual relationship for ASR men have been changing with the asylum system in Hong Kong. From the earlier mode of meeting with non-Chinese women for the fulfillment of sexual and quotidian needs when government support was non-existent, to pursuing a “hope for the future” when the prospects of getting recognized as refugees became illusory. Asylum-seekers come to inhabit a disposition to look for romantic and marital partners, i.e. HK Chinese, who could translate their lives from one of precarity into material, financial, as well as immigration security. One particular unexpected research finding was how artistic expressions play an important role in many ASR lives – musical creation, lyrics expressing their aspirations and frustrations about life and love in Hong Kong, as well as their displacement experiences. These artistic expressions also become a way for them to bond with each other and create communities for different purposes. There is one aspect that may be inadequately achieved: the importance and meanings of sex to both the men and women. There has been some resistance to discussions about this subject for the women in particular. With the men, there are findings that demonstrate how satisfypre-marital and extra-marital sex are not just expressions of a raging libido, but means of reclaiming masculinity - particularly a version of virile African masculinity. However, it was difficult to open up a discussion with the women about this subject, and all findings are limited to reproduction-related sexuality, rather than about sexual pleasures and intimacy.

14607415.label: Major findings and research outcome
14607415.value: My findings show convincingly that the racial-border regime reconfigure ideas of gender and intimacy. In particular, I develop the notion of Choreography of Masculinity in displacement to illuminate how these ideas change across borders and time, and how intimacy and marriage are integrally related to masculinities. A marriage-minded masculinity for asylum-seekers is a future-oriented masculinity focused on regularizing one’s life socially, and hopefully legally, through the acquisition of respectable roles and capacities as husband, father, and breadwinner.This is distinct but not necessarily disconnected from the pursuit of masculine recognition through sexual conquests or religious leadership. Therefore, the pursuits of intimacy and marriage for asylum-seeking men provide insights into how individuals negotiate their own subjectivity in relation to different sets of gendered expectations, racial hierarchies, and border regimes, pertinent to their meaning-making projects in displacement. Recognizing masculinity as spatialized and temporal practices, I trace asylum-seeking men’s changing subjectivities and corresponding pursuit for intimacy, marriage, and immigration status in Hong Kong. The racialization and marginalization of African asylum-seekers and refugees in Hong Kong are experienced as both embodied and structural vulnerabilities, and a suspension between the past and the future. These struggles go beyond the interpersonal realm and are enmeshed in the legacies of colonialism, imperialism, and transnational capitalism that have shaped matrices of gender, sexuality, race, and class; they have informed the way intimacies and borders are forged and contested. Another major finding is about how “love in waiting” is central to making relationships and lives meaningful for displaced persons, and how these public and private struggles are intertwined for asylum-seekers, and how displacement operates to shape subjectivity. Through intimate relationships of love, sex, and marriage with local women, African men create “a breach in their marginality” (Pinelli 2013:29) as circumscribed by the asylum regime, creating “a set of virtual possibilities for the present” (Bear 2014:27), and scripting “plausible alternative future” (Smith 2016:420) for themselves. “Love in waiting” is therefore a form of productive agency in time.

14607415.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14607415.value: I am currently working on a book proposal to publish the research findings and analysis in a manuscript titled "Love in Limbo: Intimacy and Masculinity for African Asylum-seeking Men in Hong Kong".

14607415.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14607415.value: As asylum-seeking and refugee men battle against the border regime and their socio-economic exclusion in Hong Kong - kept in waiting for sometimes over a decade, prohibited from work, study, and even volunteering, they turn to interpersonal relationships as a site of action. While their freedom and independence are highly circumscribed as asylum-seekers and refugees, and therefore many of them feel "unmanly" and lacking a future, they do aspire for love as a form of self-affirmation, and as a means to pursue possible new beginnings. The analysis focused on the dilemmas that asylum-seeking men confront as they pursue love as modern autonomous individuals, and how love offers a way out of their limbo. I look at how these men’s need for residence threatens the authenticity of their romantic pursuits, which in turn is shaped by their circumstances” of material, social, and political marginalization. By looking at the struggles that people in African-Chinese relationships face with regards to their friends, families, and the government policies, this research raises questions about racial stereotypes, the asylum system, border control, and history of colonialism shape the experiences of people in these cross-ethnic relationships, and open up new ways to think of love and intimacy.

14609215.label: Project Objectives
14609215.value: To trace the rise of strategic litigation in international and domestic settings as a tool for effectuating legal reform, distilling the key emerging trends. To ascertain what is the optimal legal environment or environments, including, potentially, multi- or trans-jurisdictional litigation pursuits, for instituting effective strategic litigation campaigns. Conversely, to identify instances where strategic litigation has failed to deliver on its objectives, where it may have even been counterproductive to the litigated cause, and where its limitations exist (e.g. problem of standing, difficulties of implementation). To identify best practices in terms of choosing appropriate clients, claims, and procedural mechanisms, including any limitations on domestic and/or international mechanisms and the factors as to why one may be better than the other in certain circumstances. To analyze budgetary concerns and constraints in conducting strategic litigation campaigns and explain why they may or may not be comparatively cost-effective in terms of initiating social justice reform. To ascertain the full extent of any professional ethical problems that may arise in strategic litigation, such as a client’s prolonged involvement for some years as appeal and international mechanisms are exhausted. To analyse the role of strategic litigation as part of the range of techniques that can be used to secure social justice, and how to use it in conjunction with other methods of seeking to reform the law (e.g. fostering public discussion, building coalitions, empowering marginalized groups), whether on a domestic or transnational scale.

14609215.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14609215.value: 着创业组织和倡导者的努力的结果，“策略性诉讼”有 产生了许多弱势群体显著的好处。术语“战略性诉讼”有 获得货币近年来，但是这是没有定义或研究的一个概念 系统。该项目的目的是确定，分析和推广最佳实践 战略性诉讼。 我们认为，“策略性诉讼”是涉及到精心挑选的律师业方法 案件采取法院和其他裁决机构，以实现影响深远的法律改革。 重点是寻求发展，将解决不仅由所带来的问题原则 客户端，但设置可以被其他人使用的先例;这可能也涉及设置建筑物 块的原则，未来的扩展。在国内法院存在这样的机制，但有 也存在可被用作一诉讼策略的一部分区域和国际机制。 这GRF项目将探索战略性诉讼的意义，作用和效用。它将提供 战略的形成，中，客户端和论坛选择方法的第一手分析 成本和实际物流方面的考虑。战略性诉讼将来自于一系列的检查 瞭望点，包括国内，国际比较的角度，以便 包容性。 该项目将产生的国际研究成果有价值，不同的利益相关者。首先，将 该项目的组成部分，是一个研讨会系列，每个专题讨论会探索不同 主题，并提供一个联络点，关键利益相关者参与知识交流和 进一步的合作。其次，每个研讨会将提供机会调查 以反映在不同上下文中战略性诉讼的用途，具有至少7轴颈 文章计划对应的研讨会系列的主题发布。第三，该 从这一提议产出还将包括建立一个战略性诉讼皮系列， 由香港中文大学的中心权利和司法研究门户管理，其上专题讨论会 参加者将被邀请提交他们的论文。研究者将寻求国际新闻 从研讨会发表的最显著文件编辑后的集合，与 调查作为卷的编辑。最后，该项目将有利于活动家，公民社会 机构，并通过了生产的实用指南，这将是对那些从事法律诊所 在这样的社区广为传播。

14609215.label: Realisation of objectives
14609215.value: All of these objectives have, to varying degrees, been met, despite the project encountering difficulties due to the unexpected resignation of its Research Assistant mid-way through the project. In total, the investigators produced three journal articles (two published and one pending) and presented at seven international conference/events. Presenting at these conferences also brought derivative benefits, in that the investigators were able to conduct interviews with practitioners of strategic litigation (in addition to presentations the investigators attended other events for information exchange with relevant stakeholders, including 'Strategic Litigation for Social Justice', held at Chatham House, London, on 14 March 2018). Such interviews in particular enriched the paper published in the Civil Justice Quarterly titled 'Defining Strategic Litigation', prepared as part of this project. The interviews also enabled the investigators to forge future collaboration links; a derivative of this project will be the production of a major multi author work 'Comparative Strategic Litigation' that is likely to be published by Edward Elgar Press (the reviews of the book proposal have been very positive subject to some minor modifications which the investigators are currently making to the proposal). That said, the number of outputs that would have enabled the full achievement in particular of objectives 3, 5 and 6 was hindered by the problem of recruiting a suitably qualified research assistant. The investigators applied for additional funding from CUHK to match the funding provided by the RGC so that the hiring of a high quality research assistant could be made possible. On this basis, a research assistant was appointed in September 2016 but she subsequently resigned with little notice in July 2017 having received a fully funded scholarship to complete an LLM in international law at Columbia Law School, Columbia University. Her sudden resignation caused difficulties in being able to recruit a suitable replacement, having regard to the completion date of the GRF and given that the principal investigator (Ramsden) was on sabbatical from October 2017 - September 2018, and prior to that on leave working at the International Criminal Court (June-September 2018). Given that the project only had a research assistant for part of its duration in turn led to the budget surplus indicated in this report, given that the majority of it was allocated for the hiring of a research assistant.

14609215.label: Major findings and research outcome
14609215.value: It is not possible to cover all of the findings here. But the major ones include: 1. Strategic litigation, despite being practiced on a transnational level, is surprisingly lacking a scholarly definition. Based upon extensive research of this practice and drawing upon our interactions with practitioners, we noted four key characteristics: (i) an extrinsic legacy component—it seeks outcomes with a long-term impact, going beyond the origins of the claimant’s complaint; (ii) it is a method of advocacy rather than a cause, and therefore adaptable to a range of purposes; (iii) its objectives are similarly multi-faceted and go beyond creating effects within the court system; (iv) it views “litigation” broadly, to include tribunals and international mechanisms of redress. 2. Strategic litigation is connected to other fields of litigation, including 'impact litigation', 'public interest litigation', or 'test case litigation', but also has a distinct meaning to denote more transnational forms of litigation. Unlike these other concepts that have come to be associated to varying degrees with social justice movement, strategic litigation is relatively value neutral and denotes a method of advocacy to effectuate change in society. 3. That said, it is apparent that strategic litigation has come to be associated with particular transnational campaigns, particularly in the attainment of a legal framework to address trafficking in persons and in the attainment of socio-economic rights. 4. Given the transnational component of strategic litigation, it is apparent that advocacy campaigns extend to the advancing of legal arguments before international and regional tribunals, and also bodies vested with quasi-judicial competencies, such subsidiary organs of the UN General Assembly or UN Human Rights Council.

14609215.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14609215.value: The three investigators have, flowing from this project, submitted a book proposal to Edward Elgar to edit a major multi-author work that explores strategic litigation from a comparative perspective. This proposal was very well received by the two reviewers of the book proposal, subject to some minor modifications of the proposal in terms of the range of countries surveyed. This book project will include contributors that we interacted with while completing the current project.

14609215.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14609215.value: Strategic litigation is everywhere, but nowhere is it defined or critiqued. The aim of this project was to fill the void through the interaction with those who engage in strategic litigation practice. It noted that strategic litigation is at a nascent stage in its development, its rise coinciding with the transnational rise legal advocacy and the understanding that legal developments in one country can affect reform in another. The project also noted some of the limitations of strategic litigation and how it might actually become a victim of its own success, where political actors seek to mobilise against progressive court judgments. This project has laid the foundation for further study of the phenomenon of strategic litigation and hopefully will prompt greater scholarly conversation across countries as to the value and utility of this practice.

14609315.label: Major findings and research outcome
14609315.value: This research examines the process of urban temple revival since the 1980s by focusing on selected temples and their interaction with state-planned urbanization. Re-opened Buddhist temples are compelled to find new niches when they encounter changed patterns of religious and urban identity. Under these circumstances, Buddhist temple revival is primarily dependent on three key factors: (1) the ability of religious agents to engage cooperatively with local state forces; (2) productive collaboration between religious leaders and commercial interests; and, most crucially, (3) the vision and determination of the temple’s abbot. PI has examined the relationship between temples restoration and the ecological approach and published two articles related to this subject: (i) [ 2019] “Urban Restructuring and the Study of Temple Agencies”, in Buddhism in the Post-Mao China, edited by Ji Zhe, Andre Laliberte, and Garth Fisher, The University of Hawaii Press, (ii) [ 2019] “閔行區龍音寺田野筆記-試從比丘尼訪談敘述分析佛教復興的政治與宗教邏輯” 《禪與人類文明研究》，香港中文大學出版社. (The details are listed in publication list.) 2. The successful restoration of 122 Buddhist temples in Shanghai city proper has led to a new myth about Buddhism serving as an enticement for neighborhood gentrification in the debates about urban planning. Drawing from the findings of my case studies of temple expansion and relocation in recent years, there are two findings in the restoration process related to gentrification: first, the significant divide between city center and suburban areas for revitalized religious and educational space in Buddhism temples that comes with political constructions, and, secondly, new relationships between religious clergy, land developers, and lay practitioners that have been created by these economic opportunities. One particular case on gentrification has been presented in a paper, “Urban Renewal and Buddhist Gentrification” in an International Conference on Metamorphosis of Buddhism in New Era China on March 22-23, 2019, at INALCO, Paris, France. 3. PI has investigated the relationship between the Buddhist temples recovery and the issue of immigration. Caused by the new city planning, the rise of non-monastic Buddhist movements that has attracted young middle-class urban inhabitants. The subject related to immigration has been published in three articles: (i) “The Place of Socially Engaged Buddhism in China– the Emerging Religious Identity in the Local Community of Urban Shanghai”, Journal of Buddhist Ethics, No. 25: 531-568, 2018; (ii) “From Structural Separation to Religious Incorporation - A Case Study of a Transnational Buddhist Group in Shanghai, China”, in Asian Migrants and Religious Experience - Transnational Religious Mobility, ed. Bernardo E. Brown and Brenda S.A. Yeoh, Amsterdam University Press, pp. 129-151, 2018; (iii) “都市佛教新貌：關於都市志願服務興起和以寺院為中心的義工的一些思考”《都市佛教的額弘法模式論文集》。 上海，華東師範大學出版社。[ 2019].

14609315.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14609315.value: 1. The studied temples with in-depth ethnographic research were mainly from the city center. Temples in the suburban area should also be studied and compared to those from the city center. This may provide an interesting comparison in a time of increased urbanization. 2. PI integrated the comments from one of grant reviewers suggesting comparing the status to Daoist temples in Shanghai. The critical condition of Daoist Temples facing the challenges of gentrification are different from those of Buddhist temples and should justify a follow-up study. PI has so far designed research and studied three Daoist Temples.

14609315.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14609315.value: This first and important study of 122 Buddhist temples in Shanghai city has discovered an increasing divide between city center and suburban areas for revitalized space in Buddhism temples. Explanatory GIS maps have been created for academic presentation and educational purpose. This study also confirmed that the hypothesis that the majority of male clergy in Shanghai are immigrants from North Jiangsu Province. As for the contemporary urban planning, the Chinese governors and land developers continue to believe that Buddhism serves as an enticement for neighborhood refurbishment. This study uncovers the important relationship between urban development and religious revitalization.

14610115.label: Project Title(Chinese)
14610115.value: 修復關係：中國家庭治療發展的民族志研究

14610115.label: Project Objectives
14610115.value: To study the development of family therapy in mainland China. To observe how family therapists adjust what they have learned in training to the actual conditions of providing therapy in the mainland Chinese context, and to the actual conditions of treating unique cases. To identify continuities and discontinuities between family therapy techniques on the one hand, and the subtle techniques ordinary people deploy in taking care of one another. To contribute to the anthropological critique of normative ethics, using the case of family therapy.
rows: To study the development of family therapy in mainland China.

To observe how family therapists adjust what they have learned in training to the actual conditions of providing therapy in the mainland Chinese context, and to the actual conditions of treating unique cases.
To identify continuities and discontinuities between family therapy techniques on the one hand, and the subtle techniques ordinary people deploy in taking care of one another.
To contribute to the anthropological critique of normative ethics, using the case of family therapy.

14610115.label: Realisation of objectives
14610115.value: Objective no. 1: the project has achieved 100% of the first objective. Data collection and analysis was entirely focused on an institute for family therapy in mainland China, where I conducted 6-months of immersive fieldwork in my role as an “intern.” I also visited other sites in the same city where family therapy was being practiced and taught. I made return trips during the summer break to participate in internship activities at the primary fieldsite and to conduct interviews with trainees. I studied and analyzed the professional literature, literature I was able to identify as salient based on what I observed in the course of fieldwork. I attended a major 3-day conference for family therapy in 2016. And lastly, I have been following WeChat groups dedicated to the study of family therapy. Objective no. 2: the project has achieved 85% of the second objective. I had ample opportunities for observing how trainees adjust what they have learned to the actual conditions of providing therapy having participated in 1) the senior supervision group, where trainees bring transcripts and videotapes from their own counseling work to receive feedback from teachers and fellow trainees, and 2) in study groups, where interns met on their own to watch videos and discuss techniques. In the latter, trainees shared their work experiences and experiences of supervision with one another in a much more relaxed and informal setting. Lastly, trainees talked with me about their professional development and counseling work in semi-structured interviews. I say only 85% of the second objective has been achieved because I still need more time to process and analyze interview transcripts. Objective no. 3: the project has achieved 100% of the third objective. Continuities and discontinuities between therapy and ordinary life were identified in the process of inductive and iterative analysis of fieldnotes and of the professional literature. I will discuss the finding in 6.1 below. Objective no. 4: the project has achieved 70% of the fourth objective. This objective is an odd one to have to quantify as the critique of normative ethics is and will continue to be a life-long project. While everything I write and publish relates to this broader theme, I say only 70% since I have one more paper to draft and complete from this project.

14610115.label: Major findings and research outcome
14610115.value: The project has thus far resulted in two peer-reviewed journal articles: the first in Culture, Medicine, and Psychiatry (2017 impact factor 1.318), the second in Ethnos: Journal of Anthropology (2017 impact factor: 1.894). I will be presenting a third paper at a major conference: the joint annual meeting of the American Anthropological Association and the Canadian Anthropology Society in Vancouver, November 2019. The conference paper shall serve as the basis for the third publication resulting from this GRF project. The findings of this project relate to how structural/systemic family therapy, as a system of knowledge and practice, offers a means for responding to the problems that arise in kin relations, broadly defined as relations between people who share time in place. This school of therapy takes the occasion of a misfortune, namely the suffering of an adolescent in the form of a psychiatric diagnosis, and sometimes, hospitalization, as an occasion for addressing relational tensions and problems that are typically not amenable to airing out in the context of everyday life. The theoretical foundation in systemic therapy with the help of a material-technical apparatus do at least three things: 1) configure the problem to be acted on in a particular way, 2) provide a laboratory-like situation that controls for external disturbances, thereby narrowing the field of possible action (important for the very possibility of action), and 3) symbolically mediates communication between family members themselves, and between family members and the therapeutic team. These findings relate to objective no. 3 in particular: what happens in family therapy is precisely what cannot happen in everyday life. A family therapy session externalizes the many ways kin injure and hurt one another, often not knowing they have done so. The practice of psychotherapy in general, and the significance of systemic therapy in particular, relates and responds to a broader social and historical context. Structural/systemic family therapy works on relational tangles that have negatively affected an adolescent, so as to set a suffering adolescent “free.” This is particularly significant in mainland China, a market-oriented society that rewards, to borrow from the words of a founding theorist, “self-directed” and “goal-oriented” human subjects who can survive and thrive in the tough competition for entry into good schools and good jobs.

14610115.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14610115.value: Firstly, I am still working through my fieldnotes and interviews from this GRF project. The third paper to be written will focus on the interview data with individual therapists and counselors, while the first two papers were based on analysis of professional literature and general observations of clinical encounters and how they realize and express a particular therapeutic logic. Secondly, I am considering another research institute in mainland China for a future fieldwork project, one that specializes in treating individual adolescents rather than family units, particularly adolescents who have withdrawn from school. The kind of therapy practiced at this institute is much closer to cognitive behavioral therapy. I am interested in understanding how different interventions arise out of differing ways of thinking about and configuring “causes.” I will seek the advice of an informant from this GRF project, who is currently playing a major role in disseminating information and facilitating study groups related to the intervention technique being developed at this other research institute. She can help to identify relevant professional literature and videos (e.g. recorded lectures), and with making contact with relevant personnel.

14610115.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14610115.value: In the United States, the birthplace of systemic family therapy, the status of such therapy is marginal and the field has taken a direction many insiders have expressed disappointment about. Major figures in the field had hoped systemic therapy could contribute to systemic change in the field of mental health services. And within the field of family therapy itself, there has been a turn away from systems and relations to the inner experience of individuals. While family therapists are relatively more reflexive about their own practice, in comparison to some other fields in human services, I believe anthropological thinking has a way of highlighting the significance of their work in a way that is unique to anthropology alone. The anti-individualist orientation of systemic therapy is important and commendable, and this investigator also harbors a hope that systemic therapy could succeed, if not in the United States, then elsewhere. The study of therapeutic interventions from an anthropological perspective contributes to an understanding of the multiple ways human societies have understood and addressed relational problems, and how questions about personhood and responsibility are raised and responded to.

14610515.label: Project Title(Chinese)
14610515.value: 三、四十年代中國現代派對法國左翼思想及文藝接受研究

14610515.label: Project Objectives
14610515.value: To investigate Chinese modernists’ reception of French leftist intellectuals’ literary and political ideas in the 1930s and 1940s. To examine the political-literary figures of the French leftist intellectuals as reconstructed by the Chinese modernists. To examine the Chinese modernists’ reinterpretation of French leftist literature in a Chinese historical context. To examine the Chinese modernists’ perspective on proletarian literature and their reflection on the dilemma between art and politics. To investigate the transcultural and hybrid nature of Chinese literary modernity.

To examine the political-literary figures of the French leftist intellectuals as reconstructed by the Chinese modernists.
To examine the Chinese modernists’ reinterpretation of French leftist literature in a Chinese historical context.
To examine the Chinese modernists’ perspective on proletarian literature and their reflection on the dilemma between art and politics.
To investigate the transcultural and hybrid nature of Chinese literary modernity.

14610515.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14610515.value: This project aims at carrying out research into the Chinese modernists’ reception of the French leftist intellectuals in the 1930s and 1940s. The Chinese modernists’ reception of the Western aesthetic modernism and their contribution to the construction of Chinese modernity have been convincingly argued by scholars in the last three decades. (Leo Ou-fan Lee; Shih Shu-mei; Peng Hsiao-yen) On the other hand, discussions on their attachment to the leftist ideologies in China and in Europe have been very limited. It was not until the 1990s that scholars have re-examined the reciprocal influences between the Chinese modernist and leftist literature (Zhang Tongdao; Liu Jianmei; Li Hongwa). A large corpus of Chinese modernists’ writings and translations related to the Leftist intellectuals in Europe, especially in France, has been overlooked, making it a missing chapter in the study of Chinese modernist literature. The Chinese modernists, deeply inspired by views of the French leftist intellectuals on aesthetics and politics, re-examined their own position on the controversial issues stemming from literature’s role in politics during the politicization of Chinese literary community, during the periods of the League of Left-wing Writers (1930-1936) and Second Sino-Japanese War (1937-1945). The project will focus on three major Chinese modernist “writers-translators-editors,” namely Shi Zhecun, Dai Wangshu and Ye Lingfeng. They translated over 80 titles of literary and political writings by Romain Rolland, André Gide, Henri Barbusse, Paul Vaillant-Couturier, Louis Aragon and André Malraux. Under their editorship, the literary journals and supplements have also published translations of articles from French leftist newspapers and literary reviews including the Humanité, the Commune, the Feuille rouge, and the Monde. By examining their criticism, translations and editorial activities, the project will investigate the Chinese modernists’ reconstruction of French leftist intellectuals’ political-literary figures as well as their re-interpretation of French leftist literature in a Chinese historical context. The project seeks to contribute to academic studies in three ways. First, it will bring forward an important but long-neglected chapter to the study of Chinese modernist literature and shed new light on the association between this study and French leftist trends. This will deepen our understanding of the transcultural and hybrid nature of Chinese literary modernity. Second, it will break new ground in the study of Twentieth-century Chinese and French comparative literature. Lastly, the project will extend the research scope of Chinese reception of leftist ideologies and literature by including the contribution from modernist writers. 本研究計劃旨在通過中國現代派作家的評論、翻譯和編輯活動，探討他們在三、四十年代中國特定歷史語境下如何理解歐洲左翼政治及文藝思潮，特別對法國左翼文學的接受及對法國左翼知識份子政治兼藝術家身分的重構。

14610515.label: Realisation of objectives
14610515.value: Our research project aims at carrying out research into the Chinese modernists’ reception of the French leftist intellectuals in the 1930s and 1940s. At the time of submission of this completion report, our research team has fully achieved the objectives of the project. Establishment of Archive The research team has completed the data collection and established an archive on critiques and translations of French, Japanese, Russian and other European leftist writers published in modernist literary journals in Shanghai in the 1930s and 1940s, as well as in literary supplements of the newspapers in Hong Kong, edited by two modernist writers, Dai Wangshu and Ye Lingfeng during the Second Sino-Japanese War. The data is classified into three categories: (i) Chinese modernists’ essays and criticism on French and other European leftist intellectuals; (ii) Chinese modernists’ translations of French and other European leftist intellectuals’ political and literary writings; (iii) Translations of articles from French leftist newspapers and reviews published in Chinese modernists’ literary journals and supplements. This database laid a solid foundation for the research project to investigate how French leftist intellectuals’ literary and political ideas travelled from Europe to Asia through Chinese modernists’ literary journals and supplements, and to examine Chinese modernists’ reinterpretation of French leftist literature in a Chinese historical context. Publication of a Single-Authored Monograph A single-authored monograph entitled Fanal Obscur: Chinese Modernists and European Leftist Literature and Art has been published in 2017. With the contradictory rhetoric of “Fanal obscure,” the book depicts the dilemmas faced by Chinese modernist writers when they explored their artistic and political path through their reflection on European modernism and leftist literature. This book, focusing on the period from the fall of the Chinese Revolution in 1927 to the end of the Second World War in 1945, reconstructs the relationship between the Chinese modernist and the European leftist literature and reveals the hybridity and heterogeneity of the Chinese modernity. The book contains seven chapters and is divided into three parts. The first part (Chapters 2 and 3), from a transcultural prospective, examines how Chinese modernists introduced the diverse perspectives on Russian-Soviet literature and Marxist literary theories to the Chinese literary circle from the Francophone leftist intellectuals’ point of view. The second part (Chapters 4 and 5) focuses on Chinese modernists’ interpretation on post-war French modernism, leftist literature and other literary trends in the historical context of the wars in Europe and Asia. The third part (Chapters 6 and 7), with the theoretical framework of avant-garde and modernism, examines Chinese modernists’ writings of proletarian literature and those of urban landscape. The monograph has been awarded the Publication Subvention Fund granted by the Faculty of Arts of the Chinese University of Hong Kong in 2017. It has been well received by the academic community and highly recommended by Prof. David Wang Der-wei, Edward C. Henderson Professor of Chinese Literature, Harvard University as well as Prof. Leo Lee Ou-fan, Wei Lun Professor of Humanities, CUHK (See Preface of the book). A favorable book review came out right after its publication in the journal Lunwen Hengshi (URL: https://mp.weixin.qq.com/s/E6v8eOpLFTUl4XCzT6tsZw ) Publication of Peer-reviewed Journal Papers Based on the findings of the research project, three academic journal papers have been or will be published, including the paper entitled “Images of Chinese and French Leftist Writers in Crossed Mirrors: Dai Wangshu, Réne Étiemble and André Malraux,” published in May 2018, examining the modernist poet, Dai Wangshu’s self-image as Marxist under the perspective of French leftist intellectuals, as well as his reconstruction of the political-literary figures of René Étiemble and André Malraux in a particular Chinese historical context. The PI has also submitted a research paper to a peer-reviewed academic journal in August 2018, entitled “The Left-wing Internationalism in the Context of European and Asian Wars: Barbusse’s Le Feu and Its Chinese Translation by Ye Lingfeng,” investigating Henri Barbusse’s Le Feu, Journal d’une Escouade (Under Fire: The Story of a Squad) and its Chinese translation by Ye Lingfeng from a transcultural and trans-historical perspective. The paper further compares and investigates Barbusse’s and Ye Lingfeng’s individual perspectives on war, internationalism and proletarian revolution, as well as the challenges facing them in Europe and Asia during the wartime. Publication of Peer-reviewed Papers at International Conferences The PI has presented seven refereed conference papers related to the research project at both local and international conferences (St. Petersburg, Taipei and Hong Kong). The conference paper entitled “Modernist and Russian Literature in Cross-cultural Perspective: Dai Wangshu’s translation of Les Poètes dans la révolution russe” has been presented at the XXIst Biennial Conference of the European Association of Chinese Studies (EACS) hosted by St. Petersburg State University, the Institute of Oriental Manuscripts RAS and the State Hermitage Museum, Russia, in August 2016. Another two conference papers investigating Ye Lingfeng’s Translation of Henri Barbusse’s Le Feu in the Contexts of Wars across Europe and Asia have been presented representatively at the International Conference on “Cultural Exchange and Reflective Imaginary: Research of Chinese Literature and Philosophy in Multi-Perspectives,” organized by the Institute of Chinese Literature and Philosophy, Academia Sinica, Taiwan, in December 2016, as well as the Biennial Conference of the Association of Chinese and Comparative Literature (ACCL), “Text, Media, and Transcultural Negotiation,” co-organized by the Association of Chinese and Comparative Literature (ACCL) and Department of Cultural and Religious Studies, The Chinese University of Hong Kong in June, 2017. The PI has also delivered two conference papers which focus on the Supplement of Li Pao and its publication of the Chinese Translation of Red Planes Fly East by a Russian communist writer, Pyotr Pavlenko, examining the anti-Japanese newspaper’s resistance strategy and its promotion of leftist ideology as well as anti-war literature in the context of the Second Sino-Japanese War. Knowledge Transfer (i) New Course for Postgraduate Students (PhD/MPhil) Based on the findings of the research project, the PI has developed a new post-graduate course “Selected Topics in Modern Chinese Literature: Chinese Modernism in a Transcultural Perspective” which aims at examining the transcultural and hybrid nature of Western and Chinese literary modernity for MPhil and PhD students. This course has been offered in 2017. (ii) Further Development of Postgraduate Course (MA Programme) The PI has offered the course “Study of Chinese Fiction and Literary Magazines in the 1930s” for MA students in 2018. Based on the findings of the research project, the PI could provide more materials and insights into the relationship of Chinese modernist literature and European leftist ideologies and literary trends. (iii) Keynote speech The PI has been invited to be the keynote speaker at the “Expressions in Humanities: The First Academic Youth Conference,” organized by the Division of Arts and Languages of the College of International Education, Hong Kong Baptist University in February 2017. More than a hundred students attended the conference and based on the findings of the research project, the PI delivered a keynote speech on Chinese modernist literature in the 1930s.

14610515.label: Major findings and research outcome
14610515.value: 1. A single-authored monograph entitled Fanal Obscur: Chinese Modernists and European Leftist Literature and Art has been published in 2017. Focusing on the period from the fall of the Chinese Revolution in 1927 to the end of the Second World War in 1945, the book depicts the dilemmas faced by Chinese modernist writers when they explored their artistic and political path through their reflection on European modernism and leftist literature. It reconstructs the relationship between the Chinese modernist and the European leftist literature and reveals the hybridity and heterogeneity of the Chinese modernity. A favorable book review came out right after its publication in the journal Lunwen Hengshi (URL: https://mp.weixin.qq.com/s/E6v8eOpLFTUl4XCzT6tsZw ) 2. Based on the findings of the research project, three academic journal papers have been or will be published. These papers include “Images of Chinese and French Leftist Writers in Crossed Mirrors: Dai Wangshu, Réne Étiemble and André Malraux,” “Shuttling between East and West: Ye Si, Hong Kong Literature and Modern Chinese Literature from the Perspectives of German and French Scholars” and “The Left-wing Internationalism in the Context of European and Asian Wars: Barbusse’s Le Feu and Its Chinese Translation by Ye Lingfeng”. (Please refer to Part C8 for details) 3. The PI has delivered seven refereed conference papers related to the research project at international conferences held in St Petersburg, Taipei and Hong Kong. These papers include “Chinese Modernists and French Leftist Intellectuals in the 1930s and 1940s: On the Translation and Transmission of Benjamin Goriély’s Les Poètes dans la révolution russe,” “The Leftist Internationalism in the Context of European and Asian Wars: Barbusse’s Le Feu and Its Translation by Ye Lingfeng,” “Sino-Japanese War and Western Literature: A Study of Ye Lingfeng’s Edition of the Supplement of Li Pao and His Chinese Translation of Red Planes Fly East” and “Revisiting and Reinvestigation: A Transcultural Dialogue on “Telling the Truth” emphasized by Ba Jin” etc. (Please refer to Part C9 for details)

14610515.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14610515.value: Based on the findings of the current research project, we propose to carry out research into the Chinese modernists’ writings and translations of war literature during the war-time period (1931-1945) in translingual and transcultural perspectives. We include in this group of modernist “writers-translators-editors” Dai Wangshu, Shi Zhecun (1905-2003), Liu Na’ou (1905-1940), Xu Xiacun (1907-1986) and Ye Lingfeng (1905-1975). We propose to conduct this new research in two stages. In the first stage, we will first examine Chinese modernists’ writing and criticism of war literature as well as their reflection on the dilemma between art and politics in the particular historical context of China. In the second stage, we intend to examine Chinese modernists’ translations and the reception of European war literature, including works about the First World War (1914-1918), the Russian Revolution (1917) and the Spanish Civil War (1936-1939) etc. Our “Research Database of Chinese modernists’ Translations in the 1930s” will provide the necessary data of these works (URL: http://www.transchimodern.hk/). We will investigate the way Chinese modernists developed their own interest in revolutionary literature, war literature or even proletarian literature in the context of wars of Europe and Asia. This project will also investigate the heterogeneity of Chinese modernity.

14610515.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14610515.value: While the Chinese modernists’ reception of the Western aesthetic modernism has been convincingly argued by scholars in the last three decades, discussions on their attachment to the leftist ideologies in China and in Europe have been very limited. This project aims at investigating the Chinese modernists’ reception of the French leftist intellectuals in the 1930s and 1940s. It brings forward an important but long-neglected chapter to the study of Chinese modernist literature and sheds new light on the association between this study and French leftist trends. This deepens our understanding of the transcultural and hybrid nature of Chinese literary modernity. Moreover, it breaks new ground in the study of Twentieth-century Chinese and French comparative literature. Lastly, as Chinese Left-wing writers were mostly influenced by the Russian and Japanese proletarian movements, this project extends the scope of research into the Chinese reception of leftist ideologies and literature, by including the contribution from modernist writers. Based on hitherto-neglected source materials and the findings of the project, a monograph entitled Fanal Obscur: Chinese Modernists and European Leftist Literature and Art as well as numerous peer-reviewed journal papers and conference papers have been published.

14610915.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14610915.value: In April 2013 asylum seekers were marching through Hong Kong, demanding faster asylum processes and improving the conditions for them in the city. The protests were taken up by international media like CNN and Al Jazeera (Ortigas, 27 April, 2013) and since then Hong Kong has been branded as a city unwelcoming to asylum seekers. This picture is paradoxical as Hong Kong is a city of refugees from Mainland China, which prides itself on its global connectivity. However, global connectivity is problematic for those who are arrested in space, such as forced migrants, who remain in transit in Hong Kong. There were thirty six million forced migrants in 2014, with Hong Kong having 1871 people seeking asylum and 126 recognized refugees (UNHCR, 2014), plus several thousands of torture claimants. The extant literature, including my own, has shown that people seeking asylum lack engagement with ICTs, caused by poverty, social isolation, gender conventions, and limited media literacy (Witteborn, 2012, 2014; Wilding & Gifford, 2013). But the literature has also started addressing the benefits of new technologies for forced migrants (Leung, 2007; Gifford & Wilding, 2013). Asylum seekers have become connected migrants (Diminescu, 2008) as they navigate their flight routes and daily life via mobile phone, connect to NGOs via websites, and use social media and Skype (Papadopoulos, Stephenson, & Tsianos, 2008). Through Youtube, Twitter and Facebook asylum seekers gain information on asylum, stay in contact with home, and mobilize politically, even while in transit. Engagement with new technologies also changes urban space as asylum seekers and their supporters can address problems via social media, as was the case in Hong Kong in 2014 when a pig farm was discovered to house asylum seekers who were eventually relocated to other parts of the city. The following main questions arise for the context of Hong Kong: Which digital practices do asylum seekers engage with to relate to each other, to existing migrant groups, and locals while being in transit? How does digital connectivity and sociocultural grouping, enabled through for and non-profit actors, shape urban space? The theoretical goal is to develop migration and communication theorizing in relation to an autonomy of migration approach (e.g., Mezzadra, 2011; Moulier Boutang, 1993) through data from (East)Asia. The practical goal is to design communication training for people seeking asylum in Hong Kong, based on their needs, which can improve their employment chances in their countries of resettlement. 2013年4月，一群尋求庇護的人士在香港街頭遊行，要求政府及聯合國難民署加快難民審批工作，以改善他們的生活條件。遊行吸引美國有線新聞網絡、半島電視台等國際媒體關注 (Ortigas, 27 April, 2013)，國際輿論頓時甚囂塵上，將香港視為不歡迎難民的城市。 香港素以「國際城市」自居，但國際間的論述似乎不認同這觀點，亦與香港過去作為內地難民聚集地的歷史相悖。香港向來自命「連接全球」，但因各種原因而停留在港的難民則被排拒在外。根據聯合國難民署(2014)資料顯示，2014年全球共有超過3600萬名難民，其中香港共有1871位尋求庇護者、126位認可難民以及數千名酷刑聲請者。這些難民在港的生活水平十分有限，當中從他們的科技資源可見一斑。現存文獻及本人過去的研究均指出，基於貧窮、社會分隔、性別傳統以及缺乏科技知識等原因，普遍難民缺乏使用資訊科技的機會 (Witteborn, 2012, 2014; Wilding & Gifford, 2013)。 不過，研究亦發現新的資訊科技能為難民帶來好處(Leung, 2007; Gifford & Wilding, 2013)。難民現在可以利用手機搜索日常生活資訊，以至逃亡路線，亦可透過網絡與志願組織聯繫，甚至可透過社交媒體及Skype等與聯絡親友 (Papadopoulos, Stephenson, & Tsianos, 2008)。難民亦可以透過YouTube、Twitter、Facebook等渠道了解他們的權益及生活狀況，甚至發起政治運動。科技運用不僅為難民自身帶來改變，也重塑城市空間。例如2014年在港難民便透過社交媒體，展露他們於養豬場居住的情況，逼使當局正視問題，為他們安排更佳居所。 基於以上論點，本研究以香港自身的環境，提出了兩大研究問題：暫時停留在港的尋求庇護者使用甚麼電子方式，與其他尋求庇護者、其他在港移民以及本地人聯繫？電子網絡、社會文化背景以及非牟利組織，如何影響城市空間的形成和變遷。 是次研究目標，主要希望透過亞洲的實例，擴充現存與移民自主權(例如 Mezzadra, 2011; Moulier Boutang, 1993) 相關的移民及傳播理論。同時亦希望利用研究結果，輔以香港難民的需要為本，設計一套能幫助他們提升就業機會的傳播訓練。

14610915.label: Realisation of objectives
14610915.value: Both objectives were fully realised. Objective 1 This study was interested in how forced migrants use digital communication practices under conditions of transit. (Hong Kong has not signed the Geneva Refugee Convention and thus resettles forced migrants, making them live in transit until resettlement.) First, the study engaged with the arguments of the Autonomy of Migration literature and how migration is an economic, social, and political force (Mezzadra & Neilson, 2013). Migration itself transforms spaces, including urban space and whole societies (Karakayali & Tsianos 2007). The study added to the arguments of the Autonomy of Migration literature by emphasizing the important role of technology in processes of migration. While being in transit in Hong Kong, asylum seekers and refugees used digital practices to participate in the social life of Hong Kong, move though the city, form cultural groups for psychological and social support in face of linguistic and cultural isolation, connect with existing diasporas, find romantic relationships, and gain language skills (Cantonese and English). While technology and digital practices helped contest a victim’s narrative (Moulier Boutang, 2007), those practices were constrained by financial dispositions of asylum seekers and education about technology use. Moreover, NGOs in Hong Kong catered to forced migrants but were not always able to keep pace with the fast-changing technological environment, including teaching the migrants about data safety and security. This study filled this gap. In the following, I will answer the research questions posed in the GRF grant. Which digital practices do asylum seekers engage with to relate to each other, to existing migrant groups, and locals while being in transit? How does digital connectivity and sociocultural grouping, enabled through for and non-profit actors, shape urban space? Which factors enable and restrain digital communicative practice under conditions of transit? Who are the actors which enable access to communication services for forced migrants? Asylum seekers and refugees are strong adopters of smart phones which they either bring from their home countries or buy cheaply in Chungking Mansions or the Mongkok area. The actors who enabled access to communication objects and services were other refugees and migrants (e.g., domestic workers), local friends, supporters (e.g., lawyers), and NGOs. Refugees received digital objects like computers and phones as well as data as gifts from those sources (Witteborn, 2019). The people engaged with social media for connecting with local friends and family abroad, to search for news, navigate the city, for translation services, and learning skills (e.g., Youtube). Some used WeChat. WhatsApp was used mostly for the creation of social groups (e.g., mother groups, sports groups) and cultural groups (e.g., co-national connection, religious grouping). Social media helped asylum seekers to connect to locals although interactions were still limited beyond NGO engagement with locals. Existing diasporas were supportive of asylum seekers from the respective countries and helped them engage in social relations or to participate in community organizations (e.g., HK African Association). The digital practices shaped Hong Kong’s urban space in three main ways. First, forced migrants used social media to organize informal get-togethers or formalized meetings (e.g., within the frame of diasporic organizations like the African Association). People met in urban spaces which were free of charge (parks and malls) and which provided technological access (Wifi) and free access to electricity (for recharging phones). Second, technology helped shape Hong Kong’s urban space as a multicultural space. Social media, Facebook and WhatsApp in particular, were used by refugees to connect with each other, locals, and NGOs and to document events and friendships. NGOs enabled the meeting between forced migrants, diasporic groups, and locals through cultural, religious, and sports events. Organizations like Table of Two Cities engaged locals, expatriates, and forced migrants through cooking and sharing food. The Centre for Refugees assisted with the creation of mixed sports teams, and offering language classes. Refugees were also regularly invited to local schools and universities to educate students on issues of forced migration. Local churches and mosques were also weekly interfaith meeting places. Food, narratives, faith, and sports became intercultural meeting points, engraving urban space as multicultural space, enabled through and documented on social media. Third, through their social media representations, refugees represented Hong Kong as a globalized and yet local place. They actively engaged with urban space by documenting their urban movement and presenting the city of Hong Kong to a global audience. But despite their active engagement with urban space through social media representation and digital connectivity with locals and other migrants, urban space also had a detrimental effect on refugees by making them feel invisible or hypervisible. The majority of asylum seekers and refugees felt not seen in the city in the physical and symbolic sense. The majority had experienced racial discrimination, especially the people from African nations. This majority felt either hyper-visualized in Hong Kong through their skin color and regular police checks or hyper-invisible through the linkage between race and asylum seeking and local Hong Kongers avoiding them in daily life. The Refugee Centre at Christian Action (social support), Refugee Union (political mobilization), and the Justice Centre (legal advice and education) are NGOs which provide Internet access and educational opportunities for refugees. Despite those services, digital practices were constrained for refugees by lack of financial resources (to buy a new phone or computer or access data packages) and lack of knowledge about data security. No problems were encountered. Objective 2 The second objective was to design a course on digital media literacy and communicating in the US as a place of settlement. The data gathered over two years show a strong preference of the forced migrants for a media literacy course that focused on how to keep their digital communication and data secure. Hence, a course was designed available on Github (https://github.com/hongkonggong/social-media-safety-asylum-seekers). This course teaches media literacy through the angle of data safety and security. The course focuses on social media companies like Facebook, which are situated in the US. Through discussions on how security settings work on Facebook and WhatsApp, how filter bubbles are produced, and what that means for news feeds and group interaction in Hong Kong, worldwide, and in the US where the company is located, this course educates refugees about digital media as well as the United States as a multicultural country with strong free market values and an individualistic culture, and what that means for newly arriving refugees in terms of acting independently and finding jobs. During a pilot study, refugees as well as NGOs were interested in a template for how to conduct this workshop and to replicate it for other refugees instead of a written report. The course itself was enthusiastically received by the refugees. Hence, myself and my assistant, security expert Jason Li, decided to create this course as a digital, open source template on Github.

14610915.label: Major findings and research outcome
14610915.value: I briefly present the main research findings and refer to Objective 1 for further explanation. Asylum seekers and refugees were strong adopters of technology to move through urban space, learn skills on Youtube, meet co-nationals, people of shared faith, and create interest groups through Facebook and WhatsApp. Social media was important to create social relations as people reported a strong sense of cultural isolation, amplified through uncertainty. People used technology for cultural encounters in urban space, mostly in the Kowloon area. People also reported how the dense urban space of Hong Kong is alienating as negative stereotypes purported by traditional and social media make them feel invisible and exposed to discrimination. NGOs were urban centers of organizing social encounters between refugees and locals, providing education on technology and free internet. Local professionals and established diasporas were important for gifting technology to refugees (phones and data) to explore urban space, stay informed, educate themselves, and find NGOs and legal/medical help. The most surprising finding was the discrepancy between how forced migrants presented themselves on social media and during interviews. Their social media performance illustrates a highly socially connected self, firmly imagined in global relations, and in Hong Kong as a global city. There was none of the loneliness and cultural isolation reported during the interviews. The people performed an aspirational mobility on social media that was strongly connected to the imagined space of Hong Kong as a socially mobile and globally connected space; types of mobility that the forced migrants wished for themselves in the future. The research has supported several publications (co-authored handbook, papers, book chapters, and one co-edited proposal to be sent out for review). A paper has been published in an SSCI journal on the topic of the digital gift. The conceptual insights from this study helped me to be co-editor of the Handbook on Migration and Media (Sage) and to select contributors on the topic of forced migration and technology as well as co-write a chapter on migration and mobility. The research project has already received much interest as I was invited as Distinguished Scholar to Israel to give a public lecture and a seminar (June 2-3, 2019) and as a paper is under review by the prestigious journal Theory, Culture & Society. The course on data safety has become a digital template; resulting in a paper for presentation at AoIR in Brisbane with top reviews. A proposal for a co-edited book is ready for submission.

14610915.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14610915.value: The grant results provide an excellent basis for developing the topics of transit space and data safety further. The researcher plans on developing the topic of transit space as infrastructural space and the implications of being in transit in this process. One of the papers coming out of the research engages with the idea of transit space as infrastructural space and the metanarrative of impermanence governing the process of transit. The goal is to outline the destructive but also generative potential of being in transit for those on the move, including asylum seekers and privileged migrants. Transit space has been described in the literature mostly as problematic space for forced migrants (Hess, 2012), a view which can be complimented through adopting perspectives from mechanical engineering and physics where transient events are regarded as generative, creating instability in a system but also reconfiguring it. Moreover, I plan a multi-sited project on what it means being in transit and the role of technology in this spatial and temporal process. I will also develop the notion of data safety for migrants; a theoretically and practically underdeveloped area, based on the paper presented at AoIR in Brisbane.

14610915.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14610915.value: This project examined forced migration and technologies within the transit space of Hong Kong. Hong Kong is a transit space as refugees have to be resettled, meaning that those seeking asylum live in a space of impermanence. This project is significant as there are hardly any studies on transit in Asia. Transit space has been described as a difficult space in the literature. This study supports this notion but also shows how transit has generative potential. People seeking asylum use platforms like Facebook and WhatsApp to connect to other migrants, communities of worship, and diasporas. The people learn skills through social media (e.g., navigation of urban space, languages, and to create social support), and they teach locals about forced migration and cultural diversity. Digital connectivity and support are important as the people are exposed to negative stereotyping, creating social isolation. Despite these experiences, the people amplify Hong Kong as a space of cultural, linguistic, and religious encounter for a global audience by presenting themselves and the city on social media. The study strengthens the argument about migration as an autonomous force which changes migrants, locals, and the places through which migrants cross but in which they can never settle.
