14612615.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14612615.value: HIV is an important public health concern over the globe. Men who have sex with men (MSM) play a critical role in the transmission of HIV in Hong Kong. Evidence has shown that HIV risk perception is strongly associated with behavioral change, however, the level of risk perception towards HIV and STD among MSM in Hong Kong is relatively low. It has been suggested that narratives, which refer to the use of personal experiences in promoting a behavior, offer a useful alternative in changing risk perceptions and behaviors. From our knowledge, no study to date utilizes narratives in changing HIV risk perception and behaviors among Chinese MSM. Moreover, the emergence of internet technology allows health interventions to be delivered in a fast and convenient manner. The proposed study aims to test the efficacy of online narratives in increasing HIV risk perception and reducing HIV risk behaviors among MSM in Hong Kong. A 2-armed randomized controlled trial is proposed, Chinese men who self-reported having anal sex with another man in the past six months will be recruited and randomly allocated into the intervention (N=238) and the control group (N=238). Participants in the intervention group will be asked to visit the study site (website or apps) which contains didactic information about HIV/STD and narratives of HIV negative and HIV positive peer MSM. Participants in the control group will only access the didactic information about HIV/STD on the study site. Participants will be evaluated at baseline, and one month and six months after the intervention using online questionnaires. The primary outcome will be unprotected anal intercourse (UAI); secondary outcomes will include perceived risk of contracting STD and HIV in the future, perceived severity of STD and HIV, condom social norms, HIV testing behavior, intention to use condom, and intention to receive HIV testing. The mechanism which the intervention influences HIV perception and risk behaviors through identification and engagement with the study site will also be tested. The proposed intervention, if found successful, will have significant implication for implementation as it can be launched in many MSM websites, NGOs or other internet-based domains, it can reach many MSM at a very low cost and has the potential to reduce the increasing HIV epidemic among MSM in Hong Kong. 愛滋病病毒（HIV）是一個重要的全球性公共衛生問題。在香港，男男性接觸者（MSM）對於HIV的傳播起著關鍵作用。已有証據表明HIV風險認知與高危行為密切相關，然而香港MSM對於HIV和性傳播疾病（STD）的風險認知水平卻較低。敘述，即運用個人經歷來促進健康行為，被認為是一種改變風險認知和行為的有效途徑。據了解，迄今為止尚沒有研究運用敘述的方法來改變中國MSM的HIV風險認知和行為。此外，網絡技術的出現使得健康干預能夠便捷地開展。 本研究旨在檢驗運用在線敘述的方法提高香港MSM的HIV風險認知以及減少HIV風險行為的效果。我們計劃開展一項雙組隨機對照試驗，招募曾在過去6個月內與男性進行過肛交的中國男性，並將他們隨機分配為干預組（N=238）和對照組（N=238）。我們將要求干預組的參加者觀看一些網上干預資料（網站或是應用程序），上面包含關於HIV/STD的信息以及一些分別是HIV陽性和陰性的MSM同伴的敘述；對照組的參加者;則只觀看網上干預中關於HIV/STD的信息。我們將採用在線問卷的方式在基線以及干預後1個月和6個月時對參加者進行測評。主要研究結果是無保護性肛交（UAI）；次要結果包括對未來感染STD和HIV風險的認知，對STD和HIV嚴重性的認知，安全套社會准則，HIV檢測行為，使用安全套的傾向以及接受HIV檢測的傾向。我們還將檢驗干預影響HIV認知和風險行為的機制。若此干預能成功改變參加者的的HIV風險認知，將有很重要的實踐意義，它能在很多MSM網站、NGO或者其他網域得到開展，以極低的成本惠及很多的MSM，並且很有可能減低香港MSM中HIV的上升趨勢。

14612615.label: Realisation of objectives
14612615.value: There are three major steps to achieve the project objectives including the design, implementation, and evaluation of the proposed intervention: 1. Designing an internet-based narrative communication intervention A video-based multi-session intervention was developed. First, themes and respective subtopics that captured different aspects of behavioral promotion for HIV prevention were identified based on both quantitative and qualitative evidence. A review of significant predictors of HIV/STI transmission and risky sexual behaviors among MSM in Hong Kong were first conducted to inform the selection of persuasive topics. A focus group discussion with five local MSM was then conducted to assess knowledge, views and information needs on specific persuasive topics under each theme, and to seek their suggestions on the development of intervention materials. The revision to session themes and subtopics was also made based on feedbacks from the collaborating NGO (AIDS Concern) staff and specialists in this field. Second, the videotaped recording of the narrative interviews was undertaken to elicit firsthand stories from selected MSM narrators who acted as different role models. Nine MSM peers were finally selected as the eligible narrators who were representative of the local MSM community in terms of the socio-demographic characteristics and were able to generate informative stories under diverse themes related to HIV prevention. Interviews were conducted with each of the narrator using the semi-structured interview guide drafted around the proposed themes and subtopics and further tailored to individual characteristics. Third, a series of intervention videos with themed messages in two formats (narrative or argumentation) were produced. The framework analysis approach was used to coalesce the original story segments into collective narrative messages for each topic. Six video themes were finally established: Knowledge about HIV/STI, Condom Use and Partnership, Condom Use and Risky Contexts, Condom Use and Substance Use, Efficacious Condom Use, HIV Testing. Topic-equivalent argumentation messages were accordingly drafted under each theme, featuring the argumentative presentation of didactic statements, logical reasons, statistical evidence and factual information. Three speakers were invited to deliver the scripted messages which were also videotape-recorded. Fourth, a dedicated website was developed as the intervention delivery platform. A content management system was established to enable the automated intervention delivery and the real-time monitoring of each participant’s engagement. An email broadcast system was used to send automated reminders when necessary. 2. Implementing a randomized controlled trial to test for the intervention efficacy First, eligible adult MSM were recruited from both online (social networking sites) and offline (popular gay venues) sources in Hong Kong. Among the MSM who showed their interest in participating in the present study, 581 logged into the study website and went through the online screening. Finally, a total of 349 eligible MSM were enrolled in the trial after completing the baseline survey online and providing consent to receive the intervention. During the recruitment, both automated and human verification approaches were used to avoid fraudulent and duplicate respondents. Each participant had a unique password-protected account, and their progression through the trial phases were automatically recorded. Second, the enrolled participants were randomly allocated by the computerized system to either the intervention group (n=174) or the control group (n=173). For both groups, the entire intervention lasted for six weeks and there were six sessions in total. Each session delivered video messages focused on a specific theme related to HIV prevention. The intervention group received two videos with narrative and argumentation messages (aka combined messages), respectively; while the control group received the argumentation one only. The intervention was implemented at an individual-level and videos were not able to be downloaded or shared outside the study, so as to avoid the potential contamination between conditions. After each video, a one-item quiz about the video content was conducted to tap the participants’ dedication. Video messages were delivered to all participants in a standardized manner; the first intervention session was open to access immediately upon the completion of baseline assessment and other sessions were then released online sequentially on a weekly basis. Each session was accessible only when the former one had been completed. Given that the increasing incentive was necessary for stimulating the adherence to a multiple-session intervention, participants were rewarded HK$ 50 for the completion of session 1-3 within three weeks; and another HK$ 100 for the completion of session 4-6 before the intervention ended. Third, a post-intervention survey was released online immediately after the intervention while a longer-term follow-up survey was released after six months. Both follow-up surveys were administered to all enrolled sample regardless of the retention status during the treatment. Notwithstanding, variables related to the treatment (e.g. engagement with messages) were not measured among treatment dropouts. A coupon of HK$ 50 was provided as an incentive to complete each follow-up survey. Appropriate confines (e.g. conditional branching, forced answering) were set to facilitate the progression through the survey and ensure the completion quality. Databases of evaluation responses could be automatically generated by the online system, and thus were not subject to the errors due to human data entry. 3. Evaluating the comparative efficacy of the intervention condition As indicators of the intervention efficacy, outcomes of behaviors and cognitions with respect to HIV prevention were repeatedly measured before and after the intervention. Theoretical determinants of HIV prevention-related behaviors were measured at all three assessment waves, including intention to consistent condom use, condom social norm, self-efficacy about consistent condom use, intention to HIV testing. Behavioral outcomes were measured at baseline and 6-month follow-up, including condom use for anal intercourses, safe sex communication and HIV testing. Indicators of information processing mechanisms were measured post-intervention among participants who completed at least one of the six intervention sessions, including engagement with video messages and identification with messengers. Background variables (e.g. ehealth literacy) and other potential confounding factors (e.g. the use of pre-exposure prophylaxis, PrEP) were measured at baseline and follow-up assessments, respectively. Finally, a total of 224 and 240 participants completed the post-intervention and 6-month follow-up assessment, respectively, and were included for the analyses. Baseline characteristics were first compared between conditions. Significant group imbalance, if found, was further controlled for as the potential confounder of intervention effects. Within-group comparisons between baseline and follow-up levels of efficacy outcomes were conducted for each condition. Between-group comparisons in efficacy outcomes were then conducted for each follow-up wave. Next, the Baron and Kenny’s principle was followed to test for the mediation effect of mechanism-related variables. The effect of intervention condition on efficacy outcomes and potential mediators was first examined. If both effects were found to be statistically significant, the indirect effect of intervention condition on efficacy outcomes through the potential mediator was further examined.

14612615.label: Major findings and research outcome
14612615.value: 1. The low level of HIV preventive behaviors among MSM in Hong Kong Of participants who self-reported having specific male sex partners in the past three months, 48.6% consistently used condoms while having anal intercourses with regular partners; and 66.1% consistently used condoms with casual partners. With respect to the role-specific sexual behaviors, 50.4% and 54.3% consistently used condoms during receptive and insertive anal intercourses. The above levels were far from the recommended one of 70%. Though 87.4% of the participants had ever taken up any HIV testing in lifetime, less than half had an HIV testing in the past six months prior to the enrollment. These findings highlighted the importance of promoting consistent condom use and regular HIV testing among this vulnerable population. 2. Intervention efficacy in improving HIV preventive behaviors and cognition Pre-post intervention comparisons showed that there was no significant change from baseline to post-intervention in any of the efficacy outcomes under each condition. However, at the 6-month follow-up, the intervention group had a significant increase in the intention to consistent condom use with regular sex partners and self-efficacy about consistent condom use with male sex partners; while the control group had a significant increase in the intention to HIV testing. Between-group comparisons showed that the intervention group had a significantly higher level of consistent condom use with casual sex partners and related behavioral intentions than the control one at the 6-month follow-up. A significant interaction between time and group effects was further detected. Both conditions conferred a comparably reduced intentions at post-intervention. However, the intention level increased during the 6-month follow-up among the intervention group whereas continued decreasing among the control group. This indicated that the use of narrative messages tended to counteract the resistance to the argumentation messages. 3. Information processing mechanisms underlying the intervention efficacy Compared with the control condition, the combined messages were found to evoke significantly greater identification with messengers at the post-intervention, which fully mediated the intervention efficacy in increasing intention to consistent use with casual sex partners at the 6-month follow-up. This indicated that the efficacy of narrative persuasion was attributed to its ability to facilitate the processing of persuasive messages. However, the intervention condition was not efficacious in evoking higher engagement with the messages. This suggested the independent role of identification with specific characters in narrative persuasion with the absence of full immersion into the overall story.

14612615.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14612615.value: Based on the current study, future research on the most optimal construction of narrative communication interventions for HIV prevention is warranted. A more complex study design (e.g. factorial design) needs to be applied to manipulate specific communication components (including message source, recipient, channel, and message) and understand their potential interplays. The most effective combination of narrative and argumentation messages needs further exploration to maximize the synergistic effect on promoting behavioral change. Also, information processing mechanisms underlying the narrative persuasion would be further examined, to inform the translation of theoretical constructs into intervention techniques. In terms of the practical applications, the present study could inform the future incorporation of narrative communication as part of the comprehensive prevention services for MSM. Given the rigorous development procedures, the narrative intervention can be efficiently replicated and adapted to other regions and high-risk populations, though its efficacy needs to be further tested in other settings. Moreover, this self-guided intervention has the potential to be scaled-up and integrated into regular prevention services when its cost-effectiveness being further demonstrated. The key actions are enhancing the population’s ehealth literacy as well as exploiting usable and sustainable ehealth platforms.

14612615.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14612615.value: The present study capitalized on narrative persuasion for HIV prevention among the MSM population. Narratives used in this study took a form of firsthand experiential stories related to HIV prevention shared by local MSM peers. A randomized controlled trial was conducted to investigate the persuasive impact of a hybrid message format featuring the narrative messages combined with overtly argumentative support relative to the standard information condition- argumentation messages only. Current findings provided empirical evidence on the superiority of the combined messages in improving intention to consistent condom use with casual sex partners and actual practices through the facilitated information processing. Following rigorous development procedures, this narrative intervention could be easily replicated and incorporated into comprehensive HIV prevention efforts. The present study also demonstrated the feasibility and acceptability of utilizing ehealth technology to deliver HIV prevention interventions among Chinese MSM. Most importantly, this self-help intervention did not require trained counselors to communicate the messages and could be easily operated through other online platforms (e.g. social networking sites). Hence, it had the potential to be scaled up and reach many MSM in a cost-effective and sustainable way.

14612715.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14612715.value: Working-class public sphere is a concept developed mostly by philosophers and historians in reaction to the Habermasian theory of bourgeois public sphere. Conceived from a social science perspective, this project examines the emergence of working-class public spheres in an era of information technology and global connectivity through an in-depth case study of media and activism, especially digitally networked action (DNA) since the “Foxconn Suicide Express” of 2010. This study will focus on, but not be limited to, Foxconn, the world’s largest electronics manufacturer, hiring 1.4 million Chinese employees who churn out iPhones, iPads, and other coveted gadgets for consumers worldwide. The working conditions are so oppressive that seventeen workers jumped from tall buildings in the first eight months of 2010. The tragedy triggered a tidal wave of media coverage and activism by NGOs, students, teachers, and citizens. Since 2012, Foxconn workers have also started to make their voices heard through DNA. Our project is guided by this basic idea: the problematic practices of capitalist industrialism stimulate working-class public spheres, a hybrid space of resistance, mobilization, and collective formation in varied forms, online and off. It is not uncommon for workers and activists to use the same gadgets assembled at Foxconn, but for purposes beyond the usual realms of individualism and consumerism, giving rise to social innovations and effective DNA campaigns. How do working-class public spheres take shape? What are the main components – such as mass media, DNA, networking among ordinary workers – and the characteristics of each? How do they interrelate – not only labor NGOs but also members of the environmental movement and consumer movement? What can be learned from this global campaign against corporate social irresponsibility? Do working-class public spheres harbor a new kind of activism? How did media, both mass media and online social media, both in China and abroad, play a role in shaping public opinion, influencing corporate behavior and state policies, ultimately affecting the fate of workers at the very bottom of the factory regime? This project shall draw from interviews, focus groups, document analysis, and participatory action research to address these questions. It shall be a benchmark empirical project for the study of working-class public spheres in the digital era, with significant theoretical contribution and broad social implication. Besides books and articles, we will explore innovative ways to communicate findings to academics, activists, and workers through new multimedia platforms. 工人階級公共領域之概念主要由哲學及史學研究者針對哈貝馬斯的資產階級公共領域理論而提出。本項目則採用社會科學視角，重點審視媒體與行動主義，特別是通過2010年富士康N連跳以來的數位聯網行動進行深入個案分析，以揭示在資訊技術與全球聯網的時代，工人階級公共領域是如何發生、如何形成多重公共領域的。 本研究重點針對全球最大的電子製造業廠商富士康，但亦涵蓋其餘類似的電子製造企業。富士康在中國大陸有約140萬工人，生產iPhone、iPad等各種在世界各地十分暢銷的電子產品。其生產壓力巨大，以至2010年頭八個月發生了17名工人跳樓自殺的慘劇，導致大量媒體報導和公民行動，後者涉及各種非政府組織、學生、教師及志願者。2012年以來，富士康工人也日益採用數位聯網行動表達他們的聲音。 這是本項目的基本想法：資本主義工業生產實踐之惡導致多重工人階級公共領域之形成；該領域乃是各種抵抗、動員與集體形成的混雜性空間，涵蓋網上與網下。在這裡，工人與行動者也採用富士康生產的電子產品，但卻試圖打破個人主義與消費主義的藩籬，創造出社會創新和有效動員的新天地。 工人階級的公共領域究竟如何形成？它包含哪些組成部分，如大眾傳媒、數位聯網行動、普通工人的網路聯繫——這些組成部分各有什麼特點？它們如何在勞工運動內部，也和環保、消費者運動等相關部門之間，發生互動？我們可從這場針對企業缺乏社會責任的全球行動中學到什麼？工人階級公共領域中能否產生新型態的行動？中國與海外的大眾傳媒及社交媒體在此扮演什麼角色？它們如何影響公共輿論、企業行為、政府決策，如何最終為改善工廠地址底層的勞工命運發生作用？ 本項目將採用訪談、焦點小組討論、文獻分析及參與式行動研究來嘗試回答上述問題。它將為數位時代的工人階級公共領域研究提供實證標桿，其理論貢獻和社會意義均比較重大。除了書籍文章的出版，我們還將嘗試運用新型多媒體平台將研究發現傳遞給更多的學者、行動者和工人群眾。

14612715.label: Realisation of objectives
14612715.value: Overall we have attained most of the goals we set out to achieve for this two-year project, while in some aspects we have exceeded our planned goals, especially that we have used this GRF as a basis to successfully apply and initiate a new CRF project entitled "Learning to Labor: Social Media and Migrant Labor Protection in Mainland China" (RGC Ref No. C5010-15GF). More specifically, we have done the following with regard to each of the project objectives: Objective 1 -- fully completed. The synthesized knowledge is presented in research outputs such as Qiu's 2016 book "Goodbye iSlave" which was recognized as the highly recommended book by the Global Media and Social Change division of International Communication Association. Work toward this goal also serves as a solid basis for the successful CRF grant application. Objective 2 -- fully completed. The framework has been used to inform the co-authored article by Qiu and Lin in 2017 and Qiu's 2018 journal article on China's digital working class. The "circuit of labor" framework has been further developed and refined through this project. Objective 3 -- fully completed as reflected in the 2017 co-authored article by Pun, Tse and Ng "Challenging Digital Capitalism" as well as Qiu's 2016 iSlave book. We have conducted in-depth case study of the anti-electronic-sweatshop campaign in Hong Kong, mainland China, Taiwan as well as internationally (e.g., in Europe). Objective 4 -- almost fully achieved. We have conducted close to interviews, focus groups, content analyses, document analyses, and extended participant observation in SACOM as well as multimedia action research through Breakthrough and Tootopia the sites of experimentation that involve students and concerned citizens in mainland China, Hong Kong, and globally. SACOM the labor NGO in Hong Kong has also benefited from this research project and used our research insights in designing and implementing its "iSlave at 10" digital media campaign in 2017. However, due to time constraint and insufficient manpower in utilizing latest Internet research tools, the WGC and online campaign analyses using digital methods remain only partially completed. Objective 5 -- almost fully achieved. The PI, Co-I, and RA of this project have disseminated knowledge and skills from this project through numerous academic publications, conference presentations, and workshop with NGOs, activists, and worker training sessions, including a book tour by the PI for his book Goodbye iSlave in several European countries from the UK to Sweden to Denmark, Belgium and Switzerland paid for by local hosts in 2017. The communication with public policymakers is not fully achieved because we have tried but so far been unsuccessful in establishing formal channels of communication with policymakers within mainland China, although we have carried this out at the international level with good results (e.g., International Labor Organization in Geneva).

14612715.label: Major findings and research outcome
14612715.value: Through in-depth study of anti-electronic-sweatshop campaigns in Hong Kong, Greater China, and globally, this study has found that, although English-language literature tends to debate on the constitution and effectiveness of public sphere historically and in the present time, in the Chinese contexts there is ample evidence that (a) public sphere formations among the working people have generated working-class public spheres with their own structures and dynamics that are distinct from the bourgeois public sphere a la Jurgen Habermas; (b) since 2010, Chinese workers, activists, and journalists have deployed digital media tools in forming transborder networks within Greater China and beyond, while campaigning against exploitation in Foxconn and similar factories; and (c) the "circuit of labor" model is helpful in not only describing but also explaining and analyzing working-class public sphere formations in particular and China's digital working class in the making. Research outcome from this project include Qiu's 2016 award-winning book "Goodbye iSlave" (Univ of Illinois Press), several book chapters and journal articles in top journals such as Information, Communication & Society, and numerous conference presentations in Asia, Europe, and North America including high-level plenary talks in London and Leicester of the UK and at Lingnan University. It also includes other invited talks and workshops with labor activists when knowledge and skills from this project were disseminated among NGOs and practitioners. This project also serves as a basis for the successful application of a three-year large-scale CRF project entitled "Learning to Labor: Social Media and Migrant Labor Protection in Mainland China" (RGC Ref No. C5010-15GF) for which PUN Ngai (co-I) of this project is the PI, and Jack Qiu (PI of this project) is one of the co-I's.

14612715.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14612715.value: Theoretically, the revised and refined framework from this project -- "circuits of labor" -- deserves further development, for which Qiu and Pun are still collaborating in co-authoring a new book entitled China's Digital Working Class. Methodologically, more actions can still be taken in the utilization of latest Internet research tools such as data mining, network analysis and data visualization that can help us better understand the dynamics online. More attempts can be made to approach public policymakers, especially in mainland China (e.g., All China Federation of Trade Unions), to make use of the findings from this project.

14612715.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14612715.value: Using a combination of conventional social science methods and innovative multimedia action design, this project studied the campaigns against electronic sweatshops since the 2010 Foxconn worker suicides. It refined the "circuit of labor" theoretical model while explicating the distinct patterns of working-class public spheres among Chinese workers, activists, and journalists, which are quite different from the bourgeois public sphere in existing literature. Digital media are found to be particularly effective in forming transborder networks within Greater China and globally. The research team has conducted solid case studies of labor campaigns on the Internet and in real-life situations, accumulated a significant amount of empirical evidence, and disseminated the knowledge and skills from this project through academic publications, training workshops and participatory action research.

14613015.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14613015.value: 目標排序的改變是老年心理學的一個常見現象。這些目標的改變在一定程度上影響老年的社會關係，決定的形成，以及社會和體能活動的程度。社會情緒選擇理論用人在年纪越大，越覺得未來短暫，因而越重視與人生意義有關之目標來解釋這些目標的改變。 但是在老年心理學以外，這個理論受另一理論所挑戰。恐懼管理理論認為人在感到死亡臨近時會感到恐懼，繼而做一些確認自我及文化價值觀的行為來減輕恐懼。支持此理論的研究指出大學生在感到死亡臨近時會增加對認同自己文化價值觀的人的正面觀感，及對反對自己的人的負面觀感。 此兩理論看似相似，覺得未來短暫的人容易覺得死亡臨近，與人生意思有關的目標也與認同自己文化的價值相關。可是，已有的在實驗室中令老年人短期地感到死亡臨近的研究沒有找到相應的目標或行為的改變。 為了解釋此予盾現象，並加深我們對成年期目標改變的理解，本研究用實驗方法來改變年青人及老年人對未來及死亡的看法，以測量這些改變對他們人生目標的影響。

14613015.label: Realisation of objectives
14613015.value: We conducted a study to address the objectives. The study contrasted the effects of limited future time perspective and mortality salience (or its more concrete form -- death reflection) on goal prioritization across adulthood. Socioemotional selectivity theory (SST) argues that people increasingly prioritize emotionally meaningful goals when they perceive future time as more limited. Terror management theory (TMT) suggests that mortality salience (i.e. the awareness of one’s mortality) drives people to prioritize the goal of perpetuating own existence through affirming cultural worldview. Method Participants In this study, 219 younger adults (140 females; 18–25 years of age, M ± SD = 18.9 ± 1.2) and 219 older adults (139 females; 57–85 years of age, M ± SD = 69.2 ± 6.0) from Hong Kong were recruited from Hong Kong. Younger participants were recruited from a local university campus through advertisement and undergraduate subject pool. Older participants were recruited from the local community. Course credit or monetary stipends were given for their participation. Older adults received HK$200 as reimbursement for their participation. Seven additional non-local participants were excluded because they might not regard recipients who held positive opinions about Hong Kong society as affirming their cultural worldviews. Procedure Participants came to our laboratory to undergo the experiment, individually, in a cubicle. The stimuli were presented on a computer and the participants completed the following tasks on the computer. After signing an informed consent form, younger and older participants were randomly assigned to 6 conditions that primed (1) limited future time (LT), (2) mortality salience (MS), (3) death reflection (DR), (4) both limited future time and mortality salience, (5) both limited future time and death reflection, or (6) none. Manipulation. Emotion closeness. To manipulate emotional closeness of recipients, participants first answered a series of daily activity questions. Afterwards, an experimenter pretended to search in a database and then reported that some recipients shared many interests with the participant while other recipients had significantly different preferences from him/her. This method has successfully manipulated “emotional closeness” in Fung, Lu and Isaacowitz (2019). Worldview affirmation. To manipulate worldview affirmation of recipients, participants read an interview transcript, which described a conversation between immigrants from Mainland China. Some immigrants expressed positive views toward Hong Kong society, while others expressed negative views. The script was taken from Zou, Morris and Benet-Martínez (2008). We only modified the evaluation object to “Hong Kong society.” Next, participants were randomly assigned into one of the six conditions (LT, MS, DR, LT-MS, LT-DR and control condition). Below we describe each condition in detail: LT condition. Participants were asked to think of a specific, meaningful location that they went to with people whom they care about. Then, they were asked to imagine that they come back to this location two months later, and then four months later. At four months later, they were told that this was the last time that they could come to this place. The above instructions, adopted from Zhang, et al. (2010), are supposed to prime future time limitations. MS condition. In order to prime mortality salience, participants answered two open-ended questions: (1) “Please briefly describe the emotions that the thought of your own death arouses in you” and (2) “Jot down, as specific as you can, what do you think will happen to you as you physically die and once you are physically dead” (Greenberg et al., 1992). DR condition. Participants were asked to imagine themselves experiencing a fatal accident in concrete details. The script was translated and back-translated from the English version that successfully elicited death reflection (Cozzolino, Staples, Meyers, & Samboceti, 2004). After the audio of scenario description, participants answered four open-ended questions: (1) “Please describe in detail the thoughts and emotions you felt while imagining the scenario”, (2) “If you did experience this event, how do you think you would handle the final moments”, (3) “Again imagining it did happen to you, describe the life you led up to that point” and (4) “how do you feel your family would react if it did happen to you?” These procedures are expected to implicitly activate near-death feelings. LT-MS condition. Participants received both priming of future time limitations and mortality salience as described above in a counterbalanced order. LT-DR condition. Participants received both priming of future time limitations and death reflection as described above in a counterbalanced order. Control condition. Participants received two sets of control instructions in a counterbalanced order. In the control instructions corresponding to the MS manipulation, participants were asked to answer two open-ended questions about dental pain (Greenberg et al., 1994): (1) Please briefly describe the emotions that the thought of dental pain arouses in you” and (2) Jot down, as specifically as you can, what you think will happen to you as you are suffered from dental pain. As for the control instructions for the LT manipulation, participants were instructed to imagine that they come to their favorite place for another time four months later without mentioning that it would be their last time to visit the place. Dependent Measures After the manipulation and a filler task, participants proceeded to the resource allocation task. There were four trials in total. In each trial, participants allocated resources to the four recipients with different levels of emotional closeness and worldview affirmation (CS, CO, NS, NO). The four recipients were presented with face pictures randomly extracted from Native Chinese Affective Picture System (Bai, Ma, Huang & Luo, 2005). In each trial, the type of resources was either HK$50,000 (approximately US$6,400) evenly divided into 10 bags (Money) or 10 hours of volunteer visiting time (Time). Their sources were either from a governmental scheme (Public) or from their own pocket (Private). For instance, in the public money condition, the participants were told “There is a caring fund from the government for the new immigrants in Hong Kong, which has HK$50,000 evenly divided into 10 bags.” Participants were told that they had the rights to freely distribute the resources, and they were reassured that the experimenter would not ask why they made such a decision to mitigate social desirability effect. All four combinations of type and source (public money, public time, private money, private time) were shown to each participant, with their order counterbalanced. The amount of the resources allocated to each recipient was the dependent variable. After the allocation task, participants rated the level of closeness they felt toward each recipient on a 9-point scale (1 = not close at all to 9 = very close). Paired t-tests showed that recipients with similar interests as the participants (M = 4.92, SD = 1.2) were rated as significantly emotionally closer than were their counterparts with different interests (M = 3.91, SD = 1.41), t(431) = 17.65, p < .001, η_p^2= 0.9. These suggested that the emotional closeness manipulation was successful. For the manipulation check of worldview affirmation, participants rated their attitude toward each recipient on a 9-point scale (1 = very unfavorable to 9 = very favorable). Paired t-tests showed that participants held significantly more positive attitude toward recipients who made positive comments on Hong Kong society (M = 5.49, SD = 1.05) than recipients who made negative comments (M = 3.98, SD = 1.17), t(429) = 20.36, p < .001, d = 1.36.

14613015.label: Major findings and research outcome
14613015.value: In this study, we compared and contrasted the effects of limited future time perspective, mortality salience, and death reflection on goal prioritization. Consistent with socioemotional selectivity theory (SST, Carstensen, Isaacowitz & Charles, 2003), we found that limited time perspective made older adults more likely to prioritize, in this case, allocated more resources, to emotionally close social partners. Younger adults did not show such effects. However, consistent with terror management theory (TMT, Pyszczynski Greenberg & Solomon, 1997, 1999), we found that older adults did not just prioritize emotionally close recipients under future time limitations, they also prioritized recipients who affirmed their cultural worldviews. These findings suggest that what get prioritized with limited future time is not just emotionally meaningful goals, but also worldview affirmation. Moreover, although priming of mortality salience did not change the goal prioritization of older adults, eliciting thoughts of a fatal accident in concrete details (called “death reflection”) did. These findings support the argument of Cozzolino (2006) that abstract concepts of mortality, as typically used in traditional TMT studies, might increase defensiveness, limiting subsequent goal changes. Instead, specific mortality concepts, such as trauma, might increase death-related growth. The findings in the current study help to integrate TMT and SST, and shed light on the mechanisms underlying these motivational changes. Our findings revealed that between future time limitations, mortality salience and death reflection, future time limitations seemed to have the greatest effect on motivational changes in old age. Death reflection, but not mortality salience, changed the goals of older adults in the same ways as did future time limitations, suggesting that old age may shift goals both because of its associated sense of anticipated endings as well as specific reminders about death. In addition, the goals that get prioritized in old age are emotional closeness as well as worldview affirmation, not just either. These findings have been published in Output #2. This is the main research output. In addition, survey data on future time perspective collected as part of the project were combined with similar data collected in Germany and the USA to test the psychometric properties of the Future Time Perspective Scale. These results are published in two journal articles (Outputs #1 & 4). Finally, age differences on survey data in meaning in life, also collected as part of the project, are written up as another manuscript that is revised and resubmitted (Output #3).

14613015.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14613015.value: Since the specific future time perspective manipulation employed in this study was about going to a personally meaningful place, whether nostalgia (Routledge, Arndt, Sedikides & Wildschut, 2008) played a role in the effect should be examined in future studies. In addition, there have been prior findings that the effect of mortality salience is more likely to be observed in experiential rather than rational mode of thinking (Simon et al., 1997). Whether this may be the reason why death reflection was more effective than abstract mortality salience in shifting goals in the current study should be further explored. Finally, it should be noted that although our theory-driven planned contrasts showed condition differences for older but not younger adults, some more nuanced condition differences for younger adults were also found. These differences among younger adults will be explored in future studies.

14613015.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14613015.value: Human behaviors are directed by goals. In the psychology and aging literature, socioemotional selectivity theory argues that when future time is perceived as increasingly limited with age, people prioritize emotionally meaningful goals (e.g., staying with family members) over future-oriented goals (e.g., knowledge acquisition). This explanation is challenged by terror management theory (TMT) in social psychology. TMT argues that the awareness of one’s mortality drives people to prioritize the goal of affirming cultural worldview, in order to buffer against death anxiety. However, no published studies have directly contrasted the effects of limited future time perception and mortality salience on goal prioritization. This project filled in this gap. We found that older adults allocated more resources to emotionally close recipients who supported their cultural worldviews in conditions involving future time limitations and death reflection. They also allocated less resources to emotionally not close recipients who did not support their cultural worldviews in conditions involving future time limitations. Younger adults did not show these differences. Nor did mortality salience have any effect. These results suggest that future time perspective and death reflection shift age-related goals more than mortality salience.

14613215.label: Realisation of objectives
14613215.value: This research project started in January 2016 and completed in June 2019. All the five research objectives set out in the study plan have been well achieved with a series of research output being generated. The first objective of the research is to examine and compare the education- and health- related outcomes of cross-border, immigrant, native-born children in Hong Kong, and HK-born children in the mainland. This is a pioneer study that includes a comprehensive sample consisting of four groups of students with different residential statuses and schooling experiences in Hong Kong and its adjacent mainland city across the border, Shenzhen, originating from the unique geo-political context in the pearl river delta region. To achieve this objective, we have conducted a large-scale survey with 4th-9th grade students in the two study sites and have collected a total of 2,610 completed valid questionnaires from twelve schools in Hong Kong and four schools in Shenzhen. The numbers of cross-border, new immigrant, local students in Hong Kong, and HK-born students in Shenzhen are 445, 348, 1387, and 430 respectively in the sample. This sample composition allows for comparison among the four student groups in terms of their education and health related outcomes. Our analyses reveal that there do exist significant differences among the groups in certain outcome measures, but not necessarily in the direction as hypothesized. For example, as reported in a manuscript under review, residential status is not associated with their self-rated health status, but new immigrant students tend to report lower levels of happiness, while cross-border students exhibit better mental well-being, which is against our original expectation considering the unique challenges faced by cross-border students due to their special living and schooling arrangement. But cross-border students do present some difficulties in their educational experiences as compared to other groups of students. The second objective of the research is to investigate how social capital embedded in the family, school, and community influences education- and health-related outcomes of children and mediates the effects of their residency statuses. Our analyses do echo findings from previous studies regarding the significant effects of social capital on children’s health and education, with different dimensions of social capital showing different strengths of effects, and various factors within each type of capital showing different effects on different outcomes. For example, family social capital is found to be most important for health related outcomes, but within this dimension, parent-child interaction is associated with all health and wellbeing measures, whereas parental monitoring does not show such effects. Moreover, children’s relationship with father and mother are both positively associated with students’ rating of happiness, while children’s relationship with father is also associated with their health status but not mental wellbeing, yet their relationship with mother is predictive of mental well-being but not health status. Likewise, school social capital has shown strongest effect on educational outcomes but also significant effect on health and wellbeing. Within school social capital, relationship with teachers and peers are both positively associated with students’ wellbeing measures, but peer relationship is not predictive of health status. Similar results are also found in the effects of social capital on educational outcomes. In terms of the mediating effects of social capital, our analyses suggest that, compared to local students, new immigrant students tend to have lower levels of family and community social capital, which lead to poorer health and educational outcomes. In contrast, cross-border students tend to have lower levels of school social capital, which influences their health and education negatively. The third objective of the research is to investigate how cultural capital acquired within the mainland and the Hong Kong cultural context respectively influences the education- and health-related outcomes of children and mediates the effects of their residency statuses. It is one of the original contributions of this research to literature by incorporating cultural capital into the integrative framework of social capital and investigating whether and how cultural capital functions on the health and educational outcomes of children independent of social capital. As presented at the Joint World Conference on Social Work, Education and Social Development, our research findings suggest that cultural capital outstrips social capital in predicting students’ educational outcomes, and cross-border children tend to possess higher levels of cultural capital, probably given their unique advantage in acquiring cultural resources from two cultural systems simultaneously, which is beneficial for their educational outcomes. In another presentation given at the East Asian Social Policy Conference, it is also reported that both social and cultural capital are predictive of children’s health and wellbeing, but cross-border children appear to have lower levels of social capital, thus leading to poorer mental health outcomes indirectly, albeit the positive direct effects of the cross-border status on mental wellbeing. The fourth objective of the research is to investigate how the functioning of social and cultural capital might differ across various groups of children with particular residency statuses. Our analyses attempt to identify the potential moderating effect of residential status in modifying the effects of social and cultural capital on health and educational outcomes. The study results have not shown significant differences in the functioning of cultural capital across the four student groups with various residential status and schooling arrangement, but social capital does operate differently across different groups, with certain dimensions of social capital exerting significant effects on certain outcomes for a particular group without demonstrating similar importance for another group. For example, in our presentation at the International Society for Quality of Life Studies Annual Conference, it is reported that, as indicators of family social capital, parent-child interaction is predictive of the health status of cross-border students, happiness of new immigrant students, and mental well-being of local students. Relationship with father is very important for the happiness and mental wellbeing of new immigrant students, while relationship with mother is more important for the mental wellbeing of cross-border and local students. With regard to school social capital, relationship with teacher is a significant predictor of all outcomes for local students, but only predictive of mental wellbeing for cross-border students. The fifth objective of the research is to understand how children with different residency-education experiences in Hong Kong and mainland China negotiate with two vastly different sociocultural systems to acquire and mobilize social and cultural resources for their own development. This objective is achieved by the qualitative part of this mixed-methods study. We have conducted semi-structured in-depth interviews with 20 students (five from each group) and tried to understand from their own perspectives how they perceive and experience the impact of social and cultural resources on their health and education. The qualitative data supplement and facilitate interpretation of the statistical findings with voices of children from these four different groups. For instance, resonating the findings from quantitative analyses, children’s narratives demonstrate that cross-border students do think more about their choices and intentionally utilize and mobilize resources in their ecological systems to achieve more favorable development. This explains why they tend to accumulate higher levels of capital that lead to better health and educational outcomes in particular dimensions. Upon achieving these objectives, this research is informative for both policymakers and service practitioners in designing policies and services that promote the health and education of children with different residential backgrounds.

14613215.label: Major findings and research outcome
14613215.value: This project involves a survey conducted in Hong Kong and Shenzhen with a total of 2,610 4th-9th grade students falling under four different residential-educational statuses: cross-border, new immigrant, local children in HK, and HK-born children in the mainland. Some major research findings have been presented in several international conferences and considered for publication in peer-reviewed journals. Below are a few highlights of the research outcomes: 1) The four groups of children with different residential status and schooling experiences present different health and educational outcomes; social capital embedded in the family, school, and community, and cultural capital acquired through two cultural systems have demonstrated significant effects on their health and education, as well as mediate the effects of residential-educational backgrounds. Different from originally hypothesized, cross-border students do not appear to experience poorer health and educational outcomes. They tend to possess higher levels of cultural capital, which associate with certain outcomes positively such as better mental wellbeing. In contrast, new immigrant students report poorer outcomes both as a consequence of their residential status and of lower levels of social and cultural capital they possess indirectly. 2) Social and cultural capital both function on children’s health and educational outcomes significantly but demonstrate different strengths of effect on different outcomes. Various dimensions of social capital are found to be more influential for health related outcomes while cultural capital exerts stronger effect on educational outcomes. Moreover, children with different residential-educational backgrounds tend to possess different levels of social and cultural capital thus leading to disparities in their health and education. Incorporating both social and cultural capital into one framework and empirically testing their independent, joint and relative effects so as to advance the theory of capital is one of the most important contributions of this research. 3) This research has also revealed an association between social capital and cultural identification (i.e., Hongkonger, mainland Chinese, dual identification, and confused identification) of children with different residential-educational backgrounds. As we have presented at the China /Hong Kong -Israel "Silk and Road" Forum, cross-border and new immigrant students are more likely to hold a dual/bicultural identification. Family and community social capital, particularly reflected by father-child and mother-child relationships as well as social cohesion and trust in the neighborhood, play significant roles in shaping the cultural identity of children. Although not among the original research objectives, this is an interesting finding that points out promising directions for future research.

14613215.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14613215.value: This project has great potential for further development. The PI has been moving forward in two promising directions to continue and enhance the social impact of the research. First, findings about the association between children’s cultural identification and social capital points out a potential direction for future research to investigate the issue of cultural identity more deeply and systematically. This has become an especially important and meaningful topic to explore in the current social atmosphere with the ongoing social movement since last year. The PI has started to develop a research proposal aiming to understand the identity formation of Hong Kong youth and the value transmission processes through the social and cultural capital theoretical framework. Second, with the growing interest in and increasing importance of the Greater Bay Area development, this research can be further expanded to investigate the capacity building, career planning and life choices of the four different groups of students through a life course perspective. The unique advantages of cross-border children as revealed in the research findings shed light on the potential that this particular group might bear in bridging the two sociocultural systems between HK and mainland China and facilitate the integration of Greater Bay Area.

14613215.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14613215.value: The unique geo-political context and increasing cross-border migration between Hong Kong and mainland China has generated four distinct student groups: local students in HK, new immigrant students (born in mainland China but have come to live in HK for less than seven years), cross-border students (born in HK, living in Shenzhen but attending school in HK on daily commute), and HK-born children who live and study in the mainland. This research aims to incorporate social and cultural capital into one integrative framework and investigate how social capital embedded in multiple social contexts and cultural capital acquired in two cultural systems might influence the health and educational outcomes of the four student groups across the HK-mainland border. The study results suggest that both types of capital are influential with social capital being more important for health related outcomes while cultural capital more important for educational outcomes. Social and cultural capital also mediate the effects of residential backgrounds and function differently on various outcomes across the four student groups. The research findings advance our understanding of the life experiences of students with different living and schooling arrangements, and provide valuable insights for policymaking and service development targeting the needs of particular groups.

14613615.label: Project Objectives
14613615.value: To identify the perceptions, attitudes, opinions, behaviour, experience and influential factors surrounding AD by interviewing a variety of stakeholders. To produce a structured questionnaire for use in a population-based telephone survey to examine the current status of and factors affecting the use of AD. To produce a conceptual model that can explain and predict AD acceptance and uptake in Hong Kong.
rows: To identify the perceptions, attitudes, opinions, behaviour, experience and influential factors surrounding AD by interviewing a variety of stakeholders.
To produce a structured questionnaire for use in a population-based telephone survey to examine the current status of and factors affecting the use of AD.
To produce a conceptual model that can explain and predict AD acceptance and uptake in Hong Kong.

14613615.label: Realisation of objectives
14613615.value: Objective 1: (PHASE I: Generation of statements) Objective 1 was achieved through qualitative interviews conducted in phase I. A total of 96 participants, including patients with life-limiting diseases, their family members, healthcare professionals (physician, nurse, social worker and chaplain) and hospital volunteers (24 from each group), were recruited from two public hospitals belonging to two clusters in Hong Kong by purposive sampling. Purposive sampling according to age and gender was not strictly applied as it was difficult to identify young patients with life-limiting diseases and young healthcare professionals having completed professional training. Nevertheless, the distribution of participants in terms of age (18-45: 24%; 46-65: 47.9%; >65: 26%) and gender (male: 42.7%; female: 57.3%) was reasonably even. After a brief introduction of advance directives (AD) to the participants, a semi-structured interview was conducted on an individual basis by a research assistant with each participant to brainstorm and develop statements regarding their perceptions, attitudes and experience on AD and the factors facilitating and hampering its utilisation. All interviews were audio-taped and field notes were taken to capture non-verbal responses. Thematic analysis was employed to summarise the views of participants and to generate statements. Objective 3: (PHASE II: Structuring of statements and concept maps) The approach previously described by Trochim (1989) was used to develop the concept map to achieve objective 3. The research team consolidated the statements identified in the interviews and the ideas extracted from the literature by removing overlaps and/or splitting statements containing multiple topics. A final set of statements was generated after discussions between the research team members on any disagreements on statement identification for reaching a consensus. Thereafter, the research team sorted the completed set of statements into groups of similar topics and a label was assigned for each group. The 96 participants recruited in phase I were then contacted and were asked to rank each statement based on their importance on a rating scale ranging from 1 (least important) to 7 (most important). However, due to participant death and participant withdrawal, only 67 participants were able to provide their ratings. Statistical techniques including multidimensional scaling (MDS) and cluster analysis were used to create the concept map. A proximity matrix in the order of number of statements * number of statements, with the distance measures between statements, was formed. The distance between each pair of statements was quantified by the average level of similarity rated by the participants. Multi-dimensional scaling was then employed to analyse the proximity matrix with solutions up to two dimensions. A Kruskal’s stress-against-dimensionality scree plot was generated to help determine the optimal dimension for the final model. Kruskal’s stress is a measure of goodness-of-fit for MDS models, with values ranging from 1 (the worst possible fit) to 0 (a perfect fit). A value of 0.285 or less is considered an acceptable fit. In addition, another commonly reported statistical parameter, the RSQ value, was also used for assessing the goodness-of-fit of the final model. The RSQ value is the square of the correlation coefficient of the input distances with the scaled distances using the MDS coordinates. The RSQ value reflects the proportion of variance accounted for in the solution: An RSQ value of 0.6 or more is considered acceptable. A point map depicting the relative distances between the statements was generated from the final MDS model. Hierarchical cluster analysis was then conducted to group the points on the point map (coordinate values) into clusters, using Ward’s algorithm. The six clusters to be retained was based on an iterative process of interpreting the cluster content, which formed the concept map. Objective 2: (PHASE III: Utilization of the map) Objective 2 was then achieved through the use of the concept map generated in phase II in the development of a questionnaire for the conduction of the telephone survey. The questionnaire consisted of five parts: (1) socio-demographic characteristics, (2) self-perception and health status, (3) prevalence of statutory written form of AD, (4) perceptions related to AD and, (5) level of agreement in making AD in various scenarios. A population-based telephone interview was conducted in Hong Kong with Chinese participants aged 18 or above. The phone interview was conducted anonymously by trained interviewers from the Telephone Survey Research Laboratory, Hong Kong Institute of Asia-Pacific Studies, the Chinese University of Hong Kong. This helps increase the cost-effectiveness of the survey as these interviewers are highly trained and experienced in conducting telephone interviews. Telephone numbers were randomly selected from updated directories developed by the Communications Authority of Hong Kong. To avoid the over- or under-sampling of the non-working population, the interviewer conducted the telephone survey in the evening between 6:15 pm and 10:15 pm. If there is more than one eligible participant in the household, the one with the birthday closest to the date of the interview was invited to take part in the survey. Eligible participants who cannot be contacted after at least two unsuccessful attempts of calling at different periods of time were not included in the survey. Apart from descriptive statistics, univariate analysis and multiple regression analysis were used to identify factors associated with AD acceptance. The level of AD acceptance in various scenarios is expressed as a summed score ranging from 0 to 100, due to the fact that the number of participants having completed AD is too low for the identification of the associated factors in regression analysis. References: Trochim, W. M. (1989). An introduction to concept mapping for planning and evaluation. Eval Prog Planning, 12, 1-16.

2. To produce a structured questionnaire for use in a population-based telephone survey to examine the current status of and factors affecting the use of AD.

14613615.label: Major findings and research outcome
14613615.value: PHASE I: Generation of statement Most participants were willing to discuss AD but had not heard of AD before the interview. In general, most participants perceived AD as an option to make their future medical decisions, while some preferred physicians to help making the decisions. Patients considered the decisions made in AD as a strategy to reduce their suffering. Family members were concerned about the psychological burden during AD discussion. Healthcare professionals focused on the logistics and process of completing AD. Interviews with hospital volunteers revealed the impact of Chinese culture on AD acceptance and these individuals also reported the lack of AD promotion in the community. PHASE II: Structuring of statements and concept maps Sixty-eight statements were generated from the participants in the qualitative interviews, while seven were derived from literature review. They were condensed into 43 final statements after the removal of overlaps. The statements were ranked based on their importance and sorted into groups based on their similarity by the participants. Multidimensional scaling was used to generate a two-dimensional point map of the statements. The goodness-of-fit indices obtained in our analysis, with Kruskal’s stress being 0.23 and RSQ being 0.90, indicated that the statement map was of a good fit to the data. Hierarchical cluster analysis was then performed to divide the statement map into clusters. A six-cluster solution was eventually identified with clusters having four to ten statements. The concept map depicted six factors that influence AD acceptance: (1) physical and illness, (2) personal situation, (3) sociocultural, (4) value system, (5) conditional, and (6) process of AD. All six clusters were rated as important by the participants. PHASE III: Utilization of the map In total, 2002 participants completed the survey. Only 18% had heard of AD and 0.5% had completed AD. However, the majority of those who had heard of AD had made or intended to make AD (80.2%). This implies that they consider AD completion acceptable. By multivariable regression, being (1) Christian, Catholics or Buddhist, (2) being optimistic, and (3) agreeing to respect patients’ wishes are independently associated with higher AD acceptance, whereas being students is associated with lower AD acceptance (all p<0.05).

14613615.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14613615.value: Our study revealed the perceptions of AD by various stakeholders and developed a concept map explaining the influential factors surrounding AD. Although the completion of AD was very low in Hong Kong, our study demonstrated that most participants consider the completion of AD acceptable. Our future studies will involve the development of culturally-relevant interventions to promote AD in the community, with the aim to increase the rate of AD uptake in Hong Kong.

14613615.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14613615.value: The study revealed a low completion rate of AD among Hong Kong Chinese and the production of a concept map to predict the acceptance of AD in Hong Kong. We first used qualitative methods to examine the perceptions of stakeholders on this topic. Building upon their ideas and relevant published studies in the literature, we developed a concept map and a structured questionnaire that was used in a large-scale population telephone survey. Finding of the study will enable clinicians to better assist individuals and families in making decisions on the end-of-life healthcare plans they desire in advance. The unique conceptual model developed based on stakeholders’ experiences and perceptions means that our findings will provide insights for the Hong Kong government on the strategies for the promotion and legislation of AD in a way that is in line with of the cultures of the Hong Kong Chinese society. It is to be hoped that such effort would result in a reduction of unnecessary medical expenditure, thereby making a positive economic and social impact on both individuals and the society as a whole. Moreover, the study findings will contribute knowledge on factors affecting AD implementation both locally and in other Asian countries.

14613815.value: 本研究重點關注當代中國抗爭政治中的官民共謀現象。所謂官民共謀﹐指的是出生于本地的政府官員與本地有影響的社會人物暗地裡合作﹐發起或堅持針對由外地調入的本地黨政一把手及其背後的上級政府某些損及地方社會精英經濟利益的決定。本研究特別探討可能導致官民共謀的結構因素﹐如主要領導幹部異地為官制度﹐幹部晉昇制度﹐地方政府與本地商業企業精英的利益重合。本研究也探討官民共謀對於地方治理和地方政治過程演變的影響﹐特別是研究重複發生的官民共謀是否會擴大社會力量對地方政治過程的參與程度和影響力﹐從而提高地方政治過程的多元化程度和開放程度。 本研究於2015年9月1日至2018年8月31日進行。研究目標是在學術期刊發表論文並準備一部書稿。

14614815.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14614815.value: This research investigates Hong Kong people’s political values, mostly the understanding and support for democracy. In particular, it examines how these values are affected by recent political movements and experiences of political participation, especially the impact of the Occupying Central Movement in September-October 2014. It will also examine if there is a new generational change in democratic values, and the impact of the use of internet and social media on political values. By dint of a household survey adopting the Wave IV core questionnaire of the Asian Barometer Survey (ABS), which is a cross-national survey on political values undertaken in 18 Asian polities, the research taps the political attitudes of Hong Kong people on various political dimensions, including various democratic values, traditional values, acceptance of alternative political forms, and other social variables. The data collected will be compared with those of previous waves of ABS surveys in 2001, 2007 and 2012. It will also allow us to compare Hong Kong’s democratic values with those in other Asian polities under the Asian Barometer survey. 本研究以「亞洲民主動態研究」的第四波調查核心問卷，以上門訪談方式，調查香港人的政治價值和對民主的看法。調查會針對近年的政治運動(包括2014年的雨傘運動)和政治參與經驗，如何影響香港人的政治和民主價值，亦會審視政治價值是否有明顯的世代差距，以及互聯網和社交媒體如何影響政治價值。 調查會觸及香港人不同層面的政治價值，包括對民主的認同、傳統的政治價值、對不同政體的接受程度、以及各種政治和社會變項如何影響政治價值等。作為「亞洲民主動態研究」的第四波研究，本研究將會與過往三波的數據，以及其他18個亞洲地區的數據比較，以加深對香港政治變化和全球民主價值的認識。

14614815.label: Realisation of objectives
14614815.value: The three research objectives are largely realized through the completion of the survey in 2016, the analysis of the data, and comparison of the data with those from other Asian states. The results and analyses were written into several conference papers, journal articles and book chapters. Results of individual questions were used in selected papers or book chapters. (Please refer to Part C for research outputs). The survey was successfully completed in 2016, with about 1200 completed household interviews and questionnaires. The data was checked, cleaned, weighted, and analyzed. The result was also presented in conferences, and compared with the data of other Asian states. The first objective is effectively fulfilled. The ABS IV survey provides a comprehensive test of the support for various aspects of democratic values in Hong Kong, as in previous waves. It also assesses the change over time, with comparison of the data from previous waves in 2001, 2006, and 2012. We test the attitudes of Hong Kong people towards various political objects related to democracy, including paternalism, equality, pluralism, checks and balances, rule of law, political efficacy and participation, and other attitudinal issues. It tests the attitude to authoritarian alternatives, and the impact of other factors (such as the attitude to the Umbrella Movement). We also asked the respondents about their evaluation on various aspects of government performance, including economic performance, the provision of goods, the upholding of procedural fairness, responsiveness, corruption, and other aspects of performance. These are analyzed with respect to different demographic variables: gender, age, education, birthplace, and other aspects. It gives us a comprehensive understanding of the current state of political values in Hong Kong, and its changes over time. For the second objective, we compare systematically the Wave III and Wave IV data on various aspects. We discovered there has not been a significant overall change in support for democratic values from 2012 to 2016. There is a slight trend of polarization in political attitudes. The most eye-catching change from Wave III (2012) to Wave IV (2016) was a substantial drop in institutional trust in many political institutions, and a higher dissatisfaction against government performance, especially on issues related to procedural fairness. There has been a steady growth in political efficacy, and the regime legitimacy is increasingly in doubt as more people believed that the current system needs fundamental reform after the Umbrella Movement. The third objective is largely fulfilled, although the results are not quite as clear-cut as the two previous objectives. It is clear that the younger and more educated respondents are usually more supportive of democracy and other related values. They are usually more unhappy about the government performance, has lower trust in government institutions, have a lower evaluation on various aspects of government performance, and they have a higher political efficacy. Those who were born in Hong Kong have similar traits as those who are young and more educated. We are not that confident about the impacts of the identity factor, as we did not have enough questions to test on the Hong Kong identity factor in the 2016 survey (due to the constraint of the length of the core questionnaire). We hope that we can have a deeper exploration of the impact of the identity factor on the political attitudes of Hong Kong in future waves of survey, when we include more questions on Hong Kong identity.

14614815.label: Major findings and research outcome
14614815.value: By 2016, the democratic values of Hong Kong people are medium-high within the Asian region. Assessing the support for authoritarian alternatives and tradiaitonal paternalistic values, the support for various core values of democracy such as equality, freedom, procedural fairness, pluralism, checks and balances, tolerance, etc., we find that for most of the indicators Hong Kong ranks at least medium-high among the 15 states involved in the Asian Barometer project. Only several mature and developed democracies such as Japan, South Korea and Taiwan have higher support for democratic values. The most important impact of the Umbrella Movement has been the decline in institutional trust in various political institutions, from 2012 to 2016. There was also a decline in evaluation in various aspects of government performance, especially on procedural fairness and the responsiveness of the system. The younger, the better educated, and those born in Hong Kong generally have lower trust in the institutions and are more dissatisfied with government performance. This brought problems of regime legitimacy, as more people believed that fundamental reforms are needed for the current system. Comparing 2012 and 2016 data, there is little change in the overall support for democracy in Hong Kong. There is a slight trend of polarization. Over the four waves of survey, there has been a steady and gradual growth in political efficacy in Hong Kong, especially among the young and more educated. Comparison with other Asian states showed that Hong Kong's support for various democratic values, and the ratio of rejection of authoritarian alternatives, was in fact quite high. On the other hand, the evaluation on various government performance indicators was only medium-low if we compare Hong Kong with other Asian states. This provides a sharp contrast with a conventional wisdom in Hong Kong politics: that Hong Kong does not have a high support for democracy but Hong Kong people are generally happy about the regime performance. In fact, Hong Kong's support for democracy is not low, and by 2016 they no longer have a high evaluation of government performance, if compared with other Asian states.

14614815.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14614815.value: The research team will make further analysis with the current data, especially in two aspects: (a) an overview of the value change in 20 years after the 1997 handover, throughout the four waves from 2001 to 2016; (b) comparison with other Asian states to situate the political values and democratic support of the Hong Kong people. The research team is contemplating co-writing a book to summarize the overall changes of political values, based on the Asian Barometer Survey data, in the last 20 years, and discussed its impacts on political development of Hong Kong. The research team is going to continue to carry out the Asian Barometer Wave V survey in late 2019. The survey will provide invaluable data for comparative study across Asia, and also longitudinal study for the understanding of the change in political values in Hong Kong. We have already started applying funding for that.

14614815.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14614815.value: The Asian Barometer Survey (ABS) is a cross-national survey involving 15 Asian states/regions since 2000, which measures comprehensively political and democratic values through a common core questionnaire. This project forms the Wave IV of the Hong Kong survey, with previous three waves conducted in 2001, 2006 and 2012. This survey allows us to assess the change of political values in Hong Kong over time, assessing the impact of major events (e.g. the Umbrella Movement), and enables comparison with other Asian states. This project, with 1200 completed cases in 2016, showed that Hong Kong has achieved a medium-high level of support for democracy among Asian states. A comparison of the 2012 and 2016 results shows a substantial decline in institutional trust, with lower evaluation of government performance in various aspects The young and the educated are especially unhappy about government performance and have less trust in the institutions, posing major problems for government legitimacy. While there is no substantive change in overall support for democracy in 2016, there is a steady growth in political efficacy. This poses major problems for governance: as the government is facing declining trust and performace evaluation, together with the rise of an increasingly efficacious public.

14615015.label: Project Title(Chinese)
14615015.value: 可再生能源與可持續供水系統在香港的整合: 模型和算法

14615015.label: Project Objectives
14615015.value: Quantifying the uncertainties of water demands and renewable energy resources through data mining and data analytics will be carried out in this work. We will collect historical and predicted data from Hong Kong water network, with both topology structures and predicted water supplies and demands. Also, we will collect information of renewable energy availabilities in different water/wastewater treatment facilities, and predictions for the amounts in different time periods. These collected data will be further processed by data clustering, regression analysis, etc., to generate typical and representative scenarios with probability distributions for modeling and tests. Designing multistage stochastic programming models and algorithms for renewable integration to the water system, and also for management and operations of the water/wastewater treatment facilities will be conducted in this work. The proposed models will incorporate renewable energy availability and uncertainty constraints, and the constraints for operations of treatment facilities in different time periods under different scenarios. The objective of the models is to minimize the total cost incurred in the water system’s operations, to satisfy the water demands. Additionally, for this special type of problems, algorithms will be designed for efficient and effective decisions, including optimal decisions for locating and deciding the capacities to install onsite renewable facilities, such as solar panels and/or wind turbines, and also optimal operations for water/wastewater facilities to meet dynamic water demands. Evaluating the proposed techniques for practical test in a real water system will be conducted in this work. The proposed model will be implemented on the data collected for some treatment facilities, and some suggestions will be provided for system planners and managers.
