15300715.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15300715.value: 在这个项目里，我们将对几个重要的结构张量，即完全正，完全可分解，平方和，柯西，希尔伯特，P和B张量进行广泛的研究，其中完全可分解张量是在本项目中首次提出。我们将证明正的柯西张量是完全正的。我们将研究希尔伯特张量及其姊妹张量的完全正分解标准形式，强正性和正交分解。我们将提出希尔伯特特征值，并研究偶数阶希尔伯特张量的姊妹张量和其它平方和张量的最小希尔伯特特征值的计算方法。我们将提出B0-张量，B0-张量将包括B0张量和希尔伯特张量的比较张量。我们将研究P0张量和H+张量，以及P张量可能的Kellogg定理。本项目的成功不仅对张量谱理论本身，同时对张量谱理论和多项式优化及张量分解的互动关系会有重大意义。

15300715.label: Realisation of objectives
15300715.value: The spectral theory of higher-order symmetric tensors is an important tool for revealing some important properties of a hypergraph via its adjacency tensor, Laplacian tensor, and signless Laplacian tensor. Owing to the sparsity of these tensors, we propose an efficient approach to calculate products of these tensors and any vectors. By using the state-of-the-art L-BFGS approach, we develop a first-order optimization algorithm for computing H- and Z-eigenvalues of these large scale sparse tensors (CEST). With the aid of the Lojasiewicz inequality, we prove that the sequence of iterates generated by CEST converges to an eigenvector of the tensor. When CEST is started from multiple random initial points, the resulting best eigenvalue could touch the extreme eigenvalue with a high probability. A spin-j state can be represented by a symmetric tensor of order N =2j and dimension 4. Here, j can be a positive integer, which corresponds to a boson; j can also be a positive half-integer, which corresponds to a fermion. We introduce regularly decomposable tensors and show that a spin-j state is classical if and only if its representing tensor is a regularly decomposable tensor. In the even-order case, a regularly decomposable tensor is a completely decomposable tensor but not vice versa; a completely decomposable tensors is a sum-of-squares (SOS) tensor but not vice versa; an SOS tensor is a positive semi-definite (PSD) tensor but not vice versa. In the odd-order case, the first row tensor of a regularly decomposable tensor is regularly decomposable and its other row tensors are induced by the regular decomposition of its first row tensor. We also show that complete decomposability and regular decomposability are invariant under orthogonal transformations, and that the completely decomposable tensor cone and the regularly decomposable tensor cone are closed convex cones. Furthermore, in the even-order case, the completely decomposable tensor cone and the PSD tensor cone are dual to each other. The Hadamard product of two completely decomposable tensors is still a completely decomposable tensor. Since one may apply the positive semi-definite programming algorithm to detect whether a symmetric tensor is an SOS tensor or not, this gives a checkable necessary condition for classicality of a spin-j state. We introduce the mth order infinite dimensional Hilbert tensor (hypermatrix) to define an (m-1)-homogeneous operator on the spaces of analytic functions, which is called the Hilbert tensor operator. The boundedness of the Hilbert tensor operator is presented on Bergman spaces A^p (p>2(m-1)). On the base of the boundedness, two positively homogeneous operators are introduced to the spaces of analytic functions, and hence the upper bounds of norm of the two operators are found on Bergman spaces A^p (p>2(m-1)). In particular, the norms of such two operators on Bergman spaces A^4(m-1) are smaller than or equal to pi and pi^(1/m-1) , respectively. Based on recent advances in spectral hypergraph theory [L. Qi and Z. Luo, Tensor Anaysis: Spectral Theory and Special Tensors, SIAM, Philadelphia, 2017], we explore the Fiedler vector of an even-uniform hypergraph, which is the Z-eigenvector associated with the second smallest Z-eigenvalue of a normalized Laplacian tensor arising from the hypergraph. Then, we develop a novel tensor-based spectral method for partitioning vertices of the hypergraph. For this purpose, we extend the normalized Laplacian matrix of a simple graph to the normalized Laplacian tensor of an even-uniform hypergraph. The corresponding Fiedler vector is related to the Cheeger constant of the hypergraph. Then, we establish a feasible optimization algorithm to compute the Fiedler vector according to the normalized Laplacian tensor. The convergence of the proposed algorithm and the probability of obtaining the Fiedler vector of the hypergraph are analyzed theoretically. Finally, preliminary numerical experiments illustrate that the new approach based on a hypergraph-based Fiedler vector is effective and promising for some combinatorial optimization problems arising from subspace partitioning and face clustering. Copositivity of tensors plays an important role in vacuum stability of a general scalar potential, polynomial optimization, tensor complementarity problem and tensor generalized eigenvalue complementarity problem. We propose a new algorithm for testing copositivity of high order tensors, and then present applications of the algorithm in physics and hypergraphs. For this purpose, we first give several new conditions for copositivity of tensors based on the representative matrix of a simplex. Then a new algorithm is proposed with the help of a proper convex subcone of the copositive tensor cone, which is defined via the copositivity of Z-tensors. Furthermore, by considering a sum-of-squares program problem, we define two new subsets of the copositive tensor cone and discuss their convexity. Finding the maximum eigenvalue of a symmetric tensor is an important topic in tensor computation and numerical multilinear algebra. We introduce a new class of structured tensors called W-tensors, which not only extends the well-studied nonnegative tensors by allowing negative entries but also covers several important tensors arising naturally from spectral hypergraph theory. We then show that finding the maximum H-eigenvalue of an even-order symmetric W-tensor is equivalent to solving a structured semidefinite program and hence can be validated in polynomial time. This yields a highly efficient semidefinite program algorithm for computing the maximum H-eigenvalue of W-tensors and is based on a new structured sums-of-squares decomposition result for a nonnegative polynomial induced by W-tensors. Numerical experiments illustrate that the proposed algorithm can successfully find the maximum H-eigenvalue of W-tensors with dimension up to 10,000, subject to machine precision. As applications, we provide a polynomial time algorithm for computing the maximum H-eigenvalues of large-size Laplacian tensors of hyperstars and hypertrees, where the algorithm can be up to 13 times faster than the state-of-the-art numerical method introduced by Ng, Qi, and Zhou in 2009. P-and P0-matrix classes have wide applications in mathematical analysis, linear and nonlinear complementarity problems, etc., since they contain many important special matrices, such as positive (semi-)definite matrices, M-matrices, diagonally dominant matrices, etc. By modifying the existing definitions of P-and P0-tensors that work only for even order tensors, we propose a homogeneous formula for the definition of P-and P0-tensors. The proposed P-and P0-tensor classes coincide the existing ones of even orders and include many important structured tensors of odd orders. We show that many checkable classes of structured tensors, such as the nonsingular M-tensors, the nonsingular H-tensors with positive diagonal entries, the strictly diagonally dominant tensors with positive diagonal entries, are P-tensors under the new definition, regardless of whether the order is even or odd. In the odd order case, our definition of P0-tensors, to some extent, can be regarded as an extension of positive semi-definite (PSD) tensors. A positive semidefinite matrix can be written as a Gramian matrix, and a completely positive matrix can therefore be written as a Gramian matrix of some nonnegative vectors. We introduce Gramian tensors and study 2-dimension completely positive tensors and {0,1}−CP tensors. Also investigated are the complete positive multi-hypergraph which are a generalized form of cp graphs. We also provide a necessary and sufficient condition for a 2-dimensional tensor to be completely positive. We propose an SDP relaxation algorithm to test the copositivity of higher order tensors. By solving finitely many SDP relaxations, the proposed algorithm can determine the copositivity of higher order tensors. Furthermore, for any copositive but not strictly copositive tensor, the algorithm can also check it exactly.

15301215.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15301215.value: Autophagy, the evolutionarily conserved cellular process of self-digestion through actions of lysosomes under physiological stress, is an essential life event that mediates the recycling of cytoplasmic components and maintains normal homeostasis and energy balance of cells; it has vital functions in immune, infection, cardiovascular, and neurodegenerative diseases, and in particular in tumors, by promoting both their survival and death. Over the past few years, it has become a research hot topic and offered abundant potential targets for scientific investigations and clinical therapies that further developing an efficient, specific, and rapid detection method of autophagy is, however, still always pressing. Therefore, we intend to combine molecular computation, synthetic chemistry, lanthanide spectroscopy and chemical biology to realize a series of newly-proposed responsive lanthanide-peptide nanomaterials for simultaneously visualizing/monitoring and inhibiting macroautophagy (the dominant type) via targeting and imaging c-CBL, a decisive autophagy-related protein. c-CBL (the E3 ubiquitin ligase) is chosen because it serves as an autophagosome cargo receptor for trafficking Src to autophagic puncta, and as the binding partner to interact with LC3B, two quintessential processes for further elucidating and exploring the nanoparticles’ regulatory pathways of autophagy. To prove our hypotheses, four preliminary proof-of-concept experiments were conducted: (1) modified synthetic peptides were shown to be c-CBL-specific; (2) significant in-vitro autophagy interruption was demonstrated upon the binding of our peptide-coated nanomaterials with c-CBL specifically; (3) the in vitro labelling of c-CBL was confirmed by live cell imaging using confocal microscopy; (4) ex vivo biodistribution studies showed the quick metabloization and exclusion of peptide-coated nanoparticles. We believe a better understanding of the various stages of autophagy in vitro, in somatic cells and tumor metastatic models, can be achieved through dynamic observation (bioimaging) endowed with time-resolved lanthanide luminescence emitted from our designed nanomaterials, on top of some organic autophagy-regulating small molecules that had been reported in literature. Deeper insights into the mysterious but miraculous autophagic phenomena can then be obtained and the de facto relationship among c-CBL, autophagy, and cancer spelt out. To the best of our knowledge, this proposal would be the first cornerstone example of dual c-CBL imaging and inhibition for in-depth autophagy research. We envision the outcomes of this work would contribute significantly to the further studies of autophagy-associated illnesses, as well as high-throughput screening for more effective and selective autophagy inducers/inhibitors; nanomedicine-oriented hematological malignancy therapy (i.e. for lymphoma or leukemia) can also sail should we develop our novel responsive lanthanide nanomaterials successfully. 多法稀土自唾顯影材料

15301215.label: Realisation of objectives
15301215.value: The first objective of this project is to design peptides that are specific towards c-CBL as autophagy vectors. After an exhaustive screening of literature reports, four different peptides that exhibited binding towards the c-CBL-TKB domain backed by isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) results were ultimately selected as candidates for this project. The first peptide is the Sprouty homolog 2 (Spry 2 49-61) with a peptide sequence of IRNTNEpYTEGPTV. It has been shown that it interacts with the c-CBL gene. The second peptide is the Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR 2063-1075), its sequence is DSFLQRpYSSDPTG. Docking results of these two peptides all showed their binding to the TKB domain. The third peptide is the Tyrosine protein Kinase (Src 412-425) with a sequence LIEDNEpYTARQGA, yet last but not least, the fourth peptide with a sequence pYTPEP was ultimately selected by our research groups due to its highest affinity to c-CBL as deteremined by confocal experiment. Two major types of lanthanide-based materials were designed and synthesized in this project. First, it is a core-shell-shell upconversion nanoparticle (UCNP). The core is made up of a NaGdF4 lattice doped with 20% Yb and 2% Er. The 1st shell consists of NaGdF4: doped with 10% Yb and 20% Nd, while the 2nd shell is made up of pure NaGdF4. The first shell, doped with Nd, introduced an additional ion to the system and the energy levels facilitated energy transfer to the emitting Er3+, creating dual emission in the green and red regions under 808 nm and 980 nm excitation. The purpose of a second shell is to minimize surface quenching by isolating the nanoparticles. The synthesis of the core-shell-shell UCNPs were characterized by transmission electron microscopy and the successful synthesis was demonstrated by the gradual increase of the layers from 13 nm to 22 nm and to 31 nm at the final core-shell-shell phase. The photophysical properties of the UCNPs were also studied under 808 nm and 980 nm excitation. When the bare UCNPs (without any shells) were excited at 808 nm, no emission was observed. This is due to the absence of Nd ions which absorbs such wavelength. With the first shell - and the presence of Nd - upconversion emission was observed. Compared to core-shell-shell, there was a huge enhancement in the emission intensity. A ~15 fold and ~37-fold enhancement was observed in the emission intensity area under curve was observed in the green and red region respectively, demonstrating the effectiveness of the outermost shell layer in minimizing surface quenching. Under 980 nm, excitation, as Yb is already present in the bare UCNPs, upconversion emission was observed. The core-shell UCNPs showed promising enhancement while, similar to under 808 nm excitation, the core-shell-shell showed the highest upconversion intensity. The surface of these UCNPs are activated first by removal of oleate by acid treatment and then capping with poly(acrylic acid) via electrostatic interaction. The ligand exchange process was evident in the change in of dynamic light scattering (DLS) and zeta-potential measurements. From here, the UCNPs are suitable for peptide conjugation through NHS/EDC chemistry. The second type of lanthanide-based material is organolanthanide complex. Our group designed and synthesized an emissive lanthanide complex conjugated to the 4th peptide mentioned above through a linker. The photophysical properties of the europium complex was studied and MTT cell viability assay in HeLa cells also revealed the organolanthanide complex conjugated with the 4th peptide is more non-cytotoxic than just the peptide itself. Co-localization experiments with commercially available LysoTracker also indicated that the lanthanide complex localized in the lysosomes. The efficacy of our Eu-complex on autophagy regluation in HeLa cells were evaluated in vitro. Conjugation with c-CBL-specific peptide altered the localization property of the Eu-complex, it became delocalized in the cell. Upon addition of an autophagy inducer, more red spots appeared under excitation from confocal microscope, corresponding to the Eu emission. This indicated that the peptide-conjugated Eu-complex interacted with c-CBL in the autophagosomes. Nevertheless, there was insufficient time to extend the study beyond the current scope. Subcutaneous lymphoma models were constructed and were tested in vivo with the 4th peptide directly injected to the tumor. While in vivo imaging results showed affinity of the peptide to c-CBL, there was little evidence to suggest regulation of autophagy was achieved. As a result, we are still encountering difficulties in finding out the mechanism in autophagy regulation and whether the mode and location of binding has any effect - positive or adverse - on regulating autophagy. Extensive docking studies were performed from a large library of peptides both from literature and newly designed ones with modifications. However, most of literature only reported isothermal titration calorimety results and no imaging experiments were performed. As a result, more time was required to test out the c-CBL affinity in terms of imaging results and ultimately, the results were unsatisfactory and did not yield results close to the 4 peptides we found from literature. As a result, the screening and identification of protein networks that were able to interact with c-CBL did not give much positive results.

15301215.label: Major findings and research outcome
15301215.value: We screened a large database of peptides from literature that reported affinity or interaction of some extent with c-CBL. Molecular docking was then performed by our team to study the interactions and selected peptides were chosen for investigating the affinity to c-CBL with imaging experiments. Eventually, our group set sight on a final peptide sequence pYTPEP that showed the highest affinity. We also designed and synthesized two luminescent systems as the imaging module. The first system is core-shell-shell upconversion nanoparticles. The two additional shells are designed for better energy transfer, ability to absorb at alternate excitation wavelength and also for minimizing surface quenching. Our UCNPs were successfully characterized by transmission electron microscopy and their photophysical properties vindicated our design rationale. Surface modifications on the UCNPs were carried out to render them suitable for peptide conjugation. In addition, we also utilized our experience and expertise in the synthesis of organolanthanide complexes in which the c-CBL-specific peptide was conjugated by chemical synthesis. The distribution of Eu complex and Eu-complex-peptide inside was investigated using confocal microsopy. The data showed that the complex alone is mainly localized in lysosome. After conjugation with peptide, the fluorescent signal from Eu-complex-peptide can be observed in the whole cell. More red sports were observed upon addition of rapamycin, an autophagy inducer, indicating the interaction of Eu-complex with c-CBL in autophagosome. Nevertheless, there was insufficient prof to show that the complex was able to regulate autophagy at this stage.

15301215.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15301215.value: The increase in emission from our Eu-complex upon addition of the autophagy inducer is a positive and encouraging result from this project. The project has always intended to extend the scope of the study autophagy to various systems covering different autophagsomes. Furthermore, it is worth looking into improving and optimizing the luminescence properties of our Eu-complex to increase its sensitivity for potential in vivo applications where tissue penetration of both the excitation and emission light will present a larger obstacle. It is also the reason that we should accelerate the investigation of using UCNPs for imaging autophagy as they have more desirable tissue penetration properties. At the same time, continual screening of protein networks should be carried out to identify better binding moieties with c-CBL.

15301215.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15301215.value: Autophagy denotes the mechanism that a cell devours itself and this process is known to bring both positive and negative influences. It can act as a timely renewal and recycle of dysfunctional components but it can also lead to unwanted cell death. It is therefore vital for researchers to understand and more ideally regulate autophagy so that harm becomes minimal. Among a pool of peptides that are specific to the c-CBL gene, we evaluated one peptide sequence with a high affinity to the gene through imaging experiments - which was not done before in literature - and conjugated it to our emissive lanthanide complex for imaging purposes. It was found that our peptide-conjugated complex showed red emission in vitro. Upon the addition of an autophagy inducer, red spots appeared and were observed under the confocal microscope. These results indicate interaction between our peptide-conjugated Eu-complex with the c-CBL gene in autophagosomes. This is an encourage result for further investigation on monitoring and regulating autophagy with improved luminescent systems and autophagy vector peptides.

15301315.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15301315.value: Carbonyl oxides (Criegee intermediates CIs) formed, from the ozonolysis of alkenes, are key species in the oxidation of volatile organic compounds (VOCs) in the atmosphere. Decomposition of CIs provides a non-photolytic source of OH radicals and some of their reactions give rise to secondary organic aerosols (SOAs). Organic hydroperoxides (ROOH) also contribute to the oxidizing capacity of the atmosphere as they are a source of the radicals OH and HO2 produced via photolysis and subsequent reaction respectively. Recent work has suggested that a Criegee intermediate can insert into a ROO-H bond to increase the carbon number and also the oxygen to carbon ratio of the new molecule, making the product more likely to have a lower vapour pressure. This will contribute to SOA formation in the atmosphere, give rise to radiative forcing and hence have an effect on climate. Scientific studies of reactions which lead to SOA formation are of particular relevance to China where aerosol pollution in the troposphere is proving to be a particular problem. This project will study a number of key CI + ROOH reactions of atmospheric importance. In the experimental part, for each reaction studied Chemical Ionisation Mass Spectrometry (CIMS) will be used to measure the overall rate coefficient. This will be followed by Photoelectron Spectroscopy (PES) measurements, which will provide channel specific rate coefficients and product branching ratios. State-of-the-art electronic structure calculations of each reaction surface will be carried out and channel specific rate coefficients will be computed for comparison with experimental values. No measurements have yet been made of the rate coefficients and product branching ratios of atmospherically relevant CI + ROOH reactions, as hydroperoxides have proved hard to detect and measure in laboratory and field measurements, and it is only recently that a convenient method has been devised to prepare CIs for laboratory study. Also, no calculations have been made of CI + ROOH reaction rate coefficients using computed potential energy surfaces. However, these rate coefficients are important as they are needed in regional and global scale modeling of the atmosphere. This combined experimental and theoretical investigation will deliver reliable channel specific rate coefficients, leading to a detailed understanding of the mechanisms of the reactions studied. This is the main objective of this research. It will allow a better understanding of the impact of CIs on the oxidizing capacity of the atmosphere and on the formation of secondary volatile organic aerosols. 烯烴的臭氧分解生成的羰基氧化物（Criegee中間體CI）是大氣中的揮發性有機化合物（VOC）的氧化的關鍵物種。CI的分解是OH自由基的非光解源，另外它們的一些反應可產生二次有機氣溶膠（SOA）。有機氫過氧化物（ROOH） 也提高大氣的氧化能力，因為它們通過光解和隨後的反應可生成OH和HO2自由基，成為大氣氧化物種的來源。最近的研究表明，一個CI中間體可插入ROO-H鍵來增加的碳原子數和新分子的氧碳比率，使得產物有較低的蒸汽壓。這將有助於SOA的形成，改變輻射驅動力（radiative forcingz )並因此影響地球的氣候。研究生成SOA的反應，對中國是十分重要，因為在對流層中氣溶膠污是個嚴重問題。 本項目將研究一些大氣的重要關鍵CI和 ROOH反應。在實驗方面，將利用化學電離質譜（CIMS）研究每個反應並測量總速率係數。隨後再利用光電子能譜（PES）的測量，提供不同反應通道的分支比。理論方面將利用最先進的方法計算每個反應表面並計算不同反應通道的反應速率係數。理論計算的結果將與實驗值進行比較。現時未有關於CI 和ROOH反應的速率係數和產品分支比的 實驗數據，因為有機氫過氧化物已被證明在實驗室和實地難於檢測和測量，並且最近才發現有效的方法生成CI 作實驗的觀測和研究。此外，CI和ROOH反應亦沒有相關的計算得出反應速率係數。可是，這些數據對區域性和全球性大氣化學模型是十分重要的。 這種結合的實驗和理論研究將提供可靠的特定反應通度的速率係數，幫助我們們了解這些化學反應的詳細機制。這是本研究的主要目的。這將有助於更好地 理解CI 對大氣的氧化能力，及對二次揮發性有機氣溶膠生成的影響。

15301315.label: Realisation of objectives
15301315.value: 1. Reaction of CI with hydroperoxide The addition reaction of hydroxymethyl hydroperoxide (HMHP, HOCH2OOH) with the simplest Criegee intermediate, CH2OO, has been examined using quantum chemical methods with transition state theory. There are three oxygen atoms in HMHP and CH2OO may add to each of them results in three addition channels. CH2OO + HOCH2OOH → HOCH2OOCH2OOH (1) CH2OO + HOCH2OOH → HOCH2O(O)CH2OOH (2) CH2OO + HOCH2OOH → HOOCH2OCH2OOH (3) Geometry optimization and IRC calculations were performed using M06-2X, MN15-L, and B2PLYP-D3 functionals in conjunction with the aug-cc-pVTZ basis set. Single point energy calculations using QCISD(T) and BD(T) with the same basis set have been performed to determine the energy of reactants, reactive complex, transition state, and products. Rate coefficients have been obtained using variational transition state theory. The most accurate method in this work is the BD(T)/AVTZ//B2PLYP-D3/AVTZ level, which gives the computed barrier heights of -6.70, -9.01 and -0.084 kcal.mol-1 for channel 1, 2 and 3, respectively. In terms of reaction energy, the computed reaction energies (ΔE_RX) at the same level were in the order: channel 2 (-20.02 kcal/mol) > channel 3 (-47.87 kcal/mol) > channel 1 (-55.32 kcal/mol), therefore, the oligomeric hydroperoxide forming channel (channel 1) is the most exothermic while the ether oxide forming channel (channel 2) is the most favorable. The reaction barrier is negative and both inner and outer transition states may contribute to the corresponding overall reactive flux. A two-transition state model has been employed to obtain reliable rate coefficients at the high-pressure limit. For the major channel, the results showed that the outer transition state dominates the overall reactive flux below 270 K while both outer and inner transition states become important from 270 K to 330 K. The pressure-dependent rate coefficient calculations using the SS-QRRK theory have shown that this channel is pressure-dependent. The ether oxide is expected to be produced in the atmosphere at the highest rate at an elevation of 12 km, corresponding to the temperature of 217 K and the pressure of 1.940 x 104 Pa. In the troposphere, where the temperature ranges from 210 K to 320 K, the production rate of the ether oxide product (channel 2) is higher than that of the oligomeric hydroperoxide product (channel 1) by a factor of 1.6 (at 210 K) to 22.8 (at 320 K). Under normal atmospheric conditions, the production rate of the ether oxide product is at least 10 times more. Although the channel 2 is the most favorable channel, the ether oxide product formed is about 30 kcal/mol higher in energy than the products of the other two channels. It is more reactive and may react with the more abundant species in the atmosphere, such as water and sulfur dioxide. Geometry optimizations of the stationary points of these reactions were performed at the M06-2X/AVDZ level only and the electronic energies were refined at the BD(T)/AVTZ level. Results suggested that the reaction HOCH2O(O)CH2OOH + SO2 → HOCH2OCH2OOH + SO3 it is a possible sink of HMHP. The potential energy surface of this reaction showed that the two reactants underwent barrierless association to form a reactant complex, with stabilization energy of 12.07 kcal.mol-1 (at the BD(T)/AVTZ//M06-2X/AVDZ level), then the reaction proceeded via a submerged barrier of -8.13 kcal/mol. It then proceeded to form a product complex with relative electronic energy of -81.27 kcal/mol and finally, it dissociated to form separate products with reaction energy of -64.35 kcal/mol. Two-transition state theory was employed to compute the rate coefficients from 200 K to 400 K. Regarding inner transition state, in view of the high computational costs of the Hessians of the reacting system along the IRC, kinner was only computed at the TST level. At 298 K, the computed rate coefficient of the HOCH2O(O)CH2OOH + SO2 → HOCH2OCH2OOH + SO3 reaction was 5.15 x 10-10 cm3molecule-1second-1. Although the TST rate coefficient might be overestimated by an order of magnitude, our results still suggest that HMHP reaction with CI may result in oxidizing of SO2 into SO3. A similar calculation has been conducted for the reaction of HMHP with OH using BD(T)//M06-2X/AVTZ and obtained a rate coefficient about 300-fold smaller than the of HMHP with CI followed by oxidation of sulphur dioxide. These results suggesting the addition reaction of HMHP with CI may be a significant sink for HMHP and this reaction could be an indirect source for generating atmospheric H2SO4, which is crucial to the formation of clouds, and it might relieve global warming. This work has been published in Physical Chemistry Chemical Physics. Theoretical study has also been conducted on the reactions of methyl hydroperoxide with the simplest CI, CH2OO has been conducted. The following channels: oxygen abstractions, hydrogen abstractions and addition reaction were considered. CH3OOH + CH2OO → CH3OOCH2OOH Addition Reaction (1a) → CH2OOH + CH3OOH Hydrogen Abstraction (1b) → CH3OOOH +CH2O Oxygen Abstraction (1c) → CH2O + HOCH2OOH Oxygen Abstraction (1d) Geometry optimization, including transition state (TS) search and intrinsic reaction coordinate (IRC) calculations, and harmonic vibrational frequency calculations were performed using the M06-2X functional with the basis set aug-cc-pvdz and 6-311G**. Higher-level ab initio electronic energy calculations were carried out using the CCSD(T*)-F12 method as implemented in MOLPRO2012. The results suggested that the addition reaction has the lowest barrier and would be the major channel. 2. Photoelectron Spectroscopy Measurement. On the experiment side, hydrogen peroxide has been studied with threshold photoelectron (TPE) spectroscopy and photoelectron (PE) spectroscopy. This is a preparation work for the experimental observation of methyl hydroperoxide and its reactions with Cregiee Intermediate. The TPE spectrum has been recorded in the 10.0−21.0 eV ionization energy region, and the PE spectrum has been recorded at 21.22 eV photon energy. The spectra obtained were assigned with the help of theoretical calculations using CCSD(T)-F12 and IP-EOM methods. The vibrational structure of the spectrum was assigned with the assistance of harmonic Franck−Condon factor calculations. This work has been published in the Journal of Physical Chemistry A. 3. Reaction of hydroperoxy radical Theoretical study on the reaction of hydroperoxy radical with BrO has also been conducted during the reporting period. Reaction enthalpies, activation energies and mechanisms have been determined for the following five reaction channels: HOO + BrO → HOBr + O2 (triplet state X3Σ) (R2a) → HOBr + O2 (single state a1Δ) (R2b) → HBr + O3 (R3) → OBrO + OH (R4) → BrOO + OH (R5) Rate coefficient calculations from computed potential energy surfaces were made for BrO + HO2 for the first time. Although channel(R2a) is the most exothermic, channel (R2b) has the lowest barrier height, which is negative (at -3.07 kcal/mol). A two transition state model involving an outer and an inner transition state has been used to describe this channel. The inner transition state was found to be the major bottleneck of the reaction in the temperature range considered. In cases like this, various TST theories are still applicable. Computed rate coefficients shows a negative temperature dependence, as observed experimentally, but are too low by approximately an order of magnitude at any selected temperature in the range 200–400 K. The results of this work have been published in PCCP.

15301315.label: Major findings and research outcome
15301315.value: This project was designed to examine the reaction between Criegee intermediates (CI) and hydroperoxide in the atmosphere as the addition reaction has been observed in laboratory. This addition reaction forms products with much lower vapour pressure and would provide a mechanism to contribute to secondary organic aerosol formation in the atmosphere. Detail reaction mechanism of Criegee intermediates is extremely important to understand its impact on oxidation capacity and formation of aerosols in the atmosphere. Hyperoxide may react with CI in a number of ways, including addition, hydrogen abstraction and oxygen abstraction. Our calculation suggested that addition reaction is indeed the most favorable reaction. Hydroxymethyl hydroperoxide (HOCH2OOH, HMHP) is among the most abundant hydroperoxides observed in the atmosphere. It is formed when the simplest CI reacts with water (or water dimer, more specifically), which is the major loss process of CH2OO in atmosphere. CH2OO may add to different oxygen atom on HMHP. If the CI adds to hydroxyl group of HMHP, an oligomer hyperoxide would formed and further addition reaction would lead to polar compounds susceptible to condensation to form aerosol. However, our theoretical study suggested that this is not the most favorable channel. The most favorable channel of the addition reaction forms an ether oxide product. In the troposphere, where the temperature ranges from 210 K to 320 K, the production rate of the ether oxide product is higher than that of the oligomeric hydroperoxide product by a factor of 1.6 (at 210 K) to 22.8 (at 320 K). Under normal atmospheric conditions, the production rate of the ether oxide product is at least 10 times more. The epoxide product is of higher energy when compared to the oligomer hyperoxide product. It is more reactive and may oxidize sulfur dioxide into sulfur trioxide very quickly. At 298 K, the computed rate coefficient of the HOCH2O(O)CH2OOH + SO2  HOCH2OCH2OOH + SO3 reaction was 5.15 x 10-10 cm3molecule-1second-1. Compare with for the reaction of HMHP with OH, the reaction rate coefficient ios about 300-fold smaller than that of HMHP with CI followed by oxidation of sulphur dioxide. These results suggesting the addition reaction of HMHP with CI may be a significant sink for HMHP and this reaction could be an indirect source for generating atmospheric H2SO4, which is crucial to the formation of clouds, and it might relieve global warming.

15301315.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15301315.value: The theoretical results of this project suggested that addition reaction with CI would be a significant sink for HMHP and this reaction could be an important indirect source for generating sulfuric acid in the atmosphere. The reaction mechanism proposed from the theoretical calculations could be incorporated in to atmospheric reaction model for simulating study to examine the importance of this in different regions. We are looking for collaboration working on atmospheric simulation to see the possibility of including the reactions described above into the chemistry model for simulation study.

15301315.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15301315.value: Chemistry of Creigee Intermediate has received a lot of attentions recently since a way to generate the species for experimental observation was discovered early this decade. Reaction with water is the most important sink of Creigee Intermediates which forms hydroxymethyl hydroperoxide (HMHP). The theoretical rate coefficient calculations suggested that addition reaction of HMHP with the Creigee Intermeidate itself could be an important sink. The ether oxide produced from this addition reaction would react very quickly with the sulfur dioxide turning them into sulfur trioxide and eventually to sulfuric acid in the atmosphere leading to formation of clouds. The results suggested that chemistry of Creigee Intermediates is not only important in forming OH, the major atmospheric oxidizing agent, it also play an important role in formation of sulfuric acid in the atmosphere.

15301615.value: 利用组合寬帶超快光譜研究高階B-型,Z-型和i-型DNA結構與DNA激發態動力學間的關係

15301615.label: Project Objectives
15301615.value: We propose to perform combined fs-TRF and fs-TA experiments to directly probe the excited-states for selected varying length alternating G-C DNAs in both B-form and Z-form structures. The experiments are aimed at exploring effect of structure and structural flexibility on the excited-states and to seek spectral signatures and excited-state dynamics distinctive to the B-form and Z-form G-C duplexes. We propose to perform comparative fs experiments on the B-form and Z-form G-C duplexes to examine effects of excitation-energy and solvent-deuteration on the excited-states. The work will provide explicit evidence for state-identifications and for assessing contributions of various competing processes to the excited-state decay. The results will allow achieving an unified picture for resolving current uncertainties on nature of excited-states and influence of structure on decay processes. We propose to perform analogous fs experiments to directly probe and study effects of excitation-energy and solvent-deuteration on the excited-states for series of C-rich DNAs including the repeats and truncated repeats of human telomeric (HT) sequences. We propose to perform the experiments in carefully controlled slightly acidic and alkaline pH to study respectively the i-motif and ss structure of the sequences. The work will allow acquisition of spectra and excited-state pathways characteristic of the two types of structures of sequences chosen. By comparing results from the sequences adopting tetramolecular, bimolecular, and unimolecular i-motif structures, this work will supply solid evidence for elucidating effect of i-motif folding topology on dynamics of excited-states. This will help resolving the long-standing issues on roles of stacking vs pairing, energy-transfer, charge-transfer, and proton-transfer in dynamics of UV-excited DNA. We propose to perform parallel fs experiments for the HT sequences at neutral and physiological pH and in the cell-mimic molecular-crowding condition. With the results from i-motif and ss structure as benchmark reference, the finding of this work will afford concrete evidence for assessing structure(s) of the sequences in biologically relevant condition. The result should prove crucial for understanding role of i-motif in vivo and in gene expression and regulation. The overall results of the proposed study will have important implication for rational design and development of the structural DNA nanotechnology.

15301615.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15301615.value: DNAs are polymorphic, can adopt various conformations different from the canonical right-handed helix B-DNA. Apart from its importance in the physiological functions, the polymorphism of DNA has been exploited in wide-ranging areas such as biosensor and molecular electronics in the nanoscale. Governed by the structural-sensitive inter-base electronic couplings, the dynamics of DNA excited-states is, on the other hand, pivotal for determining the molecular origin of DNA photo-stability and photo-damage. However, due to the intrinsic complex nature of DNA excited-states and thereby the enormous difficulty in the study of these systems, the understanding of DNA excited-states is up to now still only rudimentary. An open question of current frontier is about the precise characters and the dynamic pathways of the excited-state and how these are affected by the various conformations of DNAs. Alternating guanine(G)-Cytosine(C) duplex can adopt either the usual B-DNA or the rare left-handed Z-DNA. Besides the single-stranded (ss) conformation, tandem C-rich sequence can fold into i-DNA, known also as i-motif, an tetraplex structure formed by two parallel duplexes through intercalated hemiprotonated base-pairs. The capacity of these DNAs in adopting the various typical structures makes them prototype for investigation of the interplay between the structure and dynamics of DNA excited-states. Aiming to explore this largely unknown area, we propose here to use our state-of-the-art femtosecond time-resolved spectroscopy to perform a systematic and in-depth study on series selected G-C DNAs and C-rich DNAs including some repeats and truncated repeats of human telomeric (HT) sequences. Our integrated application of femtosecond broadband time-resolved fluorescence, transient absorption and picosecond time-resolved resonance Raman spectroscopy provide an ideal method for revealing spectral signatures and structural fingerprints for excited-states of the B-form or Z-form structure of the G-C duplexes and the i-motif or ss structure of the C-rich sequences. The proposed research will enable the first direct and comprehensive probe of dynamic evolution of the excite-states and will allow acquisition of the unique sets of photophysical parameters diagnostic to each type of the structure investigated. In this way, the results of proposed work will allow revealing the key structural element(s) that affect(s) most the excited-state dynamics. The results will provide important new insights that will help to resolve the current controversies and will also significantly enrich our knowledge of the DNA excited-states. The work will prove useful in development of the structural DNA nanotechnology. 除了最常見的右手螺旋B-型結構，DNA可採取多種不同的構型。DNA構型的多樣性不僅在生理功能方面有其重要性，在其它例如生物傳感器和納米分子電子學等領域也有著廣泛的應用。 DNA激發態的動力學受控於DNA中鹼基間的電子耦合，對DNA的光穩定性和光損傷起決定性作用。然而，由於DNA激發態的複雜性，目前對其動力學的研究非常困難，對激發態動力學的了解也十分有限。DNA激發態如何受DNA構型的影響是當前激發態研究的一個熱點問題。由鳥嘌呤（G）和胞嘧啶（C）交替組成的雙鏈DNA可以採取常見的B-型結構或較少見的左手螺旋Z-型結構。除單鏈構型，由C組成的DNA可以折疊成i-型結構，也被稱為i-DNA，即一種由兩個平行的雙鏈構成的四聚體結構。這些不同構型的GC DNA和C DNA為研究DNA結構與激發態動力學間的關係提供了重要的模型體系。為了探索這個未知的領域，我們建議採用先進的寬帶飛秒時間分辨光譜方法對一系列GC DNA，C DNA和人類端粒DNA進行深入而系統的研究。我們的組合寬帶飛秒時間分辨熒光，瞬態吸收和皮秒時間分辨共振拉曼光譜技術為研究所選DNA系列的激發態提供了理想的實驗手段，可以直接並全面地跟踪激發態的動態演化過程，進而獲得一系列重要的光物理參數及其與DNA結構的關聯。這項研究的結果將揭示影響DNA激發態動力學的關鍵結構因素，並有助於澄清目前對DNA激發態的各種爭議，加深對DNA激發態的認知。這項研究的結果也會促進DNA在納米結構技術方面的發展和應用。

15301615.value: For objective 1: 100% achieved We have performed an integrated spectroscopic investigation where we combined steady-state absorption and fluorescence, femtosecond time-resolved fluorescence (fs-TRF) and femtosecond transient absorption (fs-TA) experiments on selected G-C DNAs in both B-form and Z-form structures. The effects of structure and structural flexibility on the excited-states dynamics of the B-form and Z-form G-C duplexes were studied. For objective 2: 90% achieved We have performed an integrated spectroscopic investigation where we combined fs-TRF and fs-TA experiments on selected B-form and Z-form G-C duplexes to examine the effect of excitation-energy on the excited-states. The investigation provides evidence that there are various competing processes to the excited-state decay. For objective 3: 100% achieved We have performed the combined fs-TRF and fs-TA experiments on selected C-rich DNAs and human telomeric (HT) sequences to study the effects of excitation-energy and solvent-deuteration. We have also performed analogous fs experiments with controlled pH on the ss and i-motif sequences. The investigations provide solid information on the effect of i-motif folding topology on dynamics of excited-states and the roles of stacking vs pairing, energy-transfer, charge-transfer, and proton-transfer on the dynamics of the excited-states. For objective 4: 90% achieved We have performed the combined fs-TRF and fs-TA experiments on selected HT sequences at neutral pH in reverse micelle condition. The investigation provides information on the effect of the cell-mimic molecular-crowding condition on the decay dynamics of UV-excited DNA. For objective 5: 90% achieved By performing the investigations to achieve the objectives 1 to 4 above, we have obtained useful information for the rational design of structural DNA nanotechnology.

rows: We propose to perform combined fs-TRF and fs-TA experiments to directly probe the excited-states for selected varying length alternating G-C DNAs in both B-form and Z-form structures. The experiments are aimed at exploring effect of structure and structural flexibility on the excited-states and to seek spectral signatures and excited-state dynamics distinctive to the B-form and Z-form G-C duplexes.

We propose to perform comparative fs experiments on the B-form and Z-form G-C duplexes to examine effects of excitation-energy and solvent-deuteration on the excited-states. The work will provide explicit evidence for state-identifications and for assessing contributions of various competing processes to the excited-state decay. The results will allow achieving an unified picture for resolving current uncertainties on nature of excited-states and influence of structure on decay processes.

We propose to perform analogous fs experiments to directly probe and study effects of excitation-energy and solvent-deuteration on the excited-states for series of C-rich DNAs including the repeats and truncated repeats of human telomeric (HT) sequences. We propose to perform the experiments in carefully controlled slightly acidic and alkaline pH to study respectively the i-motif and ss structure of the sequences. The work will allow acquisition of spectra and excited-state pathways characteristic of the two types of structures of sequences chosen. By comparing results from the sequences adopting tetramolecular, bimolecular, and unimolecular i-motif structures, this work will supply solid evidence for elucidating effect of i-motif folding topology on dynamics of excited-states. This will help resolving the long-standing issues on roles of stacking vs pairing, energy-transfer, charge-transfer, and proton-transfer in dynamics of UV-excited DNA.

We propose to perform parallel fs experiments for the HT sequences at neutral and physiological pH and in the cell-mimic molecular-crowding condition. With the results from i-motif and ss structure as benchmark reference, the finding of this work will afford concrete evidence for assessing structure(s) of the sequences in biologically relevant condition. The result should prove crucial for understanding role of i-motif in vivo and in gene expression and regulation.
The overall results of the proposed study will have important implication for rational design and development of the structural DNA nanotechnology.

15301615.label: Major findings and research outcome
15301615.value: We have conducted most of the experiments planned in this project. Through these measurements, expected evidences have been obtained for addressing most of the questions posed in the proposal. Our study provides direct observation of intrinsic fluorescence and the first full probe of the real-time dynamics of the intrinsic fluorescence from i-motifs formed from varied sequences and pH conditions. The results obtained demonstrate concrete evidence for the existence at neutral pH of i-motifs from both dC20 and the HTS. It also identifies that, under neutral conditions, the i-motif from dC20 adopting the bimolecular folding structure is significantly more stable than the HTS i-motif featuring the unimolecular topology. Our TRF study unveils excitation dynamics distinctive of the interdigitated architecture of i-motifs with the excited states involved exhibiting deactivation over a remarkably broad timescale through multiple channels involving proton-coupled electron transfer lasting tens of picoseconds, as signified by the solvent kinetic isotope effect, and structure-dependent charge recombination in the hundreds of picoseconds to tens of nanoseconds time regime. Our study also unveils an unusual multichannel nonradiative mechanism dominated by states with varying character of charge transfer lasting ten and hundreds of picoseconds, accounting altogether for an overwhelming ∼85% of the overall deactivation involving proton transfer. Our comparative study shows that encapsulating the GQ in nanocavity water pool or changing it into hydrid-type topologies with the presence of K+ ions alter differently energies and lifetimes of these states, yet without affecting the nature of the electronic excitation involved. The finding of this work underscores a leading role of structural rigidity in regulating the interplay with the microenvironment of photoexcited monomolecularly folded HT-GQs.

15301615.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15301615.value: Based on the outcome of this project, further research will be attempted to perform more combined fs-TRF and fs-TA experiments to directly probe the dynamics and spectra of the excited-states for more selected G-C, human telomeric and i-motif sequences.

15301615.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15301615.value: Following the research plan suggested in the proposal, some selected G-C, human telomeric and i-motif sequences were investigated using femtosecond time-resolved fluorescence, femtosecond transient absorption spectroscopy. The spectra and dynamics signatures for intrinsic excited-states and associated emission pathways were obtained. The effects of excitation-energy, solvent-deuteration and molecular-crowding conditions on the excited-state decay were also investigated. The outcomes of this project have led to several publications in top international journals. The research grant enables the PI to participate international conferences and give invited talks in these conferences. It also allows training of several students, at both the undergraduate and post graduated levels.

15303015.label: Project Objectives
15303015.value: To fabricate atomically thin 2D materials, especially molybdenum disulphide and tungsten disulphide nanosheets by chemical vapour deposition. To fabricate strained 2D nanosheets with a spatially varying strain profile. To investigate the strain-tunable valley-orbit coupling properties in 2D materials. To fabricate strained 2D nanosheets with a spatially varying strain profile.
To investigate the strain-tunable valley-orbit coupling properties in 2D materials.
To explore the solar funnel effect in strained 2D materials.

15303015.label: Realisation of objectives
15303015.value: Objective 1: We have acquired a chemical vapor deposition system which is capable of depositing continuous monolayer to few layers MoS2 and WS2 films. The set up can also be used to prepare other layered transition metal dichalcogenides such as PtSe2 and NiSe2. The PtSe2 and NiSe2 were found to be interesting electrocatlaysts for hydrogen evolution reaction. Objective 2: We employed focused ion beam technique to etch trenches onto the substrates. Due to the FIB process, the trenches consist of an inclined plane at one end and a shape edge in the other end. Then the 2D materials were transferred onto the trenches. The continuous strain profile of the 2D material can be observed. However, the technique is not very reproducible and the yield for the strained 2D materials is very low. A systematic study was performed to investigate the process to produce strained 2D materials onto the trench. It is found that a channel is needed in each trench to drain the liquid during the transfer process. In turn, a large strain profile can be induced onto the layer. Based on the Raman shifts, the estimated maximum compressive and tensile strain of the MoS2 layer are 2% and 5%, respectively. The effect of uniaxial tensile strain on the shear mode (C mode) and layer breathing mode (LB mode) of few layers MoS2 were also studied using a bending technique. The C mode is doubly degenerated into two sub-peaks as applied strain increases. No measurable Raman shift for the LB mode is observed, while its Raman intensity decreases gradually as the strain increases. In addition, the C and LB modes exhibit distinguished thickness dependence. The C mode shows a clear blue shift as the strain increases, while the LB mode is softened in the process. Moreover, the evolution of C mode with thickness follows an enhanced linear-chain model plus a linear component very well. It implies that the C mode is a better thickness navigator as compared to the L mode. The technique was also employed to study black phosphorus and found its giant anisotropic Raman response. Objective 3: The valley-orbit coupling of the strained MoS2 was studied in collaboration with Prof Hui Zhao from the University of Kansas. Although various strained MoS2 were measured, no obvious splitting of the exciton into two linearly polarized modes (perpendicular and parallel to the strain) could be observed. The compressive and tensile strained MoS2 may be insufficient to generate the splitting of the exciton. Despite the negative results in MoS2, the ultrafast laser spectroscopy technique was applied to measure the photocarrier transport properties of ultrathin amorphous black phosphorus. Objective 4: In collaboration with Prof Jr-hau He from the King Abdullah, University of Science and Technology, we have developed various solar cells such as graphene dot/PEDOT:PSS composite for flexible solar cells, graphene quantum dot-Modified Organic/Silicon hybrid device, and Si hybrid solar cells. By patterning the p-Si substrates with an array of trenches with specified sizes using focused ion beam, the strained MoS2 was generated onto Si solar cells. However, no obvious improvement of the solar cell performance could be observed as compared with the unstrained MoS2/Si solar cells. The strain induced in the MoS2 seems to be insufficient to generate sufficient band gap variation.

15303015.label: Major findings and research outcome
15303015.value: The experimental set up of chemical vapour deposition system was developed which enabled us not only to fabricate MoS2 and WS2 films but also for various layered transition metal dichalcogenides such as PtSe2 and NiSe2. These materials exhibited interesting hydrogen evolution reaction and two papers were published. A bending technique was developed to study the shear mode and breathing mode of MoS2. A paper was published. The same technique was also applied to study black phosphorus. The result was published in Advanced Functional Materials. Ultrafast laser spectroscopy was employed to study the strained MoS2. The work was also extended to study ultrathin amorphous black phosphorus. A paper was published in 2D Materials. Due to the knowledge gained in the course of the study, we published four review papers in the topics of 2D Materials and black phosphorus.

15303015.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15303015.value: Strained engineering is an emerging approach to tune the bandgap of 2D materials. It has been predicted that strain-tunable valley-orbit coupling could lead to new structures of excition condensates, new functionalities of excitonic circuits as well as valleytronics. Thus, it is of fundamental and technological importance to explore various strain-engineered 2D materials and to monitor their responses in optical properties. Our works provided insight to the topic. Further works are needed to demonstrate the strain-tunable valley-orbit coupling.

15303015.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15303015.value: Strain engineering is a process of tuning a material’s electronic structure by changing its lattice constant, thereby creating new properties. Due to reduced dimensions, 2D materials become more flexible to be highly strained, which leaves more space for strain engineering. It is anticipated that the strained 2D materials would lead to strain-tunable valley-orbit coupling as well as the development of solar funnels which is capable of harvesting a broad range of solar spectrum. Our experimental works suggest that the strain level of the 2D materials should be more than 10% in order to observe these properties. More works are needed to search for suitable 2D materials and to develop new strain engineering techniques.

15303115.label: Realisation of objectives
15303115.value: 1. In order to achieve the project objective 1, we design different types of vertical graphene tunnelling heterostructures with a variety of ultrathin ferroelectric films. For the Si back-gated one, the monolayer graphene films synthesized on copper foils by chemical vapor deposition (CVD) were transferred onto SiO2/Si substrates using a standard wet-transfer process. The ultrathin BiFeO3 (BFO) films, with a thickness of 10 nm, were grown on the transferred graphene by pulsed laser deposition (PLD). After the PLD growth, the samples were in situ annealed at 450 oC in 100 Pa oxygen atmosphere to remove the potential oxygen vacancies. Finally, metal Au was deposited to form electrodes of source and drain by thermal evaporation. For the top-gated one, some ferroelectrics such as typical BaTiO3 (BTO) thin films were deposited on single crystal Nb: SrTiO3 (STO) by PLD. PMMA-coated graphene/Cu sheets were cut into small pieces, etched with APS and transferred onto BTO/Nb:STO by standard wet transfer process. After the sample was soaked with acetone to remove PMMA residues, HfO2 dielectric films were deposited on BTO through PLD. Au electrodes were deposited by thermal metal evaporation for subsequent electrical measurement. The sample was soaked with acetone to remove the PMMA layer. Au electrodes dots with 200 μm diameter and 90 nm thickness were deposited on the sample by thermal evaporation for electrical measurement. Finally, asymmetric FTJs comprising Nb:STO bottom electrodes, 5nm-thick BTO tunnel barrier, graphene interface layer and Au top electrodes were fabricated. 2. To achieve the objective 2, we have used a variety of techniques including X-ray diffraction (XRD) and X-ray photoemission spectroscopy (XPS), Raman spectroscopy (Horiba, HR800) using a laser excitation source with a wavelength of 488 nm to characterize structural characteristics of the fabricated heterostructures. Regarding electrical transport characteristics, we have measured current-voltage (I–V) curves of the heterostructured field-effect transistors (FET) by a semiconductor analyzer (Agilent 4156C). Also, The electrical properties of the ferroelectric tunneling junction (FTJ) were performed on Lakeshore probe station equipped with a Keithley 4200 SourceMeter to characterize electroic transport characteristics. In addition, piezoelectric force microscopy (PFM) tests were employed to measure the local ferroelectric hysteresis loops and acquire polarization images using a scanning probe microscope (Asylum Research). Through these characterizations, physical mechanism behind the observations have been studied through theoretical modelling and simulations based on the Fowler-Nordheim (FN) tunneling model. 3. To achieve the objective 3, we have designed and fabricated an unexplored type of ferroelectric vertical graphene heterostructure FET by coupling FTJ to graphene FET. This is fundamentally different from existing planar graphene FETs. Differing from conventional tunnel junctions, the tunneling barrier height in FTJ can be modulated by spontaneous polarization. Therefore, we have focused on the ferroelectric behaviors of ultrathin films using PFM and studied the out-of-plane PFM amplitude and phase images of the film after poling with alternative +10 and −10 V bias. We found that the contrast of the amplitude signal is uniform from up and down domains except at the domain walls. The 180° phase contrast illustrates that the polarization is anti-parallel in the adjacent two domains. Most importantly, through ferroelectric switching from the ferroelectric ultrathin film, we realize ultrahigh current on/off ratio (I(on)/I(off)>10,000,000) of the FET. Such a tunnel device also inherently provides an opportunity to overcome the intrinsic limit of subthreshold swing (SS) for conventional metal-oxidesemiconductor FET (MOSFET). 4. In summary, we have fully realized the three objectives of the project. Particularly, 6 high-quality papers are published with acknowledgements of this project, including the papers in top-tier journals (2 papers in Advanced Materials with IF= 25.809, and 1 paper in ACS Nano with IF= 13.903). One postgraduate student has been under training during this period. The student CHAN Hung-Lit has published journal papers as the first author and successfully obtain his postgraduate degree under the support of the GRF grant. The PI was invited to write review articles because of our research impact in this field. To disseminate our results, the PI has given keynote/invited talks in several recognized international conferences held in China, India and Japan.

15303115.label: Major findings and research outcome
15303115.value: 1. We have proposed to design and construct VGTH using ultrathin ferroelectric film as a barrier. This idea has proven to be interesting. Compared to conventional VGTH, our proposed heterostructure using the functional tunnel barrier has offered new degrees of tunability and functionality via coupling between ferroelectricity and tunnel current, which not only results in much higher performance device, but also brings additional attractive features. With the unique ferroelectric switching resulting in large amplification of tunneling current, we have demonstrated a room-temperature current on/off ratio of above 10,000,000. Based on the ferroelectric polarization switching, our developed strategy in this project could be expanded to other advanced electronic and optoelectronic heterostructure devices. (see: Part C: Journal 1, 5, 6, Conference: 1,3,4). 2. We found that ferroelectric polarization and interface have played an important role in electronic transport properties in graphene heterostructure FETs. The co-existing effects of ferroelectric gating and interface charge trapping on the transport properties of graphene are observed in graphene structure. The underlying physical mechanism has been understood. During the entire process, the transport properties of graphene are found to be tuned by multiple factors, including ferroelectric polarization, non-volatility and charge trapping. (see: Part C: Journal 4, Conference 2,5,6). 3. Regarding vertical graphene tunnelling heterostructures with ultrathin films of various ferroelectric materials, we found that PLD is a very useful technique to make the designed 2D materials and devices. In our experiments for this project, PLD has proven to be a powerful tool not only in depositing a single layer of thin film, but also in in situ fabricating heterostructures via sequentially rotating different targets without breaking the vacuum. (see: Part C: Journal 2,3, Conference 2,7). 4. We achieved the novel vertical heterostructures employing monolayer graphene as a top electrode on the ultrathin ferroelectric barrier with Nb:STO semiconductor bottom electrode. The ferroelectric domains can be written by applying positive and negative DC voltages through a conductive tip on the BTO and BFO surface. The high current ON/OFF ratio of the structures can be achieved at room temperature. Regarding physical mechanism behind the observations, we found that our measured results can match the FN tunneling model well. This finding suggests that the mechanism of FN tunneling through a triangular potential barrier provides a realistic explanation for understanding our measured results. (see: Part C: Journal 1,5, Conference 5,7).

15303115.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15303115.value: We have realized vertical graphene tunneling heterostructures using ultrathin pulsed laser deposited ferroelectric film as a barrier. Moreover, the fabricated FETs with the complementary structures possess low subthreshold swing, wafer-scale barrier, non-volatile memory and tunable transport characteristics. The results demonstrate the employment of graphene as an electrode not only enhances the electroresistance effect of FTJs, but also opens the possibility to modulate the performance of the transistors through field-effect approaches. Therefore, it is expected that the new family of atomic-scale heterostructures in this study will provide a platform with more degrees of freedom to investigate the underlying mechanisms of tunnelling phenomena in the future studies. The results will be furthered developed to more nanoscale electronic and optoelectronic devices, including digital integrated devices, non-volatile memories, and phototransistors, and so on. On the other hand, we have successfully to use PLD for making graphene and ferroelectric oxide-based heterostructures and FETs, which has proved to be an alternative way to the most reported chemical vapor deposition (CVD) method for obtaining ultrathin 2D layered films because of its remarkable advantages. It is believed that PLD will play an important role in making various 2D based heterostructures for device applications in the future.

15303115.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15303115.value: The shrinking of the geometrical dimensions of current semiconductor devices has required the adoption of new materials and new device geometries. Graphene-based field effect transistor (GFET) has been among the breakthrough results of electronic devices at nanoscale. However, an obstacle to application for all types of developed planar GFETs is their quite low current on/off ratio, which is ascribed to the absence of an energy gap in graphene. Therefore, a low current on/off ratio makes the use in digital logic application unrealistic. A new conceptual GFET, namely vertical graphene heterostructure FET (VGHFET) completed in this project is attractive. We have developed a novel FET with the complementary heterostructure possessing the features of both ferroelectricity and conventional GFET. Taking advantage of the enhanced performance, the gate modulation ability of GFETs will become stronger, and the power consumption will become lower. Our work presents the possibility of creating various multifunctional nanoscale devices by engineering a ferroelectric tunnel layer with 2D layer building blocks. The strategy in this project could be further expanded to other systems, which will contribute to the development of nanoscale electronic and optoelectronic devices, including digital integrated devices, non-volatile memories, and phototransistors, and so on.

15303215.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15303215.value: 這份計劃主要研究帶有對數敏感的一類有名的趣化性模型的行波解的穩定性。 這個模型首先由Keller-Segel在1971年提出來描述在實驗中觀測到的細菌趣化性導致的行波傳播現象， 後來被Levine, Sleeman和 Nilson-Hamilton 用來描述早期腫瘤血管生成中表皮細胞和增長因子的互相作用。所以研究趣化性模型的行波的穩定性就有著非常重要的應用意義。 我們所研究的模型是一個強耦合的雙曲拋物系統。模型的特點就是有一個奇性。雖然這個奇性給數學研究帶來了非常大的困難， 但它是模型產生行波解的一個必要條件。同時由於模型的雙曲特徵，線性化方程的本質譜含有正特徵根，因此傳統的研究行波解穩定性的譜方法就不再方便使用。因為上述的困難，此類趣化性模型的行波解的穩定性一直都是公開問題。 我們的研究目標就是發展一些新穎的方法去克服上面提到的困難， 從而建立帶有對數敏感的趣化性模型的行波解的穩定性。我們的結果將是第一手的結果。 在我們的研究當中， 很精細的能量方法將會使用去克服雙曲性所帶來的困難，雙位勢权函數和合適的初值將會使用去克服奇性所帶來的困難。

15303215.label: Realisation of objectives
15303215.value: We have successfully achieved all objectives listed above. For Objective 1, we have established the stability of traveling wave solutions with large amplitudes to the singular Chemotaxis (i.e. Keller-Segel) model with large initial data (see research Output Item 1 and 2). For Objective 2, we have used the Cole-Hopf transformation to resolve the singularity of the Keller-Segel model and achieved various results like stability of traveling wave solutions (see Output Item 1 and Item 2), Global solvability (see Output Item 2 and Item 4), boundary-layer solutions (see Output Item 3 and 5). For Objective 3, we have developed some new ideas like weighted energy estimates to study the global existence and asymptotic behavior of solutions to the chemotaxis with density-suppressed motility (see Output Item 6). For Objective 4, we have introduced the biological background and potential applications of our research results in each of research outputs (i.e. publications).

15303215.label: Major findings and research outcome
15303215.value: In the research outcomes related to this project, we have three major findings. First we establish the stability of traveling wave solutions with large amplitudes to the singular Chemotaxis (i.e. Keller-Segel) model with large initial data. Second, we systematically studied the Cauchy problem of the singular Keller-Segel system in one-dimensional space and find the large-time behavior of its solutions. Thirdly, beyond the proposed objectives, we investigates the boundary layer solutions of the singular Keller-Segel model. Our research results have been published in many prestigious journals in the filed such as Journal of Differential Equations, SIAM J. Math. Anal., SIAM J. Appl. Math., Indiana University Mathematics Journal, and Kinetic and Related Models.

15303215.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15303215.value: In the project, we have started to explore the chemotaxis model with density-suppressed motility (see research output Item 6) and develop a new idea ``weighted energy estimate'' to resolve the degeneracy caused by the density-suppressed motility. In this project, we have gained the first-hand analytical results of the chemotaxis model with density-suppressed motility. Our new ideas and research results developed in this project will stimulate more research works for the chemotaxis model with more general density-dependent motility in the future.

15303215.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15303215.value: The propagation of traveling waves was the mostly prominent patterns observed in various experiments of chemotaxis. Hence the study of traveling waves of chemotaxis models including existence and stability will not only be of mathematical interest, but also be of importance in corroborating the understanding of the mechanisms underlying the experimental patterns. The results we obtained have partially solved the stability of traveling waves of the well-known singular Keller-Segel system in the case of linear consumption rate, which has remained as a long-standing question over many years. The effort made in this project will substantially contribute to the complete understanding of the stability of traveling waves of the singular Keller-Segel system. Our results have also revealed the roles of system parameters like chemotactic sensitivity and nutrient consumption rate in the formation of steady chemotactic wave propagation, which will be helpful to understand the modeling aspect of the Chemotaxis models.

15303415.label: Realisation of objectives
15303415.value: This is the final report of Project 1530341. In the research project period, the PI research team (FY Kwong) relocated from The Hong Kong Polytechnic University to The Chinese University of Hong Kong. The PI put extensive efforts in setting up the laboratory as well as purchasing equipment in the new location. PI chased the previously delayed progress in mid-2017 to 2018. Attempted study of highly active Pd catalyst generation was successful. With the newly developed palladium catalyst system, we were able to reach the parts per million level of catalyst for the cross-coupling of alkenes and heterocycles. This finding offered us rich potential to further establish a variety of catalytic system for other relevant cross-coupling reactions. This research contribution was published in Organic Letters in 2016, (Organic Letters 2016, 18, 5300-5303). In continuing screening of other electrophilic coupling component, we found that alkenyl tosylates were excellent partners in the mono-alkenylation reactions. This palladium catalyst system was published in early 2017 in Chemical Communications, (Chemical Communications, 2017, 53, 952-955). In addition to alkenyl tosylates, the even more inert aryl tosylates was found able to be activated by the new Pd(0) reaction system. The Pd-catalyzed alpha-arylation of oxindoles was found to proceed well. These represented the first examples of using aryl tosylates for this alpha-arylation process. This finding was published in mid-2017 in The Journal of Organic Chemistry, (Journal of Organic Chemistry, 2017, 82, 6468-6473). The PI team had also tackled the challenge of highly steric congested coupling reactions. The tetra-ortho-substituted biaryls (the highly steric hindered biaryls) were reached by palladium complexed with triarylphosphine ligands. It should be noted that by simply using the -PPh2 moiety (instead of expensive -PCy2 group), the coupling process proceeded even better. This interesting finding was published in 2018 in The Journal of Organic Chemistry, (Journal of Organic Chemistry, 2018, 83, 9008-9017). In continuing the research focusing on difficult (steric hindered) coupling reactions, the PI team also established a facile synthetic method for assembling carbazolyl-derived ligands. With rich supply of these easily accessible ligands, this team conducted a variety of screening of reaction parameters. The most steric congested aromatic C-N bond-forming reaction was realized. This practical finding was published in Organic Process Research & Development in early 2019, (Organic Process Research & Development, 2019, 23, 1602-1609). In addition to simple steric encumbered biaryls, there has been a challenge for targeting heterobiaryl frameworks. The PI team played extensive efforts in solving this problem using palladium catalysis, yet only moderate results were obtained. Fortunately, the team found a complementary pathway for accessing steric hindered heterobiaryls. In the presence of inexpensive ZnI2 catalyst, the steric congested frameworks, in which they have heterocyclic moiety, were synthesized in good-to-excellent yield under ambient conditions. This regioselective cascade process was published in Chemical Communications in 2019, (Communications, 2019, Just Accepted, DOI: 10.1039/c9cc07054k). The PI team put extensive effort to prepare the mono-phosphine with axial chirality. This team reported the new carbazolyl-derived P,N type ligand composing pi-extended features. Initial results found that these ligand allowed to promote the steric hindered amination process under palladium catalysis. With this ground work, the team continued to resolve this ligand type featuring pi-extended wall, using diasteromeric pathway. Yet, by installing a different commonly available chiral auxillaries to this ligand scaffold, the team found the d.r. selectivity not higher than 60%. Further recrystallization did not afford enantiomerically pure mono-phosphine ligands. Excluded the chiral ligand synthesis part, the former steric hindered C-N bond coupling results were published in Synthesis in early 2019, (Synthesis 2019, 51, 2678-2686).

15303415.label: Major findings and research outcome
15303415.value: The aim of this research project is to explore highly active palladium catalysts fit for cross-coupling reactions. With the new ligand design and synthesis, the Project team had been able to investigate the highly challenging steric hindered cross-coupling processes. In the proposed study, the team developed the exceedingly reactive catalyst, which allowed the alkenylation (coupling between alkenes and heterocycles), under parts per million low level of catalyst loading. Moreover, this related system was shown to be applicable to other difficult coupling reactions. The team also established a new and facile method for accessing a variety of carbazolyl-derived phosphine ligand, with high efficiency.

15303415.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15303415.value: This proposed study has high potential for further development. Fine-tuning of the catalyst structure, especially fit for specific window of particular cross-coupling, is the necessity action. This direction of research is highly significant in the genuine pharmaceutical or material synthesis as chemists prefer to have a chemical reaction occurring in a specific site, yet other irrelevant functional groups remain intact.

15303415.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15303415.value: This project is to fundamentally investigate and develop highly efficient catalysts for versatile chemical bond-forming processes. With this catalyst establishment, the assembling of molecule (naturally or unnaturally) will become easy. Particularly enjoying the ability of catalyst, the molecule manufacturing process will become atom- and step-economical, and thus reaching the ultimate goad of green and sustainable environment.
