16101515.label: Major findings and research outcome
16101515.value: In our laboratory, we have been focusing on the development of efficient expression systems for the production of useful/valuable heterologous proteins. Recently, we have employed inteins, also known as protein introns, to engineer intein-mediated protein expression systems using E. coli and B. subtilis as hosts. In 2013, making use of an intein, VMA, for the first time, we demonstrated co-expression of authentic EGF and bFGF in E. coli. In this project, we further explored the feasibility of employing other inteins to facilitate co-expression of two widely different proteins: EGF and endoglucanase. The positive results supported our postulation that existing inteins might be genetically engineered for efficient expression of various heterologous proteins in E. coli (Part C Research Output No.1). Furthermore, the resulting EGF was shown to be fully bioactive and effective in treating wounds like scalds as reported in our publication (Part C Research Output No. 2). Despite the availability of many reports on the employment of various inteins for heterologous protein expression in E. coli, unfortunately, the target proteins were expressed as insoluble aggregates and isoforms possessing unauthentic primary structures. However, in our work, all of the recombinant proteins mediated by intein expression are soluble and authentic in structure; more importantly, they are biologically active. To emphasize the importance of an authentic structure to the function of a recombinant protein, a review article elaborating the differences in bioactivity, stability and performance in wound healing between authentic EGF and its isoforms was recently published by our group (Part C Research Output No.4). Although not much is known regarding how inteins may operate in B. subtilis, our results of protein fusions engineered among a cellulose binding domain (CellBD), intein DnaB, and bFGF clearly demonstrated the feasibility of intein-mediated protein expression in B. subtilis, employing expression of authentic bFGF as an example (Part C Research Output No.5). More importantly, applying a genetic optimization method, and a refined fed-batch fermentation protocol, we were successful in expressing a high level of 610 mg/L of authentic bFGF (Part C Research Output No. 3). A purification protocol was then developed to efficiently purify authentic bFGF from both the culture supernatant and cell lysate (Part C Research Output No. 6). As a result of our involvement in various approaches for protein expression in E. coli, very recently, we have been invited to contribute a book chapter on recombinant protein expression (Part C Research Output No. 7)

16101515.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16101515.value: In this project, we have developed various intein-mediated expression systems in both E. coli and B. subtilis for heterologous protein expression. Employing the inteins in combination with other genetic regulatory elements, the target proteins may be efficiently expressed as a soluble, authentic and biologically potent product. The mentioned properties are all important characters for a recombinant protein to possess if it is desired to be developed for commercial application(s). To further develop intein-mediated expression for the production of recombinant proteins, e.g., bFGF and EGF, for commercial applications, the feasibility of their production on a large scale such as a pilot scale needs to be studied. On the other hand, our findings support that B. subtilis is also feasible to be developed for intein-mediated protein expression. Being generally recognized as safe (GRAS), if intein-mediated protein expression proves to be a practical approach for general application in B. subtilis, this bacterium may be applied as a valuable host for the expression of medically important or food related proteins. Thus, much more research should be undertaken to help evaluate whether B. subtilis in conjunction with intein-protein expression may work well to formulate a general system for efficient production of useful/valuable proteins.

16101515.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16101515.value: Since the advent of recombinant DNA technology in the 1970s, different approaches have been developed to express recombinant proteins. Major difficulties in recombinant protein expression include low yields, formation of insoluble aggregates, and attainment of isoforms that are structurally different from the target proteins. Our recent success in exploiting inteins (protein introns) to mediate co-expression of EGF and bFGF as authentic and bioactive products in E. coli has revolutionized the process of recombinant protein expression. The resulting proteins are not only expressed as soluble proteins in the cytoplasm, but also auto-catalytically processed to achieve their authentic structures, thus leading to also bioactive products. Taking advantage of our novel findings and genetic optimization, we achieved dramatic enhancement of bFGF production and the development of an efficient protocol for its purification. Although the presence of inteins has not been confirmed in B. subtilis, we have been successful in extending the application of inteins to protein expression in B. subtilis. With more research conducted along the same direction, B. subtilis, being regarded as GRAS, may prove to be useful as a general system for efficient expression of useful/valuable proteins, including those may contribute as active ingredients in medically and food related products.

16101615.label: Realisation of objectives
16101615.value: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) are devastating neurological diseases. Abnormal expansion of a hexanucleotide repeat, (GGGGCC)n, is the most common genetic cause of familial and sporadic forms of ALS and FTD. This nucleotide repeat element is located in a non-protein-coding region of the C9orf72 gene. Previous studies suggested that the C9orf72 hexanucleotide repeat expansion (HRE), either as DNA or the transcribed RNA, can fold into G-quadruplexes with distinct structures. These structural polymorphisms lead to C9orf72 HRE-containing abortive transcripts, which may aggregate and form RNA foci in patient cells. Despite the critical connection of C9orf72 HRE G-quadruplexes to the pathogenic mechanism of C9orf72 HRE-linked ALS/FTD, the molecular basis of G-quadruplex formation by C9orf72 HRE remains elusive. In this project, we listed three objectives. For objective 1, we performed systematic biochemical and structural characterizations for C9orf72 HRE G-quadruplexes. First, we determined the topology of G-quadruplex DNA d(GGGGCC)4, using the nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) approach. It forms a chair-type G-quadruplex with a four-layer antiparallel G-tetra core and three edgewise loops, which is distinct from known structures of chair-type G-quadruplexes. The hydrogen-bond directionalities of the four G-tetrads are clockwise, anti-clockwise, clockwise and anti-clockwise, respectively. The glycosidic conformations of guanines around the tetrads are syn•anti•syn•anti. The G-tetrad core is the antiparallel-type, in which each G-tetrad is oriented in opposite direction with respect to its neighboring ones. This work was published in Scientific Reports 5:16673 (2015). We further showed that the two-repeat G4C2 DNA, d(G4C2)2, simultaneously formed parallel and antiparallel G-quadruplex conformations in the potassium solution. We separated different folds of d(G4C2)2 by anion exchange chromatography, followed with characterizations by circular dichroism and nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy. The parallel d(G4C2)2 G-quadruplex folded as a symmetric tetramer, while the antiparallel d(G4C2)2 adopted the topology of an asymmetric dimer. These folds are distinct from the antiparallel chair-type conformation we previously identified for the d(G4C2)4 G-quadruplex. This work was published in Scientific Reports 8:2366 (2018). We also determined the first crystal structure of an eight-layer parallel tetrameric G-quadruplex formed by two repeats of C9orf72 HRE DNA, d(G4C2)2, in Ba2+ and K+ solution respectively. Two d(G4C2)2 oligonucleotides form a parallel propeller-type dimeric G-quadruplex which stacks in 5'-to-5' arrangement making up a tetramer. Intriguingly, two kinds of 5'-to-5' orientation, Form I and Form II, were observed in the Ba2+/K+ crystal G-quadruplex structure. One of the dimeric G-quadruplex in Form I rotates 90℃ compared with the corresponding dimeric one in Form II. Each dimeric G-quadruplex is composed of four G-tetrads connected by two CC double-chain-reversal loops. The two cytosine bases located at 3' end of each stand protrude out or fold back with or without formation of C·C+•C·C/C·C+•C·C+ quadruple base pair which stacks on the neighbouring dimeric block. The hydrogen-bond directionalities of the four G-tetrads in each dimeric block are clockwise with all Hoogsteen N1-O6 and N2-N7 hydrogen bonds intact. The glycosidic conformations of guanines in each dimeric G-quadruplex are anti. All guanine bases in the quartets are approximately coplanar. This manuscript will be submitted soon. For objective 2, based on the successful experience on C9orf72 HRE DNA structure determination, we investigated C9orf72 HRE RNA in a similar way. Based on our previous work, we first focused on r(G4C2)G4 for further structure determination. After we collected all NMR spectra data, we found it difficult to assign the peaks, probably due to its inhomogeneity. After spending great efforts and time to collect NMR spectra, assign the peaks and connect the NOEs, we still could not make clear assignments because this sample likely have multiple conformations. Then we started to search for other RNA sequences suitable for structure determination. The native PAGE result showed that r(G4C2)2 and r(G4C2)4 have only one band, indicating the relatively homogeneous conformation. The imino region of 1D 1H spectrum of r(G4C2)2 showed 6 main peaks, indicating the symmetric conformation. The imino region of 1D 1H spectrum of r(G4C2)4 only showed a broaden peak, indicating multiple conformations. Therefore, we focused on r(G4C2)2 for further study. We performed NMR and X-ray crystallography experiments with this optimized RNA sample. The assignments and structure determination are in progress. And we also obtained high-resolution diffraction data with optimized crystals. The structure determination work is still on progress. For objective 3, the NMR titration experiments demonstrated that the RNA-binding domains RBD1-2 and RBD3-4 in NCL specifically bound to the C9orf72 HRE G-quadruplex DNA and RNA. Since previous report demonstrated that NCL preferentially interacted with C9orf72 HRE G-quadruplex RNA, we focused on the interaction between NCL RBD1-2 and C9orf72 HRE RNA in the study. Through NMR titration experiments, we found that RBD1 or RBD2 alone didn’t bind r(G4C2)2 efficiently, while RBD1-2 strongly interacted with r(G4C2)2. This binding mode may be comparable with the reported interaction between NCL RBD1-2 and a pre-rRNA. In that complex structure, the two RBDs of NCL bind on opposite sides of the pre-rRNA stem-loop and form a molecular clamp which stabilizes the loop conformation. Then we tried different approaches to obtain the complex structure. We collected NMR spectra and obtained the backbone assignment of RBD1-2. We also collected the intermolecular NOE spectra between r(G4C2)2 and RBD1-2, and obtained some binding interface information. We can get the final complex structure once the r(G4C2)2 structure is determined. Meanwhile, we also tried very hard to perform the crystallization of this nucleoprotein complex. Till now, we are still optimizing the crystallization conditions. The outcome of the proposed research will not only provide insight into the molecular mechanism underlying the C9orf72 HRE G-quadruplex formation in the etiology of ALS/FTD, but may also lay the necessary basis for designing small molecules that therapeutically target C9orf72 HRE G-quadruplexes for the modulation of ALS/FTD pathogenesis. Supported by this grant, we published 2 papers and presented our results in four conferences. We collaborated with several groups on the G-quadruplex project. Under the support of this project, one student got Ph.D. degree.

16101615.label: Major findings and research outcome
16101615.value: In this project, we performed systematic biochemical and structural characterizations for C9orf72 HRE G-quadruplexes. First, we determined the topology of G-quadruplex DNA d(GGGGCC)4, using the nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) approach. It forms a chair-type G-quadruplex with a four-layer antiparallel G-tetra core and three edgewise loops, which is distinct from known structures of chair-type G-quadruplexes. The hydrogen-bond directionalities of the four G-tetrads are clockwise, anti-clockwise, clockwise and anti-clockwise, respectively. The glycosidic conformations of guanines around the tetrads are syn•anti•syn•anti. The G-tetrad core is the antiparallel-type, in which each G-tetrad is oriented in opposite direction with respect to its neighboring ones. This work was published in Scientific Reports 5:16673 (2015). We further showed that the two-repeat G4C2 DNA, d(G4C2)2, simultaneously formed parallel and antiparallel G-quadruplex conformations in the potassium solution. We separated different folds of d(G4C2)2 by anion exchange chromatography, followed with characterizations by circular dichroism and nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy. The parallel d(G4C2)2 G-quadruplex folded as a symmetric tetramer, while the antiparallel d(G4C2)2 adopted the topology of an asymmetric dimer. These folds are distinct from the antiparallel chair-type conformation we previously identified for the d(G4C2)4 G-quadruplex. This work was published in Scientific Reports 8:2366 (2018). We also determined the first crystal structure of an eight-layer parallel tetrameric G-quadruplex formed by two repeats of C9orf72 HRE DNA, d(G4C2)2, in Ba2+ and K+ solution respectively. Two d(G4C2)2 oligonucleotides form a parallel propeller-type dimeric G-quadruplex which stacks in 5'-to-5' arrangement making up a tetramer. Intriguingly, two kinds of 5'-to-5' orientation, Form I and Form II, were observed in the Ba2+/K+ crystal G-quadruplex structure. One of the dimeric G-quadruplex in Form I rotates 90℃ compared with the corresponding dimeric one in Form II. Each dimeric G-quadruplex is composed of four G-tetrads connected by two CC double-chain-reversal loops. The two cytosine bases located at 3' end of each stand protrude out or fold back with or without formation of C·C+•C·C/C·C+•C·C+ quadruple base pair which stacks on the neighbouring dimeric block. The hydrogen-bond directionalities of the four G-tetrads in each dimeric block are clockwise with all Hoogsteen N1-O6 and N2-N7 hydrogen bonds intact. The glycosidic conformations of guanines in each dimeric G-quadruplex are anti. All guanine bases in the quartets are approximately coplanar. This manuscript will be submitted soon.

16101615.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16101615.value: The formation of G-quadruplexes in the non-coding region of C9orf72 within the expanded d(G4C2) repeats has been proposed as a cause of genetic instability, which is the most common genetic cause of ALS and FTD, and lead to aberrant gene transcription resulting in the development of ALS and FTD. It has been demonstrated that d(G4C2) repeats form G-quadruplex structures in vitro and the structural polymorphism within expanded GGGGCC repeat, including G-quadruplex structures at both DNA and RNA level, is implicated in the development of ALS and FTD. Atomic details of the C9orf72 HRE DNA structure discovered in our work shed light on the structural diversity of G-quadruplexes adopted by d(G4C2) repeats and allow us to design small molecules to modulate aberrant transcription of C9orf72 gene related with ALS and FTD in particular by in silico drug screening studies.

16101615.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16101615.value: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) are devastating neurological diseases. The etiology of these diseases remains unclear which hampers effective therapeutic interventions. Recently, large expansions of a GGGGCC hexanucleotide repeat in the first intron of the C9orf72 gene have been demonstrated to cause ALS and FTD. The structural conformations of both the DNA and RNA hexanucleotide repeat expansion (HRE) were suggested as fundamental determinants of the pathogenic mechanisms of C9orf72 HRE-linked ALS/FTD. Various small molecules have been used to target the G-quadruplex-forming sequences, to either enhance or perturb structure formation to modulate the maintenance of telomere lengths or gene activity. Similarly, as multimerization of C9orf72 HRE G-quadruplexes may exacerbate the formation of RNA foci and cause neuron-toxicity in ALS-FTD, disruption of these foci by targeting C9orf72 HRE G-quadruplexes may have beneficial outcomes in the treatment of these diseases. The detailed structural information of C9orf72 HRE DNA/RNA G-quadruplexes in this project will not only provide insight into the disease mechanism of C9orf72 HRE-caused ALS/FTD, but may also build the basis for designing small molecules which can therapeutically target C9orf72 HRE to modulate ALS/FTD pathogenesis.

16102415.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16102415.value: ANO1 (TMEM16) 蛋白已知為鈣激活氯離子通道蛋白,其在調節感知信號轉導、上皮細胞分泌、平滑肌蠕動和細胞增殖/遷移等生理過程中均發揮重要作用。在許多生理及病理狀況下尤其是多種癌癥細胞中，ANO1的蛋白及mRNA水平均有改變；然而，在這類狀況下調節ANO1改變的分子機制仍屬未知。泛素化系統可調節諸多離子通道的蛋白水平，對於通道蛋白自細胞膜表面回收過程尤為重要。然而，目前尚無對於泛素化系統與ANO1的關系的研究報導。 最近，我們發現E3泛素連接酶TRIM23可與ANO1相互作用並且將後者泛素化。更為重要的是，在HEK293T細胞系中共表達野生型TRIM23可以顯著降低ANO1在全細胞以及細胞膜上的蛋白水平，而共表達TRIM23缺乏泛素連接酶活性的突變體則無此效果。作為對照，在呼吸道上皮癌細胞系A549中幹擾內源TRIM23的表達可顯著增升內源ANO1的蛋白水平。基於這些發現，我們作出如下假設，即E3泛素連接酶TRIM23可直接泛素化ANO1並由此導致ANO1在全細胞水平及細胞膜上蛋白量的下調。另外，ANO1的mRNA及蛋白水平在乳腺癌細胞中均有上調，而ANO1的表達量與乳腺癌病理分級呈正相關；較高ANO1表達量亦會導致較差的預後。有趣的是，我們對有關於TRIM23的已發表數據的分析表明，與ANO1相反，TRIM23在許多腫瘤細胞中均下調，而TRIM23的mRNA的缺失亦與乳腺癌的較差預後正相關。基於TRIM23與ANO1在表達以及乳腺癌患者預後方面的強烈負相關關系，我們假設幹擾TRIM23通過泛素化途徑降低ANO1蛋白水平這一過程將會加速乳腺癌的腫瘤生成。我們的具體目標包括：（1）驗證TRIM23與ANO1的相互作用及TRIM23是否泛素化ANO1；（2）探討泛素連接酶TRIM23是否以及如何通過泛素化途徑調節ANO1的表達量；（3）分析在乳腺癌細胞中，TRIM23能否通過泛素化調控降解ANO1並阻抑乳腺癌的腫瘤生成。 在此研究中，我們將會分析ANO1是否通過泛素連接酶TRIM23介導的泛素化途徑降解，以及ANO1-TRIM23關系軸是否對於乳腺癌的腫瘤生成有重要意義。我們的發現將有助於說明TRIM23作為抑癌基因如何發揮功能，並由此打開尋找乳腺癌藥物靶標的新途徑。

16102415.label: Realisation of objectives
16102415.value: Note: all figures mentioned below is in the PDF file “ figures in the report” in the conference paper category. 1. To test whether TRIM23 interacts with and directly ubiquitinates ANO1. To examine the interaction of endogenous TRIM23 and ANO1 and map the binding sites. During this report period, we found that endogenous ANO1 and TRIM23 co-IPed in ZR-75-1 cells, suggesting the physical interaction of endogenous TRIM23 and ANO1 (Fig. 1D). To map ANO1 binding region in TRIM23, the GST-pull down assay was performed. The ARF+ domain (aa 402-574) appeared to be necessary and sufficient for interacting with ANO1 whereas the RING and B-box/B-box/coiled-coil domains are not involved in ANO1 binding (Fig. 1E). All the data on physical interaction of ANO1 and TRIM23 are summarized in Fig. 1 for preparing a manuscript. To test whether TRIM23 directly ubiquitinates ANO1 in in-vitro assays. We assembled an in vitro ubiquitination system that contained the E1 ubiquitin-activating enzyme (Uba1), the E2 ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme (UbcH5c), ATP, ubiquitin, and the protein substrate ANO1. The addition of TRIM23 but TRIM23RING led to ANO1 ubiquitination (Fig. 3C). These results clearly demonstrated that TRIM23 directly ubiquitinates ANO1 through its RING domain. To test whether TRIM23 ubiquitinates ANO1 in the cell and in vivo. Expressing TRIM23-HA but not TRIM23RING-HA considerably elevated both the ubiquitination and the expression of exogenous ANO1-V5 protein in HEK293T cells (Fig. 3A). These data suggest that TRIM23 ubiquitinates ANO1 through its RING E3 ligase and stabilizes ANO1 protein expression. Supporting this notion, TRIM23 knockout drastically lowered endogenous ANO1 ubiquitination in ZR-75-1 cells (Fig. 3B). To identify the ubiquitin-conjugation sites in other parts of ANO1. We mutated all 6 lysine residues in ANO1 C-terminus to arginine and examine their effect on TRIM23-mediated ubiquitination. K221R mutant ANO1 did not express, presumably because the mutation disrupted gross structure of ANO1 and destabilized it. Among the other five mutants, we found that K996R abolished TRIM23-induced ubiquitination. These data suggest that K966R is the major, if not the only, TRIM23-mediated ubiquitin-conjugation site in ANO1. These data are being finalized for publication. 2. To examine whether and how TRIM23 E3 ligase-dependent ubiquitination modulates ANO1 protein expression. To examine whether TRIM23 reduces ANO1 protein levels in cells. HA-TRIM23 expression dramatically increased endogenous ANO1 protein level by 1.5 fold (Fig. 2A); by contrast, expressing HA-TRIM23RING had little effect (Fig. 1A). Notably, HA-TRIM23RING and ANO1 still physically interacted (Fig. 1C-E). Taken together, these observations suggest that the E3 ligase activity of TRIM23 stabilized ANO1 protein. Previous studies from other laboratories showed that ubiquitination could have non-proteolytic functions including stabilizing protein expression, in addition to its widely-studied proteolytic effect (Hirano et al., 2013). To further examine the stabilizing effect of endogenous TRIM23 on ANO1, TRIM23 in ZR-75-1 cells was knocked down using RNA interference techniques. TRIM23 knockdown halved ANO1 protein expression (Fig. 2B). To more rigorously demonstrate TRIM23’s anti-proteolytic effect on ANO1 and facilitate subsequent investigation of the underlying mechanism, we generated a TRIM23 knockout ZR-75-1 cell line by using CRISPR/Cas9 techniques (Fig. 2C). Homozygous TRIM23 knockout (KO) ZR-75-1 cells exhibited undetectable TRIM23 expression as intended, and featured remarkably down-regulated global and cell-surface ANO1 level (Fig. 2D). In addition, the RT-PCR result indicated no significant change in ANO1 mRNA level in TRIM23 KO cells (Fig. 2D), implying a post-transcriptional regulation of ANO1 by TRIM23. Taken together, the results in Fig. 2 suggest that TRIM23 stabilizes global and cell-surface ANO1 through its RING domain. To examine whether TRIM23 exerts an anti-proteolytic effect on ANO1 in vivo, Trim23 gene in the mouse was knocked out using CRISPR/Cas9 techniques (Fig. 4A). No off-target mutation was detected in several top-scored non-coding and coding regions that are potentially targeted by the single guide RNA (sgRNA) of TRIM23 (Supplementary table 1). Previous studies suggest that ANO1 is expressed in the dorsal root ganglia (DRG), the salivary gland, and the lung. ANO1 protein level was halved in the DRG and salivary gland and reduced by 20% in the lung tissue in TRIM23 KO mice (Fig. 4C), suggesting that TRIM23 stabilizes ANO1 in vivo. By contrast, TRPV1 channel expression in the DRG had no change in TRIM23 KO mice (not shown), indicating a specific effect of TRIM23 on ANO1 channel. Similar to the results in TRIM23 KO ZR-35-1 cells (Fig. 2D), ANO1 mRNA has no change in TRIM23 KO tissues (Fig. 4D), suggesting that TRIM23 stabilizes ANO1 protein at the posttranscriptional level in vivo. To investigate the underlying mechanism of TRIM23-mediated ANO1 degradation. We used the cycloheximide (CHX) chase assay, in which protein synthesis is blocked by CHX treatment. Knocking out TRIM23 substantially accelerated endogenous ANO1 degradation (Fig. 2E). The degradation of endogenous ANO1 in the absence of TRIM23 seemed to be mainly through a lysosomal pathway, as expected for degradation of most ubiquitinated membrane proteins, because lysosomal but not proteasomal inhibitors significantly elevated ANO1 expression in TRIM23 KO cells (Fig. 2F). In the presence of TRIM23 in WT cells, the lysosomal inhibitors had little effect (Fig. 2F), agreeing with the notion that TRIM23 suppresses the lysosomal degradation of ANO1 and thereby stabilizes ANO1. 3. To assess whether TRIM23 suppresses tumorigenesis of breast cancer through ubiqui-tin-dependent degradation of ANO1. We tested the effect of TRIM23 on cell proliferation. Knocking out TRIM23 significantly increased the proliferation of ZR-75-1 cells in MTT assays. In addition, this increase was sensitive to the ANO1 channel blocker TMEM16A-inh01. These data is consistent with the notion that TRIM23 suppresses tumorigenesis of breast cancer through ANO1 (not shown). Moreover, we look at other functional impact of TRIM23-KO-induced ANO1 reduction. Knocking out TRIM23 suppressed the total licking time by 1.5 fold in the capsaicin-induced pain sensation assay, suggesting that reduced ANO1 in the DRG neurons of TRIM23 knock mice is required for the chemical (TRPV1)-induced pain sensation (Fig. 4E); this pain-sensation reduction is not due to any change in the expression TRPV1 (Supplementary Fig. 2), the receptor of capsaicin (Takayama et al., 2015). By contrast, TRIM23 KO mice showed little difference in von Frey filament experiments, which tests mechanical-pain sensation that does not involve ANO1 (Fig. 4F). Interestingly, knocking out TRIM23 also increased the heart rate by approximately 20% (Fig. 4G). Knocking out TRIM23 also decreased ANO1 protein level in the heart (not shown, a few more experiments are being carried out). One explanation is that ANO1 hyperpolarizes cardiomyocytes. If so, lowering ANO1 would depolarizes cardiomyocytes and accelerates the heart rate. In addition, we looked at whether TRIM23 links ANO1 regulation by EGF and other physiological modulators. A previous study suggests that chronic epidermal growth factor (EGF) treatment of epithelial T84 cells upregulates ANO1 protein and mRNA levels (Mroz and Keely). However, the underlying molecular mechanism of EFG regulation of ANO1 was not explored in the previous study (Mroz and Keely). Our results suggest that EGF regulates ANO1 protein expression exclusively through TRIM23 in ZR-75-1 cells. EGF signalling, including EGF secretion and EGF receptor (EGFR) expression, are under tight regulation of a wide array of signalling molecules, including estrogen/androgen, growth hormone, and calcitriol/parathyroid hormone. Therefore, our findings on the EGF-TRIM23 signalling axis indicate that TRIM23 might play an important role in ANO1 regulation by many physiological modulators.

16102415.label: Major findings and research outcome
16102415.value: Summary of Major Findings: By using the yeast-two hybrid assay and examining published interactome data, we identified TRIM23 and TRIM21, as binding partners of ANO1, respectively. The physical interaction of TRIM23 or TRIM21 with ANO1, specifically the carboxyl terminus of ANO1, was further confirmed through GST-pull down and co-immunoprecipitation assays. Surprisingly, both the protein expression and the ubiquitination of endogenous ANO1 in breast cancer ZR-75-1 cells was markedly elevated by overexpressing TRIM23 or decreased by knocking down or knocking out TRIM23, suggesting that TRIM23-induced ubiquitination stabilizes rather than degrades ANO1. More importantly, knocking out TRIM23 in the mouse decreased ANO1 protein expression without any effect on ANO1 transcripts in various tissues including the dorsal root ganglia (DRG) neurons and the salivary gland. Consistent with ANO1’s role in pain sensation and ANO1 protein reduction in DRG neurons, TRIM23 knockout mice displayed reduced pain sensation in capsaicin-evoked pain licking assays. Moreover, TRIM23 is required for EGF (epidermal growth factor)-induced increase in ANO1 protein expression. In contrast, ANO1 protein expression was reduced by overexpressing TRIM21 or increased by knocking down TRIM21 in ZR-75-1 cells. Significantly, knocking out TRIM21 in the mouse robustly increased ANO1 protein expression in the salivary gland and the heart. Our study revealed that the two antagonizing E3 ligases work together to control ANO1 channel homeostasis under physiological conditions. 16102415.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16102415.value: ANO1 (TMEM16A) is a physiologically and clinically important chloride channel. However, how ANO1 protein level is altered under distinct physiological and pathological conditions (such as cancer) remain unclear. By using the yeast-two hybrid assay and examining published interactome data, we identified two E3 ligases TRIM23 and TRIM21, as binding partners of ANO1, respectively. The physical interaction of TRIM23 or TRIM21 with ANO1 was further confirmed through GST-pull down and co-immunoprecipitation assays. Surprisingly, both the protein expression and the ubiquitination of endogenous ANO1 in breast cancer ZR-75-1 cells and in mice was markedly elevated by overexpressing TRIM23 or decreased by knocking down or knocking out TRIM23, suggesting that TRIM23-induced ubiquitination stabilizes rather than degrades ANO1. Consistent with ANO1’s role in pain sensation and ANO1 protein reduction in DRG neurons, TRIM23 knockout mice displayed reduced pain sensation in capsaicin-evoked pain licking assays. Moreover, TRIM23 is required for EGF (epidermal growth factor)-induced increase in ANO1 protein expression. In contrast, ANO1 protein expression was reduced by overexpressing TRIM21 or increased by knocking down or knocking out TRIM21 in ZR-75-1 cells or in mice. 16102615.label: Realisation of objectives
16102615.value: 1. Determine whether deletion of p110α of PI3K in MuSCs completely blocks or just delays injury-induced muscle regeneration. To address this question, we first generated a tamoxifen-inducible and MuSC-specific p110α knockout mouse line. When mice were at or older than 8-week-old, tamoxifen was injected to induce p110α deletion. One month after tamoxifen-induced gene deletion, we injured the tibialis anterior (TA) muscles of the control and p110α-null mice with cardiotoxin CTX) and examined muscle satellite cell (MuSC)-mediated muscle regeneration at day 5, 14 and 30 after the CTX injury. In control mice, the injured TA muscles were largely repaired by 14 days post injury (dpi). In contrast, no regenerated muscles were found in mutant mice at 14 dpi. Even, at 30 dpi, there was still no sign of muscle regeneration. Thus, we concluded that loss of p110α completely blocked injury-induced muscle regeneration. This objective was fully achieved. 2. Characterize the role of p110α in MuSC quiescence establishment during normal development and quiescence re-entry after injury. To address the role of p110α in MuSC quiescence establishment, we started to induce p110α deletion by tamoxifen in P10 mice. When mice were 8-week-old or older, we examined the number of Ki67-/Pax7+ (i.e., quiescent) MuSCs. We found that there was an obvious reduction in the number of quiescent MuSCs in p110α-null mice. This indicates that p110α plays a role in quiescence establishment. As p110α-null MuSCs could not exit quiescence upon injury, to study whether PI3K plays a role in quiescence re-entry, we induced p110α deletion by tamoxifen injection starting at two days after injury for five consecutive days. One month after the last tamoxifen injection, we examined the number of Pax7+/Ki67- MuSCs. We found that the number of quiescent MuSCs decreased in p110a-null SCs. This suggests that p110α of PI3K is required for both establishment of the quiescent SC pool during normal development and for quiescence re-entry after injury-induced regeneration. 3. Characterize the role of p110α in MuSC long-term maintenance and/or survival in adult mice. To address this question, we deleted p110α in adult mice and waited for 1, 2, 3, 6, and 12 months. We then examined the number of quiescent MuSCs at these different time points. We found that loss of p110α did not affect the long-term maintenance or survival of adult MuSCs. 4. Examine whether the deletion of p110α in QSCs affects their activation. To address this question, we first isolated MuSCs by a fluorescence-activated cell sorter (FACS) and grown them in culture in the presence of EdU. For control MuSCs, in 48 hours, more than 80% of them became EdU+, in contrast, EdU+ MuSCs were barely detectable. We also confirmed this result in vivo. Using the Pax7-CreER:Rosa26-stop-YFP strain, we first labeled quiescent MuSCs with YFP by tamoxifen injection followed by cardiotoxin (CTX)-induced muscle injury. Two and a half days after the CTX injury, we examined YFP+ SCs. While the number of YFP+ SCs nearly tripled, only a few YFP+ cells were found in mutant mice. We also examined the size of SCs, MyoD protein expression by immunostaining, and new RNA synthesis by pyronin Y and Hoechst 33342 double staining. We found that p110α-null SCs were smaller than freshly-isolated control SCs and had little new RNA synthesis. In addition, mutant SCs did not express MyoD. Our data showed that loss of p110α prevented SCs from quiescence exit. 5. Examine whether mTOR is a key signal transducer downstream of p110α in MuSCs. To address this issue, we generated an inducible Pax7-CreER:p110αf/f:Tsc1f/f:Rosa26-stop-YFP double knockout strain (dKO). As Tsc1 is a known repressor of mTORC1, deletion of Tsc1 is known to result in constitutive activation of mTORC1. When we isolated quiescent MuSCs from p110α-null (also called conditional knockout of cKO) and p110α/Tsc1 dKO mice and grew them in culture for 48 hours in the presence of EdU, SCs from cKO mice barely incorporated EdU as expected. In contrast, 50-60% of SCs from dKO mice became EdU+. As FoxOs are also signal transducers downstream of PI3K, we also examined whether knockdown of FoxOs in p110α-null SCs rescued defects in quiescence exit and cell cycle re-entry. Our results showed this is indeed the case. Thus, our data demonstrated that both mTORC1 and FoxOs are signal transducers downstream of p110α in regulating quiescence exit in MuSCs. 6. Mechanistic study to understand the role of p110α PI3K in MuSCs. We also searched for key downstream targets of PI3K in MuSCs by comparing transcriptomes of freshly-isolated control SCs and p110α-null SCs using RNA-seq. We found that members of AP1 (e.g., Jun, Fos, JunB, etc) and several other immediate-early genes were downregulated in p110α-null SCs. We asked whether re-expression of some of these genes in p110α-null SCs could rescue the defects in quiescence exit. We isolated p110α-null SCs by FACS and infected them with control lentivirus, Jun-expressing lentivirus, or Fos-expressing lentivirus. Only Jun-expressing lentivirus partially (~40%) rescued the defects in quiescence exit and cell cycle re-entry.

16102615.label: Major findings and research outcome
16102615.value: Adult mouse muscle satellite cells (MuSCs) are quiescent in uninjured muscles. Upon injury, MuSCs undergo quiescence exit, re-enter the cell cycle to proliferate, then differentiate to repair the damaged muscles. It remains unclear which extrinsic signal activates the quiescent MuSCs upon injury and which intrinsic signaling pathway regulates quiescence exit during MuSC activation. Here, we demonstrated that inducible MuSC-specific deletion of p110α, a catalytic subunit of phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K), rendered MuSCs unable to exit quiescence, resulting in severely-impaired MuSC proliferation and muscle regeneration. Genetic reactivation of mTORC1, overexpression of Jun, or knockdown of FoxOs in p110α-null MuSCs partially rescued the above defects, making them key effectors downstream of PI3K in regulating quiescence exit. Moreover, constitutive activation of PI3K in quiescent MuSCs induced spontaneous quiescence exit in uninjured muscles leading to their gradual depletion. Thus, PI3K is both necessary and sufficient for MuSCs to exit quiescence in response to activating signals. This work was published in EMBO J last year along with a featured “News and Views” by Frederic Relaix and Leo Machado.

16102615.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16102615.value: Although it is well established that adult MuSC will exit quiescence and re-enter the cell cycle upon muscle injury, it remains a mystery how quiescent MuSCs exit quiescence. Using genetic approach, we demonstrated that the PI3K signaling is both necessary and sufficient for quiescence exit. It remains unclear what signals trigger PI3K activation and which receptor is involved. As receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) are known to engage PI3K, we plan to focus on RTKs first. We are using a combination of different approaches (e.g., small-molecule inhibitors, CRISPR/Cas9, etc) to tackle the problem.

16102615.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16102615.value: Adult muscle stem cells (MuSCs) are localized on the surface of muscle fibers in small numbers and are mostly dormant in uninjured muscles. Upon muscle injury, these dormant MuSCs are activated and re-enter the cell cycle to increase in numbers. They can then go on to differentiate to repair the damaged muscles. For many years, it remains unclear how dormant MuSCs are activated. Our work here identified p110α, a catalytic subunit of PI3K (a lipid kinase), as a key molecule that controls activation of dormant MuSCs. Loss of p110α in MuSCs permanently arrests them in the dormant state, which totally abolishes injury-induced muscle regeneration. We also identified additional signaling molecules downstream of p110α in regulating activation of dormant MuSCs. Our work pave the way for subsequent identification of extracellular signals and membrane-bound receptors that engages the PI3K signaling pathway during early activation of dormant MuSCs upon muscle injury. A thorough understanding of molecular mechanisms underlying the functions of muscle stem cells during injury-induced muscle regeneration will provide valuable targets for effective regenerative medicine in the future.

16102715.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16102715.value: Synaptic plasticity, which is the modification of the strength and efficacy of synaptic communication among neurons, is a major cellular mechanism underlying learning and memory. Dysfunction or failure of hippocampal synaptic plasticity is associated with the development of cognitive decline in Alzheimer’s disease. Thus, studies of the functional regulation of synaptic plasticity not only enhance our understanding of learning and memory, but also help to elucidate the pathophysiological mechanisms of dementia-related neurodegenerative diseases. The pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC)-derived peptides melanocortins, which were originally shown to regulate energy metabolism, have been implicated in learning and memory. We recently reported that activation of a member of the melanocortin family, melanocortin 4 receptor (MC4R), enhances the structural and functional plasticity of hippocampal neurons. However, the circuit organization of the melanocortin pathway in the hippocampus and the mechanisms underlying its activation in synaptic plasticity remain largely unclear. The study proposed herein aims to map and characterize the POMC circuitry in the mouse hippocampus. First, using a POMC-Cre transgenic mouse line together with fluorescence-tagged reporter virus, we will investigate the distribution of POMC neurons in the hippocampus. We will then examine whether and how the synthesis and secretion of melanocortins is regulated in the hippocampus upon neuronal activity stimulation. Furthermore, the activity input that controls the melanocortin micro-circuit in mouse hippocampus will be identified. Finally, we will determine the functional importance of the POMC/MCR circuitry in hippocampal synaptic plasticity and hence in learning and memory using different memory tasks. These findings will enhance our knowledge of the hippocampal circuitry involved in learning and memory as well as the functions of the melanocortin system in the human brain. Our proposed study may also reveal a functional association between metabolism and cognition.

16102715.label: Realisation of objectives
16102715.value: Hippocampal synaptic plasticity is important for learning and memory, whereas dysfunctioning of the synaptic plasticity is associated with cognitive decline in neurodegenerative disease, i.e. Alzheimer’s disease (AD). This form of synaptic plasticity is regulated by neuromodulators such as neuropeptides, which function by binding to specific G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs). The neuropeptide alpha-melanocyte–stimulating hormone (α-MSH) is generated from the cleavage of proopiomelanocortin (POMC), which is the endogenous ligand for the GPCR melanocortin 4 receptor (MC4R) and controls energy expenditure mediated by G protein α subunit s (Gs) signaling. MC4R is prominently expressed in the postsynaptic regions of the mouse hippocampus. Accordingly, we demonstrated that MC4R activation in hippocampal pyramidal neurons in mice by exogenous ligand administration enhances structural and functional plasticity. These findings collectively suggest that α-MSH/MC4R signaling plays an important role in hippocampal synaptic functions. However, little is known about the regulation of the neural circuits involved MC4R and its functional roles in the hippocampus. Hence, we aimed to understand the regulation of hippocampal POMC/MC4R circuit and its involvement in hippocampal synaptic plasticity in health and in diseased condition (Shen et al., 2016; Lau et al., under review). In this study, we aimed to determine the presence of a specific hippocampal circuit for MC4R activation by examining the expression of POMC-positive neurons, which produce α-MSH. Specifically, to visualize the distribution of hippocampal POMC neurons, POMC-Cre mice were subjected to intra-hippocampal injection of AAV-FLEX-GFP. POMC-positive cells marked by GFP were predominantly identified in the cornu ammonis (CA) 2/3 pyramidal layers of the adult hippocampus, which were particularly confined to the dorsal CA3 region. In contrast, the POMC-positive cells were absent from the CA1 area. Upon co-staining with specific neuronal markers, most POMC cells were positive for calcium/calmodulin-dependent kinase II alpha subunit (CaMKIIα), an excitatory neuronal marker. These observations was corroborated with the findings showing that mRNA expression of Pomc was mainly detected in the CA3 region (Shen et al., 2016; Lau et al., under review). This result suggests that the POMC+ neurons in the CA3 region secrete α-MSH and activate MC4R in CA1 neurons. We found that the expression of Pomc gene markedly decrease in the hippocampal CA2/3 region in the amyloid precursor protein (APP)/presenilin 1 (PS1) mouse model of AD, at the onset of synaptic impairment from 4 to 6 months of age, suggesting that hippocampal POMC/MC4R signaling is disrupted in the early stage of AD. Therefore, we examined the impacts of manipulating hippocampal POMC/MC4R neurons on synaptic functions in AD. Accordingly, we specifically targeted the restoration of POMC expression in POMC neurons in the CA3 region in 8-month-old APP/PS1 mice for 4 weeks. The efficacy of such AAV-mediated POMC overexpression was validated. The POMC restoration in CA3 significantly alleviated the Aβ-deposition pathology, shown by a ~50% decrease in Aβ plaque area in the entire hippocampus. Similar reduction was not observed in the cortex in the same mice, indicating the hippocampus-specific effects of POMC-expressed CA3 neurons on the amelioration of amyloid plaque deposition. These results collectively suggest that replenishment of melanocortin signaling in the hippocampus alleviates amyloid pathology in AD-like conditions. Hippocampal synaptic plasticity impairment is believed to contribute to the cognitive decline in AD. Our findings showed that stimulation of the hippocampal POMC/MC4R circuit by overexpression of POMC in hippocampal POMC cells or treatment with an MC4R agonist—D-tyrosine (D-Tyr) melanotan-II (MTII) rescued the abovementioned synaptic defects in APP/PS1 mice at 6 months of age, when LTP impairment is first observed (Shen et al., 2016). These findings collectively show that enhancement of hippocampal POMC/MC4R signaling alleviates both the pre- and postsynaptic dysfunctions in APP/PS1 mice. As MC4R is a GPCR that functions via Gs signaling, which involves a cascade of downstream pathways and components, we determined the involvement of specific players in the hippocampal POMC/MC4R-mediated rescue of the synaptic deficits in APP/PS1 mice. MC4R activation promotes adenylyl cyclase through Gs, which subsequently increases intracellular cAMP levels and enhances downstream effectors including PKA. We further investigated CREB, which is a transcription factor and cellular target of PKA signaling that has been suggested to be downregulated in AD pathology. Accordingly, we observed reduced CREB activation in both Aβ-treated acute mouse hippocampal slices and APP/PS1 mouse hippocampal slices; however, this decrease was restored by D-Tyr MTII treatment. Furthermore, the D-Tyr MTII-mediated rescue of the Aβ-induced deficits in synaptic transmission was abolished in cultured hippocampal neurons overexpressing CREB mutants. This suggests that PKA/CREB-dependent signaling and transcriptional pathways is pivotal for the MC4R-stimulated protective effects in hippocampal synapses (Shen et al., 2016). Thus, our results collectively indicate that the activation of hippocampal MC4R/Gs/cAMP/PKA/CREB signaling alleviates hippocampal synaptic plasticity impairment and hence Aβ-induced synaptic dysfunction during AD progression. We then examined the underlying mechanisms of melancortin/MC4R signaling in the amelioration of AD pathology, in particular whether and how it is mediated through the CREB-dependent transcriptional pathways. We performed a microarray analysis on D-Tyr–treated acute hippocampal slices. Transcriptome analysis identified that upon D-Tyr administration, 349 genes (i.e., 156 upregulated and 193 downregulated) were differentially regulated in hippocampal slices prepared from C57 mice. Top upregulated candidate genes include Pcdhb4 (Protocadherin gamma subfamily B, 4), Igfbp4 (insulin growth factor binding protein 4), Ociad2 (OCIA domain containing protein 2), Ppp1r3g (protein phosphatase 1 regulatory subunit 3G), while the top downrguated genes include Mmgt2 (membrane magnesium transporter 2), Rbm12b1 (RNA binding motif protein 12 B1) and Pcdh7 (protocadherin 7). To examine the functional implications of the transcriptomic signatures in the hippocampus stimulated upon MC4R activation, we performed pathway analysis to annotate these differentially expressed genes upon D-Tyr MTII administration. Both Gene Ontology (GO) and protein–protein interaction analyses showed that the upregulated genes were associated with regulation of peroxidase activity, protein kinase B signaling, ERK1/2 cascade and neuropeptide processing; meanwhile, the downregulated genes were associated with the regulation of axoneme assembly, vasculogenesis, cell projection assembly and sensory processing (Lau et al., under review).

16102715.label: Major findings and research outcome
16102715.value: This study aimed to understand the hippocampal POMC/MC4R circuit and its functional role in the regulation of hippocampal synaptic plasticity. • Hippocampal POMC expression is confined to the presynaptic CA3 region POMC-positive cells were mainly present in the CA2/3 pyramidal layers of the mouse hippocampus, primarily in CA3 pyramidal neurons (Shen et al. 2016; Lau et al., under review), suggesting that the hippocampal melanocortin circuit might modulate the classical excitatory trisynaptic pathway. • The activation of hippocampal POMC/MC4R signaling rescues the hippocampal synaptic defects in APP/PS1 mice, respectively Blockade of the hippocampal POMC/MC4R circuit by deletion of POMC cells in the CA3 region or inhibition of MC4R activity in CA1 neurons by overexpression of its endogenous inverse agonist or RNAi-mediated MC4R knockdown led to precocious and exacerbated hippocampal LTP impairment in APP/PS1 mice. Activation of the POMC/MC4R circuit by exogenous administration of MC4R agonist or replenishment of POMC in the hippocampus rescued the synaptic plasticity impairment in APP/PS1 mice (Shen et al. 2016). This demonstrates the importance of the cells that synthesize the presynaptic ligand and the postsynaptic receptors that mediate the protective effects of the circuit. • MC4R/Gs/cAMP/PKA/CREB signaling ameliorates hippocampal synaptic plasticity impairment and rescues oligomeric Aβ-induced synaptic dysfunction in the hippocampus Activation of MC4R-coupled Gs signaling rescued hippocampal LTP impairment in APP/PS1 mice. MC4R activation by D-Tyr MTII treatment rescued LTP impairment in APP/PS1 mice in a PKA/CREB-dependent manner (Shen et al. 2016) as well as the Aβ-induced impairment in hippocampal LTP and synaptic transmission in acute mouse hippocampal slices and cultured rat hippocampal neurons, respectively. We also conducted further studies to demonstrate that MC4R activation causes reduction of amyloid deposition and associated pathology in AD conditions. Transcriptome analysis revealed that MCR activation restores the impaired homeostatic processes and microglial reactivity in the hippocampus in APP/PS1 mice (Lau et al., under review).

16102715.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16102715.value: To our knowledge, the present study is the first to map and demonstrate the importance of a functional hippocampal POMC/MC4R circuit in the regulation of synaptic plasticity in an AD mouse model. Our results provide a foundation for alternative approaches to AD treatment. As MC4R activation reverses synaptic plasticity impairment in AD, it would be invaluable to further explore the beneficial effects of replenishment of MC4R ligand on AD pathology. Accordingly, the identification of a mechanistic means to protect POMC neurons and maintain a reserve of POMC-derived peptides has immense potential for alleviating hippocampal synaptic deficits. Given that systemic administration of MC4R agonists into AD mouse models improves synaptic function, the POMC/MC4R circuit is a potential therapeutic target for cognitive dysfunctions. Future work will investigate the functional roles of the POMC/MC4R circuit in hippocampus-dependent learning and memory, which is largely unexplored. To elucidate the functional role of this circuit in learning and memory, we will selectively ablate or stimulate POMC-containing neurons in experimental mice and subject them to a battery of behavioral tests. The results will enhance our understanding of the relationship between hippocampal synaptic plasticity and cognitive function under regulation by the melanocortin circuit.

16102715.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16102715.value: The modulation of the strength and efficacy of synaptic communication among neurons in the hippocampus is termed “synaptic plasticity.” Its dysfunction contributes to the cognitive decline apparent in Alzheimer’s disease. Melanocortins, which are peptides derived from proopiomelanocortin (POMC), and melanocortin 4 receptor (MC4R) are implicated in synaptic plasticity in the hippocampus. However, the organization of the POMC/MC4R pathway in the hippocampus and the mechanisms by which it is involved in synaptic plasticity remain unclear. In this study, we mapped and characterized a POMC neurocircuit in the mouse hippocampus; POMC neurons in a specific hippocampal region synthesize and secrete alpha-melanocyte–stimulating hormone, which activates MC4R on their targeting neurons. Suppressing MC4R activity in the hippocampus in a mouse model of Alzheimer’s disease worsened their existing synaptic dysfunction, which was improved by restoring the activity of POMC or MC4R in the hippocampus. Meanwhile, stimulating this melanocortin neurocircuit restored synaptic functions in these mice. Therefore, the disruption of hippocampal POMC/MC4R signaling might contribute to the synaptic impairment observed in Alzheimer’s disease. This study improves our understanding of how the hippocampus is involved in synaptic plasticity, which will help delineate the mechanisms of dementia-related neurodegenerative diseases.

16102815.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16102815.value: Learning and memory require the orchestrated regulation of both neuronal connections and synaptic strength in the hippocampus. Any defect in the neural circuitry (i.e., dysregulation of synaptic transmission or plasticity) severely impairs hippocampus-dependent memory. G protein-coupled receptors can regulate diverse physiological functions through the activation of different G proteins. The activities of particular Gαs protein-coupled receptors in the hippocampus play crucial roles in the circuitry regulation and contribute to memory formation and consolidation. Nonetheless, how Gαs protein-coupled receptors exert their specific regulatory effects with high spatiotemporal resolution is poorly understood. The proposed study will overcome this problem through pharmacogenetics technology, specifically “Designer Receptors Exclusively Activated by Designer Drugs” (DREADD), and optogenetics technology. By expressing drug-activated Gαs/Gαi protein-coupled receptors or light-controlled Gαs protein-coupled receptors (opto-XR), we can easily and precisely modulate Gαs mediated signaling in the mouse hippocampal circuit, specifically the CA3–CA1 pathway, by drug or light stimulation. First, we will examine the modulatory function of Gαs signaling during long-term potentiation in the CA3–CA1 pathway, demonstrating the role of Gαs signaling in the regulation of synaptic plasticity. Then, we will examine the involvement of Gαs protein-coupled receptor signaling in the regulation of mouse performance in different phases of memory (i.e., memory formation, consolidation, or retrieval) using the fear conditioning behavioral task. We will further investigate if a spatial pattern-dependent activation is required for the modulatory effect of Gαs protein-coupled receptor on memory encoding. The specific population of CA1 neurons activated by exposure to a particular context (known as memory traces) will be labeled and overexpressed with engineered Gαs/Gαi protein-coupled receptors. We will then modulate the G protein signaling in these tagged cells specifically by activation or inhibition of the G protein-coupled receptors during contextual fear conditioning and determine if an engram-related pattern of Gαs signaling activation is required for its modulation in memory processes. The proposed study will greatly expand our knowledge of the functional roles of Gαs protein-coupled receptors in hippocampus-dependent learning and memory with high spatiotemporal resolution and hence provide insights into the development of therapeutic strategies for memory impairment.

16102815.label: Realisation of objectives
16102815.value: In this study, we aimed to understand the functional roles of Gαs protein-coupled receptors in hippocampal synaptic plasticity and hence hippocampus-dependent learning and memory. To achieve this, we expressed an engineered Gs protein-coupled receptor in the postsynaptic CA1 region of the hippocampus and validated its activation within the hippocampal circuitry. To easily and precisely modulate Gαs-mediated signaling in the mouse hippocampal circuit, we utilized the pharmacogenetic technology “Designer Receptors Exclusively Activated by Designer Drugs” (DREADD) and expressed a Gαs protein-coupled receptor termed Gs-DREADD (GsD) that can be activated by clozapine-N-oxide (CNO). We then co-injected adeno-associated virus (AAV) containing GsD and virus expressing mCitrine fluorescent protein into the CA1 region of the mouse hippocampus. Three weeks after virus injection, we observed yellow fluorescence from mCitrine in the CA1 pyramidal cell layer, suggesting that GsD was successfully expressed. We then confirmed the expression of Gs-DREADD protein in the pyramidal neurons of the hippocampal CA1 region using immunocytochemical analysis. These results collectively demonstrate that GsD was successfully expressed in the hippocampus Our next aim was to investigate the spatiotemporal regulation of hippocampal synaptic plasticity by Gαs protein-coupled receptor signaling. We showed that both in vitro and in vivo activation of GsD increased the phosphorylation of AMPA (α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid) receptor subunit GluA1 at Ser845, which is critical for the synaptic trafficking of GluA1. We stimulated hippocampal slices derived from AAV5-GsD-expressing mice with different doses of CNO and subjected the slices to western blot analysis for GluA1 phosphorylation. We demonstrated that CNO treatment increased GluA1 phosphorylation at Ser845 in acute hippocampal slices prepared from AAV5-GsD–infected mice but not in slices prepared from AAV5-GFP–infected mice (as a control). Furthermore, we found that intraperitoneal injection of CNO into AAV5-GsD–infected mice increased GluA1 phosphorylation at Ser845 in the hippocampus. Together, these findings suggest that specific activation of postsynaptic Gαs enhances synaptic transmission in hippocampal neurons through the phosphorylation of GluA1 and regulation of its synaptic trafficking. Long-term potentiation (LTP) refers to the enhancement of synaptic transmission after rapid and repeated neuronal activation and is believed to be an important molecular mechanism underlying learning and memory. To examine whether Gαs activation enhances the LTP formation in vitro, we incubated acute hippocampal slices prepared from AAV5-GsD–infected mice with CNO. We induced LTP in the Schaffer collateral pathway and measured it using a multi-electrode array system. Consistent with the GsD-dependent increase of GluA1 phosphorylation, in vitro activation of GsD increased LTP in the Schaffer collateral pathway in the hippocampal slices, suggesting that Gαs activation enhances hippocampal synaptic plasticity. In contrast, activation of Gq or Gi protein-coupled receptor signaling did not increase hippocampal LTP, suggesting that the enhancement of hippocampal synaptic plasticity is dependent on Gs. After demonstrating that GsD activation enhances hippocampal synaptic plasticity, we assessed the physiological roles of GsD in the regulation of hippocampus-dependent learning and memory by submitting mice to the fear-conditioning test. In this test, we placed the mice in a specific context and subsequently administered a foot shock. If the animals learn the association between the context and the foot shock, which is hippocampus dependent, they will freeze when they are returned to the context in which they received the foot shock. The time that the mice remain frozen reflects the strength of the context-based fear memory formed. While GsD activation did not affect the basal level of freezing during training, it resulted in a significant increase in time spent frozen in the retrieval test. This finding suggests that activation of GsD signaling enhances hippocampus-dependent learning and memory.

16102815.label: Major findings and research outcome
16102815.value: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), the largest superfamily of cell-surface receptors, are important for diverse physiological functions through the coupling of different G proteins and subsequent activation of downstream effector signaling pathways. The coupling of GPCRs to different Gα protein subtypes (e.g., Gαs or Gαi/o) leads to different physiological outcomes. The activities of specific Gαs protein-coupled receptors in the hippocampus play crucial roles in regulating neuronal connectivity and activity, which contribute to memory formation and consolidation. However, the molecular mechanisms of GPCRs underlying memory formation remain unclear. In this study, we used the pharmacogenetic technology, DREADD, to study the function of Gαs protein-coupled receptors in the hippocampus. We showed that specific activation of Gαs protein-coupled receptors in the postsynaptic CA1 region of the mouse hippocampus enhances synaptic plasticity by regulating synaptic trafficking of AMPA receptors, the major glutamatergic receptor for excitatory neurotransmission. Furthermore, activation of Gαs protein-coupled receptors significantly enhanced hippocampus-dependent contextual memory. These findings reveal that Gαs protein-coupled receptors play a positive role in hippocampal synaptic plasticity and facilitating memory formation. Our examination of the underlying mechanisms of Gαs protein-coupled receptors at hippocampal excitatory synapses showed that Gαs activation regulated AMPA receptor trafficking through the activation of the cAMP/PKA-dependent pathway followed by Ser845 phosphorylation of AMPA receptor subunit GluA1; the Ser835 phosphorylation of GluA1 ultimately facilitated the insertion of AMPA receptors into synapses. Furthermore, the cAMP/PKA pathway enhanced gene expression through the activation of a key transcription factor CREB, which potentiates long-term synaptic plasticity. Infusing PKA inhibitor into the hippocampus impaired spatial memory in mice, whereas overexpression of adenylyl cyclase in the mouse forebrain facilitated the formation of long-term potentiation and memory. These findings collectively demonstrate that cAMP/PKA signaling plays a positive role in synaptic plasticity and memory formation, suggesting that Gαs protein-coupled receptors function in the hippocampus. Some of the findings described herein are reported in Shen et al, Cell Reports, 2016 (see attached).

16102815.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16102815.value: The findings of the current study demonstrate that GPCR/Gαs signaling plays a role in enhancing hippocampal synaptic plasticity and hippocampus-dependent learning and memory. This finding lays the foundation for us to examine the involvement of GPCR/Gs signaling in synaptic impairment in different neurological disorders. For example, we can examine whether reduced phosphorylation of GluA1 and the deregulated synaptic targeting of AMPA receptors can be used as an indicator for studying the dysfunctions of GPCR signaling in the hippocampus. Furthermore, we can examine whether enhancing the deregulated Gs signaling pathway can restore the impaired hippocampal functions and synaptic impairment in different disease mouse models.

16102815.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16102815.value: Communication between neurons occurs at specialized sites called synapses. The dysfunction of synapses in the hippocampus is believed to be a major cause of memory impairment in Alzheimer’s disease. Thus, studying how synaptic communication is regulated in the hippocampus enhances our understanding of learning and memory. While modulation of cell-surface receptors, specifically G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), is suggested to shape the morphology and function of hippocampal synapses, mapping the activation of GPCRs and their subsequent signaling in the hippocampus is critical for our understanding of the functions of hippocampal synapses and hence learning and memory. We showed that specific stimulation of Gαs signaling, which occurs after GPCRs, in specific areas of the hippocampus regulates the functions of neurotransmitter receptors and the changes in synaptic transmission between neurons. This finding suggests that GPCR/Gαs activation is critical for modulating hippocampal functions and thus enhancing learning and memory. The findings regarding the spatial- and time-specific activation of Gαs signaling in the mouse hippocampus bolsters our understanding of the molecular and cellular bases of learning and memory. In addition, these findings provide insights into the mechanisms underlying the synaptic impairment in Alzheimer’s disease.

16103015.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16103015.value: Melatonin is a neurohormone synthesized and secreted by the pineal gland during darkness in a normal diurnal cycle. Its regulatory role in controlling circadian rhythm is well-established and the signal is mediated through the activation of two mammalian G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) designated as MT1 and MT2. The two melatonin receptor subtypes are widely expressed in both the central nervous system as well as peripheral tissues, and they display similar binding affinity for melatonin and are linked to a multitude of signaling pathways. Recent genome-wide association studies and the use of MT1/MT2 knockout mice have greatly expanded our understanding of the physiological roles of melatonin. There is increasing evidence to implicate the MT2 receptor in the pathophysiology of type 2 diabetes and various neuro-disorders including depression. Given that GPCRs represent one of the most exploited pharmacological targets, there is tremendous therapeutic potential for developing melatonin-like drugs (or melatoninergics). This is especially true for small molecules that can distinguish between the two receptor subtypes because each subtype can be linked to specific functional responses at the target tissues. However, most of the melatoninergics in the market act on both MT1 and MT2 receptors almost indiscriminately. The difficulty in designing subtype-selective melatoninergics is largely due to incomplete mapping of the ligand binding pockets of the two receptors. In this regard, the Principal Investigator (PI) has successfully identified several novel isoquinolinone derivatives that exhibit remarkable selectivity for MT2 (up to 1,800-fold). Recent characterization of the isoquinolinones revealed that they can modulate a variety of intracellular signals in a receptor-dependent manner and yet they appear to bind to the MT2 receptor in a fashion distinct from melatonin. These compounds thus represent powerful tools to examine the biological functions of MT2 and for elucidating the structural differences between MT1 and MT2. The present proposal aims to identify the molecular determinants that distinguish MT2 from MT1 receptors. Homology modeling based on recently resolved GPCR structures coupled with conventional mutagenesis approaches will be employed to identify possible ligand-interacting residues that form the binding pocket of MT2. Identification of conserved and/or distinct residues will help to provide the molecular basis distinguishing the two receptors from each other, and pave the way forward for the rational design of highly selective ligands as therapeutic agents for human diseases and disorders associated with defects in specific melatonin receptors.

16103015.label: Realisation of objectives
16103015.value: Objective 1: At the time of project commencement, no crystal structure of MT1 or MT2 melatonin receptor was available. Hence, it necessitated the generation of a homology model of the MT2 receptor. This was achieved by using the SWISS-MODEL tool in the ExPASy Bioinformatics resource portal. The crystal structure of the active conformation of the human β2-adrenergic receptor (PDB access code 3P0G) was employed as a template. Ligand structures were constructed with ChemDraw and converted into 3D structures by AutoDock Tools. The putative ligand binding pocket was generated by SITEHOUND and FunFOLD. Molecular modelling and ligand docking approaches were employed to predict residues involved in forming interactions with the MT2-selective isoquinolinones. Seven conserved residues (Asn175, His208, Trp264, Asn268, Gly271, Tyr294 and Tyr298) were selected as targets for site-directed mutagenesis. Ca2+ mobilization, cAMP inhibition, phosphorylation of extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK), and ligand binding assays were performed to functionally characterize the receptor mutants in transfected CHO cells. In the receptor model, the 5-methoxy moiety of melatonin is positioned near TM5 and forms a hydrogen bond between the methoxy oxygen and the imidazole ring of His208. This may explain the reduced melatonin potency (decreased 44-fold) for Ca2+ mobilization in the H208A mutant. In contrast to melatonin, however, functional agonist activities of isoquinolinones bearing a 3-methoxybenzyloxyl substituent were unaffected by alanine substitution at His208 of MT2. The putative binding pocket of melatonin receptor is delimited by two conserved tyrosine residues (Tyr294 and Tyr298) on TM7 separated by approximately one helix turn. The Y298A mutant exhibited a 3-fold decrease in melatonin potency, while the EC50 values of isoquinolinones (7b-c and 15b-c) were hindered by 15- to 80-fold. Compounds 7b, 14b and 15b that possess a 3-methoxybenzyloxy substituent at C6, C7 or C5 position, respectively, exhibited large potency differences (EC50 values from 0.14 nM to 49 nM) in wild-type MT2 receptor, but displayed similar potencies ranging between 0.5 nM and 1.6 nM in the Y294A mutant, while isoquinolinones bearing a 3,5-dimethoxybenzyloxyl substituent (7c, 14c and 15c) had reduced efficacies. These results suggested that the Tyr294 on TM7 may regulate ligand selectivity of the MT2 receptor. Although alanine substitutions at Tyr294 or Tyr298 reduced the potency of melatonin and several isoquinolinones on MT2, similar mutations on MT1 allowed five hitherto ineffective isoquinolinones to act as agonists. Interestingly, an isoquinolinone antagonist bearing a 4-methoxybenzyloxyl moiety turned into an agonist at H208A, Y294A, and Y298A mutants. The potency of melatonin at N175A was approximately 4-fold lower than the wild-type receptor, while the potency of isoquinolinone compounds (7b-d and 15b-c) was significantly reduced by 30-120 folds at N175A. The efficacy of melatonin at the W264A mutant was significantly reduced to 50% of wild-type MT2. Collectively, these results indicate that a subset of residues is apparently involved in forming a hydrophobic binding cavity to confer selectivity upon the aromatic substituent of isoquinolinone compounds. Two conserved tyrosine residues (Tyr281/294 and Tyr285/298) on TM7 may confer ligand selectivity at MT1 and MT2 receptors, while a conserved histidine on TM5 is apparently involved in receptor activation. These studies have successfully mapped several residues that are crucial for the binding of MT2-selective isoquinolinones. Objective 2: Among the various nonsynonymous MTNR1B variants known to be associated with type-2 diabetes (T2D), mutants that exhibit defective Gi-signaling without significant impairment in ligand binding were selected for functional characterization. These mutants may adopt conformations that can be “tweaked” by the isoquinolinones into active receptors more easily than mutants that are incapable of binding melatonin. A panel of mutants with mutations at TM1-5 were constructed by site-directed mutagenesis: A52T, A74T, R138C, L166I, and R222H, respectively. These MT2 mutants were stably expressed in HEK293 cells and assayed for agonist-induced Ca2+ mobilization, cAMP inhibition, and ERK phosphorylation. A52T, A74T, and L166I mutants exhibited ~30% reduction in efficacy upon treatment with melatonin or isoquinolinone 7b. Interestingly, R138C displayed a complete loss of response to either melatonin or compound 7b, while melatonin (but not compound 7b) became a partial agonist at the R222H mutant. ERK phosphorylations induced by either melatonin or 7b were similar between the wild-type and MT2 mutants (A52T, A74T, L166I and R222H), but the isoquinolinone was generally more potent. Again, R138C did not respond to either ligand. Similar results were obtained in cAMP inhibition assays. Surprisingly, compound 14b (which does not bind to MT1) potently stimulated Ca2+ mobilization in cells coexpressing R138C and MT1; this response was blocked by the MT2 antagonist 4P-PDOT. Collectively, these studies suggest that isoquinolinones may be less affected by T2D-associated nonsynonymous MTNR1B variants. Objective 3: Since it remains controversial whether melatonin receptor is predominantly expressed in pancreatic β-cells versus α-cells, several pancreatic cell lines were characterized. Murine INS-1E, α-TC1 and β-TC6 insulinomas, as well as the human MIN6 pseudoislets were subjected to RT-PCR for determining the transcripts of melatonin receptors. Although both MT1 and MT2 transcripts were detected in INS-1E, β-TC6 and MIN6 cells, it required extended PCR cycles (60 cycles), and MT2 generally displayed a lower transcript level than MT1. In contrast, only MT1 transcript was detected in α-TC1 cells. As compared to primary islet cells (transcripts detected at 35 cycles), the expression levels of melatonin receptors are apparently much lower in pancreatic β cell lines. This prompted us to examine if melatonin can elicit any functional response in these cells before proceeding to shRNA-mediated knockdown of MT1 or MT2 receptors. In accordance to the proposal, we examined the ability of melatonin to suppress insulin secretion in the presence of low/high glucose stimulation. Serum-starved INS-1E, β-TC6, and MIN6 cells were washed twice and incubated with serum-free Krebs-Ringer buffer for an hour, before being challenged with various concentrations of glucose (1 to 28 mM; 1 hour). Insulin released into the culture medium was subsequently determined by ELISA. As expected, glucose dose-dependently stimulated insulin secretion (reaching 250 ng/ml), while isoprenaline, epinephrine, and somatostatin effectively suppressed this response to basal (~90 ng/ml). Disappointingly, melatonin did not inhibit glucose-stimulated insulin secretion in all experimental conditions tested. Manipulations on glucose concentration, incubation time, melatonin concentration, and co-incubation with other ligands (glucagon, epinephrine, or somatostatin) all failed to demonstrate any ability of melatonin to inhibit insulin secretion. These results are in stark contrast to published in vivo data. Since robust inhibition of insulin secretion could not be achieved, attempts were made to develop surrogate readouts for melatonin receptor activation in pancreatic cell lines. INS-1E, β-TC6, and MIN6 cells were examined for melatonin-induced inhibition of adenylyl cyclase, phosphorylation of ERK, and suppression of CREB phosphorylation. Selection of readouts was based on the typical functions of Gi-coupled receptors. Despite clear demonstration of functional responses to epinephrine and somatostatin in these assays, none of the pancreatic cell lines responded to melatonin (up to 1 uM) consistently. Although overexpression of MT2 enabled detection of melatonin-induced inhibition of adenylyl cyclase and CREB phosphorylation in INS-1E and β-TC6 cells, these responses were relatively weak (as compared to similar studies in HEK293 cells) and were not observed in MIN6 cells. These results suggest that melatonin signaling may be atypical in pancreatic cells and, in the absence of a reliable cellular readout, they precluded further analysis of the roles of isoquinolinones and MT2 mutants in regulating insulin release.
