16206915.label: Major findings and research outcome
16206915.value: 1) We fabricated PFC nanodroplets with controlled size and high monodispersity using our novel micro/nanofluidc devices and synthesis methods. In the first design, we developed a flame-shaped glass capillary and PDMS hybrid device for synthesis of PFC nanodroplets as small as 200 nm in diameter with PDI <0.04. (Lab on a Chip, 2017, J1). In the second design, we developed a novel method to produce monodisperse PFC nanodroplets by the Ouzo effect using a staggered herringbone micromixer. We fabricated PFC nanodroplets from ~ 200 to ~ 700 nm in diameter with a narrow size distribution (PDI <0.1) and the throughput of nanodroplet production could be as high as 0.48 ml/h. (Microfluidics and Nanofluidics, 2019, J4). Finally, ultrasound imaging was conducted to demonstrate the feasibility of PFC nanodroplets as ultrasound contrast agents. 2) To tackle the limitations of lipid or surfactant coated nano/microcapsules including poor stability and shorter lifetime for ultrasound imaging, we developed a microfluidic flow-focusing approach to produce monodisperse nano/micro bubbles stabilized by PLGA as the polymer shell. The size of PLGA bubbles can be tightly controlled from ∼600 nm to ∼7 μm with PDI < 4% for ensuring highly homogeneous echogenic behavior in ultrasound fields. (ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces, 2018, J2). 3) We further explored the potentials using the developed nano/microcapsules for cancer therapy. Hypoxia in solid tumors may be a hindrance to effective treatments of tumors in achieving their therapeutic potential, especially for photodynamic therapy (PDT) which requires oxygen as the supplement substrate. We designed lipid-polymer bilaminar oxygen nanobubbles with chlorin e6 conjugated to the polymer shell as a novel oxygen self-supplement agent for PDT. Using the oxygen nanobubbles for PDT, a significant enhancement of therapeutic efficacy and survival rates was achieved on C6 glioma-bearing mice. (ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces, 2018, J3) 4) We found the conventional oxygen delivery systems require external stimuli to release the oxygen. To enhance oxygen delivery to tumor tissues in vivo, we designed oxygen carriers preferentially possess stimuli-responsive properties for pH-responsive controlled release. Our strategy is to adopt delicately tailored materials with pH-labile groups or cross-linkers such as PEG-poly(-amino ester), poly(amidoamine) dendrimers which release the encapsulated cargoes by a hydrophobic-to-hydrophilic transformation induced by acidic pH. We developed oxygen nanobubbles that were enclosed by the acetalated dextran polymer shells and the external stimuli-free supply of oxygen was evaluated on CNE2 tumorbearing mice to show 6-fold, increase of the intratumoral oxygen level. (Langmuir, 2019, J5)

16206915.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16206915.value: Suggested work for further development: 1) In this project, we demonstrated the feasibility of PFC nanodroplets as ultrasound contrast agents but have not thoroughly investigated the viscoelastic and acoustic properties of the developed contrast agents. In future work, a systematic characterizations of the contrast agents in terms of their temporal response to ultrasound activation, the correlations of nano capsule size, shell composition and thickness with ultrasound frequency and intensity will be conducted to provide more understanding for nanomaterial design. 2) For targeted ultrasound imaging and therapy using functional nanomaterials, enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effect need to be greatly enhanced to achieve nanomaterial accumulation in the target regions. Both passive or active mechanisms will be explored to improve the EPR effect. Microfluidic devices can be utilized to establish model systems for in vitro studies. 3) The developed microfluidic based methods can be used for synthesis of other functional nanomaterials. The nanomaterials can be designed to have multifunctional agents for targeted diagnosis and therapy.

16206915.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16206915.value: Ultrasound has been extensively employed in biomedical fields of diagnosis, therapy, and imaging-guided drug delivery in combination with ultrasound contrast agents. Commercially available contrast agents, lipid microbubbles of 1–8 μm in diameter, have drawbacks such as limited stability, short lifetime, and poor accessibility in extravascular sites like tumors or inflammation due to their relative large size compared to the inter-endothelial cell gaps (e.g., 400–800 nm). Perfluorocarbon (PFC) nanocapsules are being exploited as the most effective contrast agents owing to the enhanced permeability and retention in tumor tissues offered by their unique properties, as well as the enhanced echogenicity of the vaporized forms upon ultrasound activation. As both the trigger frequency for vaporization and resonance frequency for imaging with ultrasound are size-dependent, the monodispersity is a critical measure. Unfortunately, conventional nanoemulsification techniques all suffer from polydisperse populations. In this project, we fabricated PFC nanocapsules with controlled size and high uniformity using microfluidic technologies. Moreover, the stability of the nanocapsules were improved by the design of lipid-polymer bilaminar shells. We investigated the conversion of nanodroplets into microbubbles and demonstrated the feasibility of using such PFC nanocapsules as theranostic agents for targeted ultrasound imaging and therapy.

16207115.label: Realisation of objectives
16207115.value: All the objectives outlined in the proposal have been achieved. Realization of each objective is described below: Object #1: Develop techniques for characterizing the interface traps and border traps and obtain understanding of the underlying physical mechanisms Fast transients of VTH shift and their impact on RON under dynamic AC (1 k-1 MHz) positive gate stress in depletion-mode (D–mode) and enhancement-mode (E-mode) MIS-HEMTs have been studied [1, 2]. We achieved data acquisition within 120 ns right after each stress pulse throughout the entire stress time range from 100 ns up to 1,000 s, by virtue of a short stress-to-sense delay of ~100 ns and high sampling rate up to 50 MSa/s. Such a characterization resolution was made possible with the fast data acquisition link between the high-speed oscilloscope and the control computer developed in house. The major challenges lies in that a large number of frames of waveforms need to be transferred to computer within a short time. Despite the considerable VTH shift, its impact on RON in D-mode and E-mode MIS-HEMT is modest, if the device is under sufficient gate overdrive. Furthermore, VTH shift and the consequent RON increase under dynamic stress, which are more relevant to high-frequency switching operation, exhibits frequency dependence within 1-kHz ~ 1-MHz and is always smaller than that under conventionally used static (constant) stress. Furthermore, distinctive Ron’s susceptibilities to Vth shift between E-mode and D-mode GaN transistors are revealed and analyzed. The correlation between Vth shift and RON facilitates the assessment on how much Vth shift a GaN power switch can tolerate. Object #2: Understand the time-dependent dielectric breakdown phenomena of the gate dielectric in GaN power MIS-HEMTs Credible reliability study has to be performed on devices fabricated with state-of-the-art technology and showing state-of-the-art performance. This is made possible with the development of SiNx grown by LPCVD (low pressure chemical vapor deposition) as the gate dielectric by our group. Up to date, LPCVD-SiNx deliver the best combinations of performance and reliability including the longest TDDB lifetime, highest breakdown field, lowest PBTI (positive bias temperature instability) and NBTI (negative bias temperature instability) when it is deposited on C-plane GaN. The superior performance and reliability are attributed to two main factors: 1) a type II band-alignment between LPCVD-SiNx and GaN that yields a large conduction band offset at around 2.4 eV at the SiNx/GaN interface. A large barrier height is presented at the critical SiNx/GaN interface to block leakage, despite the relatively small bandgap of SiNx; 2) high deposition temperature (~780 degree Celsius) of LPCVD-SiNx that leads to dense film with low defect density. Atomic layer deposition (ALD) usually features much lower temperature (typically around 300 degree Celsius) and high temperature annealing does not generate the same benefits as high temperature deposition. In addition, many commonly used dielectric materials (such as AlN, Al2O3) have relatively low crystallization temperature and thus cannot sustain high temperature annealing. High temperature deposition needs to be designed carefully. For example, SiNx grown by MOCVD (metal organic chemical vapor deposition) at ~1,000 degree Celsius delivers low interface state density, but not long lifetime, probably due to partial crystallization of SiNx at such a high temperature. Time-dependent dielectric breakdown (TDDB) test was performed to evaluate the gate dielectric reliability of the LPCVD-SiNx MIS-HEMTs [3]. Considering distinct gate leakage mechanisms within different bias ranges, a combined model including both Fowler-Nordheim (FN) model (for high bias) and Poole-Frenkel (PF) model (for low bias) was proposed and used to predict the lifetime of LPCVD-SiNx gate dielectric. We have also demonstrated that the highly effective AlN/SiNx passivation technique is compatible with high-performance LPCVD-SiNx gate dielectric to deliver superior current collapse suppression and gate reliability simultaneously for GaN-based power MIS-HEMTs [4]. Supported by hard-switching and soft-switching tests, the AlN/SiNx passivation after being subjected to a high temperature of 780 oC during the LPCVD-SiNx deposition can still suppress the current collapse effectively, confirming the compatibility of the passivation technology with high temperature process. Object #3: Identify the dominant and representative modes and mechanisms of gate dielectric failure in GaN power MIS-HEMTs To achieve the E-mode operation, one of the most attractive approaches is to fabricate MIS-FET with a fully recessed gate structure. Compared with the MIS-HEMT with a partially recessed gate structure, the MIS-FET exhibits substantial robustness in recess depth control. We have successfully integrated the highly reliable LPCVD-SiNx with the fully recessed gate structure to achieve high-performance GaN MIS-FET with normally-off operation. In particular, we demonstrated that an interfacial protection layer could effectively prevent the etched GaN surface from degradation during the high-temperature LPCVD-SiNx, and is essential for achieving a high-quality dielectric/GaN interface [5, 6]. We investigated the threshold voltage VTH stability under reverse-bias step-stress in the E-mode LPCVD-SiNx/PECVD-SiNx/GaN MIS-FET [7]. Under the OFF-state reverse-bias stress with the same net gate-to-drain voltage (VGD), the VTH shift shows an obvious dependence on the negative gate bias. With a VGS of 0 V, the VTH shift is small and recoverable, while the VTH shifts are substantially larger with more negative gate bias (VGS = −20 V). In addition to the PECVD-SiNx interlayer protection, we also developed another approach of obtaining such a protection layer using oxygen-plasma treatment followed by in situ annealing prior to the LPCVD-SiNx deposition [8]. 16207115.value: • Fast transients of VTH shift and their impact on RON under dynamic AC (1 k-1 MHz) positive gate stress in depletion-mode (D–mode) and enhancement-mode (E-mode) MIS-HEMTs have been studied [1, 2]. We achieved data acquisition within 120 ns right after each stress pulse throughout the entire stress time range from 100 ns up to 1,000 s, by virtue of a short stress-to-sense delay of ~100 ns and high sampling rate up to 50 MSa/s. • We found that VTH shift and the consequent RON increase under dynamic stress, which are more relevant to high-frequency switching operation, exhibits frequency dependence within 1-kHz ~ 1-MHz and is always smaller than that under conventionally used static (constant) stress. A model to explain such a phenomenon has been developed. • Distinctive Ron’s susceptibilities to Vth shift between E-mode and D-mode GaN transistors are revealed and analyzed. The correlation between Vth shift and RON facilitates the assessment on how much Vth shift a GaN power switch can tolerate. • Systematically developed LPCVD-SiNx as the most promising gate dielectric for GaN MIS-gate transistors: major findings include identification of the large conduction band offset between LPCVD-SiNx and GaN, long TDDB lifetime, high breakdown electric field, etc. • Developed effective interface protection techniques for etched GaN surface to endure high temperature process such as LPCVD • Identified a new hole induced gate dielectric degradation mechanism under high-voltage reverse-bias stress • Research results published in 6 journal papers, 5 conference presentations. 16207115.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16207115.value: Over the course of this project, great progress has been made in identifying and developing suitable gate dielectric for GaN MIS-gate transistors. Time-dependent dielectric breakdown (TDDB) lifetime close to what is required in applications has been finally within our reach. It is believed that GaN MIS-gate power devices, especially the enhancement-mode ones, will continue to attract great interests in the community of GaN power transistors. This is because the p-GaN junction gate HEMT currently being commercialized has faced many reliability issues in application, and one of the major reasons is that the gate structure is not based on MIS or MOS structures that have been proven in Si and SiC based power MOSFETs. Further course of action will be to seek close collaboration with industry, and promote transfer of the technology and knowhow from this project.

16207115.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16207115.value: This project has focused on the reliability of gate dielectrics in GaN power MIS-gate heterojunction transistors. The studies were conducted on state-of-the-art devices fabricated with advanced deposition and reliability enhancement techniques. Characterization techniques were developed to reveal reliability issues under static and dynamic operating conditions that take place in practical power switching applications. Key failure modes and mechanisms have been revealed with in-depth understanding. The fundamental understanding of the reliability issues have led to successful development of new interface protection techniques that are capable of delivering GaN power MIS-gate transistors with record performance and lifetime. The outputs from this project will pave the way toward eventual commercialization of GaN MIS-gate power transistors.

16207415.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16207415.value: In cellular mobile communications, due to the path loss effect as radio frequency signals propagate, sufficient power is required to combat noise and reliably transmit data from the base station to a mobile terminal, say, located near the cell edge. However, raising transmission power levels from base stations increases adjacent cell interference, which reduces the user capacity or the number of mobile terminals to be accommodated in a cell. A more power efficient alternative to extend signal coverage of the base station is to deploy a relay which forwards a copy of its received signal from the base station to the mobile terminal. There exist several types of relaying strategies, decode-and-forward, amplify-and-forward, compress-and-forward, etc. Among them, the most practical relaying strategy is arguably decode-and-forward (DF), in which the relay receives a coded packet from the base station, attempts to decode it and forward the re-encoded packet to the mobile terminal. There is a large volume of literature reporting various DF-related schemes for a wide range of wireless networking scenarios, but all such schemes were designed based on completely ignoring or inaccurately modeling the effect of decoding error at the delay. In this project, we propose a new method to accurately model the effect of decoding error at the relay, and based on which, near-optimal decoding at the destination can be developed. Contrary to the conventional wisdom, our result suggests that with (near) optimal decoding at the destination, the fixed DF (in spite of having error propagation) is superior in bit-error-rate performance to the selective DF. By fully developing the potential of our methods of decoding error modeling and near-optimal decoding, this project aims to bring about better understanding, design and implementation of various DF relaying strategies which are applicable to general multiple relay networks. 在蜂窩移動通信中，由於射頻信號在傳播過程中的路徑損耗效應，需要足夠大的功率以對抗噪聲以及保證數據在基站和位於蜂窩邊緣的移動終端之間的可靠傳輸。然而，提高基站傳輸功率會增加對鄰近蜂窩的干擾，從而降低用戶容量或容納於單位蜂窩的移動終端的數量。為了擴大基站信號的覆蓋範圍，一個更節省功率的替代方案是部署中繼以轉發其從基站接收的信號到移動終端。現有幾種類型的中繼策略，例如譯碼轉發，放大轉發，壓縮轉發等。其中，最實用的被認為是譯碼轉發，在此中繼策略中，中繼從基站接收到一個編碼數據包，然後嘗試對其進行譯碼並轉發重新編碼的數據包到移動終端。現有大量的文獻報告了廣泛適用於無線網絡場景的各種譯碼轉發相關方案，但是所有上述方案的設計都基於對中繼端譯碼錯誤的完全忽略或不准確建模。在此項目中，我們提出了一種全新的方法來對中繼譯碼錯誤進行精確建模，基於此模型，我們開發了在接收端的擬最優譯碼算法。與傳統經驗不同的是，我們的結果表明通過在接收端的擬最優譯碼，固定型譯碼轉發(儘管存在錯誤傳播)在誤碼率方面可以優於選擇型譯碼轉發。通過全面發掘我們的譯碼錯誤模型和擬最優譯碼的潛能，此項目旨在提供對於適用於一般多中繼網絡的各類​​譯碼轉發策略的更好理解，設計，以及實現。

16207415.label: Realisation of objectives
16207415.value: To meet Objective 1, the decoding problem in the convolutionally coded decode-and-forward (DF) relay channel representing a 3-node source-relay-destination network has been re-examined. By tackling the challenge of accurately modeling the decoding errors at the relay, a near BER-optimal decoder (NBOD) at the destination has been derived based on a product trellis representation and Viterbi decoding. Its decoding complexity is linear in the information block length, while the existence of the exact BER-optimal decoder with sub-exponential complexity is still unknown. Since the major approximation involved in the derivation of the NBOD is the pairwise error probability approximation that is known to incur an insignificant degradation from the optimal BER performance. To achieve Objective 2, accurate BER bounds for the near maximum likelihood decoding (MLD) decoder and the linear-combining-based decoders (including fixed DF with cooperative maximal-ratio combining (MRC) and selective DF with MRC) in the three-node one-way relay channel scenario have been derived. Their accuracy has been verified by computer simulation. Our simulation results confirms that the proposed NBOD can perform close to the MLD performance and outperform the existing combining-based decoders in the three-node single DF relay network scenario. Besides, the NBOD has been extended for more general multiple DF relay networks. Simulation results further verify that the proposed NBOD can outperform existing decoders based on MRC and selective DF in various relay channel scenarios at the cost of higher complexity. To meet Objective 3, we interpret the trellis error model (TEM) implicit in the product trellis representation of the NBOD algorithm as a component code in a distributed Turbo coding (DTC) system, in which the relay performs the decode-interleave-reencode-forward operation. By applying the famous Turbo principle, efficient TEM-based iterative decoders (TEM-ID) achieving excellent performance-complexity tradeoffs compared with the NBOD has been proposed. For finite block lengths, a near MLD bound for DTC under the of uniform interleaving assumption was derived. Our simulation results showed that the performance of TEM-ID can approach the bound to within 0.2 dB and is superior to that of the existing decoders which were introduced based on some less accurate error models. For large block lengths, the asymptotic performance (or decoding threshold) of the proposed TEM-ID was predicted using the EXIT chart technique and it can be approached by the simulated performance with a block length of 10,000 bits. To achieve Objective 4, the TEM-ID has been extended to a graph-based iterative decoder for a general distributed concatenated coded network with any number of relays, and the decoding errors at each relay are accurately modeled. Besides, efficient LDLC message passing decoder based on list sphere decoding with capacity-approach performance was devised. The NBOD has also been extended for convolutionally coded asynchronous physical layer network coded (APNC) two-way relay network with analytical performance bound analysis. These new decoders give near-optimal performance and are superior to the known counterparts due to their better performance and/or lower complexity. In addition, to minimize the training overhead associated with channel estimation, we proposed a new low-complexity detector for non-coherent DF relay networks with optimized generalized differential modulation (GDM) and derived the associated performance bounds. Furthermore, as performance evaluation by theoretical analysis is not always tractable and Monte Carlo simulation is time-consuming, a new minimum-variance importance sampling estimator has been derived for fast simulation of the error performance of coded systems. In summary, we have successfully achieved Objectives 1-4.

16207415.label: Major findings and research outcome
16207415.value: The major findings of this project have been detailed in Section 5.3. The research outcomes associated with Objectives 1-4 have been disseminated in four journal papers (including two published in IEEE Transactions on Wireless Communications [J1], [J2], one published in IEEE Transactions on Vehicular Technology [J3], and one currently under second review for possible publication in IEEE Transactions on Wireless Communications [J4]) as well as seven conference papers/posters [C1]-[C7]. 16207415.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16207415.value: The proposed error model-based decoders (NBOD, TEM-ID, and their extensions) have been shown to achieve near-optimal performance for DF relay networks and their complexities grow nearly with the code length. However, their complexities may still be too high for some important applications, e.g. when the cooperative network mainly consists of battery-operated sensor nodes. Hence, an important further development is to devise simplified versions of the proposed decoders which can provide flexible complexity-performance tradeoffs to match with a wide range of practical application scenarios. This is particularly important for large networks because under the current framework, the proposed decoder views the whole network as a concatenated code whose length scales with the size of the network. In this case, performance evaluation becomes prohibitively time-consuming. To meet the system design requirements, novel time-efficient techniques for performance evaluation are needed. From the perspective of real-world application developments, the complexity of the proposed TEM-ID should be affordable for some three-node fixed wireless networks, e.g. Wifi home networks. It is of practical interest to launch an ITF project to build a prototype to demonstrate the achievable extended coverage of a Wifi router, say.

16207415.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16207415.value: Decode-and-forward (DF) relaying is one of the most practical cooperative communication strategies to extend the signal coverage of a wireless network. While the efficient optimal decoder (e.g. Viterbi decoder) for a convolutionally coded point-to-point channel is well-known, the corresponding decoder for a convolutionally coded DF relay network has a complexity that grows exponentially with the code length. Known efficient suboptimal decoders were devised under the unrealistic assumption that the decoding errors at the delay can be neglected or represented by some over-simplistic models. This limits the full potential of signal coverage and power efficiency of a relay network. In this project, by introducing a new error model to accurately represent the decoding errors at the delay, a new near-optimal decoder with complexity linear in the code length for a coded DF relay network has been developed. Its near-optimal performance is guaranteed by theoretical analysis. The new approach to design efficient near-optimal decoders has been successfully extended for general multiple DF relay networks and distributed coded networks. The near-optimal decoder designs resulted from this project can realize the full potential of decode-and-forward relaying to enhance signal coverage and power efficiency of cooperative wireless networks.

16207515.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16207515.value: The behavior of a multicomponent droplet impinging, spreading and evaporating on a wettability-patterned surface is of significant fundamental interest and also has a broad range of applications, including inkjet printing, hot spot cooling, surface patterning, droplet-based microfluidics, painting, anti-fogging, DNA microarray formation and nano-spray for thin film deposition. Recently, experimental and numerical investigations have been focused on multicomponent droplet impact and evaporation because most applications involve multicomponent droplets but the mechanism of the process is more complex than with monocomponent droplets. The wettability of the surface, surface temperature, droplet impact velocity and size, liquid components, and the thermal properties of the liquid, all affect the droplet dynamics, evaporation and resulting micro-droplet formation. For a surface with patterned wettability, the pattern will confine liquid spreading, droplet shape formation and spontaneous droplet motion. The transient interaction between the droplet and mciro/nanostructured pattern has significant effects on the liquid’s spreading dynamics, and on heat transfer and evaporation. Furthermore, an evaporating multicomponent droplet will form concentration gradient inside the droplet which will be affected the internal flow circulation caused transient contact line variations around by the patterned surfaces. Therefore, it is essential to understand the effects of various parameters on the impingement, spreading and evaporation processes to engineer the various processes mentioned above. Wettability patterned surfaces can be fabricated utilizing micro/nanostructures. Nanofabrication techniques for fabricating transparent nanopillars will be developed for providing transparent patterned surfaces. Experiments will be carried out to investigate the impact dynamics, heat transfer and evaporation of water droplets on the wettability patterned surfaces using time-resolved micro-resolution particle image velocimetry (µPIV), advanced 3-component phase-Doppler anemometry (PDA), a high speed fringe interference measurement system, a fast response temperature micro-sensor array and a scanning electron microscope (SEM). These measuring techniques will provide the information about droplet size and velocity, droplet contact diameter, dynamic contact angle, internal flow of the droplet, the temperature distribution on the surface, liquid spreading and evaporation processes for various wettability patterns and surface morphologies. The transient substrate temperature and variable droplet profile will provide the boundary conditions for numerical modeling and simulation which was not considered in previous studies. Based on the results of the proposed study, an optimization method for patterning to improve the surface wettability control and multicomponent droplet evaporation will be suggested. The corresponding microstructures, droplet velocity and size, substrate temperature distribution, liquid properties, and surface patterns will be modeled and compared through experiment.

16207515.label: Realisation of objectives
16207515.value: To study multicomponent droplet dynamics and evaporation on wettability-patterned surfaces, it is important to understand the contact line dynamics and heat transfer of a sessile multicomponent droplet on a heated surface. Specifically, a detection technique that can measure local concentration of an evaporating multicomponent droplet and the contact line dynamics under different thermal boundary conditions and surface wettabilities are crucial. Therefore, it is important to predict contact line dynamics and local concentration under different surface wetting conditions in order to understand their effects on the response of evaporation. To measure the internal flow dynamics during multicomponent droplet spreading and evaporation on different surfaces, a novel AIE based direct visualization technique has been developed. The research is the first demonstration of local concentration mapping inside an evaporating binary droplets utilizing the Aggregation-Induced Emission material. The concentration gradients of the evaporating binary THF/water droplets can be visualized and investigated by tracking the fluorescence intensity profile of p-AIEgens. Using the function of fluorescence intensity versus water volume fraction in THF/water mixtures, the average concentration kinetics of the evaporating droplets can be determined. Fluorescence intensity difference along the droplet surface layer can be observed during the first and second evaporation stages, which can be translated as the local concentration. This offers the possibility to obtain the local surface tension difference on the drop surface. We also studied the evaporation of sessile THF/water droplet on a heated surface to understand multicomponent droplet evaporation process. Fluorescence intensity enhancement had been observed when the droplet was evaporating on the heated substrate. Hence the high substrate temperature enhances the THF evaporation of the binary droplet during the first two evaporation stages. Moreover, the increment of intensity caused by heating is varied along the droplet surface. The intensity increment near the edge area is larger than it at the apex area, which indicates that the higher substrate temperate enhance the THF evaporation on the droplet surface layer, especially near the contact line area. Additionally, p-AIEgen is selected for this work due to the following characteristics: a. the increasing fluorescence intensity is in a monotonic fashion upon the water adding; b. p-AIEgen is suitable in a range of particle size that is small enough to be evenly dispersed in the droplet; c. This p-AIEgen shows good photo-stability upon continuous laser excitation during the first and second evaporation stage without any fluorescence intensity quenched. The method of using AIEgens to visualize the concentration distribution can be used for different binary water/solvent systems. To understand the evaporation/boiling on a wettability-patterned surface, experimental investigations were conducted to compare a hydrophilic surface with a wettability-patterned surface significantly enhanced the heat transfer performance under flow boiling conditions. It is found that on a wettability-patterned surface, the liquid will first nucleate on the hydrophobic islands and the shapes will be affected by the patterns. This significantly increase the nucleation site density. The vapor on the wettability-patterned surface shows longer triple contact lines, which increases evaporation flux and helps dissipate the heat flux. The vapor will “jump” from the hydrophilic networks to hydrophobic islands when they reach the hydrophilic and hydrophobic boundary, which helps improve the vapor mobility. Experimental results show that the heat transfer performance of a wettability-patterned microchannel outweighs the hydrophilic one. Vapor dynamics help reveal the mechanics behind this significant improvement. We compared the flow boiling performance on the patterned surface at three mass fluxes and found that when the mass flux increases, heat transfer performance will improve accordingly and flow patterns will affect the heat transfer performance. An analytical model of local forces on a three-phase line is applied to analyze the minimum requirement for the bubbles to depart/move. With wettability data of both surfaces, the local forces model proves that the minimum requirement of vapor departure/movement on a wettability-patterned surface is much smaller than on a hydrophobic surface. This model also gives a useful insight to combine different wettability characteristics, such as pitch sizes and distances to increase vapor departure frequency/mobility and then improve flow boiling heat transfer in a microchannel. To study the droplet impact dynamics and heat transfer on a micro/nanostructured surface with heat transfer, a novel doubly reentrant microcavity with different cell sizes were fabricated utilizing improved fabrication techniques. Compared with conventional closed cell only structure, pillared and doubly reentrant pillared surfaces, the new design demonstrated better static repellency and dynamic pressure resistance in both room/freezing temperature conditions under different Webber number conditions. The newly developed surface can not only successfully suspend the liquid with extremely low surface tension but also can repel droplets with an impact Weber number as high as 1000 under a room temperature condition which is twice higher than previous research. The contact time during impacting on the new surface was highly reduced compared with traditional superhydrophobic surface. Theoretical analysis of estimating the droplet impacting pressure at the initial phase, adiabatic compression model, noted as ‘air-spring’ effect, which was used to describe the pressure change inside the cavities, and Laplace breakthrough & Canthotaxis effect was conducted for the micro wetting behavior at the top. Calculation results revealed the breakthrough pressure for our new surface was three times as large as that of closed cell surface, which was the best traditional design. The two mechanisms work together in hybrid state to render the new surface with higher wetting resistance ability.

16207515.label: Major findings and research outcome
16207515.value: In this research, utilizing novel Aggregation-Induced Emission (AIE) visualization technique, it is found that the internal flow and contact line dynamics of a multicomponent droplet can be visualized as the following: the internal flow is manipulated by the thermal boundary conditions with very strong solutal and thermal Marangoni effects; the liquid composition near the contact line is mainly water because THF is more volatile than water (Cai et al. 2017). Therefore, the contact line dynamics of a multicomponent droplet is similar to a pure water droplet under heating and evaporating conditions which is competing with the solutal Marangoni effect. This process can significantly affect droplet dynamics and evaporation which are important in multicomponent droplet evaporation prediction and control. Furthermore, it is the first time the instantaneous local component concentration can be measured utilizing the novel AIE technique. The interfacial contact line dynamics on wettability-patterned surfaces and micro/nanostructured surfaces are found to have unique features which can be used to further manipulate the contact line dynamics and heat transfer. It is possible to control the droplet dynamics under very low temperature by using novel doubly reentrant microcavity with different cell sizes (Liao et al. 2019). This newly developed surfaces can rebound high Weber number droplet under very low surface temperature compared to the dynamics process of a droplet on a conventional micro/nanostructured surface. An improved local pinning/depinning force model on the wettability-patterned surface was employed for analyzing the critical receding contact angles on homogenous and patterned surfaces. We systematically studied the full spectrum of dynamics of droplets/bubbles on hydrophobic-network surfaces under different heating conditions. It is found that wettability-patterned surfaces can significantly manipulate the contact lines and hence the heat transfer (Wang et al. 2019). We also developed general models for analysis and accurately predicted the stage transition.

16207515.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16207515.value: The newly developed wettability-patterned hydrophilic/hydrophobic and nanostructured surfaces can control the droplet dynamics and heat transfer. The pattern size, pitch distance and wettability are three key parameters affecting the contact line dynamics and heat transfer which need to be optimized. It was found that the multicomponent droplet contact line dynamics is similar to the pure water’s ones which help us better understanding in numerical modeling. Furthermore, the wettability patterned surfaces and micro/nanostructured surfaces can be further developed for different applications. The pattern size confines the size of the droplet/bubble and the pitch distance controls the interaction of the adjacent droplets/bubbles. Since the heat transfer efficiency changes with the heat flux, the patterns with different sizes and pitch distances should have different optimal working conditions. Optimization of these two variables is a complicated but interesting topic. Systematic research on this topic would provide key parameters for better control of droplet dynamics, contact line pinning/depinning and irregular droplet/bubble shape and droplet/bubble array formation which have promising potential in evaporation control, electronics cooling and other droplet/bubble microfluidic applications.

16207515.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16207515.value: Contact line dynamics and evaporation of multicomponent droplets at the microscale is relevant to microfluidics, drop on demand 3D printing devices, lab-on-a-chip devices and industrial applications. The current project focused on the fundamental phenomena of droplet dynamics, contact line behavior and heating microdroplets on wettability-patterned surfaces that affect droplet internal flow, shape, evaporation, and interaction in mini/micro spaces. Interfacial contact line dynamics on wettability-patterned surface is found to have a significant impact on multicomponent droplet evaporation, flow boiling and anti-icing applications. The effects of surface wetting contact line length, droplet pinning and depinning on droplet dynamics and heat transfer are investigated for the first time. It was crucial to non-invasively measure transient droplet contact line and film thickness in mini/micro spaces, especially, near the interface between the micro droplet and the wall surface. A novel AIE visualization technique for a mini/micro space measurement has been developed. Internal local concentration of a multicomponent droplet is visualized at the first time. Based on our findings, because surface-wettability patterns have a significant impact on the droplet dynamics, pinning/depinning, evaporation, heat and mass transfer processes, the technique helps to better design and optimize microfluidic droplet/bubble devices, such as droplet evaporators, electronics cooling devices, etc.

16207615.label: Realisation of objectives
16207615.value: Following the original submitted proposal, we have carefully conducted this project aiming at matching closely its objectives. We give details below and in a companion attachment in section 11. Objective 1: We studied the impact of the A-site composition by changing the ratio of La to Sr in the original material as well as the nonstoichiometry. We have investigated the effect that such a modification has on the conductivity, electrochemical activity, as well as the speed at which the nanoparticles exsolve. We monitored the latter by electrochemical impedance spectra and ex-situ scanning electron microscopy. We found the A-site element to have a significant impact on the conductivity but no impact on the nanoparticle growth dynamics and the relative activity improvement following the nanoparticle growth. Objective 2: Complimentarily with Objective 1, we studied the impact of the B-site composition and nonstoichiometry on the electrochemical properties (conductivity and electrochemical activity). As we did for the A-site element study, we tracked conductivity, electrochemical activity, and the growth rate of the nanoparticles. The latter property was studied by ex-situ scanning electron microscopy at different exsolution times and by monitoring the evolution of the electrochemical impedance spectra during exsolution. According to our findings, the B-site element has a significant impact on all the above-mentioned properties. The nanoparticle growth speed and the activities are higher the more reducible the B-site transition metal is. B-site nonstoichiometry is detrimental to the stability of the material. Objective 3: We has benchmarked the materials and documented their stable activity in a lab-scale setup for over 100 hours, we found the conductivity to be stable and all studied indicators of the activity to be stable over that timeframe. Even the introduction of Si in the B-site of the studied material had no visible effect on these properties. Meanwhile, the activity and conductivity were enhanced. Objective 4: We deposited well-defined thin films made by PLD and tested the films' characteristics. The deposited films were dense, as shown in Section 11, and stable under the conditions representative of anode operation. Objective 5: The deposited materials have been studied using scanning probe microscopy to determine the surface characteristics. Density functional theory has been employed to compare the exsolution behavior under a number of conditions, including surface terminations and orientations representative of real operating conditions. The exsolution energetics and surface stability have also been studied as a function of these properties. Objective 6: We extended the thin film models to the situation where the current collector is embedded beneath the surface to maximize the area available to reactions. In conditions representative of anode material operation, we discovered that the current collector position, spacing, and width have a substantial impact on the measured impedance and the observed area-specific resistance. We also developed a continuum-level model for the nanoparticle exsolution dynamics to interpret some of the results obtained as part of Objectives 1 and 2. The model allowed us to study of the factors limiting the nanoparticle size evolution versus exsolution time. We found the nanoparticle growth dynamics to be controlled either by the availability of reducible B-site dopants or the intrinsic nanoparticles’ strain. Our modeling results have been used by other research groups in high-profile articles. Objective 7: To gain additional mechanistic insight, we have developed a mechano-chemical model aimed at elucidating the impact of the strain and external chemical environment on the surface composition of thin films and bulk samples. The continuum model solves is thermodynamically consistent and solves for the concentration of defects, electric field, and stresses using the Poisson-Nernst-Planck set of equations couples with mechanical equilibrium condition. The results of the simulations with this model have been compared to the XPS experiments.

16207615.label: Major findings and research outcome
16207615.value: Firstly, we have investigated the factors that affect the exsolution mechanism anode materials for solid oxide fuel cells (SOFCs). We also linked that insight to the electrochemical activity and the embedded nanoparticle growth dynamics. The insight was gained thanks to a combined experimental and modeling effort. From the experimental point of view, we synthesized materials of various compositions, monitored their electrochemical impedance response through time, and tested their surface characteristics, including composition, the oxidation state of elements, and catalytic activity. This data allowed us to benchmark continuum-level models for the growth of the nanoparticles, for the catalytic response of thin films, and for the energetics of atomic segregation towards surfaces. The important insight gained mainly center around two areas. First, we were able to propose new materials compositions that are more catalytically active in comparison to previously existing materials. In addition to that, we found that surface termination and B-site cationic composition are two major factors affecting the composition of the surface where the A-site element has an impact only on the concentration of defects. Second, we developed new models that are now used widely to assess the nanoparticle growth dynamics and responses of thin films, allowing the identification of the surface reaction rate k and the bulk diffusion coefficient D underpinning the reactivity of the materials. These findings are now serving as a reference for the rational development of SOFC anode materials capable of exsolution.

16207615.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16207615.value: The research grant allowed us to 1) understand the growth mechanism of nanoparticles; 2) design new high-performance compositions. This was possible because experiments and computations were combined. Looking forward, there are tremendous opportunities for follow-up works. First, we could refine the current continuum models to further improve their predictive power and to probe the nucleation and growth of nanoparticles in dedicated in-situ experiments. Second, since the density functional theory models have been validated through this project, it would be interesting to run high-throughput calculations aiming at studying the stability and activity of the materials. This effort could be coupled with machine learning to allow an additional optimization of high-performance compositions.

16207615.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16207615.value: SOFCs are very promising energy conversion devices because of their high thermodynamic efficiency. However, the stability of their materials can still be improved by adding highly stable nanoparticles. During this project, we studied several oxide materials that can grow catalytically active embedded nanoparticles on their surfaces. We investigated such materials by a combined experimental and computational effort. Thanks to that, we unraveled the relationship between chemical composition and optimal nanoparticle size as well as rationale guidelines for the development of new anode materials. Leveraging this fundamental study, we synthesized for the first time La0.4Sr0.4Sc0.9Ni0.1O3-δ (LSSN), a highly active and stable material showing considerable promise as an electrode for SOFCs.

16207715.value: 模拟等离子运动的多尺度气体动理学方法

16207715.label: Project Objectives
16207715.value: To develop a unified kinetic scheme based on the simplified Vlasov-BGK-Poisson equation. This scheme will be used to simulate the plasma dynamics in both the collisionless and MHD regimes to validate the basic approach. To construct the interface flux through integral solution of the Fokker-Planck equation, which incorporates the magnetic field and Landau operator. In order to improve the accuracy, the magneto-electric field equations and the kinetic equation for the charged particles will be coupled and solved simultaneously. To apply the scheme to complex cross-regime test cases and compare the results with experimental data and benchmark solutions from other schemes.

16207715.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16207715.value: The study of non-equilibrium gases and plasmas is very important in science and engineering. The aim of this proposal is to develop physical models and numerical methods for simulating non-equilibrium plasmas. The related aerospace applications include electric propulsion for spacecraft control and hypersonic aerothermodynamics for flight at high speed. For non-equilibrium flows, the current simulation methods are mostly particle methods, such as direct simulation Monte Carlo, particle-in- ell, and molecular dynamics. For equilibrium flows, the continuum methods based on the Euler, Navier-Stokes, and magneto-hydrodynamics equations are commonly used. The major difficulties in plasma simulation are capturing the flow physics between the kinetic and hydrodynamic regimes, and that many plasma phenomena have to be studied in this transition regime. A multi-scale method should be able to properly capture the flow physics from the particle transport and collision in the kinetic scale, to the accumulating wave propagation in the hydrodynamic scale. Due to the unified treatment of particle transport and collision in direct modeling, a unified gas kinetic scheme (UGKS) has been successfully developed and used for the non-equilibrium neutral gas simulation. The current research project is to further develop the unified scheme for the plasma flow simulation. More specifically, we will construct and use a multiple scale integral solution of the Fokker-Planck model for the numerical flux evaluation in the numerical scheme. The scheme will capture the flow physics from the Fokker-Planck transport in the kinetic scale to the magneto-hydrodynamics in the continuum one.

16207715.label: Realisation of objectives
16207715.value: Through this project, we have conducted research in the following aspects. For the first time, a unified gas kinetic scheme (UGKS) for multi-scale and multi-component plasma transport was constructed. The current scheme is a direct modeling method, where the time evolution solutions from the Vlasov-BGK equations of electron and ion and the Maxwell equations are used to construct a scale-dependent plasma simulation model. As a result, with the changing of modeling scales of cell Knudsen number and Larmor radius, which are defined as the ratio of particle mean free path over the cell size and the circulating radius of electron around magnetic field lines, the plasma physics from the collisionless particle transport to the magneto-hydrodynamic evolution is captured. In other words, the discretized UGKS formulation covers a wide range of plasma evolution regimes. The physics recovered in UGKS ranges from the Vlasov equation in the kinetic scale to different-type magneto-hydrodynamic (MHD) equations in the hydrodynamic scale. The UGKS provides a more general evolution model than the Vlasov equation in the kinetic scale and many types of MHD equations in the hydrodynamic scale, such as the two fluids model, the Hall, the resistive, and the ideal MHD equations. All above specific governing equations become the subsets of the UGKS. The key dynamics in UGKS is the un-splitting treatment of particle collision, acceleration, and transport in the construction of numerical flux across a cell interface, and this flux is a scale-dependent evolving solution of the Vlasov-BGK model. At the same time, the plasma evolution is coupled with the Maxwell equations in an implicit way, which automatically provides a smooth transition between the Ampere's law and the Ohm's law for the calculation of electric field. The time step of UGKS is not limited by the relaxation time, the cyclotron period, and the speed of light in the MHD regime. Our scheme is able to give a physically accurate solution for plasma simulation with a large variation of Knudsen number and normalized Larmor radius. It can be used to simulate the phenomena from the Vlasov limit to the scale of plasma skin depth for the capturing of two-fluid effect, and the phenomena in the plasma transition regime with a modest Knudsen number and Larmor radius in a unified smoothly transitional way. The UGKS is validated by numerical test cases, such as the Landau damping and two stream instability in the kinetic regime, and the Brio-Wu shock tube problem and the Orszag-Tang MHD turbulence problem in the hydrodynamic regime. The scheme is also used to study the geospace environment modeling (GEM), such as the challenging magnetic reconnection problem in the transition regime. At the same time, the magnetic reconnection mechanism of the Sweet-Parker model and the Hall effect model can be connected smoothly through the variation of Larmor radius in the UGKS simulations. Overall, the UGKS is a physically reliable multi-scale plasma simulation method. It provides a powerful and unified approach for the study of plasma physics. Through the current study, a better way to discreize the Maxwell equations and incorporate it with the evolution equations of ions and electrons has been figured out, and an enlarged time step has been used. At the same time, a two fluids model for magneto-hydrodynamics (MHD) has been developed and compared its solutions with the single component MHD equations. The acceleration technique for the UGKS has been tested with the increase its efficiency. Recently, the wave-particle version of UGKS for plasma simulation without using discrete particle velocity space has been constructed and the computational efficiency can be improved by hundreds of times in the hypersonic flow computation. The memory cost of the wave particle version method can be reduced by two orders of magnitudes in comparison with the original UGKS-plasma.

16207715.label: Major findings and research outcome
16207715.value: Through this project, a multi-scale numerical method for multi-species plasma simulation in the whole flow regimes has been constructed. The UGKS takes into account the collisions among electrons and ions, and their coupling with the full Maxwell equations. The UGKS describes the plasma evolution on the mesh size and time step scales, which intrinsically provides the fundamental multi-scale discretized governing equations. The flow physics covered by the current scheme is more general than those from either the collisionless Vlasov equation or MHD equations in the corresponding kinetic or hydrodynamic limit alone. More importantly, the UGKS can give a reliable physical solution in the transitional regime as well, which has not been fully explored before from the particle-based and MHD-based numerical methods. In the generalized Brio-Wu test case, the UGKS presents a smooth transition from neutral fluid results to the MHD solutions. At the same time, with the time evolution the results from the kinetic Vlasov equation and the solutions from the hydrodynamic two-fluid system have been recovered in the single UGKS formulation. The study of the Orszag-Tang turbulence problem shows the ability of the UGKS in capturing all kinds of MHD solutions and recovering the magnetic reconnection mechanism under different conditions. The UGKS is also able to capture the phenomena on the scale of Debye length, such as the fast magnetic reconnection in GEM case. The direct modeling methodology makes it possible to construct UGKS for the study of multi-scale transport in the rarefied gas dynamics, radiative transfer, and plasma physics.

16207715.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16207715.value: The unified gas-kinetic scheme (UGKS) provides a framework for simulating multiscale transport with the updates of both gas distribution function and macroscopic flow variables on the cell size and time step scales. The multiscale dynamics in UGKS is achieved through the coupled particle transport and collision in the particle evolution process within a time step. In order to further improve the numerical method, under the UGKS framework, we are proposing an efficient multiscale unified gas-kinetic wave-particle (UGKWP) method. The gas dynamics in UGKWP method is described by the individual particle movement coupled with the evolution of the probability density function (PDF). During a time step, the trajectories of simulation particles are tracked until collision happens, and the post-collision particles are evolved collectively through the evolution of the corresponding distribution function. The evolution of simulation particles and distribution function is guided by the evolution of macroscopic variables, and guarantees the conservation of the scheme in the final wave-particle formulation. The computational cost of the scheme including the computational time and memory cost is on the same level as the most efficient method in the corresponding regime, such as the particle methods in the rarefied regime and hydrodynamic solvers in continuum regime.

16207715.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16207715.value: Generally, plasma is a medium with positive, negative, and neutral particles. It is quasi-neutral on the length scale larger than the Debye length. The plasma concerned is the weakly coupled plasma, such as the plasma in the solar corona, the magnetosphere around the Earth, the plasma inside a Tokamak. The motion of charged particles in a plasma is coupled with the evolution of electromagnetic field. The flow regime of a plasma is more complex than that of a neutral gas. Numerical methods have been developed for plasma simulation since 1950s, such as the particle-in-cell (PIC) method, the kinetic Vlasov solvers, and the hydrodynamic MHD solvers. In this project, for the first time a multi-scale method is developed for the plasma simulation. The corresponding scheme is based on the space and time evolution solution of the Vlasov-BGK equations for electron and ion, and the Maxwell equations for electromagnetic field. With the variation of Knudsen number, inter-species collision frequency, and dimensionless Larmor radius, the scheme unifies the solutions in the kinetic Vlasov regime, the two-fluid regime, and the MHD regime with a smooth transition among them.

16207915.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16207915.value: The past few years have witnessed an explosion of data in wide-ranging applications, and this is creating major opportunities and novel scientific challenges. A difficult task is extracting informative, but typically well-hidden patterns from such data for various purposes. For example, data collected from large-scale distributed sensor networks must be processed to facilitate real-time environmental monitoring, while the wealth of recently available DNA sequences may be processed to guide novel vaccine design against infectious diseases. Due to the unprecedented size and complexity of modern data sets, developing novel statistical techniques that can identify hidden patterns in big data has become critically important. Conventional statistical tools are typically equipped to only handle relationships that are either (i) linear or (ii) specialized for two variables. These tools are ill-suited to identifying complex patterns in big data applications that often manifest as complicated non-linear associations between multiple variables. There is an urgent need to develop tools that can account for such complexities and extract meaningful inference. The proposed project will address this critical requirement by developing a powerful statistical framework for accurately quantifying non-linear associations between multiple variables, and then use these associations to develop efficient density estimation algorithms. The first step will be to propose a novel and accurate multi-variate association measure based on the information-theoretic concept of mutual information. The second step will involve designing innovative noise-cleaning methods to improve the accuracy of the multi-variate association measure, using ideas from tensor theory. The third step will employ the association measure to develop a sophisticated, fast and accurate density estimation algorithm. These three innovations will form the backbone of a powerful statistical inference framework with wide applicability to numerous scientific fields. The utility of the proposed framework will be demonstrated by expanding upon the PI and Co-Is’ preliminary work [1,2,22] in designing vaccines for hepatitis C and HIV, which only considered linear associations between variable pairs. The PI and Co-I McKay have strong backgrounds in information theory, multivariate statistics and random matrix theory, which are the key mathematical techniques required for the successful completion of the project. Co-I Chakraborty is a world-expert in immunology and computational biology, and his experience will be essential in applying the association measure to vaccine design. 過去幾年見證了爆發的數據廣泛應用於各領域，此情況正在創造大量機會以及新穎的科學挑戰。難處在於從用於各種目的的數據當中提取資訊的模式，而此種模式往往是隱藏的。例如，必須處理從大規模分佈式傳感器網路收集而來的數據，以便於即時監測環境，而最近可獲得的豐富的DNA序列可被處理，從而引導對抗傳染病的新型疫苗設計。由於現代數據庫空前的規模和複雜性，發展可識別大數據中隱藏模式的新統計方法日益重要。傳統的統計工具通常只配備處理的關係是(i)線性的或(ii)特定於兩個變量。在大數據應用中，這些工具不適合識別複雜的模式，這些複雜的模式經常表現為多變量之間的複雜非線性關聯。目前迫切需要發展出可說明此種複雜性並提取有意義推理的工具。 藉由發展出能夠精準量化多變量之間的非線性關聯的強大統計架構，我們提出的計畫將解決這個關鍵的需求，並且利用這些關聯，發展出有效的密度估算法。第一步驟是基於互信息的信息論概念，提出一新穎且準確的多元關聯測量。第二步驟中，利用張量理論的概念，設計創新的干擾清除法以改善多元關聯測量的精準度。第三步驟將採用關聯測量，以發展一成熟、快速且準確的密度估算法。這三個創新將形成強大的統計推理架構骨幹，且廣泛適用於眾多科學領域。藉由擴展C型肝炎和HIV設計疫苗中PI與Co-Is的前期工作 [1,2,22]，將能說明該架構的效用，其中前期工作[1,2,22]僅考慮變量對之間的線性關聯。

16207915.label: Realisation of objectives
16207915.value: All key objectives have been successfully met. The project has produced numerous contributions, leading to 4 publications in leading journals. It has supported 1 Ph.D. student. Objective 1: Investigate suitable novel association measures that can detect and quantify nonlinear associations between multiple variables. The first objective was completely addressed, with the main results reported in Journal Paper 1 and Journal Paper 4. We introduced a computational framework to infer a “direct information” measure which can detect and quantify nonlinear associations between multiple variables. In this framework, we first introduced an approach to determine the optimal number of parameters to be estimated. Secondly, we extended upon an algorithm from statistical physics called “Minimum Probability Flow”. We considered both a “Potts” extension which accounts for more than two values per variable, and a data-driven regularization procedure. As a final step, we refined the parameters using a gradient descent algorithm. These parameters were then used to form the association measure. We verified the accuracy of the association measure by applying it to an important biological application: detecting contact residues in a protein. Specifically, we compared our measure with the native crystal structure of the protein, which is indicative of the residues in contact. We also considered other association measures, such as mutual information and Pearson correlation. Our results indicate our measure had the highest predictive accuracy. This is because of its ability to detect direct association between variables, in contrast to other measures like mutual information which also detects indirect associations, thus producing false positives. We applied this measure to real protein sequence data collected from multiple patients, including the p24, gp41 and gp120 proteins in HIV. These proteins are large in size, i.e., there are a large number of variables, and thus conventional algorithms do not scale well. In contrast, our framework was able to infer association measures for these large proteins quite fast, in some cases, orders of magnitude faster than previous algorithms. Methods for estimating non-linear association measures were also presented in Journal Paper 2. Here, we proposed a new tool called RoCA (robust co-evolutionary analysis), a random-matrix-based sparse principal component analysis (PCA) algorithm. We showed RoCA was able to reliably predict co-evolutionary sectors of various proteins. Sectors are comprised of non-linearly-associated amino acids, and we showed that our inferred sectors showed close correspondence with experimentally-known biochemical domains, verifying the accuracy of RoCA. The non-linear association measures developed in this project are important, and have led to important contributions by presenting fast and accurate algorithms to infer association measures for high-dimensional data. Objective 2: Investigate novel noise-cleaning approaches for providing robust estimates of the proposed association measure with limited data samples. This objective was completely addressed, with the main results reported in Journal Paper 1 and Journal Paper 4. Our computational framework to estimate the association measures contained two key noise-cleaning procedures, both attempting to achieve a balance between overfitting and underfitting the data. First, we found that due to sampling noise, estimating too many parameters had the negative effect of overfitting to noise. We thus implemented a data-driven approach to choose the number of parameters to achieve a good balance between overfitting and underfitting. We verified this approach by comparison with models with different numbers of parameters, and showed that the model with the number of parameters chosen by our method was able to better predict the fitness of HIV strains. Secondly, we applied regularization to both the algorithm used to initially estimate the parameters required for the association measure, and the gradient descent algorithm to refine these parameters. We employed L1 and L2 regularization, to adjust the parameters to achieve a balance between overfitting and underfitting the data. The regularization parameters were chosen using a data-driven approach, and were found to result in very accurate association measures, when compared with viral protein contact information. In addition, we introduced noise-cleaning methods in Journal Paper 2, based on random matrix theory and sophisticated sparsity techniques, resulting in our proposed RoCA algorithm. These techniques resulted in robust estimation of protein sectors, which we showed were highly correlated with structural or functional domains. We compared our methods to the conventional “Statistical Coupling Analysis” (SCA) algorithm and classical PCA methods. Our results revealed that these methods are highly sensitive to noise, while RoCA was able to distinguish structural or functional domains with a high degree of accuracy. We applied our methods to a number of proteins in HCV in addition to other proteins, demonstrating robustness and range of applicability. Robust performance was also demonstrated on ground-truth synthetic tests. Our work is important as we proposed highly-effective noise cleaning approaches, which we showed were robust to limited data samples. Objective 3: Design a novel density estimation algorithm that can capture non-linear associations between multiple variables in big data. This objective was completely addressed, with results in Journal Paper 1 and 4. The computational framework we developed was used to estimate the density of multiple-variables, accounting for non-linear associations. Specifically, the density is represented by the so-called “maximum entropy” model. This model requires estimation of two types of parameters, the “field” and “coupling” parameters. The coupling parameters capture the non-linear association between variables. A key contribution of our framework is to accurately and efficiently estimate both the field and coupling parameters. These parameters can simply be plugged into the maximum entropy model, to obtain an estimate of the density. We successfully applied this framework to a “big-data” scenario, specifically gp160, the largest protein of HIV, which comprises of millions of parameters. Objective 4: Apply the density estimation algorithm to design enhanced vaccine strategies for viruses. This objective was successfully completed in Journal Papers 1 and 3. In Journal Paper 1, we applied the computational framework developed in the previous objectives to the gp160 protein in HIV. Gp160 is the external protein of HIV, and is the key target for an antibody-based design. Using our framework, we found potential hot-spots of the gp160 protein, which when targeted by the immune system, can result in a significant reduction in viral fitness. This can subsequently lead to a reduction in viral load and thus can be used to design enhanced vaccine strategies which can elicit an immune response against these hot-spots. We then applied the same framework to the E2 protein of HCV in Journal Paper 3. We combined our framework with a sophisticated evolutionary model to determine the antibodies which can result in the most significant reduction in viral-load. This allowed us to quantify the effectiveness of a vaccine with these antibodies.

16207915.label: Major findings and research outcome
16207915.value: Below is a brief summary of some the major contributions in this project: [Journal Papers 1 and 4]: These papers proposed a new computational framework to infer association measures between random variables, which subsequently can be used for density estimation with application to vaccine design strategies. The proposed framework allowed for fast and accurate estimation of association measures which are resilient to noise. This is achieved through sophisticated data-driven parameter selection and regularization. We applied this framework to the external protein of HIV, where we found vulnerable regions which when targeted, can lead to a reduced viral load. Knowledge of these regions can thus inform the design of effective vaccines which can induce an immune response targeting these regions. The proposed framework would be of interest to researchers and practitioners who seek to obtain fast and accurate association measures, and who seek to analyze viral data. [Journal Paper 2]: The paper introduced efficient, noise-robust methods using ideas from random matrix theory for inferring non-linear associations between groups of interacting variables, from a high-dimensional data set. The results showed excellent performance when applied to protein data for HIV and HCV, and on synthetic model constructions. In addition, the results were compared against other benchmark techniques, and revealed significantly improved performance. The developed methods, RoCA, presents a useful tool for bioinformatic analysis of high-dimensional data. [Journal Paper 3]: This paper presented a quantitative comparison of the effectiveness of antibodies targeting the E2 protein in HCV. This was achieved through a sophisticated evolutionary simulation model combined with the computational framework in Journal Papers 1 and 4, which was used to infer association measures. We found a specific antigenic domain which we predicted to be an ideal target for an antibody-based vaccine, due to reduction in viral load as a consequence of escape mutations in this domain. Our computational approach presents an effective technique to determine effective vaccines, and alleviates the need for expensive and time-consuming experiments. The results of the project were published in high-impact journals, including PNAS and Nature Communications. Their impact was also reported in local and international media, at the Annual Convention of the Hong Kong Hospital Authority, and through an invited talk at the World Economic Forum (see Part C of this completion report).

16207915.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16207915.value: There are various avenues for further development. Here we briefly indicate a few such directions. We have applied our algorithms to the external protein of specific viral subtypes of HIV and HCV, which infect a certain fraction of the population. Two immediate extensions are possible. The first is to apply these algorithms to other subtypes, with the aim of developing a vaccine which can be effective for a large group of people. One difficultly lies in the number of sequences available for these other subtypes. More stringent noise-cleaning approaches will need to be investigated. The second is to apply our algorithms to other proteins, which are the target of T-cell based vaccines. In-silico or experimentally determined methods can be used to obtain the T-cell epitopes for HIV or HCV. Another avenue for development is using the proposed framework to design the optimal combination of antibodies and T-cell responses, instead of designing a vaccine for just one antibody. This will require extensions to the evolutionary algorithm to account for this additional complexity, and has the potential to lead to more efficient vaccines.

16207915.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16207915.value: The project has provided new computational algorithms to estimate non-linear association measures between random variables. Our algorithms are fast, accurate, and robust to limited data. We verified our algorithms through extensive comparisons with biological data, and showed our algorithms perform favorably compared to existing algorithms. We applied our algorithms to viral data with the aim of predicting vulnerable regions of the viral proteins, and to quantify the effectiveness of different antibodies. This has the potential to inform effective vaccine design, alleviating the need for costly and time-consuming experiments.

16208115.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16208115.value: Major cities around the world are becoming more and more congested due to economic development and urbanization. To efficiently make use of space to relieve traffic congestion, and to protect the environment from excessive energy consumption and emissions due to traffic jams, it appears that underground metro systems have become the only viable transportation solution for many cosmopolitan cities worldwide such as New York, London, Singapore, Hong Kong and Shanghai. Due to an increasing demand for underground space, modern tunnels are constructed closer and closer to each other, particularly at the intersection of different metro lines. Any tunnel construction will inevitably cause stress changes in the ground and hence induce ground movements. Uncontrollable ground movements may cause adverse effects on nearby tunnels. It is not uncommon to encounter existing non-circular tunnels such as horseshoe and oval shaped during the construction of new shield driven circular tunnels, yet there is a lack of systematic investigation of interaction among multiple existing non-circular tunnels and modern new circular tunnels. Previous studies have mainly focused on the response of circular tunnels, however, the stress redistribution and deformation induced by adjacent new tunnel excavation may cause considerable large deformation and bending moment in non-circular tunnels due to their discontinuous hoop thrust transmission, possibly resulting in excessive tensile stress and cracking in the existing non-circular tunnel lining. In this proposed project, carefully planned, systematic three-dimensional centrifuge model tests will be carried out using the state-of-the-art geotechnical centrifuge at HKUST to investigate and understand closely spaced interactions among an existing non-circular (i.e., horseshoe and oval shaped) tunnel and up to two new perpendicularly crossing circular tunnels in sand and clay. By using advanced constitutive models, which can capture strain-dependent and stress path-dependent soil stiffness at small strains, three-dimensional numerical back-analyses of selected centrifuge model tests and a parametric study will be carried out to improve our fundamental understanding of closely spaced tunnel interactions and to develop design calculation charts for the safe and economical designs of modern circular tunnels adjacent to existing non-circular tunnels. Based on research findings, design guidelines and calculation charts will be developed to benefit the engineering profession directly and they will also have significant and positive impacts on the environment and the economy of major congested cities around the world.

All these two problems were tackled by further active recruitment and careful project management and planning. The project objectives were all met satisfactorily.
