16301415.label: Major findings and research outcome
16301415.value: 1. We measured high-bias conductance of single polyporphyrin molecular wires with the distance from 1.3 nm to 13 nm. We observed multiple sharp conductance peaks, conductance as high as 20 nS in wires of more than 10 nm long, and nearly length-independent conductance (attenuation < 0.001 Å−1). We revealed that the measured conductance is coherent resonant transport via a delocalized molecular orbital. (J. Am. Chem. Soc. 138, 11140 (2016).) 2. Spin crossover (SCO) is demonstrated in the single-molecule junctions of Fe-porphyrin formed in a scanning tunneling microscope, where the Fe spin state is reversibly and repeatedly switched between S=2 and S=1 by mechanically stretching or squeezing the junctions. These findings unravel how to realize robust and reversible manipulation of single-molecule spin states. (ACS Nano, 11, 6295 (2017).) 3. We study negative differential conductance (NDC) effects in polyporphyrin oligomers with nonlinear backbones. We selectively controlled the charge transport path in single oligomer wires. We observed robust NDC when charge passed through a T-shape junction, bistable NDC when charge passed through a 90° kink and no NDC when charge passed through a 120° kink. We attributed this backbone-dependent NDC to bias-modulated hybridization of the electrode states with the resonant transport molecular orbital. (J. Am. Chem. Soc. 140, 570 (2018).) 4. We show the on-surface synthesis of bimetallic porphyrin molecules on Au(111). We observed that three different species conformed the self-assembled molecular arrays. Their structural properties are studied by scanning tunneling microscopy and the inelastic spin excitations are spatially-resolved through low-temperature scanning tunneling spectroscopy. (manuscript of "Spin excitation in bimetallic porphyrin complexes") 5. We achieved the collective spin crossover of multiple Ni atoms by the correlated switching in the coordination chains on Au(111). The combined STM, STS and DFT investigations reveal the alternate arrangement of HS-Ni and LS-Ni atoms along the coordination chains. The spin states of the Ni atoms in the same coordination chain were found to switch collectively upon the local tip-excitation, resulting in the correlated manipulation of spin state of the Ni atoms. These results open up a way to employ the correlated process as an efficient approach to tuning the spintronic properties of supramolecular systems. (manuscript "Collectively Switching Spin State of Multiple Nickel Atoms by Single-Atom Stimulation in Coordination Chains" ) 6. We investigated the conformation relaxation and stabilization processes of two porphyrin derivatives from dome to saddle conformations on Au(111) and Pb(111). (J. Phys. Chem. Lett.2017, 8, 6, 1241-1247)

16301415.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16301415.value: The rich electronic and magnetic properties discovered in our studies open many new possibilities for further investigations, including mechanical, optical and chemical controlled conductivity of single molecules and molecular wires. For example, the object 4, which we have not fully explored, can be a very interesting work to do. To measure spin-dependent transport of the Ni wires synthesized in work (5) is also highly appealing since this system is a promising candidate for single-molecular spintronic device.

16301415.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16301415.value: In this project, we have synthesized series of molecular and macromolecular systems containing metal centers and measure their conductance. The ultimate goal is to use single molecules as electronic or magnetic devices, such as tiny conducting wires, switches, transistors or data storage medium. Our discoveries exemplify that the molecular and macromolecular systems exhibit some superb properties listed below. 1. A molecule wire can transmit electronic current with very low energy loss up to 10 nm, the record length reported in the literature. 2. A single magnet molecule can change its "magnet" when it is stressed slightly, making it a good candidate for information technology. 3. A molecular wire with a junction can be used as switch or transistor. 4. A chain of single atom "magnets" can be switched simultaneously and collectively like a domino.

16301515.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16301515.value: For the last twenty more years, physicists have used physical methods and concepts, which are not established mathematically and hence not accessible to mathematicians, to get a lot of predications which can be translated into mathematical conjectures. One of the most famous examples is the Gromov-Witten theory. In this theory, one studies a collection of formal power series (Gromov-Witten (GW) invariants) indexed by non-negative integers called genus. They are obtained from a space called Calabi-Yau (CY) three-fold. Even though the mathematical theory of Gromov-Witten theory is well-established, the verification of the physical predications is only done mathematically for genus equal to zero and one. Nevertheless, these are already great achievements which attract lots of talented people to work in this area and lead to many mathematical discoveries in terms of new concepts as well as new tools. Another example is the Landau-Ginzburg (LG) theory, which is mathematically constructed only recently. The so-called "space" here is a polynomial in several variables. This theory also has a collection of formal power series (Fan-Jarvis-Ruan-Witten (FJRW) invariants) indexed by the genus. Physicists believe that these two theories are the same in the physical terms. Mathematically, GW invariants and FJRW invariants should be related in a highly non-trivial way. This relation is called CY-LG correspondence. In mathematical physics, E. Witten proposed a gauged linear sigma model (GLSM) to link GW theory and FJRW theory using infinite dimensional path integrals. However, this method lacks a rigorous mathematics treatment. In this proposal, we plan to use the lately discovered "MSP field moduli" to calculate FJRW invariants and GW invariants for the quintic Calabi-Yau threefold. After the "cosection localization'' technique was invented, the PI with collaborators constructed through rigorous mathematics the algebro-geometric GW invariants as a nonaffine Landau-Ginzburg theory using P-fields, and the FJRW invariants as a Landau-Ginzburg theory using spin-fields. That work was funded by project GRF Grant 600711. Recently the PI and his collaborators (Jun Li, Weiping Li and Melissa Liu) have discovered that "mixed-spin-P fields"(MSP fields) create the background space in which one can relate these two LG-type of invariants naturally. From the physical point of view such a space unifies different moduli spaces of Witten's GLSM into one space. The goal of this proposed study is to use this master moduli space to find a correspondence between the GW invariants and FJRW invariants, and moreover, to compute both of them. 過去二十多年物理學家使用方法和概念得到很多數學上的猜想和預測. 然而這些方法多數在數學上是無法嚴格定義因此數學家無法直接使用. 一個最有名的例子是Gromov-Witten(GW)理論: 其中從一個給定的卡拉比-丘空間 人們 對每一個“虧格數”g=0,1,2,3...定義了一個冪級數Fg（係數為該空間的ＧＷ不變量）. 雖然該定義是數學上嚴格的, 對物理學家預測的Fg之計算, 數學家只能驗證 g=0的情形, 並對g>0(高虧格)情形束手無策. 無論如何 這些結果已吸引了非常多人並且引出了很多數學上的新發現,新概念,和新方法. 另外一個例子是Landau-Ginzburg(LG) 奇異點不變量, 其數學構造也是近幾年才完成. 這LG理論也是對每一個虧格數g=0,1,2..定義了一個冪級數(使用了FJRW不變量). 物理學家相信上述的GW和LG兩個看似極為不同的理論其實是“等價”的. 但要給出嚴格的兩理論間之數學關係 是一個非常困難並且至今尚未有明顯的辦法的問題. 此關係也被稱呼為”CY-LG”對應. 雖然E. Witten提出用規範線性sigma模式的無線維路徑積分(GLSM)來連結兩個理論, 這個方法在數學上很難加以嚴格定義並且研究. 主因是幾何上GW中出現的場無法真的在GLSM中變形成FJRW理論中的場. 在此項目中我們計劃使用最新發展的”MSP場”來計算五次三維卡拉比-丘空間的FJRW和ＧＷ不變量. 在”餘截面局部化”的技術被發現後, PI和合作者們在數學上嚴格的用非仿射平坦(帶曲率)LG模型來構造了代數幾何的GW不變量, 該構造的一主要想法是引入了所謂的”P場”. 平行地我們也利用所謂的”自旋場”來獲得FJRW理論的代數幾何構造. 這兩個工作是由GRF 600711經費資助的. 最近PI和合作者(李駿,李衛平,劉秋菊)發現使用”自旋場和P場的混合場”（簡稱混合自旋P場)可以將兩個上述的LG理論放在同一個幾何空間中以得到兩種理論的互相作用. 從物理的觀點”混合自旋P場”的模空間是把各種不同參數的Witten的GLSM模空間統一起來成為一整體空間. 本研究項目的目的是使用這個模空間來,數學上嚴格的,獲得兩個理論 (GW 和 FJRW)的明確關係. 這提供了第一個能連結兩個高虧格理論的幾何方法.

16301515.label: Realisation of objectives
16301515.value: For objective 1, PI and collaborators has complete the full construction in sequence of papers. For objective 2, PI and collaborators did use torus localization and obtain the wanted combinatorial relations between GW and FJRW invariants, for all genus. For determination of low genus GW invariants, PI and collaborators managed to obtain g=1 and g=2 GW invariants of quintic completely. As for g=3, we obtain full infinite sequence of g=3 invariants up to 3g-3=6 many rational numbers as initial conditions. In this sense g=3 is also almost obtained. For FJRW invariants, the g=1 is obtained and the packaged algorithm toward determining g=2 is discovered in this project. The g=3 FJRW invariants remains a puzzle, but again, by the package, only up to 3g-3 conditions. PI and collaborators has managed to find very effective methods to package the CY invariant's structure. The method does use cosmological field theories. The package (from BCOV point of view) is completed for CY invariants, and expected to work for LG invariants in continuing project. This establish the hope of CY-LG correspondence rigorously.

16301515.label: Major findings and research outcome
16301515.value: The major finding in this project (2015-2018) is that the original proposed geometry does give very unexpected beautiful structures among the invariants of study, which was not even thought possible at the time the proposal was written. Roughly a Feynman structure between the curve counting theory of Calabi Yau threefold is exhibited, using the moduli of mixed spin P fields, the main object of study in this project. This solves a 25 year conjecture in mathematics raised from string theory. And as a consequence this determines the difficult invariants up to finite conditions. The case of g=2 Gromov Witten invariants are easily determined afterwards. To obtain this far-better-than-expected result, PI and collaborators wrote a sequence of papers(around 10 many) to establish every intermediate stages of argument. Namely the program was divided several stages of problems, each took 1 or more papers to be nailed. The last of these papers is "BCOV's Feynman rule of quintic 3- folds via NMSP" under review.

16301515.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16301515.value: There are many directions that our result opens up, such as (i) general method to handle arbitrary Calabi Yau threefold as complete intersections, (ii) constructions of the MSP moduli for Fano hyper surfaces, (iii) deeper relation between twisted large projective spaces' GW theory with that of B model antiholomorphic path integral, etc. Our research team (PI and collaborators) are moving toward these further directions of research, with more new students or postdocs joining us.

16301515.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16301515.value: The modern knowledge of Quantum Field Theory(QFT) is based on a kind of integral over infinite dimension bases. The infinity cause many obstructions for the mathematics to access the foundations of QFT. String theory aims to combine QFT with gravity. Surprisingly some versions of string theory provide a channel for mathematics to find a ``finite" counterpart of the infinite integral. Finiteness makes researcher excited and easier to give precise extension of the subject. However, as there are many ingredients and notions in original QFT, only very few parts of them admits finite counterparts. This research project helps find a new finite counterpart of the so called ``B twisted global topological string theory", in A model mathematics. This should revolutionize the future research of the A-B symmetric, called Mirror Symmetry.

16301815.label: Realisation of objectives
16301815.value: The objective of this project is to synthesize high-valent heterometallic nitrido complexes and to study their bonding, structure, electrochemistry and reactivity. The application of bimetallic nitrido complexes as catalysts for organic reactions has been explored. In this project, we have developed a synthetic route to heterometallic nitrido complexes starting from terminal nitrido complexes. Specifically, a family of heterometallic nitrido porphyrin complexes of group 8 and 9 metals have been synthesized and structurally characterized. This offers us an opportunity to elucidate the factors that affect their bonding, electrochemistry and reactivity. In addition, a series of Ru-N-Fe(IV) nitrido complexes supported by phthalocyanine and Schiff base ligands have been synthesized. Our results have shown that the redox properties of the M-N-M’ complexes can be tuned by the metal centers and ligands. Depending on the metal and/or ligand, chemical oxidation of M-N-M’ complexes generated reactive high valent heterometallic nitrido species that are capable of oxidizing organic substrates. We found that oxidation of a Ru-N-Fe(IV) phthalocyanine complex produced a phthalocyanine cation radical or hydroxy-phthalocyanine complex, showing the rich oxidation chemistry of heterometallic iron(IV) nitrides. In addition, we have synthesized dinuclear and tetranuclear ruthenium cyclopentadienyl nitrido complexes that can serve as a good platform for the study of the organometallic chemistry of high-valent ruthenium. Finally, we have shown that heterometallic Ru-N-Fe porphyrin complexes are efficient catalysts for alkene oxidation, presumably via nitrido-bridged dimetal-oxo species. The results of this project have demonstrated that high-valent heterometallic complexes with multiply bonded ligands are chemically accessible and such complexes can have potential applications as reagents/catalysts for organic transformations.

16301815.label: Major findings and research outcome
16301815.value: (i) We have developed a general method to synthesize heterometallic nitrido porphyrin complexes of group 8 and 9 metals. Their bonding, structure, electrochemistry and reactivity have been studied systematically. (ii) Heterodinuclear Fe(IV) nitrido porphyrin, phthalocyanine and Schiff base complexes containing various axial ligands have been isolated. This offers us an opportunity to elucidate the factors affecting the redox and reaction chemistry of Fe(IV) complexes. (iii) We have shown that the redox behavior of M-N-M’ complexes can be controlled by the metal centers M and M’ and coligands. Oxidation of M(IV)-N-Fe(IV) complexes generate reactive high-valent bimetallic species with oxidizing equivalent being held either on the metal (e.g. M = Os) or the ligand (phthalocyanine) site of the complexes. (iii) The first heterometallic iridium porphyrin complexes with bridging nitrido ligands have been isolated and structurally characterized. X-ray diffraction indicated that these Ir complexes feature short Ir=N bonds that are consistent with double bonds. These iridium nitrido complexes can serve as a good platform for the study of high-valent iridium chemistry. (iv) We found that the oxidation of an Ru-N-Fe(IV) phthalocyanine complex with PhI(CF3CO2)2 yielded a hydroxyphthalocyanine complex. To our knowledge this is the first report of addition of hydroxyl group to the inner ring of the phthalocyanine ligand that is otherwise resistant to chemical transformations. (v) We have demonstrated that a Ru(VI) nitride reacted with Ru(II) pentamethylcyclopentadienyl complexes to yield tetranuclear Ru nitrido complexes that can serve as starting materials for Ru(IV) cyclopentadienyl complexes. In addition, the Ru(VI) nitride reacted with cyclopentadienyl to yield a cyclopent-4-ene-1,3-diimine ligand, showing the potential application of electrophilic metal nitrides in C-H bond activation and functionalization. (vi) We found that the Fe(IV) nitrido complex LOEtRu-N-Fe(TPP) can catalyze the oxidation of alkenes efficiently, possibly via a Ru-N-Fe=O active species. Therefore, with judicious choice of metal and ligand, M-N-M’ oxo/imido complexes can be stable enough for isolation and such complexes can find applications in atom/group transfer reactions. (vi) We have synthesized and structurally the first Fe(IV) Schiff base complexes containing bridging nitrido ligands. Importantly, abstraction of chloride from a Ru(IV)-N-Fe(IV) Schiff base complex led to isolation of a tetranuclear Ru-N-Fe-O-Fe-N-Ru complex. The elucidation of the pathway by which Fe(IV) aqua complexes is oxidized to hydroxo/oxo species can provide new insights into the oxidation chemistry of high-valent iron.

16301815.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16301815.value: In the future, research should be directed toward the isolation of high-valent heterometallic nitrido complexes derived from chemical oxidation of the M-N-M’ precursors. The kinetics of oxidation of organic substrates by the resulting high-valent M-N-M’ complexes should be studied in order to elucidate the mechanisms of their electron and atom transfer reactions. The oxidation of M-N-Fe(IV) aqua complexes to give hydroxo and oxo species is of significance because it is relevant to an active intermediate of heme enzymes. In this regard, Fe(IV) aqua complexes should be prepared and their oxidation should be studied. To facilitate the oxidation of the iron complexes, efforts should be made to prepare water-soluble heterometallic iron aqua complexes, which can be oxidized to hydroxo and oxo species through via proton-coupled electron transfer in aqueous media. In addition, we have shown that heterometallic iridium nitrido complexes can be prepared by reaction of iridium porphyrin or organometallic complexes with metal nitrides. These iridium nitrido complexes can serve as good starting materials for high-valent iridium compounds. Therefore, efforts should be made to prepare high-valent iridium oxo, imido and carbene complexes by reactions of M-N-Ir complexes with oxo, nitrene and carbene donors.

16301815.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16301815.value: The nitrido group is a strong electron-donating ligand that can stabilize metal ions in high oxidation states. Of interest are dinuclear nitrido complexes featuring M-N-M units that can catalyze oxidation of organic compounds via dimetal-oxo active species. In this project, we have developed a general method to synthesize heterometallic M-N-M’ (where M and M' are group 8 or 9 metals) nitrido complexes starting from terminal nitrido complexes. A series of M-N-M’ complexes containing various metals and chelating ligands have been synthesized, thus offering us an opportunity to elucidate the factors that affect the redox properties and reactivity of heterometallic nitrido complexes. Our electrochemical studies have shown that the redox behavior of M-N-M’ complexes can be controlled by the metals and/or ligands. In addition, we have synthesized a series of dinuclear and tetranuclear ruthenium cyclopentadienyl nitrido complexes, showing that the bridge nitride is a good supporting ligand for high-valent organoruthenium complexes. Also, we found that M-N-M’ porphyrin complexes are efficient catalysts for alkene oxidation, presumably via reactive heterobimetallic oxo intermediates. The results of this project demonstrate that redox-active heterometallic M-N-M’ complexes can serve as a good platform for the study of catalytic chemistry of high-valent metal complexes.

16301915.label: Project Title(Chinese)
16301915.value: 關於約化群的Hecke 代數的研究

16301915.label: Project Objectives
16301915.value: PI Moy will investigate with Prof. Dan Barbasch of Cornell University precise relationships between the Iwahori-Hecke algebra and a related Hecke algebra involving the `1st congruence' subgroup instead of the Iwahori subgroup. The latter Hecke algebra has a natural algebra anti-involution, which Moy and Barbasch hope to relate to a less natural algebra anti-involution of the Iwahori-Hecke algebra. Co-PIs Moy and Wong propose to compute the group character of certain tempered representations of a p-adic group by combining previous results of Moy with recent work of Kim-Lusztig. Success in these computations would form the basis to compute other functions related to the proposed investigation of Moy and Barbasch mentioned above. Co-I Wong will investigate with collaborator Mr. Kei Yuen Chan of the University of Utah/Universiteit van Amsterdam to study theta-elliptic pairing theory on graded Hecke algebra. This will provide a generalization of previous works by Ciubotaru, He and Reeder.

16301915.label: Major findings and research outcome
16301915.value: Moy in work with Prof Dan Barbasch established the Morita equivalence of the Iwahori Hecke algebra of a p-adic group and a related Hecke algebra introduced by them call Peter-Weyl Hecke algebra. The Morita equivalence established by Moy and Barbasch was also shown preserve Hermitian and unitary modules. Later it turned out that the Hecke algebra idempotents used to define the Peter-Weyl Hecke algebras could be grouped into equivariant systems of idempotents indexed by the facets of the Bruhat-Tits building.

16301915.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16301915.value: The idempotents introduced by Moy and Barbasch to define the Peter-Weyl Hecke algebra can be indexed by the facets of the Bruhat-Tits building. This has led to a promising new research avenue which gives presentations of very important invariant distributions on the p-adic group -- the so-called Bernstein center distributions -- as Euler-Poincare of idempotents over the facets of the Bruhat-Tits building.

16301915.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16301915.value: The research involves investigations into mathematical objects called groups which describe the symmetry of number systems. The study of certain functions on the groups is called harmonic analysis and representation theory on the group. The entire system of such functions can often be related to physical systems in science and engineering. A goal is to partition the entire system of functions into smaller collections of functions called representations. Properties of entire system of functions (for example energy in a physical system) is then related to the same properties for the smaller collection.

16302115.label: Project Objectives
16302115.value: To develop a dislocation climb formulation based on the Green’s functions for arbitrarily curved and multiple dislocations in three-dimensions. To develop a numerical discretization method of the obtained Green’s function formulation for discrete dislocation dynamics simulations. To examine the assumptions and address the associated limitations of the commonly used dislocation climb model based on which the climb velocity formulations are derived, including full diffusion or diffusion equilibrium of vacancy concentrations, additional types of point defect sources or sinks, finite domains, and the elastic interaction between dislocations and point defects, etc.

16302115.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16302115.value: Dislocations are line defects in crystals and the primary carriers of plastic deformation. Discrete dislocation dynamics simulations of collective motion and interactions of dislocation ensembles have revealed many interesting mechanical and plastic properties of crystalline materials. The climb motion of dislocations, in which absorption and/or emission of lattice vacancies are involved, plays important roles at high temperatures, for example in dislocation creep. Attempts of discrete dislocation dynamics simulations incorporating dislocation climb have been performed in the literature. However, the existing formulations for the coupling between dislocation climb and vacancy diffusion are derived for single, straight dislocations and depend locally on the climb component of the Peach-Koehler force on dislocations. On the other hand, dislocation dynamics simulations commonly model the evolution of dislocation structures containing large numbers of dislocations with arbitrary shape. In this proposed project, we will develop a general dislocation climb formulation based on the Green’s functions for arbitrarily curved dislocations in three-dimensions. In this new formulation, the dislocation climb velocity is determined from the Peach-Koehler force on dislocations through vacancy diffusion in a nonlocal manner. This long-range contribution to dislocation climb is associated with vacancy diffusion rather than from the well-known long-range effect captured in the Peach-Koehler force. Both long-range effects are important in determining the climb velocity of dislocations. Preliminary examples show that the widely used local climb formula based on straight infinite dislocations is not generally applicable, except for a few special cases. We will also develop numerical discretization methods for this Green’s function formulation for discrete dislocation dynamics simulations. In the discrete dislocation dynamics implementation, the long-range Peach-Koehler force is calculated as is commonly done, then a linear system is solved for the climb velocity from the force. This implementation is done within the same order of computational cost as the existing discrete dislocation dynamics methods. Besides the local approximation, the commonly used dislocation climb model is based upon several other assumptions, and therefore, has several limitations. In this project, we will also systematically address these limitations, including full diffusion or diffusion equilibrium of vacancy concentrations, additional types of point defect sources or sinks, finite domains, and the elastic interaction between dislocations and point defects. The obtained formulations and numerical methods for discrete dislocation dynamics will provide a tool for more accurate simulations and deeper understandings of dislocation climb and related mechanical and plastic properties of crystalline materials.

16302115.label: Realisation of objectives
16302115.value: The three objectives of this project have been fully achieved. Objective 1: We have derived a Green's function formulation for the climb of curved dislocations and multiple dislocations in three-dimensions [1]. In this new dislocation climb formulation, the dislocation climb velocity is determined from the Peach-Koehler force on dislocations through vacancy diffusion in a non-local manner. The long-range contribution to the dislocation climb velocity is associated with vacancy diffusion and are important in determining the climb velocity of dislocations. Analytical and numerical examples show that the widely used local climb formula, based on straight infinite dislocations, is not generally applicable, except for a small set of special cases. We have also developed the Green's function formulation for solving the full vacancy diffusion equation [2]. We also developed a mesoscopic dislocation dynamics model for vacancy-assisted dislocation climb by upscalings from an atomistic-scale model [3]. Effects of the jog structure and vacancy pipe diffusion on dislocations are incorporated by a Robin boundary condition near the dislocations for the bulk diffusion equation and a new contribution in the dislocation climb velocity due to vacancy pipe diffusion (self-climb) driven by the stress variation along the dislocation. As shown by simulations, our formulation is the first pointwise DDD model that is able to quantitatively describe the conservative translation and coalescence of prismatic loops at low temperatures observed in experiments and atomistic simulations [4]. We have generalized the developed Green's function formulation to study the properties of low angle grain boundaries that are associated with climb of the constituent dislocations [7, 8, 9, 10, 11]. We have studied the relaxation of perturbed low-angle tilt grain boundaries by climb of the constituent dislocations due to vacancy bulk diffusion [7] and vacancy pipe diffusion [8]. The relaxations of these two mechanisms are quantitatively different from the relaxation due to dislocation glide motion. We have also obtained a new analytical model to quantify the role of dislocation climb assisted by vacancy pipe and bulk diffusion in controlling the damage resistance. The extent of this self-healing increases with decreasing grain size, which explains the enhanced damage resistance of nanocrystalline materials. We have also derived jump Robin type condition at a coarse-grained level for the point defect absorption at interfaces [9, 10]. The role of interface microstructure is effectively taken into account in this model. We have developed a three-scale homogenisation approach to the prediction of long-time absorption of radiation induced interstitials by nanovoids at interfaces [11], and this model incorporates the collective effect of multiple sinks on interstitial migration which is not fully taken into account in conventional works. Objective 2: We have presented a numerical discretization method of this Green's function formulation appropriate for implementation in discrete dislocation dynamics (DDD) simulations [1]. In DDD implementations, the long-range Peach-Koehler force is calculated as is commonly done, then a linear system is solved for the climb velocity using these forces. This is also done within the same order of computational cost as existing discrete dislocation dynamics methods. We have also presented an efficient high order method for dislocation dynamics simulation of vacancy-assisted dislocation climb in two dimensions [5]. The method is based on a second kind integral equation (SKIE) formulation that represents the vacancy concentration via the sum of double layer potentials and point sources located at each dislocation center. The method discretizes the interfaces only. The number of unknowns in the linear system to achieve certain accuracy is optimal for typical settings in dislocation dynamics. Three different ways of solving the resulting linear system have been compared. We have also developed an efficient numerical implementation method for solving the full vacancy diffusion equation under the Green's function formulation [2]. The singular integrals in time are evaluated efficiently by separation of history and local parts. Efficient simulation model based on the phase field approach for conservative dislocation climb by vacancy pipe diffusion has been developed [6]. This model has the advantage of handling the geometric and topological changes of the prismatic dislocation loops during the evolution process. Objective 3: We have made discussion on different types of the available methods for dislocation climb in dislocation dynamics simulations, including the mobility law type models, the vacancy equilibrium approximation, and solving the full vacancy diffusion equation [2]. Advantages and limitations of each type of methods have been discussed, and the conditions under which each of type methods are applicable have been examined. We have also discussed the influence of the elastic effect [1]. We have derived the dislocation dynamics model for vacancy-assisted dislocation climb by upscalings from a stochastic model on the atomistic scale [3], in which various microscopic mechanisms associated with vacancy bulk diffusion and pipe diffusion and vacancy attachment-detachment kinetics at jogs are incorporated. This derivation has validated the dislocation climb models and more accurate formulation has been obtained. We have examined the common assumption that grain boundaries are ideal sinks for point defects by comparing and contrasting its implications with an explicit model of a low-angle tilt boundary described by an array of edge dislocations which annihilate point defects by climbing [9]. When the constituent dislocation spacing is small (large misorientation), the grain boundary sink efficiency approaches that of the ideal sink. However, for small misorientations, the grain boundary sink efficiency drops rapidly to zero and the ideal sink assumption for the grain boundary fails dramatically. We also derived a reduced dimension description of grain boundaries where the influence of grain boundary structure is captured in a single parameter in a Robin boundary condition for the diffusion equation. 16302115.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16302115.value: The dislocation climb formulations and numerical methods for discrete dislocation dynamics obtained in this project will provide a basis for more accurate simulations and deeper understandings of dislocation climb and related mechanical and plastic properties of crystalline materials. Further development may include: (1) Incorporation of the developed dislocation climb formulations into the available dislocation dynamics simulation methods and codes or development of new software packages based on the new formulations, (2) Employing the developed formulations to perform large scale dislocation dynamics simulations to study the materials properties (e.g. materials under irradiation) under combined effects of dislocation motions of glide, climb by vacancy bulk diffusion, and self-climb by vacancy pipe diffusion, (3) Development of dislocation density based models on larger length and times scales from the obtained dislocation climb formulations, and (4) Incorporation of stochastic effects in the materials.

16302115.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16302115.value: Dislocations are line defects in crystals. Discrete dislocation dynamics (DDD) is a powerful simulation tool for crystalline materials. The climb motion of dislocations, which couples with vacancy diffusion, plays important roles for materials properties. Most of the existing dislocation climb models were derived based on single straight dislocations. Whereas DDD simulations commonly model the evolution of microstructures containing large amounts of dislocations with arbitrary shape. In this project, we have developed dislocation climb formulations based on the Green’s functions for multiple, arbitrarily curved dislocations, in which the climb velocity is determined from the force on dislocations through vacancy diffusion in a nonlocal manner. We have also developed a DDD model for the self-climb of dislocations by vacancy pipe diffusion, which is able to quantitatively describe experimental observations of conservative motions of dislocation loops. We have also developed efficient numerical methods for the new formulations, which have the same order of computational cost as the existing DDD methods. We have also systematically discussed the assumptions and their limitations and influences of the dislocation climb models. The obtained formulations and numerical methods will provide a tool for more accurate DDD simulations and deeper understandings of dislocation climb and related materials properties.

16302215.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16302215.value: Resonant impurities are rather unique structures of disorder in graphene. They usually create resonant quasi-localized states near the charge neutrality point and have profound impacts on graphene’s extraordinary properties. The global behavior of resonant impurities in graphene has not been examined deeply. The main reason is due to the difficulty in distinguishing resonant impurities from other types of existing disorder by traditional electrical transport measurements. Investigations of the electronic properties and modification of the band structure of graphene by different impurities have triggered debates over the origins and mechanisms underlying the interaction between resonant impurities and graphene. Recently, we discovered that silver (Ag) adatoms and electron beam induced hydrogenation generated resonant impurities in graphene in a controlled fashion. Different from other types of impurities, Ag atoms form very weak covalent bonds with graphene. Using quantum capacitance measurement techniques, we first experimentally evidenced that Ag adatoms induced resonant states and had very weak localization effects. We observed unconventional phenomena such as negative quantum capacitance. The relationship between resonant states and property modulation of graphene by different forms of resonant impurities is important for better understanding the fundamental issues of graphene’s properties and device application. We propose to systematically investigate the fundamental aspects of different resonant impurities and their effects on graphene properties with the aim of clarifying the formation and detailed scattering mechanisms of resonant impurities. Some important issues such as the relationship between resonant states and electron kinetic energy, pseudo magnetic effects, electron-electron interaction enhancement mechanisms and the origin of the negative quantum capacitance will be systematically investigated. For practical application, impurities or disorder structures are often intentionally introduced to modify the properties of devices. This project will not only provide a better understanding of the fundamental aspects of graphene’s properties but also generate useful information needed for artificial modulation of graphene electronic band structure and electronic properties with resonant impurities for potential applications. 共振杂质缺陷在石墨烯中是一类特殊的缺陷。他们通常会产生局域态而极大的影响石墨烯的优异性能。这类缺陷目前还没有被深入研究，主要原因是这类缺陷通常与其他缺陷混杂一起。研究石墨烯的电子能带结构与这类杂质的交互作用会极大的帮助理解共振杂质缺陷与石墨烯的作用原理。我们在石墨烯吸附的银原子态中发现了不同于其他杂质的共振杂质缺陷态，同时证实了共振态的存在和负电容现象。在此项研究中，我们计划进行深入研究，特别是共振杂质缺陷形成机制，作用原理，电子的交互作用，以及负电容的产生机理。这项研究不仅仅聚焦在基础研究方向，我们同时也会关注共振杂质缺陷对石墨烯性质的修饰和在电子器件的潜在应用。

16302215.label: Realisation of objectives
16302215.value: The purpose of the first part of this research is to characterize the resonant impurities and their unconventional behavior induced in graphene. We have explored different metal clusters, hydrogenation treatments and atomically thin crystalline materials as impurities for graphene. After initial investigation, we concluded that Ag clusters deposited on single layer graphene showed the strongest effects as reflected by the unconventional phenomenon of negative quantum capacitance. Then, we further verified that this kind of resonant impurities caused the formation of flat impurity bands near the Dirac point in graphene and thus modulated the quantum capacitance properties. We have calculated the flat bands and analyzed theoretically on the flat band structures. We confirmed that these flat bands normally formed near the Dirac point of graphene. Different from exfoliated graphene, however, we observed no resonant impurity effect in large-area CVD grown graphene. Although metal clusters, such as Cu clusters were introduced. Through a rapid thermal treatment method, we found that the charge carrier mobility of the CVD grown graphene could be largely improved. This method provided a promising simple transfer-free approach using solid carbon sources to obtain high-quality graphene for future study of impurity effects. To elucidate the relationships between resonant states and electron-electron interaction enhancement mechanisms and the origin of the negative electronic compressibility observed in graphene, we extended our research to non-metallic resonant impurities and found that semiconductors, such as atomically thin layered-structures of black phosphorus induced a very similar negative compressibility as observed in Ag-graphene structures. Through a collaboration with Dr. Brian Skinner at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, we evidenced that the negative electronic compressibility is generated near the band edges of few-layer black phosphorus. Similar electronic band structure modulations happened in other type of layered 2D semiconductors. We interpreted that the formation of the resonant states could quench the electron kinetic energy. In the case, the electron-electron interaction as reflected by the Coulomb energy of the 2D system effect could be enhanced. We extended our research from single layer graphene to few-layer graphene and few-layer transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs) which have a structure very similar to that of graphene. Although we did not detected the negative compressibility effect in TMDCs, some interesting relevant properties have been detected and studied. One of the differences between monolayer and few-layer graphene is the interlayer interaction effects. There is no such an effect in monolayer graphene. In the study of few-layer TMDCs, we first realized the universal low-temperature Ohmic contacts for probing quantum transport in TMDCs. This is an important step for realizing high-quality field-effect transistors in semiconducting TMDCs. We discovered that the Zeeman energy is about 3 times as large as the cyclotron energy near the valence band top at the Γ valley. This result implies the significant roles played by the exchange interactions in p-type few-layer WSe2, in which itinerant or quantum Hall ferromagnetism likely occurs. We developed a method for fabricating multilayer graphene field-effect double-layer transistors biased through ionic liquid gating. We believe that the interface between graphene and the liquid impurity is highly modulated by this method. Phase transitions at the interface or on the surface of electrostatically doped multilayer graphene occurred. We have also explored artificial modulation of graphene electronic properties with other semi-liquid impurities. For example, in iodine-doped bilayer graphene devices, we observed fluctuation-induced tunneling conduction. We demonstrated that the properties of semimetallic bilayer graphene can be controllably tuned to either metallic or insulating by a simple way of iodine molecular doping. The transport properties of iodine-doped bilayer graphene have been systematically investigated. At high iodine doping concentrations, the Fermi level shifts by approximately 0.35 eV to the metallic region because of the symmetric doping on the top and bottom bilayer surfaces. At low iodine doping concentrations, small energy gaps open in local areas due to the asymmetric doping between the top and the bottom graphene layers. In this case, an insulating behavior at low temperatures is observed, which can be well explained by employing the fluctuation-induced tunneling (FIT) model. At medium iodine doping concentrations, both metallic and insulating behaviors can be observed at different temperatures, implying that both FIT and metallic mechanisms take effect. Our work may have potential applications in functional on/off controllable electronic devices, gas sensors, and transparent flexible electrode in optoelectronics.

16302215.label: Major findings and research outcome
16302215.value: We developed new methods to introduce different types of impurities into graphene and study their effects on electrical property modifications. We discovered negative compressibility in graphene-semiconductor 2D heterostructures. We have elucidated the relationships between resonant states and electron-electron interaction enhancement mechanisms and the origin of the negative electronic compressibility observed in our samples. We extended our research from single layer graphene to multi-layer graphene, few-layer black phosphorus and few-layer TMDCs. We have explored artificial modulation of graphene electronic properties with different types of impurities. In iodine-doped bilayer graphene devices, we observed fluctuation-induced tunneling conduction. We demonstrated that the properties of semimetallic bilayer graphene can be controllably tuned to either metallic or insulating by a simple way of iodine molecular doping. Our work may have potential applications in functional on/off controllable electronic devices, gas sensors, and transparent flexible electrode in optoelectronics (JOURNAL OF APPLIED PHYSICS 123, 244302 (2018)). Atomically-thin black phosphorus (BP) field-effect transistors show strong-weak localization transition, which is tunable through gate voltages. Hopping transports through charge impurity induced localized states are observed at low carrier density regime. Variable-range hopping model is applied to simulate scattering behaviors of charge carriers. (Nanotechnology 29 (2018) 035204) We developed universal low-temperature Ohmic contacts for semiconducting transition metal dichalcogenides (2D Mater. 3 (2016) 021007) and therefore realized a record-high mobility in p-type few-layer WSe2 field-effect transistors. We first observed a series of quantum Hall (QH) states following an unconventional sequence predominated by odd-integer states under a moderate strength magnetic field. We discovered that the Zeeman energy is about 3 times as large as the cyclotron energy near the valence band top at the Γ valley. This result implies the significant roles played by the exchange interactions in p-type few-layer WSe2, in which itinerant or quantum Hall ferromagnetism likely occurs. All these properties have not been observed in graphene. (Phys. Rev. Lett. 118, 067702 (2017)). In few-layer MoS2, we observed even–odd layer-dependent magnetotransport of high-mobility Q-valley electrons. The high-quality MoS2 FET devices pave the way for understanding the multi-valley band structures of few-layer TMDCs (NATURE COMMUNICATIONS 7 (2016) 12955).

16302215.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16302215.value: We have systematically investigated the effects of different impurities introduced into graphene and other two-dimensional layered materials. Some of the impurities have generated strong negative quantum capacitance and negative electronic compressibility effects which may have potential applications. The outcome of this research indicate great potential for further development of our research in particular in two-dimensional atomically thin heterostructures (not limited to graphene) and nano-device design. The heterostructures made by graphene and TMDCs have potential for further development in quantum transport devices.

16302215.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16302215.value: This project has led to new methods for the preparation and characterization of rather unique disorder structures of resonant impurities in graphene and related 2D layered materials. Using quantum capacitance and electrical transport measurements, we have investigated resonant impurity related disorder structures and property modifications. This project provides useful information needed for artificial modulation of electronic band structure and electronic properties for potential applications. We have extended our research to different semiconducting 2D layered materials (e.g., few-layer black phosphorus and few-layer TMDCs), which have a very similar geometry with graphene. We discovered some interesting properties, such as even–odd layer-dependent magnetotransport, quantum Hall states following an unconventional sequence predominated by odd-integer states and fluctuation-induced tunneling conduction. The knowledge gained from this study is highly relevant to fabricating nano- and quantum-devices from graphene and related 2D layered materials.

16302415.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16302415.value: 在过去的30年， DNA程序化自组装为我们提供了很多新颖的结构以及在纳米技术上的各种应用。应用DNA特有的程序化的结构设计，各种DNA结构模板先后问世，诸如DX（双交叉模板），TX（三交叉模板），PX（平行交叉模板）等等。然而我们面临的最大挑战是在运用上述模板构建DNA结构时，结构终极尺寸无法被控制。在我们近期发表的工作的基础上，我们提出了用线框有限尺度设计DNA自组装结构的设想，进而搭建DNA二维和三维的纳米结构。

16302415.label: Realisation of objectives
16302415.value: All six objectives have been realised. In details, we have built the hierarchical assembly of DNA nanostructures based on four-way toehold mediated strand displacement. The widely adopted strategy to combine individual units is to directly design different units with different sets of connection elements of desired matching scheme. However, structures from SSTs would not self-assemble well with too many single-stranded overhangs and that is exactly the case for individual structural units with connection tiles at vertical boundaries. That is why we need to cover the single-stranded overhangs of the connection tiles by protection tiles in forming the individual units before they are combined. However, we believe such a strand displacement process helps to reduce undesired binding by random sticky end cohesion hence preserve matching fidelity, since sticky ends are not exposed when the assembly to higher order takes place. Higher annealing temperature can encourage the combination of matching units but the structural integrity can get compromised if the temperature is too high. Especially, the protection tiles attach to the structure by single 10/11nt domains are prone to fall off from structure in high temperature. Once the protection tiles fall off, the single-stranded overhangs from the connection tiles are exposed to encourage undesired random aggregation. Fortunately, the 10/11nt domain provide binding that is stable enough at typical annealing temperatures (e.g. 37 °C). Potentially, when the structural units of enhanced thermal stability are adopted (e.g. longer binding domains or enzymatic/chemical ligation to stitch multiple domains), higher annealing temperatures could be applied for higher assembly yields of higher-order structures. Lastly, As the analogy of LEGO bricks in the macroscopic world goes, when bricks of different shapes and properties are included, one can build sophisticated models more easily. We believe the similar scenario applies to building blocks of structural DNA nanotechnology and that is the rationale behind our development to adopt different motifs, including ones in this study, to build complex DNA nanostructures. When building blocks of different fine structural features are available, one can build versatile DNA nanostructures with high level of controllability, precision and functionality.

16302715.label: Project Objectives
16302715.value: Develop an efficient numerical model for drop impact on rough surfaces with decorated posts. The approach will be based on the two-phase model developed previously with special attention on setting up and implementation in three dimensional complex geometry. Study numerically the detailed dynamics behavior of drop impact on flat surfaces. Our main objective is to quantify the influence of individual parameters (impact velocity, drop size, density and viscosity of the liquid, the surface tension, and wettability of the surface) on the out-come of the impact leading to phenomena of adherence, bouncing, partial bouncing and splashing. We also hope to quantify the transition between adherence, bouncing and splashing. In the bouncing regime, the effect of these parameters on the contact time will also be studied. Investigate numerically the dynamic behaviour of a drop impacting on rough and chemically patterned superhydrophobic surfaces. We will study the effect of roughness on the spreading and recoiling process after the impact. We will also try to understand the mechanism leading to the fingering and formation of patterns in the spreading and recoiling stage. The numerical results will be compared to the experimental results.

16302715.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16302715.value: The impacting and spreading of liquid drops are key elements of a wide variety of phenomena encountered in technical applications where knowledge of drop impingement is required for process improvement. Ink-jet printing and emerging applications such as organic light emitting diode fabrication, or deoxyribonucleic acid in situ synthesis are examples where drop impact is crucial to performance. A particular area of active research focuses on the hydrodynamics of liquid drops behaviour on superhydrophobic surfaces. In this project , we are interested in modeling and simulation of dynamics of a drop impacting on both rough surfaces with decorated posts and the super-wettability contrast patterns. We will first develop a numerical model for simulating the drop impact on rough and chemically patterned surfaces based on our recent breakthrough on modeling the two phase moving contact line problem. We then study numerically the dynamic behaviour of a drop impacting and the effect of the wettability and roughness of the surface on the impacting. 液滴在固体表面的撞击和扩散的研究在多个科技领域有广泛的应用，比如新打印技术，有机发光二极管的制作以及原位合成脱氧核糖核酸等等。一个热点的领域是超疏水表面上液滴的流体力学行为的研究。在本研究计划里，我们对液滴在粗糙固体表面的撞击和扩散进行建模和数值模拟以研究固体表面的各种性质对撞击和扩散的影响。

16302715.label: Realisation of objectives
16302715.value: An accurate description of the dynamics of the contact line is important in modeling the impact dynamics. We use a phase field model consisting of a coupled system of the Cahn-Hilliard (CH) equation and Navier-Stokes (NS) equations with the generalized Navier boundary condition (GNBC) proposed recently by us to model the moving contact line problem. The new model has the advantage of providing a more accurate description of contact line motion which is an important factor in droplet impacting and spreading on solid surfaces. The model has also been demonstrated to be accurate and used to study two phase flows on various rough and patterned surfaces. Using the phase field model also enables us to handle the topological changes of the droplet shape more easily. In this project, this phase field model in axisymmetric coordinates is used to numerically investigate the dynamics of droplet impact on solid surfaces. The numerical method is based on the energy stable scheme developed by Gao and Wang in previous research. Our objective is to quantify the influence of individual parameters on the droplet impact dynamics. Ranges of the Weber number, Reynolds number, and equilibrium contact angle leading to phenomena of adherence, bouncing, partial bouncing, and splashing are obtained. The effect of slip length, density ratio, and viscosity ratio is also studied. Droplet-impact maps are generated under axisymmetric conditions, in which the outcomes of the impact are characterized by different effects of these parameters. Using the model in axisymmetric coordinates enables us to reduce the computational cost significantly. However, this also implies that we cannot simulate the real splashing when the impacting droplet breaks into smaller bouncing droplets which is essentially a nonsymmetric phenomenon. In the axisymmetric case, we define splashing to be the case when the impacting droplet breaks into multiple rings that bounce off (which would break into small droplets in a fully three dimensional simulation). We observe numerically droplet spreading, receding and rebounding (total and partial) off the solid surface. We study systematically the effect of the parameters (Reynolds number, Weber Number, density ratio, and viscosity ratio, and the equilibrium contact angle of the solid surface) on the dynamic process and outcome of the impact. The Reynolds number plays a dominant role in the spreading stage of the impact. But during droplet receding, the Weber number plays a more significant role. The wettability of the solid surface is found to affect the entire impact process. Bouncing and splashing are more likely to occur on hydrophobic surfaces. We also obtain near quantitative agreement with the experimental results, which demonstrates that our phase field model can satisfactorily describe the droplet impact phenomena.

16302715.label: Major findings and research outcome
16302715.value: We simulate a droplet impacting on a solid surface using a phase field model consisting of the Cahn-Hilliard and Navier Stokes equations with the generalized Navier boundary condition. An efficient gradient stable scheme is used to solve the system in axisymmetric coordinates. Our objective is to understand numerically the mechanisms leading to different impacting phenomena such as adherence, bouncing, partial bouncing, and splashing. In particular, we study how various processes are affected by the relevant dimensionless parameters: the Reynolds number, Weber number, density ratio, viscosity ratio, and the wettability of the solid surface. We also compare our numerical results with the experimental results and observe almost quantitative agreement.

16302715.value: Droplet-impact maps are generated under axisymmetric conditions, in which the outcomes of the impact are characterized by different effects of these parameters. In this project, we use the model in axisymmetric coordinates reduce the computational cost significantly. However, this also implies that we cannot simulate the real splashing when the impacting droplet breaks into smaller bouncing droplets which is essentially a nonsymmetric phenomenon. A more general simulation (using supercomputer) is needed to understand the real splashing phenomena.

16302715.value: We use computer to simulate a droplet impacting on a solid surface. This kind of simulations require accurate modeling, efficient numerical method and good understanding of the phenomena. In particular, we want to understand the mechanisms leading to different impacting phenomena such as adherence, bouncing, partial bouncing, and splashing. The numerical modeling will have significant applications in future engineering design.

This new signal amplification strategy will be the basis upon which novel ultrasensitive DNA sensing methods will be developed in the proposed study. Enzyme-free and immobilization-free electrochemical nucleic acid sensing utilizing non-linear hybridization chain reaction. Integrating the enzyme-free non-linear hybridization chain reaction with an immobilization-free electrochemical DNA detection technology previously developed by the PI’s group, an extremely sensitive electrochemical DNA detection method will be demonstrated Non-fluorescent (e.g., colorimetric) nucleic acid sensing utilizing the enzyme-free non-linear hybridization chain reaction. In order to develop a nucleic acid sensing technology that requires minimum instrumentation and extremely easy operation, non-fluorescent ( e.g., colorimetric) nucleic acid sensing method will be developed based on the enzyme-free non-linear hybridization chain reaction, which will be especially suitable for applications in resource-limited scenarios.

16302815.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16302815.value: Nucleic acid sequences and biomolecules (e.g., proteins, ATP) are important bio-analytes for pathogen detection and disease diagnostics. Recently, a class of short non-coding ribonucleic acid sequences, known as microRNAs (miRNAs), has been shown to be a promising biomarker in the blood, the presence of which correlates with disease development. Traditionally, the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is a well-established amplification method to enrich dilute DNA samples prior to detection. This PCR-based sample enrichment process “exponentially” increases analyte quantity in a short time, improves detection specificity and amplifies the analyte-derived signal. However, its procedure requires enzymes and temperature control. Because of technological advances in DNA synthesis, the cost and the delivery time for short synthetic DNA sequences have been much reduced. Using DNA self-assembly, many DNA nanostructures have been demonstrated. An innovative one was the concept of hybridization chain reaction (HCR) where a cascade of hybridization could be initiated in the presence of a specific DNA sequence. This HCR strategy converts a short sequence of DNA hairpins, through repetitive, enzyme-free “polymerization” steps, into a linear DNA polymer with a molecular weight inversely correlated with the concentration of the specific initiating DNA strand. Although this HCR strategy could only achieve a linear version of amplification, its triggering of assembly has attracted a lot of interest for biosensing applications. The PI’s team has recently demonstrated a non-linear version of HCR where a 2D DNA dendrimer could be grown after a DNA analyte triggers the reaction. Leveraging the progress, this proposed project aims to develop an ultrasensitive and enzyme-free sensing platform for important biomolecules including nucleic acids as well as heavy metal ions such as mercury, using innovative, non-linear HCR amplification strategy and kinetically controlled self-assembly. This new method needs no enzyme and does not require an additional amplicon enrichment step. The working principle of this approach involves the use of several specifically-designed reactant sequences according to the sequence of the analyte target. An analyte single-stranded DNA would hybridize to a complementary toehold region of a designed double-stranded DNA. This initiating step would trigger a cascade of autonomous and catalytic hybridization reactions, leading to the formation of a two-dimensional branch of DNA self-assembly network. This branched-growth algorithm mimics PCR-like exponential amplification and it can be easily developed into ultrasensitive fluorescent, electrochemical and colorimetric sensing platforms through the incorporation of a fluorescent reporter, an electrochemically active label, and thiol groups on the terminal nucleotide. 核酸序列和生物分子（例如蛋白質，ATP）是病原檢測和疾病診斷中重要的目標生物分析物。目前發現血液中一類被稱為微小RNA（簡稱miRNAs）的非編碼RNA短序列可被用作有效的潛在生物標誌物，其出現及存在狀態與疾病的發生發展呈現相關性。一般地，在檢測之前，稀釋後樣品中的DNA需要通過成熟完善的聚合酶鏈式反應（PCR）進行擴增。這種基於PCR的擴增方式可以在短時間內使分析物數量得到指數增長，從而提高檢測特異性，同時增強分析物產生的響應信號。然而這個過程需要酶的參與和對溫度的控制。 隨著DNA合成技術的發展，人工合成DNA短序列已變得愈發便宜和快速。運用DNA自組裝原理，可以實現許多DNA納米構造的表達。雜交鏈式反應（HCR）即是其中富有創造性的代表，目標DNA序列的出現可啟動串聯式的雜交反應過程。HCR技術在沒有酶參與的情況下，通過重復的“聚合反應“步驟，將具有發夾結構的DNA短序列轉化為大分子量的線性DNA聚合物，而線性DNA聚合物的分子量和目標DNA的濃度相關。雖然HCR技術中的擴增過程為線性過程，其觸發組裝的概念在生物檢測應用方面已吸引了諸多關註。 截止目前，PI研究團隊已論證一種非線性版本的HCR技術，通過目標DNA分析物來觸發二維DNA樹狀分子的生長。推而廣之，本提案旨在通過新型非線性HCR擴增技術和動力學控制自組裝過程，建立超敏無酶生物檢測平臺，此平臺將用於檢測包括核酸和ATP在內的重要生物分子以及重金屬離子，如汞離子等。此新型檢測方法不需要酶的參與以及額外的分析物擴增步驟。本方法的工作原理為：數條參與反應序列基於目標分析物進行特殊設計；目標分析物單鏈DNA將和特殊設計的雙鏈反應物序列上互補的toehold部位發生雜交；此啟動步驟將觸發一串聯自發雜交反應過程，進而形成二維樹狀DNA自組裝網絡。此樹狀擴增的法則為類似PCR的指數擴增，且易於通過分別結合熒光標記、電化學標記和末端核苷酸巰基修飾，發展成為高靈敏度的熒光檢測、電化學檢測和比色檢測平臺。

16302815.label: Major findings and research outcome
16302815.value: We have demonstrated a new highly sensitive nucleic acid based sensing strategy through the integration of upstream catalytic (target recycling) circuit with the downstream sequence-triggered nonlinear hybridization chair reaction (NL-HCR). This work has been reported in the journal "Nanoscale" (paper 2 in Section C). We have also shown that enzyme-free and immobilization-free sensing strategies utilizing NR-HCR principles could be achieved (paper 3 and 4 in Section C). In addition, a platform using kinectically modulated DNA self-assembly circuit (paper 5 of Section C) could be developed for point of care applications in resource-limited scenarios. An invited review article "Rational Design of Electrochemical DNA Biosensors for Point-of-Care Applications" (paper 1 of Section C) provides a nice perspective of DNA-assembly based strategics for PoC applications.

16303215.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16303215.value: The goal of the proposed experimental research is to study the fluctuation spectra of micromechanical devices in the presence of nonlinear effects and/or frequency noise. Micromechanical resonators are widely used as sensors and actuators. In resonant sensors, vibrations of the micromechanical element are the strongest around the resonance frequency. By tracking changes in the resonant frequencies, the devices can be used in applications ranging from inertial sensing to high sensitivity force and mass detection. Fluctuational phenomena are of paramount importance in mechanical resonators. For instance, damping associated with energy losses tends to increase the spectral width so that the strong vibrations occur over a large range of frequencies, limiting the accuracy at which the resonance frequency of the oscillator can be measured. As the trend of miniaturization continues, factors other than damping play an increasingly important role in determining the spectral response of mechanical devices. The emphasis of the proposed research will be placed on revealing the various mechanisms that can affect the spectral line shape of mechanical resonators. By designing resonators with tunable nonlinearity, we plan to explore the effects of nonlinearity, fluctuations and their interplay on the spectral line shape. In conventional systems, the spectral linewidth is expected to increase with noise intensity. However, for systems where the dependence of the eigenfrequency on energy is non-monotonic, the dispersion of the eigenfrequency is zero at the extremum energy. We propose to explore a wide range of “zero-dispersion” phenomena that have been predicted, including noise induced spectral narrowing and development of sharp peaks in the fluctuation spectrum. Furthermore, we plan to investigate the fluctuation spectrum of a nonlinear resonator under periodic drive in the presence of frequency noise. Successful implementation of the proposed projects will not only verify the validity of various theoretical approaches, answer open questions and stimulate new theoretical research, but could also lead to micromechanical detectors of improved sensitivity and functionality. The PI has extensive experience with fluctuational phenomena in micromechanical devices. In the past few years, his group performed an extensive investigation of the switching between coexisting vibration states induced by Gaussian and Poisson noise on a nonlinear micromechanical torsional oscillator under strong periodic drive. The PI will work closely with Prof. Mark Dykman and Dr. Stanislav Soskin, theorists at Michigan State University and National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine respectively, to reveal novel behaviors of the fluctuation spectra of nonlinear micromechanical resonators. 我們建議的實驗研究的目標是研究在非線性效應和/或頻率噪聲影響下的微機械器件的波動譜。微機械諧振器被廣泛用作傳感器和製動器。在諧振傳感器中，其機械部分的振動在共振頻率附近達到最大。通過追蹤其共振頻率的變化，這些器件可用於慣性傳感以及力和質量的高精度測量等應用中。波動現象對於機械諧振器是非常重要的。例如，與能量損耗相關的阻尼會導致頻譜寬度增加，以至於在較大的頻率範圍內都有較強的振動出現，其結果是限制了測量諧振器頻率的準確性。 隨著機械器件尺寸的不斷微型化，阻尼之外的其他因素在決定機械諧振器的頻譜反應上扮演著越來越重要的角色。建議研究的重點將在於揭示影響機械諧振器頻譜形狀的多種機制。通過設計非線性可調的諧振器，我們計劃探索研究非線性、波動以及它們之間的相互作用對頻譜形狀的影響。在常規的系統中，頻譜的線寬預計會隨著噪聲強度的增加而增加。然而，對于本征頻率與能量非單調相關的系統，本征頻率在能量極值點的離散度是零。我們建議探索研究一系列已經被預測的“零-離散度”現象，包括噪聲導致的頻譜窄化和波動譜中尖峰的出現。此外，我們計劃探究週期性驅動的非線性諧振器在有頻率噪聲時的波動譜。建議研究的成功實施不僅將驗證各種理論方法的正確性，回答尚未解決的問題，並促进新理論的研究，更將提高微機械探測器的靈敏度和功能性。 主要研究者在研究微機械諧振器的波動現象方面擁有豐富的經驗。在過去幾年裡，他的團隊對於在強力的周期性驅動下，非線性微機械扭轉諧振器在由於高斯噪聲和泊松噪聲的激發而產生的共存振動狀態之間的跳轉做了大量的研究。主要研究者將會與來自密歇根州立大學的Mark Dykman教授和來自烏克蘭國家科學院的Stanislav Soskin博士緊密合作，揭示非線性微機械諧振器波動譜的新現象。

16303215.label: Realisation of objectives
16303215.value: During the reporting period, we carried out an investigation of the effects of nonlinearity and zero dispersion on the fluctuation spectra and frequency noise of micromechanical resonators. We achieved the project objectives of investigating noise-induced spectral broadening in an underdamped nonlinear micromechanical resonator, exploring noise-induced spectral narrowing in a zero dispersion system and investigating the fluctuation spectrum of a nonlinear resonator in the presence of frequency noise. Our findings were presented in four international/local conferences and published in Nature Communications and Applied Physics Letters. One PG student was trained. He is currently writing his PhD thesis. To achieve the project objectives, we designed and fabricated a micromechanical resonator that can be tuned by dc voltage applied to an underlying electrode to yield either monotonic or non-monotonic dependence of the eigenfrequency on energy. We found that the interplay between nonlinearity, fluctuations and relaxation have a profound effect on the fluctuation spectrum. For small noise intensities, the fluctuation spectrum peaks at the natural frequency omega_1 with a width that is only determined by the damping constant Gamma. As the noise intensity increases, we show that the resonator can show different behaviors. For a resonator with ordinary monotonic dependence of the eigenfrequency on energy, we demonstrate that the fluctuation spectrum broadens with noise intensity. The width is no longer solely determined by the damping constant. Next we tuned the dc voltage to make the dependence of eigenfrequency on energy non-monotonic. Such a zero-dispersion system gives a fluctuation spectrum that first broadens and then narrows as the noise intensity is increased. We also investigated the effect of frequency noise that originates from charge fluctuations in the silicon nitride layer that insulates the device from the substrate. The frequency noise was detected by measuring the amplitude fluctuations in the presence of a periodic drive at a fixed frequency. The micromechanical device consists of a highly-doped polycrystalline silicon plate (3.5 um by 300 um by 300 um) suspended by springs at its four corners. Electrical voltage V is applied to a fixed electrode of the same size underneath the top plate to excite vibrations of the top plate in the fundamental mode that involves translational motion normal to the substrate. This device provides an ideal platform for investigating a wealth of zero-dispersion phenomena that are associated with the large contribution of vibrations over a range of energies in the vicinity of E_zd occurring at almost the same frequency. In our mechanical resonator, the non-monotonic dependence of omega on energy E is achieved by tuning the negative nonlinearity induced by electrostatic force from a nearby electrode relative to the positive intrinsic nonlinearity of the springs. At the extremum energy E_zd, the dispersion of omega(E) is zero so that d omega/dE = 0. To demonstrate a different kind of zero dispersion effect, we set our devices into self-sustained oscillations with active feedback where the mechanical resonator serves as the frequency-selecting element. The standard deviation of the oscillation frequency at the optimal vibration amplitude is demonstrated to be a factor of ~3 smaller in the zero-dispersion regime compared to the minimal noise in the conventional nonlinear regime. To our knowledge, zero-dispersion phenomena have not been directly observed in physical systems other than analog circuits and computer simulations. Our findings demonstrate that zero-dispersion phenomena can play an important role in micro/nano mechanical systems, potentially leading to new methods of detection and frequency stabilization. The main problem encountered and solved include the necessity to design a resonator with a large ratio of (omega_zd - omega_1)/Gamma, under the constraint of our fabrication process where the gap between the movable plate and the electrode is fixed at 2 um. We spent much effort in exploring many different sizes of the vibrating plate and different values of V_dc to maximize effects of the zero dispersion phenomena in our devices. Specifically, the optimal stability of self-sustained oscillations shows a factor of 3 improvement compared to conventional nonlinear resonators.

16303215.label: Major findings and research outcome
16303215.value: The research in this project represents the first realization of a zero dispersion system apart from circuit simulations. Major findings include demonstration that the width of the fluctuation spectra of micromechanical resonators is determined by the interplay of damping, nonlinearity and additive noise. In a conventional nonlinear oscillator, where the dependence of eigenfrequency on energy is monotonic, the fluctuation spectrum peak widens as the noise intensity increases. For a resonator with zero dispersion, where the dependence of eigenfrequency on energy is non-monotonic, the spectral peak undergoes narrowing as the noise intensity is increased in some range related to E_zd, in agreement with theoretical calculations. For the zero-dispersion resonator, the optimal frequency stability of self-sustained oscillations shows a considerable improvement as compared to conventional nonlinear resonator. The findings are of general interests to the scientific community because mechanical resonators are widely used as precision clocks and sensitive detectors that rely on the stability of their eigenfrequencies. The phase noise is determined by different factors including thermal noise, frequency noise of the resonator and noise in the feedback circuitry. Increasing the vibration amplitude can mitigate some of these effects but the improvements are limited by nonlinearities that are particularly strong for miniaturized micro- and nano-mechanical systems. Our findings demonstrate that zero-dispersion phenomena can play an important role in micro/nano mechanical systems, potentially leading to new methods of detection and frequency stabilization. The outcome of our research includes two papers (one published in Nature Communications and one in Applied physics letters) and 4 presentations at conferences. One PG student was trained. He is currently writing his PhD thesis.

16303215.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16303215.value: The optimal phase stability for self-sustained oscillations is achieved at the vibration amplitude A_zd at which d omega/dE = 0. By eliminating the extra contributions to phase noise converted from amplitude noise, the phase stability becomes comparable to an oscillator undergoing purely linear vibrations at amplitude A_zd. It is well-known that for linear resonators, the frequency standard deviation for self-sustained vibrations is inversely proportional to the vibration amplitude. Therefore, the optimal frequency standard deviation for an oscillator in the zero dispersion regime is expected to follow a similar dependence on A_zd, i.e. proportional to 1/ A_zd. Ideally, the phase stability can be further improved by choosing A_zd to be as large as possible. Promising future research directions for phase stabilization using zero dispersion include new approaches to yield large A_zd, as well as the effect on the phase stability due to other phenomena that emerges when the vibration amplitude becomes large, such as nonlinear friction.

16303215.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16303215.value: The frequency stability of mechanical resonators plays a central role in applications such as time keeping and sensing. While clocks in integrated circuits are largely based on quartz resonators, silicon micro- and nanomechanical devices have become viable alternatives because of their small size, low power consumption and reliability in extreme conditions. However, the operation of such devices at large amplitudes is limited by their nonlinearities: the eigenfrequency typically changes with energy monotonically, converting amplitude noise into unwanted phase noise. In this project, we design an electromechanical resonator with non-monotonic dependence of its vibrational eigenfrequency on energy, so that the dispersion of the eigenfrequency is zero at the extremum point. With vibrations at energies around the extremum point all contributing to almost the same frequency, we show that the width of the spectral peak, one of the most important parameters of resonant systems, undergoes counter-intuitive narrowing instead of broadening when the noise intensity is increased. The spectral narrowing directly leads to improved frequency stability when the resonator is driven into self-sustained oscillations via a feedback loop. Our findings represent a first step in investigating and exploiting zero-dispersion phenomena in mesoscopic resonators.

16303415.label: Project Objectives
16303415.value: To work out the detailed theoretical and computational approaches for calculating the electrophoresis effect, based on the self-consistent approach for a single spherical particle in a cylindrical channel whose radius is several times the Debye layer thickness, coupled to the Navier-Stokes equation. To extend the theory to those cases in which we have different salt concentrations and different acidity or alkalinity. The experiment will be conducted in collaboration with Prof. Daniel Ouyang of Lehigh University.

16303415.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16303415.value: Electrophoresis refers to the phenomenon wherein a particulate substance acquires a charged interface with liquid, such as water, and under an externally applied electric field moves with a fixed velocity along the electric field direction. This effect is tremendously important in biological experiments, known as gel electrophoresis, wherein the bio materials such as DNA, RNA and proteins can be separated in accordance with their size and amount of charges carried. Here the basic principle is simply that the smaller, or shorter molecules would move faster through the gel under an electric field, thereby achieving the separation. Electrophoresis also belongs to the larger class of phenomena known as electrokinetics. They share the common characteristics of having a charged surface (negatively charged in the case of water/silica interface), in conjunction with a diffuse charged layer generally known as the Debye layer. Recently we have advanced a theory of electrokinetics, based on the constraint of global charge neutrality (Physical Review X 4, 011042 (2014)), that for the first time enabled the joint consideration of the surface ions and the diffuse layer’s counterions under the minimum free energy condition. With only one parameter, this new theory is able to correctly predict the many behaviors of electrokinetics, especially for the nanoscale systems. It is the purpose of the present proposal to extend this theory to the description of electrophoresis, by coupling it to the Navier-Stokes equation that is essential for the fluid flow. In conjunction with the theory, we intend to carry out experiments involving one single spherical particle, microns in size, that can be manipulated by a technique known as optical tweezers. The experiment will measure both the drag force as well as the velocity of the particle under a given applied electric field. The comparison between such experimental results with the theory prediction can yield unprecedented details about the electrophoretic phenomenon. In particular, the completion of this proposal can provide a calibration to the traditional theories and measurement techniques involving the assumption that the electrophoresis velocity is always directly proportional to the zeta potential, traditionally regarded as a fixed constant for a particular solid/liquid interface.
