17502915.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17502915.value: Corporate governance essentially deals with the ways that different capital providers of a firm ensure a return on their respective investment (Shleifer and Vishnny, 1997). Due to conflicting interests, governance policies in favor of one party do not necessarily create value for the other, which is manifested by the agency cost of debt and asset substitution problems (Jensen and Meckling, 1976; Myers, 1977). While the impact of corporate governance on shareholder value has been well documented, wealth implications on debtholders remain under-investigated and undetermined. On the one hand, corporate governance can enhance debtholder value because stronger governance mechanisms help mitigate managerial self-dealing activities and lower credit risk (Djankov, LaPorta, Lopez-de-Silanes and Shleifer, 2008; Lin, Ma, Malatesta and Xuan, 2011). On the other hand, stronger shareholder rights may induce risk-shifting activities or investment distortion that transfers wealth from debtholders to shareholders (Jensen and Meckling, 1976; Myers, 1977; Parrino and Weisbach, 1999). In view of the competing hypotheses, it remains an empirical question whether corporate governance enhances or decreases debtholder value. Furthermore, debtholders are among the most heavyweight stakeholders of a firm, contributing more than 50% of funding to a median U.S. firm (DeAngelo and Roll, 2014). Therefore, it is even more compelling to examine the impact of corporate governance on debtholder value. Literature hitherto provides mixed evidence regarding the impact of corporate governance on debtholder value. With a focus on anti-takeover provisions, Klock, Mansi and Maxwell (2005) among others find a negative relation between anti-takeover provision and the cost of debt but they fail to incorporate the costs associated with more anti-takeover provisions. There are two major concerns. First, they focus on cross-sectional relation that is likely to be biased by omitted variables. Second, they measure credit market reaction over a long window, during which many irrelevant factors can arise to confound the true relation. This paper addresses these concerns 1) uses abnormal bond return around shareholder voting to capture more responsive bond market reaction (event study); 2) resorts to regression discontinuity design (RDD) to identify causal relation by comparing the abnormal bond returns of firms holding close-call proposals (e.g. 50.1% vs. 49.% vote shares). We further group the governance proposals into three categories, namely, repealing anti-takeover provisions, executive compensation and board, to analyze their respective impact on debtholder value. Finally, we explore the channels driving corporate governance and debtholder value using subsamples divided by information opacity, default risk and growth opportunities. 大部分的 公司治理研究都集中在股东回报上， 仅有很少的项目研究公司治理对债权人的影响。本项目旨在利用股东投票作为公司重要事件来研究公司治理对债权人权益的影响。 债权人权益将通过债券市场交易以及回报的事件分析来衡量。该研究对投资策略以及证券业监管有着直接的参考建议作用。

17502915.label: Realisation of objectives
17502915.value: After the approval of this proposal, we noticed that another group of authors had completed a paper on almost the same topic and started circulating it on line. Their paper entitled "The Impact of Stronger Shareholder Control on Bondholders", which can be retrieved from "https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2542878", examines whether the passage of governance-related shareholder proposal affects debtholder value. They use the spreads on credit default swap (CDS) as an inverse proxy for debtholder value and employ the same sample and Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD) approach as we proposed. They find that stronger shareholder rights benefit debtholders and lead to lower CDS spreads. They also find that stronger shareholder rights lead to an increase in credit ratings and operating performance in the long run. In view of the competing paper, we slightly revised the first objective of our research. Instead of examining other similar properties of debtholders, we differentiate by exploring the underlying channels through information production. That is, we try to understand the bond value implications of stronger shareholder rights by examining whether the passage of these governance proposals leads to better corporate information environment. We assess corporate information production from various dimensions, such as intensity, precision, accuracy and news content, so as to portray a comprehensive picture on the impact of stronger shareholder rights on such an important corporate policy. As information environment exerts a direct impact on debtholder value, the revised direction of examination is closely related to our initially proposed topic and significantly complements it. Specifically, we revised objective 1 is as follows: identify the impact of corporate governance on corporate information production, which casts implications for debtholder value. Below is how and to what extent these objectives have been achieved: 1. Using more than 3000 shareholder proposals that aim to remove entrenchment mechanisms of managers in a firm and following standard implementation of RDD, we identify a positive effect of passing entrenchment-mitigating proposals on the provision of corporate information in the form of managerial earnings forecasts. We have conducted McCrary test and balance test, and employed graphical illustration to support the validity of our RDD setting. That is, firms are randomly located around the cutoff vote share (i.e., 50%) within an optimally defined local bandwidth, thus they share similar characteristics before the voting. Besides, we have constructed a variety of measures to measure different dimension of managerial earnings forecasts, including occurrence, frequency, precision, horizon, accuracy and news content (conservative and negative news). Therefore, we have been able to provide a comprehensive picture on how stronger shareholder rights affect corporate disclosure policy, which contains value implications for the firm. As information production certainly provides a channel for debtholders to learn about the firm, our results also cast implications on debtholder benefits. Thus, the first (revised) objective is considered fully achieved; the original objective is achieved in an indirect manner. For future exploration of the direct impact on debtholders along the initially proposed line, we can examine the effect of shareholder voting on bond liquidity, the portion of institutional holding of outstanding bonds, and bond trading volumes by types (investment grade bonds vs. high-yield bonds). 2. We have classified governance proposals into three categories: anti-takeover, board and voting, which are closely related to the mechanisms entrenching managers. The RAs hired have helped us clean and classify these proposals into different categories and provided on-going support. We first test and report that the number of entrenchment mechanisms decreases following the passage of these proposals, which is direct evidence that "anti-takeover" proposals are on average effective. Our channel tests suggest that, passing these proposals can help increase board independence, which validate the importance of "board"-related proposals in particular, but also that of other governance-related proposals in general as they can have aggregate effect on the overall improvement of corporate governance. We also find that the effect of shareholder voting is stronger if firms have poorer alignment of incentives via low power incentive contracts, which offers support on effectiveness of "compensation"-related proposals. We further confirm that the effect is not driven by the proposals that aim to change corporate disclosure policies directly. Thus, the second objective is considered fully achieved. 3. We have conducted three sub-sample test to understand the channel. (1) We partition the sample by information asymmetries. We use two measures, namely asset intangibility and industry valuation dispersion, to gauge the degree of corporate information asymmetry. We find that the effect of passing an entrenchment-related shareholder proposal is larger among the subgroups with higher pre-existing information asymmetries before the voting. (2) We partition the sample by incentive alignment between managers and shareholders. We obtain compensation data from ExecuComp use the percentage of equity compensation to proxy for the degree of incentive alignment prior to the shareholder voting. We find that the effect of passing an entrenchment-related shareholder proposal is larger among the subgroups with poorer incentive alignment before the voting. (3) We partition the sample by the legal expertise of management. We obtain relevant information from ExecuComp and Morse, Wang, and Wu (2016) to identify and classify the top management according to their legal expertise. We find that the effect of passing an entrenchment-related shareholder proposal is larger among the subgroups with few legal experts in the management team before the voting. Overall, these sub-sample tests suggest that passing governance-related shareholder proposals helps discipline the managers and reduce agency conflicts between managers and shareholders, thereby enhancing managerial incentives to product information. Thus, the third objective is considered fully achieved. The research output has been accepted by Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis, a top journal in finance.

17502915.label: Major findings and research outcome
17502915.value: The paper mainly evaluates whether and how managerial entrenchment affects corporate information production. We have obtained the following findings and outcomes: 1. In the baseline analysis (with optimal bandwidth), we use shareholder proposals around the passing threshold at 50% vote share and employ RDD to identify the causal effect on corporate information production. We find that, passing an entrenchment-related proposal helps improve corporate information production. Specifically, it leads to a higher likelihood of firms' issuing management earnings forecasts and a greater number of earnings forecasts. The format of issued forecasts also becomes more precise; forecasts are issued earlier in a quarter and contain fewer errors (compared with the actual earnings). In terms of news content, the proportion that the issued forecasts contain negative or conservative news increases following the passage of these proposals. When it comes to the economic magnitude, a "pass" firm on average is 66% more likely to issue earnings forecasts in a quarter than a "reject" firm; it issues one more forecast, issues forecasts of 1.38 higher precision score (from a qualitative statement to an open-ended estimate) and 0.8 accuracy score in a quarter than a "reject" firm; it also tends to issue a quarterly forecast 29 days ahead of a "reject" firm within a quarter, so that the information is disclosed in a more timely way. Finally, the fraction of forecasts containing negative or conservative news increases by 60% and 64% respectively more than the "reject" firm. The results are presented in Table 3-5 of the paper attached to Part C. The findings are robust to alternative specifications, such as (1) wider or smaller bandwidth, (2) global bandwidth with a higher degrees of polynomials, (3) additional firm-level controls, and (4) longer window, as shown in Table A3. 2. We find the effect of passing a entrenchment-related proposal leads to greater improvement of information product among firms with (1) greater information asymmetries (Table 6), (2) poorer alignment of incentives between managers and shareholders (Table 7), (3) few legal experts in the top management team (Table 8) prior to the voting. These sub-sample tests confirms the channel that the passage of the proposals improve corporate information disclosure by reducing agency conflicts between managers and shareholders. 3. We also find direct support for the agency channel that passing an entrenchment-related proposal on corporate governance quality leads to more independent board and audit / governance committees subsequently. The paper (“Managerial Entrenchment and Information Production”) has been accepted by Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis, a top journal in finance.

17502915.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17502915.value: For future exploration of direct impact on debtholders along the initially proposed line, we can examine the effect of shareholder voting on bond liquidity, the portion of institutional holding of outstanding bonds, and bond trading volumes by types (investment grade vs. high-yield bonds).

17502915.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17502915.value: This research examines whether and how managerial entrenchment affects corporate information production. Managerial entrenchment is a phenomenon that managers use an assortment of mechanisms to shield them from market disciplines. Therefore, they can take activities that benefit themselves at the cost of shareholders and other stakeholders. While previous studies have examined the effect of managerial entrenchment on corporate outcomes and valuation, whether and how it affects corporate information production is unclear. Since corporate information production is an important channel through which outside investors form their valuation and investment decisions, our research can improves people's understanding about the impact of corporate governance on information policies and related valuation implications. Moreover, we are able to make causal inferences using shareholder proposals aiming to reduce managerial entrenchment that just pass or fail in a meeting. These firms are comparable in all dimensions except that one's governance is improved while the other's remain. In this way, we can identify the causal effect of reducing managerial entrenchment, which is not fully accomplished in previous related studies.

17503115.label: Project Title(Chinese)
17503115.value: 出口国别、产品质量、以及中国产品在世界市场的利润率

17503115.label: Project Objectives
17503115.value: To develop a (global comparable) measure of product quality based on observed data. To examine how product quality differs both across firms in the domestic and export markets. To investigate how past export experience and other investments affect product quality. To understand firms’ dynamic decisions on investments in R&D and advertisement in order to improve productivity and (perceived) product quality. To apply this model to examine the product quality, productivity, and export performance of Chinese firms, and to provide a micro-based guideline for Chinese firms and policy makers to improve the serious quality concern of Chinese products in the international markets.

17503115.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17503115.value: How consumers perceive the quality of products provided by a firm is an important factor determining demand for this firm. A high quality product not only earns larger a market share, but also admits larger market power and allows the firm to charge a higher margin. Unlike the effect of productivity, which changes production costs, product quality affects firm profit by changing demand. In the context of international trade, product quality is more important. It determines where the firm can export, how much to export, and the profit margin in each market. At the macro level, product quality largely determines the direction of international trade across countries, how countries specialize in production, and terms of trade. For Chinese exports, the issue of product quality is even more important. As is well known, Chinese exports have been generally deemed as of low quality in most foreign markets, and Chinese firms earn a very low margin internationally. However, over the past decades, firms have been encouraged to upgrade their product quality and productivity in China. This comes along with a fast and persistent expansion after the opening-up policy in 1980s. The export-GDP ratio reached 26.40% in 2013 according to World Bank, which is a significant increase compared with only around 10% in 1980. Is this fast export expansion mainly driven by quality or productivity? How does the quality of Chinese exports change over time? How much does it contribute to the growth of exports? The goals of this project are to examine how the product quality of Chinese exports differs across firms and changes over time, how the quality differs in different export markets, and how forward-looking firms determine where to export and how much to invest to improve product quality and productivity. We will take two steps to achieve these goals. First, we develop a unified framework to recover the firm-market-time specific product quality and firm-time-specific productivity using data on inputs, outputs, and export volume, destination, and prices of Chinese manufacturers. The key is that these measures are comparable across firms and markets and over time. Second, we will study firms’ dynamic optimal decisions on pricing, quality, and export destinations by estimating a structural model. The model provides a comprehensive way to evaluate and explain both the growth and expansion of Chinese exports. The dataset linking together the Chinese Manufacturing Survey and Chinese Custom Report provides rich information for the empirical analysis. 企业产品质量决定了消费者对其产品的需求。高质量的产品不仅能带来更大的市场份额，更能为企业带来更高的市场支配力和利润率。企业生产率可以通过降低生产成本来提高效益，而产品质量则可以通过改进需求来达到类似的效果。在国际贸易中，产品质量非常重要。它决定了一个企业能出口到哪里，能出口多少，以及在每个市场的利润率。在宏观层次上，产品质量在很大程度上决定了国与国之间国际贸易的方向，每个国家的专业化分工，以及贸易条件。对中国的出口来说，产品质量就更为重要。长期以来中国出口的产品都被认为是低质量的代名词，因而中国企业出口利润率也较低。然而，中国政府在过去一二十年来一直致力于鼓励中国企业提高产品质量和生产率。在1980年改革开放以后，中国产品出口得到了快速稳定的发展。根据世界银行的统计数据，中国的出口-国内生产总值比率在30年间从1980年的10%左右上升到2013年的26.40%。中国出口的高速增长到底是仅仅源于生产率的提高，还是伴随着产品质量的显著提高？中国出口产品质量到底有多大进步？它对出口增长的贡献有多大？本课题将致力于回答这些问题。具体地讲，本课题将研究中国出口产品质量在企业间的异质性及其随时间的变化趋势，中国产品质量在不同市场的差别，前瞻性的企业如何内生的选择出口目的地，以及如何选择旨在提高产品质量以及生产率的研发投资。我们将分两步来回答这些问题。首先，我们会发展建立一个统一的框架利用现有的数据（包括投入，产出，出口量，出口价格，目的地等）来建立每个企业生产率和产品质量的指标。其中，生产率是企业-时点异质性的，而产品质量则随企业、时间、以及市场的不同而有差异。这个框架相对于现有文献的创新之处在于产品质量的指标在不同市场间是可比的。然后，我们会建立一个动态模型来解释企业对产品定价、质量选择、和出口目的地选择的最优决策。这个模型将为解释中国企业出口的扩张提供一个综合的微观分析框架。基于这个模型,我们将利用中国制造业企业调查数据和中国海关交易数据构成的联立数据库进行实证分析。

17503115.label: Realisation of objectives
17503115.value: We developed a general framework to disentangle firm-level product quality and productivity (Objective 1). One major advantage of our method is that the developed product quality measure is comparable across markets, because our method combines information from demand, supply, and market competition across firms in multiple markets. In the application to the Chinese export data during 2000-2006, we find systematic quality sorting of Chinese exports in the global market. Firms tend to export high quality products to more developed countries and low quality products to low-income countries (Objective 2). However, due to the intensive competition from other high-quality products, Chinese exports are still considered as of low quality by consumers in the developed countries. This results in lower margins of Chinese export in many developed countries, compared with that of exports to low-income countries. We find that past exporting experience has a positive impact on firms' quality choice (Objective 3 and 4). We also find substantial improvement of export quality by Chinese firms in the global market over time, especially after China's accession to WTO in 2002. The model is ready to be used to provide a micro-based guideline for Chinese firms and policy makers to improve the serious quality concern of Chinese products in the international markets (Objective 5), for which we are conducting further counterfactual experiments to evaluate the impact of different policy choices. The results are summarised in two papers. 1. "Product Quality, Productivity, and Margins of Chinese Exports in the Global Markets", by Shengyu Li and Hongsong Zhang. 2. "Input Prices, Productivity and Trade Dynamics: Long-run Effects of Liberalization on Chinese Paint Manufacturer", by Paul Grieco, Shengyu Li, and Hongsong Zhang.

17503115.label: Major findings and research outcome
17503115.value: In the first paper, "Product Quality, Productivity, and Margins of Chinese Exports in the Global Markets", we examine the dispersion of Chinese product quality in different export markets, and how the destination-based quality sorting determines the export margins of Chinese firms in the global markets. We develop a general framework to disentangle firm-level product quality and productivity. One major advantage of our method is that the developed product quality measure is comparable across markets, because our method combines information from demand, supply, and market competition across firms in multiple markets. In the application to the Chinese export data during 2000-2006, we find systematic quality sorting of Chinese exports in the global market. Firms tend to export high quality products to more developed countries and low quality products to low-income countries. However, due to the intensive competition from other high-quality products, Chinese exports are still considered as of low quality by consumers in the developed countries. This results in lower margins of Chinese export in many developed countries, compared with that of exports to low-income countries. We also find substantial improvement of export quality by Chinese firms in the global market over time, especially after China's accession to WTO in 2002. In the second paper, "Input Prices, Productivity and Trade Dynamics: Long-run Effects of Liberalization on Chinese Paint Manufacturer", we develop a dynamic structural model to analyze the impact of input tariff liberalization on input prices, trading decisions, productivity, and firm performance. While input tariff liberalization directly affects input price benefits of importing, its impact on trade participation generates indirect benefits through additional channels, such as productivity improvements and complementarity between importing and exporting. To disentangle these effects, our model separately measures importing's effect on intermediate input prices and productivity. We apply the model to examine the reaction of Chinese paint manufacturers to China's accession to the World Trade Organization (WTO). We find a mild short-term effect of input tariff liberalization in the industry. The effect is amplified in the long run by induced trade participation, resulting in even higher aggregate productivity and lower input prices. Overall, this effect increases the average present firm value by 2.3 percent.

17503115.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17503115.value: Based on the first paper, we plan to further study the importance of within- and cross-firm quality sorting in different destinations in the global market, and how export quality and domestic quality provision interact as firms participate in international trade. Moreover, the globally comparable measure of output quality can be applied to study many relevant economic questions that require a precise measure of output quality.

17503115.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17503115.value: How consumers perceive the quality of products provided by a firm is an important factor determining demand for this firm. In the context of international trade, product quality is more important. It determines where the firm can export, how much to export, and the profit margin in each market. Based on a new measure of output quality that is comparable across markets, the first paper of this project examines how the product quality of Chinese exports differs across firms and markets and how quality, productivity, and competitor's quality determine the export margins of Chinese firms in the global markets. The model provides a comprehensive way to evaluate and explain both the growth and expansion of Chinese exports in the global markets. The second paper of this project provides a systematic framework to quantify the impact of input tariff liberalization on the performance of importers in the short run and long run. While input tariff liberalization directly affects input price benefits of importing, its impact on trade participation generates indirect benefits through additional channels, such as productivity improvements and complementarity between importing and exporting. The paper finds a mild short-term effect of input tariff liberalization; the long-run effect is amplified by induced trade participation.

17503815.label: Project Objectives
17503815.value: This research aims to develop a theory-driven model of CHIT-based disease self-monitoring behavior to improve the understanding of the key factors that drive such behavior. Specifically, we will examine the effects of pertinent factors that determine self-monitoring of vital signs using a tablet-based self-monitoring system among chronically ill patients. The specific aims and objectives of this study are (A1) to assess the key factors that affect the intention to perform CHIT-based disease self-monitoring and actual performance of such behavior among patients with co-morbid type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension; and (A2) to evaluate the magnitude of the effects of these factors using structural equation modeling. Throughout the study, we will aim to provide recommendations and strategies for the effective design of patient-focused CHIT-augmented self-monitoring interventions.

17600015.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17600015.value: 本課題嘗試探討徽州商業家族中的博學女性基於商業與文化資本的結合為其家族謀求 “進身之階”的努力。近年來，徽學備受關注，尤以徽州商業家族在明代中後期至清代中後期（或稱“早期現代”）的繁榮為海內外研究的重心。有關商業家族與士紳階層的相互滲透已有詳盡研究，這些家族以徽州為發源地向商業中心城市（如：揚州、蘇州、杭州、上海）的遷移也為更大範圍內探討這一時期社會、經濟多方面的變化提供了極為豐富的研究資料。儘管如此，女性在徽州商業家族中所發揮的作用卻往往受到忽略。現有的零星研究或強調徽州大為盛行的貞孝節烈觀對女性的殘害，或試圖在宗譜資料中尋找有關女性重視商業活動的有限記錄，並以此作為這些女性有“反封建”傾向的證據。本課題的目的正是為了彌補現有研究的不足及糾正其偏差。 博學女性在徽州商業家族中的出現本身即反映了廣泛的社會、經濟以及性別關係的變化，同時也推動這些變化的發展。與這一時期繁盛的江南閨秀文化相呼應，徽州商業家族重視女性的教育並視其為家族文化資本，遷移至江南一帶商業中心城市的徽州宗族更以其女性成員融入江南閨秀文化為傲。以汪氏、程氏、方氏、曹氏等鹽商大族為例，女性以詩、文著稱者代不乏人，她們廣泛的文化活動以及與江南一帶世家閨秀的互通聲氣留下了諸多歷史記錄。本課題結合宗譜、地方誌、文人筆記、閨秀詩歌總集等資料，嘗試勾勒出這一系列文化活動及其重心遷移的地圖，並利用近年來大量翻印、再版的明清女性詩文別集及資料庫，進一步詳細探討這些女性在家族教育與其他事務、文學與藝術事業、精英社會關係網、慈善活動等方面發揮的關鍵作用。

17600415.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17600415.value: Painting, sculpture, installation art, conceptual art, and performance art are just some of the genres and traditions of fine arts that have used language (writing and speech) as their material and medium of expression. In early Italian Renaissance painting, language inscriptions may have been marginal to the overall composition, but they served the symbolic function of representing characters, for example, as ‘foreign’ or ‘otherworldly’. Since the 1960s, international conceptual art made ‘language’, (writing in particular) its key material and a form of representation closely linked to the New Left, feminism, civil and gay rights movement, and counterculture. This project offers to formulate the first systematic theoretical account of language in art, i.e. in works for which language is the sole or key component of their visuality and meaning making. A sizable body of art historical and art critical work has dealt with different aspects of writing and speech in art, but it has largely focused on the iconographic aspects of texts, their representation and meaning in individual artists, schools or movements. So far, no extended account of language use in art has been attempted in sociolinguistics. Yet, art has not only been a site of aesthetic visualisation of the ‘poetic’ in language (Jakobson, 1960). On the contrary, artists have used a range of genres and modalities to research and experiment with the boundaries of linguistic communication as forms of political expression and subversion, social activism and technological innovation. Frequently and unjustifiably dismissed as whimsical and elitist, or as a negligible embellishment, linguistic innovation in art has given rise to a whole array of sociolinguistic practices in contemporary social life. The influences of the typographic discoveries of the European avant-garde, or pop art’s experiments with language are now commonplace in the global semioscape; Cimabue’s or Jan van Eyck’s ‘pseudoscripts’ long predate the ‘polylingual or ‘metrolingual’ play of contemporary youth cultures; Alighiero Boetti’s and others’ mail art demonstrated how language can be ‘deterritorialized’ decades before it has become commonplace in ‘new’ mobile media and the internet. This project aims to bring text-based art to the attention of Sociolinguists and Discourse Analysts as a notable area of social action and performativity, and to understand the linguistic processes of meaning-making in art through the frameworks of both these disciplines. 在藝術傳統中有很多藝術形式，包括繪畫，雕塑，裝置藝術，觀念藝術和表演藝術等，都使用語言（包括書寫和語音）作為藝術表現的材料和媒介。在早期意大利文藝復興繪畫中，雖然語言題字的作用對於整體構圖無足輕重，但它們具備像征意義：代表‘外來的’或‘來自神秘的另一個世界的’。自1960年以來，國際觀念藝術廣泛使用‘語言’（尤其是書寫）作為主要的材料和表達形式。這一轉變和新左運動，女權主義，民權和同性戀權利運動，以及反文化運動密切相關。本研究項目將第一次系統的理論化研究藝術中（尤其是那些語言作為唯一或首要的視覺及意義表達工具的藝術作品）的語言。 在藝術史和藝術批判學科中，已經有學者研究藝術作品中的書寫和語音，但是他們關注的都是語言的圖像意義，或語言使用在某個藝術家或某個流派，運動中的意義。到目前為止，社會語言學還沒有詳細研究藝術中的語言使用。而實際上，在各種藝術形式中，不僅語言的‘詩學’功能（Jakobson，1960）得到美學上的運用，很多藝術家開始通過各種體裁和模式來研究和探索語言交流形式應用於政治表達和顛覆，社會行動主義，科技創新等領域的可能性。雖然經常被誤解為古怪的，精英主義的，或者可有可無的裝飾，藝術中的語言創新已經影響了當代生活一系列的社會語言實踐。歐洲前衛藝術的字體創新，或波普藝術的語言實驗的影響，已經遍及全球符號景觀；契馬布埃（Cimabue）或揚•凡•艾克（Jan Van Eyck）使用的‘偽文字’早在當代年輕人中流行的雜糅多種語言的做法之前；阿裡傑羅•波提（Alighiero Boetti）及其他藝術家的郵寄藝術也早在‘新’移動媒體和互聯網之前就展示了語言如何被‘解域化’。 該研究項目旨在將基於文本的藝術置於社會語言學和話語分析研究者的視野之中，強調這些語言藝術形式作為社會行動和表演性的特征，並通過這兩個學科現有的理論框架來理解藝術作品運用語言表達意義的過程。

17600415.label: Realisation of objectives
17600415.value: Objective 4 deals with the specific vehicles by means of which the other objectives were realized and their results disseminated transnationally. My goal of publishing two journal papers and a book manuscript was transformed into the publication of multiple, stand-alone outputs. A book manuscript continues to be developed. Due to obstacles produced by pandemic conditions, my plan to produce an edited collection based on an invited conference panel (SS23) did not materialize due to authors’ inability to deliver their contributions. The number of print publications directly tied to this project is 14 (with 12 published, one in press, and one under review). These include 7 articles in peer-reviewed journals, 6 book chapters, and 1 edited special issue. Between 2016 and 2020, I presented research directly relating to this project and its objectives at 18 international conferences in 12 countries/regions, excluding one recent and two forthcoming conferences that I was forced to pull out of due to a major health crisis. Objectives 1 and 2 are closely connected to one another in that the broadening of the scope of theorizing key concepts in sociolinguistics (Objective 2) has been achieved through my synthesis of two different ways of doing sociolinguistics—social semiotics and linguistic anthropology—to present a coherent sociolinguistic account of language as a medium in the visual arts (Objective 1). This work is encapsulated in a conference presentation (SS23) in which I explore some synergies and points of contact between social semiotics and linguistic anthropology in the study of text based-art. With specific reference to the abstract art of asemic writing by Cy Twombly, I draw parallels between social semiotics and linguistic anthropology (twin disciplines that are not commonly considered together across sociolinguistics). In particular, I elucidate new connections between two pairs of critical concepts from these respective fields: affordances and resemiotisation (in social semiotics) and indexicality and enregisterment (in linguistic anthropology). The interdisciplinary approach to sociolinguistics provides fertile ground for combining analyses of linguistic and non-linguistic modes of communication. Another example of how the project offered an insightful and coherent sociolinguistic account of language as a medium and form of expression in the visual arts (Objective 1) concerns the connections it establishes between so-called “high art,” (as in my work on Xu Bing, Robert Indiana, and the avant-garde practice of assemblage) and more commercial or popular forms (i.e. public monuments, commercial signage, T-shirts, etc.). In terms of the broadening of the scope of theorization of sociolinguistic concepts (Objective 2), in addition to the concepts described above, my research has resulted in the expansion of the theoretical application of the following terms to text-based visual art, thereby further contributing to Objective 1: AUTHENCITY: I compare “new writing” (Van Leeuwen) in advertising, corporate communication, and education with its precursors in text-based art of the early 20th century avant-garde, contemporary conceptual and abstract art. Although the tradition of combining writing and graphic design spans millennia (cf. Rypson), I trace the origins of new writing to Guillaume Apollinaire's picture-poems (‘calligrams’), cubist papiers collés, Marinetti’s idea of “words at liberty”, conceptual art, and so on. In my account, what is different between corporate/educational new writing and its artistic precedents is that the former derives its linguistic authority from the principle of anonymity, while the latter from the principle of authenticity (Woolard; Gal and Woolard). CREATIVITY: Creativity is closely bound up with transformation. I examine different semiotic processes, such as translation (“moving” meaning “within” and “across” modes), transformation (changes in representation with no change in mode, e.g. translation of a novel from English to German), and transduction (also known as intersemiotic translation or transmutation—that is, moving across modes, for example from image to speech). The project exemplifies a wide range of creative and social processes across artistic texts (conceptual, abstract, figurative, and multimodal). IDEOLOGY: One of the fundamental aspects of sociolinguistic research concerns the referential and relational meaning of language and its social and cultural contexts. Ideology (alongside form, use, and domain) is one of the four aspects of language—Silverstein’s total linguistic fact. In my work on Xu Bing, I demonstrate how contemporary visual artists experiment with new ways of displaying language, employing forms of symbolic manipulation that subvert dominant language ideologies. In my research on the Ibsen Sitat, a text-based public monument, I argue that, as a national symbol, its placement at street level espouses an egalitarian, or democratic nationalist ethos. My research on sculptural place names proposes that such manifestations of visual art can be seen as mediators of elitism and egalitarianism, with implications for how we understand gentrified urban spaces. MATERIALITY: While the study of the symbolic dimension of language has been a concern in sociolinguistics, its materiality has been relatively neglected. In this project, the materiality of language—especially of writing—is considered as a rich and important semiotic resource in terms of its affordances and indexicalities. My research explores the juxtaposition of elements, objects, and materials in the artistic assemblages of 20th Century avant-garde art and draws parallels with the concept of semiotic assemblages used today by applied linguists, highlighting how the latter needs to be retheorized in light of these early experiments in the visual arts. MEDIATION: In my work on Robert Indiana’s text-based art, I show how his meticulously detailed artist books, poems and artist statements meld into a chain of creative remediations of his “primary” artworks. Likewise, subsequent recontextualizations of his personal stories as visual spectacles create chains of transformations in content and form. I further explore this with relation to the mediatization of art in broadcast media (TV), especially with reference to performance between the operating logics of immediacy and hypermediacy. SPECTACLE: What I call ‘spectacular writing’ typically bears the following characteristics: large scale; extravagant; immersive; one off / repetitive; self-referential; self-reflexive; diverse materially; performative. I discuss three approaches to spectacular language in the visual arts based on three, interdisciplinary frameworks: “consumerist representation” (Debord), “visual pleasure’ (Mulvey), “grotesque ritual” (Bakhtin, 1968). My findings on the relationship between avant-garde and semiotic assemblages speaks to the way in which I bridge the gap between sociolinguistic and art historical research (Objective 3). Language display in art and public spaces has been conceptualised as a semiotic assemblage, and my revision of this concept adds a dynamic dimension of linguistic mobility captured by the term moiré effect, directly linked to design and visual art, especially kinetic sculpture and installations. Linguistic-semiotic landscapes are inherently chaotic, unpredictable, and multifarious. It is precisely because of these empirical complexities, marked by shifting, shimmering layers of semiotic resources and actions, that I propose to view semiotic relations as moiré-like in their apparent or actual motion as the patterns created by the overlaying movements, sounds, texts, artefacts, spaces, and bodies fluctuate in a constant ebb and flow of interactional synchronicity and rupture. In my work on Robert Indiana, I use art historical research to inform my sociolinguistic analyses of his text-based pieces from a narrative point of view (as ‘small stories’). This dialogue between sociolinguistics and art history is a recurring feature of the work relating to this project, whether this be accomplished through the application of sociolinguistic concepts to objects traditionally studied by art historians, or by drawing from art historical discourses and objects of analysis to further enrich the field of sociolinguistics

17600415.label: Major findings and research outcome
17600415.value: The major findings can be summarized in relation to the following interrelated areas: the interdisciplinary synthesis of discourses, methods, and theoretical approaches used in the sociolinguistic analysis of language in art; the insights produced by broadening the remit of the analysis of text-based art across elite and egalitarian platforms; and the re-theorization of a number of key concepts in sociolinguistics in light of such interdisciplinary cross-fertilizations. My research on the synergies between the cognate disciplines of social semiotics and linguistic anthropology (conference paper at SS23) established critical correspondences between concepts in these respective fields (i.e. affordances and resemiotisation; indexicality and enregisterment). I further demonstrate how an interdisciplinary synthesis between social semiotics and linguistic anthropology can be mobilized to enrich the sociolinguistic analysis of linguistic and non-linguistic modes of communication, as I do in my work on writing in the city (Jaworski and Li) and on the text displayed on T-shirts of mobile urban subjects (Jaworski and Lou). My research on the relationship between the avant-garde art of assemblage and the concept of semiotic assemblage (Jaworski 2017, 2020a, 2020b) is similarly based on an interdisciplinary approach located at the intersection of sociolinguistics and art history. My research broadens the remit of the analysis of text-based art across elite and egalitarian platforms, demonstrating that there is only a fine line dividing commercially driven language display and conceptual text-based art, which is itself a commercial activity (Jaworski 2018; 2020a, 2020b, etc.). My research findings shed new light on the nature of sociolinguistic objects of inquiry, drawing parallels between text-based art (Cubism, Dada) and more mundane public texts (street signs, advertisements). Consequently, I have exposed various continuities between these two realms—links between the interpretation of artistic and non-artistic publicly displayed texts—which have in turn enriched my exploration of key sociolinguistic concepts, such as ideology, creativity, materiality, etc. (e.g. Jaworski 2019a, 2019b) Ideology is one of the sociolinguistic concepts that has been theorized in light of this project’s interdisciplinary approach. My findings demonstrate, for example, that national language ideologies in text-based art are malleable (Jaworski, 2018); national-literary monuments blurring the boundaries between literature and visual arts (in this case, sculpture) espouse two conflicting stances, the egalitarian and elitist (Jaworski and Gonçalves in press); and upmarket commercial spaces style their marketing resources (signage, visual imagery) drawing on diverse artistic sources such as minimalist painting, baroque sculpture, and surrealism (Jaworski 2019b).

17600415.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17600415.value: Preparation of the manuscript for my monograph on “Language and art” is ongoing. The diverse array of more specific and contextualized analyses of text-based art in the research outputs, as well as the richly productive dialogues with artists and scholars conducted outside of the remit of this project, have functioned to clarify both my more general theoretical framing and the overall conceptual structure and organization. With respect to the former, my findings on the synergies between the cognate fields of social semiotics and linguistic anthropology and my interdisciplinary engagement with art historical discourses and objects of analysis have contributed to the development of a coherent sociolinguistic approach to text-based art—one that foregrounds and elucidates the continuities between language in art as it is manifest in both avant-garde and so-called “high” cultural production and more popular, commercial, or public forms of art. The project’s objective of broadening the scope of sociolinguistic concepts has in turn informed its structure, providing the basis for planned individual chapters around particular concepts, some of which have been developed in the project, and some that are currently being drafted: Assemblage; Creativity; Diversity; Genre; Ideology; Materiality; Self-referentiality; Signatures; Spectacle; Participation; Performativity.

17600415.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17600415.value: The project examines text and language as a medium and form of communication in the visual arts. Bridging the gap between text and image, the research synthesizes social approaches to the study of language and art history. The insights broaden the scope of the analysis of text-based art across elite (so called “high art”) and egalitarian (the quotidian) platforms such as the mass media and commerce. The project mobilizes an interdisciplinary toolbox spanning semiotic theory, narrative analysis, multimodality, etc., to analyze linguistic and non-linguistic modes of communication. Insights about the use of language in art are drawn from the 20th century avant-garde, pop art, conceptual art, etc., as well as the mundane writing displayed in the city, such as text displayed on T-shirts, information signage, advertising, public sculptures, etc. A monograph on “Language and art” is underway and will be organised around a long list of analytic terms analysing text in modern and contemporary art: Assemblage; Creativity; Diversity; Genre; Ideology; Materiality; Self-referentiality; Signatures; Spectacle; Participation; Performativity; Titles.

17600515.label: Project Objectives
17600515.value: To write a critical monograph on John Kneubuhl's dramatic work in its entirety spanning fifty years (1942 to 1992), focusing on the evolution of its thematic concerns and formal affiliations and innovations, especially regarding the working together of Western and Polynesian traditions. To situate Kneubuhl's work historically in the specific local contexts in which his plays have been produced to date (in the 1940s, the 1970s, the 1990s, and the present), focusing especially on the connections between Kneubuhl's evolving notion of theatricality, as expressed in his plays and his directorial efforts, and changing conditions and conventions of theatrical production. To trace the coherence and evolution of Kneubuhl's vision of a Pacific theatre, in both his dramatic and non-dramatic writing, and to address its place and significance in the emergence of a popular Pacific theatre in the late twentieth century. To initiate and encourage further critical study and debate of Kneubuhl's work and its value by presenting preliminary findings at conferences and in other forms of publication, with a view to furthering the archival preservation and possible dissemination of his dramatic work as a resource for future scholarly and creative pursuits in the Pacific and elsewhere.

17600515.value: The main objective of this project is to write the first book-length critical study of the work of Samoan playwright John Kneubuhl (1920-1992). Kneubuhl is generally acknowledged as a pioneer of contemporary Pacific theatre, yet to date his dramatic work is not widely known and remains little studied, largely due to his indifference, if not reluctance, to see it published in print until quite late in his life. Still, Kneubuhls career and achievements are remarkable: born in American Samoa and later educated in Hawai‘i, his talent for playwriting was recognized at Yale University when he was the first undergraduate to be admitted to the prestigious Workshop 47 and saw his first two plays produced before graduating. After the Second World War, as a young playwright and associate director at the Honolulu Community Theatre, he left his mark promoting the development of a local theatre through both original plays and local adaptations of classics. After writing and directing the first feature film by a Pacific Islander, he left Honolulu for Hollywood where he spent the next eighteen years as a successful script writer for television, only to abruptly turn his back on the business and return to Samoa and Hawai‘i, where he would spend the rest of his life as a teacher of Polynesian culture and history and a mentor of local theatre in Hawai‘i, while completing his last three plays. His last play was premiered in Pago Pago the day he died and produced with great success in Auckland a year later and has since become the focus of most of the small number of critical discussions of Kneubuhl's work. This project aims to substantially advance the critical recognition of Kneubuhl's dramatic work by studying it in its entirety spanning fifty years (1942-1992), based on unpublished scripts and related manuscript material collected in various locations in Hawai‘i. This will result in the first study to trace and interpret the coherence and evolution of Kneubuhl's thematic concerns and theatrical vision across his work and to situate it historically and critically in its various contexts of theatrical production. By focusing particularly on Kneubuhl's treatment of local histories, his bilingual and multilingual dramatic experimentation, and his working together of Polynesian theatrical traditions and Western dramatic forms, this project will make a significant contribution to the study of the emergence of a popular Pacific theatre and will stimulate further critical engagement with Kneubuhl's work. 本硏究計劃的主要目的，在於深入研究撒摩亞劇作家約翰．紐布爾 (1920 - 1992) 的作品，撰寫成這個課題的第一本學術專著。紐布爾是公認為當代太平洋區域戲劇創作的先驅，然而其作品既未廣為人知，研究更屬寥寥，主因是紐布爾本人直到晚年都不熟衷甚至不願意把劇作印行出版。儘管如此，卻無損於他在劇壇的卓越成就。紐布爾生於太平洋美屬的撒摩亞，在夏威夷上學，就讀於耶魯大學期間已嶄露頭角，發揮戲劇才華，成為著名的「四十七號戲劇坊」的第一位本科生，大學還未畢業已經製作搬演了首兩部作品。第二次世界大戰結束後，青壯之年的紐布爾出任檀香山社區劇團的副團長，演出原創劇及改編的經典劇目，推進當地的劇運，成績斐然。他在轉往荷里活發展前，還在夏威夷創作了一個電影劇本並親自執導，開太平洋地區島民之先河。他在荷里活十八年，為電視節目撰稿，本來做得很不錯，卻遽然放棄，回到撒摩亞和夏威夷，貢獻餘生於太平洋島嶼的文化歷史的教育工作，並推動培育夏威夷當地的劇運發展。他最後的三個劇作，都完成於這個時期。紐布爾離世之日，正是他最後一個劇本在撒摩亞首府帕果．帕果首演當天；翌年此劇在紐西蘭的奧克蘭演出，非常成功，至今探硏紐布爾的劇作為數不多，但大都以此劇為焦點。本研究計劃旨在大力提高對紐布爾劇作的認識及成就的認同，研究範圍包括其長達五十年的創作生涯 (1942 - 1992)；研究取材宏富，資料包括在夏威夷當地搜羅所得的未刊劇稿及其他相關稿件，從而深入了解創作的主題用意及劇劇意念，將有助於尋本探源，剖釋演變，開啟紐布爾硏究的新局面。本硏究尤其注意紐布爾對於當地歷史的處理丶在雙語及多元文化方面的戲劇實驗，以及如何揉合太平洋島嶼的戲劇傳統及西方的戲劇形式等。本硏究對於現在已廣受注意的太平洋地區大眾島民的戲劇研究，將會成為重要的學術貢獻，並開啟對紐布爾作品探研的大門。

17600515.label: Realisation of objectives
17600515.value: The four objectives have been mostly realized as follows: 1. To write a critical monograph on John Kneubuhl's dramatic work in its entirety spanning fifty years (1942 to 1992), focusing on the evolution of its thematic concerns and formal affiliations and innovations, especially regarding the working together of Western and Polynesian traditions. This objective has been realized to about 75%. The implementation of the research plan had to be adjusted in connection with other teaching and research commitments in the first year of the project. I was teaching two new courses in the first half of 2016 (including a common core course) and was co-organizing a conference (unrelated to the project) at HKU in March 2016, following which I was co-editing a special themed section of the Island Studies Journal. I was also invited to give a keynote lecture (unrelated to the project) at a conference in London in July 2016, followed by the writing up of the lead essay of a special section in the journal Interventions. Due to these commitments, I was only able to undertake the two planned research trips in 2017 and as a result my progress on the monograph was delayed. However, I have succeeded in collecting and reading/viewing all the primary material needed and have also acquired and almost completed reading the additional sources related to Pacific theatre, collected in New Zealand and Hawaii in 2017. The draft of the monograph is in progress and will be completed in 2019. 2. To situate Kneubuhl's work historically in the specific local contexts in which his plays have been produced to date (in the 1940s, the 1970s, the 1990s, and the present), focusing especially on the connections between Kneubuhl's evolving notion of theatricality, as expressed in his plays and his directorial efforts, and changing conditions and conventions of theatrical production. This objective has been fully realized and has resulted in several publications. Based on unpublished play scripts and contextual material collected before the start of the project, I was able to present a paper on Kneubuhl’s Hawaiian plays (from the 1940s to 1990) at a conference in Fiji in April 2016. The paper demonstrated the continuity and the transformation of Kneubuhl’s theatrical vision across his career, notably including work he produced and directed while living in Hollywood. I was able to research contexts of Kneubuhl’s writing and the production of his works further during my research trips to New Zealand in March-April 2017 and to Hawaii in October 2017, which included both meetings with important resource persons and archival research, sourcing and examining audio recordings. In Auckland I met with the husband of the (recently deceased) producer of the first production of Kneubuhl’s last play in 1993 and was able to acquire important documents related to this show as well as to view partial footage of it. I also met with the director of a more recent production of another play by Kneubuhl, staged in Auckland in 2013, which I was able to view on DVD and to collect important documents, including photographs, related to it. In Wellington, I met with the director of the first two productions of Think of a Garden, Nathaniel Lees, to discuss the process and impact of these shows. I also met with current Maori and Pacific theatre directors and producers who remember these shows and who shared their own theatrical work and vision with me. At the National Library of New Zealand, I was also able to collect important material related to the development of Pacific theatre in New Zealand since the 1990s. In Hawaii, I was able to complete archival research, both from the private collection of Kneubuhl’s niece, playwright and novelist Victoria Nalani Kneubuhl, and in the archive of the Bishop Museum. The latter in particular yielded a fascinating disvovery: an audio recording of a long conversation between Maiki Aiu Lake and Mary Kawena Pukui from 1962, when Aiu was choreographing the dances for the pageant Kneubuhl had written and was directing for the 1962 Aloha Week festival. Two essays, written about Kneubuhl’s work in connection with the work of other Pacific playwrights, will be published in 2019. 3. To trace the coherence and evolution of Kneubuhl's vision of a Pacific theatre, in both his dramatic and non-dramatic writing, and to address its place and significance in the emergence of a popular Pacific theatre in the late twentieth century. This objective has been fully realized and has resulted in the publication of a journal article. Studying Kneubuhl’s writings on Polynesian and Samoan history, as well as on play writing, and reading the transcripts of two long life history interviews he made with two friends and colleagues in American Samoa and Hawaii, I was able to trace the evolution of his vision of a Pacific theatre and to situate his plays in connection with his non-dramatic work, especially in oral history. In Hawaii I was also given a copy of an unpublished novel Kneubuhl wrote while in Hollywood, which, focusing on a well-known missionary to the Pacific, provides an important facet to Kneubuhl’s lifelong interest in missionary lives and stories, including those of his own Pritchard ancestors. Victoria Kneubuhl introduced me to her brother who lives in American Samoa and in connection with a conference in Apia Samoa in Nov.-Dec. 2017, I was able to visit Kneubuhl’s birthplace (and grave) and to meet with his nephew there, who in turn introduced me to Kneubuhl’s daughter, who is aware and approves of my writing about her father and his work. Just as I was revising the article on Kneubuhl and oral history, I was alerted to the production of his autobiographical last play in Auckland in January 2018, which I was able to attend and discuss with the director, Anapela Polata’ivao. 4. To initiate and encourage further critical study and debate of Kneubuhl's work and its value by presenting preliminary findings at conferences and in other forms of publication, with a view to furthering the archival preservation and possible dissemination of his dramatic work as a resource for future scholarly and creative pursuits in the Pacific and elsewhere. This objective has been fully realized. At the biannual conference of the Pacific History Association in Guam in May 2016, I met the librarian of the Hawaiian and Pacific section of the Hamilton Library at University of Hawaii in Manoa and discussed the prospect of archiving John Kneubuhl’s unpublished scripts. This process is now underway, with audio recordings of his radio talks and life history interviews now accessible at the library. I returned to Hawaii in October 2017 to listen to these recordings and wrote my article on Kneubuhl and oral history based on this archival material. I also presented this paper at the Center for Biographical Research at the University of Hawaii where I had collected much of the material for my research. I also presented papers at the University of Fiji in April 2016 and at the 13th International Small Island Cultures conference in St. John’s, Newfoundland, in June 2017. I have shared my work with theatre directors and producers in New Zealand and Hawaii and have asked about plans for new productions, possibly coinciding with the Festival of Pacific Arts & Culture in Hawaii in 2020.

17600515.label: Major findings and research outcome
17600515.value: The research findings and discoveries that this project has enabled me to gain have exceeded my expectations. From preliminary research that formed the basis of my GRF application, I had a good sense of the trajectory of John Kneubuhl’s career as a playwright from the1940s to the 1990s. This project allowed me time to read closely all the material I had previously collected, to complete gaps in my research and to meet and discuss Kneubuhl’s work with knowledgeable resource persons in the field of Pacific theatre and writing. In the process, I made some astonishing discoveries. Reading all of Kneubuhl’s extant Hawaiian plays, I was able to trace the development of Kneubuhl’s theatrical vision and to recognize the importance of Hawai’i in the formation of his emphatically Polynesian (and not simply Samoan) identification. What was particularly striking was the continuity of his cultural and theatrical concerns and interests over several decades and how each play built on and transformed the material and shapes established by its predecessor. Most exciting was the discovery of the script of a pageant, “The Hula Dancer,” which Kneubuhl wrote for the Honolulu Aloha Week festival in 1962 (when he was working in Hollywood), and which forms a pivotal work linking his earliest Hawaiian play, Harp in the Willows (1947), and his return to Hawai’i after returning to Samoa, with Hello Hello Hello and especially Mele Kanikau in the 1970s. Another major discovery was Kneubuhl’s investment in oral history after his return to Samoa from Hollywood in 1968, which resulted in a series of radio talks (broadcast in American Samoa), a long life history interview, as well as several lectures and the manuscript of a Samoan cultural history. Reading and listening to these, I have been able to identify the connections between Kneubuhl’s late dramatic work and his deep immersion in Polynesian and Samoan culture and history. And yet another major discovery, made possible by this project, was the extent to which Kneubuhl is remembered and respected among the Pacific diaspora today. This was particularly evident in New Zealand where I met with several well-known Polynesian directors, actors and playwrights, who were involved in the production of two of his plays in New Zealand in 1993, 1995 and 2013. Through these contacts, I was also able to return to Auckland to see the latest production of his last play, Think of a Garden, in January 2018.

17600515.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17600515.value: Over the two years working on this project, I have not only become conversant with the body of John Kneubuhl’s unpublished work, but I have also met and established good relationships with many important people close to John Kneubuhl and working in Pacific theatre, including members of his family and playwrights, directors and producers in Hawai’i and New Zealand. Based on some of these contacts, I have already organized a small conference at the University of Hong Kong in 2018, bringing together theatre practitioners and scholars from New Zealand and Hawai‘i, as well as Hong Kong and other countries. The trust and shared vision and interest that has been established will be a basis for future collaborations, possibly in connection with John Kneubuhl’s centenary in 2020, when the four-yearly Festival of Pacific Arts & Culture will be held in Hawai‘i. With the preliminary archiving of some of Kneubuhl’s unpublished materials (especially audio recordings) in the Hamilton library at the University of Hawai‘i, it will also be possible to push for a more complete acquisition and cataloguing of all of Kneubuhl’s unpublished writings there, most importantly his play scripts. The publication of my monograph on Kneubuhl will lend support to such endeavors.

17600515.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17600515.value: This research project funded by the General Research Fund has undertaken an in-depth study of the leading Pacific playwright, John Kneubuhl from Samoa (1920-1992), who was also a highly successful screenwriter in Hollywood in the1950s and 60s and a renowned authority and teacher of Polynesian culture and history. The project has involved the collection and close examination of all of Kneubuhl’s published and unpublished plays, as well as his unpublished lectures, radio talks, interviews and correspondence, resulting in several publications and conference presentations on Kneubuhl’s contribution to Hawaiian theatre, his place in Pacific theatre, his vision of a Polynesian theatre, and his involvement in oral history. The project has also aimed to promote efforts to establish an archive of Kneubuhl’s largely unpublished writings and audio recordings and some of these are now accessible at the library of the University of Hawaii in Manoa. The project also sought to ascertain and assess the importance of Kneubuhl’s work for contemporary Pacific theatre, especially in New Zealand and Hawai‘i, through a series of interviews with important writers, directors and producers, and attendance, in January 2018, at a production of his last play in Auckland. The project findings will be published in a book.

17600915.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17600915.value: The proposed research aims to develop an account of the normative ethical views of the Zhuangzi, evaluate the plausibility of these views, and situate them in the context of ethical discourse today. The project will produce two journal articles, one on Zhuangist ethics of interpersonal conduct and one relating the Zhuangzi to contemporary philosophical ethics. The project will also produce the manuscript of a book entitled _Zhuangzi: Ways of Wandering_ incorporating material from the two journal articles along with content from several of the PI’s previous publications. Classical Chinese philosophy was characterized by lively, provocative discourse concerning the nature and content of the dao (way), the proper course of personal and sociopolitical life. Prominent movements such as the Confucians and Mohists grounded their normative account of the dao in moral values such as ren (benevolence), yi (right), and li (ritual propriety). These movements shared the conviction that moral ideals are central to the theory and practice of the dao. The Daoist anthology Zhuangzi offers a skeptical critique of such conceptions of dao, which motivates an alternative approach by which dao is not framed in terms of moral values. Instead, as one Zhuangzi passage proposes, we are to directly “conduct ourselves through de (potency, virtuosity) and move by following dao.” In developing this alternative ethical vision, the writings collected in the Zhuangzi present a eudaimonistic conception of the good individual life, a constructive account of the process of ethical development by which agents can come to realize these eudaimonistic ideals, and an inchoate, pragmatic approach to normative evaluation of actions or courses of action. The proposed project builds on the principal investigator’s previous work on skepticism, ethics, and psychology in the Zhuangzi to develop an interpretation of a Zhuangist approach to normative ethics, especially the relatively unexplored topic of interpersonal conduct. The primarily work of the project is to formulate the Zhuangist normative vision as presented through concepts such as “walking two ways” (liang xing), “competence” (tong), and “the right is set by the fitting” (yi she yu shi). A secondary aspect of the project will be to relate Zhuangist ethics to contemporary philosophical ethics, in particular by comparing and contrasting it with recent moral particularism, as articulated by McDowell, Dancy, and others. By way of this comparative work, the project will explore the significance of Zhuangist ethics for contemporary ethical discourse.

17600915.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17600915.value: The various threads of discourse preserved in the Zhuāngzǐ present a radical challenge to prevailing ways of thinking about ethics. The dominant stance in the Zhuāngzǐ is to reject orthodox moral norms or values on grounds that they are ineffective guides to dao (the way). In their place, Zhuangist writings focus directly on the concepts of dao and de (power, agency), along with interrelated conceptions of the well-lived life. The project explored the attitudes and conduct toward other agents that go hand in hand with the admirable individual life, as depicted in the Zhuāngzǐ. It found that on a Zhuangist understanding, interpersonal ethics is a special case of competence or adroitness in applying dé (agency) and following dào (ways). The general ideal of exemplary activity is to employ our dé to find a fitting, free-flowing dào by which to navigate through contingent, changing circumstances. Interpersonal ethics is an application of this ideal to cases in which other agents and our relations with them are prominent features of our circumstances. The ethics of interacting with others is thus not a distinct subject area in Zhuangist discourse but one application of more general views about dào, dé, and exemplary activity.

17601715.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17601715.value: In today's increasingly globalised world, English is widely recognised as the world’s lingua franca. Content and Language Integrated Learning (CLIL), which is characterised by the use of a second language (L2) as the language of instruction in content subjects, has emerged as an appealing approach that enables students to learn the L2 (very often English) and content knowledge simultaneously. However, the academic language involved in learning content subjects poses difficulties for L2 learners, requiring CLIL teachers to provide more explicit instruction and scaffolding with regard to academic language. Grounded in systemic functional linguistics, genre-based pedagogy emphasises contextualised language learning and use to achieve social purposes. The approach is widely applied to the teaching of school genres to disadvantaged students in Anglophone countries, and L2 writing instruction and English for Specific Purposes courses around the world. Recently, CLIL researchers in Europe have also adopted genre-based pedagogy to design curriculum and scaffold L2 learners' academic literacy in content subject lessons. The aim of the proposed study is to apply this approach to the CLIL context in Asia (Hong Kong) and investigate its impact on student learning of both content knowledge and academic literacy. The study will employ a quasi-experimental approach. Three Liberal Studies teachers from three English-medium secondary schools in Hong Kong will be recruited, and two Grade 10 classes taught by the teacher participant in each school selected. Using materials co-designed with the research team, the teacher participants will implement genre-based pedagogy in one class (the experimental group) and their normal content-oriented teaching style in the other (the comparison group). The intervention will include two teaching units, and the experimental and comparison groups will be swapped around in the second unit to achieve within-subject control and alleviate ethical concerns. Students' performance on pre- and post-tests will constitute the major source of data, complemented by lesson observations and interviews to explore the participants' perceptions of genre-based pedagogy. The test scores will be subjected to rigorous statistical analysis, which will then be complemented by systematic analysis of the other data sources. This study will then provide empirical evidence of whether genre-based pedagogy can be effectively applied in CLIL in an Asian context, which is considered as more examination-oriented. Further, this study will inform how teachers can successfully integrate content and language teaching in CLIL, something which has posed challenges to CLIL teachers. This will in turn illuminate potential directions for CLIL teacher education. 在全球化的趨勢下，英語被廣泛認為是世界通用語言。學科内容與語言融合教學（CLIL）漸漸成為一個極具吸引力的教學法，其特點是使用第二語言作為教授非語文學科的語言，讓學生能同時學習第二語言（通常為英文）和學科的內容知識。然而，不少學生以第二語言學習學科內容時皆面對很多困難，尤其是當中涉及的學術語言。因此，教師須在學術語言方面為學生提供更多的輔助。以系統功能語言學為本的語體教學法（genre-based pedagogy）強調語言在實際情況下的學習和運用，以實現語言在溝通的功能。此教學法被廣泛應用於英語國家中在主流學校就讀的弱勢學生，以及在世界各地的英語寫作教學和（English for Specific Purposes）課程。最近，在歐洲研究CLIL的學者也開始採用語體教學法設計課程，以及為學生的學術語言發展提供更多支援。本研究的目的是試行在亞洲（香港）的CLIL教學環境中應用語體教學法，並探討其對學生學習學科知識和學術語言的影響。 這項研究將採用準實驗的方法。三位來自三所中學、並以英語教授通識科的教師，以及他們任教的兩班中四級學生將會參與這項研究。參與的教師將使用與研究隊伍一起設計的教材在其中一班採用語體教學法（實驗組），同時在另一班採用他們一貫的教學法（對照組）。整個實驗將包括兩個教學單元，實驗組和對照組將會在教授第二個單元時調換，以減輕準實驗中選樣偏差和研究道德的問題。此研究的主要數據來源為參與學生在前後測試中的表現，輔以觀課和訪談，以探討參與者對語體教學法的看法。學生的測試成績將經過統計分析，並聯同其他資料以解答研究問題。 這項研究將提供證據，反映語體教學法能否有效地應用於亞洲、一向被認為較考試主導的CLIL教學環境中。另外，此研究對於教師如何能成功在課堂上結合學科知識和語言教學，以及教師培訓方面，將帶來一些啟示。

17601715.label: Realisation of objectives
17601715.value: Research objectives 1 and 2 concern the development of students’ content knowledge and language (especially their academic literacy), and whether there is any trade-off. To achieve these two objectives, intervention of genre-based pedagogy was implemented in three schools (more details below) and students’ performance before and after intervention was tracked to evaluate the impact of genre-based pedagogy. Regarding objective 3, which concerns teachers’ and students’ beliefs and attitudes towards genre-based pedagogy, the results were obtained through semi-structured interviews with the participating teacher and students. Research participants and setting Three teachers working in three secondary schools agreed to participate in the project. The details of the three teachers, their working contexts and the implementation of the project are as follows: In School A, Miss A, together with two classes of Grade 8 students (51 students), were involved. The research team helped Miss A to design one set of materials based on genre-based pedagogy. The two classes of students experienced the pre-test, intervention and post-test. There was no comparison group in this school, as Miss A felt that it was unethical and unfair to deprive the other classes of students of the potential benefit of genre-based pedagogy. In School B, two classes of Mr B’s Grade 9 students (55 students) were recruited as the experimental group, whereas the other two classes in the same grade level were treated as the comparison group. The experimental group experienced the pre-test, intervention and post-test; the comparison group, taught by Mr B’s colleague without using genre-based pedagogy, completed the pre-test. Then the examination scripts of the students were collected and the questions related to the target genres in the intervention were analysed to see if there were any differences in the performance of students in the experimental group and comparison group. School C was an international school located in Mainland China. Miss C graduated from a master’s programme that the Principal Investigator taught on, and hence she was recruited as a participant. The school followed the International General Certificate of Secondary Education (IGCSE) curriculum. Miss C was teaching one class of Grade 10 students (20 students) (i.e. the experimental group), and another class of students taught by Miss C’s colleague served as the comparison group. The research team designed two sets of materials for Miss C, who used them in the experimental group. Students’ work before and after the intervention was collected, and students’ results in the final examination were collected and compared with those in the comparison group. In all the schools, the lessons in which the designed materials were used by the teacher participants were video or audio-recorded for more detailed analysis. Semi-structured interviews were also conducted with the teachers and selected groups of students (6-10 students from each school). Students’ performance in the pre-test and post-test were analysed, both quantitatively and qualitatively. In Schools A and B, specific assessment rubrics were developed to mark the pre- and post-tests, so that the progress in the content and language dimensions were diagnosed separately. The “content” aspect covered students’ abilities to understand the task and their abilities to express their content knowledge to address the question, whereas the “language” aspect covered grammar, vocabulary, sentence and text structure. In School C, Miss C preferred using the marking scheme of the IGCSE examination, and hence the marking of students’ work followed the stipulated marking scheme. Detailed text analyses were also conducted to all students’ scripts collected, so as to identify in which aspects students improved in their academic literacies. Such analyses focused on students’ use of academic vocabulary, sentence patterns and text structure. To summarise, a total of three teachers and 126 students were involved in the experimental group in this study. Intervention based on genre-based pedagogy was implemented. Students’ performance on the pre-test and post-test were analysed, and compared with those in the comparison group whenever possible. Findings in relation to the objectives With regard to objectives 1 and 2, the findings of this study show that genre-based pedagogy could facilitate students’ development of academic literacies, without trade-off in content knowledge. Such a conclusion is supported by the fact that in the three schools, students’ performance in the post-test was significantly better than that in the pre-test. Such significant improvement was found in both the language and content aspects (when students’ performance in the two dimensions was analysed separately). When comparing the performance of students in the experimental and control group, the students in the former could produce better writing, in terms of organisation, logical development and connection of ideas, as well as appropriate use of connectives and academic vocabulary. These results demonstrate that implementation of the genre-based pedagogy helped students express their content knowledge in appropriate academic language, without trade-off in their content learning. It is also observed that students with lower English proficiency and general academic ability made more progress than their counterparts. When it comes to objective 3 (i.e. the beliefs and attitudes of teachers and students regarding genre-based pedagogy), teachers and students alike were rather positive towards genre-based pedagogy, and they believed it was effective. For example, Miss A believed that focusing on teaching genre would enable the students to better understand the structure of their writing, and the materials designed based on the genre-based pedagogy “definitely benefit students because you’re making everything very clear and organised”. This was echoed by the other two teachers, with Mr B suggesting that “adopting the genre-based pedagogies allows us to do this (to help his students learn academic language) in a more systematic way”, and Miss C noticing the obvious improvement in her students’ performance, especially “those lower achievers … their essays are better structured now”. The teachers’ positive attitude was shared by their students. The student interviewees in Schools A and B commented that the approach helped them learn the structure of the target essay, and such writing skills could be applied to other subjects. Students in School C appreciated Miss C’s efforts in helping them understand “the structure of the sample answer (of the IGCSE)”, so that they could “learn how to express their ideas, instead of memorising the model answer”. When asked whether they felt that the lesson was turned into a language lesson, most students did not have the feeling. Instead, they felt that some language elements were integrated into the lessons. Such a feeling of content and language integration was exactly what the project tried to achieve through the implementation of genre-based pedagogy. While all the teachers believed in the effectiveness of the method, they did feel the time constraint. For example, Mr B reflected, “it was time consuming”, especially there were only two lessons allocated to his subject, so “it will be a very challenging for teachers to squeeze lesson time for the language part”. Such a concern was shared by the other two teachers. However, Miss A believed that if teachers only focus on one or two genres for each grade level and keep recycling them throughout the year, it would be more time efficient in helping students to develop academic literacy gradually. To conclude, all the three objectives of this project have been achieved, with interesting findings that can illuminate effective CLIL pedagogy.
