17605015.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17605015.value: The underrepresentation of women in senior academic and managerial roles in higher education is an international phenomenon and an issue of growing concern. In 2012, for example, academics put forward a manifesto for change to increase women’s participation as academic leaders globally. The problem is particularly acute in Hong Kong. Only 7.3% of women occupy the most senior leadership positions – at the level of Dean and above. Moreover, there are no women university presidents. This represents a significant loss of human capital to the Hong Kong university sector. Research indicates that inclusive, diverse leadership leads to better organizational performance and that women bring enhancement to the leadership process; they exhibit transformational leadership styles which are associated with effective outcomes. Furthermore, inclusive leadership reflects more accurately the diversity of the student body, university staff and wider community, and demonstrates an institutional commitment to the values of diversity and equality. Previous research considers how and why the gender gap is maintained, but only elsewhere in the world. Thus, there is great scope to increase our understanding of this issue in Hong Kong. The aim of this study is twofold. First, to consider how, and to what extent, universities in Hong Kong are supporting the career progression of women and their entry to leadership roles. Second, to explore the local enablers and barriers to women academics progressing through the academic hierarchy and becoming leaders. A documentary analysis of diversity and equality policies, initiatives and strategies that have put in place to support women academics will be carried out. Semi-structured interviews with women academics at different points in their careers and in different disciplines will also be undertaken. The findings of the study will be distributed widely and in different formats for maximum impact. This will include, for example, policy briefing documents aimed at informing key bodies and personnel responsible for diversity and equality issues. The aim is to inform and invigorate discussion with respect to the issue of inclusive leadership in the Hong Kong higher education sector. 高等教育機構的高級學術和管理層中，女性比例較低是一個國際現象，也是日益受到關注的議題。例如，2012年，學者們發表了一個呼籲提高全球女性學術領導者比例的變革宣言。這問題在香港高校尤其尖銳。在香港高校的院長及以上級別高層領導者中，女性的比例只有7.3%；且沒有女性擔任大學校長一職。 對香港高等教育界而言，這是一個嚴重的人力資本缺失。研究表明，包容性的、多樣化的領導可以提升組織績效；而善於採用變革式領導風格的女性領導者在此功不可沒，因其不僅可以體現領導藝術，而且有助於提升組織效能。另外，包容性領導也可以更好地反映學生群體、高校教職工和社區的多樣性，有助於高等院校展示其在推動多元化和平等的使命。 既有研究已經以多個國家和地方為例，探討了性別不平等何以及為何被延續，但是尚未涉足香港高等院校性別不平的問題；這是值得關注的問題。本研究目標有二：一是瞭解香港高等院校如何、及在多大程度上支持女性學者的職業發展、促進其進入到領導崗位；二是探索促進和阻礙女性學者職業晉升和擔任領導者的因素。為了實現這些研究目標，本研究採用兩種資料收集方法：文獻分析和半結構式訪談。其中，文獻包括多元化和平等的政策，及現行的、支持女性學者的方案和策略；被訪者是來自不同職業生涯階段和不同學科的女性學者。 為了引發社會對此問題的關注，研究結果將會以不同形式廣泛傳播，例如，向負責多元化和平等問題的核心團體和部門發送政策簡報分享研究成果。這旨在喚起和激發人們關注和討論香港高等教育界的包容性領導諸問題。

17605015.label: Realisation of objectives
17605015.value: Objective 1: How, and to what extent, are universities in HK supporting the career progression of women academics and their entry to senior leadership roles? Documentary Analysis: Part 1 of documentary analysis has been completed. The websites of the 8 UGC-funded institutions have been analysed to look at publicly available documents/statements that indicate policies and strategies, which are publicly visible, to support the career progression of women academics. All the webpages of each institution were looked at. This level of analysis indicates that three out of the eight universities – coincidentally the case-study universities related to Objective 2 - appear to be more proactive than the other five. Part 2 - requesting internal documents from the universities was not completed as the Co-I (Sarah Jane Aiston) left the University of Hong Kong. Please note 50% of the research funding is to be returned to the RGC. Objective 2: What are the enablers and barriers to career progression and entry to senior leadership roles within the HK context? Semi-structured interviews: The interview schedule was constructed in reference to the existing research literature base. The interview was constructed as follows: the interviewees’ reflections on their own career trajectory (enablers, barriers and forward progression), the impact of a Chinese cultural context, their thoughts on their research profile (linked into the Co-Is research on the gendered research productivity gap, see Aiston and Jung, 2015), as well their thoughts more generally on why they think women are underrepresented in the senior levels of the HK academy. And finally, the extent to which they felt their own institution, and the HK sector as a whole, is committed to the advancement of women academics. Responses to this final question were analysed against the interviewees’ institutional policies and strategies. This provided an insight into the extent to which the interviewees’ were aware of their institution’s policies/support. The sampling strategy (as outlined in the original proposal) was to interview women academics from HKU, HKUST and CHUK. The sample was stratified by two key variables: academic rank - Assistant, Associate and Full Professor - and discipline – Science (Sc), Business (B) and Engineering (E), Arts and Humanities and Social Science (SS). The target was 25% of all women academics in Sc, B and E (19 interviewees) and 25% of all women academics in Arts and SS (25 interviewees). In total 35 interviews were conducted by the Co-I and Research Assistant, consisting of 13 academic women employed in science and engineering (below the target figure of 19) and 22 in social sciences and humanities (below the target figure of 25). Fourty-nine academic women responded to the first email, with 45 agreeing to participate initially. Four women rejected the invitation due to tight schedules and one respondent due to a lack of interest in the topic. Ten of the 45 women later went on to withdraw from participating in the study; 8 of them did not reply after several follow-up emails were sent out, 1 withdrew due to a busy schedule after 5 months of email communication and one woman preferred to talk to the PI instead of the Research Assistant. The PI was not in Hong Kong and offered a different format – Skype or telephone – but did not hear again from the respondent. Seventeen of the interviewees were Assistant Professors, 8 Associate Professors and 10 Full Professors. The majority of the interviewees (30) received their PhD from overseas and 5 received their PhD from a local institution in Hong Kong. Twenty-six interviewees had experienced working abroad (i.e. outside of Hong Kong) either as tenure-track staff (such as Assistant Professor or Lecturer), or non-tenure-track staff (such as Research Fellow, Postdoctoral Fellow or Research Assistant Professor). Twenty-nine of the interviewees were Asian (20 of them were ethically Chinese and 8 non-Chinese), whilst 7 were non-Asian. Voluntary consent was sought and a consent form was signed by each interviewee. All interviews were audio-recorded and transcribed verbatim into a word file. The data collected was then anonymised and individuals and institutions have not been identified. The initial analysis adopted a three-stage coding approach as set out in the research grant application (Coffey and Atkinson, 1996). First, basic coding was carried out, for example, to identify the ‘enablers’ to career progression, or academic women’s career aspirations in the academy. Second, attention were given to the content of what was said, to generate themes to reflect the language the interviewees used. Third, abstraction from what the interviewees had said, to the creation of broad analytic themes took place. Attention were also given to the interconnections between the codes to see if any of them were dimensions of a broader phenomenon. The data were analysed with the aid of NVivo. The use of this software enabled themes identified to be cross-checked with variables such as academic rank and discipline. In this way it became possible not only to look at the data set as whole, but also more easily analyse sub-sets with the data, for example, experiences and views of an assistant professor in STEM-related discipline. However, having ‘carved up’ the data in numerous ways and on re-reading codes and themes, the Co-I then returned to the full length transcrips to be immersed in each individual narrative to re-check codes and themes.

17605015.label: Major findings and research outcome
17605015.value: Journal article: The Silence/ing of Academic Women This article presents a new conceptual dimension to our understanding of how and why women academics experience the higher education profession differently to their male colleagues and the factors, or forces that prevent women academics from leading in the academy (linked to Objective 2 of the research objectives). Based on interviews with women academics from the case-study universities, the article presents a two-part conceptual framework – the silence/ing of academic women. The article also explores the issue of silence/ing in relation to cultural context. On exploring the concept of silence/ing, ‘micro-inequities’, ‘micro-aggressions’ and ‘micro-politics’ became relevant as a theoretical framework. The article suggests that the organizational organisational cultural of higher education in Hong Kong continues to expect women to ‘fit in’. Normative expectations of how women should act in turn opens up the ‘space’ for micro-inequities to be let in, with women struggling to negotiate how they should act. Paradoxically, women’s silence is both an enabler and a barrier to their career progression. Journal Article: Enabling Women Academics: Problematic Policies and Strategies This article aims to begin to gain an insight into the ‘policy’ response to the absence of women as senior leaders in Hong Kong in the three case-study universities (linked to Objective 1 and 2 of the research objectives). The article firstly reports on the policies, initiatives and strategies put in place to support academic women. It is evident the ‘policy response’ from the three universities was largely family-focused, suggesting that institutions’ understanding of the barriers academic women face largely coalesced around caring responsibilities. The interviewees identified ‘gaps’ between institutions voicing a commitment to gender equality and actual practice, and pinpointed middle management as a potential ‘sticking point’ in bringing about change. The interviewees questioned the extent to which male colleagues understood, or even recognized the barriers academic women face in the profession. However, interviewees expressed concerns around affirmative action, particularly in relation to academic appointments. Both the documentary analysis and interviews suggest that the case-study institutions are at the early stages of promoting/supporting women’s career advancement. Book: Politics, Neoliberalism, and University Governance This book started with a concern arising from literature review on university leadership and gender for this project: university leadership and governance in policymaking. The study finds that university councils have freedom to make policy in response to changing domestic/global contexts. This has significant implication for gender diversity in university leadership.

17605015.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17605015.value: This research project has found that gender diversity in university leadership is related to the micro-politics and culture within universities and is constrained by the macro-contexts in which they are situated. Futher research can be conducted to explore how university's organizational culture and politics can be reshaped to create a level-playing field for female academics in career advancement in university leadership. Another potential research project is to study the issues arising from the dilemma between the policy of affirmative action for female academics in recruitment for senior posts and the law protecting equal opportunity for males and females in employment and promotion.

17605015.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17605015.value: The underrepresentation of women academics in the most senior ranks and leadership roles in higher is both an international phenomenon and enduring social justice issue. The Hong Kong higher education is no exception; women are woefully underrepresented comprising only 8% of senior academic leaders across the 8 UGC-funded universities (Aiston and Yang, 2017). Funded by the Research Grants Council, this project makes an original contribution to our understanding of 1) how, and to what extent, three case-study universities in Hong Kong are supporting the career progression of women academics, and 2) the enablers and barriers to career progression and entry to senior leadership roles for academic women. The research indicates that the Hong Kong higher education sector is only at the early stages of promoting/supporting gender equality – the three case-study universities appearing to be at the forefront of this emerging agenda. Support for women academics at this point largely coalesces around caring responsibilities. However, this research, along with extensive scholarship in the field of gender and higher education, highlights that caring responsibilities are only one aspect of what is a complicated and multifaceted problem.

17605215.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17605215.value: Chinese characters are formed of components and structure. Contemporary Chinese consists of simplified and traditional written forms, the latter of which has more character components and a more complex structure. The proposed study aims to investigate the component and structural sensitivity of Hong Kong (HK) ethnic minority (EM) students in regard to traditional Chinese characters. It will focus on the 26 single characters (with high configuration ability) and 15 spatial configurations forming the highest frequency words in HK. Five hundred Grades 7 and 8 Pakistani and Nepalese students (representing the two major EM groups in HK) will participate. The students are required to complete six tasks under four categories along the sequence of language development: (1) Visual (Lexical Decision Task, Chinese Structure Test); (2) Visual-Phonetic (Lexical Naming Task); (3) Visual-Semantic (Orthographic Choice Task, Orthographic Choice in Context Task); and (4) Visual-Phonetic-Semantic (Character Familiarity Task). All tests will be conducted in school hours on different days, and their duration ranges from 10 to 30 minutes. To control the order effects, rotated forms with different sequences and combinations of tasks will be presented. Besides descriptive statistical analyses, multi-dimensional scaling will be used for each participant group in each test to generate a production matrix for each component and structure. The findings will help to identify underlying dimensions while explaining observed similarities or dissimilarities between the investigated objects in each test. Correlation analyses will also be conducted using the production matrices to check for the presence of correlation between each participant group, the findings of which will show within group differences, i.e., whether EM students in each subgroup classified by ethnicity and time of arrival have different lexical processing characteristics. Furthermore, exploratory factor analysis will be used to uncover the internal structure amongst all dependent variables, and to identify the underlying constructs behind the variables; whereas the hierarchical multiple regression will be used to investigate the internal structure of dependent variables. Results will significantly enhance our theoretical repertoire, lead to new understanding of Chinese as a second language (CSL) learning useful for developing effective curricula and teaching materials for EM students in HK, and inform teachers of teaching and learning strategies pertinent to the compositional relationship between components and structures for Chinese character learning.

17605215.label: Realisation of objectives
17605215.value: 1. It was found that there is a developmental process for EM students to be aware of the orthographic legality of Traditional Chinese characters. Without orthographic knowledge, EM students can hardly recognize Chinese characters. Thus, their exposure of characters and components in everyday use has very limited contribution to the development of orthographic knowledge. 2. The findings showed that EM students performed the best on recognizing Chinese characters with left-right structure, then top-down structure, and they did not perform very well in recognizing the remaining structures of Chinese characters. They also found single-component characters are difficult for recognition. 3. The preliminary findings showed that it takes about 2 years for EM students to develop orthographic sensitivity in formal educational setting, if sufficient orthographic analogies input has been provided. 4 & 5. No differences were found across different ethnic groups. Orthographic knowledge plays a more important role than the length of time spent studying CSL in terms of their orthographic sensitivity of EM students.

17605215.label: Major findings and research outcome
17605215.value: The project examined how Chinese as a second language (CSL) learners perceive patterns of Chinese character (Loh, Leung, Tam & Lau, 2016), and explored the role of orthographic knowledge in character learning. We have proved that component knowledge plays an important role for Chinese characters learning (Loh, Liao & Leung, under preparation), and structural knowledge has mediation effect on the application of component knowledge for character construction (Loh, Liao & Leung, 2018). The findings supported “learner framework for processing CSL” and further extended the evidence from adults to younger learners.

17605215.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17605215.value: Due to the complication of the Chinese characters recognition process which goes through various cognitive operational procedures, it is hypothesized that learners' executive functioning ability may affect the Chinese character recognition performance. As a result, we suggest further exploration of the relationship between Chinese as a second language learners' executive function on Chinese character recognition and their character learning ability.

17605215.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17605215.value: The project examined how Chinese as a second language (CSL) learners read the patterns of Chinese character, and explored the role of orthographic knowledge in character learning. We have proved that component knowledge plays an important role for Chinese characters learning, and structural knowledge has mediation effect on the application of component knowledge for character construction. As a result, it is recommended that teachers teach CSL learners the component and structural knowledge of Chinese characters, as well as provide them with explicit learning experiences on using component and structural knowledge to form Chinese characters.

17605415.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17605415.value: This project aims to investigate the effectiveness of Halliday’s Sydney School genre-based approach in teaching Chinese written composition to South Asian ethnic minority students in Hong Kong. Chinese language, with its heightened status in Hong Kong, holds a key for South Asians with low socio-economic status to obtain upward mobility (Shum, Gao, Tsung, & Ki, 2011). However, South Asian ethnic minority students, as a disadvantaged group of second language learners, lack efficient pedagogical support in Chinese language learning in Hong Kong. Thus, the genre-based pedagogy derived from Halliday’s (1985) Systemic Functional Linguistics (SFL) will be applied in this study to improve Chinese language performance of South Asian ethnic minority students for better chance to participate in mainstream society. The SFL approach is primarily concerned with language choice in social situations and has been widely applied in sociolinguistics (Hyland, 2007, 2012). Its latest model in language teaching methodology, the ’Reading to Learn, Learning to Write’ (R2L) pedagogy, is a genre-based teaching strategy which is designed to guide students to experience different levels of language through extensive classroom reading and writing activities with selected texts. An SFL-based genre approach has been used by the Principal Investigator of the project to explore the subject-specific genres of various school subjects, and the proposed study is to extend the approach to teaching and learning Chinese as a second language. The employment of genre-based pedagogy aims to support South Asian students for their learning of Chinese written composition in the senior secondary curriculum. The study comprises three related parts. First, the Chinese teachers involved will be provided with appropriate training in the genre-based approach to language teaching focusing on the genres of narration, explanation, and argumentation. Secondly, research data will be collected while teachers begin to use the genre-based teaching approach, by means of pre- and post-tests before and after genre instruction, semi-structured interviews, tasks and documentary evidence. Thirdly, SFL criteria will be employed to analyze students’ written composition in both pre- and post-tests in order to understand the effectiveness of the genre-based pedagogy in teaching Chinese as a second language. Based on the findings, the research will suggest teaching strategies to enhance the learning of Chinese by ethnic minority students in Hong Kong and beyond.

17605415.label: Realisation of objectives
17605415.value: This study is of great significance in language teaching, learning, and assessment. In order to facilitate the teaching process, an identification of the symptom faced by the students is a prerequisite to a thorough understanding of their learning process. Hence, with a view to helping students improve their writing skills, revealing their difficulties in their L2 Chinese writing is the first step and a key to gaining access to the ways that improve the students’ writing capacity. Based on the text analysis by means of Reading to Learn (R2L) assessment criteria, the students’ writing difficulties on the word level, sentence level and the whole text level have been revealed from the inspection of the students with different level of learning abilities. In response to the students’ learning difficulties identified from their pre-tests, the genre-based R2L pedagogic intervention was conducted in the experiment groups, with no treatment applied to the control groups to measure the effectiveness of the genre-based pedagogy in enhancing Chinese written composition performance by South Asian ethnic minority students in Hong Kong. There were 2 groups of participants in this research, namely, a non-Chinese speaking target group and a non-Chinese speaking control group. The target group of the research will be 116 non-Chinese speaking students aged 13-15 from Secondary 2 - 3 classes, consisting mostly of South Asian students, as they have already possessed a fundamental level of spoken Cantonese and modern written Chinese. Another 112 non-Chinese speaking Secondary 2 - 3 students from the same schools as the control group students will participate as the non-treatment group. The classes of this group will apply the “traditional” teaching practice, thus serving as the control reference. In the “traditional” practice, teaching of reading involves mainly the whole text level, with little support on the reading of sentences and words, and the writing tasks are usually unrelated to the reading tasks (Martin, 2012; Rose & Martin, 2012; Rose, 2012). In contrast, the genre-based pedagogy emphasizes preparation before the reading tasks, and the reading tasks are organized with sufficient support at 3 levels of scaffolding support as mentioned above, so that the reading tasks act as preparation for the writing tasks, and the teaching of reading and writing is closely connected (Rose & Martin, 2012). Grounded upon detailed reading, students were scaffolded from joint rewriting and construction to individual rewriting and construction. In addition to the emphasis on the relationship between writing and reading, the genre-based approach to writing accentuates the inculcation of text types and meanings with clear-cut schematic structure and specific lexico-grammatical knowledge to facilitate students’ learning of writing. It is of great help for students to have explicit step-by-step guidance and scaffolding as to how writing is performed. The research recruited 3 in-service Chinese language teachers as teaching researchers. The four cases were selected based on reputational case selection (Miles, Huberman, & Saldaña, 2014). They received training in the genre-based “Reading to Learn, Learning to Write” (R2L) pedagogy before applying it in the target groups. Intensive training was offered for the teachers in the experiment group before the pedagogic intervention mainly based on the researchers’ introduction to R2L pedagogy and its resource package with video demonstration (Rose, 2012). The research team also cooperated with the teachers to write up detailed lesson plans based on the texts they were going to teach in the semester. Upon the commencement of the teaching intervention, each of the teachers’ lessons from experiment group was video recorded on a daily basis. Weekly school visit and monthly meeting of progress report with teacher researchers were also conducted to discuss the lesson plans, provide pedagogic suggestions and track the progress of the teaching for record in order to cater for the different learning needs of the students under treatment. In order to investigate the effectiveness of the genre-based pedagogy, data were collected by pre- and post-test of task writing in the two different genres of narration and explanation. Both groups of students were required to write two essays of each genre at the beginning and the end of the treatment. The pre-test and post-test were used to measure students’ performance in Chinese written composition. The marks of both the pre- and post-tests were compared and analyzed statistically by means of ANCOVA for each genre of writing and reading in both schools with two assigned groups (Control & Experimental). The progress rate was also measured via Independent Samples T-test for both reading and writing in each genre (Narration & Explanation) in both School A and B. The students’ writings were also evaluated by text analysis with Halliday’s Systemic Functional Linguistics. Semi-structured interviews with the students were also conducted in order to understand the shareholders’ opinions on the R2L pedagogy. By means of the quantitative and qualitative mixed research method, both of the project objectives have been achieved, with the majoring findings and the research outcomes reported in the next Section 6.

17605415.label: Major findings and research outcome
17605415.value: On the whole text level, the students at all levels of achievement were found to have difficulty in constructing correctly the schematic structure and the staging of narration and explanation. Their writing performance of these two genres indicates explanatory composition is harder than narration writing. Without the support of accurate stages and detailed elaboration in phases, the writing purpose can only be partially fulfilled, leading to an underdevelopment of field, tenor, and mode for content delivery and reader engagement. On the sentence and word level, the students were confronted with a deficiency of lexico-grammatical knowledge for syntactical and lexical variation to build the field. Some students with weaker language proficiency felt especially difficult in Chinese character writing, even using English for meaning making in Chinese language writing. In the process of discourse construction, students have little awareness of using appraisal to express personal feelings or subjective reflection towards the happenings in narrative writing, neither using it to appreciate the target surroundings in explanatory composition. All writings were loosely constructed without strong connections by conjunctions. Repetition of noun subjects instead of using pronouns was usually detected in the writings of relatively lower achievers. In response to the students’ learning difficulties identified from their pre-tests, the genre-based R2L pedagogic intervention was conducted in the experiment groups, with no treatment applied to the control groups. The statistical results has suggested that “Reading to Learning” is more effective than the traditional teaching method in improving the Chinese writing of two genres, i.e. narration and explanation. After the comparison between the writing performances of the high, medium and low achievers from the experiment group and its counterparts from the control group in response to the literacy tasks of both narrative and explanatory writing via text analysis, it was also found the students at the high, medium, and low levels improved both in the construction of schematic structure and the variation of lexico-grammatical choices from the whole-text, sentence and word levels respectively, but more scaffolding needs to be provided for the low level students in the generic construction for explanation.

17605415.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17605415.value: By means of both quantitative and qualitative mixed research method employed in the current study, enhancement of Chinese written composition performance among south Asian ethnic minority students in Hong Kong was found evident. It is hoped that this effective application of genre-based pedagogy in the current research can provide a source for further application within Hong Kong and suggest new directions for teaching and learning Chinese as a second language. Encouraged by the research findings as to the effectiveness of the genre-based approach in Chinese language education, curriculum design and pedagogical innovations for NCS students’ language development and educational attainment will be promoted and widely disseminated by providing more teacher training with regard to the implementation of genre-based approach in the L2 Chinese language classrooms. The further development of the current research will help bring robust evidence to theory building in the field of Chinese language as a second language pedagogies, curriculum development and teacher education both in Hong Kong and can be generalized to other contexts which also struggle for the better support of Chinese language teaching and learning.

17605415.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17605415.value: The R2L pedagogy discards the traditional manner of language instruction and explicitly makes clear what is to be learnt to facilitate the acquisition of literacy skills, specifically in writing. It provides a systematic and coherent framework in focusing on both language and contexts, and ensures that course objectives and content are derived from students’ needs. Second, it discards the traditional, teacher-centered teaching pedagogy. Instead, it adopts a constructivist perspective in language teaching, and gives teachers a facilitator role in scaffolding students’ learning. Third, it allows access to the patterns and possibilities of text variations by ethnic minority students, and gives students the resources to understand and challenge these discourses. Fourth, it adopts functional linguistic theory to analyze classroom discourse and student writings. The application of Systemic Functional Grammar changes traditional language assessment, and increases teachers’ awareness of texts, enabling them confidently to advise students on improving their reading and writing. It is thus hoped that the research findings will contribute to the improvement of Chinese language skills and educational achievement among ethnic minority students. It is also expected to suggest new directions for research on the utilization of the genre-based approach in teaching and learning Chinese as a second language.

17605815.value: 過度活躍與兒童受虐：全港人口性研究 背景: 過度活躍症及兒童虐待兩者皆是重要的兒童健康和心理社會問題。臨床觀察和初階的研究發現了兩者間有可能的關聯。雖然過度活躍與兒童受虐過往時間在香港皆同步增加，可是兩者間是否有關連及當中的機制還有待進一步的研究證實。 目標: 1. 估量當下香港初小學生的過度活躍比率 2. 研究過度活躍與兒童受虐兩者間的關係 3. 探索其中重要的兒童及家庭因素 研究設計: 此次的人口性研究將採用分層性隨機抽樣方法。全港18區中的36間小學的5184個小一至小三的學生及其家長將被邀請參與此研究。參與此計劃的家長將填寫一份與過度活躍，照顧兒童與家庭情況有關的問卷。相關的數據將有助我們更了解當下香港兒童的過度活躍情況和與兒童受虐之間的關係。 研究的重要性: 這將是首個在中國人中研究過度活躍與兒童虐待的計劃。研究的數據將有助於我們推動香港兒童的健康發展，減少過度活躍與兒童受虐所帶來的傷害。有關發現亦將可成為發展未來綜合或治療計劃的導引。

17605815.label: Realisation of objectives
17605815.value: Using stratified random sampling, 51 primary schools were selected and participated in this population-representative study. All of the 10,278 Grades 1-3 students were invited to participate, in which 7,585 (73.8%) have completed the assessments. Among 7,585 children recruited, 4,127 (54.4%) were boys. Mean (SD) age of the participants were 8.15 (0.88), with a range of 6 to 9. Mean (SD) family income was $31,853 ($28,662) per month. There was no significant difference between the sample's family income and the median monthly income of Hong Kong ($32,700; P=0.99). 186 (2.5%) and 347 (4.6%) of the fathers and mothers respectively reported to have any mental disorders, while 65 (0.9%) and 56 (0.7%) of the fathers and mothers respectively reported to be diagnosed of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder. A total of 4,805 (63.3%), 1,739 (22.9%), and 95 (1.3%) of children have been reported to experience minor, severe, and very severe physical abuse respectively in the past year, in addition to 6,373 (84.0%) and 1,770 (23.3%) to experience psychological abuse and neglect respectively. Objective 1 - To estimate the prevalence of ADHD amongst primary school children in Hong Kong as a whole and in individual districts The mean (SD) symptom score of ADHD was -0.38 (0.99), indicating that the parents, in general, perceived their child to have slightly fewer ADHD symptoms than the average kid. Nonetheless, when using the clinical cut-off of the Chinese SWAN ADHD assessment, 536 (7.0%) were categorised with probable ADHD, while 329 (4.3%) were reported by parents to have ADHD diagnosis. The prevalence of probable ADHD was 4.9% and 8.9% for girls and boys respectively, and that for Hong Kong Island, East Kowloon, West Kowloon, East New Territories, and West New Territories was 7.8%, 8.3%, 6.3%, 6.2%, and 6.2% respectively. After accounting for misspecification of the SWAN assessment with the published statistics on sensitivity and specificity, the estimated prevalence of ADHD in Hong Kong was 8.39%. That for girls and boys was 2.98% and 13.43% respectively. District-specific prevalence was 10.8%, 12.5%, 5.8%, 5.4%, and 5.5% for Hong Kong Island, East Kowloon, West Kowloon, East New Territories, and West New Territories. ADHD prevalence was not significantly associated with district after adjusting for intra-school correlation (P > 0.05). Objective 2 - To investigate the association between ADHD and child maltreatment Generalised linear model analyses were conducted to investigate the association between ADHD and child maltreatment. Exposure to child maltreatment was generally associated with ADHD. Using Poisson regression with robust standard error, parent-report ADHD diagnosis was associated minor (prevalence ratio [PR] 1.73, 95% CI 1.35-2.21, P < 0.001) and severe physical abuse (2.15, 1.73-2.66, P < 0.001), psychological abuse (1.56, 1.10-2.19, P = 0.01), and neglect (1.38, 1.10-1.73, P = 0.005). Similarly, SWAN-measured probable ADHD was associated with minor (1.57, 1.30-1.90, P < 0.001), severe (2.18, 1.85-2.58, P < 0.001), and very severe physical abuse (2.11, 1.31-3.42, P = 0.002), and neglect (1.44, 1.21-1.73, P < 0.001). In fact, ADHD symptom of all participants was associated with all types of child maltreatment, i.e. minor (standardised coefficient 0.36, 95% CI 0.32-0.41, P < 0.001), severe (0.41, 0.36-0.47, P < 0.001), and very severe physical abuse (0.33, 0.13-0.53, P = 0.001), as well as psychological abuse (0.40, 0.34-0.46, P < 0.001), and neglect (0.24, 0.18-0.29, P < 0.001). All the analyses have been adjusted for age and sex of the child, family income, and ADHD diagnosis of parents. Sensitivity analysis has shown that similar results were found using ADHD-inattention and ADHD-hyperactivity subtypes. Objective 3 - To investigate the extent to which the relation between ADHD and child maltreatment is moderated by affecting factors at the child and family levels A series of moderation analyses have been conducted to examine the role of parenting stress, parent-child relationship, parenting style, as well as the child’s peer interaction, emotional stability, conduct problems, and prosocial behaviour. Parenting stress, parent-child relationship, parenting style, child’s peer problems, and prosocial behaviours were not significant moderators to the associations between ADHD and child maltreatment. On the other hand, child’s emotional instability and conduct problem intensifies the association of physical maltreatment and ADHD symptom. Both interaction terms were significant with standardised coefficients 0.85 (95% CI 0.30-1.39, P = 0.002) and 0.77 (0.26-1.29, P = 0.003) respectively. In summary, this research project has successfully completed all the proposed objectives. ADHD prevalence was found to be at about 8%. All types of child maltreatment were found to be associated with risk and symptom of ADHD, while children with emotional instabilities and conduct problems being more susceptible to the association.

17605815.label: Major findings and research outcome
17605815.value: The study has identified an elevated ADHD prevalence in Hong Kong using a population-representative sample of 7,585 children aged 6¬–9 years. It was estimated to be 8.39% in the whole territory. That for girls and boys was 2.98% and 13.43% respectively. District-specific prevalence was 10.8%, 12.5%, 5.8%, 5.4%, and 5.5% for Hong Kong Island, East Kowloon, West Kowloon, East New Territories, and West New Territories. The association between child maltreatment and ADHD is statistically significant with a small-to-medium effect size on symptom (standardised coefficient 0.24-0.40) and prevalence ratios of 1.44-2.18. Generally speaking, the associations were weakest with neglect and strongest with severe physical abuse. Among an array of parental and child factors, only the child’s emotional stability and conduct problems appears to moderate the associations between maltreatment and ADHD. Both factors amplified the associations.

17605815.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17605815.value: This study lays the important foundation of the current prevalence of ADHD in Hong Kong, demonstrating the increasing burden in the community and healthcare system. This is in complement with the Mental Health Review 2017 of the Hong Kong Food and Health Bureau, which reported ADHD as a major burden to the healthcare system. Even more importantly, this study filled in the important research gap on the association between ADHD and child maltreatment, as found in the meta-analysis on Chinese population. This confirms the potential relationship between the two prevalent child health conditions and opens an area for future research. Based on this project, future longitudinal studies can be designed to delineate the potential casual pathways. The result of this study also alerts clinicians during their management of child maltreatment and ADHD cases, particularly those with comorbid emotional and conduct problems.

17605815.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17605815.value: This research project estimated about 8.39% of the children aged 6-9 to have attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, an important health condition that severely impairs children’s learning and development. The percentage is higher than the previous estimates, suggesting that a potential increasing trend in ADHD. This new finding is significant in that government and healthcare providers can plan for relevant resource allocation. In addition, this study also found children suffered from maltreatment in the past year were more likely to have ADHD. In this study, even though we cannot ascertain the causality of the relationship, such discovery can also be meaningful to clinical management. For example, clinicians should be careful of the co-occurrence of these conditions in managing these cases. The study will also be a foundation in further investigation on the causality of the relationship.

17606015.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17606015.value: 鼻咽癌是香港第七大常見的癌症（香港癌症登記處，2012）。電療或同步化療是鼻咽癌最主要的治療方法。過去的研究發現在接受過電療的鼻咽癌倖存者中，電療會引發言語和吞嚥問題。鼻咽癌倖存者的言語問題主要指不清晰的發音和音質的改變。吞嚥問題主要指食物或液體從口進入胃的過程中有障礙。研究顯示言語和吞嚥問題對鼻咽癌倖存者的生活質素有負面影響。對於接受過電療的鼻咽癌患者而言，高達85%的人會發生吞嚥問題。 過去的研究發現，鼻咽癌、癌症晚期、同步化療以及在癌症治療中使用的電療劑量會增加頭頸癌倖存者患有言語和吞嚥問題的風險因素。隨著電療技術的進步，臨床醫生可以分別採用強度調控電療，以調整和設計應用於腫瘤部位和周圍非腫瘤部位的電療劑量。近期的調強電療治療頭頸癌的研究發現，如果嚥縮肌和喉部接受的輻射劑量減少，在電療後的頭兩年言語和吞嚥功能會得到較好的保存。然而，大部分的研究並沒有特別針對鼻咽癌倖存者、沒有全面的評估工具、也沒有針對超過電療兩年後的言語和吞嚥問題。 目前的研究旨在調查以下兩方面：（1）癌症治療在言語和吞嚥問題上的影響；（2）電療劑量與鼻咽癌倖存者接受調強電療後3至5年的言語和吞嚥功能的關係。研究一共會招募130個接受過調強電療的鼻咽癌倖存者。言語和吞嚥功能的評估會包括患者的自我報告和儀器測量。病史和癌症治療的放射劑量等資訊將會從醫療記錄中被檢索出。本研究推測如與言語和吞嚥功能有關的結構接觸到高劑量的電療，言語和吞嚥功能會有較大機會減弱。本研究將有助進一步了解電療對言語和吞嚥功能的影響，從而提供更好的健康教育和治療方案以改善鼻咽癌倖存者的生活質素。

17606015.label: Realisation of objectives
17606015.value: To meet with objective one, 30 nasopharyngeal cancer survivors who were more than three years post-radiotherapy were recruited from the community. The participants underwent instrumental swallowing assessments (videofluoroscopic swallowing studies or flexible endoscopic swallowing studies), self-report on swallowing related quality of life and speech assessments. To meet with objective one and two, an additional 80 nasopharyngeal cancer survivors who were three to five years post-radiation therapy were recruited from Queen Mary Hospital. Two participants did not have radiation data available, therefore a total of 78 participants were included in the analysis. Radiation dosage to 12 structures in the head and neck were obtained from hospital records, these were: 1) oral cavity, 2) ipsilateral parotid, 3) contralateral parotid, 4) base of tongue, 5) superior pharyngeal constrictor, 6) middle pharyngeal constrictor, 7) inferior pharyngeal constrictor, 8) pharyngeal constrictors, 9) cricopharyngeus, 10) glottic larynx, 11) supraglottic larynx, 12) whole larynx. Each structure was identified by the oncologist in the computer tomography scan of the participants, then delineated using tissue contouring via computer software. All participants underwent videofluoroscopic swallowing examination, audio-recoding of speech for perceptual analysis and self-report on swallowing-related quality of life. Results obtained: Objective 1 The swallowing data from the first 52 participants recruited were extracted and presented at an international conference (8th European Society for Swallowing Disorders Annual Congress. Dublin, Ireland). Results showed that participants who were five or more years post-treatment (chronic group) had significantly higher penetration (45%) and aspiration rates (30%) than the 3-5 years post-treatment group (25% and 8.3% respectively). Higher penetration and aspiration rates suggest higher risk for aspiration pneumonia and poorer swallowing functions and quality of life. Results also showed that the swallowing difficulties had significantly more impact on the chronic group's interpersonal relationships than the 3-5 years group. No significant impact on articulation and voice functions has been identified on the 3-5 years group. Further acoustic analysis will be performed to detect for early subtle changes in articulation and voice. Objective 2 All dose data have been recently obtained and currently being analysed. There were delays in obtaining the dose data because of technical and personnel issues but all issues are resolved. Based on initial analysis of 39 participants who we have complete dosage data for, four structures were correlated with significant differences in swallowing function as measured by kinematic measures of swallowing structures. These were the inferior pharyngeal constrictors, glottic larynx, cricopharyngeus, and base of tongue. Past studies on head and neck cancer suggested to limit radiation dose to pharyngeal constrictors to <60 Gy. Current study has found that participants who had received dosages above 60Gy at the pharyngeal constrictors had significantly worse swallowing functions than the lower-dose (<60 Gy) participants. Further analysis will be conducted using additional measures of swallowing function, including participant-completed swallowing-related questionnaires, to identify structures that may be responsible for subjective and objective standards of dysphagia. The data will be written up and submitted to Laryngoscope in early 2020.

17606015.label: Major findings and research outcome
17606015.value: Three research outputs have been published and one manuscript is in preparation. 1. Analysis based on the first 52 participants recruited have found that NPC survivors who were five or more years post radiotherapy had significantly worse airway protection during swallowing than the 3 to 5 years post-radiotherapy survivors. Poorer airway protection led to penetration and aspiration during swallowing and this would put the participants at higher risk of developing aspiration pneumonia. The results were presented at the 8th European Society for Swallowing Disorders (Part C-conference #2). 2. All participants completed two self-report on swallowing-related quality of life, the M.D. Anderson Dysphagia Inventory and a new questionnaire developed for this study, the Head-and-Neck Cancer Survivors' Assessment of Mealtimes (HNSAM). The HNSAM was designed based on previous qualitative study by one of the co-investigators (Prof. Ward) and followed the World Health Organization's International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health framework. The HNSAM was found to have good validity and reliability. The development of HNSAM was reported in Laryngoscope (Part C- publication #1). 3. High radiation dose (>60Gy) to the pharyngeal constrictors have been associated with poorer swallowing functions in the current study. Further analysis to other swallowing related structures will be conducted. The results will be submitted to Laryngoscope in early 2020. Preliminary data on dose and swallowing functions were presented at the 10th Asia Pacific Conference on Speech, Language and Hearing (Part C-conference #1).

17606015.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17606015.value: The current study has confirmed that swallowing functions decline as early as three years post-radiotherapy for nasopharyngeal cancer survivors. Therefore, it is important to provide swallowing therapy for these patients. Currently the PI and a Co-I (Dr. Raymond Tsang) are conducting a GRF project together to investigate the effect of swallowing exercises during radiotherapy for preventing long-term swallowing difficulties. The PI is also conducting pilot studies on the effect of swallowing exercises for chronic NPC survivors. The pilot data will be used for future GRF applications to conduct larger scale RCT treatment studies for chronic NPC survivors.

17606015.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17606015.value: The current study looked at the relationship between radiation dose received by swallowing-related structures and the swallowing functions in nasopharyngeal cancer survivors. The study recruited 110 nasopharyngeal cancer survivors who had received radiotherapy three or more years prior to participation. The participants received clinical and instrumental swallowing examinations and completed self-report questionnaires on the impact of swallowing difficulties on daily living. The study found that participants who were five or more years post-radiotherapy had poorer swallowing functions than those who were 3 to 5 years post-radiotherapy. The study also found that for those who had received higher radiation dose to swallowing-related structures during their cancer treatment had poorer swallowing functions 3 to 5 years post cancer treatment. The current study confirmed that NPC survivors may face swallowing difficulties as early as three years post cancer treatment. It is proposed that early swallowing management should be provided to this population to enhance swallowing functions and prevent aspiration pneumonia. The radiation dose imposed on swallowing structures should also be carefully reviewed and maintained below <60Gy where possible without affecting cancer treatment outcomes.

17606415.value: 「第五屆香港小四學生中英雙語閱讀能力研究」(BR2016) 是一個探討香港小四學生中文及英文閱讀能力的趨勢 研究，此研究先後於2004年（第一屆）、2007年（第二屆）、2010年（第三屆）及2013年（第四屆）舉行。本研究旨在學生的閱讀能力發展，跟他們的閱讀興趣和態度的關係，並深入了解教育政策和語文評估對閱讀能力發展的影響。 「香港小四學生中英雙語閱讀能力研究」的研究框架和評估工具，沿自另一國際大型閱讀能力研究：「全球學生閱讀能力進展研究」計劃(PIRLS)，此研究由國際教育成績評估(International Association for the Evaluation of Educational Achievement, IEA)主辦，每五年一次調查全球不同國家及地區小四學生的閱讀能力及發展趨勢。PIRLS研究的參與國家地區成員，由PIRLS 2001年的35個增加至PIRLS 2011年的46個，預計PIRLS 2016年時會有超過50國家地區參與研究。 「香港小四學生中英雙語閱讀能力研究」(BR2016) 研究團隊會隨機抽樣和邀請全港40所學校的校長、中英文科老師共80人、2400名小四學生和他們的家長參與研究，填寫不同的問卷，學生亦需要進行中、英文的閱讀理解測試。研究員同時亦會邀請在職語文教師，組成焦點小組，仔細審視研究的數據，在語文課程、閱讀教學實踐方面提供專業的意見，幫助研究團隊總結研究結果，為政府當局、學校、教師和家長等不同持分者提供合適的建議。 本研究從下列各方面蒐集資料:小學的語文課程、閱讀教學、社區的閱讀氣氛、大眾的閱讀態度、學生的背景、家庭對閱讀的支援等。研究再結合學生的閱讀成績基線進行分析，調查不同因素對香港學生閱讀能力的影響。 本計劃還會就其他語文教育議題進行調查，包括： (1) 中文課堂的教學語言問題：近年愈來愈多小學以普通話作為中文科的授課語言，本研究會嘗試探討「普教中」的教學效能以及對學生中文閱讀能力的影響。 (2) 自主學習：近年香港不少學校把自主學習定為發展目標，鼓勵學生積極參與和主動學習。本研究會了解學生自主學習 與閱讀能力的關係。 我們深信本研究的發現和結果，能幫助社區各界、教育當局、學校課程發展人員、學校教師和家長，深入了解香港學生閱 讀現況。我們預期本計劃將發表的學術成果和報告，能通過不同渠道，幫助提升香港小學學生中、英雙語的閱讀能力。

17606415.label: Realisation of objectives
17606415.value: Objective 1 To study the effects of using Cantonese and/ or Putonghua as the MoI on Chinese reading literacy The first objective has been generally achieved. The data show that students who used Putonghua to study Chinese performed better on the Chinese reading test than did peers using Cantonese. However, in interpreting this finding, one needs to consider the following phenomena. SCOLAR conducted a survey about the medium of instruction (MoI) used in Hong Kong primary schools in 2015/16. Some 16.4% and 28.3% of schools respectively employed Putonghua or Cantonese as the MoI with all classes. However, 55.3% of schools employed Putonghua and/or Cantonese in some part of lessons, meaning that Putonghua was used for about 50% of the instruction time, while Cantonese was used in the rest of the lessons. However, not all schools followed the exact proportions of language usage with all classes. In addition, schools were asked to provide information about the children in participating classes in the questionnaire (elite class, normal class or remedial class). Unfortunately, most schools refused to disclose such information in full. Furthermore, the researchers did not know each school’s policy on how they decided which language to use in Chinese Language lessons for every class. For example, some schools might assign Putonghua as the MoI in elite classes and Cantonese in remaining classes. Hence, the correlational analyses between students’ reading scores and the extent of their usage of either Putonghua or Cantonese as MoI in lessons need to be interpreted with great care. The research team took every step possible to avoid sampling errors, and consultations were held at every stage with school staff. Although sampling errors were kept to an absolute minimum, the research team hesitates to draw very firm conclusions and it warns against speculative proposals and interpretations. Objective 2 To examine the impact of “self-directed learning” on students’ reading performance in Chinese and English separately The objective has been realized, the findings below being yielded. Once again, great caution is required in interpreting the evidence and the findings outlined below. Key Findings In examining the impact of “self-directed learning” on students’ reading performance, great caution is needed. No significant effect of planning stood out, and a factor relating to self-directed learning, was noted in the students’ Chinese reading performance (see one-way ANOVA.) However, positive effects of monitoring decisions during occasions of self-directed learning in students’ Chinese reading performance emerged (F(2, 3428)= 22.92, p & lt; .001). There was a significant effect of planning on P4 students English reading performance (F(2, 3402)=10.86, p< .001). A significant effect of monitoring was also found on students English reading performance (F(2, 3392)= 61.84, p< .001). Objective 3 The impact on bilingual reading performance of students’ reading habits, self-concept as readers, attitudes towards reading, teaching methods and classroom reading activities, home reading environment and parents’ attitudes toward reading will be investigated. The objectives above have partly been realized, but caution is advised in drawing conclusions. The following are the findings. Generally speaking, student reading habits; self-concept as readers; attitudes towards reading; teaching methods and classroom reading activities; home reading environment; and parents’ attitude towards readings have affected the Chinese and English reading performance of P4 students. Objective 4 BR2016 is the fifth study in a series (following BR 2004, BR 2007, BR 2010 and BR 2013). The overall programme of research operates in a three-year cycle of assessment and will continue to measure trends and patterns in children’s bilingual reading literacy attainment and their attributions such as policy and practice changes. The objective has been realized. Below, see the main findings: This research found that the Primary 4 students’ English reading performance in BR 2016 was 79.22% of the average Chinese reading score. Comparing 70% (BR2004), 74% (BR2007), 76% (BR2010), and 75% (BR2013), there were significant improvements in students’ English reading test performance in BR 2016, especially in the overall reading test scores. Comparing students who were competent in using English and Chinese, there was a growth from 5.44% in BR2013 to 8.10% in BR2016. There was also an increase of students with bilingual attainment over 500 (international mean): from 12.76% in BR2013 to 22.48% in BR2016. In general, the percentage of competent P4 bilingual students is growing.

17606415.label: Major findings and research outcome
17606415.value: The study found that P4 students’ average English reading performance in BR2016 was 79.22% of that of their average Chinese reading score. Comparing 70%(BR2004), 74%(BR2007), 76%(BR2010) and 75%(BR2013), there were clear improvements in students’ English test performance in BR 2016. At the same time, there was an increase in students’ bilingual attainment scores over 500 (international mean) from 12.76% in BR2013 to 22.48% in BR2016. Generally, the percentage of competent P4 bilingual students had grown. Turning to the impact of “self-directed learning” on students’ reading performance, no significant effect of planning, one factor of self-directed learning, were found in students’ Chinese reading performance (one-way analysis of variance). However, there was a significantly positive effect in terms of monitoring (the other factor in self-directed learning) on students’ Chinese reading performance (F(2, 3428)= 22.92, p< .001). There was a significant effect of planning on the students English reading performance (F(2, 3402)=10.86, p< .001). A significant effect of monitoring was also found on students’ English performance (F(2, 3392)= 61.84, p & lt; .001). Since 2006, the EDB has encouraged schools to use Putonghua as the medium of instruction(MOI). Additional teachers, school-based support and resources have also been provided. More than 70% of primary schools used Putonghua as the MOI. Consequently, the results of the independent-samples t-test showed that P4 students from schools using Putonghua as the MoI (M=561.72,SD=50.96) performed better than those in schools using Cantonese (M= 557.04, SD= 51.77) in the Chinese reading test (t(2720)= 2.37, p< .05). The study showed that (a) learning resources at home; (b) parents who themselves enjoyed reading; (c) parents who regularly engaged their offspring in literacy activities before entering primary school and regularly engaged children in reading activities outside school had a markedly positive impact on students’ bilingual reading ability. In general, HK P4 students seemed not to be avidly engaged in reading lessons, although well motivated students usually obtained higher reading scores. Regarding students’ reading confidence, 38.6% of students were found to have difficulties in reading Chinese, and 43.5 % had difficulties in reading English. Generally, the longer students had had to engage in tutorial sessions (usually for remedial purposes), the lower their reading score. Most teacher participants said that they mainly used textbooks as primary materials for reading instruction, whilst some also used reading series as supplementary material.

17606415.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17606415.value: First and foremost, this is the only high level, scientific, in-depth research focusing on P4 students’ Chinese and English reading ability in Hong Kong on five occasions. The Government, the general public and schools have displayed considerable interest in the findings. Furthermore, after the data are professionally analyzed, an individual report will be prepared for every participating school. Details of student performance on different reading tasks will be revealed and scrutinized, together with suggestions for future improvement. Schools can use the evidence presented to adjust to their own school-based curriculum and teaching methods. Parents will also be provided with access to the report so they can learn more about their children’s reading attainment and better assist their learning at home. Moreover, a publication for schools, parents and educators is also planned to promote bilingual reading literacy. A comprehensive overview of P4 students’ bilingual reading ability in Hong Kong will be included, combining data from the past five studies. The book will also suggest ways for parents to help their children develop a keen interest in reading. It is with gratitude that we once again ask for RGC support for this crucial research project.

17606415.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17606415.value: The study compared the Chinese and English reading performance of Primary 4 students(P4) in Hong Kong(HK) in 2016. It was the fifth round of testing in a series of studies since 2004. It was found that P4 students’ English reading performance had improved and was 79.22% of the average Chinese reading score. Comparing the numbers of students who were competent in using both languages, growth was evident in the numbers found: from 5.44% in 2013 to 8.10% in 2016. There was also an increase student number with bilingual attainment over 500(the international mean) from 12.76% in 2013 to 22.48% Turning to the impact of ‘self-directed learning’, a significant and positive effect of monitoring was found in Chinese and English reading performance. A significant impact of planning on English reading performance was noted. This was the first time since 2004 that P4 students from schools using Putonghua as the Medium of Instruction performed better than those from schools using Cantonese in the Chinese reading test. The study provides information for the Government(EDB), and schools to help them formulate education policies, and improve their pedagogy and curriculum. It can also parents to help their children to build up reading habits and skills.

17606515.label: Project Objectives
17606515.value: To trace the change in the FLG’s collective actions from the mid-1990s to the mid-2010s, and to identify the pattern(s) of change, especially from 1999 onwards. To examine FLG’s collective action frames and framing processes in different periods, and to analyze how these frames and framing processes are constituted by the ideological content of the FLG. To investigate the role of the charismatic leader in orchestrating collective actions, and to understand the perceptions and the meaning-making of ordinary followers in carrying out these actions. To compare FLG’s collective actions in temporal and geographical dimensions so as to analyze how they are conditioned by the Chinese state’s actions and policies, and by their immediate social and political contexts. To offer sociological analyses of the evolution of a movement, with an emphasis on explaining why the FLG as a movement and its individual followers have engaged in activities that have made them lose public support and sympathy over time. To theorize the processes and the mechanisms of collective action frame transformation in relation to ideology, the charismatic leader, and socio-political forces.

17606515.label: Realisation of objectives
17606515.value: The objectives of this project, to a large extent, have been achieved. Three of the six original objectives were achieved 100% and the other three were achieved 80-90%. The major reason for some objectives falling under 100% is that when I was about to write up the paper that will meet all these objectives, a book entitled Becoming Activists in Global China by Andrew Junker (Cambridge U Press) was published in 2019. Two of the chapters in this book largely overlap with my research question about FLG’s collective action frames and their change over time. With the appearance of this book, the chance of my paper getting accepted for publication in a top-tier journal was lessened. I therefore added a new research objective to examine the public reception to FLG’s activism in different socio-political contexts. None of the extant literature ever explores the publics’ views on FLG and this is a crucial missing gap in the studies of FLG. The new objective was added in the last minute toward the end of the funding period in the second half of 2019 and therefore I did not get a chance to apply for a revision of the objectives. This new objective (#7) was 100% achieved and I have been writing up a paper with a tentative title “Public Reception to Falun Gong’s Activism and Crusaders in Hong Kong, Taiwan, and North America” for publication. Because I have to submit this completion report six months earlier than the original due date in order to be eligible for the forthcoming round of GRF teaching relief, the paper is still in progress. It should be ready to be submitted for review by May-June 2020. My research assistants and I had gathered a large volume of data from participant observations and interviews in Hong Kong, Taiwan, and a number of cities in the United States. In addition, we collected a large volume of FLG’s documents, including the charismatic leader’s writings, that stretches over a decade long from their websites. We also collected newspaper reports of FLG’s activism over a decade long period. With these data, I was able to achieve objectives (#1), (#4), and (#5) that aim to trace the change in FLG’s collective actions from the mid-1990s to the mid-2010s, identity the pattern of change, compare their actions in both temporal and geographic dimensions, analyze sociologically its evolution, and explain why individual followers persistently engaged in activism and why they lose public support and sympathy over time. The findings and analyses were presented at international conferences and written in the two papers listed under Part C Research Output. Objectives (#2), (#3), and (#6) were achieved 80-90%. All relevant data related to FLG’s ideology and how it was related to FLG’s collective action frames were collected and the initial findings and the substantial findings and analyses were presented at the ISA Forum of Sociology and at the Annual Meeting of Hong Kong Sociological Association respectively. However, as I explained at the beginning why I did not write up a paper to address all these questions in particular. Objective (#3) about the role of the charismatic leader was achieved 80% because the leader was physically inaccessible to academic researchers and some of the core followers were cautious and reserved when responding to questions related to the charismatic leader. Fortunately, I was still able to learn about his role by reading the texts he wrote, watching FLG’s media, and interviewing with a few core followers who were relatively open and honest.

To compare FLG’s collective actions in temporal and geographical dimensions so as to analyze how they are conditioned by the Chinese state’s actions and policies, and by their immediate social and political contexts.

To offer sociological analyses of the evolution of a movement, with an emphasis on explaining why the FLG as a movement and its individual followers have engaged in activities that have made them lose public support and sympathy over time.
To theorize the processes and the mechanisms of collective action frame transformation in relation to ideology, the charismatic leader, and socio-political forces.
To compare the public receptions to FLG and their collective actions in different socio-political contexts.

17606515.label: Major findings and research outcome
17606515.value: 1. Data Collected: 1.1. From February 2016 to December 2019, a total of 157 interviews with mainly FLG followers, anti-FLG members, and audiences (publics) were conducted by myself or my research assistants in Hong Kong, Taipei, Kao Hsiung, Chicago, New York City, Boston, Deerpark Town and Middletown in New York state. At the same time, we conducted a total of 85 participant observations of FLG’s collective actions, anti-FLG’s actions, and FLG’s interactions with anti-FLG and with the publics in these cities. These data allow me to analyze FLG’s collective actions and the publics’ reception to FLG in different socio-political contexts. They also allow me to analyze the impacts of the anti-FLG campaign on FLG in Hong Kong. Together with the data I collected earlier from 1999 to 2014, I was able to trace the evolution of FLG as a religious-cum-social movement. 1.2. Newspaper reports on FLG were collected from 1999 to 2009 to trace the evolution of FLG’s collective actions. To strike a balance of different political positions of the newspapers, all of the reports on FLG from Mingpao, Wenweipao, and SCMP were collected for the case of Hong Kong. At the same time, all the reports on FLG from Washington Post and New York Times were also collected to understand FLG’s activities in North America. 1.3. FLG’s own publications include books, the Epoch Times, and articles posted in their website called Minghui Net were collected. The charismatic leader’s writings from 2000 to 2011, a time when he was most active in communicating with his followers via writing, were also collected. This set of data allows me to analyze FLG’s action frames and the role of the charismatic leader. 2. Conference Presentations and Publications: Two papers were presented at five international conferences, and one of these papers was already accepted for publication in a top-tier area studies journal, Modern China. Another paper was not intended for publication because, as I explained in section 5.3, the research question was already addressed by a recently published book (2019) by another author. I took an immediate remedy by shifting the focus to address a missing question in the literature of FLG, which is the public reception in different socio-political contexts. The new paper is under preparation and an incomplete draft is attached. I plan on sending it to China Journal (ranked No.1 in area studies journal in 2018) for review in May-June 2020.

17606515.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17606515.value: My initial findings from this study indicate that one of the changes of FLG is its institutionalization of the organization. FLG’s collective actions in the past were more spontaneous but they have become much more organized with a clear division of labor among the followers. Some followers were assigned to distribute flyers and the Epoch Times and they were instructed not to speak to the publics. When non-FLG people have any questions, they were referred to some senior followers or spokespersons for some rather standardized answers. Such a practice, in fact, resembled the organizational practice of some large transnational corporations that aim at controlling the public images of the companies. Future studies on FLG can focus on the institutionalization process and the organizational aspect of FLG.

17606515.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17606515.value: All of us must have seen the booths of Falun Gong (FLG) on Causeway Bay, Mongkok, or Hung Hom train station before. Some of us might have seen their parade that lasted for hours. FLG people distributed flyers and the Epoch Times and they displayed banners with slogans “Down the criminal Jiang Zemin” and “Heaven Destroy the Chinese Community Party.” What is FLG and why do FLG people demonstrate on streets almost every day? Their collective actions in the public space in Hong Kong appeared as early as 1999. Twenty years later FLG were still around and their collective actions never faded out. FLG’s activism is present not only in Hong Kong but also in Taiwan, North America, Australia, and Europe. At the same time, we have been anti-FLG booths standing side by side with FLG’s in Hong Kong. What is the anti-FLG campaign about? How did it affect FLG? This study collects data in Hong Kong, Taiwan, and North America to examine FLG’s evolution and change over time as a religious and social movement, the impact of the anti-FLG campaign on FLG, and the public reception to FLG’s collective actions in different social and political contexts.
