17606715.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17606715.value: This study employs Learning Study to examine the impact of teachers’ efficacy and creative behaviors on the development of writing and reading literacy of non-Chinese speaking (NCS) primary school students. Method: A total of 48 P.3 & 4 teachers are recruited from 12 primary schools and randomly allocated to the intervention and comparison groups. Intervention group teachers receive a professional training approach, Learning Study, while teachers in the comparison group do not. The intervention group teachers use learned creative and culturally responsive teaching strategies to teach Chinese language while teachers in the comparison group adopt traditional teaching. Participating teachers are observed and videotaped four times which are rated independently by two trained raters using the Creative Teaching Framework. Teachers have to complete the Culturally Responsive Teaching Self-Efficacy Scale (CRTSE) and the Culturally Responsive Teaching Outcome Expectancy (CRTOE) Scale before and after the intervention. 400 P.3 and 4 NCS students in these schools are recruited (with informed consent) and studied from 2015 to 2017. The Chinese Character Test, Pre-PIRLS Reading Assessment Test, and the Chinese Creative Writing Scale are used to assess the reading and writing achievements of the students. Student outcome measures are administered before the intervention at the beginning of the academic year (pre-test), towards the end of the academic year (post-test), and four months after the Learning Study (delayed post-test). Repeated measures ANOVA with post hoc comparisons are carried out to determine whether significant difference occurs between scores of the teacher and student participants in both groups along the different time intervals. Hierarchical linear modeling is employed to assess if teaching efficacy and creative teaching behaviors can predict students’ writing and reading performance. Significance: There is a dire need for the 6.4 % of ethnic minority citizens in HK to have a basic competence in the Chinese language for the education system to offer them the opportunity to be linguistically integrated into the Hong Kong society. This study addresses such important local need of how Chinese as a Second language (CSL) could be taught and learnt. It gives a better understanding of the relationship between teacher creative behaviors, efficacy and NCS student achievement which is original in HK. Teachers teaching CSL can acquire skills and dispositions that expand their culturally responsive instructional strategies to exercise creative teaching techniques that promote student learning. The insights gained have relevance to a worldwide interest in learning CSL and general educational contexts.

17606715.label: Realisation of objectives
17606715.value: The objectives of the project were achieved. Teachers in linguistically diverse classrooms often feel underprepared when they teach students from a different linguistic background. They are urgently in need of developing cultural relevancy in their own teaching self-efficacy and Chinese language teaching so that they can address non-Chinese students’ needs. This study developed the Chinese Culturally Responsive Teaching Self-Efficacy and Creative Teaching Framework. The sample comprised of 498 in-service teachers teaching in culturally-diverse classrooms in Hong Kong schools. Exploratory Factor Analysis was first conducted and then tested by Confirmatory Factor Analysis. The findings indicated a five-factor structure with “Efficacy to accommodate diversity” having the highest loading. This became an effective instrument for assessing teachers’ self-efficacy and creativity in teaching linguistically diverse students in the intervention of learning studies. The follow-up study recruited 183 teachers who teach Chinese as a second language. There were 69 teachers in the control group, 65 teachers who joined the professional training of the learning studies but did not conduct learning studies in class, and 49 teachers who attended professional training and applied learning studies in their culturally responsive classrooms. All teacher participants were invited to complete this questionnaire (the Chinese Culturally Responsive Teaching Self-Efficacy and Creative Teaching Framework) after the intervention. Repeated measures ANOVA were used to test the impact of learning studies on teaching and lessons. From the quantitative data and lesson analysis, teachers’ efficacy to accommodate diversity, to create a positive and trusting relationship, to develop school-based curricula, to engage effectively with parents displayed a significant positive change among teacher participants after the learning study intervention. These are important findings. Furthermore, the outcomes illustrated that teachers improved in their ability to connect theory to practice. This connection is important in all pedagogical contexts. In order to indicate non-Chinese students’ word-level ability which is the foundation in learning Chinese language, this study developed the Chinese Character Acquisition Assessment (CCAA) to measure non-Chinese students’ abilities to make associations among the forms, sounds, and meanings of the Chinese characters, and administered it to 173 young learners in Hong Kong. High model-to-data fit was found using the two-parameter logistic Item Response Theory model (MSinfit = .87 to 1.07, ps > .41). Of the 40 items, 36 exhibited a range of difficulty and good discrimination. Facing the serious inqdequacy of research to understand the needs of multilingual learners in leanring Chinese which is an important global language, the development of CCAA to assess the L2 students’ Chinese abilities in unique in Hong Kong where Cantonese is the main medium of instruction in primary schools. The PI and co-I also revisited the parental and student factors affecting reading achievement of Hong Kong students in the PIRLS 2011 study, focusing on parental and student factors and used the Pre-PIRLS Reading Comprehension to test the reading outcomes of the students. There were 418 students of Grade 3 and 4 coming from 12 primary schools participating in the learning studies. Results from the pre-test and post-test before and after the learning studies were analyzed and investigated. Result from the Paired t-test on pre- and post-test showed that the students had an overall improvement on the Structured Test on CCAA, Mental Lexicon and Pre-PIRLS Reading Comprehension with a t-value of 7.036 (p<.005). Students improved significantly in the CCAA from the pre-test with a t-value of 6.164 (p<.005), in the Mental Lexicon section with a t-value of 5.675 (p<.005) and with a t-value of 2.249 (p<.005) in the Pre-PIRLS Reading Comprehension section. Result revealed that students improved significantly on the word-level and text-level reading ability. As for the Chinese Creative Writing Scale, the overall effect was significant in fluency (F = 28.64, df = (2,260), p < 0.0125); originality (F = 25.67, df = (2,260), p < 0.0125); and the total score (F = 24.87, df = (2,259), p < 0.0125). Result revealed that students improved significantly on the word-level, text-level reading ability and writing ability. A paper is in preparation and is intended to be submitted to the International Journal of Bilingual Education and Bilingualism. There is wide engagement with local stakeholders to disseminate the findings of this study through keynote lectures in territory–wide local conferences: - Cheung, W. M. (2019). Picture Books Make Me Love My School, keynote speech at the “Conference on Empowering Multicultural Learners, Unleashing Potential for Transition” at University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong on 5 January 2019 - Cheung, W. M. (2017). An Innovative Model of Teacher Professional Development to Enhance Multicultural Learners’ Chinese Learning, keynote speech at the “From Isolation to Collaboration: Conference on working together and looking forward in the L & T of Chinese for multi-cultural learners” at University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong on 22 April 2017 In the two territory-wide conferences, there were 7 presentations related to reading and writing from teachers from 7 different primary schools sharing findings, their teaching strategies, progress, challenges and outcomes generated from our learning studies. In addition to wide engagement with local stakeholder, the research in this study has also been disseminated internationally through international conferences on education (such as EARLI and AERA) and international invitation: Cheung, W. M. (2018). Innovative Teacher Professional Development to Support the Quest for Equitable Educational Opportunity in Teaching Chinese as a Second Language, an invited talk at the Department of Education, University of Oxford on 3 May 2018. Reports on the study have been sent to all participating schools. The PI and collaborating teachers published their good practices of various learning studies that enhanced Chinese reading and writing abilities among multicultural students in two books (Cheung, Chan, Leung, Cheng & Chen, 2017; Cheung, 2018). These books conceptualized the knowledge and strategies generated from this study, and have been uploaded to the EDB website to be shared with all teachers in HK. Furthermore, the outcomes have led to journal articles and conference papers which will disseminate the outcomes internationally. Seven papers on the findings have been presented in international conferences. Five international journal papers have been published. One paper is under review and three other papers are in preparation. There is also an important impact on academic work from the perspectives of support for students (PhDs, MPhil).

17606715.label: Major findings and research outcome
17606715.value: This study developed and validated the Chinese Culturally Responsive Teaching Self-Efficacy (CRTSE) and Creative Teaching Framework (Cheung, Huang, Chan & Tsang, 2018; Cheung, Huang, Wong, Chan & Tsang, under review) from 498 teachers teaching in culturally-diverse classrooms in Hong Kong schools. The findings indicated a five-factor structure which accounted for 69.62% of the variability with a good model fit, which indicates that it is an effective instrument for assessing teachers in culturally responsive education and teachers’ creative teaching professional development. This study also developed the Chinese Character Acquisition Assessment (CCAA) to measure second language learners’ abilities to make associations among the forms, sounds, and meanings of 40 characters (Chan, Cheung, Huang, Lam & Lin, 2020). This assessment tool exhibited good discrimination with high internal consistency reliability and inter-rater reliability. The instrument is a valid and reliable one for assessing multicultural learners in Chinese language. As requested by participating teachers teaching non-Chinese students to understand the factors leading to reading achievements of HK primary school students, we analyzed the PIRLS 2011 data to investigate the reasons behind 4th grade students’ reading achievement in Hong Kong. Data of 3875 fourth graders from 132 primary schools and 3682 parents were involved in the analysis. A 10-factor structure model of student factor and a 7-factor structure model of home factor have been identified by exploratory factor analysis (EFA) and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) (Lam, Cheung, Au, Tsang, So & Zhu, 2016; Cheung, Lam, Au, Tsang & Chan, 2016). Structural equation modeling revealed that parental background posed an indirect effect on reading achievement via books at home and early reading abilities, which in turn influences reading motivation and reading self-efficacy (Cheung, Lam, Au, So, Huang &Tsang, 2017). Such results shed light on the planning of the learning studies related to factors like student motivation and student engagement in reading lessons. To enhance the teaching efficacy and creative teaching of teachers, the PI and Co-I started work collaboratively with teachers to address the question of “what is to be learned” in learning studies (Marton, Cheung & Chan, 2019). Learning studies provided professional development to teachers by analyzing the learning of reading and writing for non-Chinese students according to the variation theory of learning which has been used the theoretical foundation to most learning studies. Guided fantasy was found to be one of the powerful creative teaching strategies in learning studies(Cheung, Huang, Chan & Zhang, 2019). The follow-up study recruited 183 teachers who teach Chinese as a second language. There were 69 teachers in the control group, 65 who joined the professional training of the learning studies but did not conduct learning studies in class, and 49 teachers who attended and applied learning studies in their culturally responsive classroom. All teacher participants were invited to complete this questionnaire (the Chinese Culturally Responsive Teaching Self-Efficacy and Creative Teaching Framework) after the intervention. Repeated measures ANOVA was be used to test the impact on teaching and lessons. Results showed that the teaching efficacy of teachers in intervention group that applied learning studies were higher than the control group. Four out of the five factors, displayed a significant positive change among teacher participants after the full participation of learning studies (Cheung & Huang, 2019; Cheung, Huang, Chan & Wong, 2018). A manuscript related to this innovative professional development model of learning studies is in preparation and will be submitted to American Educational Research Journal.

17606715.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17606715.value: It is important to investigate further on developmental trends of the Chinese literacy of non-Chinese learners, by allowing comparisons both with other age groups and with native Chinese students of the same age using CCAA, Pre-PIRLS Reading Assessment and Chinese Creative Writing Scale. There is also a need to include foreign language anxiety impacts upon Chinese language learning and performance for non-Chinese students (Cheung & Kong, 2019). Successful completion of the study showed that learning study intervention is an effective model to address the fragmentation of professional development of teaching Chinese as a Second language. There should be more attempts of employing learning study intervention in kindergartens and primary schools with non-Chinese students to learn Chinese listening and speaking. The outcome of learning study intervention is the formation of a team of educational architects and a community of dedicated professionals in collaborating schools. In the long term, there should be a study on the effect of innovative Professional Development inspired by learning study in Hong Kong. The strategies generated from various learning studies provided evidences of effective teacher training in learning Chinese as a L2.

17606715.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17606715.value: This study employs Learning Study to enhance the impact of teachers’ efficacy and creative behaviors on the development of writing and reading literacy of non-Chinese primary school students. In Phase 1, we developed and validated the Chinese Culturally Responsive Teaching Self-Efficacy and Creative Teaching Framework from 498 teachers teaching in culturally-diverse classrooms in Hong Kong schools. The findings indicated that it is an effective instrument for assessing teachers’ self-efficacy and creativity in teaching linguistically diverse students. There were 183 teachers involved in Phase 2. Among them, 49 teachers who joined and applied learning studies displayed a significant positive change and higher self-efficacy after the intervention. This showed that learning study is an effective professional model to help teachers learn about best practice in supporting multilingual learners to develop and implement specific reading and writing strategies. There were 418 students of Grade 3 and 4 coming from 12 primary schools participating in the learning studies. Result revealed that students improved significantly on the word-level, text-level reading ability and writing ability. This project improved teachers’ teaching and students’ learning for social inclusion and have implications for research in culturally responsive education and teachers’ creative teaching professional development.

17606815.label: Project Objectives

17606815.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17606815.value: Southeast Asia is a major sending region of contract labour migrants who support infrastructure production and social reproduction in middle and higher income countries globally, including in Hong Kong. These migrations have led to the rising prominence of transnational families, where children grow up with one or both parents away during significant childhood years. One of the primary motivations for parental migration is to provide better opportunities for their children’s future prospects. However, whether or how parental migration improves the life chances of those left behind remains unclear. A growing body of research from Asia and other sending regions is demonstrating a complex web of costs and benefits for left-behind children and families. Despite recent advances, there is a significant knowledge gap about the long-term impacts of growing up in a transnational family on later transition to adult roles, including participation in higher education, entry to employment, partnering and parenting. This research study draws on child development and transnational family literature to focus on the key transition period when children pass into young adulthood. The conceptual framework draws on the theory of New Economics of Labor Migration and incorporates aspects of the emotional economy of family relations, non-economic outcomes and structural components conditioning migration experiences. This framework will guide the mixed-methods analysis and interrogation of longitudinal data to address questions on how the experience of growing up in a transnational household influences physical and psychological health, health risk behaviours, education and employment, and family relationships during the transition to adulthood. The study will collect data (survey and in-depth interviews) from a cohort of youth aged 17 to 19 in 2016 (projected start date) in two countries, Indonesia and the Philippines. These data will be linked to baseline data collected from households, child caregivers and the young people themselves in 2008 by the same research team in the CHAMPSEA research project on Child Health and Parental Migration in South-East Asia. The proposed study will thus create a unique mixed-method longitudinal dataset that, for the first time, will allow insight into the long-term consequences of parental absence overseas during formative childhood years. The comparative design of the study, in combination with consideration of the wider context of transnational exchanges, will produce evidence to inform parents, NGOs working with migrant’s families, and those responsible for national policy agreements, as well as advancing scholarly knowledge on transnational families and the youth transition to adulthood. 東南亞各國是世界主要的勞工輸出區域。這些勞工支撐著中高收入國家和地區，包括香港在內，的基礎設施建設和社會再生產。同時，大量的人口流動也導致了跨境家庭的產生。這些家庭中的兒童往往成長於缺乏父、母，乃至雙親陪伴的環境中。對於身為跨國勞工的父母來說，為子女提供更好的成長機遇是他們背井離鄉打拼的最大動力之一。然而，究竟出外打工而不能親自照顧子女，是否真的有益於，又或者是如何影響到子女的個人生活機遇，是並不清晰的。越來越多關於亞洲及其它勞工輸出區域的研究表明：如何計算留守兒童及其家庭的得失，相當複雜。儘管相關也取得了一定的進展，但關於人口流動對於跨境家庭的長期影響以及對家庭成員從兒童過渡到成人過程的影響，包括接受高等教育、就業、未來的夫妻之間和他們同子女關係等方面，仍然有著巨大的認知鴻溝。 本項研究著重關注的是在跨境家庭中，兒童在進入成人這個關鍵期時候的成長。理論架構主要參考了勞動力遷移的新經濟學以及涉及到家庭關係的情感支出和兒童發展的文獻。同時，經濟以外的因素和結構對遷移經驗的影響也被考慮在內。研究方法則主要是多種方法並用的數據分析以及長期的數據追蹤。研究希望以此來釐清，逐漸成年的兒童成長在跨境家庭的經驗，將怎樣影響到兒童身體和心理的健康狀況，他們的教育、就業以及家庭關係。 研究將於2016開始，向一批年齡在17到19歲的印度尼西亞和菲律賓的兒童（青年）收集數據。同時研究將采用2008年獲得的關於兒童健康和出外務工父母的數據作為基線數據。這些數據是由同一個研究小組在2008年的CHAMPSEA項目中向同一批兒童、他們的家庭成員以及兒童照顧者取得的。因此，該項目將第一次建立一個使用混合研究法的、長期數據追蹤的數據集合。從而能夠揭示父母長時間位於海外，疏於照顧，將對處於性格塑造期的兒童帶來怎樣的影響。而由於考慮到了跨境的背景，這樣的研究設計將會為跨境勞工父母自身、服務移民家庭的非政府組織，相關政策責任人以及學術界提供更多的關於跨境家庭和該類家庭中兒童成長的了解和洞見

17606815.label: Realisation of objectives
17606815.value: Our project objectives have been largely achieved, although the analysis of the completed datasets and the writing of papers continues. In terms of publications, we have published (or accepted for publication) 2 internationally refereed journal papers in reputable journals (such as Global Networks, Population, Space and Place) and 1 book chapter in state-of-the-art handbook collections and specialist volumes published by (See publications listing). In addition, we have three additional papers under review and have an accepted special issue collection of papers which will contain 7 papers with publication expected within 2020. The introduction which covers the broad introduction of the CHAMPSEA young adult cohort paper is led by Jordan. All of the papers focus on different aspects of the young adult CHAMPSEA children’s well-being to achieve the different objectives of the project (psychological and physical well-being, livelihoods trajectories of education and employment, risk behaviors) covering objectives 1-4 out of 5. We have set a target of completing 4 additional papers in the next six months of 2020 with multiple papers under review and accepted for workshops and other types of academic dissemination. An important achievement is the completion of a longitudinal dataset of about 1,000 households across the two countries including quantitative and qualitative data. This dataset features households with different migration characteristics (mother-migrant, father-migrant, both-parents-migrant, and non-migrant households) and with young adults aged 17-20. In each household, separate structured surveys were conducted using specially designed survey instruments with the index child (young adult) and the responsible adult in the household. CHAMPSEA (Waves 1 and 2) is the first of its kind to develop a longitudinal mixed-methods dataset that can cast light on the long-term impact of parental international migration on the care, health and well-being of left-behind Young Adults in Southeast Asia. The quantitative dataset is complemented by qualitative methods of data collection that yielded 54 paired life-story interviews (from the same household) with parental/non-parental adults and their children. By implementing robust tracking procedures and working with local collaborators with in-depth knowledge of ground conditions, we were able to minimize the overall attrition rate between CHAMPSEA Wave 1 and Wave 2 (8 years apart) to 16.4% (higher in the Philippines and lower in Indonesia given the higher rate of geographical mobility in the former compared to the latter). The combined power of CHAMPSEA Wave 1 and Wave 2 has allowed us to make significant contributions to understanding the culturally contextualized relationships between parental migration and child well-being as the children enter adulthood. For example, we were able to examine the way care relations are negotiated longitudinally across two interacting sets of temporalities: A ‘migration trajectory’ structured by permutations of gender-differentiated (non)-migration episodes (for example, mother migrants may be replaced by father migrants over time, or non-migration may alternate with parental migration); and A ‘family trajectory’ marked by life-course events (for example, when finish schooling) and unexpected crises (such as divorce, death or serious illness). By collecting data from the child and the responsible adult in each household, we were able to examine different points of view in recognising the complexity of personal relationships and household dynamics in influencing a range of child outcomes. In terms of future research, CHAMPSEA provides an important impetus for stimulating more scholarly work. Methodologically and theoretically, it has been observed that families are still predominantly conceived of as nuclear, living together, and bounded by the nation state. In reality, many families – including low-income families in less developed countries – are coping with developmental pressures by assuming transnational family formations where productive (breadwinning) and reproductive (caring for children) work are spatially split across two nation-states. CHAMPSEA is a frontrunner in conducting research on this phenomenon and has already stimulated interest in extending this work to other countries. The PI Dr. Jordan was asked to lead a similar consultancy study in Cambodia, and the UGC has awarded funding for an extension of the CHAMPSEA study in Thailand in 2017 to the PI. Given the strong foundation that we have constructed through CHAMPSEA Wave 1 and Wave 2, we anticipate working on Wave 3 further down the road. We have thus far been able to track the migration trajectories of the same families with children from pre-school years to to young adulthood over an 8-year period. Conducting CHAMPSEA Wave 3 would allow us to track some of the children through to a phase of adulthood characterised by marriage, child bearing and entry into the workforce. This will not only allow us to study more deeply the transitions to adulthood (decision-making with regard to education, employment, marriage and migration) over time, but also allow us to match children’s aspirations (articulated when they were in middle childhood or on the cusp of adulthood) with actual outcomes. This vein of research is important in order to better understand generational effects of parental migration on their children, and CHAMPSEA 3 would allow for better understanding the intergenerational effect of migration as the original CHAMPSEA children transition to adult roles of marriage, childbearing and employment, including migration. The newly started work in Thailand where the CHAMPSEA children are 3 years older than they were in this study indicates rising participation in migration and childbearing of these young adults. There is very little empirical research that has examined the intergenerational influence of migration. One major limitation with this type of research is the scale of resources needed to efficiently work with the data, and also to prepare the data for public use. To date, the project team has managed to combine resources of UGC in Hong Kong, the Ministry of Education in Singapore with the original funding from the Wellcome Trust. In order to maximise the current extensive data resources, reach broader audiences via data sharing, and collect and manage complex multicountry research larger scale and multiple year funding is necessary. The PI and co-investigative team luckily have been able to draw on additional resources (eg. Consultancy funding, strong relationships with in-country collaborators). In sum the major problem encountered is resources (financial to fund adequate human resources and technical aspects of the research including virtual support resources and publicly accessible and staff-supported data infrastructure). This low level of resources is one reason the timestamp of the extensive publications that are forthcoming is noted in this summary.

17606815.label: Major findings and research outcome
17606815.value: The combined power of CHAMPSEA Wave 1 and Wave 2 has allowed us to make significant contributions to understanding the culturally contextualized relationships between parental migration and child well-being. We are able to attend to the creation of new knowledge by introducing a temporal element in our analysis and track change over time rather than projecting or imputing change. CHAMPSEA is able to add considerable value to existing research by studying how children’s care needs and well-being change over time in relation to both family and migration trajectories. For example, we were able to examine the way care relations are negotiated longitudinally across two interacting sets of temporalities: A ‘migration trajectory’ structured by permutations of gender-differentiated (non)-migration episodes (for example, mother migrants may be replaced by father migrants over time, or non-migration may alternate with parental migration); and A ‘family trajectory’ marked by life-course events (for example, when children reach school-going age, or finish schooling) and unexpected crises (such as divorce, death or serious illness). By collecting data from the child and the responsible adult in each household, we were able to examine different points of view in recognising the complexity of personal relationships and household dynamics in influencing a range of childcare arrangements and child outcomes. 17606815.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17606815.value: The Child Health and Migrant Parents in South-East Asia (CHAMPSEA) Young Adults study seeks to enhance knowledge and understanding of the health and well-being of children left behind in Southeast Asia – specifically Indonesia and the Philippines – when one or both of their parents migrate overseas for work. By examining the comparative impacts of paternal and maternal migration on the care of children as well as child health and well -being over time, this study contributes to academic, practice and policy debates within the Southeast Asian region and beyond on larger questions relating to the feminization of ‘care migration’, the provision of care for children, and the health and well -being outcomes for children in migrant-sending villages. The study addresses key research questions including the impact of the migration of one or both parents on physical health, psychological well-being, health-related behaviours, schooling and educational achievements, aspirations relating to education, work, marriage and migration, and subjective happiness of children young adulthood (where possible in comparison with children in non-migrant household). CHAMPSEA is a pioneering study that continues to throw light on the lives of millions of so-called “left -behind” children.

17607315.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17607315.value: While low level of concerns about the potential threat of cancer recurrence is a normal, realistic response, high fear of cancer recurrence can be detrimental, affecting individuals’ quality of life and functional capacity. Locally, one in four cancer survivors reported high fear of cancer recurrence. However, little is known about the mechanisms contributing to fear of cancer recurrence. The present study proposes a test of the Self-Regulatory Executive Function (S-REF) model which was developed to explain anxiety syndromes, and predicates “thinking about thinking” (metacognitions) as core elements in the maintenance of anxiety. The S-REF model proposes that negative thinking styles (e.g. persistent rumination and worry) are maintained by maladaptive metacognitive beliefs about coping. Such styles of thinking can then become habitual and persistent leading to chronic anxiety states, a process labelled “cognitive attentional syndrome”. So far research has been limited to generalized anxiety states but not to cancer-related anxiety and distress. However, negative cancer-related rumination, intrusive thoughts and hypervigilance characterize cancer-related distress. It therefore seems S-REF would be potentially useful in understanding this. Therefore, applying the S-REF model, we aim to test if maladaptive metacognitive beliefs about negative thinking (e.g. rumination and worry) promote negative styles of thinking (i.e. cognitive attentional syndrome including intrusive thoughts, thought suppression, and attention bias toward threat-related information) thereby leading to fear of cancer recurrence. A longitudinal study is proposed to address the study questions. Eligible participants are Chinese patients newly diagnosed with breast cancer or colorectal cancer. Approximately 150 patients from each cancer type, together 300 patients, will be recruited. Eligible patients will be approached within 4 week after the surgery. Those agreeing to participate complete an interview (baseline) and follow-up at 3-month (FU1), 6-months (FU2), and 12-months (FU3) post-baseline. At baseline, we assess metacognitive beliefs, intrusive thoughts, thought avoidance, attention bias toward threat-related information, and fear of cancer recurrence; follow-ups assess fear of cancer recurrence. A dot probe task, the technique commonly used to assess attention bias will be used to assess attention bias toward threat-related information, whereas validated subject-reported questionnaire will be used to assess other study variables. Latent growth mixture modeling will be used to examine the growth trajectories of fear of cancer recurrence, as well as to test the effect of metacognitive beliefs and cognitive attentional syndrome on the growth trajectories of fear of cancer recurrence.

17607315.label: Realisation of objectives
17607315.value: We had successfully completed the longitudinal study examining the trajectories of fear of cancer recurrence (FCR) over the first year of diagnosis among patients with breast or colorectal cancer, as well las examined the role of metacognition and its indirect effect through attentional bias, intrusive thoughts and avoidance (the CAS) in predicting FCR trajectory. To conduct this study, ethical approval was obtained (ref: UW 15153). Chinese cancer patients who (i) were Cantonese- or Mandarin-speaker; (ii) were recently diagnosed with curable BC or CRC (stage 0 to III); (iii) had surgery as primary treatment within the past eight weeks were recruited at two breast centers and two CRC surgical-oncology units in Hong Kong during their post-surgical follow-up medical appointment. Participants were excluded if they were diagnosed with metastatic BC or CRC, and had linguistic or intellectual difficulties to complete the questionnaires or dot-probe tasks. Written informed consent was sought from potential patients after an explanation of the study nature. Participants completed a standardized face-to-face questionnaire-based interview immediately (baseline), and follow-up interview at 3-month, 6-month, and 12-month post-baseline. In the present study, a total of 293 of eligible patients were recruited from two breast centres and two colorectal cancer surgical-oncology units under the Hospital Authority and gave informed consent, then completed the baseline assessment. The attrition rates for the follow-up assessments were within 14%, resulting a total of 270 patients completed the longitudinal study. At baseline, participants completed the measures of FCR, Metacognition, Intrusive and Avoidant Thoughts, plus the dot-probe tasks assessing attentional bias. Participants’ socio-demographics (age, gender, marital status, education, family monthly income, and occupation) were self-reported on baseline questionnaire, whereas clinical data were extracted from their medical records after the completion of the study. To assess attentional bias, two modified dot-probe tasks using word stimuli as target stimuli were implemented. The paradigm was presented on a Samsung laptop with 15.6-inch monitor by E-Prime. Participants were instructed to sit approximately 50 cm away from the laptop. For negatively-valences stimuli, a word set comprised by 32 negative (e.g. “suicide”) and 32 positive (e.g. “happiness”) two-character Chinese compound words in which have been validated previously were used. Each target word was paired with a neutral word (e.g. “height”). Each trial began with a fixation for 500ms. A priming condition, subliminal exposure of a two-character Chinese compound words either “cancer” (target prime) or “sky” (neutral prime) for 20ms was then incoporated to examine the effect of cancer-related context on attentional bias). Following a pattern mask for 500ms, a pair of word stimuli comprised by one target word and one neutral word (e.g. negative-neutral word pair) appeared side-by-side on the screen for either a subliminal (500ms) or supraliminal (1250ms) duration in order to assess automatic and later strategic attentional processing. After the offset of the paired stimuli, a probe (i.e. a dot) appeared at the location that previously occupied by one of the paired words. Participants were asked to indicate the location of the probe as quickly as possible by pressing the corresponding keys. Reaction latency was recorded. The priming condition, exposure duration, location of the target word, and probe location were counterbalanced generating 64 trials. Four practice trials were given preceding the test trials. Reaction time from correct trials were included for analysis. Reaction time <200ms and >3000ms, and more than 3 SDs above each participants’ mean were discarded as outliners. It has been assumed that individuals who demonstrate attentional bias towards target words would have reaction time advantage when in response to probes replacing negative or positive words (i.e. congruent trials) compared to probes replacing neutral words (i.e. incongruent trials). Hence, attentional bias is inferred from mean difference of reaction time between congruent and incongruent trials. Bias index was calculated by using the formula: Bias Index=((trpl-tlpl)+(tlpr-trpr))/2 where t= target word; p=probe location; r=right side; and l=left side. A positive bias index represents a tendency of attending towards the target stimulus; whereas a negative bias index represents a tendency of attending away from the target stimulus. For cancer-related information, in this task, in order to examine thematically-specific nature of attentional bias, 32 Cancer-related Chinese compound words, rather than negatively-valenced words, were used as target words. As such, there was no priming condition. Otherwise, the setting and procedure were identical to the described one. Cancer-related or positive two-character Chinese compound words were paired with neutral words respectively to produce 64 trials. For data analysis, standard descriptive analyses were conducted to assess sample characteristics. Trajectories of FCR over the 12-month follow-up were identified using a latent growth mixture model (LGMM), derived using Mplus Version 8.2. A robust full information maximum likelihood (FIML) estimations procedure, with an assumption that missing data are unrelated to the outcome variable (missing at random), was used to handle missing data. As such, deceased patients during the study were excluded from the analyses. To generate reliable estimates of the missing data, participants with more than two missing assessment points were also excluded.Three steps were taken to conduct the LGMM analyses (34). Firstly, a univariate single-class growth model without covariates was obtained. Next, to determine the optimal number of trajectories, a series of unconditional growth mixture models was performed. Model indices, namely the Bayesian (BIC), sample-sized adjusted Bayesian (SSBIC), Aikaike information criteria (AIC), entropy values, the Lo-Mendell-Rubin likelihood test (LRT) and the bootstrap likelihood ratio test (BLRT) were assessed and compared across the models. Both models in which growth parameters and associated covariances were constrained to be equivalent across classes, and models in which these constraints were relaxed were examined. Lower values for the BIC, AIC, SSBIC, higher entropy values, and significant p-values (p<0.05) for both the LRT and the BLRT indicate better model fit. Additionally, the proportions for each class must be above 1% of the sample. Thirdly, a conditional growth mixture model was performed by including covariates of class-membership. Since adding too many covariates can raise convergence problems, only the study covariates (MCQ scores and bias indices) were included in this step. Univariate analyses were initially conducted to explore the relationships of FCR trajectories with each of demographic and clinical variables. Only variables significant at a 0.05 level were include in subsequent analyses. To test the mediating effect of the proposed models, Baron and Kenny proposed a 4-step approach in which a series of adjusted regression analyses were conducted. Firstly, a multinomial logistic regression model of FCR trajectory on metacognition was established (Model 1). Next, avoidance, intrusive thoughts and attentional bias (the proposed mediators) were independently regressed on metacognition (Model 2), which was followed by Model 3, where multinomial logistic regression models of FCR trajectory on each of the proposed mediators were developed. Lastly, a regression analysis of FCR trajectory on metacognition and the proposed mediators was conducted (Model 4). Given significant associations were shown in model 1 to model 3, a post-hoc path analysis was applied using INDIRECT macro within SPSS to test the significance of the indirect pathway, that metacognition affects FCR trajectory through its effect on the CAS.

17607315.label: Major findings and research outcome
17607315.value: Latent growth mixed modelling results indicated better model fit for the three-class model. Using the subclinical and clinical cut-off scores of 13-21 and great than 22 as references, most patients (62.4%) were assigned to a ‘Low-stable’ class characterized by having stably low FCR scores. 29% of the sample featuring stably high FCR scores over time, which exceeded the subclinical cut-off score were assigned to a ‘High-stable’ class. The remaining patients (8.3%) evidenced a ‘Recovery’ trajectory, featuring high FCR score with a subsequent decline to the normal range. We then proceeded to examined the role of metacognition and its indirect effect through attentional bias, intrusive thoughts and avoidance (the CAS) in predicting FCR trajectory. Objective 1. Compared with the Low-stable group, patients assigned to the High-stable or the Recovery group reported marginally-significantly and significantly greater Negative beliefs about worry, respectively (High-stable: OR=1.08, p=0.055; Recovery: OR=1.13, p=0.035). Patients in the High-stable group also reported poorer confidence in capabilities of their memory measured by Cognitive confidence (OR=1.12, p=0.004) and were younger (OR=0.95, p=0.001) than the Low-stable group. Therefore, Negative beliefs about worry and Cognitive confidence were retained in the final model delineating predictors of the FCR trajectories. Objective 2. Cognitive confidence did not associate with any of the three CAS. Negative beliefs about worry was positively associated with Avoidance (B = 0.062, p<0.001) and Intrusive thought (B=0.098, p<0.001). Subliminal (but not supraliminal) attentional bias for negatively-valenced words in the priming condition and for cancer-related words were negatively correlated with Negative beliefs about worry (B=-3.86, p=0.017). Avoidance (p=0.003) and Intrusive thoughts (p=0.001) significantly predicted FCR trajectories, whereas attentional bias did not predict FCR and therefore, it was excluded from the subsequent meditation analysis. Objective 3. Bootstrapping procedures with 1000 iterations were used to test mediation effect. Indirect effects of Negative beliefs about worry on FCR trajectories through avoidance (B=0.064, 95% CIs 0.027, 0.12) and intrusive thoughts (B=0.14, 95% CIs 0.083, 0.20) were identified, respectively. After controlling for the mediator, Avoidance, the direct effect of Negative beliefs about worry on FCR trajectories was reduced but remained significant, B =0.078, p=0.036, suggesting that Avoidance partially mediates the association between Negative beliefs about worry and FCR trajectories. Conversely, the direct effect of Negative beliefs about worry was no longer significant after controlling for Intrusive thoughts, B =0.011, p=0.81, indicating a full mediation of Intrusive thoughts.

17607315.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17607315.value: FCR trajectory analyses revealed that while most Chinese cancer patients were resilient to FCR over 12 month, about 3 in 10 demonstrated persistently high FCR above the subclinical casesness threshold, who might be vulnearable to long-term psychosocial maladjustment. The reported findings correspond to the S-REF model, highlighting the centrality of intrusive thought in enhancing and maintaining FCR. More importantly, the subset of affected patients who held greater negative belief about worry and had more intrusive thoughts might be likely to use avoidant coping. Such disengagement coping can impair adaptation, which may counterproductively persist FCR. This specific population may benefit from culturally adapting the existing therapeutic intervention targeting at modifying metacognitive knowledge and interrupting maladaptive information processing including intrusion and avoidance, which should be implemented at the initial diagnostic stage. To build on the findings of the present study, we are currently piloting a metacognition-based, manualized intervention for patients with high fear of cancer recurrence, assessing its feasibility o as well as its preliminary effectiveness. The pilot study is funded by the internal seed funding. We have also submitted a grant application to conduct a randomised controlled trial to test its effectiveness. We are awaiting for the funding results.

17607315.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17607315.value: This longitudinal study identified distinct trajectories of Fear of cancer recurrence (FCR) over 12 months among patients with breast (BC) or colorectal (CRC) cancer, and examined the role of metacognition and its indirect effect through attentional bias, intrusive thoughts and avoidance (the CAS) in predicting FCR trajectory. Three distinct FCR trajectories were identified, namely, Low-stable (62.4%), High-stable (29.2%) and Recovery (8.3%). Negative beliefs about worry, Cognitive confidence, and age predicted FCR trajectories. Compared with the Low-stable group, the Recovery FCR group had greater Negative belief about worry and the High-stable group reported poorer Cognitive confidence. The effect of Negative beliefs about worry were partially mediated by avoidance and fully mediated by intrusive thoughts. Attentional bias did not predict FCR trajectories. While most patients experienced little FCR, 3 in 10 persistently worried about cancer returning over the first 12-month post-surgery. Therapeutic interventions should target patients at risk of persistent FCR by modifying their metacognitive knowledge and interrupting maladaptive cognitive processing including intrusion and avoidance.

17607415.label: Project Title(Chinese)
17607415.value: 科技帝國主義和全球衛生的起源

17607415.label: Project Objectives
17607415.value: Examine how communication technologies were deployed for intelligence gathering and disease surveillance across British territories in Asia between the 1870s and WWII. Preliminary research has suggested that telegraphy transformed routine practices of government, accentuating the importance of intelligence in policy and decision-making. Although a preoccupation with intelligence gathering within the Empire clearly predated electrical technologies, I hypothesise from pervious research that near-instantaneous transcolonial and imperial communication made this intelligence actionable in new ways. Explore how imperial communication systems developed in dynamic response to specific disease threats, including epidemics of cholera, plague, and influenza. To what extent were these systems employed in different ways to deal with different diseases or was the effect the same, regardless? In the 1870s and 1880s, as much of Asia was being linked by cable, laboratory science began to underpin sanitary and public health interventions. How did these coincidental innovations in biomedicine and communication technologies reinforce each other? Investigate the role of non-governmental institutions in shaping official information-collecting practices and intelligence-assessment methods. Previous research has shown how the expansion of telegraphy in the 1870s (and later of telephony and radio) was crucial for the distension of a global media. While news and government intelligence were relayed along the same pathways, agencies such as Reuters became vital to the processes of imperial governance and global commerce. What were the consequences of these convergences and how did governmental and non-governmental agencies interact to produce actionable intelligence? Assess the extent to which communication technologies produced disruptive feedbacks, amplifying the crises they sought to manage. I hypothesise, based on previous research, that these technologies frequently had countervailing effects, necessitating the development of other, ‘corrective’ technologies. Relatedly, the project will assess the uneven appropriation of these technologies across the Empire in Asia. Document the interrelationship between war, technology, and disease, with a particular focus on the role of communication systems during and after the influenza pandemic of 1918 to 1920. Did military conflicts create favourable conditions for the take-up and development of communication technologies and, specifically, their repurposing for disease prevention and control? Consider the degree to which transformative technologies were generated through recombinations of older technologies with a focus on the shift from telegraphy to ‘wireless’ communication, and the arrival of radio in the 1920s and 1930s. How were existing appliances and networks adapted and how did these adaptations impact upon the meaning and scope of ‘intelligence’? The purpose is also to track continuities – and discontinuities – between earlier practices for acquiring and disseminating information that pre-dated the telegraph (for example, the Lloyd’s agency network). Reflect on how communication technologies helped to produce a new arena of pan-Asian intervention. How did imperial concerns about the transnational threat posed by infectious disease impact upon local practices and knowledge? And to what extent did local priorities shape an incipient global regime of health?

17607415.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17607415.value: This project will transform our understanding of the role played by telecommunications in the development of disease surveillance during the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Many historians have argued that new modes of communication, in particular long-distance electrical communication, were crucial to the expansion and consolidation of European empires from the 1870s. Telegraphy enabled rapid communication on a global scale, producing and intensifying interconnectedness. Notwithstanding these claims, surprisingly little study has been made of the specific uses to which the telegraph, telephone, and radio, were put on the ground. How did these technologies reshape practices of imperial and colonial governance? In what ways did they reinforce transcolonial ties and materialise empire’s global rule? This project will address these key questions by investigating the role of technology in British intelligence gathering from the late nineteenth century to WWII, principally in relation to the perceived threats posed by infectious disease across colonial sites in Asia: Aden, Bombay, Colombo, Rangoon, Singapore, and Hong Kong. The project will be the first to examine how telecommunications were instrumentalised to forestall and manage epidemics of cholera, plague, and influenza. It will explore the extent to which a transnational information regime, predicated on health but influenced by the tactics of counterinsurgency and mass communication, produced an incipient ‘global’ consciousness through the collection of epidemiological information. Drawing on material in government and company archives, private papers and newspaper reports, the resulting monograph will contribute substantially to the scholarship on empire and colonialism. It will revise conventional genealogies of global health, which have tended to concentrate on public health efforts after 1945, including the formation of the WHO and the role of international non-governmental organisations in mass immunisation programmes. Instead, the book will track pan-Asian disease concerns back from the post-WWII period of decolonisation to a ‘techno-imperialism’ in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Engaging with recent work that has begun to reappraise the role of technological systems in empire-making, it will examine the ideological meanings vested in new communication technologies, as well as the complex and contradictory factors driving their development. In short, this project will illuminate the crucial role played by disease intelligence gathering in imperial governance, showing how the repurposing of telecommunications for epidemic surveillance helped to delineate the ‘global’ as an object of intervention. The project will furnish fresh perspectives on the contemporary mobilisation of electronic surveillance networks for health security, while providing a new analytics of the global. 電訊科技對於在十九、二十世紀時，疾病監控的發展扮演了什麼角色？這學術研究計劃將改變我們對電訊功用的理解。許多歷史學家都認為，新的通訊方式，尤其是長途電子通信，是歐洲帝國自1870 年代起擴張的重要原因 。人們大多認為電報促使全球通訊傳播更加快捷，加強各地相互聯繫。儘管這個說法很普遍，現今的學術研究卻鮮有提及有關電報、電話、無線電廣播對帝國擴張的影響。 究竟這些通訊科技如何改變帝國和殖民地的統治方式？又，這些科技何以加深跨殖民聯繫, 並實現帝國的殖民統治？這學術研究計劃針對十九世紀末到二次世界大戰期間，英國將科技應用到情報收集，收集有關傳染病威脅亞洲殖民地的信息，所觸及的殖民地包括亞丁、孟買、可倫坡、仰光、新加坡和香港 。 這是首個著重於電訊科技應用在傳染病的防護和控制的硏究計劃。跨國所收集的流行病學資料—— 其中包括霍亂、鼠疫、流感，大前題雖是以健康衛生為主，但其實情報卻同時受當時帝國反叛亂的策略和大眾傳播的影響。收集各種傳染病相關信息，某程度上形成了「全球」的概念。 一向以來，全球衛生的討論往往側重於1945年後公共衛生的發展，包括世衛組織的成立和國際非政府組織的大規模免疫接種計劃。相反，這學術研究計劃將重點推前，專注於十九、二十世紀初的「科技帝國」。 透過分柝和引述政府機構、公司的檔案、私人文件和報紙報導，本論著將對日後帝國和殖民主義研究有深遠影響。 近期已有學術研究嘗試重新評估電訊科技對帝國擴張的影響。本論著探討新的通信技術的意識含義，並點出推動科技發展的因素既複雜且矛盾。 簡而言之，這研究計劃將揭示疫情數據收集對帝國統治所發揮的重要作用，同時，藉著疫情監測科技，「全球」亦成為了被干預的對象。換言之，這計劃以新角度檢視當代電子監控網絡對健康衛生安全，亦同時重新分析全球化的現象。

17607915.label: Project Title(Chinese)
17607915.value: 人类视觉控制朝向目标运动的神经机制

17607915.label: Co - Investigator(s)
17607915.value: Prof Fang, Fang Dr Field, David T

17607915.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17607915.value: One important locomotion task that we face in our daily life is to successfully walk or steer toward a goal. How do we accomplish this task? Much research in the last two decades has studied this question and the findings support the use of two competing visual strategies, i.e., we can walk or steer toward a target by aligning our instantaneous direction of travel (i.e., heading) with the target (the heading strategy; Gibson, 1950, 1958), or by centering the target straight ahead (the egocentric direction strategy; Rushton et al., 1998). While many neurophysiological studies have examined the neural systems engaged in the perception of heading and target egocentric direction cues during self-motion, no study has examined the neural bases for the visual control of goal-oriented locomotion l in humans. The proposed research addresses this question using both task-activation and resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). First, using a steering control task and a model-based fMRI analysis approach, we will identify the brain networks subserving the heading and the egocentric direction strategies using individual differences in the reliance on these two strategies for steering control. We will then vary task instructions and use the effect of task instructions on the control strategy selection to confirm the identified brain networks subserving the two control strategies. In addition, we will examine whether the resting-state functional connectivity of the identified brain networks correlates with the observed individual differences in the reliance on the two control strategies and whether it also predicts the change of the reliance when the task instructions change. Second, to uncover the common (i.e., task-independent) neural bases for the visual control of goal-oriented locomotion, we will examine whether the brain networks identified using the steering control task also subserve the control of walking toward a goal. Last, we will examine how extensive training to use a specific control strategy modulates the activities and connections of the identified brain networks using both the steering and walking tasks. The findings of the proposed research will provide the first evidence regarding the architecture and plasticity of the neural bases for the visual control of goal-oriented locomotion in humans. 成功的控制自身运动从而朝向特定的目标行进（行走或驾驶行为）是人们日常 生活中一项非常重要的活动。在过去的二十年中，人们展开了大量的研究探讨 这项活动是如何完成的。现有的研究成果支持两种相对立的依赖于不同视觉信 息的控制策略。一种是运动方向策略，指的是将由光流信息所指示的运动方向 始终对准目标的运动控制方式(Gibson, 1950, 1958)。另一种是目标参照方向 策略,指的是在行进时始终将目标维持在身体正前方的运动控制方式(Rushton et al.,1998)。目前为止人们对于运动方向和目标参照方向这两种视觉信息的 知觉所涉及的神经系统的探讨已经积累了大量的神经生理学研究，但对于使用 运动方向和目标参照方向这两种视觉信息控制朝向目标行进这一活动所涉及的 神经系统的研究还未开始。本研究将使用任务态功能磁共振以及静息态功能磁 共振的方法解决这一问题。研究第一步，我们将使用基于模型的功能磁共振分 析方法，利用不同个体在行进控制任务中对于运动方向策略和目标参照方向策 略依赖的差异，识别出在控制朝向目标行进的驾驶任务中使用运动方向策略和 目标参照方向策略所分别对应的神经网络。之后我们将操控实验指导语以改变 被试对于运动方向策略和目标参照方向策略的偏好，从而对于之前所定位的两 种控制策略所对应的神经网络进行再验证。此外，我们还将探讨两种策略所对 应的神经网络内脑区之间联系的强弱和所观察到的个体对于不同策略所依赖的 权重是否相关联，以及此关联是否能够预测个体由于实验指导语的变化而改变 的对于不同策略的依赖权重。研究第二步，为了揭示使用视觉信息控制朝向目 标行进所涉及的非特定神经基础（即与特定任务无关），我们将探讨在研究第 一步所识别的基于朝向目标行进的驾驶任务的神经网络是否可扩展到朝向目标 行进的行走任务。最后，我们将使用朝向目标行进的驾驶任务和行走任务来探 讨对于特定策略的训练是否能够改变此策略所对应的神经网络内脑区的激活强 度以及脑区之间联系的强弱。本研究的结果将为朝向目标行进时使用不同控制 策略所涉及的神经网络的结构以及神经网络结构的可塑性提供首个实验结论。

17608515.label: Project Title(Chinese)
17608515.value: 無律師代表的訴訟人在特定類型民事訴訟中所得的結果

17608515.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17608515.value: The issue of access to justice for those without private legal representation is not new; however, whilst the growing proportions of these litigants in person (“LiPs”) appearing in civil courts is an increasing concern, little has been achieved to ensure their cases are fully ventilated and rights fully protected. This study proposes to examine the presence of unrepresented litigants in the civil courts by way of a quantitative study of judgments. Initial findings from a pilot study of civil cases in Hong Kong from 2005 – 2013 showed higher proportions of LiPs in bankruptcy proceedings (50%), family court proceedings (31%), employees’ compensation cases (30%) and personal injuries cases (21%), in contrast with the 21% mean of all civil cases in the Court of First Instance of the High Court and 29% in the District Court. The proposed study thus focuses on LiPs in the areas of insolvency, family and tort law – in narrowing down the study to specific types of cases, this study distinguishes itself further from previous broadbrush approaches to LiPs. The methodology of this study will be to capture all such cases within the period of study, ensuring representativeness of the set of data, in contrast with the sampling methods and risk of potential bias the higher number of cases in other common law jurisdictions necessitate. The study will focus on the measurable impact of LiPs on the court system in comparison with represented parties in terms of time, costs, and significantly, outcomes of their cases. Such a study has never been carried out in Hong Kong, and will capture more detail than previous studies on LiPs. The same methodology will then be applied to comparative studies of judgments from other common law jurisdictions for the purposes of consistency, though of smaller sample size, not only to enhance the impact and international relevance of this study, but also to identify issues that are potentially systemic to the common law litigation system. This particularized methodology could enable specific reforms to be developed; e.g. the high proportion of bankruptcy cases arising from judgment debt found in the pilot study might be addressed by development of post-litigation mediation of award satisfaction. This quantitative study will be supplemented and contextualised with judicial statistics on LiP participation in civil court hearings, Daily Cause Lists data, and qualitative studies such as surveys, interviews and observation of court cases to enhance the interpretation of the data. 有關無私人律師代表的訴訟人向法院提出訴訟的議題一直存在，然而，儘管在民事法庭中，無律師代表的訴訟人比例不斷增長，而情況愈來愈備受關注，但目前仍未有充足措施，能確保他們的案件得到充分聽取，並且充分保障他們的權利。本研究擬通過對判決書的定量研究，探討在民事法庭中出現無律師代表訴訟人的情況。 根據於2005年至2013年在香港進行的民事案件試點研究，初步結果顯示，無律師代表的訴訟人在以下案件中出現的比例較高：破產程序(50％)、家事法庭訴訟程序(31％)、僱員補償案件(30％)、人身傷害案件(21％)，對比高等法院原訟法庭所有民事案件中，無律師代表的案件平均數為21％，而區域法院則為29％。此擬議之研究主要探討在破產、家庭法和侵權法範疇內無律師代表的訴訟人──藉着將研究範圍收窄至特定類型的案件，本研究將更加有別於以往對無律師代表訴訟人的概括性研究。 本研究所採用的方法，將涵蓋研究期間內的所有此等案件，以確保數據的代表性，這樣會與其他普通法司法管轄區研究較大量案件時所使用的抽樣方法和所可能產生的偏差而有所不同。 本研究集中了解在時間、費用以及更重要的是在案件結果方面，無律師代表的訴訟人對比有律師代表的訴訟方，對法庭系統的可衡量的影響。此種研究從未在香港進行，並且相比以往針對無律師代表訴訟人的研究，將涉獵更多細節。為確保一致性，對其他普通法司法管轄區的判決書進行比較研究時將採用同樣方法，惟取樣數目較小，藉此不但可提升本研究的影響力和國際意義，更可找出可能影響整體普通法訴訟制度的問題。 此具體化的方法可促使特定的改革發展，例如試點研究發現破產案件大部分由判定債項所產生，對應這情況的方法可以是研究在訴訟後就清償判給額進行調解。 為加強數據的詮釋，本定量研究的補充資料及背景資料將包括無律師代表訴訟人參與民事法庭聆訊的司法機構數據、審訊案件表及定性研究，如法庭案件的調查、訪問和觀察。

17608615.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17608615.value: This project examines policy controversies over the inadequate housing problem in Hong Kong. While there is an extensive literature on slum housing in developing countries, there are relatively fewer studies on inadequate housing in the developed world. In reality, inadequate housing also exists in highly developed cities, such as Hong Kong, where tens of thousands of households live in overcrowded sub-divided flats. However, just because a problem is serious does not mean that it is high on the political agenda, since there are multiple issues clamouring for the attention of policymakers. In the case of Hong Kong, inadequate housing did not feature explicitly on the political agenda until around 2012, when the government began to review its Long Term Housing Strategy. Thus, the first phase of this project is to outline the changing visibility of the inadequate housing problem in Hong Kong, through examining statistical data and news reports. In particular, it attempts to explain the rapid entrance of this problem onto the political agenda over the last few years. The second phase of the project applies the method of framing analysis, to analyse why policy controversies emerged, despite consensus over the severity of the inadequate housing problem. The framing method goes beyond conventional policy analysis methods, which tend to focus on the efficiency or cost-effectiveness of different policy interventions. It acknowledges the prevalence of controversies in public policymaking, since policy actors have divergent interpretations about the causes of a problem, and hence the appropriateness of different policy responses. Using the tools of framing analysis, the project will analyse policy documents and news reports, to identify the frames adopted by different actors to shape public perceptions about the causes of and solutions to the inadequate housing problem. The final phase of the project involves interviewing policy actors, to examine how framing strategies interact with the material resources and socio-political power possessed by different actors, and how the local policymaking context influences the choice of particular courses of action. Overall, the project seeks to deepen our understanding of the role of framing strategies in the policymaking process. This approach helps explain why particular policies emerge in response to the inadequate housing problem, and why controversies persist. In addition, it provides insights into possible strategies for re-framing, such as the generation of new frames that could potentially bridge the divide between adversaries, and could pave the way towards more consensual solutions. 本研究旨在解讀香港劏房問題的政策爭論。劏房問題一直存在，為何過去幾年始受廣泛關注，成為數一數二的政治議題? 研究嘗試闡釋以上現象，再透過框架理論，分析不同持份者如何詮釋劏房問題的成因和應對政策。框架理論有助我們跳出狹窄的成本效益分析，更深入地了解詮釋框架對政策制定的影響。

17608615.label: Realisation of objectives
17608615.value: The primary aim of this research was to analyse policy responses and controversies in relation to the inadequate housing problem in Hong Kong, which adds to the literature on inadequate housing in developed cities. In particular, the research applied framing theories from the sociological literature, thus going beyond conventional approaches to policy analysis. The first objective of the research was to outline the changing visibility of the inadequate housing problem in Hong Kong, and explain its rapid entrance onto the political agenda in recent years. This objective was successfully achieved through a systematic review of secondary data, including census data, policy documents and media articles on inadequate housing, especially sub-divided flats in the private rental sector. Through documentary analysis, this phase of the research identified key moments in the rent regulation debate in Hong Kong, including abolition of rent control in the late 1990s, and removal of security of tenure in the early 2000s, both of which contributed to unaffordability and housing insecurity problems among low-income tenants. The second objective was to identify the strategies which different actors adopted to frame the causes of and solutions to the inadequate housing problem. This objective was also successfully achieved. Prior to collecting primary data, the researcher reviewed key concepts and theories in the sociological framing literature, including the key concepts of diagnostic and prognostic frames, in order to develop an analytical framework for interpretation of the interview data. Also, through review of documentary data and media articles, the key actors associated with the rent regulation debate, such as representatives of low-income tenant advocacy groups, were identified and compiled into a list to facilitate arrangement of in-depth interviews. Subsequently, the researcher conducted in-depth qualitative interviews with key actors, in order to understand how these actors attribute the causes of proliferation of sub-divided flats, and how they justify the solutions which they propose. As expected, it was not easy to secure interviews with all of these key actors, since the rent regulation debate has extended over a long period of time, and some of these actors have already left the institutions which they served. Nevertheless, the snowballing technique was adopted, i.e. asking interviewees to recommend other people in their networks, in order to maximize the number of interviews. This enabled the researcher to secure interviews with actors from a variety of backgrounds, including representatives of lobbying groups and legislative councillors. In the data analysis stage, the researcher applied the analytical framework to make sense of competing arguments of the interviewees. Furthermore, during the process of data collection and analysis, it became obvious that inadequate housing in Hong Kong is not limited to sub-divided flats in the low-end rental sector, but also includes micro-flats in the higher end of the sector, which lack sufficient housing space. Thus, the researcher also examined recent growth of micro-flats in the higher-end rental sector. This involved reviewing government data on micro-flats, as well as interviews with residents of micro-flats, in order to understand the reasons behind the growth of micro-flats, the characteristics of micro-flat dwellers, and their perceptions of housing space problems. The third objective of the study was to analyse how framing strategies interact with material resources, political power and the policymaking context, to shape the set of policy responses in Hong Kong. This objective was also achieved through in-depth interview data collection. Interviewees were asked to assess their financial and political resources in relation to other actors, and to consider how this has affected their lobbying efforts and outcomes. In addition, the meeting minutes of Legislative Council meetings were analysed in detail, in order to understand the influence of political ideology and power relations on the contest between legislative councillors, especially during key moments in the rent regulation debate. The fourth objective was to explain why controversies emerged during the policymaking process, despite consensus over the severity of the inadequate housing problem. This was achieved through applying concepts from framing theories to interpret the in-depth interview data, especially the concepts of diagnostic, prognostic and motivational frames. As elaborated in one of the journal publications, although there was a general convergence of diagnostic frames between different actors, there were major divergences in terms of prognostic frames. Furthermore, low-income advocacy groups were not able to mobilise widespread support for rent regulation in recent years, due to weak motivational frames. The fifth and final objective was to identify possibilities for re-framing the inadequate housing debate towards more consensual solutions. This objective was achieved through the reflections in two journal publications, which highlighted recent shifts of the framing strategies of tenant advocacy groups from rent regulation towards community-based housing solutions. As elaborated in the publications, these reframed solutions are more consensual, and are supported by most of the key actors, although they run the risk of diluting previous debates on rent regulation. Overall, all of the study objectives have been achieved. Different approaches to data collection, including documentary analysis and in-depth interviews, were implemented according to the research plan. The data was thoroughly analysed through applying the concepts and theories that were extracted from the literature review.

17608615.label: Major findings and research outcome
17608615.value: The major findings in this research have been disseminated through four peer-reviewed publications, including three journal publications and one book chapter. The first set of important findings were published in two journal papers, including one paper entitled “"Lobbying for rent regulation in Hong Kong: Rental market politics and framing strategies", published in Housing Studies, and another paper entitled “Community-based housing solutions in Hong Kong: How and why have they emerged?”, published in the International Journal of Housing Policy. These papers provide evidence on the framing strategies of lobbying groups in Hong Kong, which explain recurrent contests over rent regulation. Furthermore, the papers argue how these framing strategies have shifted in recent years, which help lobbying groups mobilise support from other actors, but which may not help address the root causes of affordability problems. The second set of important findings were published in a journal paper entitled “Housing size and housing market dynamics: The case of micro-flats in Hong Kong”, published in Land Use Policy. This paper provides new empirical evidence on recent growth of micro-flats in Hong Kong, the reasons behind this growth, resident perceptions of housing space and why they trade off housing space with other factors. The paper contributes to ongoing academic and policy debates about decline in housing space in the context of housing affordability problems. The third set of important findings were elaborated in a book chapter entitled “Speculative sub-division of private rental flats in Hong Kong”, which is part of a larger book project entitled The Speculative City. The findings reveal that the growth of sub-divided flats cannot be solely attributed to undersupply of public rental flats. This phenomenon is linked to housing speculation in Hong Kong, including the construction of large, luxury flats, which tend to be bought by property speculators. The book chapter argues that these speculative activities have led to spillover effects, including reduced supply of small to medium-sized flats, leading to intensified competition for a limited stock of rental flats among lower-middle income households. Apart from the above research publications, the major findings of the research were presented in four international conferences, including the Asia-Pacific Network for Housing Research (APNHR) Conference and European Network for Housing Research (ENHR) Conference, in order to disseminate the findings among other housing researchers.

17608615.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17608615.value: The research findings highlight an interesting issue which has potential for further investigation. Currently, low-income advocacy groups have conducted some studies on the health impacts of living in overcrowded flats in the low-end private rental sector. However, as this research indicates, the housing space problem affects not only low-income renters in Hong Kong, but also higher-income households renting micro-flats in the inner urban area, as well as households who have bought micro-flats in suburban areas. In other words, the housing space problem is widespread. Thus, it is worth exploring the socio-psychological impacts of living in different types of small-sized flats. These households are likely to experience a range of problems such as privacy problems and lack of family interaction space, which have potential implications for psychological health. Nevertheless, there are few studies on the psychological dimensions of the housing space problem. The Principal Investigator plans to explore the literature on this topic, with the aim of developing a new research project.

17608615.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17608615.value: This research explores an increasingly important topic in housing studies, namely the growth of private renting in the context of severe affordability problems and difficulties in accessing homeownership. While there is a lot of research on the private rental sector in other places, such as England, Germany and Australia, there are very few studies on the private rental sector in Hong Kong. Through qualitative research methods, this study provides new empirical knowledge of recent developments in the private rental sector in Hong Kong, including developments in the low-end private rental sector (proliferation of sub-divided flats rented by low-income households), as well as developments in the higher end of the sector (growth of micro-flats rented by high-income professionals). Furthermore, the study explores power relations among key actors in the private rental sector, including landlords, tenants, tenant advocacy groups, and policymakers. The study applies framing theories from the sociological literature to interpret these policy contests, such as contests over rent control and security of tenure, which go beyond conventional approaches to policy analysis. Overall, the study extends existing academic and policy discussions on rental-ownership dynamics, by highlighting locally-specific manifestations of affordability problems, while introducing new theoretical frameworks for interpreting these problems.

17608715.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17608715.value: This is a longitudinal study of teenage immigrant students in Hong Kong to understand their academic trajectories and identity formation. Annually about 5,000 newly-arrived children are first admitted to primary and secondary schools in Hong Kong. Educational pathway and identity construction, which this research will focus on, are the two key issues relating to the future development and integration of these young immigrants. This proposal is a continuation and expansion of my PhD dissertation which, conducted from 2008 to 2012, ethnographically explored the academic trajectories and identity formation of newly-arrived immigrant youth in Hong Kong secondary schools as they adapted to schooling and life. They were the teenage children of the two largest incoming groups to Hong Kong: from Mainland China and from South Asia. These two groups formed the focus and were an excellent pair for comparison because 1) they were the two largest immigrant groups; and 2) they represented one Chinese group, sharing similar ethnic and cultural backgrounds with local Hong Kong Chinese, and one non-Chinese group, having utterly different ethnic and cultural backgrounds. At the time of my dissertation research, these students had been in the Hong Kong education system for less than one year. I interviewed 87 students aged between 12 and 18. Now, two to six years later, it is high time to revisit these young people to keep track of their transformations. Although some of them might have left school and are no longer students, and some might have grown to young adults and are no longer teenagers, for the purpose of this study, they will still be included because they came to Hong Kong as teenage students. Their life stories will still be traced. This project will continue the line of inquiry of my dissertation to investigate the life stories of young immigrants in Hong Kong with special reference to academic trajectories and identity formation through 1) in-depth interviews; 2) participant observation; and 3) class shadowing for those who are at school. This investigation seeks to illuminate the full complexity of young immigrants’ situations in their first five to ten years as they adapt to schooling and life in Hong Kong. It will particularly elucidate the promises and obstacles along their academic pathway, and the complex process of identity construction. It will offer informed suggestions as to what kind of support and intervention might be most effective in advancing educational equity and social integration. 是項調查採用追蹤研究，以期了解青少年移民學生在香港的教育途徑以及身份建構。每年約有五千名新來港學童入讀中小學，教育途徑及身份建構兩大議題，與這批年青移民的將來發展及社會融合息息相關，也就是這項研究的焦點所在。 這個研究是我博士論文的延伸，論文研究在2008年至2012年進行，以民族誌調查方法，探索新來港中學生的教育途徑及身份建構，以中國內地及南亞國家來港的青少年為主。而當前這個研究比較這兩大群體，不單是因為他們佔青少年移民的大多數，也是因為他們文化背景迴異，一群來自中國內地，與香港有共同的中華文化背景，而另一群則與香港的民族文化截然不同。 當時我的博士論文研究對象在香港讀書不到一年，年齡介乎12至18歲，我訪問了87位同學，今天相距當時訪談二至六年，正是合適時機重訪這班年青人，去追蹤他們的改變。雖然他們有些已經離校不再是學生，有些亦不再是十幾歲，但是他們還是會包括在是次研究，因為他們到港的時候還是十幾歲的少年，這項研究會繼續追蹤他們的生活故事。 如前所述，是項研究會延續我的博士論文，去探究在香港的青少年移民的故事，著眼點放在教育途徑以及身份建構。研究方法將採用深入訪談、參與觀察等，對於仍在學的青少年，還會進行課堂觀察。研究目的是希望可以了解青少年移民在香港首五至十年的情況，探索他們如何適應在香港的教育以至生活，闡述他們教育的前景及障礙，並闡明身份建構的複雜過程，研究還會提出建議，以期可以更有效地達到公平教育以及社會融合。
