17611815.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17611815.value: BACKGROUND: The 12-month point prevalence rate of bipolar disorder in Hong Kong is estimated to be between 0.5 and 1.8, affecting between 36,000 and 129,000 individuals. The illness often develops in young adults and, in many cases, has long-term effects on their life trajectory, negatively influencing their ability to sustain employment or establish and maintain a family. The costs to society lie in the provision of treatment and loss of economic productivity. Treatment is often typically with medication, but such treatment does not address the emotional and social sequaelae of the illness, which may be better addressed by peer-supporters. AIMS AND DESIGN: The overall aim of this study is to examine how individuals with bipolar disorder (BD) seek, assess and use professional and expert-by-experience knowledge (provided by peer-supporters based on their own lived experience of mental illness) to make positive changes as part of the recovery process. The study will adopt a qualitative paradigm underpinned by an interpretive approach representing a social constructionist view of reality. Data will be collected from 32 service users selected with purposive sampling using interviews and vignettes. A family member (n=16), peer-supporter (n=8) and professional staff (n=8) member will also be interviewed, for a total of 64 interviews. Data will be analysed according to standard thematic analysis techniques aided by the NVivo computer program. All results will be presented to the interviewees as part of a reality-checking process and to allow them to provide any additional comments. The two co-investigators will be persons who have recovered from serious mental illness. SIGNIFICANCE: The originality of the proposed study lies in its potential to advance knowledge by extending our epistemological understanding of credible knowledge, as interpreted by various stakeholders in mental healthcare settings. Collaborative research incorporating individuals with lived experience of mental illness is at the cutting edge of research in this area. These individuals will join the study as named co-investigators and will thus have real authority to influence its design and execution. The results will inform practice and training in psychiatric settings and encourage the creative incorporation of peer-supporters into the recovery process, thereby facilitating both qualitative and quantitative improvements in service provision in a resource-limited health sector.

17611815.label: Realisation of objectives
17611815.value: 1) Execution of the Project to achieve the Research Objectives: To achieve the research objectives, 65 (original target, N=64) in-depth individual interviews were conducted between April 2016 and July 2017 with four categories of participants: i) 32 service users, ii) 16 family caregivers, iii) nine peer support workers and iv) eight mental health professionals. In order to recruit service users and family caregivers, we contacted a public hospital, five Integrated Community Centres for Mental Wellness (ICCMWs) and non-government organisations (NGO). The mental health professional were members of multidisciplinary teams (e.g., psychiatrist, nurse, social worker, occupational therapist) in hospital or community-based settings; whereas the peer support workers held a paid position as a PSW to support clients in hospital or ICCMW. The interviews lasted between 40 and 90 minutes and were performed by a trained researcher. The team developed a semi-structured interview guides which contains questions covering the following areas: experiences of caregiving (family members) or recovery journey (service users), mental health services received or delivered, their understanding of recovery, the perception of peer support service and knowledge or information they gained from professionals and PSWs (professional and expert-by-experience knowledge). The were two methodological innovations introduced to the present project. First, two case vignettes, one on medication and one on employment, were used for the interviews with professionals and PSWs for direct comparison. After presented the vignettes, participants were asked what they would typically do, what kind of information or advice they would give to the client, and how mental health professionals and peer supporters can help the client to manage medication or to seek a job. The vignette approach was used as it is “an efficient way of collecting data, provide[s] balance between flexibility and structure, and enhance[s] the researcher’s depth of understanding” about the topic under investigation (Jackson, Harrison, Swinburn, & Lawrence, 2015, p. 1405). Additionally, the vignette solicited different participants’ responses to a uniform scenario and ascertained what they would do while reducing halo effect (Barter & Renold, 1999; Holley & Gillard, 2017). Responses were analysed to reveal the level of harmony or discord between the two groups concerning the topic under study. The vignette and interview guide were previewed by two peer researchers with lived experience of BD and were modified based on their feedback: for example, questions were added on what services clients were using, and who they would turn to when clients felt unwell. Second, peer researchers as Named Investigators were invited to participate in this project; for details on peer researcher in mental health see www.centreformentalhealth.org.uk/work-us/action-research-and-peer-involvement. The two colleagues helped to refine the implementation of the study and to aid interpretation of the data was another innovative approach adapted in the present study. Upon reflection, it worked well on two counts: i) they helped to promote participants recruitment, and ii) to verify and make sense of the research results. The audio recordings were transcribed verbatim in Chinese by professional transcribers for subsequent analysis and interpretation. All personally identifiable information was removed from the texts to ensure confidentiality and quality checks were performed by comparing the recordings to transcripts. During the data collection phase, the team reviewed the emerging findings and discussed any additional questions to explore deeper meanings of the themes. Following the six steps of thematic analysis, the principal investigator (Tse) and the researcher (Yuen) read the interview transcripts independently to familiarise themselves with the data, then the two researchers met several times to discuss the initial codes and were open to any new codes generated from the data. The interviews were coded using the agreed system (aided by NVivo). Potential themes were then identified, refined and finalised. The findings were shared with members of the wider team (Davidson and Murray) including the peer researchers (Kan and Kwan) of this project and a group of peer support workers for verification. The study showed differences in the perception of expert-by-experience knowledge and those from regular mental health professionals by the four groups of participants. Additionally, different knowledge was needed and delivered at different stages of the recovery. 2) Challenges: 2.1 Overall: The recruitment of service users and family caregivers slowed down after six months commencing the study. Peer support service is a new form of mental service in Hong Kong which has created a few challenges for this project. Firstly, there were only limited number of service users or family members fulfilled the inclusion criteria that the service users were diagnosed with bipolar disorder and receiving peer support services at the same time. Secondly, the field or peer support services are not ready for this project’s recruitment for instance, they needed time to define the job description, set the scope of the services, and prepare the entire workplace to integrate the new emerging workforce of peer supporters into the existing healthcare services/ settings. In one instance, a NGO asked us to contact them again after six months. Thirdly, at the time of the commencement of the project (late December 2015), the three originally partnering NGOs were not in a position to support this project as they were already engaged in another major project (funded by Mindset, Jardine Ambassadors Programme). We requested an extension of six months successfully; we approached new NGOs e.g., Family Links, family services at Baptist Oi Kwan ICCMW to recruit participants. 2.2 For Objective 2, some service users had difficulty in self-reporting the subtypes of their bipolar illness; the interview data revealed some participants recalled vivid experience during their depressed (e.g., low motivation, dragging for very long period of time) or elated episodes (e.g., overspending, conflicts [related agitated mood] at home resulted in family calling the police), whereas the social service agencies did not have such information. Nevertheless, the research participants were able to recall the year of receiving the diagnosis. It afforded us the opportunity to examine the experience of interacting with/ obtaining knowledge from peer support workers and mental health professionals across individuals with different years of illness. We performed further analyses by using NVivo: Any differences in themes (sub-themes) across years of illness (less than 10 years, 11-20 years or those had BD for more than 20 years). Two differences were found across those three groups in terms of: i) participants with less than 10 years of BD appreciated that PSW would see them as a person first not merely a "mentally-ill patient"; and ii) participants with more than 10 years of BD reported the communication (with mental health professionals were often about the routine "stuff" (e.g., how was your sleep, taking meds, mood). The Nvivo nodes of themes and sub-themes and trails of analyses are available upon request. 3) Beyond Achieving the Objectives: A forum was held for PSWs and social workers, over 50 people in total, in June 2018. Other activities (e.g., presenting public lecture, 2 articles published in local Chinese newspaper, see Part C- Research Outputs) were completed to create greater impact on different sectors of the community. For details of the research results, please see Section 6 Research Outcome and the FULL MANUSCRIPTS are attached in this Report. We are keen to update RGC the publication status of the 3 manuscripts already submitted to reputable journals (currently under review) by June 2019, if required.

17611815.label: Major findings and research outcome
17611815.value: Several themes related to knowledge acquisition (or "knowledge sharing" a more helpful expression when interviewing research participants) and peer support services: 1) Understanding of recovery The service users and family caregivers gave a multifaceted definition of recovery. While some of them viewed that recovery as returning to the status before the onset of illness and being able to stop medication, others indicated that medication and fluctuations in mood may be present, but they were able to go out into the community and sustain a job. They gained this understanding from different sources (e.g., reflecting upon own experience, information from health professionals, attending talks and groups). 2) Comparison of regular mental health professionals and peer support services 2.1 Service user participants described in general, PSW (expert-by-experience) and health professionals have their own focus in practice and contributed in a “complementary” ways to their recovery from bipolar disorder (BD). 2.2 Professional participants generally expressed that information on medication offered by people who were not medical professionals may be “inaccurate”. The service users and PSWs shared the view that psychiatrists were the expert in medication and they were cautious when talking about medication. 2.3 Service users perceived that medication was only one component in supporting recovery, other aspects, such as engaging in other activities and advices from PSW, were also helpful. Many clients had strong tendency to cut down medication (understably); PSW would explain that the goal should be to foster good role functioning and being stable. 2.4 Overall, participants did not reveal any unpleasant experience in terms of receiving any conflicting information about the condition or treatments. Mental health professionals delivered knowledge on medical (e.g. symptoms, diagnosis, medication) and psycho-social aspects (e.g. interpersonal relationships, accommodation and financial situation) whereas PSWs (who have expert-by-experience knowledge) focused on practical and daily issues, such as advices on navigating the health systems and participation in community activities. 3) The unique features of PSWs PSWs had the natural ability to connect with the service users and foster hope. They also helped family caregivers to better understand their loved ones' illness and change their perception about their family members' recovery. 4) Elements to facilitate knowledge acquisition Participants reported that a respectful attitude and being non-judgmental facilitated the trust between service users and mental health staff and PSWs. Furthermore, there could be tailor-made approach to share knowledge with individuals with BD, for example, using rhetorical questions and offering them with alternative perspectives.

17611815.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17611815.value: Research and clinical implications: 1) Future research can be extended to examine the perceptions of PSWs and investigate the mechanism of PSWs impact on caregivers with a more representative sample of caregivers, including caregivers coming from different family structures, such as remarriage/blended families, three-generation families. Future research should also systematically investigate the mechanisms of PSWs’ impact on caregivers. 2) More open and respectful communication between mental health professionals and PSWs. The current data highlight the different approaches of the two groups of people providing support for people with BD. Mental health workers are well placed to help PSWs develop a language around medication prescription which is a good fit to PSWs’ expertise and background; we can also imagine in multi-disciplinary teams where PSWs help mental health workers with appropriate language around lived experience to maximize health workers’ engagement with their clients. 3) PSWs can effect a more structured intervention, for instance, active dialogues on medication management, without jeopardizing the authenticity of peer-to-peer support in mental health. 4) Findings from the present study should be widely disseminated not only to PSWs but also their peer colleagues, supervisors and policy/ service planners to improve their understanding of peer services- characteristics of the services, contributions and constrains

17611815.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17611815.value: Peer support services provide expert-by-experience knowledge and has been adopted in Hong Kong and other Western regions, but little is known about how knowledge is disseminated by peer support workers (PSWs) as compared to mental health professionals. The current qualitative study using individual in-depth interviews was conducted with 65 participants (32 service users, 16 family caregivers, 9 PSWs and 8 mental health professionals). This was the first research in the region to examine the view of the key stakeholders on PSWs and recovery from bipolar disorder. Knowledge delivered by the PSWs offered a helpful perspective for the service users. In addition to the practical advices from PSWs, they were also able to foster hope, provide emotional support and be their companion throughout service users’ recovery journey. This study generated significant implications for the services provided in a Chinese context. PSWs has a role to play in medication management. A more open and respectful communication between health professionals and PSWs, organizational readiness, staff preparation, clear policies and procedures are required to enhance mental health services. Caregivers began to understand the benefits of PSWs after experiencing their services. Peer-led services could be a helpful support for both service users and family caregivers.

17612015.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17612015.value: 日常生活中，年輕人在不同事情，例如物質濫用，升學，和就業發展等的決策上也需管理風險，以確保良好生活質素。科學研究以睡眠剝奪實驗已證明睡眠質量會影響風險決策能力。然而，儘管日間小睡較無眠或睡眠剝奪較為常見，目前幾乎沒有任何檢視日間小睡，睡眠習慣，與風險決策能力關係的研究。 透過採用主觀和客觀的睡眠評估工具和日間小睡實驗，此研究旨在探討睡眠在風險決策能力中擔當的角色，以及其他相關的因素。基於目前科研數據，我們的主要研究假設包括：（1）相對睡眠充足的人，睡眠時間較短的人的風險決策能力將會較差，而睡眠時間及風險決策能力的關係是受著個人睡眠需要及實際睡眠時間差異的影響；（2）小睡組將較對照實驗組（沒有小睡機會）有更佳的風險決策能力；（3）小睡與風險決策能力的關係會受著個人睡眠需要及實際睡眠時間的差異影響；（4）小睡對風險決策能力的裨益與在多導睡眠圖（PSG）檢測的睡眠神經生理因素（例如，快速眼動睡眠和慢波睡眠的長短及遲滯期）相關；（5）睡眠時間及小睡透過影響其他腦神經心理功能（例如工作記憶及警覺性）影響風險決策能力。 大約一百名研究參加者將完成情緒，智能，睡眠，小睡習慣和看法的評估。研究為期7日，參加者在首5日填寫睡眠日記，並戴著腕動計作為睡眠習慣的量度。參加者將在第6日來到睡眠實驗室進行兩節腦神經心理功能評估（包括風險決策能力，警覺性，工作記憶，抑鬱控制和情緒）。在兩節評估之間，參加者將被隨機分配到小睡組或對照實驗組，當中只有小睡組會有小睡機會，並在睡眠期間接受多導睡眠圖檢測睡眠神經生理因素。完成兩節腦神經心理功能評估後，參加者將會再戴著腕動計和填寫睡眠日記一日，以探討日間小睡對晚間睡眠質量的潛在影響。 研究結果將對睡眠科學帶來新的知識，尤其是睡眠與小睡在風險決策能力之間的互為影響及背後相關的腦神經心理及電生理的因素。研究結果將提供科研數據裨益學生健康教育和公共政策（例如從事高風險決策工作人仕的工時）。

17612015.label: Realisation of objectives
17612015.value: All three objectives were achieved successfully. Objective #1: The associations between habitual sleep behaviors, sleep need, and risk-related decision-making among college students We examined the relationship between habitual sleep behaviors, sleep need and risk-related decision making in our sample. Significant associations among our research variables were identified. Our sample showed high day-to-day sleep timing variability, had short sleep duration and Excessive Daytime Sleepiness (EDS), with 11-16% sleeping less than the threshold of 6 hours per night and 66% with EDS (c.f., 25% in US college population). Using the Risky-Gains task (RGT), we found that sleep timing variability was cross-sectionally correlated with risk-taking behaviors. We further found that individual differences in subjective sleep need moderated the influence of short sleep duration on risk-taking behaviors. Greater perceived sleep need predicted more risk taking among habitual short sleepers, but decreased risk taking among habitual normal sleepers. Further details of the associations can be found in attachment (Lau*, Wong, Rusak et al. in press). Such findings were presented at two international conferences, 23rd Congress of The European Sleep Research Society and 31st Annual Meeting of the Associated Professional Sleep Societies, and published in the Journal Psychology & Health. Objective #2: The effects of a daytime sleep opportunity (i.e., a nap) on risk-related decision-making We assessed the effect of sleep on risk-related decision making in young adults using multiple neurobehavioral assessments using a daytime sleep paradigm. Our experimental data showed that young adults generally had deteriorated vigilance and increased impulsive decision-making tendency throughout the day. Specifically, participants without a daytime sleep opportunity showed poorer planning and psychomotor vigilance performance during the second set of assessments, but they responded faster in making risky choices. On the other hand, a 90-min daytime sleep opportunity reduced impulsivity in decision making; participants given a sleep opportunity showed better planning performance and improved psychomotor vigilance than those in the Wake group. Sleep spindle in central region was additionally found to be correlated with impulsive decision-making tendency among the youths with the sleep opportunity, suggesting potential physiological mechanism of sleep’s protective effect on impulsive decision-making among youths. These findings indicate that a 90-min daytime sleep opportunity improved planning and decision making in tasks related to risk taking. Further details of the associations can be found in attachment (Wong, Lau*, Lam et al. submitted). Such findings were presented at an international conference, World Sleep 2017 Congress, and submitted to the Journal SLEEP. Objective #3: The moderators and mediators involved in the napping effects on risk-related decision-making Regarding Objective #3, we explored the moderating effects of depressed mood among the Sleep group. Participants in the Sleep group were further divided into those with/without depressed mood using the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale, and the napping effects on RGT performance were examined among both groups. At the pre-condition assessment, after a punishment 80 trial, those with depressed mood had significant lower tendency to select another highly risky decision, than the non-depressed group, t(103)=-2.416, p=.018. A mixed model ANOVA revealed a significant main effect of time, F(1,91)=7.261, p=.008, and an interaction effect between time and depressed mood, F(1,91)=4.161, p=.044. Post-hoc analyses showed that, following the nap, participants with depressed mood had significantly increased tendency to select a highly risky choice after being punished, t(35)=-3.411, p=.002, where the non-depressed group did not have significantly different performance on the same measure, t(57)=-.494, p=.623. The data suggest a sub-optimal punishment learning in risky decision making among individuals with depressed mood, which appeared to have improved and comparable to those without depressed mood after a daytime nap. We shall continue to look for other theoretically meaningful mediators and moderators involved in the napping effects on risk-related decision-making, and to uncover the potential mechanisms of the effect, e.g. sleep spindles, or moderators like premorbid sleep duration or quality. We are preparing a third manuscript on these findings. As a whole, all three objectives were realized by using validated subjective and objective measures of naturalistic nighttime sleep and experimental daytime sleep. We investigated the complex role of sleep in making risk-related decisions, and the associated electrophysiological and neuropsychological moderators and mediators, through the support of this project grant.

17612015.label: Major findings and research outcome
17612015.value: In the original proposal, we stated five hypotheses for testing. We are listing them below, as well as the findings and research outcome pertaining to those hypotheses. H1: individuals with habitual short sleep duration would have worse risk-related decision-making ability than those with normal sleep duration, and such association would be related to the discrepancies of their subjective sleep need and habitual sleep duration In support of H1, individual’s baseline sleep need and sleep duration interacted in predicting risk-related decision making. Individuals with high sleep need but short sleep duration showed more risk-taking behaviors (Lau*, Wong, Rusak, et al., in press) H2: the Nap group would have improved risk-related decision-making ability compared to the No-nap group H3: the napping effects would be moderated by their habitual sleep duration and sleep need H4: the benefits of daytime napping on risk-related decision-making would be associated with polysomnographic (PSG) features (e.g. duration and latency of rapid eye movement sleep and slow wave sleep) In support of H2 and H4, our data suggested that a 90-min midday sleep opportunity reduced the risk of impulsive decision making among young adults. Risk-related Impulsive decision making after a sleep opportunity was correlated with features of sleep spindles in central region during the nap, suggesting a role for this sleep feature in modulating the executive and other functions involved in risk-related decision making. In relations to H3, our data showed that habitual sleep duration and sleep need did not moderate the impact of napping effect on risk-related impulsive decision-making. H5: the effect of short sleep duration and daytime sleep on risk-related decision-making ability would be mediated by other neuropsychological functions (e.g., working memory, vigilance). Our experimental data showed that youth generally exhibited worse vigilance with increased impulsive decision-making tendency throughout the day. However, when given a short sleep opportunity, youths displayed a profile of maintained decision-making tendency with improved vigilance. However, working memory and vigilance does not seem to mediate the effect of short sleep duration and daytime sleep on risk-related decision-making ability. Instead, we identified a moderating role of depressed mood on the napping effects on risk-related decision-making ability. The data suggest a sub-optimal punishment learning in risky decision making among individuals with depressed mood, which appeared to have improved and comparable to those without depressed mood after a daytime nap.

17612015.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17612015.value: With respect to the moderators and mediators involved in the napping effects on risk-related decision-making, so far we have investigated how depressed mood may moderate the impacts of a daytime nap on risky decision making. Our findings pave the way to investigate the potential mechanisms underlying the associations. We are currently preparing another manuscript in this direction of investigation, examining the moderating role of depressed moods on the napping effects (findings of H5). In addition, whereas the sample in the current study consisted of mainly healthy youths, our findings provided foundation for further research to be conducted in populations with mood conditions to further elucidate the complex role of sleep in risky decision making. Further, post-nap performance was measured only once so it remained unknown whether learning and improvement might take place after a longer period of time post-nap, or with repeated naps in subsequent days and be correlated with sleep physiology. Studies assessing the impact of different nighttime sleep patterns (e.g. short versus long sleepers, insomniac versus good sleepers) on changes in decision making during daytime sleep would help determine if any specific population might benefit more after daytime sleep.

17612015.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17612015.value: This research project adopted a multi-method approach in measuring sleep and its functional outcomes to investigate the role and interplay of nighttime and daytime sleep in making risk-related decisions, as well as the moderators and mediators of the relationships. Results from the research indicated a correlation between more variable sleep timing and increased risk taking. Young adults sleeping less than 6 hours nightly coupled with high perceived sleep need were also more likely to take risks. Additionally, a 90-minute midday sleep opportunity reduced the risk of impulsive decision making among young adults. The benefits of daytime napping on risk-related decision-making was associated with features of sleep spindles during the nap, suggesting a role for this sleep feature in modulating the executive and other functions involved in decision making. Our data suggested that individual difference in sleep-wake behaviors, including sleep need, sleep-wake timing and duration are important factors that interplay in affecting risky decision making among young adults; sleep health education in college should include promotion of regularity of sleep-wake timing in addition to adequate sleep duration and quality sleep.

17612215.value: 本研究的目的是分析及評估從香港的自由幹預主義系統轉移補貼性住房政策至屬市場化社會主義系統的深圳的可能性，來促進住房比較學的住房政策轉移性的理論構建，及提高兩城市可負擔住房政策的績效。1997年的亞洲金融風暴及2008年的全球金融風暴曾引致亞洲主要經濟體系對補貼性住房政策作出重大修改。在此過程中，參考其他國家的經驗是必走的一步。中國的中央政府曾宣佈要在第十二個五年計劃（2011-2015）內興建三千六百萬個保障性住房來解決因經濟發展而引致的住房負擔能力問題，並要求各城市的政府向外地學習，特別是香港及新加坡。但是，在住房比較學的文獻中，政策的可轉移性及政策的轉移過程鮮有討論。這空隙急需填補，以便促進有效的政策轉移，及增進政策轉移的理論的討論以豐富住房比較學的文獻。研究香港補貼性住房轉移至深圳的可能性，並以兩地政府對住房市場幹預的分異作爲研究基礎，是實行這類研究的一個好開端。 此研究的理論概念將引用政策研究學的政策轉移理論及其分析工具。首先，本研究會找出現時香港與深圳的補貼性住房政策的異同來確定2011年中央政府的指引有否帶來政策轉移。跟著，兩地政策的異同會從幾方面來解釋。首先會研究香港住房政策環境的可複製性及相容性，及深圳的政策環境，旨在鑒定影響政策轉移的宏觀及中觀限制及機會。跟著研究的是深圳複製香港有關的政策環境的能力及意欲。最後，會研究深圳對於轉移香港政策的考慮，對政策模式的優先選擇，及轉移政策的過程等，以便能解釋深圳現行的住房補貼政策及績效。此研究引用的二手資料主要是政府報告及統計資料，學術論文及專業期刊等。一手資料則包括實地考察、訪問政府官員、研究員及與住房有關的專業人士等。 在理論的層面，由於本研究建基於政策轉移的概念並引用豐富的佐證，將會對自由幹預主義系統及市場化社會主義系統的住房政策可轉移性做出貢獻。這項研究意義重大，因爲政策學的有關理論會被首次借用，應用，及測試於一項大型的住房研究項目。由是，此研究的理論和分析構架及成果將對以後住房政策轉移的研究有重大的參考價值。在實踐方面，此研究將對中國政府希望借鑒香港房屋政策的意向是否適合及有用做出驗證。廣義來説，此研究亦會對其他有意引用香港住房政策的政府有所幫助。同樣的，本研究所構建的相容性及能力性研究方法及研究成果將會幫助政府明白如何依據城市的特性來考慮他地的政策轉移。

17612215.label: Realisation of objectives
17612215.value: Objective 1: To establish the extent of subsidized policy transfer from Hong Kong to Shenzhen since 2011 by investigating the convergence and divergence in policy trends. The convergence and divergence in subsidized housing policy design and approaches in Hong Kong and Shenzhen since 2011 were ascertained according to the conceptual framework. Field trips to Shenzhen were conducted in March and April 2017. Discussion sessions and interviews were undertaken with leading officials of the Shenzhen Municipality Housing and Construction Bureau and Shenzhen Land and Planning Bureau, Director of the Shenzhen Real Estate Research Centre, and the former Head of the Department of Urban Planning, Shenzhen University. Field trips to housing estates of different types were also made, and discussion with officials and property managers during the site visits were also useful. Secondary data were collected by reviewing academic and government publications and the websites of related government websites. By applying the analytical framework in the project proposal to the data collected from Shenzhen and Hong Kong, it was found that from the 1990’s to mid-2000’s, Shenzhen adopted and adapted Hong Kong’s model of a dual-track and three-level housing system. But since then Shenzhen’s subsidized housing policy and diversity of programs have gone significantly beyond that of Hong Kong, though the subsidized housing stock is only one-third of that of Hong Kong. Shenzhen also covers a much wider spectrum of income groups, but its policy focus on ‘talents’ in fact resembles the economic function of Hong Kong’s public rental housing program in the 1960’s and 1970’s. While similarly owning two major factors of housing production – land ownership and development right – Shenzhen uses more market sources and tools to provide subsidized housing. Overall, the intricate interplay of market principles and forces with state authority and resources marks the major difference between Hong Kong’s model of liberal interventionist with Shenzhen’s marketized socialist regime. Objectives 2: To explain the extent of policy transfer by investigating the compatibility of the subsidized housing policy contexts between Hong Kong and Shenzhen. The interviews and discussion sessions were useful in understanding compatibility of the subsidized housing policy contexts between Hong Kong and Shenzhen. Government documents especially the announcement of various subsidized housing schemes provide useful information about policy targets and why. Research materials presented by the Shenzhen Real Estate Research Centre during the interviews and the invitation to give expert opinion to the policy paper to be submitted to the Central Government provided useful contextual information. The compatibility framework of the project proposal was used to interpret information and data collected from these activities. Policy contexts accounted for the weakening transferability of policy design and measures between the two cities. Given the differences in the developmental stage, socio-political situation, demographic structure and residency issues, the thrust of the subsidized housing policy differs, with Hong Kong giving increasing attention to social and political functions of housing policy since the early 1970’s, and Shenzhen on economic functions. Thus, the scale of subsidized housing programs, allocation priority, tenancy policy inevitably differ. The compatibility of policy contexts affected the desirability of Shenzhen to borrow housing policy design from Hong Kong. Objectives 3: To further explain the extent of policy transfer by assessing Shenzhen’s capability and desire to replicate the policy environment of Hong Kong’s subsidized housing policies. The policy environment analytical framework of the project proposal was used to analyse the policy environment data collected from interviews, government documents and research materials collected as described above. It was found that in terms of total land area, sources of developable land, usable government land, efficiency in the planning process, Shenzhen is more favourable than Hong Kong in enhancing housing production. However, in terms of advancing housing conditions and quantity through improving land utility efficiency, enhancing land value by improving infrastructure and connectivity, upgrading urban landscape quality, and instituting a more participatory mode of governance in the planning process, Hong Kong may have more experience to share with Shenzhen, though Shenzhen’s desirability to take on this may not be strong at this stage of its development. The model of financing housing subsidy bears greater resemblance between Hong Kong and Shenzhen as both governments own land and development rights, which are the fundamental resources affecting the capability for housing subsidy provision. The difference is, on top of these fundamental resources, how the roles of the state and market play out to best utilize these resources. While the self-finance model of Hong Kong has proven to be practicable and effective in the past three decades, Shenzhen’s multiple nexuses between the government and market enterprises, and the newly established state-owned non-profitable housing company are in the making of marketized socialist models effective in delivering housing subsidy to the needy families and to social groups needed for economic and social development. Objective 4: To identify critical concerns in the transferability consideration process that have affected the policy choice and the subsequent performance of the transferred policy. In addition to the information and data collected as described for Objective 1, 2 and 3, the PI was invited by a consultancy company of Shenzhen to comment on their study reports proposing subsidized housing programs to two district governments. The review and discussion with the lead researcher of the two studies provided chances for the PI to understand their concerns of transferring the Hong Kong experience. This study finds that the two analytical frameworks proposed in the project proposal were able to identify the critical concerns in the transferability consideration process. Only minor amendments were made to the proposed frameworks in the actual analyses. The critical concerns in examining the compatibility of the policy contexts are the changing societal functions of the subsidized housing policy, the planning and design of residential forms, and housing culture and livability (revised from socio-cultural habits of housing consumption). Replicability of the policy environment components are land policy, planning policy, housing finance and subsidy (revised from subsidy policy) and governance policy. Objective 5: To pioneer conceptual constructs for explaining and evaluating housing policy transferability across a liberal interventionist and a marketized socialist housing system under the ‘one country, two systems’ context. Overall, this study proposes that transferability of housing policy between different housing regimes may work at the initial stage. But as the policy reform deepens, institutional and ideological differences may give rise to different policy measures and policy priorities and targets, especially if the transferring and the transferred cities or countries are at different stages of development, giving rise to different policy contexts. Policy environment has important implications for capability and desirability to borrow external experiences, especially the extent of government possession of fundamental factors of production. On top of these fundamental factors, the institutional ability of the government to effectively use these resources and the allowance of the political and economic ideology to maximize the use of market forces to co-provide housing subsidy to achieve housing and non-housing objectives are crucial in the consideration of housing policy transfer.

17612215.label: Major findings and research outcome
17612215.value: From 1990’s to mid-2000’s, Shenzhen adopted and adapted Hong Kong’s model of a dual-track and three-level housing system. But since then Shenzhen’s subsidized housing policy and diversity of programs have gone significantly beyond that of Hong Kong, though the scale of subsidized housing is only one-third of Hong Kong. Government involvement takes a different form in the liberal-interventionist model of Hong Kong, by which the subsidized housing sector clearly demarcates itself away from the private sector (#8(1), 8(2), 9(1)). In Shenzhen’s marketized socialist system, the government controls the production factors of land and development right, but opens the sources of finance to the market. It also controls provision right and decision of market players (#8(3), 8(4)). What is most notable is the setting up of a state-owned enterprise operating on market principles to produce and provide subsidized housing combining market efficiency with state power and support (#8(4). Policy contexts also accounts for the weakening transferability of policy design and measures. Given the differences in the developmental stage, socio-political situation, demographic structure and residency issues, the thrust of the subsidized housing policy differs, with Hong Kong giving increasing attention to social and political functions of housing policy since the early 1970’s, and Shenzhen on economic functions (#8(2),8(4),9(2)). The policy environment directly affects capability to borrow external housing experience. As a bigger city spatially and with a rural hinterland, Shenzhen owns more natural resources. Its less open planning process with stronger government steer also enables more efficient delivery of land for housing development. However, a more participatory mode of urban governance and planning governance may be needed to improve urban quality and livability, as proven in the case of Hong Kong after 1997 (#8(2),8(4)). The model of financing housing subsidy bears greater resemblance between Hong Kong and Shenzhen as both governments own land and development rights, which are the fundamental resources affecting the capability for housing subsidy provision. The difference is, on top of these fundamental resources, how the roles of the state and market play out to best utilize these resources (#8(1),8(4)). Overall, the study argues that transferability of housing policy between different housing regimes may work at the initial stage. But as the policy reform deepens, institutional and ideological differences may give rise to different policy measures and policy priorities and targets, especially if the involved cities are at different stages of development, giving rise to different policy contexts (#8(4)).

17612215.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17612215.value: The research can be developed by investigating the transferability of similar housing regimes but of similar stages of economic, social and urban development such as England and Hong Kong, both of which are liberal interventionist system but with different extent of government intervention to the housing market, Vietnam and China with different levels of marketization within a socialist state. The research can also be extended to investigate transferability between other housing regimes such as the social democratic systems of Sweden/Germany and free market systems of the U.S. and Taiwan. These investigations will enrich the concepts and theories of policy transfer generally, and housing policy specifically, contributing to comparative (housing) policy study and actual government policy making.

17612215.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17612215.value: This study aims to enrich the application of policy transfer concepts to strengthen the ‘lesson borrowing’ research in comparative housing studies, by analysing the transferability of liberal-interventionist Hong Kong’s subsidized housing policy to the neighbouring marketized socialist Shenzhen. It argues that transferring housing policy between different housing regimes may work initially. But as the policy reform deepens, institutional and ideological differences may give rise to different policy measures and policy priorities and targets, especially if the stages of development of the two cities differ, incurring different policy contexts and policy aims. At the implementation level, policy environment has important implications for capability and desirability to borrow external experiences, especially crucial are government possession of fundamental factors of production, government’s ability to effectively use these resources, and the extent that political and economic ideologies allow the use of market forces to co-provide housing subsidy to achieve housing and non-housing objectives.

17612315.value: To evaluate whether proportionality is a valid moral principle in criminal punishment
rows: To evaluate whether proportionality is a valid moral principle in criminal punishment

17612315.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17612315.value: 本研究旨在探討“刑事處罰相稱”是否是道德上正確的原則。刑事處罰相稱，是指刑罰的輕重應取決於罪行的嚴重性(而罪行的嚴重性取決於罪行所做成的傷害及犯人犯案時的心態及動機) 。 刑事處罰相稱原則在香港及其他很多地方也是判刑的重要考慮因素之一。很多人也認為它是的道德上正確的：很多人認為把一個小偷處以終身監禁及向連環殺人犯處以輕微罰款是道德上不正確的。然而，這觀點是正確的嗎？如是，它的理由為何？文獻對這問題並沒有一致性的答案。本項目旨在對此作出深入探討。

17612315.label: Realisation of objectives
17612315.value: The objective of this two-year project is “to evaluate whether proportionality is a valid moral principle in criminal punishment”, and I believe the objective has been satisfactorily realized. Let me begin by outlining the background of my project. Traditionally, the benefit-fairness theory, which appeals to some alleged benefits received by the offender, and the expressive theory, which appeals to expressive concerns, are the most prominent justifications for proportionate punishment. The two theories have been subjected to heavy (and what many people would regard to be decisive) criticisms. However, the two traditional theories have received recent enthusiastic defences in the literature. Moreover, theories which appeal neither to the benefits received by the offender nor expressive concerns have recently been offered to justify proportionate punishment. My project, accordingly, proceeds through a critical engagement with the recent developments in punishment theory in order to explore whether such developments can ultimately help to justify proportionate punishment. My focus, in particular, is on the theories which have not been answered satisfactorily in the literature yet. My conclusion is that we do not have good reasons to accept proportionality. For clarity of exposition, my project may be divided into two main parts: first, a consideration of whether the recent innovative defences of the two traditional theories can satisfactorily answer the existing objections to them and thus ground proportionate punishment; and second, a consideration of whether there are good defences for proportionate punishment other than the benefit-fairness theory and the expressive theory. Concerning the first part of my project, I have considered the recent defence of the expressive theory by Christopher Bennett and the recent defence of the benefit-fairness theory by Zachery Hoskins. In my view, each of these improves upon the traditional theories in original ways. But I have argued, nonetheless, they are ultimately unsuccessful. My discussion of Bennett’s expressive theory is published as “Bennett’s Expressive Justification of Punishment” in Criminal Law and Philosophy (Rank A journal by the Australian Research Council) and my discussion of Hoskins’s theory is published as “Hoskins’s New Benefit-Fairness Theory of Punishment” in Criminal Law and Philosophy. Concerning the second part of my project, I have examined, amongst others, the justification of punishment that appeals to the loss (such loss need not be material) suffered by the victim rather than the benefits received by the offender. A version of loss-based justification of proportionate punishment has been recently offered (independently) by Daniel McDermott, Richard Lippke and Göran Duus-Otterström. I have considered two variations of the loss-based theory, and I have found both of them to be unsuccessful. My discussion of the loss-based theory is published as “Loss-Based Retributive Justifications of Punishment” in the Oxford Journal of Legal Studies (Rank A* journal by the Australian Research Council). I consider the objective of my project to have been successfully realized because of three reasons. First, my project has considered the most promising recent defences of proportionate punishment and provided original critiques of them. Second, I promised “three to four journal articles in top-tier journals” in my grant proposal as output for the project. I believe the publications arising out of the project satisfy the criteria since the Oxford Journal of Legal Studies is one of the best-regarded generalist law journals and Criminal Law and Philosophy is one of the top specialist journals in my field. Third, I promised to prepare an elective course on punishment theory as educational outcome. I have submitted the course proposal (as a complete revamping of the dormant course “Punishment and Society”) to the HKU Law Department in 2017, which has been approved. (Originally the elective course would be offered in 2017-18, but it is delayed because my co-teacher on the Criminal Law compulsory course is on leave during the first semester of 2017-18 so I spent all my teaching hours this year teaching Criminal Law.)

17612315.label: Major findings and research outcome
17612315.value: The major finding of this project is that we do not have adequate reasons to accept proportionality in criminal punishment, as none of the recent important attempts to rescue proportionate punishment from objections works. In particular, Hoskins’s recent defence of the benefit-fairness theory, Bennett’s recent defence of the expressive theory, and the loss-based theory offered (independently) by Daniel McDermott, Richard Lippke and Göran Duus-Otterström have been carefully considered and are found to be unsuccessful.

17612315.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17612315.value: There are two main possible further developments. The first is to consider justifications for proportionate punishment that are not considered in this project. While the most promising justifications for proportionate punishment recently offered in the literature have been, I believe, considered in this project, it is of course possible that new theories (or new developments of existing theories) may be offered in the future. The second is to consider how the Hong Kong sentencing system should be restructured if proportionality is no longer regarded as a valid consideration in sentencing. The issue of how to structure a sentencing system without regard to proportionality has of course been considered in the literature before, but I think it is fair to say that most of the contributions are not about Hong Kong in particular. If the amount of appropriate punishment is determined not by proportionality but instead by empirical concerns such as deterrence, then given that empirical circumstances vary amongst places, findings about other places need not be directly applicable to Hong Kong and Hong Kong must, to quote from Quentin Skinner, “do our thinking for ourselves” (Visions of Politics, 88).

17612315.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17612315.value: The aim of this project is to consider whether proportionality in criminal punishment, i.e. the idea that the severity of punishment should depend on the seriousness of the crime, is justified. The proportionality principle is quite intuitive. It has also been regarded as a valid sentencing principle in most jurisdictions including Hong Kong. That said, the justification for the principle remains elusive as the traditional justifications offered for it in the literature have been subjected to criticisms which many would regard decisive. Recently, however, enthusiastic new defences for the principle have been offered in the literature. This project considers whether they work. This project has found that none of the recent defences for proportionate punishment can withstand critical scrutiny. Therefore, in absence of further defences for proportionate punishment, we should accept the (perhaps counter-intuitive) conclusion that there is not always a reason (not even a defeasible one) to make the punishment fit the crime. Given that proportionality is an entrenched principle in our sentencing system, it is important, as a matter of justice, to question whether it is really morally valid. If I am right that proportionality cannot be justified, then we should rationally reform the system such that it is instead structured by other considerations.

17613415.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17613415.value: Mongolia is facing a critical moment in its urban evolution. The economic reforms following Soviet withdrawal in 1990 coupled with the discovery of vast reserves of coal, gold, and copper led to massive rural migration to the capital city: Ulaanbataar. Predicted GDP growth rates of 17% in 2011 and the promise of development projects lead nomadic herdsman to sell their livestock and move to the city in search of a better life. The population of the city doubled since 1989 and city’s territory expanded from 130km2 to 4700 km2. The extremely cold winter (zud) in 2010 that killed many livestock sealed the fate of many, leaving them little choice other than to move to the city. The nomads settle on any available land, occupying residual inner areas, slopes and the periphery of the city. When migrants arrive they erect a traditional felt tent - a ger - and surround the plot with a wooden fence. The extent and rapidity of their growth has meant that the provision of the most basic services of urban life has not been viable: water is fetched from kiosks; pit latrines are dug on site; and garbage goes uncollected. Coal smog hovers throughout the city during the winter as ger residents burn fuel to stay warm. As this population has no prior experience living amongst others - there is no word for “community” in Mongolian - or in situ, in one home on a single plot of land, other problems ensue such as solid waste disposal and a consideration of shared public space. Compounding these issues is widespread unemployment, alcoholism and health problems. Unlike other informal settlements in developing countries, these districts are not illegal as each new migrant, as a Mongolian national, has the right to land ownership. However, they are still stigmatized as problem areas - effectively slums - that are seen as a hindrance to Ulaanbaatar’s evolution into a “modern” capital. This project seeks to understand the spatial characteristics of this unique rural-urban fringe as a unique example of informal settlements. Through the research, the aim is to develop innovative architectural prototypes that can contribute to the integration of the Ger districts into a viable urban construct. Through this methodology the aim is to create an alternative urban model of development for “slum” areas, other than wholesale demolition. 外蒙古现在正面临着城市发展的关键时刻。因为1990年苏联撤出，加上国家发现了煤炭，黄金，和铜的储量，所以导致了大量的牧民迁移到蒙古首都：乌兰巴托。 2011 年的预测国内生产总值达到了17%，而城里的开发项目也预计增加。因此，游牧牧民为了寻求更好的生活，都纷纷卖掉了自己的牲畜，迁移到城市。 自1989年来，乌兰巴托的人口已增加了一倍，而城市面积也从130平方公里增加到4700平方公里。2010年，一个极度寒冷的冬天 (zud) 杀掉了很多畜生，使更多牧民别无选择地迁移到城市里。 游牧民迁移到城市时，会选择在任何可用的土地定居，例如：在城中的剩余区域，斜坡，或者城市外围。决定了定居地方后，牧民会在空地里建立一个传统的蒙古包 (ger)，而且会用木栅栏围着空地。这种定居地增加得又快又广，令城市没法供应基本的生活设施: 水要从储水亭取，坑式厕所直接在现场挖，垃圾也没人来收。在冬天，煤炭造成的烟雾覆盖着整个城市，因为住在蒙古包里的居民要烧炭取暖。新迁移到乌兰巴托的牧民都没有跟其他人一起住的经验 - 蒙古话里没有“社区”这个词 - 也没有长期在一个地方定居的习惯。这个情况导致了很多问题，例如：固体废物要处置，和对公共空间的考虑。这些问题可以带来失业，酗酒和健康问题。 这些“蒙古包区”(ger areas) 是跟其他发展中国家的贫民窟有区别的，因为在这些地区里建的房子是没有违法的。在乌兰巴托定居的每一位移民者，作为一个蒙古人，都拥有土地所有权。尽管如此，蒙古包区仍然是被视为问题区域，普众也会觉得它会令乌兰巴托难以成为一个“现代”城市。 这个项目旨在了解蒙古包区这个城村结合中的空间特征，也视它为一个独特的非正式定居点。此研究的最终目标是设计能够帮助“蒙古包区”与城市融合的创新建筑原型。通过这种研究方法，我们希望可以找到完全拆除“贫民窟”以外的城市发展方法。

17613415.label: Realisation of objectives
17613415.value: Objective 1 The spatial characteristics of the ger districts were documented through site surveys, conducting over 80 household visits resulting in the creation of plan and sectional drawings of people’s homes and gers. This demonstrated how each family made incremental changes to their plot including modifications to the ger, adding a kitchen building, storage unit or constructing a small house. Additionally, the majority of houses did not have internal sanitation facilities. (Report Section 1B, Survey Drawings) Interviews from 19 families in Chingeltei-16 and Sukhbaatar-16 provided a detailed understanding of when people moved to the city, exchanges with their rural relatives, and their daily and weekly movements between the ger districts and the city. These findings are documented in the Report (Section 1B, Interview Analysis) and in the journal article ’“Settling the Nomads”, Joshua Bolchover in Designing the Rural: A Global Countryside in Flux, Architectural Design Series, Wiley London, 2016’ that describes how the spatial characteristics of the ger districts reflect the process of assimilation from nomadic to sedentary life as well as introducing and conceptualising Objectives 3 and 4. To understand the personal geographies of the residents, six families were selected to be interviewed and their everyday lives’ documented through a series of videos produced in collaboration with Dulguun Bayasgalan. These were exhibited as “Ger District Portraits” as part of “Settling the Nomads”, 2016 Venice Biennale and “City of Nomads” as part of “Fear and Love: Reactions to a Complex World” at the inaugural exhibition at the Design Museum, London. Objective 2 By comparing google earth imagery with our own drone footage of three sites that are representative of urban, mid, and fringe scenarios, we were able to investigate patterns of growth in the urban fabric over a 8 year period, from 2009-2017. A total of 24 maps were drawn (documented in the Report Section 1C, District Transformation). These gave us both a spatial and empirical understanding, through comparative data sets, on the transformation process of the ger districts. The process of transformation was drawn and published in the journal paper “Seeding the City in Ulaanbaatar’s Ger Districts: Urbanisation from the Inside-out”, Monu No. 27 Small Urbanism, Bruil, Netherlands, which also introduces a new model of informal settlement upgrading (Objective 4). This knowledge of the process of transformation of the ger districts enabled us to compare it with examples of informal urban growth in sample sites of Paraisopolis, Brazil and Baishizhou, Shenzhen. Comparative drawings were produced to illustrate the analysed information about the different typologies and position the ger districts as a unique example given the security of land tenure that is not present in the other examples of “informal” settlement. (Report Section 1D, Informal Settlement - Typology) This was also presented in a series of invited lectures and panel discussions including “Designing for Contraditions Part 1” The University of Delft, Rural Urban Framework: Incremental Urbanism, Ulaanbaatar's Ger Settlements, Settling the Nomads, Scarcity: Meetings on Architecture”, Venice Biennale Event, Sept 2016. Each lecture positioned the ger district as a unique typology of informal settlement based on the spatial characteristics and process of urban growth. Objective 3 Research obtained for Objectives 1 and 2, supported the argument for an incremental strategy as it would harness the existing process of development in the ger districts. Based on the findings from the interviews, 10 prototypes were conceived to address their most pressing needs. The feasibility of the designs was tested with stakeholders during three community workshops in February 2016, March 2017, and July 2018 involving over 50 local residents, 36 students, the NGO GerHub, M.A.D, and the Institute of Engineering and Technology in Mongolia (Report Section 2B, Prototype Testing). Two prototypes were selected to be implemented in the ger districts. The Ger Plug-in addresses the need for affordable housing with decentralised infrastructure in the fringe districts, and the Ger Innovation Hub (currently under construction) provides community infrastructure for public meetings and events (Report Section 2C, Selected Prototypes). The need for community resources within the incremental strategy was presented in ‘Incremental Urbanism. Enabling Common Good in Ulaanbaatar’, Common Good, New South Books, MAAS Media, March 2018. As part of the development process, we tested structural and spatial ideas through 1:1 tectonic prototypes at 3 exhibitions– “Settling the Nomads” at la Biennale di Venezia, “City of Nomads” at The Design Museum, London, and “Ger District Hub” at the Museum for Applied Arts and Sciences, Sydney. The details between the existing timber structure of the ger and modern timber construction, developed in the research for the exhibitions, were applied in the construction of the Ger Plug-In. This innovation allowed the two central columns of the ger to be removed allowing the ger to be extended for new uses. Each of the exhibitions also disseminated research outcomes from Objective 1 and 4. Three incremental strategies addressing the three different site conditions were developed after evaluating the prototypes through feedback sessions and open-house events (Objective 3). A scenario for each was drawn and projected over time to demonstrate how the urban ecology would be altered. The conference paper “Incremental Urbanism: Designing a Resilient Urban Strategy for the Ger Districts of Ulaanbaatar.” 11th International Forum on Urbanism (IFoU) Congress 2018” presented these findings alongside a mechanism for implementation by accessing low interest mortgages through the Green Climate Fund. (Report: Executive Summary). Objective 4 In order to understand current development strategies for the ger districts, we mapped both top down plans led by the Asian Development Bank and the municipality of Ulaanbaatar and bottom up strategies by NGOs and local district governors, which can be found in the Report (Section 1E, Existing Initiatives). The identification of a need to engage a more agile strategy for the fringe districts that was not being addressed by either current top or bottom down plans, became the driver for our proposal, and was discussed in the journal article “Seeding the City in Ulaanbaatar’s Ger Districts: Urbanisation from the Inside-out”, Monu No. 27 Small Urbanism, Bruil, Netherlands. This knowledge was disseminated in a meeting with 17 stakeholders and experts at the Ger Plug-in prototype to discuss the potential impact of the proposed upgrading strategy. Attendees included the CEO of Mongolia’s largest bank, the Canadian Development Bank, eco-banking divisions of local banks, private equity investors, the Environment, Science, and Health Officer of the US Embassy, representatives from UNICEF, GIZ, Novaterra, Engie Mongolia, and the President of the Institute of Engineering and Technology in Mongolia. An implementation plan was developed following these meetings and presented in “Incremental Urbanism: Designing a Resilient Urban Strategy for the Ger Districts of Ulaanbaatar.” 11th International Forum on Urbanism (IFoU) Congress 2018.” Furthermore, it was presented to key stakeholders such as Gerhub, Gund Investment, Xac Bank, and the Mongolian Sustainable Finance Association in October 2018. The Report titled “Incremental Urbanism: Ulaanbaatar’s Ger Districts” which includes the realisation of all the objectives, architectural prototypes, knowledge on informal settlement upgrading and, the incremental urban strategy has been disseminated in December 2018 to organizations such as the Asian Development Bank, Xac Bank, Lorinet Foundation, Geres, Clean Energy Asia LLC, and JICA Mongolia, which were followed by a series of meetings held in January 2019.

17613415.label: Major findings and research outcome
17613415.value: The research revealed that: over time ger districts densify without improvements to infrastructure through a process of subdivision; proposed city masterplans and certain initiatives by the Asian Development Bank have been difficult to implement; and that the extent of the problems in the ger districts including lack of infrastructure, air pollution and lack of civic services is not only severe, but growing each year. A comprehensive research report compiled this information including: Base mapping: A series of maps located existing development initiatives, formal and informal infrastructure. Archival information of the historical transformation of Ulaanbaatar was collected showing how the city’s administrative territory has expanded to over 30 times its original size and the urban population has doubled since the 1990 democratic revolution. Ger district analysis: By drawing the transformation of the change in urban morphology from 2009-2017 in Chingeltei-16 and Sukhbaatar-16, we demonstrated that the central, mid and fringe typologies, which equate to different densities and housing types, exist within single khoroos. Both Chingeltei-16 and Sukhbaatar-16 are densifying through sub-division. This process was compared to examples of urban growth in sample sites of Paraisopolis, Brazil and Baishizhou, Shenzhen to understand the ger district as a unique example of an informal settlement. Stakeholder and resident interviews: Interviews and stakeholder meetings (engaging over 170 local residents and 35 stakeholders) were conducted to understand the personal geographies of residents. Prototype designs were initiated and two were selected for further development and presented to residents, community leaders and NGOs. Assessment of current masterplans for the ger districts: The Asian Development Bank working with the Municipality of Ulaanbaatar and the Government of Mongolia is the main agent for ger district redevelopment. However, many ger district inhabitants are situated outside of the geographical development boundary and so will be unaffected by these initiatives. As the fringe is growing by 35,000 residents per year, it is essential that a strategy can be developed for these areas. Incremental urban strategy: Based on these findings, an incremental urban strategy was defined including: - a strategy to develop shared infrastructure between resident families - a design for an affordable housing prototype based on plugging into a traditional ger - a design for a community hub to support community needs - a proposal to provide access to low interest mortgages through the Green Climate Fund - a holistic strategy to decrease reliance on coal and thereby improve air quality.

17613415.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17613415.value: The project concluded that there is a current gap in ger district development strategies for the outer, fringe settlements. The aim of further research is to develop the guidelines from the incremental strategy into a manual for implementation for these areas. The objective is to provide a mechanism for residents to develop their land themselves to create a more sustainable community with access to infrastructure and reduced air pollution. The proposed course of action is to create a baseline study into the current thermal performance of each household coupled with their consumption of water, electricity and coal, in order to specify, size, and cost the required infrastructure necessary to upgrade a four plot fringe site. Designs for housing and community components will be created to devise a menu of options for residents to choose how they wish to develop their land. Each of these designs will be audited to meet the criteria, including environmental standards, so they can be accepted by banks and other mortgage lenders. This way we can provide residents access to financial tools to implement the construction of affordable and sustainable homes with access to infrastructure and improved community provision.

17613415.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17613415.value: Over 70% of the population of Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia live in the Ger Districts –settlements made of traditional felt tents and single story houses. The majority of this population do not have centrally supplied water, heating or sewers. The very cold winters mean that each ger district household uses around 3.8 tonnes of unrefined coal as their main heating source, producing some of the highest levels of air pollution worldwide, with ger districts experiencing winter PM2.5 concentrations more than 100 times the World Health Organization 24-hour guideline. The research analyses the spatial characteristics of these areas and understands how they are formed to position the districts as a significant case study of an “informal settlement”. Using that knowledge, an incremental upgrading strategy has been proposed to provide an alternative model for ger district redevelopment that has been shared with stakeholders including the Asian Development Bank; local mortgage providers; and NGOs. If taken up as a model for upgrading it has the potential to impact thousands of people in the ger districts. As the ger district phenomenon is not just specific to Ulaanbaatar, but exists in every urban area of Mongolia, it could have widespread ramifications for the entire country.

17613515.label: Project Objectives
17613515.value: To examine the process through which public interest lawyers develop a legal community with shared mission, identity and interest; To study the extent to which public interest lawyers are able to build bridges with the respective civil society organizations and establish a stable and mutually benefiting relationship with those communities that lawyers regularly represent; To explore the interaction between the community of public interest lawyers and the legislature, government agencies and in particular the courts; To study the mechanisms through which public interest lawyers mobilize themselves in limiting arbitrary powers; and To place the development of Chinese public interest lawyers in a larger comparative context of East Asia with a particular focus on the experiences of Taiwan's legal development during Taiwan's democratic transition.

17613515.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17613515.value: Chinese public interest lawyers are well known for being brave but lone fighters. Can they put aside their individual differences and work collectively as a community? Can they build a legal complex (Halliday and Karpik, 1997; 2007) for the rule of law? This proposed research aims to identify the circumstances in which Chinese public interest lawyers can develop a common professional identity and advance their collective interest and explore the multidimensional process in which lawyers build trust. After the 2010-2011 repressive episode against human rights lawyers in China, most of those lawyers have adopted different strategies. They have toned down their political rhetoric and meet some of their less politicized colleagues mid-way who, shocked by the wanton abuse of power on the part of the state, act collectively in defending the rule of law. What united the two groups of lawyers is a profound professional agenda: lawyers, because of their education and nature of their work, share a common identity and objectives. There is of course instrumental value for lawyers to act together— “to keep warm by getting together”— because lawyers are vulnerable in what they do in China. Building trust and working in cooperation are the best survival strategies in China’s hostile legal environment. Beyond the instrumental value, however, the professional identity and common interest provide a strong thread to tie lawyers together. Professionalism matters tremendously in the formation of a legal community in China. Based on this common identity and shared interest, and in pursuit of the same objectives of rule of law and accountable government, lawyers are reaching out to each other and increasingly cooperating in high-impact cases. They are also reaching out to other civil society organizations, to either search for mutual support or to extend their influence. And, finally, they are linking up with institutional actors, courts in particular, through dialogue. There is not yet a legal complex in China in which legally trained lawyers—broadly defined to include lawyers, judges, and prosecutors, among others—can form a liberal-leaning alliance in fighting for a more limited state and a larger realm of freedom. This proposed research seeks to explore the possibility for lawyers to build such a complex with public interest law as an entry point and a catalyst. 中国的公益律师通常被誉为勇敢的侠士， 但他们能否摒弃自己的个人喜好或成见，而努力去构造一个能通过法律去限制公权力的公益律师共同体？本项研究旨从比较的视角去探索中国公益律师形成其职业认同和发展自身共同利益的主客观环境、以及他们共建互信的多重过程。本项目着重研究公益律师发展的三个不同层面： 1）不同类型的公益律师之间相互了解、沟通和支持；特别是公益律师“抱团取暖”的工作方式； 2）公益律师和公民社会组织多元的、相互支持和依赖的关系；3）律师和权力机关之间复杂的互动。

17613515.label: Major findings and research outcome
17613515.value: Legal advocacy and activism are possible in authoritarian states because the regimes' need for law and legality to provide political legitimacy, promote economic growth, and improve governance. As long as that foundational need remains, law is relevant and meaningful and lawyers have some political space for meaningful engagement in courts and other public spaces. China’s Party-state follows a legal reform path, as it does in both rhetoric and, to a limited degree, practices, it remains possible for lawyers, together with other civil society actors, to retain and grow their political and legal space to advocate for changes. Legal profession is both politically embedded and politically challenging. According to the prevailing conceptualization, the legal profession can be as profit-driven as business and serve as a hired gun for power or money. Given that reliance, public interest and a progressive political role with commitment to liberalism seem a remote possibility. In addition, the legal profession has its own interest to guard against either the grabbing hands of the state or a demanding society. However, as this research finds, in China, as the case elsewhere, lawyering is an inherently political profession with public interest and political emancipation at its heart. In the right circumstances, lawyers will mobilize themselves, build alliance, and use legal or political mechanisms to advance a liberal cause – a limited state in which rights and freedom of the citizens are effectively protected. Chinese lawyers follow that worthy tradition. Leaders emerge in the process who would play an indispensable role in organizing and coordinating the collective action among lawyers. It is hard to organize collective action everywhere, and it is harder to organize collective action among lawyers. Here we see a key difference between authoritarianism and democracy – while legal mobilization and political protest is an inherent right for citizens in democracy, it is prohibited, tightly controlled and harshly repressed under authoritarianism. While an authoritarian state promotes legal rights, it controls collective legal action and individualizes rights claims, making collective action politically risky. Lawyers who are politically motivated and use lawyering for change are forced to act in a cage. To be resilient in the fight for emancipation, lawyers have to be embedded in communities working through and working with grass-roots organization. Lawyers become politically meaningful, legally effectively, and socially embraced when they are embedded in their respective communities and work on prevalent social problems such as labor rights, gender equality, or consumer protection with mass participation.

17613515.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17613515.value: Based on the research, I have started to explore the deeper structure of authoritarian law by identifying the core, the pillars and foundation of authoritarian power. This can be done in two ways. First, through documenting and analyzing lawyers' struggle for political accountability and the rule of law, scholars gain an entry point to the operation of political power. Having observed the power in display from the backstage, scholars can develop a better understanding of authoritarian resilience and fragility. Second, China is not exceptional in its political and legal development and its one-Party authoritarianism can be compared with authoritarianism elsewhere, including current authoritarian states and those which have experienced democratic transition. The PI is exploring deeper and comparative studies of authoritarian Constitutional system. The research, with its sharp focus on lawyers in action, provides an excellent opportunity for knowledge transfer. The research outputs can be used, and, as it happens, have been used to inform and guide legal advocacy and activism. The transmission from theory to practice can provide further opportunities and incentives for theory-building.

17613515.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17613515.value: In an authoritarian system that restricts political participation and prohibits social mobilization, law becomes the principal platform for justice. Law offers legal remedies that are otherwise not available, but the Party state exerts tight control over the legal process. Law, as a double-edged sword, ignites hope and empowers people, but at the same time, marginalizes politics and limits the potentials of structural and transformative changes. Legal advocacy and activism are possible in authoritarian states because the regimes' partial commitment to the rule of law. As long as that foundational need remains, it remains possible for lawyers to retain and grow their political and legal space to advocate for changes. In China, as the case elsewhere, lawyering is an inherently political profession with public interest and political emancipation at its heart. In the right circumstances, lawyers will mobilize themselves, build alliance, and use legal or political opportunities to advance a liberal cause – a limited state in which rights and freedom of the citizens are effectively protected. Chinese lawyers follow that worthy tradition.
