18602415.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18602415.value: The subjugation of women in Irish literature has been criticized in recent years. The subordinated status of women becomes apparent when one compares Yeats and Lady Gregory. While Yeats is universally acknowledged as the spokesman of the Irish Literary Revival and the symbol of modern Irish literature, Lady Gregory is ridiculed by George Bernard Shaw as the “charwoman of the Abbey Theater” (Gilbert & Gubar 1115). Her influence on the Celtic Revival is known but not so well researched. However, it is Lady Gregory’s devotion that makes possible the popularity and prosperity of the Abbey Theater. But, pitiably her works are not so well discussed, though she is a prolific and qualified writer and translator. This study aims to re-evaluate Lady Gregory and her writings. By bringing into discussion the socio-historical aspects of Irish Literary Renaissance, the systematic engagement of textual analysis of Gregory’s literary works, and relevant feminist theories (eg. proposed by feminist ethicists such as Carol Gilligan, and French feminists such as Hélène Cixous and Luce Irigaray), it is expected that many gaps in our understanding of the position of women in Irish Literary Renaissance (as well as modern Irish literature), the connection between nation and women, and the construction/deconstruction of women in modern Irish culture will be filled in by this study. Also, the research aims at helping clarify the nature of female writing and justify Lady Gregory’s contribution to modern Irish literature. 中文摘要 近年來，愛爾蘭文學中女性的次等地位飽受批評。我們只要比較葉慈和格雷格里夫人，便能了解這樣的性別不平等。葉慈經常被視為愛爾蘭文藝復興運動的代言人，儼然是現代愛爾蘭文學的象徵。但是，格雷格里夫人卻被蕭伯納說成是「艾比劇場的清潔女工」(Gilbert & Gubar 1115)。格雷格里夫人對塞爾特文藝復興運動的影響眾所皆知，但相關的研究卻明顯不足。然而，要不是因為她的奉獻，艾比劇場就不會那麼有名。可惜的是，雖然格雷格里夫人是位質量俱佳的作者和譯者，相關的討論並不多。本研究計畫重新評估格雷格里夫人及其作品的重要性。藉由探討愛爾蘭文藝復興運動的社會歷史面向，詳細深入閱讀格雷格里夫人的作品，以及援引相關的女性主義理論(例如，卡蘿‧吉利根等人提出的女性倫理學、法國女性主義者如艾蓮那‧西蘇和露西‧伊瑞嘉嘿等人的理論)，研究者希望彌補現有研究的不足，並進一步了解女性在愛爾蘭文藝復興運動裡面扮演的角色、女性和國家的關係，以及女性在愛爾蘭文化當中的建構/解構。同時，本研究希望釐清女性寫作的特質，並證明格雷格里夫人對現代愛爾蘭文學的貢獻。

18602415.label: Realisation of objectives
18602415.value: This study aims at investigating Lady Gregory and her writings, including her plays, essays, translations, and prose writings. By discussing the socio-historical backgrounds of the Celtic Revival in the early twentieth century, a systematic analysis of Lady Gregory’s literary creations alongside relevant literary theory (for example, Carol Gilligan’s feminist ethics), it is expected that we can better understand the role of women in Irish Literary Renaissance and twentieth-century Irish literature as a whole, the relationship between nation and women, and the construction/deconstruction of women in modern Irish culture. In order to help achieve the goal, four objectives are proposed in my research: (1) To investigate the major characteristics of Irish Literary Renaissance and the role women play in the movement (2) To thoroughly study the primary texts by (and secondary materials on) Lady Gregory and re-assess her position in twentieth century Irish literature (3) To investigate the nature of woman’s writing by comparing and contrasting male writing and female writing (4) To serve as a reference point for future studies on modern and contemporary Irish (female) writings. In the following, I will explain how the objectives have been achieved with the completion of this research project. First, in reference to investigating the major characteristics of Irish Literary Renaissance and the role women play in the movement, it was found that in the wake of Irish nationalism popular in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, Irish women during the Celtic Revival were often thrown into the verge of their existence and were therefore imprisoned by male dominance. To get free from this maze of patriarchy proves to be very difficult. Anti-colonial revolutions in the early twentieth century were always accompanied by notions such as equalities between men and women in different aspects; however, ironically the equality of both sexes was only a myth in the real world. In addition to Irish nationalism in political terms, women in Ireland in the early twentieth century also suffered from marginalization due to another campaign, Irish cultural nationalism. No matter how powerful Irish political nationalism was, it was tarnished by the scandal of Charles Stuart Parnell, leader of Irish Parliamentary Party. Accordingly, the influence of political nationalism was followed by cultural nationalism, which was evidenced by the establishment of the Gaelic League launched by Douglas Hyde. Nonetheless, the well-intentioned actions initiated by cultural nationalists turned out to be an exclusion inflicted on women. Namely, among Irish cultural nationalists’ efforts, women were estranged from the center of power. Pitiably, Irish women at that time were always urged to fulfill their duty of motherhood and were therefore subjugated as merely helping maids of Irish nationalism. When they restricted themselves to household chores, they were forced to be responsible for preserving their indigenous culture and educating their children simultaneously, as specified in Irish Constitution made in 1937. Second, regarding thoroughly studying the primary texts by and secondary materials on Lady Gregory and re-assessing her position in twentieth century Irish literature, the principal investigator has tried his best to collect and investigate relevant primary and secondary materials available in Ireland and Asia. Some selected texts reviewed during this research include: (1) Selected Plays of Lady Gregory (e.g. plays such as The Travelling Man, Spreading the News, Kincora, Hyacinth Halvey, The Gaol Gate, The Rising of the Moon, Dervorgilla, The Workhouse Ward, Grania, and Dave, and critical essays such as “Lady Gregory on Playwriting and her Plays” and “First Performances”) (2) Lady Gregory: Selected Writings (3) Lady Gregory and Irish National Theatre (4) Lady Gregory: Interviews & Recollections (5) Lady Gregory: Fifty Years After (6) The Irish Dramatic Revival 1899-1939 (7) Inventing Ireland (8) Celtic Dawn: A Portrait of the Irish Literary Renaissance (9) Handbook of the Irish Revival (10) Gods and Fighting Men (11) French Feminist Theory (12) Lady Gregory, etc.) It was found that Lady Gregory has not been critically acclaimed partly because of the socio-historical context of in the early-twentieth-century, which was very unfriendly to women. Nevertheless, as this research indicates, women in Lady Gregory’s plays are not really so fragile and wicked. For example, as my paper “Re-evaluating Lady Gregory in Modern Irish Literature: A Feminist Ethics Study” demonstrates, women in Gregory’s plays seem to be negative because most readers often read them from a rationalistic perspective, paying little attention to the ethics of care and relationships which better mirrors women’s relationships with other people. This unique feature of caring is echoed in Lady Gregory’s engagement in the Irish Renaissance campaigns. In fact, many of her plays challenge the stereotype of women as impotent and immoral. Third, in relation to investigating the nature of woman’s writing by comparing and contrasting male writing and female writing, it was found that, although women and female writing tended to be limited by nationalism and patriarchy, they are by no means as stable as most people understand. We can find certain conflicts between nation and women in the plays of Yeats, Lady Gregory and J.M. Synge. This has a lot to do with the influence of nationalism, patriarchy, and the Catholic Church in the early decades of the 20th century. However, Lady Gregory and her writing also demonstrate women’s strong desire for love, sext, and control. As is found in this research, Lady Gregory was a woman who craved love and emotional and sexual gratification, as evidenced in her love affair with Wilfrid Scawen Blunt. However, to a certain degree, Lady Gregory’s intelligence and her sexuality were ruthlessly stifled by her self-imposed monitoring as well as the hostile patriarchal culture of the early twentieth century. ColmTóibín’s research on Lady Gregory and his quasi-biographical and fictional sketches of this long neglected woman via the story “Silence” helps us revisit these lesser-known aspects of her personality. I argue that Tóibín’s attempt to recreate Lady Gregory as both a rational and emotional, traditional and rebellious female figure should be acknowledged. By composing poetry and re-telling her love story, Lady Gregory succeeded in giving herself a public voice despite societal expectations about the appropriate role of women. In this sense, she is anything but only a charwoman of the Abbey Theater. Fourth, in reference to serving as a reference point for future studies on modern and contemporary Irish (female) writings, the findings contribute to our better understanding of a less well discussed aspect of women in Lady Gregory’s plays and add critical varieties to the existing research. As this study implies, although women appear to be subjugated in traditional male-dominated moral thinking, they are more positive and admirable when evaluated from ethical feminism, though to a certain extent they are also limited in traditional societies. This attention to women’s characteristics paves the way for our further exploration of some other women’s writing in modern and contemporary Irish literature (e.g. female writings by Edna O’Brien, Eavan Boland, Emma Donoghue, Maeve Binchy, Anne Enright, Eithne Strong, Marinna Carr, and Nuala Ní Dhomhnaill, etc).

18602415.label: Major findings and research outcome
18602415.value: Overall, this research helps the PI better understand Lady Gregory, her works, and the position of Irish women in modern Irish literature. More detailed findings and relevant research outcomes in my study are indicated below. (1) Different from traditional studies on Lady Gregory and her plays, which concentrates on women’s subjugation in the male-dominated Irish society, the main findings of this research help shed new lights on the value of women in Gregory’s plays via an ethical feminist approach. (Publication: “Re-evaluating Lady Gregory in Modern Irish Literature: A Feminist Ethics Study”. GEMA Online Journal of Language Studies 18(3): 101-13. (2) When faced with nationalism, women’s rights and their concerns are constantly cast aside. Accordingly, due to nationalism, a grand narrative in Ireland, Irish women were comparatively invisible. (Conference Paper: “Women, Nationalism, and Identity in Lady Gregory and Her Plays” (3) By examining Lady Gregory by reading Colm Tóibín’s short story “Silence” in conjunction with examples from her plays and Andrea Dworkin’s feminist theory, it is found that, despite the docility typically associated with Lady Gregory and Irish women, she is not just a helping maid but a proto-feminist in twentieth-century Irish literature. (Paper under Review: “Sense and Sexuality: Lady Gregory via Colm Tóibín” Tamkang Review) (4) While women are often demonized, literally or metaphorically, in Gregory’s plays, they are cherished and re-evaluated in Eavan Boland’s and Nuala Ní Dhomhnaill’s poetry, as evidenced in their re-examination of history and myth. (Paper under Review: “Irish Women Then and Now.” 3L: Language, Linguistics, Literature) (5) Traditional stereotypes of heroes are closely related to the history of colonization/de-colonization in Irish history, which is evident in plays by W.B. Yeats and Lady Gregory. (Book Chapter: “Heroes and Myth,” to be published by National Taiwan University Press in 2019/20)

18602415.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18602415.value: As the research findings demonstrate, this study helps us understand the problems of Irish women in the early twentieth century and potentially highlight the plight of women globally. In the wake of nationalism, Catholicism, and other patriarchal conventions, Irish women in the early decades of the twentieth century were unfairly restricted within family and traditional roles. However, as exemplified in Lady Gregory and her works and works on her, traditional stereotypes imposed on women are problematic because, instead of being confined to patriarchal conventions, women are intellectually gifted and sexually sensitive. This understanding can help us further investigate relevant topics about women. Potential development may include: (1) A comparative study of Lady Gregory and other modern and contemporary Irish female playwrights (e.g. Marianna Carr) in 2-3 years (2) A comparative study of Lady Gregory and other female writers (e.g. Eileen Chang in modern Chinese literature) in non-Irish literature in 2-3 years (3) A monograph based on the research findings and the follow-up research within 3-5 years

18602415.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18602415.value: Lady Gregory significantly impacted modern Irish literature not only because she helped nurture some aspects of W.B. Yeats’s literary career but because she was committed to fostering and promoting the Irish people’s indigenous cultural identity through her writings. However, Lady Gregory’s identity as an intelligent woman is not given adequate credit, and nor are works about her well discussed. This literary study helps us re-examine this great female writer in Irish literature. Lady Gregory’s devotion to the establishment and the management of the Abbey Theater and her plays which promote Irish nationalism belie the fact that, in addition to being a qualified theater runner and supporter, she was also an intelligent woman. Moreover, Lady Gregory was a woman who craved emotional and sexual satisfaction. Nonetheless, Lady Gregory’s intelligence and her sexuality were, to a certain degree, hampered by her self-imposed monitoring as well as the hostile patriarchal culture of the early twentieth century. By investigating Lady Gregory and her works and works on her, this study enables us to better understand the conflict and compromise of being a woman and a writer in a male-dominated society and hopefully paves the way for our understanding of women in the 21st century.

18603515.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18603515.value: 身份認同形成是青少年階段的一項重要發展議題(Erickson, 1968)。不少研究已探究影響青少年身份認同的因素，有研究發現，參與社會服務有助青少年在不同範疇發展身份認同(Hardy et al., 2011)。然而，社會服務的類型十分多樣，究竟服務活動的哪些要素有助青少年發展及增進個人作為社會一員的認同，我們卻知之甚少。 過去半個世紀，學者們已發展出多個理論來描述和解釋身份認同形成的過程(Schwartz, Lukckx & Vignoles, 2011)。其中Marcia (1966) 提出的身份認同狀態理論對青少年身份認同是如何發展及變化這一問題提供了一個描述架構。具體而言，根據青少年探索及承諾於某些特定價值觀或社會意識型態的程度，Marcia區分出四種身份認同狀態：身份認同達成﹙經歷過探索並決定投身於某些價值觀念的實踐﹚，身份認同延緩﹙仍處於探索階段，還未作出選擇﹚，身份認同早閉﹙甚少探索的經歷，但已根據父母或權威人士意見對某些觀念作出承諾﹚，身份認同擴散﹙甚少探索，亦無作出決定﹚。本研究即採用Marcia的身份認同狀態理論來探究香港青少年身份認同之模式和特點，並著重考察青少年參與社會服務與其身份認同狀態的關係。本研究根據服務學習質素指標(Service-Learning Quality Indicators, National Youth Leadership Council, 2008), 將對以下社會服務要素作出檢視：服務活動持續的時間與密集程度、有意義的服務活動、服務與課程之關聯、反省機會、接觸多樣人群、青少年自主及發言權、學校與服務機構之合作、在服務過程中對學生提供指導。 本研究採混合研究方法，量化方法用於檢測社會服務的哪些要素有助青少年理解其身份。具體而言，本研究將使用修定後的自我身份認同狀態量表(the Modified Extended Objective Measure of Ego Identity Status)實施前後測，測量青少年的身份認同狀態在一年時間有何變化。青少年服務活動列表(The Youth Inventory of Involvement)及服務學習質素指標(Service-Learning Quality Indicators)用於測量青少年參與服務活動的狀況及他們對社會服務要素的評價。研究者亦會邀請中學生參加半結構訪談，以探究參加社會服務的過程中，青少年的身份狀態是如何發生變化以及與社會服務的哪些因素相關。

18603515.label: Realisation of objectives
18603515.value: The present study set out to explore which community service program factors provide opportunities for adolescents to develop an increased understanding of their membership in society. A Chinese version of Modified EOMEIS, developed from the present study, in the form of pretest/posttest were administered to assess over 1600 secondary school students’ identity status change within a half year time-span. Students’ community service involvement were reported in both pre and post surveys while key factors in service learning were administered post-project to assess their evaluation of service program quality. Semi-structured interviews with 29 students from three secondary schools were conducted to explain how students with various community service experiences perceived their identity formation in the context of school-based community service programs. The researchers have performed the analysis on the pretest survey data and interview data. The findings of the relationship between community service involvement and adolescents’ overall sense of identity status as well as identity formation in specific domains have been reported from the quantitative data. It was found that 95.9% of the students can be categorized into a particular status, and 31.7%, 25.6%, 20.4%, 22.3% of the students were assigned as diffusion, foreclosure, moratorium, and achievement statuses respectively. Spearman correlation was performed and the results showed that students’ willingness to participate in service, perceived importance of service and previous service experience were positively correlated with levels of self-status, suggesting that more positive service attitudes (i.e., willingness and importance) and more engagement in social service (more time) are associated with the formation of more mature self-status. Ordinal Logistic regression was performed to examine the unique contributions of the service variables in predicting the individual differences in identity status. After parental engagement in service and time spent in service were considered, students attitudes toward social service was a significant predictor of overall self-status. This suggests that the students who regard service as important and willing to participate were more likely to arrive in moratorium or achievement self-statuses, regardless of whether they actually engaged in any service in the past. Compared to the students who did not provide any service in the past 12 months, the students who served were more likely to achieve a higher level of identity status, although the students who spent more time on service were not different with those who spent less time. It appeared that service attitude is a stronger predictor of students’ overall self-status. When predicting overall self-status, service attitude is more important than actual experience. Ordinal logistic regression analyses were also performed on each of the four aspects of identity status. After service time and parental engagement in service were partialled out, students’ service attitude was a significant predictor of all four aspects of identity status. In contrast, time spent in service predicted identity status in lifestyle and occupation, but not in friendship and education. Thus, service experiences exert more impacts on the formation of self-identity in some life areas; but for other areas, they may have no impact – this explains the less effect on overall self-status. Compared to other aspects of identity status, expenditure of more time in social service has a stronger effect on the development of identity in occupation area, suggesting that regardless of ones’ attitudes toward service, service experience may make students progress to more mature identity status. To follow, the relationship between the types of community service and identity formation in the domains of lifestyle and career has been further identified from interview data. Twenty-nine secondary school students in three schools in Hong Kong were interviewed and three main findings were reported from the data. Service experiences that students participated in required and voluntary service were different. Community service no matter required service or voluntary service had similar impacts upon adolescents' understanding of lifestyle, while the more positive impact on career exploration was reported in voluntary service than in required service. The various interplay of students’ personal characteristics (previous service experience, motivation to participate in service), service program features (pre-service training and preparation, direct or indirect contact with service recipients, reflection that focusing on the desired learning outcomes) and social context had led to individual difference in the exploration of lifestyle and career. The abovementioned findings provide evidence that project objectives 1-4 have been achieved to a large extent. The findings of influential factors in the qualitative study have confirmed the necessity to integrate high impact practice into the design of a service program/project. High impact practice includes the role of reflection, a longer period of time investigating in service, direct contact with service recipients in the state of need, and self-determination in making decision and choices. The present study also suggests that the community service with a purpose to enhance students’ understanding of lifestyle and career may consider providing a diversity of opportunities for students to approach to service recipients with various backgrounds, as well as directing students to find the relevancy between service experience and their own characteristics. The findings of some students’ low motivation and unwilling to be involved in required service reflect the negative side of this policy. The above findings and suggestions provide implication for NSS curriculum policy and school practice with reference to community service (objective 5). What remains on-going is data analysis on the change patterns of identity statuses in different domains as well as the quantitative examination of the association between community service program factors and identity statuses. The delay of data analysis and reporting was explained in the remaining section. The current project originally had a mix-methods design, including pre-posttest surveys (six-month interval) with around 30 schools and 1800 students and interviews with 36 students from six schools. Since the project was originally funded only for a period of 12 months, the research team encountered several challenges due to the tight schedule. For example, development of a Chinese version of questionnaire and difficulties in liaising with schools. Regarding the development of the questionnaire, the research team originally planned to adopt an existing Chinese version of the instrument, however, due to the unavailability of the Chinese version of the questionnaire, we decided to do the translation and pilot the Chinese version by the research team. Such change caused the delay of the project yet the good thing is that an additional deliverable, a Chinese version of the Objective Measure of Ego Identity Status (OMEIS-2), has been produced from the project. Apart from the development of research instrument, one of the other major challenges we encountered is inviting schools to participate in the project with a very tight schedule. The research team tried to liaise with secondary schools by using different approaches at the early stage of data collection. Fifteen schools and over 900 students returned the pre-test questionnaire by July 2016. After the approval of the extension of the project was obtained, the PI had contacted the Social Science Data Laboratory (SSDL) of EdUHK and subsequently outsourced the part of data collection work to SSDL. With the support of SSDL, additional around 700 students from 11 schools completed the pre-pretest survey by Aug 2017. Thus, the data analysis on the post-test survey has been delayed.

18603515.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18603515.value: The present study has provided empirical evidence that community service exerted more influence in the domain of lifestyle and occupational than that in friendship and education. This finding attaches important to devote more effort to the investigation of identity formation in specific domains. Two specific domains of identity – moral and civic identities may be examined in the future study since the two domains have been stressed in Hong Kong secondary curriculum (CDC, 2013,2017). The present study has also revealed the complexity of service, which covers multiple purposes with different service settings facing a variety of backgrounds of people to be served directly or indirectly. Without differentiating among the service types, it would be ambiguous to simply generalize the kind of benefits that youth would gain in the process of performing service. Given that the complexity of community service is reflected in the interplay of multiple variables in a service program, the further study may examine the interplay of variables in a service program, such as required or voluntary service, service that directly or indirectly contact service recipients, and different degrees of self-determination.

18603515.value: The present study investigated how community service program factors provided opportunities for adolescents to develop an increased understanding of their membership in the society and how they interplay with each other. A mixed methods design were employed to investigate how adolescent identity status changes within the context of community service. The quantitative findings revealed the relationship between community service and adolescents’ overall sense of identity status as well as identity formation in specific domains. Qualitative data showed that service experiences that students participated in required and voluntary service were different and the interplay of students’ personal characteristics, service program features, and social context had led to individual differences in the exploration of lifestyle and career.

18604515.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18604515.value: In the past decade, much psychometric research interest has been given to statistical models with latent constructs that classify respondents for the purpose of a fine-grained diagnosis. Cognitive diagnosis models (CDMs) can provide detailed diagnostic information to stakeholders about their mastery of the skills. The development of CDMs is still in its early stages. The proposed project aims to contribute to the development by focusing on three important and challenging issues that arise from common practices in cognitive diagnostic tests and concern test fairness and validity: (1) Measurement Invariance/Differential Item Functioning Assessment of differential item functioning (DIF) has been routinely conducted to ensure test fairness across different groups of test-takers. All existing DIF studies in CDMs have a fundamental and logical fallacy: the latent attributes derived from a test with DIF items are mistakenly treated as comparable across groups, making the findings misleading. The fallacy will be corrected through theoretical analysis, simulation evaluation, and empirical evidence. The definition of DIF will be clarified and the assessment of DIF in the CDM framework will be evaluated. Scale purification procedures and the DIF-free-then-DIF strategy that are developed in the item response theory (IRT) framework will be adapted to the CDM framework. (2) Rater CDMs Existing CDMs have two facets – person and item. When a student’s performance is graded by teachers or a patient’s behavior is judged by a psychopathologist, raters also play a significant role in the test score. Ignoring rater effects will lead to biased parameter estimates and inaccurate classification of latent attributes. To resolve this problem, we will develop rater CDMs based on two philosophies: the facets model and the hierarchical rater model. (3) Multilevel CDMs Existing CDMs are not applicable for multilevel data (e.g., students are nested in schools) or longitudinal data (e.g., students are repeatedly assessed). Ignoring multilevel structures will yield biased parameter estimates and inaccurate standard errors. We will thus develop multilevel CDMs with both the latent continuous variable approach and the multivariate Bernoulli distribution approach to account for the multilevel structure. The proposed project aims to provide solutions to these three challenging problems, conduct simulations to evaluate these new models and methods, and demonstrate their implications and applications through several real datasets. Accomplishment of this project will (a) correct the DIF fallacy, (b) advance CDMs to ensure test fairness and improve test validity, and (c) offer a free and standard-alone computer program to promote the new CDMs.

18604515.label: Realisation of objectives
18604515.value: Objective 1: Advance CDMs by correcting the DIF fallacy and developing new models and methods to account for assessments of DIF, rater effects, and multilevel structures (January 2016 to May 2017) To achieve Objective 1, we have clarified the fundamental fallacy for the DIF assessment under CDMs in existing studies. We have theoretically analyzed the problems embedded in the DIF definition, methods, and results and proposed a general definition of DIF assessment which include various types of DIF: (a) differential items parameters, (b) differential Q-matrices, and (c) differential measurement model between groups. Additionally, we have successfully developed new DIF detection methods which are easy-to-use and powerful in detecting DIF in CDMs. The scale purification procedure as well as the DIF-free-then-DIF strategy which were developed under the item response theory (IRT) models framework have been successfully adapted to CDM framework. With regard to the CDMs for rater effects, out team has developed new CDMs to consider the rater effects within the framework of facets models and hierarchical rater model. For multilevel modeling of CDMs, our team has successfully developed multilevel CDMs using the latent continuous variable approach and the multivariate Bernoulli distribution approach to account for multilevel data structures, which are often used in large-scale educational assessments or longitudinal testing. Finally, our team has developed a new model with higher-order structures in CDMs to increase the manageability of the parameter estimates for polytomous or continuous attributes. Objective 2: Evaluate these new initiatives with comprehensive simulations (October 2016 to October 2017) To achieve Objective 2, we have conducted comprehensive simulation studies to explore the performance of new methods, the parameter recovery and model-data fit of the new models. For example, in simulation studies for DIF assessment in CDMs, we have manipulated the number of DIF items and different DIF types. In simulation studies for multilevel CDMs, we have manipulated number of attributes, number of schools, test length, and magnitude of multilevel effects. Two kinds of estimation methods have been implemented and investigated in this project: the expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm and the Bayesian estimation with Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method. We have developed the efficient Mantel-Haenszel method for DIF assessment in CDMs in R, which implements the EM algorithm, and the program for rater CDMs and multilevel CDMs in JAGS, which is a freeware that implements the MCMC method. Objective 3: Demonstrate the implications and applications of these initiatives using empirical examples (July 2017 to December 2017) The new models have been applied to empirical data to illustrate the implications and applications, including the 2003 Trends in International Mathematics and Science Study (TIMSS) eighth grade mathematical test, an English academic essay, an exam for the certificate of proficiency in English and so on. In addition, this project introduced a new item selection algorithms of computerized adaptive testing (CDM) for CDMs. The new method outperformed the existing algorithm in terms of classification accuracy, as well as item bank usage and test efficiency. The study suggests the practicability of the new method in CAT for CDMs. Objective 4: Develop a free and stand-alone computer program with manuals and examples to promote the new initiatives (January 2018 to June 2018) To promote the new models, we have established a website to allow users to free download the examples, computer code, and instructions.

18604515.label: Major findings and research outcome
18604515.value: Major findings include: 1. The fundamental fallacy in previous studies for DIF assessment in CDMs have been clarified and new methods that are easy-to-use and powerful in detecting DIF in CDMs have been proposed. The new methods are applicable for detecting various types of DIF, including the differential item parameters, differential Q-matrices, and differential measurement models in CDMs. 2. A new class of CDMs that account for rater effects within the frameworks of facets models and hierarchical rater models have been successfully developed. 3. A new class of CDMs that considering the hierarchal data structuring which often observe in large-scale assessments or longitudinal testing have been developed using the latent continuous variable approach and the multivariate Bernoulli distribution approach. 4. The parameters of the rater CDMs and multilevel CDMs can be well recovered by using the MCMC method implemented in WinBUGS/JAGS. The new models yielded accurate item parameters estimates and person classification. The outcomes from this project have substantial impacts both theoretically and practically. Specifically, the accomplishment of this project have not only corrected the fundamental fallacy of previous studies in DIF assessment for CDMs, have improved the accuracy and efficiency of detecting DIF, especially when there are many DIF items, but also created a new research paradigm of DIF assessment in CDMs. In addition, this project have taken the complicated data structure (i.e., rater effect, hierarchical data structure, polytomous responses) in real tests into account so as to yield scores that are fair and valid. Findings have been widely disseminated in various forms as an article published in world-leading journal, book chapter, and conference papers. The detailed information can be found in Part C of this report. The project team will continue to prepare manuscripts for publication and generate more outcomes. Finally, a website has been constructed where the empirical examples, computer code, and instructions can be freely downloaded. Researchers and practitioners can directly apply the new methods or models to their real tests by using the developed programs in this project.

18604515.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18604515.value: Although we have conducted pioneering work for CDMs, more studies are in need. Two issues are listed as an example: (1) in addition to the MH method that has been adapted in this project for DIF assessment in CDMs, the logistic regression method that is commonly used in IRT can be adapted as well, (2) item parameters in CDMs (e.g., the slip parameter and guessing parameter in the DINA model) are often treated as fixed effects, indicating that they are identical across persons. For example, the levels of slipping may depend on examinee motivation, and the levels of guessing may be related to examinee ability. When appropriate, the random-effect approach proposed can be incorporated in multilevel CDMs. More outcomes will be disseminated in the conferences and academic journals.

18604515.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18604515.value: Cognitive diagnosis models (CDMs) can provide detailed diagnostic information to stakeholders about their mastery of the skills for the purpose of a fine-grained diagnosis. The development of CDMs is still in its early stages. This project aims to contribute to its development by focusing on three important and challenging issues that arise from common practices in cognitive diagnostic tests and concern test fairness and validity: measurement invariance or DIF, rater effect, and multilevel CDMs. This project proposes new methods for DIF assessment in CDMs to correct the fundamental fallacy in all existing DIF studies in CDMs and ensure test fairness and validity. Moreover, this project develops a new class of IRT models for CDMs to account for rater effects and multilevel data structure and investigate relevant technical and practical issues. These news models and new methods have been well established, evaluated via extensive simulation studies, and applied to several empirical datasets. This project has generated a long-standing impacts on theoretical and practical advancements of CDMs. Theoretically, this project has shed new light on the three important issues and created new research lines for CDMs. Practically, this project has provided the most cutting edge methods for analyzing the data in CDMs.

18605015.label: Project Title(Chinese)
18605015.value: 香港與英國中學生對生物保育議題的決策：跨文化、年齡及性別研究

18605015.label: Project Objectives
18605015.value: To explore how students make decisions about issues concerning biological conservation through multi-perspective reasoning, utilization of scientific evidence, and differentiation of alternatives. To find out how the decision-making interactions of students within and between two cultural localities, Hong Kong and the UK, impact the three processes and outcomes mentioned in objective (1) in their decision-making process. To investigate how the findings regarding objectives (1) and (2) vary with age, gender, and cultural contexts.

18605015.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18605015.value: The proposed research explores secondary students’ decision making about socio-scientific issues (SSIs) related to biological conservation, from cross-cultural, cross-age and cross-gender perspectives. Many of these SSIs have profound repercussions on global environmental sustainability that transcend cultural boundaries, and that entail international negotiation. In science education, SSIs can contribute to the development of students’ scientific literacy which embraces the ability to be engaged “intelligently in public discourse and debate about matters of scientific and technological concern” (NRC, 1996, p. 13). Furthermore, making informed decisions about SSIs entails critical reasoning and the exercising of responsible citizenship, which are the thrusts of new interdisciplinary curricula in both Hong Kong (e.g. Liberal Studies), and the UK (e.g., citizenship education). SSIs typically involve disagreements over conflicting science-related claims, evaluation of the trustworthiness of those claims based on evidence, and considerations of the pros and cons of decision alternatives from multiple perspectives. Research on SSIs has been focused on multi-perspective reasoning, the evaluation of evidence, value judgement, and the formulation of the criteria for decision-making. The possible role of culture, gender, and age-related developmental factors as mediators of decision making about SSIs has been under-explored, and more so for the impact of intercultural interactions on the quality of decision making despite the fact that appreciating cultural connections within these issues is important in achieving intercultural understanding. Culture, gender and age-related development must be taken into account when developing pedagogical approaches to SSI education at the different stages of schooling. This study adopts a comparative perspective and uses a qualitative approach supplemented with quantitative methods. Four secondary schools, two in Hong Kong and the other two in the UK, will be involved in decision making about sociocultural issues and in cross-cultural exchange to study the impact of culture and cross-cultural exchange on students’ decision making about conservation issues. Students from four classes in each school will be engaged as participants, two from the age range of 12-14, and the other two from 16-18 to explore age-related differences in decision making. Students in each class are presented in turn with two conservation issues – animal culling and shark hunting. Data about how students make decisions about the issues before and after interacting with their peers within and outside their locality will be collected through discussion records, supplemented with focus-group interviews. The data will be analysed to reflect the effects of age, gender and cultural contexts on students’ decision-making. 香港與英國中學生對生物保育議題的決策：跨文化、年齡及性別研究 本研究旨在探討中學生對與社會有關的科學議題所作的決策。 課題以生物保育為主， 並以跨文化，年齡及性別的角度進行探討。 為確保全球環境的可持續性， 面對這些複雜議題，國際間跨文化及地域的合作至為重要。 探討此類議題有助培養學生的科學素養， 以及發展學生的批判思維及公民責任感， 對實踐跨學科課程也有莫大幫助。 一向以來，科學議題的研究主要針對多角度思考， 證據評估， 價值判斷，及決策標準的釐定等方面， 卻甚少考慮文化， 年齡及性別所起的作用，尤以跨文化互動對議題決策的影響為然， 而不同學習階段的課程設計，更應對這些因素予以考慮。 本研究從比較角度，選擇港、英兩地各兩所中學的學生為研究對象。從每所學校分別選取12至14歲，及16 至18歲兩個年齡組別，探討年齡、性別及地域文化對兩項動物保育議題的決策的影響。本研究利用量性及質性方法相配合，就學生的討論所得及與研究員的面談所搜集的數據進行分析，以反映年齡、性別及文化對學生作決策的影響。

18605015.label: Realisation of objectives
18605015.value: The following are the objectives stated in the proposal:- 1. To explore how students make decisions about issues concerning biological conservation through multi-perspective reasoning, utilization of scientific evidence, and differentiation of alternatives. 2. To find out how the decision-making interactions of students within and between two cultural localities, Hong Kong and the UK, impact the three processes and outcomes mentioned in objective (1) in their decision-making process. 3. To investigate how the findings regarding objectives (1) and (2) vary with age, gender, and cultural contexts. These objectives have been achieved to a satisfactory extent. Analysis has been carried out to explore how student participants made decisions about two animal conservation issues namely shark hunting and badger culling. Students’ decision making with respect to three levels were analysed including the stakeholders (human or non-human) targeted by the students, and the means of control and concerns underpinning their decisions. There were variations in students’ decisions between the HK and UK, though there were similarities as well. Some age-related differences were observed between the junior secondary and senior secondary groups. Gender differences were less conspicuous than age-related differences.

18605015.label: Major findings and research outcome
18605015.value: The outcomes regarding the issue of shark fishing were used to illustrate the research outcomes. The three levels, namely targets or stakeholders, means of control and areas of concerns constitute a common structure of decision-making by students within and across cultures, which was used as a basis for further comparison across culture, age and gender. For the ‘targets’ level, both HK and UK students targeted shark fishing or fishermen rather than consumers or traders. As for the means of control, those who preferred legislative means also focused on curbing shark fishing rather than trading or consuming sharks, showing shark fishing as the most widely recognized culprit in the issue. Culture appears to have mediated the initial decision making by the students through the cultural context in which they have been brought up. Difference due to culture seemed to have greater effects than age and gender. HK students suggested more varied means of control compared with their UK counterparts at the beginning of the activity, although the difference disappeared toward the end of the activity. HK students also show a wider range of concerns than UK students throughout from the beginning to the end of the activity. HK junior students in particular suggested a wider range of targets and means of control, and a wider range of concerns than their UK counterparts. The greater richness of thoughts exhibited by HK students may be explained by their heightened awareness toward shark fishing due to the greater relevance of the issue to the culture of HK, the controversy about shark fishing in recent years, and the advocacy by pressure groups to eliminate shark fins from Chinese banquets. As shown by this study, UK students seemed to have little knowledge about the issue, despite the fact that shark meat has been utilized in their region. These students were not aware of the consumption of shark products in their region as sources of meat and tended to regard it as a cultural issue in other parts of the world. Despite their cultural links with shark fishing, did not appear to show a stronger identification with or support for this practice than UK students. By contrast, UK students, despite not perceiving the issue as relevant to their culture, seemed to be more sympathetic toward cultural and economic concerns after the activity than they were before the activity.

18605015.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18605015.value: The findings have provided insights into cross-cultural comparison of students’ decision-making, which have implications for preparing students to make decisions about global conservation issues as future global citizens. The findings as regards cultural, age and gender differences are noteworthy from an educational point of view, particularly from a pedagogical perspective. Intra-cultural group discussion and intercultural exchange seems able to exert a certain degree of impact on students’ final decision in terms of the nature and number of perspectives they draw upon. Future studies could explore the impact of more direct forms of cultural exchange such as videoconferencing or detailed reciprocal feedback. A greater sample of students could be involved in future studies to validate the present findings with respect to age-related and gender differences. Other animal conservation issues could be used to further examine the relationship between the nature of the issue and the animals involved and students’ decision-making. The findings of the study will be reported in the coming WERA Focal Meeting & HKERA International Conference to be held in 30 Nov – 2 Dec 2017 in Hong Kong. A paper which is to be submitted to an international science education journal is now at the final drafting stage.

18605015.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18605015.value: The study explored secondary students’ decision making about socio-scientific issues related to biological conservation, from cross-cultural, cross-age and cross-gender perspectives. Two groups of junior and senior students from UK and HK respectively were engaged in decision making about two conservation issues - shark hunting and badger culling. The findings showed while the majority of students in both localities inclined to protect animals from being hunted or culled, there were differences across age, gender and culture in various aspects of their decisions including their justifications. After the activity, senior students seemed to have considered a wider range of options than junior students; more senior students in both localities resorted to education as a means to protect sharks than their junior counterparts; and more junior students in both localities thought they needed further information for making decision about the issue than their senior counterparts. Gender differences were not obvious for both localities for the shark hunting issue. However, for badger culling, female students tended to develop a wider range of ideas and concerns than male students. This kind of cultural exchange between the two localities seemed to have an impact on students’ decision making through enhancing their understanding of the issues.

18605515.label: Project Title(Chinese)
18605515.value: “真實的痕跡：後殖民及離散文學中攝影缺席的在場”

18605515.label: Project Objectives
18605515.value: This project overcomes the disciplinary divisions between literature, photography and postcolonial studies. It posits a reading of photographs and photography as a trope or metaphor that offers us insights into postcolonial literature and new ways of reading this literature. This project attempts to analyze the extent to which photography in postcolonial literature offers a means of “talking back” to Empire. Bringing together the complex disciplines of postcolonial and migration studies, photography and literature this project aims to bring to the fore some of the dialectical interrelations between these already multidisciplinary fields. By focusing on the written rather than visual representation of photographs in literary texts, this project attempts to problematize some of the claims of photography that arise from its visuality. By analyzing the role of photographs in ameliorating or heightening the trauma of migration, this project attempts to overcome a perceived divide between postcolonial literature and trauma studies. This project aims to shed light on the often overlooked figure of the photographer in postcolonial literature and to assess his role as a postcolonial intellectual.

18605515.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18605515.value: Literature and photography are often regarded as sister arts, their cominglings latent in the very etymology of the word “photography” meaning “writing with light.” While many scholars have studied their productive interactions, there is scant scholarly work about the use of photography as a trope or metaphor in literary texts. This project aims to shift the scholarship from an intense focus on text-image relations to the presence and function of verbalized or narrated images in literary texts. Some scholars have propounded the textuality of images by viewing images as texts that can be read and deciphered (Mitchell 1995, Petit 2006), but none have analysed the narrated image in literature. I argue that narrated images in literary texts provide a moment that is twice removed – once in being captured as a photograph (which doesn’t really exist) and again in being described by the narrator. Photographs are often seen as absent presences – making a now absent moment from the past, present for eternity. The narrated image in literary texts I argue, function as a similar absent presence. By limiting the scope of the project to the study of postcolonial and diasporic literature, I attempt to hypothesise on the relationship between postcoloniality and photography. Photography in colonial times, often served to justify the project of colonialism by presenting the colonized as fetishized types rather than as real individuals. Photography in postcolonial literature may then be seen as an attempt at authentic self-representation, an attempt to regain voice and agency. However, I argue that while the power of images may give agency and validity to the photographer, the inherently paradoxical nature of photography, always/already undercuts such attempts at representing the “real.” Diasporic literature with its attendant themes of loss, longing, mourning and trauma, has obvious resonances with photography. By studying the presence of the narrated photographs in many recent diasporic novels, I attempt to hypothesize the ways in which photography represents an endless regression of infinite melancholia for the diasporic characters in these novels. By bringing together the multidisciplinary fields of postcolonial literature, migration studies and photography, this project aims to overcome the disciplinary divisions between these fields and shift the debate on the interactions between these sister arts. It attempts to study not the interaction of the written word and the visual image, but rather the written image which functions as a photographic metaphor to enhance the themes of the literary text. 文學和攝影經常被認為是姊妹藝術，它們的混合性可見於攝影 (Photography) 的詞源，即「以光書寫」。儘管不少學者已研究過兩者在製作方面的共通之處，可是針對文學作品中以攝影作比喻或象徵的研究卻仍見貧乏。 本研究正是旨在離開一般只集中在文字和影像之關係的學研方向，並將焦點轉移至影像在文學作品中以口述或敘述的存在形式和作用。部份學者曾提出影像有其文本性：它們能被閱讀和闡釋(Mitchell 1995, Petit 2006)，但仍未有研究分析過文本中被敘述的影像。我認為這種敘述影像是被雙重移除的：它們曾經被攝為一幀照片(這照片其實也是不存在的)，而後又被敘事者轉述。攝影經常被視為“缺席的在場”— 再現了一個已成過去的瞬間，並使這瞬間永遠存在。我認為在文學作品中被敘述的影像也有一種類似的—“缺席的在場”的—性質。 我希望將研究範圍限於後殖民和離散文學，並對後殖民性和攝影的關係作出推測。在殖民時期，攝影經常被用來再現被殖民者，將他們的血肉之軀物化為影像，從而合理化殖民主義。而在後殖民文學裏的攝影則可被視為一種主權的自我表現、一種重奪發言權和代理權的嘗試。然而，我認為影像的力量固然有機會給予攝影者代理權和真確性，但攝影固有的弔詭本質經已削弱了這“真實”的表現。 離散文學與其伴隨的主題—失落、渴望、哀悼和創傷—與攝影有明顯的共鳴。透過研究大量近期離散小說中被敍述照片的狀態，我希望揣摩離散小說的角色如何藉著照片回顧他們無盡的哀傷。 此研究結合後殖民文學、移民研究和攝影等不同學科，旨在克服學科之間的差異和轉移有關研究中的固有側重。這項研究的重點不在於文字和影像的互動性，反之為探討被書寫的影像、其攝影性的象徵作用和對文學主題的提升。

18605515.label: Realisation of objectives
18605515.value: All 7 objectives of the project have been fully realized. The project was proposed as a book project. I have now completed drafts of 5 of the 6 proposed chapters of the book and also prepared the book proposal which is currently under review for publication. I am currently working on the introductory chapter. The book comprises of the following chapters: Introduction: Photography and the Postcolonial Chapter 1: The False Promise of Affective Intentionality: The Violence of Documentary Photography in Train to Pakistan Chapter 2: Imagistic Haunting: Photographic Traces and Posthuman Photography in Animal’s People and Pterodactyl, Puran Sahay and Pirtha Chapter 3: Picturing Atrocity: Postcolonial Trauma and the Photographic Eye in Anil’s Ghost and Choli ke Pichhe Chapter 4: The Punctum of Loss: Photography and the Vision of Loss in “Hema and Kaushik.” Chapter 5: Finding Gauri: Photography and a Reappraisal of Diasporic Womanhood in The Lowland. Conclusion Traces of the Real shifts the scholarship from an intense focus on text-image relations to the presence and function in literary texts of the photographic in various absent or indirect forms – primarily the image in absentia, either ekphrastically evoked or via allusions to iconic photographs that exist outside the fictional text - but also the photographic eye or characters who are photographers in the texts. In doing so it overcomes the disciplinary divisions between literature, photography and postcolonial studies and provides new ways of reading this literature. (Objectives 1 and 2). The book opens at the cusp of South Asian postcoloniality with a discussion of Khushwant Singh’s novel Train to Pakistan, written nine brief years after Indian independence. Contrary to the book’s avowed intention of focusing on the image in absentia, the opening chapter of the book does include analyses of real photographs. However, these are photographs that were added fifty years after the first publication of the novel; so these photographs, by dint of their belatedness, are also an absent presence in the novel. On the occasion of the 50th anniversary of the publication of Khushwant Singh’s Train to Pakistan, Roli Books launched a special illustrated edition of the novel in 2006. Edited by Pramod Kapoor, this edition of Singh’s novel is supplemented by sixty five hitherto unpublished photographs taken by the celebrated American photographer Margaret Bourke-White for LIFE magazine during her stay in India in 1946 and 1947. The chapter begins by tracing the history of photography in India from its indexical origins under the project of colonialism to its opposing practices which attempted an authentic self-representation running counter to colonial representations (Objective 3). I situate Bourke-White’s Partition photographs within this spectrum while also attempting to understand what she wanted her images to convey. Citing critics like John Tagg who have called into question documentary photography’s capacity to bear witness, I argue that despite being politically progressive, Margaret Bourke-White’s photographs of Partition convey an ideological naivete and evidence of what Tagg calls “the pleasures of the paternalistic gaze” (xxxiii). This chapter also considers the affective consequences of the coupling of Singh’s text with Bourke-White’s images. Despite the affective intentionality of the belated inclusion of photographs in Singh’s novel, I read this as an act of violence and violation. The always already present discourse of colonial photography, coupled with Bourke-White’s often staged and artificial documenting of the Great Migration of India’s Partition and the trauma it brought to millions, ensures that such a naive coupling of text and image can never be straightforward (Objective 4 and 5). Rather than add affective dimensionality to Singh’s powerful novel, I argue that Bourke-White’s photos work at cross purposes to Singh’s storytelling in Train to Pakistan. In Chapter 3, I provide a reading Michael Ondaatje’s novel Anil’s Ghost (2000) and Mahasweta Devi’s short story “Choli ke Pichhe” (Behind the Bodice) as correctives to the Eurocentric bias of much of trauma studies (Objective 6). Ondaatje’s novel about the Sri Lankan civil war is the story of Anil Tissera, a Sri Lankan born, western educated forensic expert who returns to her homeland to investigate possible atrocities committed by the government. In Ondaatje’s novel, as a Westernized, diasporic individual, Anil replicates the Eurocentric view of trauma. I argue that by making his protagonist somewhat of an outsider and by further aligning her gaze to the Western gaze and the supposedly “objective” camera eye, Ondaatje complicates the notion of postcolonial witnessing and representation. Ondaatje considers the utility of photographs as a means of witnessing, recording and providing testimonials about postcolonial trauma. Drawing on discussions of the photography of torture and atrocity (Prosser 2005; Sontag 2004 and Butler 2009), this chapter seeks to explore the ways in which photography and the narrated image complicate Ondaatje’s themes of trauma, truth and testimony. I question whether photography’s inherent contradictions – objectivity vs framing, immediacy vs. distance - allow the characters in the novel to access the truth about violence and trauma in an alternative way or whether they painfully heighten the impossibility of this endeavor (Objectives 5 and 6). Finally, I argue that Ondaatje proposes several modes of seeing in this novel. He aligns the photographic eye with a western notion of documentation and truth telling which, he argues fails in the context of postcolonial trauma which calls for a more localized, grounded, intuitive and even spiritual way of seeing (Objective 5). This alternative vision is what I call “the optics of blindness” or, somewhat contradictorily, a blind seeing, a way of intuitively apprehending what is not obvious. I turn my attention to the figure of the photographer in postcolonial literature in the latter half of Chapter 3 (Objective 7). In “Behind the Bodice” Devi connects visuality and trauma (Objective 6) through the figure of Upin Puri whose photographic gaze is transformed into a scopophilic one and works to objectify the protagonist Gangor’s body. At the end of this story we have a strange but powerful reversal. Instead of the photograph standing in and speaking for the unspeakable traumatic act, the victim remains articulate and resilient, while Upin the author of the image, becomes traumatized, haunted by his work of art and his own unwitting role in causing the traumatic act. Chapter 4 further explores the relationship between trauma studies and postcolonial literature (Objective 6). Through a reading of Jhumpa Lahiri’s novella Hema and Kaushik, I argue that the contradictions within photography provide Lahiri with the means to reflect on the ambivalent nature of home, belonging and diaspora for characters like Hema and Kaushik. Instead of providing him with roots and an access into the past that can give him a secure sense of his diasporic identity, photographs and photography simply exacerbates Kaushik’s sense of phantom loss and diasporic mourning. Parallels between photography, on the one hand, and the trauma and haunting that sometimes come with diasporic movement, on the other, suggest both the appropriateness of Lahiri’s use of photography as a trope as well as the necessity of its deliberate structural failure in the story. Using writings on photography theory by Roland Barthes, Susan Sontag and others, I analyze the trope of photography in the story and posit a relation between the desire to photograph and the immigrant condition.

18605515.label: Major findings and research outcome
18605515.value: The major research outcome of the project is the monograph, Traces of the Real. I have also published two refereed journal articles, delivered one invited lecture and presented my work at three international conferences. In addition to the 2016 conference paper which led to a subsequent publication in 2017 (summarized in the midterm report), I had the opportunity to present parts of Chapter 5 (“Photography and a Reappraisal of Diasporic Woman hood in The Lowland”) at two separate talks in 2017. The first of these was for an invited lecture at St. Lawrence University. The talk was titled “Becoming Udayan: Photography and the Devastating Doubling of Brothers in Jhumpa Lahiri’s The Lowland.” This talk was derived from the second part of the chapter where I analyze a death portrait to suggest that the brothers in the novel, Subhash and Udayan are inextricably “twinned” such that the protagonist Gauri remains haunted by the past and her memories of Udayan even after she comes to America. The second talk was delivered at the conference of the Society for the Study of American Women Writers in July 2017 entitled “Allo-portraits of a mother: Photography and Diasporic motherhood in Jhumpa Lahiri’s The Lowland.” This talk was based on the first part of the chapter where I use Marianne Hirsch’s work on family photographs, the familial gaze and the connection between photography and motherhood, to argue that Lahiri’s protagonist Gauri is a more sympathetic character than critics have argued who fails to fulfil the hegemonic familial ideology imposed upon her. During my visit to Canton, NY to deliver the invited lecture, I also attended a conference at Cornell University called Utopia After the Human where I delivered a paper, “Posthuman Utopias: Inter-species Assemblages and Migranthood in Shaun Tan’s The Arrival.” Though this is not from the book itself, it helped me consolidate my ideas on posthumanism, particularly in relation to the postcolonial, in preparation for what became Chapter 2 of the book – “Imagistic Haunting: Photographic Traces and Posthuman Photography in Animal’s People and Pterodactyl, Puran Sahay and Pirtha.” I was also able to include a version of a small part of Chapter 3 in a forthcoming publication, “Defiance and the Speakability of Rape: Decolonizing Trauma Studies in Mahasweta Devi’s Fiction” included in Trauma, Memory and Healing in Asian Literature (Routledge, 2019) edited by Sharanya Jayawickrama.

18605515.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18605515.value: This project has allowed me to continue to explore the relation between visual studies and postcoloniality more generally. I have just submitted another RGC grant application for a project on the refugee graphic novel called “Picturing Precarity.” Following critics like Simon Gikandi (2010) and Giorgio Agamben (1998, 2000) who have theorized the refugee as a new kind of Other that challenges global cultural flows, “Picturing Precarity” calls for an alternative migration framework based on spatiality as well as a more individualized and humanized visual frame for depicting the refugee. These I wager, can be found in the refugee graphic novels of the last decade. In particular, this project considers the depiction of “nonplaces” such as the open sea, detention centres and refugee camps in refugee graphic novels, arguing that these offer us a new migration framework based on reconfiguring spatiality. This project considers the politics of photographic depictions of refugees in the media. I argue that despite the visibility of such coverage, the dehistoricized and dehumanizing visual framing of refugees in these images, negatively influences the discourse framing questions of asylum in particular countries.

18605515.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18605515.value: In the first of his “Seven theses on photography” (2012), Christopher Pinney laments what he calls the “problem of ex-nomination” in photography studies. This arises from the predominance of Western photography in the field which gives it a privileged place of global recognition while photography from the non-Western world is always characterized as having a local rather than a global flavor. While in literature, the Empire has written back and has been doing so for several decades, the harnessing of photographic discourses to bolster the truth of dominant ideologies, often remains unacknowledged. This book argues that by using photography as a metaphor in a variety of ways in their writing, South Asian postcolonial writers are undermining the truth-telling power and indexicality of photography, thereby challenging the hegemony of Western photographic discourse. In the discussion of novels by Michael Ondaatje, Jhumpa Lahiri, Indra Sinha and others, this book proposes alternative photographic visions more suited to the postcolonial project. This is the first extensive study of photography as a metaphor in South Asian postcolonial and diasporic literature, and as yet, there are no obvious direct competitors to the book.

18605715.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18605715.value: 當前的國際教育改革致力於培養學生的自主學習能力，這一能力強調學習的自主性和學生的自我管理。作為自主學習的一個核心技巧，自我評估要求學生承擔尋求反饋、描述和評估自己學習情況的責任。為了實現自我評估，學生需要收集能夠反映自己學習表現的反饋信息。自我評估的校準依賴從多種途徑獲得反饋，以確認或者修正學生對學業質量的初始判斷。反饋可以來自外部（即，過往測試，教師、同學或者家長給予的評價），也可以來自內部（例如，情緒、動機、信念和身體感覺）。這即是引導自我評估的校準機制。學生自我評估的某些方面至今並未得到很好地理解，尤其是在受儒家文化影響的學習環境中。例如，學生自我評估時從不同途徑獲得反饋的頻率和程度是怎樣的？自我評估校準在自主學習三個關鍵過程中（即，預想、執行和反思）(Zimmerman & Moylan, 2009)是否存在不同特征？什麼預測因子會影響學生的自我評估意願和實踐？儘管現有文獻認為自我評估與學業表現呈正相關，但是，在不同學習階段它們之間的關係到底是怎樣的？ 本研究旨在探討香港學生自我評估的校準、預測因子及其影響。研究目標包括：（1）探究自主學習三個不同階段自我評估校準的特征；（2）探索學生自我評估意願和實踐的預測因子；以及（3）檢測自我評估對學生學業成績的影響。 本研究採用焦點團體訪談和問卷調查相結合的混合研究方法。為探究研究目標1和2，將邀請約60名小四至中三的學生參與焦點團體訪談。為探究研究目標1、2、3，本研究將對來自20所香港學校（十所小學、十所中學）小四至中三的3600名學生進行問卷調查。所使用的問卷來自於之前設計的自我報告式問卷（例如，Yan, 2014a; Yan & Cheng, in press; Yan, 2014b）和從訪談研究中產生的新問題。 本研究探究學生自我評估的整個“鏈條”，從自我評估的預測因子（例如：態度、主觀規範、理解的行為約束），到自主學習不同階段的自我評估校準（依據內部和外部反饋），再到自我評估對學生學習結果的影響。研究結果將會從理論上和實踐上增強我們對學生自我評估的認識。本研究能讓教師對自我評估的功能有更好的見解，使學生有更好的進行自我評估的元認知意識，從而推動教育評估理論的發展。而且，本研究還將從心理學理論的角度對文化於自我評估的影響提供有益啟示。

18605715.label: Realisation of objectives
18605715.value: Research objective 1: To investigate the characteristics of self-assessment calibration in the three different phases of self-regulated learning This objective has been 100% achieved. The characteristics of self-assessment calibration in the three different phases of self-regulated learning have been investigated through interview and survey studies. Focus group interviews with 30 secondary students and individual interviews with 17 undergraduate students have been conducted. The interviews have obtained in-depth information regarding the common actions students engage in when calibrating self-assessments in different phases of self-regulated learning. Furthermore, the results and insights generated from interviews have helped to fine-tune the theoretical framework used in this study and develop the self-assessment scale used in the subsequent survey. Based on the results of the interview study, a journal article entitled “A cyclical self-assessment process: Towards a model of how students engage in self-assessment” was published in Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education in 2017. The proposed model identified three actions that are commonly undertaken in the self-assessment calibration process: (1) determining the performance criteria, (2) self-directed feedback seeking, and (3) self-reflection. Based on the above-mentioned theoretical framework of the cyclical self-assessment process, the Self-assessment Practice Scale (SaPS), an instrument for assessing students’ actions in self-assessment calibration, has been developed. A validation study has been conducted on a sample of 3,059 Hong Kong students ranging from Primary 4 to Secondary 3. A journal article entitled “The Self-assessment Practice Scale (SaPS) for students: Development and psychometric studies” was published in The Asia-Pacific Education Researcher in 2018. The development of the SaPS provides a useful tool for measuring various self-assessment actions of primary, secondary, and university students. In addition, a longitudinal survey of 63 university students has been conducted to investigate the characteristics of self-assessment practices in different self-regulated learning phases (Preparatory, Performance, and Appraisal phases). A journal article entitled “Self-assessment in the process of self-regulated learning and its relationship with academic achievement” was submitted to Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education for review in 2019. It was found that self-assessment is a fundamental skill for self-regulated learning and occurs in each self-regulated learning phase with different patterns. Research objective 2: To explore the predictors of students’ self-assessment intentions and practices This objective has been 100% achieved. The predictors of students’ self-assessment intentions and practices have been identified through interview and survey studies. The above-mentioned interviews have also enabled an in-depth understanding of the possible predictors that influence students’ self-assessment intentions and practices. Based on the interview study, a questionnaire has been developed to assess students’ self-assessment intentions and practices as well as the predictors, including Affective attitude, Instrumental attitude, Subjective norms, Controlability, Self-efficacy, and Psychological safety. This questionnaire has been administered to half of the sample, as described in Research objective 1 (i.e., 1,425 students), to explore the relationship between students’ self-assessment intentions and practices and its predictors. A journal article entitled “Student self-assessment: Why do they do it?” was submitted to Educational Psychology for review in 2019. The results showed that instrumental attitude had the most significant impact on intention to self-assess, while self-efficacy was the strongest factor in predicting self-assessment practices. Research objective 3: To examine the effects of self-assessment on students’ academic performance This objective has been 100% achieved. The effects of self-assessment on students’ academic performance have been examined through cross-sectional and longitudinal survey studies. A survey has been conducted on another sample of 980 Hong Kong students, ranging from Primary 4 to Secondary 3, to examine the effects of self-assessment on students’ academic performance. The survey collected data on students’ self-assessment practice and their performance in school-based assessments. According to the review comment on the comparability of internal exam scores from different schools in the 1st annual progress report, the standardized z-scores of school-based assessments were used instead of raw scores and multiple-level analysis was applied. A journal paper based on the survey results is under preparation. The results revealed a general positive relationship between self-assessment practices and academic achievement. The longitudinal survey study, mentioned under Research objective 1, also investigated the impact of self-assessment practices in different self-regulated learning phases on academic achievement (on the same assessment task). It was found that seeking feedback for self-assessment through monitoring in the Performance phase was the strongest and most positive predictor of academic achievement. Furthermore, a small-scale experimental study on the effects of self-assessment on students’ academic performance has been conducted. The results indicated that a self-assessment diary intervention could significantly enhance students’ academic achievement and self-efficacy. Although not planned in the original proposal, this additional study extends this line of research and serves as a pilot study that might result in another GRF project.

18605715.label: Major findings and research outcome
18605715.value: The research findings generated from this GRF project have made theoretical and practical contributions to the literature, and have great potential to inform future policies related to educational assessment. • Key research finding 1 (self-assessment theory): Yan and Brown (2017) developed a cyclical self-assessment process model that depicts the inner processes and common actions (i.e., determining assessment criteria, self-directed feedback seeking, and self-reflection) in self-assessment. Yan (under review) found that self-assessment is a fundamental skill for self-regulated learning and occurs in each self-regulated learning phase with different patterns. Significance: The processes by which students conduct their self-assessments are not clear in literature. Yan and Brown’s (2017) work was the most recent update in this field and, as such, its in-depth understanding of self-assessment processes have laid a foundation for future investigations in this field. The finding about self-assessment practices in different self-regulated learning phases may enable a better understanding of the complexity of self-assessment and the mechanism of the effects of self-assessment. • Key research finding 2 (measurement of self-assessment practices): Based on the above model, Yan (2018) developed the Self-assessment Practice Scale (SaPS) for assessing self-assessment practices. The SaPS contains 20 items in four subscales assessing students’ actions in self-assessment, including seeking external feedback through monitoring, seeking external feedback through inquiry, seeking internal feedback, and self-reﬂection. Significance: The SaPS is the first scale to be explicitly based on a theoretical model of self-assessment and was developed specifically for assessment of concrete self-assessment actions. • Key research finding 3 (predictors of students’ self-assessment intentions and practices): Yan, Brown, Lee, and Qiu (under review) found that attitude, subjective norms, self-efficacy, and perceived controllability were statistically significant predictors of intention to self-assess, while self-efficacy and intention had a significant influence on self-assessment practice. Psychological safety also had a relatively weak but significant impact on self-assessment intention and practice. Significance: This study identified predictors of self-assessment intentionality and behavior and therefore has important implications regarding how to promote meaningful self-assessment behavior, which is crucial for self-regulated and lifelong learning. • Key research finding 4 (effects of self-assessment): Yan (under review) revealed that self-assessment has a generally positive impact on students’ academic performance. Feedback seeking through monitoring in the Performance phase of self-regulated learning was the strongest and most positive predictor of academic achievement. Significance: The finding about the general positive impact of self-assessment echoed the results of previous studies regarding the effectiveness of self-assessment and justified the inclusion of self-assessment in schooling.

18605715.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18605715.value: There are two directions in which to further develop this line of research. First, it will be meaningful to design sustainable instructional strategies/interventions that can promote meaningful self-assessment practices without introducing excessive teaching and learning workloads in natural learning contexts. A GRF proposal on this topic was developed and submitted in November 2018. Second, it is important to explore how to promote the uptake of self-assessment and maximize its positive impact in classrooms. A large-scale project, in collaboration with the HKEAA and local schools, is under preparation. This project aims to develop a learning support system centered on self-assessment with the support of digital technologies. This learning support system could be a pivot point for facilitating the attainment of the goals of educational reform, such as self-regulated learning and lifelong learning. The advantages of this system include: 1) it benefits all relevant stakeholders including schools, teachers, students, and parents; 2) it enhances students’ learning performance (both long-term and short-term) by placing students in the central role with other stakeholders as supporters; 3) it reduces teachers’ workload and facilitates teaching by changing their working convention; and 4) it brings social and economic benefits by enhancing the effectiveness of the education system.

18605715.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18605715.value: This GRF project has investigated the “chain” of student self-assessment from predictors of self-assessment, through calibration of self-assessment, to its impact on student learning outcomes. The research outcomes of this project have addressed four important issues: 1) uncovering the inner process of self-assessment calibration and identifying the common actions students engage in during self-assessment; 2) developing a valid instrument (Self-assessment Practice Scale [SaPS]) for assessing self-assessment practice; 3) identifying predictors that influence students’ intentions and practices regarding self-assessment; and 4) demonstrating the positive effects of self-assessment on students’ learning outcomes and identifying a possible mechanism of the effects of self-assessment. This study has contributed to the theoretical development of self-assessment by breaking down the “black box” of the inner process of self-assessment calibration. The cyclical process model of self-assessment, together with the SaPS, laid a solid foundation for future research on self-assessment. The findings about the characteristics of self-assessment practices and the predictors of self-assessment can inform optimized use of self-assessment in learning and teaching practice. The empirical evidence regarding the positive effects of self-assessment on student learning justifies the inclusion of self-assessment in schooling at the policy-making level.
