18606215.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18606215.value: In the 2008 Hong Kong Literature Festival, the veteran poet Wu Yin Ching 胡燕青 gave an interesting paper titled "Food, Clothing, Housing and Transportation in Hong Kong New Poetry" (xianggang xinshi li de yishizhuxing). The Chinese expression "yishizhuxing" 衣食住行 refers to the basic necessities of life. As the most mundane part of our daily existence, such needs and activities might not seem to be particularly poetic to many readers. But some of Wu’s examples are remarkably lively, imbued with deep emotions without giving in to sentimentality; some deal with disagreeable urban experiences, yet enlivened by personal reflections and aesthetic devices. The object of this project is the poetic treatments of everyday modernity in 1970s Hong Kong, but not restricted to the four basic necessities mentioned above. By “modernity” we mean the social changes brought about by urbanization, commercialization and other socio-economic forces of capitalist development. Such social changes and their diverse effects as experienced in people’s everyday life were particularly palpable during the 1970s, when rapid development took place in Hong Kong due to the “economic take-off,” social changes and urban development. The importance of Hong Kong poetry about daily urban experience in the 1970s lies not only in its function as vivid historical documents. Some of them are of high literary merits. Many poets concerned had developed their writing skills with inspirations from Western modernist arts and literature or from classical and modern Chinese poetry, including the modernist variety in Taiwan. Writing poems of such lyrical quality or personal insights about the commonplace is always a great challenge. The best of Hong Kong poets at that time succeeded and left us a rich literary legacy. This project investigates the thematic nuances and literary skills in these poems, focusing in particular on the subtle expressions of emotions and self-reflections, examining how poetry serves as a privileged medium bridging private experiences and larger social or cultural concerns. The project will make use of and further develop existing scholarships of modern Chinese poetry as well as Western modernisms. Thematic and theoretical inspirations will also be drawn from research on everyday life and modernity in sociological and cultural studies. As a vibrant meeting place between East and West, 1970s Hong Kong produced some of the best, or at least most interesting, modern Chinese poems, which may be hybrid in language or artistic conception; thus a comparative perspective will be adopted where appropriate.

18607515.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18607515.value: Harnessing information technology in education is believed to strengthen and facilitate learning and teaching in the 21st century. The Hong Kong government has shown its determination to promote e-learning by launching three Information Technology in Education strategies and a series of major initiatives such as the Pilot Scheme on E-Learning in Schools, and the E-Textbook Market Development Scheme. These schemes have encouraged the development of e-textbooks that align with the local curricula. However, use of e-textbooks in classrooms is seen as a challenge for teachers and learners. Whether the adoption of e-textbooks can bring fundamental changes to teachers’ practices to offer meaningful learning experience and educational learning environment for students is a concern for local educators. In order to respond to this concern, evidence should be collected to explain how teachers' practical theories and their pedagogical practices are influenced through the process of using e-textbook and how students' learning is facilitated in the same process. The evidence will also constitute a solid foundation for the further revision of e-textbook and the design of teacher professional development programme for using e-textbooks. These are the major objectives of the current research. In this study, a set of the newly designed e-textbooks of the core subject General Studies at primary level included in the recommended e-textbook list is chosen for use. General Studies is interdisciplinary in nature, which emphasises on an inquiry approach, and is widely considered as complementary to e-learning. Design-based research methodology will be adopted considering its potential to facilitate generation of new theories for conceptualising learning, instruction and design processes. Four schools randomly selected from the Pilot Scheme on E-learning Schools, each with two teachers of varied teaching experiences and their students, will be invited as research participants. Teachers will be involved in two cycles of inquiry into their use of e-textbook in two consecutive school semesters. Each cycle is made up of four stages, namely analysis of teachers’ practical theories of teaching with e-textbook, lesson planning, implementation and reflection on teaching. Various methods such as interviews, classroom observations and reflective journals will be used to capture teachers’ conceptual changes and corresponding pedagogical practices with e-textbook. Analytics in education such as log file analysis and cognitive walkthrough will be conducted with students to acquire better understanding of learning processes and to inform teaching improvement.

18607515.label: Realisation of objectives
18607515.value: To address these objectives, data of eight teachers and their students from Grades 3 to 6 in four schools were collected through lesson observations, teacher reflective journals, individual teacher interviews, and student cognitive walkthrough. In total, 51 lessons were observed, 33 reflections were collected (Due to three teachers being busy with teaching and other work and changing school after a semester, their reflections were unable to be collected), 28 interviews with teachers were conducted, and 48 cognitive walkthroughs were conducted. All data were video- or audio-taped for further transcription and analysis. For data analysis, to address objective 1, teacher interview data were analysed through content analysis. Themes used to understand teachers’ existing perceptions of e-textbook use for science learning included: (1) Usefulness – beliefs of the usefulness of e-learning resources for achieving learning goals (2) Proper teaching approaches– perceptions of effective teaching methods for e-learning in the classroom, and (3) Barriers to implementing e-learning – beliefs about the degree to which barriers (e.g. lack of support, time limitation) would affect instruction. To address objective 2, data from teacher interviews and student cognitive walkthroughs were used. Changes in teachers’ perceptions of teaching with e-textbooks were tracked through comparing teachers’ interviews before and after their teaching practices. Factors influencing teacher practice were explored in terms of personal factors (e.g. the teacher’s own teaching style) and contextual factors (e.g. student-related factors, technical issues). To address objective 3, lesson observation data were analyzed based on the Resource-based e-Learning Environment (RBeLEs) framework which consists of four dimensions: contexts created, use of resources, use of tools, and adoption of scaffolds. The findings from analyzing lesson observation data and the findings from analyzing teacher interview data (objective 2) were combined in order to understand the relationships between teacher practices and their belief change. To address objective 4, student data collected from cognitive walkthrough were used to explore students’ perceptions and experiences of learning with e-learning resources and multi-media. Through linking these findings with the findings related to teachers’ belief change and their pedagogical practices (objectives 2 and 3), how student-related factors affect teachers’ textbook acceptance and adoption was further studied. To address objective 5, the patterns of scientific inquiry activities in the e-textbook were analyzed. Then, models for each (Evidence-based approach, Experiential approach, Predict-observe-explain approach) were consolidated to show how the combined use of multimedia resources and inquiry approaches can support students’ inquiry of science phenomena for conceptual understanding. Based on the above analysis, six conference papers and presentations were submitted to and accepted by five international conferences. Four journal articles were completed, in which three have been accepted for publication in academic journals.

18607515.label: Major findings and research outcome
18607515.value: Major findings include: a. Through analyzing teachers’ beliefs and e-textbook use, it was found in this study that teachers mostly perceived e-textbooks as acceptable, appealing, useful, and easy to use. Some teachers were concerned about the decrease in teacher/student interaction and the difficulties in managing classrooms, as students were likely to be overexcited about using tablets during lessons. b. Teachers’ use of e-textbooks in the classroom was greatly influenced by their own teaching style, students’ over-excitement about iPad use, the adaptability of e-learning resources, as well as technical limitations. Teachers’ pedagogical beliefs fundamentally influenced their practices. Teachers’ beliefs about technology affected and was affected by their experience of teaching with e-textbooks. c. Based on the Resource-Based e-Learning Environment (RBeLEs) framework, analysis of lesson observation data indicated that the teachers created contexts that were teacher determined or teacher-and-students negotiated. They made more use of static resources and provided tools of ‘information processing’ and ‘communicating’ and scaffolds including ‘doing and observing’, ‘asking and discussing’ and ‘summarising and conceptualising’ to stimulate students’ inquiry learning. d. The analysis of students’ interview data revealed that the use of the e-textbook provided a platform for students’ self-regulated learning. However, for effective self-regulated learning, students need scaffolds from the e-textbook and teachers to face several challenges, such as developing an understanding of the nature of scientific inquiry, or making effective use of e-learning tools. e. By analyzing how the primary students learned about the seasons with the e-learning resources, the results also indicated that the process of discussing prior knowledge of the seasons through online forums as well as analysing the weather data of temperature, humidity, and rainfall as evidence to explain seasons helped to facilitate the students’ conceptual changes and construction, as well as their awareness and skills of evidence use in scientific explanations. f. A framework/model highlighting three approaches to scientific inquiry, namely evidence-based approach, experimental approach, and predict-observe-explain approach, was proposed for designing inquiry activities in e-textbooks for science teaching and learning.

18607515.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18607515.value: a. Further research on teacher professional development related to technology use is needed, on one hand, to help teachers with traditional beliefs change their beliefs to be more constructivist and to implement e-learning or technology-supported learning in more student-centred way; on the other hand, to help teachers develop knowledge and skills of scaffolding students’ self-regulated learning in e-learning environments. b. Further research on improving the quality of e-learning resources (e.g., e-textbooks) is needed. Particularly, it is important to improve the pedagogical aspects of e-learning resources to meet the needs of both teachers and students. c. Sustained efforts to develop infrastructure to ensure the readiness of computing hardware and Internet connectivity in schools is still needed to better motivate teachers’ technology integrations in their teaching.

18607515.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18607515.value: This study investigated teachers’ practical theories and practice with e-textbooks, as well as students’ e-learning patterns through lesson observations and interviews. The findings in this study contributed to the understandings of the features of teachers’ beliefs about teaching and technology, practices with e-textbook, and the relations between belief and practice. In addition, this study explored the patterns or challenges of students’ learning with e-textbooks, which can be used to inform teachers’ effective implementation of e-learning in the classroom. Moreover, this study had practical implications for decision makers, educators, and publishers to maximize the positive impacts of curricula and teacher education related to e-learning. The framework generated can serve as a basis to design more adaptive e-textbooks and as a reference to design training programmes within and beyond schools to facilitate teachers’ sharing of pedagogical considerations and changes in beliefs and practices regarding technology-based learning so as to ensure more effective classroom use of technologies including e-textbooks.

18608315.label: Project Objectives
18608315.value: Explain findings of cultural differences in variability in behavior by reference to both emic Chinese moral values and etic principles of responsible behavior. Empirically demonstrate that compared to Westerners, Chinese perceive relationally variable behavior to indicate good moral character more than Americans do. Empirically demonstrate that compared to those with worse moral character, Chinese participants with more salient or excellent moral character will be more likely to show relationally variable behavior. Through the above empirical demonstrations, build evidence that cultural differences in behavioral variability are not only a descriptive norm (what is done), but encouraged by injunctive norms (what is valued).

18608315.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18608315.value: Is it morally good to treat different people differently? While Confucianism relationalism emphasizes the importance of attending to social ties (Hwang, 2012), Western moral philosophy emphasizes the importance of applying abstract moral principles with little regard for relationships (Rosemont & Ames, 2009). Previous cultural psychology studies have shown that East Asian participants display more behavioral variability across different relationship roles than Western participants do, but the cultural cause of this difference has not been empirically identified (e.g. Katigbak et al., 2013). Among Chinese participants, is such role-based variability not only a descriptive norm, but an injunctive norm-- reflecting moral values about how one ought to act? With a series of experimental and correlational studies, using cross-cultural comparisons as well as comparisons of Chinese participants with higher and lower moral character, this project will amass evidence that behavioral variability across social roles is supported by moral norms in Chinese culture. The studies build on previous work by the PI outlining lay beliefs about the important factors of Chinese moral character, and extend this work to showing how moral beliefs influence daily perceptions and behavior. Findings will help explain how cultural differences in personality variability may be supported by cultural differences in moral principles, and may be extended to practical problems such as moral conundrums in the workplace. 對不同人士有不同的對待，在道德上是否正確呢？儒家倫理主義強調人與人之間社會關係的重要性（Hwang, 2012），而西方道德哲學則強調切實執行道德原則時，盡量減少考慮人際關係（Rosemont & Ames, 2009）。過往的文化心理學研究指出，東亞地區的參與者較西方地區的參與者在不同的身份角色上，表現出更多的行為差異，但這種東、西方文化差別的原因尚未被研究確定（如Katigbak et al., 2013）。在中國，這種以身份角色為基礎的行為差異，是否不只是一種普通的行為常態，而是一種猶如禁令般的規範—會否反映出一些規範人們應該如何行動的道德價值？隨著一系列的實驗性和相關性研究，透過跨文化的比較，以及比較中國參與者中擁有較高和較低道德觀的參與者，本研究項目將印證不同身份角色下的行為差異是否基於中國文化中的道德標準。本研究建基於主研究員早前一個概述中式道德品格的重要因素的研究，並延展該研究以顯示道德價值如何影響日常的觀念和行為。研究結果將有助理解不同文化的人的性格差異程度不同，是否由於其道德原則的文化差異，甚而有助理解一些實際問題，例如在工作中遇到的道德難題。

To identify the relationship between teacher professional development and the roles played by facilitators in practitioner research.
To construct a model for facilitating sustainable teacher professional development through practitioner research by defining the roles of teachers, facilitators and researchers.

18608615.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18608615.value: There has been a call in the education literature over the last two decades for making Practitioner Research (PR) a key characteristic of high quality Teacher Professional Development (TPD). There are extensive reports on the positive and profound impacts of PR on TPD, and a positive relationship between PR and the sustainability of TPD has been shown. As there is a lack of research on the development of teachers’ research ability in PR, this study addresses the research gap through investigating 16 Hong Kong Liberal Studies teachers’ development in relation to both teaching and research through conducting PR on teaching critical thinking in secondary classrooms. Moreover, it looks into the relationship between teacher development and the roles played by the facilitators. A model of facilitating sustainable teacher professional development through PR will be generated by synthesizing the findings and reflections of teachers, facilitators and researchers. A total of four schools, with four teachers from each school, will participate in the study. Each school will be assigned a facilitator who is one of the project team members. After attending a total of 10 hours of professional workshops focusing on teaching critical thinking and conducting PR, the teachers will be involved in two cycles of inquiry into teaching critical thinking. Each cycle will consist of five stages of PR, namely wondering, experimentation, evaluation, learning, and sharing. At the end of each cycle, a sharing session will be held which will be attended by all the participating teachers in the project. Data will be collected through (i) interviews with teachers and facilitators, (ii) observations of lessons, lessons involving teachers’ research, post-lesson discussion, group meetings, individual meetings, and sharing sessions, and (iii) documentary analysis of teachers and facilitators’ logbooks, materials associated with the observed lessons (including lesson plans, worksheets, quizzes, and reading materials), notes of meetings, emails between teachers and facilitators, as well as teachers’ research plans and reports. This study will advance our understanding of TPD on two main fronts. Firstly, it will add to the literature knowledge about the process of TPD in both research and teaching through PR, as well as the relationship between TPD and the roles played by the facilitators in PR. Secondly, the study will build a model for facilitating sustainable teacher professional development through PR, which will provide insights into the design of similar projects or programmes. 教育文獻於過去二十年來認為實踐者研究可以成為促進高質素教師專業發展的一個主要研究方法。多份研究報告經已指出實踐者研究對教師專業發展有著積極而深遠的影響，並且肯定實踐者研究與教師專業可持續發展存在正面的關係。然而，有見現時以實踐者研究方法探究教師發展仍然缺乏，因此，本研究計劃的目的是希望填補該研究範疇的裂縫。計劃將邀請香港十六位任教通識科目的中學教師參與，從觀察及研究其於課堂教授批判思維的表現，以實踐者研究的方法探究教師於教學及研究方面的專業發展，同時亦研究協調員於教師發展中所扮演的角色及彼此的關係，最後綜合教師、協調員及研究人員的反饋及研究所得，以建構促進教師專業可持續發展的模式。 計劃將邀請四所中學各派出四位教師參與。每所中學會獲委派一位研究計劃小組成員作為協調員。經過完成共十小時有關批判思維教學的專業工作坊及進行實踐者研究後，教師們會經歷兩輪批判思維教學的探究過程，而每一輪都必須經過實踐者研究的五個階段，分別為懷疑、實驗、評估、學習及分享。每一個循環的終結時，所有參與研究計劃的教師們都需出席分享會。而研究數據會經以下方式搜集：1) 與教師及協調員面談；2) 觀課，內容包括教師們的研究計劃、課後討論、小組會議、個人會議及分享會；3) 就教師及協調員的活動日誌、與課堂有關的材料 (包括教學計劃、工作紙、測驗卷及其他閱讀材料)、會議紀錄、教師及協調員的電郵往來及教師們的研究計劃及報告進行文本分析。 本研究計劃將會增進我們對教師專業發展兩個不同向度的了解。第一，透過實踐者研究以及教師專業發展與協調員角色的關係，為教師專業發展過程提供研究及教學層面的文獻紀錄；第二，通過實踐者研究以建構一個促進教師專業可持續發展的模式，從而為日後相類似的研究計劃提供新的視角。

18608615.label: Realisation of objectives
18608615.value: The objectives have been achieved to a satisfactory extent. Outputs include one published article, one submitted manuscript, one draft in preparation for submission, and three conference presentations. Financial support from GRF was acknowledged for all the outputs. Objective 1: To understand the outcomes of teacher professional development in both research and teaching through practitioner research (PR). The objective was achieved by analyzing data gathered from teacher interviews, reflective field notes, teacher self-evaluation of their lessons, and student surveys. Findings showed that despite contextual challenges, teachers re-defined their role in creating a supportive classroom atmosphere which promotes interaction and hence facilitates students’ development of critical thinking (CT). Detailed qualitative findings were reported in the manuscript submitted to the Journal of Professional Development in Education (Cheng & Li, submitted). Teachers were engaged in reflecting on evidence of student learning during the PR. They observed an improvement in student performance in CT and engagement. Detailed results related to student data as an outcome of PR can be found in the published paper (Cheng & Wan, 2017) and the paper presented at the AERA 2018 annual meeting (Cheng & Li, 2018). Objective 2: To identify the relationship between teacher professional development and the roles played by facilitators in practitioner research. The research confirmed the important role played by the teachers and the facilitation of the research team in improving students’ CT in the process of teachers’ PR in the classroom. Findings related to lesson observation were reported at the HKERA conference (Cheng & Li, 2017). Instead of seeing the university team or facilitators as experts possessing knowledge, knowledge was shared throughout the proposed PR process and developed interactively between the teachers and the university team. Knowledge of the innovative teaching strategies and reference materials related to teaching content, innovative teaching strategies and approaches to facilitating students’ development of CT are shared by the teachers who actively select and adapt those relevant to their teaching context. Input from the university team is provided not only at the beginning but also when teachers have completed the first inquiry cycle and are reflecting on their teaching and the learning of their students. The university team serves as a critical friend as well as a collaborator in PR, offering feedback and support in collecting and analysing evidence of student learning which forms the basis of teachers’ reflection. Findings can be found in the manuscript submitted to the Journal of Professional Development in Education (Cheng & Li, submitted). Objective 3: To construct a model for facilitating sustainable teacher professional development through practitioner research by defining the roles of teachers, facilitators and researchers. Our pilot findings suggest more frequent one-off training workshops and seminars were perceived as too theoretical, while teachers found forming teams and being engaged in co-teaching and co-planning to be more effective. Sustainable PD needs to involve teachers in lesson observations and reflection on teaching. Findings were reported at the 8th TEAN Annual Conference (Cheng, Lee, & Yu, 2017). At the conclusion of this PR project, to make PR feasible, a university and teacher collaborative approach to PR is proposed. This approach emphasizes interaction and communication between the university team and the teachers. PR adopting this collaborative approach involves co-planning in at least two cycles of inquiry. This allows teachers to build up their confidence, develop a collaborative relationship with the university team and reflect on their teaching based on their experience and data on student performance in the first cycle. Teachers become ready to move out of their comfort zone, and are open to their own reflections and to suggestions from the university team as a critical friend. The second cycle involves teachers re-visiting their plans and enhancing their designs. After the two cycles of inquiry, the experienced teachers are ready to analyse the impact of PR on the learning of the students and to chart their directions, which can further enhance their teaching. This approach was elaborated in the paper submitted to the Journal of Professional Development in Education (Cheng & Li, submitted).

18608615.label: Major findings and research outcome
18608615.value: The major findings include: 1) The impact of PR on teachers’ professional development a. adopting new teaching strategies; b. using evidence to support reflection on student learning and teaching; c. communicating and collaborating with other teachers; d. and the redefining of teachers’ roles. The impact on teacher professional development involves fundamental changes as teachers work and improve their teaching as a team, conduct reflection based on evidence of student learning, and are open to unfamiliar teaching strategies as a group. The teachers re-define their roles as promoting participation and interaction to facilitate students’ development of CT (see Cheng, Lee, & Yu, 2017; Cheng & Li, 2017; Cheng & Li, submitted). 2) The impact of PR on student learning a. improved student performance in critical thinking development; b. improved student lesson engagement. Results showed a consistent improvement in students’ critical thinking behaviors across dimensions, regarding both CT propensity and skills. Findings reflect improved student engagement in the classroom both from behavioral and cognitive perspectives. There was also a significant increase in student higher order thinking behaviors comparing the first and second inquiry cycle (see Cheng & Li, 2018; Cheng & Wan, 2017). 3) The contextual challenges of conducting PR identified by Hong Kong secondary school teachers: a. a tight teaching schedule; b. increased teacher workload; c. adoption of new teaching strategies. The findings echo the recommendation from previous research that support for schools is essential to make teacher professional development effective, and that sufficient time and space are required (Cheng & Li, submitted). 4) Effective facilitation with a collaborative approach, which led to positive impacts on student learning and teacher professional developments: a. providing reference materials; b. enhancing teachers’ understanding of the teaching innovations; c. providing support for analysing data related to student performance; d. providing feedback on teaching. The research outcome proposes a university school collaboration approach to facilitating PR which takes into account the challenging school factors in an Asia-Pacific context (Cheng & Li, submitted).

18608615.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18608615.value: Building on this GRF project, further research may investigate ways to maximize the impact or benefits of PR such as: 1) tracking the continuous professional development among the teachers in this study, 2) stimulating or promoting in-depth reflection among the teachers, 3) enhancing cooperation between teachers across subject teams, and 4) encouraging teachers experienced in PR to provide mentoring for pre-service teachers by conducting PR during the field experience period.

18608615.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18608615.value: This project contributes to the literature by providing evidence of the effectiveness of practitioner research (PR) as a sustainable teacher professional development strategy in the Asia-Pacific context. The impact of PR includes improved student performance and engagement, motivating teachers to adopt innovative teaching approaches and fundamental changes as they collaborate in teams and redefine their roles in the classroom. Findings reflect the challenges in conducting PR in an Asia-Pacific context including tight teaching schedules, heavy teaching workload and adapting to new teaching approaches. Despite the challenges, effective support and collaborative strategies adopted by the university team during PR, such as providing reference materials related to teaching content and innovative teaching strategies; enhancing teachers’ understanding of critical thinking; providing feedback on teaching; and providing support for data analysis, were identified by teachers. The project has generated findings and suggestions that can guide teacher educators, university research academics and school administrators in establishing a collaborative, research-rich environment to encourage teachers to conduct inquiry in their classrooms, to better assume their roles as knowledge producers, and ultimately, to improve the effectiveness of their classroom teaching. Finally, a collaborative approach for PR involving co-planning in at least two cycles of inquiry is proposed.

18609415.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18609415.value: 香港性小眾在社會服務界是否受到平等對待仍然面臨挑戰。社會工作學者認為社會人士對性小眾的負面態度可以透過培訓而改變。本計劃的目標是： 1)發展社會工作者性別多元化培訓課程; 2) 評估上述課程在消除負面態度的成效。與此同時，本計劃將探討相關的社會工作實務及専業守則，探討如何達到平等共融的社會工作理念。

18609415.label: Realisation of objectives
18609415.value: Objective 1 Objective achieved through the following tasks: Through document analysis and literature review, we found that heterosexism and prejudice against sexual minorities persist in most Asian Chinese societies, including Hong Kong, where anti-prejudice policies and support programs for service users and helping professionals were rare and insufficient. Based on this review and other community observations in public forums, we realized the challenges of facing prejudice as research team members and the difficulties in recruiting informants under heteronormative atmosphere. Strategies were used to overcome the challenges, such as prolonged engagement, persistent community observations, using ethnographic observational strategies, obtaining institutional supports, and offering alternative ways of interviews etc. to maintain collaborative relationship with stake holders, so as to collect information rich data. By using these strategies, we were able to recruit more than 100 informants and such sample size has surpassed the originally proposed size (40 informants). We learnt from informants on how they perceived sexual diversity, sexual prejudice, sexual minority students’ experiences, and how sexual prejudice has been constructed in the society and in social service settings. They also informed us about accounts of diverse sexual identities, including those with fluid, non-binary, and multiple identities on the sexuality spectrum, in addition to those whose sexual identities fall within the binary spectrum. Additional difficulties were found in a subgroup of informants who have trans identities, and those with mental health and disability concerns. They faced multiple layers of barriers in help seeking process, such as individual level engagement barriers, agency level and professional level barriers, by not being acknowledged of their sexualities in their life, in addition to accessibility of services. We also learned that informants in the social service sectors faced dilemma/institutional barriers in understanding diverse sexualities of service users, including sexual, gender, disability, and other social identities. Training themes, cultural limitations, and strategies in conducting sexual diversity training were informed by the informants. Objective 2 The following tasks were completed to achieve the objective: Related to informants’ suggestions from qualitative interviews, we modified the recruitment and sampling method, as well as training content and format to better engage participants joining the training. Training location was suggested to be changed to professional organizations and training institutes; non-random sampling was adopted instead of random sampling. Examples of the contents included critical awareness - cultural construction of sexual prejudice within the social service context, connecting social work and sexuality, code of ethics and reflective social work practice, and contacts and dialogue. The training with experimental intervention-control-group design were conducted with 333 participants. Scales examining the training effectiveness were validated with good to excellent internal consistency, convergent, and discriminant validities. Results from one-way between-group ANCOVA showed that significant differences were found between the control and experimental group across the scale scores. Participants in the experimental group were found to have significantly less negative attitude, more favorable civil right attitude, more perceived and actual knowledge, and more ready to adopt affirmative practice in working with sexual minority issues.

18609415.label: Major findings and research outcome
18609415.value: Review of literature found that heterosexism against sexual minorities persist in most Asian societies, where anti-heterosexist policies and social service programs were uncommon or non-existent, except in Taiwan, where the government has established legal and institutional supports to sexual minorities. Heteronormative socio-cultural climate in Hong Kong, both within the social service system and in the wider society, makes it challenging to build in LGBT-friendly programs within mainstream social service agencies without government initiatives and institutional supports. Transcripts from over 100 informants were derived in the qualitative research, with semi-structured in-depth interviews and ethnographic observations, in sexual minority and social service communities. Result found that social work informants, although one group of them were knowledgeable about the concepts of sexual orientation, some were uncomfortable to talk about sexuality as non-binary, fluid, or spectrum-based concepts, especially those informants working in clinical settings and/or religious affiliated services. Another group of social work informants, with the training or work context implementing rights-based approaches, adopted broad spectrum and non-binary conceptions. Sexual minority informants, in addition to the traditional binary concept of sex, were also aware of the ignored intersex, multiple dimensions of gender and sexuality. They experienced double or triple layers of barriers within social services, having help-seeking and engagement barriers, institutional/agency level barriers. Both social workers and sexual minority informants indicated that Confucians’ familial value and colonial religiosity embedded in Hong Kong social service context might well be important cultural forces contributing to sexual prejudice manifested in service delivery to sexual minorities. Although human rights and social justice concepts were embedded in professional code of practice of social work profession, sexual minority informants found that not all social workers were able to handle their dilemma well in their service delivery process, because of their personal and institution’s cultural and/or religious backgrounds. Based on the themes, the training with experimental intervention-control-group design were conducted with 333 participants. Scales examining the training effectiveness were validated with good to excellent internal consistency, convergent, and discriminant validities. Results from one-way between-group ANCOVA showed that significant differences were found between the control and experimental group across the scale scores. Participants in the experimental group were found to have significantly less negative attitude, more favorable civil right attitude, more perceived and actual knowledge, and more ready to adopt affirmative practice in working with sexual minority issues.

18609415.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18609415.value: Based on this research experience, we found that sexual minorities with non-binary or fluid identities faced visibility and multiple help-seeking barriers in health and social service settings, especially those who are gender variant, non-binary, with chronic illness/disability, and mental health concerns. This group of informants suffered multiple marginalization. A project proposal on trans-prejudice has been submitted and approved, which has been started for few months. Collaboration with community agencies with grant support from the Equal Opportunities Commission will be started in July 2019, to work on a trans visibility project. A postgraduate student under the PI’s supervision has started a project on sexuality and special educational needs. A conference on Asian Sexuality Education, with focus to address diversity and inclusiveness has been under planning at EdUHK, with P.I. as one of the organizing committee member, and collaborating with the Family Planning Association of Hong Kong, to address challenges of developing and implementing sexuality education for sexual minorities and other disability/marginalized groups. Keynote speakers from international sexual health research institutions and UNESCO Asia/China have been invited by the P.I.. Further research possibilities will be explored.

18609415.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18609415.value: The study is of significance by reporting the difficulties, barriers, dilemma, and professional training themes of social workers in delivery social work services to sexual minorities in Hong Kong. It also reveals and acknowledges the existence of diverse, fluid sexual expressions/identities of some sexual minorities in Chinese society, challenging the essentialist and binary paradigm of gender and sexuality. Validation of the Chinese translated scales to measure attitudes, knowledge and intended behaviors of social workers to support sexual minorities has contributed to the advancement of quantitative measurement for researchers in Hong Kong or those in greater Chinese-speaking regions. Qualitative study was adopted to understand social worker training themes, and the cultural barriers to implement the training in Hong Kong. Quantitative study has confirmed that the training is effective in enhancing social worker’s attitudes and knowledge/intended practice behaviors to support sexual minorities.

18610515.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18610515.value: 對於高中階段的學生，有明確的職業定位，以及與職業相關的能力、目標、興趣和選擇對生涯規劃是重要的。在香港，為了加強不同學習能力的中學生職業指導和生涯規劃， “自2014至2015學年開始，政府將給所有開設高中課程的公立學校提供源源不斷的資金支持，用於拓展學校老師和教學人員的能力，使其更好地服務于本校的高中生職業指導和生涯規劃教育”（教育局，2014，第三頁）。雖然針對此議題已制定初步的指導方針和資源提供，但是在香港本地，關於高中生職業指導和生涯規劃如何實施和怎樣評估的研究卻遠遠不夠。雖然越來越多的研究開始關注高中生的職業生涯規劃教育，但是，到目前為止，還沒有研究去探索香港或者亞洲地區有關特殊教育需要學生和正常學生的職業生涯規劃教育的效果。本研究目的在與探索職業生涯規劃教育對香港融合教育背景下有特殊教育需要學生和正常學生的長遠影響。研究同時採取了橫向和縱向的研究設計。數據收集對象為中四至中六學生，收集時間分別為取樣學校開展年度生涯規劃教育之前和之後。縱向研究設計有助於了解職業發展過程中，學生在關鍵的心理變量上發生的變化。除了通過不同的測量工具研究個體在職業生涯規劃教育中的變化，本研究還採取了深度訪談的研究方法，用於了解不同持份者對職業生涯規劃教育的看法，以及分析職業生涯規劃項目實施過程中遭遇的不同類型的支持和阻力。研究最終結果會幫助改善職業生涯規劃教育項目，以及提供建議改善相關政策用於支援融合教育實踐中能力不同學生的職業發展。

18610515.label: Realisation of objectives
18610515.value: According to the proposal, the research team conducted two rounds of data collection, including survey and focus group interview, to fulfill the 4 proposed research questions. During the two-year study, 14 secondary schools were recruited. At the first-round (pre-test) of survey study, SEN students (N=204) from 10 schools returned their questionnaire, a matching sample of non-SEN students were also involved to help generate a good understanding of SEN students’ characteristics in terms of these career-related variables tested in this study. Students’ age ranged from 14 to 22 with mean =16.39 and SD=1.158. Among these SEN students, nine categories of special needs were reported. 39.6% reported with more than one category of special needs. 24.3% with SpLD and 11.9% with ADHD. Other SEN categories including SLI (7.3%), EBD (5.6%), VI (3.4%), ASD (2.3%), CD (2.3%), HI (1.7%) and ID (1.7%). In post-test survey study, SEN students (N=195) from 9 schools returned their questionnaire, a matching sample of non-SEN students were also involved for comparison purposes as designed in this study. For further understanding the implication situation of school-based career education programme, the research team conducted a series of interview, participants were schoolteachers, students and parents. Among the 14 school which joined the survey part of this study, 4 schools agreed to arrange focus group interviews for research team. During the pretest, 13 teachers (4 groups) from school career guidance team and 12 teachers (4 group) from other subjects joined the focus group interviews. Only 3 schools agreed to arrange students and their parents’ interview. The number of participants were 8 Non-SEN students, 4 Non-SEN parents, 6 SEN students and 5 SEN parents. Concerned the labeling issue and participants requirements, these group of interviews were conducted one by one or two as a group. Objective 1 “compare SEN and regular senior secondary students’ cognitive-person gains from career planning programs in terms of their career decision self-efficacy, career outcome expectations, career-related goals, career planning and career exploration. We measured the variables listed in objective 1 with career adaptabilities scale (Maggiori, Rossier, Savickas, 2015) and career development self-efficacy inventory (Yuen, Gysbers, Chan, Lau, Leung, Hui, & Shea, 2005). Regarding to the students’ career development self-efficacy, in general, there are no significant difference between Non-SEN group and SEN group students p>.05 in both pretest and posttest. However, in pretest, students from SEN group have higher confidence in career planning and career goal setting than that of student from Non-SEN group. Interestingly, SEN students’ confidence on career goal setting became lower than that of Non-SEN student in posttest although no statistic significant was found, p>.05. After one-year interval, student from SEN group obtained higher score on career planning (p<.01) and career goal setting(p>.05) subscale during the post-test. However, situation in Non-SEN group didn’t change too much. Concern to students’ career adaptabilities, in general, Non-SEN group has higher score than that of SEN group in pretest but with no statistic significant difference, p>.05. However, after one-year interval, this situation reversed in posttest. SEN group gained higher score in control, curiosity and confidence subscales even though no significant difference was found, p>.05. In Non-SEN group, compared with the pretest, students scored lower on whole scale and the four subscales (concern, control, curiosity and confidence) in posttest but has no statistic significant (p>.05). Different from Non-SEN group, students from SEN group had higher score in posttest than they did in pretest in terms of whole scale and the four subscales. Still this difference has not reached statistic significant (p>.05). Objective 2. examine SEN and regular senior secondary students’ perceived career supports on these key cognitive-person variables in career development process; We examined students’ perspective about the support from teachers, parents and their friends with career influence inventory (Fisher & Stafford, 1999). The results show that compared with student form SEN group, students from Non-SEN group held stronger perspective that their teachers, parents and friends have greater influence on their career, but only parents influence reached statistic significant, p<.01. Compared with pretest, in posttest, student with SEN reported their teachers, parents and peers pay more attention on their career planning, but only teacher’s influence has statistic significant. The same situation was also found in Non-SEN group except parent’s influent declined a little bit Objective 3. identify the developmental changes of both cognitive-person gains and perceived career supports and barriers to career development needs of students with and without SEN. From the survey data, as mentioned above in objective 2, while SEN student believed their parents pay more attention in posttest than that in pretest, Non-SEN student’s perception on their parents’ support to their career development declined in posttest. According to the interview data, the possible reasons maybe, on one hand, parents of Non-SEN students have no useful information to share with their children. From the interview, we learned that parents of Non-SEN student know little about their children’s participant situation of school-based career education activities. They seldom attend career education lectures/workshop/activities as well. On the other hand, there’s communication problem between parents and students. From interview we found that some SEN student seldom had discussions with their parents on the topic of their career plans. For example, when students were asked about their career plans, the only response would be “No” or “I don’t know. Will think about it later” Regarding to students needs to empower their career development, Non-SEN students hoped the school could provide more academic support and more opportunities to known/experience different jobs. For SEN student, they wish to know more detailed information about the jobs they interested. Objective 4. review the effectiveness of career planning programs for students with and without SEN to offer recommendations for policy-making and instructional practice We assessed students’ attitude toward the careen planning and life education programme in terms of their perceptions on their performance during the career education related activities and their attitude toward the advantage of school-based careen planning and life education programme. The result shows, SEN student gained higher score than Non-SEN student in terms of their perceptions on their performance on career education related activities. Both SEN and Non-SEN students held a positive attitude toward the career planning and life education program, as all the item mean score were larger than 2.7 (4 is the maximum value). They agreed that the programme would help them set career goals, make career decisions based on their interests and abilities and guide them to achieve their career goals. Although SEN group scored higher than Non-SEN group did in terms of their Perception on the advantage of career planning and life education course, no significant difference was found between the two groups. In short, all the objectives have been achieved accordingly, with the support of the stakeholders in the sample schools. The data pool provided evidences for understanding the contextual development on career planning and support to SEN students. The outcome is helpful for the knowledge dissemination and policy support for SEN students in the mainstreaming schools. It shed lights to the future intervention support in regard to the inclusion development in Hong Kong.

18610515.label: Major findings and research outcome
18610515.value: Based on the survey data , we found that the career adaptability of both SEN student and Non-SEN student improved after one-year interval. The career development self-efficacy of SEN students become higher in terms of career planning and career goal settings. Both SEN and Non-SEN students hold a positive attitude toward the school-based career guidance programme. While data of SEN students showed teachers, parents and peers pay more attention to their career development, data of Non-SEN students indicated their perception about their parents support on their career panning declined. This part of findings have been presented in the “HKERA International Conference 2018” and the “Learning & Teaching Expo Hong Kong 2018”. According to the focus group interview, we noticed that both SEN and Non-SEN students were clear about their interests but only few of them have a clear career goal. They were searching and adjusting their career goals based on the information or experiences they learned from the career guidance programme. From career guidance teachers point of view, there were two concerns 1) lack of information about the service related to career education. They need spent lot of time searching service/ resource for school’s career guidance programme. 2) Lack of manpower and time for out-school training. Substitute teachers are needed when career guidance teacher attend the training courses, however, there’s difficulty for hiring short term substitute teacher. We also found that lower participant rate of career education related parent activities arranged by schools were reported by the career guidance teacher. Similarly, parents of Non-SEN students reported they know little about the career education related activities their children attended at school. However on the other hand, compared to the parents of Non-SEN student, parents of student with SEN know more about the schools’ career education. This may partly explained the different changes of SEN and Non-SEN students' attitude toward their parents' support on their career development showed in the survey findings. Regarding the suggestions/ expectation about the school-based career education, different from parents of Non-SEN students that they preferred their children would get more academic support, parents of SEN students wished the school could provide more information about job experience/practice activities that suitable for their children. This part of finding has been presented on the “Autumn Forum: Advances and emerging issues in international and comparative education research 2018” and in the SEN theatre of “Learning & Teaching Expo Hong Kong 2018”.

18610515.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18610515.value: For future studies to test the effectiveness of career planning education in affecting diverse students’ career development needs, the following aspects 1)Strengthen professional training to school teachers, not only career-guidance coordinator, SENCO, but also other school subject teachers to implement the whole school approach to career guidance and support to students 2)Develop enhancement programs on career adaptability for diverse learners. According to findings in this study interventions aiming at the concern and control aspects for Non-SEN students would be more effective while SEN students may need focused interventions on the control and confidence aspects. 3)Enhance students’ career panning abilities and career goal setting abilities through school-based career guidance programs /activities. 4)Enhance the school-family communication and cooperation not only for students’ academic performance, but also for career education, e.g. the partnership with ADHD and SpLD Parent Associations for the support 5)Provide more information and supporting resources to career guidance team to further improve the school-based career guidance programs development, e.g. the collaboration with the Resource centre with the Society for the Deaf and for the Blind. 6)Initiate further support to SEN school leavers for further life-long learning, e.g. proposal submission to Jockey Club Charities Trust CE Community Project

18610515.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18610515.value: With both survey and interview methods this study evaluated the career development changes of senior secondary student with and without special educational needs (SEN and Non-SEN ) after the school-based career planning and life education programme was implemented. Participants were 204 SEN students and 204 Non-SEN students from 10 senior secondary schools. Two rounds of data were collected with one-year interval. Interviews, including teachers, parents and students, were conducted half year after each round of survey. The results showed that the career adaptability of both SEN student and Non-SEN student improved after one-year interval. The career development self-efficacy of SEN students become higher in terms of career planning and career goal settings. Both SEN and Non-SEN students hold a positive attitude toward the school-based career guidance programme. Teachers, parents and peers pay more attention to SEN students’ career development. Based on the interview data, more work needs to be done to strengthen professional training to schoolteachers, not only career-guidance coordinator, SENCO, but also other school subject teachers to implement the whole school approach to career guidance and support to students. School-family communication and cooperation for both students’ academic performance and career education is another point needs to pay more attention.

18610915.label: Project Title(Chinese)
18610915.value: 促進學校策略規劃能力的知識管理：檢視SECI知識管理模型在學校情境中的應用

18610915.label: Project Objectives
18610915.value: To determine the extent to which SECI knowledge processes enhance strategic planning capacity in the context of Hong Kong school education; and to identify the critical success factors for institutionalising the SECI knowledge creation mechanism for enhancing the strategic planning capacity of schools.
rows: To determine the extent to which SECI knowledge processes enhance strategic planning capacity in the context of Hong Kong school education; and
to identify the critical success factors for institutionalising the SECI knowledge creation mechanism for enhancing the strategic planning capacity of schools.

18610915.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18610915.value: This project applies the subject of knowledge management (KM) to the study of school management. KM is related to strategy management that makes use of information and knowledge as organisational resources for improving management processes including formulating, implementing, monitoring and evaluating strategic plans and thus enhancing organisational performance. KM aims to support organisations in the creation of a capable structure and mechanism that acquires, applies, shares, retains and even creates knowledge. KM can be used not only for problem solving and decision making but also for crafting strategies. Institutionalising a knowledge management mechanism in schools may support schools to enhance the strategic planning capacity so as to cope with the rapid changes generated from the complex and challenging policy environment. The project seeks to identify the critical success factors that facilitate the institutionalisation of the Nonaka’s (1994) SECI knowledge creation mechanism within schools. This study will examine whether institutionalising the mechanism in schools could enhance their strategic planning capacities. The education quality assurance policy and the high speed of knowledge expansion knowledge have impacted on and created challenges for school management. The nature of school management becomes more challenging, complex, analytic and data driven. Developing an innovative management approach to support schools to leverage knowledge from the existing organisational information and data resources to plan for improvement will provide practical help to school leaders and also contribute to the existing school management theories. Experimental research design with a mixed-method approach will be adopted as the research strategy. A quantitative questionnaire survey and qualitative interviews will be conducted to collect data. Multilevel structural equation modelling will be applied to examine the predictive effects of the mechanism on strategic planning capacity and to identify the school level and teacher level contextual factors for institutionalising the SECI mechanism. Effective KM practices and the corresponding contextual factors will be identified through analysing the narrative patterns in interview scripts. Significant outcomes are expected from this study. First, the results will provide insights in applying theories of KM for streamlining strategic management in the school context. Second, contextual factors for institutionalizing the SECI mechanism in schools will be identified. This will respond to the international debate of the culture and context dependent issues on using Nonaka’s SECI model for knowledge creation (Glisby & Holden 2003; Hong 2012). Third, the study will identify effective management practices to school leaders for crafting strategies. 本計劃將知識管理概念應用於學校管理的研究之中。知識管理是策略管理的一種，其將資訊和知識作為組織資源應用於改善管理過程，包括策略規劃的制定、實施、監督及評估，從而提升組織的表現。知識管理的目的是支持組織建立知識獲取、應用、分享、保存甚至創造所需的結構與機制。除了能夠用於解決問題和作出決策，知識管理還可幫助制定策略。在學校將知識管理機制制度化可以協助學校提高策略規劃的能力，從而適應複雜及具挑戰性的政策環境所造成的變化。本計劃旨在探究在學校環境中將Nonaka （1994）的SECI知識創造機制制度化的關鍵成功因素。此研究將會探索在學校將該機制制度化能否提升學校的策略規劃能力。教育的質素保證政策以及高速的知識擴張已為學校的管理帶來衝擊和挑戰。學校管理變得越來越複雜及具挑戰性，越來越需要分析和以數據為導向。發展一個創新的管理方式來協助學校從現有的組織資訊與數據資源中創造可用於制定改善規劃的知識能夠為學校領導層帶來實際的幫助，並為現存的學校管理理論作出貢獻。此研究將採用混合方法實驗設計作為研究策略。量性問卷調查及質性面談將會用於收集數據。多層結構方程模型將會用以檢定SECI知識創造機制對策略規劃能力的預測效果和探究在學校與老師層面上將該機制制度化的環境因素。透過分析面談謄錄中的敘述模式，有效的知識管理實踐和相應的環境因素將可被辨識。此研究將會得到以下顯著的成果。第一，此研究的結果將幫助深入了解知識管理理論在精簡學校策略管理上的應用；第二，學校中協助SECI機制制度化的環境因素將會被識別，從而回應國際間有關Nonaka的SECI模型在知識創造的應用上文化和環境依存問題的爭論(Glisby & Holden 2003; Hong 2012)；第三，此研究將可發現協助學校領導層制定策略的有效管理實踐。

18610915.label: Realisation of objectives
18610915.value: The project fully achieved its primary objective, confirming the value of the SECI model in enhancing strategic planning capacity in Hong Kong school education. Strategic planning is empirically constructed as the process of planning, implementation, and evaluation. The knowledge externalization process predicts the knowledge combination process, and the knowledge combination process, in turn, predicts the process of planning, implementation, and evaluation. The project also fully achieved objective 2, identifying collaborative culture, organizational trust, justice, shared vision and systems thinking as critical factors for institutionalizing the SECI knowledge creation mechanism to enhance strategic planning capacity in schools. Mixed methods analysis was applied to realize these two objectives. The process involved a quantitative questionnaire survey, documentary analysis, and conducting qualitative interviews to collect data. We applied two-level structural equation modelling to examine the predictive effects of the SECI mechanism on strategic planning capacity and to examine the collaborative culture for institutionalizing the SECI mechanism. Analysis of narrative patterns in interview scripts allowed us to identify effective KM practices, cultural elements and contextual factors for school planning. The sample for the survey consisted of 42 principals/vice principals and 462 teachers (11 teachers/per school x 42 schools). A total of 392 principals and teachers returned completed questionnaires with signed consent forms, a response rate of 84.8%. Group A included 17 schools (9 primary schools and 8 secondary schools) in Hong Kong that had participated in a QEF project entitled “Applying Knowledge Management Practices in School Education for Sustainable Development” and institutionalized the SECI model for KM implementation. Group B consisted of 25 schools (12 primary schools and 13 secondary schools) randomly sampled from around 1000 Hong Kong schools. The principals and 10 HODs (or senior teachers) in each school who had taken part in the development of school plans were invited to participate in the survey and interviews. The aim of the survey was to collect data to explore the relationship between the SECI model and the school’s strategic planning capacity and to investigate the contextual factors for institutionalizing the SECI model in the school context. The reliability coefficient of all scales ranged from 0.777 to 0.926, which was judged adequate for this study. Initially, a single-level SEM model was established to explore the relationship between the knowledge conversation processes of the SECI model and the strategic planning capacity of schools. As most schools in Hong Kong conduct strategic planning via the planning-implementation-evaluation (P-I-E) cycle, the project team also re-conceptualized the strategic planning capacity of schools using the P-I-E cycle. A two-level SEM confirms the theoretical framework of this study. The model fits the data reasonably well. (RMSEA = 0.050 < 0.08; CFI = 0.939 > 0.9; TLI = 0.929 > 0.9; SRMR(W) = 0.035 < 0.08; SRMR(B) = 0.072 < 0.08). The teacher level SEM shows that the knowledge combination process predicts planning (β = 0.752, p < 0.01), implementation (β = 0.759, p < 0.01) and evaluation (β = 0.741, p < 0.01). Furthermore, the knowledge externalization process predicts the knowledge combination process (β = 0.936, p < 0.01). The school level SEM also shows that the knowledge combination process predicts planning (β = 0.902, p < 0.01), implementation (β = 0.924, p < 0.01) and evaluation (β = 0.931, p < 0.01). The knowledge externalization process also serves as a predictor for the knowledge combination process (β = 0.943, p < 0.01). The collaborative culture predicts the externalization process (β = 0.793, p < 0.01). All the paths in the model were significant at the 0.05 level. Four primary schools and 4 secondary schools with the highest and lowest scores in strategic planning (SP) capacity in their sector were selected from the 42 schools. The principals of the 8 schools received cover letters explaining the research activities. Documentary analysis and narrative inquiry were conducted for all case schools. Documents reviewed and analyzed included school development plans and reports, subject (departments) annual plans and reports in the latest three-year developmental cycle. Documentary analysis was used to identify the major concerns stated in the school plans, as well as the strategies adopted by schools and subjects to address those concerns. A Plan-Implement-Evaluation (PIE) planning cycle, as framed as a management cycle by the Education Bureau of Hong Kong under the School-based Management and Quality Assurance policy, was identified in all case schools. The major concerns and key contents of all the school plans focus on developing teaching and learning, e.g. developing students with self-regulated abilities, problem solving skills, creative thinking skills and proficiency in STEM education. The school documents stipulated routine meetings to implement and evaluate the effectiveness of teaching and learning plans. The strategies to realize the school plans included subject-level and school-level collaborative curriculum planning, curriculum implementation and curriculum evaluation. The practice of Lesson Study, a Japanese school-based collaborative teacher professional model for creating knowledge to bridge the implementation gaps of school plans, was identified in almost all the case schools. The researchers conducted in-depth interviews with principals/vice-principals, HODs, and senior teachers. In each school, 9 to 12 teachers, including the principal, were interviewed. In the group of 8 schools, 85 teachers participated in interviews. NVivo was applied to manage the large amount of text in interview scripts of the 8 case schools for data reduction and identification of emerging key themes and issues, and for comparison with those in other schools. We compared and contrasted the collaborative culture and its elements between the case schools with highest and lowest scores in SP. We also examined the common pattern of practices and activities for the PIE process. A culture of organizational trust and justice that promoted collaboration was seen in the schools with the highest SP score. On the other hand, the schools with the lowest SP score exhibited feelings of animosity, enmity and conflict between teachers and school leaders which discouraged collaboration. The results show that collegial trust among teachers is a crucial force in encouraging peer-to-peer knowledge sharing, and that collaborative cultures promote the knowledge externalization process. A shared vision, and acceptance of the major concerns of teachers, were identified in teachers who wanted to share knowledge with others. Department heads with a systems-thinking mindset tend to participate more in the knowledge combination process. The qualitative evidence supports the quantitative finding that collaborative culture enabled the case schools to construct and combine knowledge for school development. The study identified meetings and teaching professional development activities related to collaborative lesson preparation and post-lesson discussion under a school culture of trust, justice, shared vison, and systems thinking as best practices for facilitating knowledge externalization and knowledge combination processes. These practices allow the teachers to externalize their personal teaching ideas and strategies on taught topics, and to combine ideas and strategies from one another to design lesson plans. This finding also verifies the degree to which the SECI model is culturally embedded in Japanese culture, in which high trust, shared vison, and systems thinking prevail.

18610915.label: Major findings and research outcome
18610915.value: In the Hong Kong school context, strategic planning capacity is empirically constructed as the planning, implementation and evaluation (PIE) process. The knowledge combination process enhances the strategic planning capacity of schools, and the knowledge externalization process facilitates the knowledge combination process. Teacher education level, ranking, and teaching experience do not have significant predictive effects on the knowledge conversion processes. On the other hand, a collaborative culture does predict an effective knowledge externalization process. These findings imply the importance of creating a collaborative culture to bond teachers from the same department so that they will externalize their tacit knowledge into explicit knowledge. They also suggest a need to construct a mechanism that optimizes, within each department, the knowledge combination process that enhances school strategic planning capacity. The PIE process of the school plan in the case schools involves school-level collaborative curriculum planning, curriculum implementation and curriculum evaluation to address major concerns in teaching and learning. In the case schools with the highest SP score, we find a high level of organizational trust. This encourages collaborative lesson preparation meetings and post-lesson discussion sessions that facilitate knowledge externalization and knowledge combination processes. The study confirms that a collaborative culture is critical in institutionalizing the SECI mechanism to create knowledge for strategic planning. It identifies organizational trust, a sense of justice, shared vision, and systems thinking as core values of the collaborative culture that supports knowledge sharing activities in the Hong Kong School context. The SECI model has emerged from Japanese culture, with its characteristic high levels of trust. This study successfully responds to the international debate on culture and context-dependent issues in using Nonaka’s SECI model for knowledge creation. Its findings also situate theories of KM into strategic management in the school context and suggest a new area of research into ways to embed KM into the field of school leadership and management.

18610915.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18610915.value: The study suggests two areas for further research. The first is an exploration of ways to cultivate organizational trust and a fertile ground to develop a collaborative culture to operate the SECI model in schools. Senge’s five disciplines for organizational learning may serve as the Ba to operate the four knowledge-conversion processes. Those five disciplines include developing personal mastery for knowledge internalization, creating an open mental model for knowledge socialization, promoting team learning for externalization of team knowledge, enhancing systems thinking to combine knowledge from different departments, and making the shared knowledge vision the driving force for KM activities The second fertile area for investigation is how the social learning process operates within the four knowledge-conversion process. This examination would explore how teachers transform the data into useful information, and how they contextualize that information into actionable knowledge for school improvement. This requires the construction of a relevant model. Boisot’s I-Space model may provide a suitable analytical framework to explain how data and information can be codified, abstracted, diffused and absorbed into knowledge assets and diffused throughout organizations. The model examines and evaluates organizations as living organisms that can develop knowledge through a process of social learning.

18610915.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18610915.value: This project applied the disciplines of knowledge management (KM) to the study of school management. It confirms KM to be an effective management approach for improving, formulating, implementing, monitoring and evaluating strategic plans. It does this by creating a mechanism capable of acquiring, applying, sharing, retaining and even creating, knowledge for crafting strategies and enhancing school performance. The study also identifies collaborative curriculum lesson planning, implementation and evaluation as effective management practices that enable school leaders to craft strategies for teaching and learning plans. It confirms that institutionalizing Nonaka’s SECI knowledge creation mechanism in schools supports those schools in enhancing strategic planning capacity to cope with the rapid changes generated within the complex and challenging policy environment. As the study identifies collaborative culture and trust as requirements for institutionalizing the SECI mechanism in the Hong Kong school context, this confirms the extent to which Nonaka’s SECI is dependent on Japanese culture and context. Nevertheless, schools can fulfill the education quality assurance policy and be more accountable to public through institutionalizing the KM mechanism. The study provides insights into ways to apply theories of KM for streamlining strategic management in the school context.

18611615.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18611615.value: 現今全球有大約10%的學生患有讀寫障礙。讀寫障礙為學生的個人心理健康及正常社交都帶來很大的負面影響。過去在兒童讀寫障礙研究中發現了一些讀寫障礙有關的認知和語言處理問題，但很少研究有跟進到青春期。雖然研究至今，已發現讀寫障礙對字母和非字母語言的單語讀者所構成的影響，但是仍然缺乏有系統地嘗試找出導致認知語言能力及執行能力偏弱的原因，以及研究這些技能與香港青少年讀寫障礙患者在學習英語作為第二語言(L2)時的關係。是次研究的主要目的，是探討青少年雙語讀者在中文(L1)和英文(L2)這兩個不同的書寫系統中，共同出現閱讀障礙的性質和程度。 這項研究也會探討各種認知語言能力、口語能力、語言理解能力及執行能力在閱讀障礙與非閱讀障礙的讀者在學習L1和L2時會有甚麼不同的影響，同時亦會了解以上4種能力對不同類型的讀寫障礙讀者在閱讀L1和L2時的影響。研究將採用多維方法，反映閱讀問題涉及以上4種能力。 在第一階段的研究中，合共260個香港中學生會被招募並分派到三個不同組別：180名有讀寫障礙學生，40名閱讀水平匹配的對照，和40名年齡匹配的對照。所有學生將會以中文和英文接受各個與閱讀障礙相關的認知語言能力、口語能力、語言理解能力、及執行能力測試。那180名有讀寫障礙的學生和40名年齡匹配的對照將會被安排在第二階段中接受類型鑑定和驗證研究。這些測試能夠顯示出語言能力、口語能力、語言理解能力、及執行能力在中英文閱讀上的角色和影響。數據分析將會以中英文測試中的數據，分析出最能識別讀寫障礙的能力，同時研究不同類型的讀寫障礙以及其根源是否與語言相關。 此研究的成果將對學術及教育層面帶來極大的意義。在學術層面上，研究結果可能帶出學生在認知語言能力、口語能力、語言理解能力及執行能力的異同，和釐清中英文這兩個語言在雙語讀者之間的關係。實際上，研究結果亦有機會帶出更敏感的診斷方法和處理讀寫障礙學生的教學策略，不論在中文或英文上，以上的研究成果都能有效地幫助不同類型的讀寫障礙學生，特別是針對一些對傳統治療和教學方法有不同反應的學生更為有效。

18611615.label: Realisation of objectives
18611615.value: This project examined the nature and degree of co-occurrence of reading difficulties in Chinese (L1) and English (L2) among Chinese adolescent readers with dyslexia learning English as L2. Specifically, it investigated the profile of adolescent readers with dyslexia and the contribution of various cognitive-linguistic skills, oral language skills, executive functioning skills and language comprehension skills to reading performance of L1 and L2. It also examined the nature of adolescent readers in L1 and L2 reading and their profiles. For Phase I and II of this project, 260 Chinese adolescents in junior secondary grades were recruited in three groups: dyslexic readers, reading level age of readers, and chronological age of readers. Thirty-three assessment measures in L1 and L2 were developed and tested in order to address the five project objectives stated in the project. Our project showed that compared with the typically developing readers, adolescent readers with dyslexia at Grade 5, and 6, and 7 showed poorer performance on the cognitive-linguistic measures of morphological awareness, phonological awareness, visual-orthographic knowledge, rapid naming, working memory, and vocabulary knowledge in L1 and L2 except for phonological awareness in Chinese. Hierarchical regression analysis indicated that for both groups of readers, morphological awareness and rapid naming contributed uniquely to word reading and spelling in L1 (Kalindi & Chung, 2018). In the subsequent findings, only rapid letter naming contributed uniquely to English word spelling in the readers at Grade 7 whereas the morphological awareness predicted both reading and spelling in L1 and L2 (Chung & Lam, 2020). Correlational analyses showed that cognitive-linguistic skills were associated with word reading and spelling in L1 and L2, suggesting that readers with dyslexia may experience difficulties in both languages, and the underlying cognitive-linguistic basis of literacy difficulties may be similar in both L1 and L2. These findings highlight the potential importance of co-occurring difficulties in L1 and L2 reading and spelling and suggest that morphological awareness and rapid naming may play a critical role in predicting word reading and spelling across languages and age groups for Chinese adolescents with dyslexia and those without difficulty. These findings have addressed Objective 1, 2, 3 and 4. Taken together, these results have been published in Frontiers in Psychology (JCR Impact Factor: 2.32; Q2 in Psychology, Multidisciplinary and Journal of Learning Disabilities (JCR impact factor: 2.58; Q1 in Education, Special), Asia Pacific Journal of Developmental Differences, and a book chapter in Writing Systems, Reading Processes, and Cross-Linguistic Influences: Reflections from the Chinese, Japanese and Korean Languages. Our project also indicated that executive functioning contributed to reading comprehension in L1 and L2 for readers with and without dyslexia. Results showed that readers with dyslexia performed less well than the typically developing readers in executive functioning of working memory, inhibition, shifting, planning, vocabulary knowledge, rapid naming, and reading comprehension (Chung, Lam, & Leung, 2020). These findings suggest that readers with dyslexia may have difficulties in executive functioning, cognitive-linguistic skills, oral language skills, and reading comprehension in both L1 and L2. The readers with dyslexia also exhibited co-occurring difficulties in reading comprehension in L1 and L2, suggesting that readers with dyslexia in L1 could have a high risk of reading difficulty for L2. Hierarchical regressions showed that working memory, inhibition, and vocabulary knowledge predicted reading comprehension in L1. Furthermore, working memory, inhibition, shifting, vocabulary knowledge, and rapid naming contributed uniquely to reading comprehension in L2. These results imply executive functioning difficulties in Chinese readers with dyslexia and underscore the differential contributions of executive functioning to Chinese and English reading comprehension. Working memory and inhibition probably play an important role in reading comprehension across alphabetic and non-alphabetic languages. These findings have addressed Objective 1, 2, 3 and 4 as well as have been published advance online in Reading and Writing (JCR impact factor: 1.94; Q2 in Education and Educational Research). Our project demonstrated that readers with dyslexia could be considered as a highly heterogeneous group and showed different cognitive and language profiles across lifespan development. The profiles of the typical-functioning dyslexics and high-functioning dyslexics with longitudinal cohorts of Chinese-speaking adolescents diagnosed with childhood dyslexia were examined (Chung, Lo, & McBride, 2018). These two groups of readers with dyslexia were followed up from childhood through adolescence. High-functioning dyslexics refer to a group of readers with dyslexia having relatively less severe manifestations of reading impairment at Grade 8. The results showed that both dyslexic groups performed less well than the typically developing readers on the measures of rapid naming, visual-orthographic knowledge, morphological skills, verbal working memory, reading and writing skills. Compared to the high-functioning dyslexics, the typical functioning dyslexics displayed a higher incidence of multiple cognitive-linguistic deficit profiles with significant deficits in rapid naming and showed more difficulties with reading and writing. Rapid naming deficit is further confirmed to be an important underlying correlate and cause of dyslexia across different languages and perhaps it is the most prominent and persistent deficit in Chinese readers with dyslexia. These results also support the multiple deficit model which suggests that dyslexia may consist of a single underlying deficit and multiple impaired skills. These findings have addressed Objective 5 in addition to the other four objectives and have been published in Annals of Dyslexia (JCR Impact Factor: 1.79; Q1 in Education, Special). Based on another set of data analysis, three subgroups of dyslexia: mild deficit, syntactic deficit, and global deficit were found by using cluster analyses with k-means (Chung, Lam, Li, & Kwok, 2019). The findings revealed that the mild deficit group performed better than the other two groups on the measures of executive functioning, word reading, one-minute word reading, reading comprehension in Chinese and one-minute word reading in English (L2). Moreover, both the mild and the syntactic deficit group outperformed the global deficit group on the measure of executive functioning, word reading and reading comprehension in L2. These results underscore the unique role of syntactic deficits in L1 and executive functioning in L2 reading. These findings also suggest that taking a more fine-grained diagnostic view on the underlying causes for subgroups of dyslexia into account may be beneficial for optimizing the outcome of reading intervention programs. These findings have addressed Objective 5 and were presented at the Twenty-Fifth Annual SSSR Meeting, Toronto, 2019. To recap, the findings of this project have addressed important questions about the cognitive-linguistic, oral language, language comprehension, and executive functioning aspects of L1 and L2 sensitivity in dyslexic and non-dyslexic adolescent readers, and their profiles and subgroups of dyslexia. Collectively, the six studies published have revealed that executive functioning, morphological skills, vocabulary knowledge, syntactic skills, and rapid naming are important for adolescent readers with and without dyslexia and these skills are worth to be considered when examining individual differences in reading acquisition and difficulties.
