21600815.label: Major findings and research outcome
21600815.value: The study was a three-wave longitudinal study examining the relationships among perceived parental sacrifices, filial piety and developmental outcomes in a sample of poor adolescents in Hong Kong over time. Cross-lagged panel analyses showed that filial piety fully mediated the relationship between perceived maternal sacrifice and adolescents’ social-oriented achievement motivation (Standardized indirect effect = .132; 95% Bias-corrected CI = .000 to .030), resilience (Standardized indirect effect = .025; 95% Bias-corrected CI = .000 to .015), hopelessness (Standardized indirect effect = -.012, 95% Bias-corrected CI = -.001 to -.029), and self-determination (Standardized indirect effect = .091, 95% Bias-corrected CI = .000 to .022) over time. However, the relationship between paternal sacrifice at Time 1 and filial piety at Time 2 was non-significant. A paper on the relationships among paternal and maternal sacrifices, filial piety (reciprocal and authoritarian) and adolescent life satisfaction at Time 1 was published, and a manuscript reporting the relationships among paternal and maternal sacrifices, filial piety and adolescent hopelessness was under review. The results of generalized linear models (GLM) showed that while paternal sacrifice was stable across time, maternal sacrifice was decreasing across time (F = 5.064, p < .05, partial Eta Squared = .010). When examining the different components of paternal and maternal sacrifice, it was found that maternal time spent (F = 14.533, p < .001, partial Eta Squared = .027), maternal restructuring of daily routine (F = 28.682, p < .001, partial Eta Squared = .052), and paternal restructuring of daily routine (F = 9.957, p < .01, partial Eta Squared = .019) were decreasing across different time points, whereas paternal shielding of worries was marginally increasing over time (F = 3.797, p = .052, partial Eta Squared = .007). Moreover, the respondents perceived higher levels of maternal sacrifice than paternal sacrifice over different time points (F = 5554.293, p < .001, partial Eta Squared = .955). Finally, paternal sacrifice moderated the associations of maternal sacrifice with resilience, self-determination, positive self-identity and self-efficacy respectively at Time 1. While perceived maternal sacrifice was positively associated with adolescent resilience, self-determination, positive self-identity and self-efficacy respectively at higher levels of perceived paternal sacrifice, the relationships became non-significant when adolescents perceived lower levels of paternal sacrifice. However, the interaction effects of paternal and maternal sacrifices on adolescent developmental outcomes were non-significant over time. A paper on the moderation effects at Time 1 was published.

21600815.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
21600815.value: The study provides important contributions on examining the relationships among perceived parental sacrifice, filial piety and developmental outcomes in a sample of Chinese adolescents in Hong Kong. The research findings were shared with social workers in Hong Kong, presented in overseas International Conferences, and incorporated in the curricula of “social work theory and practice” subjects of social work undergraduate and postgraduate programs, and subject curriculum for Master Program of Family Practice and Family Therapy. Moreover, the findings provide insightful ideas for the development of other practice and research proposals on family processes among families experiencing economic disadvantage, including a research proposal supported by General Research Fund on filial responsibilities, adolescent developmental outcomes and maternal wellbeing among poor single-mother families, as well as a family resilience intervention project proposal applied to other charitable fund. The study focused mainly on a sample of early adolescents. The study can be expanded to cover different target groups (e.g., late adolescents and emerging adults). Moreover, this study adopted the perspectives of adolescents in examining the relationship of perceived parental sacrifice and their developmental outcomes. It is methodologically preferable to collect data from multiple sources of informants (i.e., parents and adolescents) in future studies.

21600815.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
21600815.value: There is a dearth of research in assessing the longitudinal effects of cultural family processes on developmental outcomes among Chinese adolescents in the context of poverty, and the pathways through which the effects happen. Employing the cultural-ecological perspectives and the Chinese socialization model, the present study was a three-wave longitudinal study examining the relationships among paternal and maternal sacrifices, filial piety and developmental outcomes among a sample of 527 Chinese junior secondary students experiencing economic disadvantage in Hong Kong. The results indicated that perceived maternal sacrifice was positively associated with adolescents’ social-oriented achievement motivation, resilience and self-determination, and negatively related to adolescent hopelessness over time, via the development of filial piety. However, perceived paternal sacrifice did not predicted adolescent filial piety over time. The study revealed that maternal sacrifice serves as a protective factor in nurturing positive outcomes of adolescents in the context of poverty. The study is pioneering in the existing social science literature and contributes to the development of family process model on resiliency applicable to Chinese communities. The findings provide practical implications on how family practitioners and social workers can help economically disadvantaged adolescents develop positively via making meanings of maternal sacrifice and promoting filial piety.

21605315.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
21605315.value: This research is interested in the current creative practices of production in video games. More specifically, our research focuses on the professionalized aesthetic strategies surrounding the use of game engines, a toolkit that offers a set of functionalities to automatize the handling of a range of process (graphics, sound, physics, networks, artificial Intelligence) during the production of video games. The specificities of video game engines as creative tools inform current artistic and aesthetic strategies in the realm of professionalized production of interactive entertainment. What defines video games as an interactive medium? This question has been addressed by numerous researchers in the field of game studies and new media studies (Galloway, 2006). Studying video games as finished products used to be the privileged approach in video game studies. It amounts to focus on the specific form of interactive narratives found in video games (Ryan, 2006) or on the ludic qualities of video games (Aarseth, 2001). Some researchers are also interested in the practices of reappropriation of video games by the players, including the reconfiguration of game levels or game characters through the manipulation of the game engine (Kirkpatrick, 2013; Sotamaa, 2003). We contend that the definition of the video game as a medium is strongly informed by the specificities of the game engines used by game developers to produce them. Aware of the latest developments in software and interface studies that seek to overcome the traditional definition of interface as neutral mediations (Andersen & Pold, 2011), the originality of our approach, is to address the question of the specificity of video games through the study of their technological conditions of possibility (game engines) rather than through the study of video game as an end product. Our focus on the aesthetic strategies developed along the use of game engines invites us to go beyond an instrumental definition of game engines and to take into account their expressive potentialities. Through the study of game engines and the differentiated artistic and aesthetic strategies attached to them, this project asks: 1/what kind of software and interface game engines used in professionalized video game production are? 2/ what are the diverse aesthetic strategies developed to tap the expressive potential of game engines? 3/ How the professionalized aesthetic strategies developed around game engines are reconfigured by the contemporary evolution of game engines. 以遊戲開發引擎用作科技及超創作媒介 是次研究主要關注現今電子遊戲生產的創作手法。這個研究更重點集中於圍繞遊戲開發引擎的專門美學策略，一套為電子遊戲生產過程中提供一系列自動（圖像、聲音、物理、網絡、人工智能）加工功能的工具組件。以電子遊戲開發引擎作為創意工具的這個特質帶出現今用於互動娛樂生產領域中的藝術及美學策略。 究竟是甚麼界定電子遊戲為互動媒介？無數遊戲研究學和新媒體學的研究人員都曾談及這問題 (Galloway, 2006)。以一件完成品角度來探討電子遊戲曾己何時是一種於電子遊戲學內很優越的研究手法。這種研究手法旨在專注於電子遊戲內互動敘事方式的獨特型態(Ryan, 2006) 或是在於電子遊戲本身的遊戲特質(Aarseth, 2001)。有一些研究人員也會對以遊戲玩家經驗重新改寫電子遊戲的研究手法感到興趣，這包括以透過操作遊戲開發引擎來重新配置遊戲程度和遊戲特性(Kirkpatrick, 2013; Sotamaa, 2003)。 我們主張以電子遊戲作為媒界這定義是由遊戲開發者使用並塑造遊戲開發引擎這個特質而釐訂的。有見於以軟件及界面研究去克服以界面作為中介這傳統定義的最新發展(Andersen & Pold, 2011)，我們最初的研究方向是以科技條件的可能性（遊戲開發引擎）而非以透過研究電子遊戲作為完成品來探討電子遊戲特質的問題。我們的研究聚焦於遊戲引擎的使用和它美學策略的同步發展，這引領我們去超越一般對遊戲引擎的工具主義定義的想法和考慮到它們表達的潛質。透過研究遊戲開發引擎和區分附屬於它們的美術和美學策略，是次研究會探討1／專業的電子遊戲生產使用甚麼遊戲開發引擎軟件和界面？2／是甚麼多樣的美學策略開啟了遊戲開發引擎的表達潛能？3／遊戲開發引擎的當代進化如何重新配置了圍繞遊戲開發引擎而發展的專業美學策略？ 關鍵字：電子遊戲開發引擎，美術工具，電子遊戲業

21605315.label: Realisation of objectives
21605315.value: Field research: Following some exploratory interviews with artists and video game workers using game engines in their professional activities, the PI did a series of in depth interviews with professionals working in the field of video game engines and video games middleware industries (computer scientists working as academics in the field of game engines, professionals working in middleware companies, specialists of in house game engines working in video game companies). Between 2016 and 2019, 12 specialists of game engines were interviewed in San Francisco, Paris, Tokyo, Aarhus and Hong Kong. Their interviews (each between 1.30 to 2 hours long) have been transcribed and analysed using Atlas.ti software for qualitative analysis. Concurrently, an ethnography of professional practices was performed in game middleware companies in Tokyo and San Francisco. Several Skype interviews between early 2016 and 2017 Fieldtrip to San Francisco (Dec 9 2016-Dec 19th 2016); Fieldtrip to Paris (Dec 19-Dec 24th 2016); Fieldtrip in Tokyo (Jan 28th – Feb 5th 2017). These interviews and field trips enabled us to understand how the emergence of game engines such as Unity has reconfigured the aesthetic strategies developed around the use of game engine inside video game developers studio (objective 2). Survey and additional interviews: Some additional research proved necessary in order to explore the situated ways in which game workers (especially non-programmers such as content developers, artists, animators, game designers) interface with different game engines. The PI conducted a survey, using Qualtrics software, on the practices of technocreatives based in Hong Kong using technologies such as game engines in their professional practices. The survey was sent to a mailing list of approximately 200 graduates of the School of Creative Media. 23 respondents provided information about the modes of acquisition of their technological skills, the contexts where these technologies are used and developed. The survey was complemented with 9 interviews of technocreatives and media artists who use game engines in their professional and artistic practices in Hong Kong. These creative were chosen for their hybrid profiles (techno professionals and artists). The rationale of the survey and the interviews was to assess the impact of the emergence of game engines aimed at the general public and to explore in which ways diverse modes of cultural production are related to video game engines (objective 3). The results of the survey contribute to the knowledge on the circulation of game engines in different creative settings, i.e. game development per se, sound art, interactive media art, and so on (objective 2). Importantly, these methods highlighted the importance of spatial and contextual conditions enabling such circulation: the availability of institutions (middleground) dedicated to the training, funding and publicizing technocreative practices, communities of support, diverse scenes of cultural production enabling hybrid creative practices, and so on. Therefore, one of the main contributions of this research is a conception of game engines as a situated instantiation of non-anthropocentric forms of creativity and specific modalities of emergent techno-human processes) (objective 4). To put it another way, game engines are produced, and influenced by a range of stakeholders, such as specialized software companies, enthusiasts’ community, video game artists. Their modes of circulation contribute to their performativity. The users of game engines (not only in the context of videogame production) are endowed with a certain power of reconfiguration of ready-made options embedded in game engines constrained by the logic of object manipulation specific to the game engine. The degree of their agency depends on their programming skills and the ways those programming skills enable a certain manipulation of the game engines in a certain sociocultural and economic context. Desk research and archive: The PI conducted a desk research for several purposes: gathering information about the different middleware companies producing game engines from available online literature; producing a database of resources and the latest development of research about game engines. This research resulted in the constitution of an archive about the different facets of game engines as tools of metacreation. This archive was used to produce the research output (conference papers and journal articles). Interface studies: The interfaces of several game engines were studied to gain an awareness of the affordances offered by different types of game engines (objective 1). This axis of research was mostly destined for the education plan aiming to help students in creative media to critically use video game engines to create interactive artwork and have a better understanding of it as a complex tool (objective 5).

21605315.label: Major findings and research outcome
21605315.value: The PI has published the findings of this research in: - 3 research papers in SSCI-ranked international journals, including Information Science Society (Sage, Q2), Organised Sound (Cambridge University Press, Q1, the most prominent journal in the field of sound studies), and Cities (Elsevier, Q1, JCR: ranked #2 in urban studies); - A 14,000 word-research paper in a prominent academic journal in Communication studies (French); - Two shorter papers in academic journals - including a book review in the prestigious journal Screen (Sage, SSCI ranked) useful for our theory-building; - A published conference presentation (book). The research was also presented at 4 international peer reviewed conferences including a conference held at Paris’ Archives Nationales with Alexander Galloway (NYU) and Nick Montfort (MIT), and the Congress of the prestigious International Association for Aesthetics. The major findings are: - The existence of differences between various game engines programming paradigms based on their ontogenetic modes of existence, that is, on their regimes of functioning. We traced the ontogenetic evolution of game engines from the manual analytic stage where the programmer is the ‘technical individual’ and the engine’s functionalities are hard-coded in the source code towards an industrial synthetic stage where the computational object (here game engine) becomes the ‘technical individual’ proper and many of its functionalities are easily modified by non-programmers in a high-level scripting language (Charrieras & Ivanova 2016; Charrieras 2016; Charrieras 2017a; Charrieras 2017b). - Game engines have impact beyond the field of videogame production. As tools to produce real time 3D environments, they can be used in a variety of ways in entertainment industries and beyond (Charrieras & Ivanova 2016; Charrieras 2018). - Two lines of enquiry stood out in our research: 1) the central role of space as a complex notion to assess game engines effectivities (as contextual setting infused with possibilities and limitations for the actualization these effectivities and as a part and product of practices involving game engines) (Charrieras 2018; Charrieras et al. 2018). 2) And the role of sound in the creation of 3D space. - The notion of 3D virtual space in game engines as used by space designers/creators benefits from the grounded notion of space we analysed in the context of underground artistic practices in Hong Kong (Charrieras & Mouillot 2015; Charrieras et al. 2018; Charrieras 2019). - The modes of computer-mediated creation in electronic music contribute to a new understanding of forms of creation using game engines beyond a dominant visual paradigm (Charrieras 2019).

21605315.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
21605315.value: Concerning the current research field of study on the cultural assessment of the impact of game engines on the contemporary creative economies and creative practices, despite the increased number of publications recently released on the subject, there is still no robust reconceptualization of creation and visualities in view of the specific effectivities of game engines in diverse fields today. This research has already generated two further GRF grants building on the findings of this research concerning the technologies of video game production as well as the modes of negotiations with creative digital interfaces, partially in the cloud and extended through AI functionalities. 21605315.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
21605315.value: This research explored the sociotechnical and cultural impact of game engines on the contemporary creative society. Game engines could be described as what defines the conditions of possibilities of the modes of creation specific to video games as an interactive medium. At a technical level, game engines can be described as a toolkit that offers a set of functionalities to automatize the handling of a range of processes (graphics, sound, physics, networks, artificial Intelligence) to produce real time 3D environment. Given their technical properties, game engines make possible or impossible certain forms of creation and emergences beyond the field of video game production. Game engines are used in different entertainment industries (television, cinema) but also in other industries (Amazon for instance has produced its own game engine). These contexts are influenced by this pervasiveness but they also influence how the effects of this technology are materialized through different practices. Our research shows how the notion of space, real time virtual environment and spatialised digital sound are reconfigured by the affordances opened by the generalisation of game engines as a medium to create 3D real time environment in a variety of creative/spatial/sonic contexts not exclusively limited to video game industries.

21605615.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
21605615.value: In line with global trends, Hong Kong has witnessed an increase in psychotropic substance abuse among young people over the last two decades. Given its dependence symptoms and bodily signs tend not to be obvious or may take longer time to become apparent, their drug abuse situation becomes more hidden and harder to reach. In 2013, half of the abusers reported having abused drugs for at least 4 years, compared to 1.9 years in 2008. Moreover, there are increasing numbers of drug abusers being identified in young adulthood instead of adolescence. Because of its chronic, hidden, hard-to-reach natures and the possible costs created for the family and community, different treatment approaches and rehabilitation services have been examined and developed worldwide. However, regardless of the type of programme employed, relapse is still highly prevalent among substance abusers. In recent years, combining the effects of cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) with the practice of mindfulness, mindfulness based relapse prevention (MBRP) approach has gained increasing attention and promising results as treatment for rehabilitating substance abusers in the West. In the Asian contexts, except for one study conducted in Taiwan, empirical study on the efficacy of the approach particularly for Chinese is almost non-existent. Therefore, the main objective of this proposed study is to develop and evaluate the short and longer-term effects of a mindfulness approach in relapse prevention for young psychotropic substance abusers in both community and residential settings in Hong Kong. This proposed study adopts a randomized control design with pre-test, post-test and 3rd month and 6th month follow-up evaluations. A total of 200 recovering participants aged between 14 and 35 will be recruited from five counselling centres and five residential homes for substances abusers and randomly assigned into the MBRP based experimental and CBT based control conditions. Eventually, ten pairs of MBRP and CBT based groups with 8 sessions will be run over a period of two and a half years. The short and sustainable effects of the MBRP programme in (1) enhancing participants’ awareness and non-judgmental attitude to their drug taking motive, (2) reducing the severity of their substance use and cravings for drugs, and (3) raising their overall sense of self-efficacy will be assessed quantitatively with a self-administered questionnaire and qualitatively with indepth interviews. It is envisaged that this MBRP programme, if demonstrated to be effective, will likely be used (with modification) for Chinese in the local and international levels.

21605915.label: Project Objectives
21605915.value: To discover the historical evolution of the binding force of guiding cases in local courts in practice, and to investigate the specific conditions under which the guiding case became essential for solving disputes in China’s legal system. The outcome of the objective will help to distinguish the difference between the binding force at the local level and the current one established by the SPC. To investigate the real mechanism of the binding force of guiding cases of the SPC, and the conditions under which such a mechanism works effectively or ineffectively in practice. The internal and external factors that can influence the binding force of guiding cases will be examined. It will deal with the specific context of China and focuses on the processes, mechanisms and conditions for the production and implementation of the SPC’s guiding cases in specific contexts rather than the grander theoretical claims about whether it works. To explore the extent to which the binding force of the Main Points of Adjudication (MPA) is different from other parts of the guiding case. The MPA mainly plays the role of interpreting statutory law, according to the current structure of guiding cases set up by the SPC. However, its binding force is different from that of abstract judicial interpretation, as well as other parts of guiding cases that have no function of statutory interpretation. To reveal the extent to which the binding force of guiding cases can change the adjudication model in practice. Upon the establishment of a guiding case with binding force, the court and the parties concerned are able to use the guiding case as a basis for a judicial decision or a cause of action in practice. As the guiding case has a place in adjudication activities, how it can interplay with the Adjudication Committee and Qingshi (requests for advisory opinion from higher courts) in dealing with hard or influential cases will be examined. To investigate the influence of the binding force of the SPC’s guiding case over other non-guiding cases. Although the guiding case is exclusively decided by the SPC, this does not prohibit the previous practice whereby the court can develop some typical cases for lower courts to study when deciding similar cases subsequently. Thus, it is necessary to clarify the different effect of these typical cases from the guiding cases. To study to what extent the binding force of the SPC’s guiding case is different from that of other civil law or common law countries. It is hoped that this will deepen the understanding and facilitate the application of guiding cases in a globalized market.

21605915.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
21605915.value: 隨著中國經濟的迅猛發展，中國的法律制度也取得了前所未有的發展。法院在中國發展的過程中扮演了重要的角色。儘管案例在大陸法系和普通法系都起了不可忽視的重要的作用，但直到2010年，中國最高人民法院才頒佈《關於案例指導工作的規定》（以下簡稱《規定》），從而初步確立了一種特別的案例制度。為此，很多研究都認為該案例制度會在中國的司法實踐中扮演非常重要的作用，但也存在很多批評的聲音，比如公佈的案例很少，指導案例沒有法定的約束力，等等。但是，這些討論都沒有從經驗的角度充分探究案例指導制度是在何種具體的社會情境下產生和發展的。 比較來看，中國作為社會主義國家，整體上遵循了大陸法系的傳統。儘管如此，案例指導制度具有截然不同的特徵。根據《規定》，只有最高人民法院才可以發佈指導案例。初審法院等其他主體只可以報送相關案例，直至最高人民法院，並最終由最高人民法院決定。而且，最高人民法院可以將“裁判要點”部分增加到報送的案例當中，並最終向社會予以公佈。初步研究表明，指導案例的不同部分（包括“裁判要點”，“相關法條”，“基本案情”，“裁判理由”，“裁判結果”，等）在司法實踐當中分別具有不同的實踐效力。 因此，該研究課題擬從經驗和比較的角度，對中國指導案例在實踐中的約束力進行研究，從而探究其所具有的與其他案例法所不同的法理。這並非要得出一種可以普遍適用的案例法理論，而是探討一種具有中國情境的附條件理論，從而有力解釋中國司法制度下案例制度的具體運作及其機理。在中國逐漸融入全球化的背景下，這對於中國司法制度的進一步發展，以及對其他國家進一步瞭解中國案例制度的具體運作等都具有重要的意義。

21605915.label: Realisation of objectives
21605915.value: This project has employed empirical methods to explore the binding force of guiding cases in the context of China. It has now achieved the specific objectives as listed in the original research plan. Specifically, this project used a combination of empirical methods in the form of interviews, and documentary and media analysis. In order to reflect regional diversity, I made three research trips to three different provincial areas of China (in March and December 2016, and August 2017), and personally conducted 50 semi-structured interviews with judges in three major cities, namely, Nanjing, Nanning and Shenzhen, and four smaller cities, i.e., Guilin, Fangchenggang, Qinzhou and Huizhou in Guangxi and Guangdong. While the vast majority of interviews were conducted with one respondent in his or her workplace, some interviews included multiple respondents and/or were conducted in places where the interviewees felt most comfortable such as restaurants. Primarily based on data analysis, it was found that the main reason why local courts began to experiment with case law was because of the increasingly perceived notion that similar cases were treated differently in practice. The famous example of this occurred in 1998 when the plaintiff Ge Rui sued three pharmacies in three different jurisdictions separately according to the rules of civil procedure but received three different decisions. This situation motivated the courts to pay more attention to establishing a suitable case law system in order to solve such issues in practice. As a result, the trial court in Zhongyuan District, Zhengzhou City issued its Regulations on the Realization of the Precedent Decision System in 2002. This stipulated that, after cases are selected and decided by the Adjudication Committee, the highest decision-making body inside China’s courts, and released by the court as precedent cases, they will be followed by judges as a point of reference, if not as the basis, to decide subsequent similar cases. If the precedent is ignored without legitimate reason, the judge who makes the incorrect decision will be sanctioned. However, once the guiding case system was adopted by the Higher People’s Courts at the provincial level, it in fact largely deviated from the original practice of guiding cases trialed in Zhongyuan District Court in the sense that only a few cases, after being selected and determined by the Higher People’s Courts, were treated as guiding cases. In reality, such a limited number of guiding cases is unable to maintain consistency for the majority of cases in practice. Although the local experiment did not fully achieve the desired effect, the Supreme People’s Court (SPC) still moved forward to establish a formal national mechanism of guiding cases in 2010 through promulgating the Provisions on Case Guidance Work. However, it further deviated from the trajectory of local experiments in that the SPC became the exclusive authority on deciding guiding cases. Such a system was further specified in the Detailed Rules of Implementation of the Provisions of the Supreme People’s Court on Case Guidance Work (hereinafter referred to as the Detailed Rules) in 2015. The Detailed Rules specified the distinctive ways that the guiding case shall be referred to in the adjudication. In principle, Article 10 of the Detailed Rules stipulates that, “[w]hen a people’s court at any level refers to a guiding case in the adjudication of a similar case, it shall quote the guiding case as part of the reasons for the judgment or ruling, but shall not quote the same as a legal basis for the judgment or ruling”. This shows that the guiding case does not have the same legislative effect as other statutory laws. Rather, it can only be treated as a reference for adjudicating similar cases. In addition, Article 11 of the Detailed Rules further states that: “Where relevant guiding cases are quoted in written judgments or rulings, the serial numbers of the guiding cases, and the Main Points of Adjudication (MPA) shall be quoted as part of the reasons for the judgment or ruling.” This shows the distinctiveness of the binding force of guiding cases, which is based on the unique structure of the guiding cases with a separate part, namely, the MPA, which is added, separate to the original judgment, by the court and finalized by the SPC. In this regard, the MPA has actually been used by the SPC as a form of statutory interpretation to clarify the ambiguities involved in statutes. Nonetheless, in practice, given the lack of judicial independence in the sense that the courts are not independent from the people’s congress system constitutionally, and at the same time are subordinate to the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) politically, it has been hard for judges to choose to make an explicit and specific statement of the rule of law out of a case at hand in a way that would develop case law in China. At the same time, given the collective model of judicial decision-making in the event of ambiguities of laws, the judges’ primary concern is not about the public consensus in the community but the will of the higher authority. Consequently, the concise style of the judicial decision without very detailed reasoning has become an obvious way for judges to protect themselves in the sense that it can, to a certain extent, avoid potential legal disputes based on the judicial decision from litigants and the public, and avoid the political risks that may occur otherwise in an authoritarian context. It has been common practice for judges to exclude details on determining factual and legal issues, including their construction of laws and the reasoning, from the judgment. This then makes it extremely difficult for the judges to identify the similarities between cases which is a precondition for the legal reasoning of case law. Following this logic, the guiding case is hardly able to function as case law; its main legal function is in fact through the MPA, which is added by the SPC and is a form of statutory interpretation. Moreover, at present, China has in fact formed a vertical hierarchy of typical cases of different types which comprises guiding cases, reference cases and typical cases. The guiding case system has been formally institutionalized by the SPC, while the reference case system has emerged in some provinces under the SPC’s policy of emphasizing case guidance work. The typical cases, mainly selected through the typical-case-selection movement, have been the main source for guiding cases and reference cases. Moreover, given the absence of case law, China appears to have created a bureaucratic model of judicial precedents within which a case can achieve a certain degree of political importance if selected as a typical case. Of course, politically, the typical-case-selection movement can also have a positive effect on the propaganda of judicial credibility in an authoritarian regime.

21605915.label: Major findings and research outcome
21605915.value: In contrast to case law systems in liberal democracies with independent judiciaries, in an authoritarian context, China’s guiding case system is distinctive and cannot simply be explained by current case law theories. This project first explores the distinctiveness of the guiding case system in the specific context of China, as opposed to other types of case law in liberal democracies, and then explains the reason why the SPC has been able to expand its judicial lawmaking authority in the sense that it is able to interpret the law through guiding cases. Furthermore, it illustrates that the MPA, as part of a guiding case, has essentially become a form of statutory interpretation which enables the SPC to independently perform a legislative function to a certain extent with no routine surveillance by the Standing Committee of the National People’s Congress, and that the effectiveness of the SPC’s lawmaking function through the guiding case system largely depends on the extent to which the courts could become independent in the context of China. In addition, the project finds that guiding cases in China hardly perform the function of a type of case law compared to judicial precedents in other jurisdictions. In practice, judges are generally reluctant to refer to a judicial precedent, including a guiding case, in the process of making a judicial decision. Moreover, it reveals that the guiding case system has effectively crystallized a bureaucratic system of judicial precedents in which guiding cases are at the top of the pyramid. Such a bureaucratic system is mainly grounded on the political hierarchy of the courts and a nationwide typical-case-selection movement in which the lower courts are politically responsible for submitting a certain number of typical cases selected from within their respective jurisdictions to the SPC annually. Finally, it develops a bureaucratic theory of judicial precedents centered on guiding cases which clearly fits into China’s authoritarian context and which is substantially different from any other type of case law in a liberal context.

21605915.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
21605915.value: With the development of China’s legal system, the factors that influence the binding force of guiding cases may change further. This largely depends on the extent to which the courts could become independent, and the judges could make judicial decisions independently. Given that China has been attempting to build up an authoritarian legal system that fits with the leadership of the CCP, more empirical research will be needed in order to address the relevant new issues that arise from the practice of the guiding case system.

21605915.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
21605915.value: This project focuses on the binding force of guiding cases. The results of the project have provided a comprehensive view of the binding force of guiding cases from comparative and empirical perspectives, which is beyond most of the literature whose focus has been on the grand theoretical claims associated with this subject. Furthermore, the project is of significant practical value and will help legal professionals to understand how the guiding case is employed in China. Moreover, it develops a bureaucratic theory of judicial precedents centered on guiding cases which clearly fits into China’s authoritarian context and which is substantially different from any other type of case law in a liberal context. This has made a significant contribution to the literature on Chinese law and China studies.

21607215.value: 買樓文化: 香港私人分層住宅發展史(1950-1980年代)

21607215.label: Project Objectives
21607215.value: To understand the formation of a homeownership culture in Hong Kong by studying how property developers instilled an ideologically grounded belief in the superiority of homeownership. To study the role of property developers in the expansion of homeownership in Hong Kong by analyzing the market initiatives they have introduced to make housing affordable to the middle-class. To explore the ways in which homeownership has become an identity tag of the middle-class by documenting homeowners’ experience of upward social mobility. To study the role of property developers in the expansion of homeownership in Hong Kong by analyzing the market initiatives they have introduced to make housing affordable to the middle-class.

21607215.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
21607215.value: Since its introduction in 1948, the condominium has become the most popular housing choice in Hong Kong. How did this historically overlooked and under-theorized architectural type become so widespread in Hong Kong, and why did it take its current form? The popularity of the condominium is commonly attributed to Hong Kong’s limited land availability and large population. Although this simplistic view holds some truth, it fails to address the postwar social conditions that enabled the spectacular growth of the homeownership rate from 20% in 1961 to 52% in 2012. The proposed research will be based on the hypothesis that the dominance of the condominium in postwar Hong Kong is a result of decades of concerted efforts from property developers to instill an ideologically grounded belief in the superiority of homeownership. The objective of the research will be to explore how such a homeownership culture was created and how it affects Hong Kong’s residential landscape and condominium design. The literature on the dominance of homeownership in societies such as the United State and Singapore mainly emphasizes state intervention. The originality of this research is that it provides another perspective to study the role of property developers in expanding homeownership, and suggests that the postwar home-buying culture is the result of a series of market initiatives. The first initiative was the invention of new legal and financial mechanisms in the 1950s, such as split of titles of multistory buildings and installment purchases of real property. The second initiative was the development of large-scale planned communities in the 1960s that fulfilled the housing demands of the growing middle-class. The last initiative was the development of mini-condominium flats, usually less than 40 square meters, in Hong Kong’s new towns in the 1970s. All of these initiatives have successfully lowered the financial threshold for becoming a homeowner and made condominium ownership a materialized form of middle-class aspiration. The significance of this research is that it will make Hong Kong people realize that homeownership is not a natural or superior preference, but a socially constructed concept promoted by the property developers. The research will also provide a historical reference to policymakers to better understand the current housing problem, and show that one of the keys to the growth of homeownership lies in the willingness of property developers to provide affordable housing, and that failure to do so will clog the path of upward social mobility.

21607215.label: Realisation of objectives
21607215.value: Objective 1: To understand the formation of a homeownership culture in Hong Kong by studying how property developers instilled an ideologically grounded belief in the superiority of homeownership. To understand the social contexts that led to massive homeownership after WWII, the project team examined historical newspapers, housing statistics, reports and correspondences from various governmental departments, and other entities. Official records show that in the first decade after WWII, the colonial government refused to use public funds to solve the housing shortage resulting from the influx of Chinese refugees. Private real estate developers took the initiative to change the tenure systems in Hong Kong in the late 1940s, allowing buyers to share the ownership of multi-unit buildings, thus lowering the cost of buying a home. Since then, the homeownership rate has steadily increased. In 1961, 20.1% of Hong Kong households owned their domestic premises. The homeownership rate increased most significantly between 1981 (27.9%) and 1986 (35.1%). To verify our hypothesis that property developers instilled an ideologically grounded belief in the superiority of homeownership, we examined several property sale advertisements published in local newspapers and old condominium sale brochures produced by various property developers from the 1950s to the 1980s. The project team observed a change in narratives in the ways property developers advertised their condominium projects. From the 1950s to the mid-1960s, property sale advertisements usually focused on the affordability of condominium flats, especially when developers offered the option of an installment purchase with small down payments for buyers. Many sale advertisements also emphasized that buying a flat could yield better economic returns than renting; however, beginning in the mid-1960s, property developers shifted the marketing strategy from housing affordability to the quality of the condominiums, emphasizing the architectural design, building materials used, and modern equipment installed in the flats. The marketing strategy shifted again toward the mid-1970s, highlighting the middle-class lifestyle associated with condominium living. Objective 2: To study the role of property developers in the expansion of homeownership in Hong Kong by analyzing the market initiatives they have introduced to make housing affordable to the middle class. The project team has completed extensive research on new market initiatives introduced by property developers from the late 1940s to the 1980s. We discovered that three market initiatives were particularly crucial to the expansion of homeownership. The first initiative was the introduction of new tenure systems that permit the subdivision of ownership of condominiums. We have examined the land leases, land registry records, and the deeds of mutual covenant of various domestic buildings as well as the correspondences between various government departments and property owners. From these records, we concluded that two tenure systems, which resemble cooperative ownership and condominium ownership in Western societies, were introduced by property developers to Hong Kong in 1947 and 1948, respectively. Both systems allow a buyer to own or to enjoy an exclusive right to a flat in a condominium, which successfully lowered the threshold for becoming a homeowner. The second initiative was the development of large-scale, high-rise planned communities in the late 1960s, providing an abundant supply of affordable flats to Hong Kong. The project team has carried out an in-depth case study on Mei Foo Sun Chuen, developed by the American oil company Mobil. The development occupied 40 acres of land formerly used as an oil depot. It consisted of 99 residential towers, housing over 80,000 tenants. By the time it was completed in the early 1970s, Mei Foo Sun Chuen was the largest privately funded housing project in the world. The project also started the trend of converting large brownfield sites near urban centers into residential developments. The final initiative was the development of mini-flats in Hong Kong’s new towns since the late 1970s. The project team has analyzed the official housing statistics and has found that from 1978 to 1989, flats under 400 sq. ft. dominated Hong Kong’s annual housing production. In addition, throughout the 1980s, more flats were completed in the New Territories than in Hong Kong Island and Kowloon. This period also had the sharpest increase in the homeownership rate. These housing figures aligned with the findings from our case study of Shatin New Town. We have collected and analyzed the building plans of all private condominiums developed in Shatin from the 1970s to the 1980s. We discovered that most of the flats completed were under 400 sq. ft. Due to the small size, the cost of buying a mini-flat in the new towns was relatively low compared to flats in the urban centers. Objective 3: To explore the ways in which homeownership has become an identity tag of the middle class by documenting homeowners’ experiences of upward social mobility. The project team has interviewed several homeowners who were first-hand or early buyers of Mei Foo Sun Chuen (completed in the late 1960s) and City One Shatin (completed in the early 1980s). These two projects, which have been selected for our case studies, were gigantic in scale (having a population of over 30,000) and represented the most up-to-date condominium design at their times. We investigated the interviewees’ experiences of home buying and their narratives of upward social mobility through achieving homeownership. Although the interviewees came from different backgrounds, their experiences were common in several aspects. Most had never owned a property before they bought their flats. Some originally lived in rental public housing estates. Most interviewees bought their flats because they planned to get married and to start a new family. They selected Mei Foo Sun Chuen or City One Shatin based on the affordable price and the pleasant environment, which was suitable for raising children. Objective 4: To chronicle the development of the condominium and to explain changes in condominium design over time through in-depth case studies. The project team has identified over 20 condominiums completed at different times for architectural analysis. We discovered that the changes in condominium designs over time were largely due to three interrelated factors: the decrease in flat sizes, the change in building codes, and the introduction of community planning. Statistical records show that Hong Kong’s household size had been decreasing gradually after WWII. Following this trend, the flat size also reduced with time. Although individual flats became smaller than before, the overall building bulk became bigger. In 1956 and 1962, respectively, the colonial government had amended the building codes to allow domestic buildings to grow larger in volume and taller in height. The 1962 building codes amendment introduced the site coverage and plot ratio control to Hong Kong. These new controls forced property developers to provide adequate open space between buildings. Since then, most condominiums have been designed in the form of slender high-rise towers. The completion of Mei Foo Sun Chuen in the late 1960s brought the concept of community planning to Hong Kong and largely raised the standard of condominium design. The estate was hailed as “a city within a city” by the developer because it had almost all amenities, such as schools, markets, shopping centers, recreational facilities, and a cinema, to make it virtually a self-contained community. Mei Foo Sun Chuen provided a planning model for many privately-owned housing estates, such as Tai Koo Shing, Whampoo Garden, and Laguna City.

21607215.label: Major findings and research outcome
21607215.value: For some time, homeownership was beyond the reach of most Hong Kong people as the ownership of a building was tied to the ownership of the land on which the building rested. The first major finding of this research is that homeownership became achievable when property developers began selling parts of buildings to individual purchasers around 1947 and 1948 through two tenure systems. First, individual purchasers could buy shares of a development company to secure the tenancy of individual flats. Second, individual purchasers could become tenants in common in equal shares and could enjoy exclusive rights to specific flats. These new tenure systems lowered the cost of becoming homeowners. Since then, condominiums rapidly became the dominant housing choice for Hong Kong citizens. The Principal Investigator (PI) has published the findings in a conference paper titled “Towards Homeownership: the Birth of Condominiums (Flatted Developments) in Post-War Hong Kong.” The second major finding is that the thriving of condominiums following WWII coincided with the government’s decision to relax building density control. To provide more floor spaces, the government amended the building codes in 1956 to allow domestic buildings to increase in height. The PI has produced a short video for the 2019 Hong Kong Biennale of Urbanism/Architecture to explain how the building codes amendment led to the construction of condominiums that were too massive in size. Realizing the problem of these massive condominiums, in 1962, the government introduced plot ratio and site coverage control to Hong Kong to ensure the provision of open spaces between buildings, thus leading to the development of slender high-rise towers. The PI analyzes various models of condominiums developed under these new controls in a journal article titled “Tower-on-Podium: A Prototype of a High-Density Residential Building Complex in Hong Kong.” The final major finding is that the expansion of homeownership served as an important index of the formation of a new middle class in post-war Hong Kong. Mei Foo Sun Chuen, a pilot high-rise planned community, became a materialized form of middle-class aspiration. The success of the estate is based on its early recognition of a growing number of young Chinese families who had more money to spend and who cared about their quality of living. The PI has consolidated the findings in a journal article titled “Housing the Nascent Middle Class: the First High-Rise Planned Community in Post-War Hong Kong,” which is currently under preparation.

21607215.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
21607215.value: This research project explores how condominiums with ownership shared among multiple buyers emerged as the most popular housing choice in post-war Hong Kong. One of the major findings of this research is that condominium ownership was introduced to Hong Kong by property developers around 1947 and 1948, which was earlier than in the United States (1958), Australia (1961), Canada (1967) and Singapore (1974). We propose that Hong Kong may be the first Asian city that adopted condominium ownership. Unfortunately, the project team has yet to locate any scholarly studies on the history of condominiums in Asia. Therefore, this research has the potential to be developed into a comparative study on the practice of condominium ownership and the design of condominiums in Asian cities. Like Hong Kong, many Asian cities have been colonized by Western powers. These cities experienced rapid population and economic growth after the war, and currently, condominiums are the most popular housing type there. It is worth investigating whether similar trajectories of condominium development and homeownership expansion can be observed between Hong Kong and other Asian cities.

21607215.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
21607215.value: Condominiums, commonly referred to as “flatted developments” in Hong Kong, became the most popular housing choice for inhabitants after the end of World War II. This research traces the beginning of condominiums in post-war Hong Kong when the colony faced an acute housing demand. It explores the role of private enterprises in the post-war shift from private renting to individual owner-occupation. It is argued that the dominance of condominiums in post-war Hong Kong is a result of decades of concerted efforts from property developers to install an ideological grounded belief in the superiority of homeownership. It highlights a series of initiatives proposed by property developers, which had successfully lowered the threshold of becoming homeowners. The first initiative was the introduction of new tenure systems, which permitted buyers to purchase only parts of a condominium. The second initiative was the development of large-scale planned communities, which allowed an abundant supply of affordable flats to the growing middle class. The final initiative was the development of mini-flats in new towns, which required lower investments from buyers. All these initiatives have contributed to the expansion of homeownership in post-war Hong Kong and have made condominiums a materialized form of middle-class aspiration.

21608215.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
21608215.value: The aim of this proposal is an innovative one, specifically, to investigate the construction of Muslim identity in Myanmar, something that has never been done. At a time when relations between various religious communities and Muslims are attracting such scrutiny, it is remarkable that no study of this kind has ever been undertaken in Myanmar, the Southeast Asian setting in which these relations are today most fraught. The proposed project will examine Buddhist-Muslim ethno-religious diversity at the intersection of social attitudes, historical legacies and government policies in contemporary Myanmar. It will do so by capitalising on the PI’s long-term scholarly engagement with the Buddhist and Muslim traditions of Myanmar, a country currently undergoing significant upheaval and transformation as it deals with change on the political, economic and social frontiers. The country is also witnessing a marked rise in instances of religious intolerance. The media and scholars in both Myanmar and the West have paid widespread attention to the most extreme acts of violence perpetrated by Buddhists against Muslims and provided Buddhist extremists with ample outlets in such publications as Time Magazine (July 2013) and New York Times (June 20, 2013), for their Islamophobic vitriol. But this media has generally neglected two longstanding, and arguably more pressing, issues: 1) the need to listen to the voices of Burmese Muslims themselves, voices that are largely absent from the prevailing discourse on the country’s current ethno-religious tensions, and 2) the general lack of understanding and trust between the Buddhist and Muslim communities and the resulting impact, not only on religious issues, but also on issues involving citizenship and ethnicity. Religion, nationalism and ethnicity are important ingredients of the decades-long identity politics and conflicts of Myanmar, with Burmese Buddhism being seen as the central source of identity. In this project, I will expand the debate beyond the traditional focus on the role of Buddhism to address issues of ethnicity, religion and nationalism as origins of Islamophobia and violence in Myanmar. My main focus will be on the individual Muslim men and women who make up two distinct Sunni Muslim communities in two Burmese cities to determine how they navigate ‘being a Muslim’ in an overwhelmingly Buddhist and increasingly violent country and how their sense of exclusion and belonging differs on the basis of ethnicity and place of residence. 此建議書的目的是創新的、未曾被研究過的，具體而言，是研究在緬甸中穆斯林身份的建構。此時各宗教團體和穆斯林之間的關係正備受關注，值得注意的是，從來沒有人研究在緬甸中穆斯林身份的建構。在當今的東南亞，這些關係是令人顧慮的。此提擬計劃將研究在當代緬甸內佛教與穆斯林之間的民族宗教多樣性的交匯，包括於社會態度、歷史遺產和政府政策。此計劃主要透過首席研究員與緬甸佛教和穆斯林傳統的長期學術接觸為起步點。緬甸目前正經歷在政治、經濟和社會上顯著動盪和變革，也見證了宗教之間互不相讓的情況有顯著上升。 在緬甸和西方國家，媒體和學者已廣泛關注到佛教徒對穆斯林以暴力犯下最極端的行為，時代雜誌(刊登於2013年7月號)和紐約時報(刊登於2013年6月20日)等已充份報導佛教極端分子對伊斯蘭恐懼症的殘酷和痛苦批評。但媒體普遍忽略了兩個長期並可以說是更迫切的議題：第一、媒體需要聽聽在緬甸的穆斯林自己的見解，這是從該國當前民族宗教關係緊張的交談中不存在的；第二、佛教徒和穆斯林社區間普遍缺乏信任和理解，這造成的影響不僅在宗教問題上，同時也涉及對公民和種族問題之間的議題。緬甸在數十年以來在宗教、民族和種族的政治身份上不段有衝突，這與緬甸的佛教被視為主要身份的來源有關。 在這個項目中，我將擴大和超越對佛教傳統焦點的角色辯論，以解決種族、宗教和民族主義的問題，這都是對伊斯蘭教的恐懼和在緬甸暴力事件的起源。我主要的重點是在個別的穆斯林男人和女人，他們如何兩個緬甸城市建立了兩個不同的遜尼派穆斯林社區，去決定他們如何在強烈佛教氣氛和日益暴力的國家下導引「成為穆斯林」，以及他們因不同種族和不同居住地的基礎上所產生的被排斥感和歸屬感是怎樣。

21608215.value: I examined the history of ethno-religious conflicts amongst Buddhists and Muslims from the pre-colonial era to the present day to identify the historical antecedents of the current anti-Muslim sentiments in Myanmar. To accomplish this, I investigated how Burmese Buddhists interpret the threat of Islam to their national identity and how that interpretation influences the legal frameworks and practices protecting the religious freedoms of Muslim minorities. To carry out such an investigation, I collected and analysed the testimonies of Muslims from two distinct ethno-religious traditions in Myanmar through participant observations, British and Burmese archival sources, and a survey of popular Muslim periodicals and a range of magazines, personal journals, songs and websites to offer the first ethnography of Burmese Muslims. The findings of this investigation found their ways into my publications. I helped run an inter-religious and inter-ethnic dialogue with members of Buddhist and Muslim communities, in conjunction with the Religions of Peace Organization and Myanmar Muslim Association.

21608215.label: Major findings and research outcome
21608215.value: Wanting to capture the dynamic between Buddhist and Muslim communities that leads to latter constructing particular kinds of identities, my research found that these identities derive from, but then contribute to variable levels of violence. Ethnicity (and spatial location) were found to be crucial to outcomes, with Muslims of Indian lineage feeling much pressure; ‘indigenous’ converts remaining assimilated more or less; while those of Chinese linage in the borderlands are left alone. Scholars have attempted to explain the recent waves of anti-Muslim violence in terms of how ancient Buddhist texts and pre-modern Buddhist societies have justified violence against non-Buddhists. However, these scholars are guilty of engaging in a kind of reverse-presentism, that is, of analysing contemporary issues by anachronistically introducing pre-modern ideas and perspectives into contemporary interpretations. In my research findings, for example, I interviewed Buddhists who admitted to engaging in hostile activities against Muslims and were certainly not acting with thoughts in mind of how their actions might be justified with reference to ancient texts or the practices of their ancestors. For them, Islam represented a real and present danger, and the only remedy was to purge it from the nation. Other scholars have attempted to humanise Buddhists who engage in various forms of violence and discrimination against Muslims. What was lacking in such studies, however, was the absence of Muslim voices. In all of this research, any reference made to Islam or Muslims is either essentialised or generalised, as if to imply that Islam is the same everywhere in Myanmar or that Muslims throughout the country speak and act in a unified manner. My research learned about the intimate lives of the variety of ‘Islams’ in Myanmar and the diversity of Muslim voices that can be heard throughout the country. I learned how Indo-Burmese Muslims in a Yangon ghetto view their sense of exclusion or belonging in the world compared with wealthy, ethnically Chinese Muslims in the suburbs of Mandalay. Islam – and being Muslim – matters for the members of these communities, not necessarily as a belief system or set of authoritative texts that must be adhered to, but as something that is discussed, practised and renegotiated in their everyday lives. The thoroughly localised forms of Islam that Burmese Muslims practise and the way in which they imagine and employ their religion in response to local conditions and circumstances lie at the heart of the research outcomes.

21608215.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
21608215.value: A glaring omission from the project is the Rohingya Muslims of Arakan State (also known as Rakhine State) in western Myanmar. The United Nations has declared the Rohingya to be one of the most persecuted religious minorities in the world. Thousands of Rohingya currently live in camps for internally displaced persons and have suffered tremendous losses during and in the aftermath of the 2012 Rakhine State Riots. Unfortunately, owing to the violence and political insecurity that still plague that area, I was unable to conduct research among the Rakhine Muslims because foreigners not working for NGOs are not allowed to enter the area.

21608215.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
21608215.value: The project explained the world of Burmese Buddhists and Muslims in terms of both the broader social, political, and religious context and the intimate roles that these religions play in people’s everyday lives. Drawing upon material and visual culture, long-term participant observation, and the testimonies of the devout the project considered certain Buddhist and Muslim beliefs and practices to be forms of defending their traditions from externally perceived threats and even to restrictive gender roles. The project also offered a new lens on the political struggles and social transformations that have taken place in Myanmar in recent years with regards to Muslims and Buddhists. Featuring close attention to the voices of individual Muslims and Buddhists themselves, the project expands our ways of thinking about the daily experience of lived religious practices.

21608915.label: Project Title(Chinese)
21608915.value: 我們在成長中學習：對青年激進主義、圖像方法學、愛滋病預防的長期觀察研究

21608915.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
21608915.value: In 2002, Thabo was an outspoken young activist around HIV prevention in his community of Khayelitsha, one of the largest and most impoverished townships in South Africa. Thabo was one of a dozen young people involved in a multi-year qualitative educational research project that included interviews, the production of literary texts, a documentary film, and a series of creative art works (Walsh 2004). Thabo became well-known youth spokesperson, and flew to conferences around the world teaching young people about HIV prevention and speaking on health-related issues. Yet over ten years later, many of his dreams were shattered as the relentless poverty around him took its toll, and he struggled to survive. What happened in the intervening years of his life? How did time, in combination with structural factors, affect the educational experiences he had as a teenager? What difference did it make? Educational research using visual methods has transformative potential, yet structural violence, poverty and other factors can inhibit the possibilities of positive life-long impacts for participants. In response, longitudinal perspectives that focus on life events through time can give researchers a better understanding of how educational work is effected as participants intersect with the communities and societies in which they live. (Mitchell 2014; Walsh 2013; Weller & Shirani 2010; Neale 2010). While these insights can be valuable into developing more effective programs, it is increasingly difficult for educational research to have the resources, or time, to conduct such long-term qualitative work. This study addresses this gap, through a longitudinal analysis of an educational research project in which we followed participants from teenagers to adults over the past 12 years. Critically, the study explores the following questions: In what ways do experiences with educational, arts-based research around HIV prevention remain with participants over their transition to adulthood? What are the limits, and potentials, of such educational projects? How do issues of gender, class, and race intersect with interventionist education initiatives? What can we learn from taking a longitudinal approach to research on HIV education that can help improve long-term outcomes? This study draws on research I started in 2002-2004, with follow up in-depth interviews and ethnographies that were done in 2006, 2008, and 2011. For this, the final phase of the project, I propose to conduct new research with participants to trace their journey from teens into adulthood, with the goal of developing a book-length manuscript of the 12 year trajectory. 2002年，在南非最大及最貧困的小鎮之一Khayelitsha，Thabo 作為一個青年社運人士積極地在他的社區宣傳如何預防愛滋病。Thabo來自一個有12位年輕人的組合，他們在進行一個長達數年的關於教育的定性研究，當中包括採訪、文學課本製作、一部紀錄片以及一系列創意藝術作品 (Walsh 2004)。Thabo 成為了出名的青年代言人，並且參與了世界各地會議，就健康衛生議題發言，教導年輕人如何預防愛滋病。但是十多年過去，他為貧困所迫，掙扎求生，夢想因而破滅。在這幾年間發生了身麼事？在他青少年歲月的教育經驗如何被時間及社會結構性的因素影響？當中有甚麼區別？ 運用圖像方法的教育研究有潛在的改革功效，但是因社會不平等引起的暴力，貧窮以及其他因素有可能會影響參與者一生。針對這些方面, 專注於生活事件的長期觀察研究方法令研究者更深入地了解參與者所在的社區和社會如何影響他們的教育工作 (Mitchell 2014; Walsh 2013; Weller & Shirani 2010; Neale 2010)。儘管這些洞察對發展更有效的課程是有價值的，但是對於教育研究，要得到資源或時間來進行這些長期的定性研究工作卻變得更加困難。 ​這個研究課題致力處理這個差距問題，為此在過去的12年間，我們在一個教育研究項目中跟隨參與者，觀察他們由青少年變為成年人的經歷。這個研究批判地探討以下問題：以藝術為基礎的關於愛滋病預防的教育研究經驗如何伴隨著參與者由青少年踏入成年歲月？這些有關教育的研究項目有何限制與潛質？性別，階級和種族這些因素如何干預教育主導權？我們利用長期觀察研究的這種方法去探究愛滋病教育得到的結論能如何改進長遠的影響？ 這個研究課題由我在2002至2004年間進行的研究開始，隨後還有在2006年，2008年及2011年進行的深入訪問與人種學研究。在此研究的最後階段，我建議進行一個新研究項目，當中研究參與者追溯由青少年變為成人的歷程，目的是以此編寫一本涵蓋這12年生命軌跡的紀錄文稿。

21610515.label: Project Objectives
21610515.value: To examine Dickens’s “connections” with China and Hong Kong in the first half of the twentieth century. To explore the translation and adaptations of the everyday in Dickens’s texts in a cross-cultural context. To offer alternative readings to cross-cultural interactions through the prism of everyday studies. To analyse the applicability of Western theorization of the everyday and of translation, adaptation and appropriation to cross-cultural contexts. To contribute to the field of literary geographies and spatiality by examining the relationship between power and narrative of space in a cross-cultural context.

21610515.label: Realisation of objectives
21610515.value: Most of the project objectives have been achieved. In what follows, I will outline how the project objectives are achieved, and areas which can be further developed. One of the major research outputs of this project is the completion and publication of my first monograph, Charles Dickens and China: Cross-Cultural Encounters (1895-1915) (New York and London: Routledge, 2017). The funding was partly used to support the final research and writing of this book, which was evolved from my PhD project in the UK. The book seeks to investigate the connections between Dickens and China through investigating the translation, adaptation and appropriation of Dickens’s works in China in the early twentieth century. The book in many ways succeed in achieving the project objectives of exploring Dickens’s connections with China in the early twentieth century and of investigating the applicability of Western theorization of the everyday and of translation, adaptation and appropriation to cross-cultural contexts. As a book that emphasizes cross-cultural interactions and the movement of texts (and people in the case of city narratives) across space and time, it contributes to the field of literary geography through attending to narratives of space and the everyday life. The idea of the everyday and its subversive potential, as Henri Lefebvre famously articulates in The Practice of Everyday Life, is being used to explore A Tale of Two Cities in both its original version and its adapted form when it was transferred to China in the early twentieth century. A result of this exploration is the last chapter of the book, ‘Reading and Reframing: History, Politics, and A Tale of Two Cities’. The relationship between space, power and place in a cross-cultural setting is a recurrent feature of my monograph. The ECS grant provides the necessary resources for me to carry out a research trip to the British Library, where I carried out an archival research into not only the first-edition Dickens’s works that I have included in the book but also the English literary journals and newspapers that published literary work in Hong Kong from the mid-nineteenth to early-twentieth centuries. The research trip has deepened my understanding of Dickens’s connections with Hong Kong in the early twentieth century. Dickens’s ‘presence’ in Hong Kong is most evident in the special Christmas edition in South China Weekly Post (1903-04), a sister publication of a leading English daily newspaper in Hong Kong, South China Morning Post (1903-). The way in which Dickens was invoked and the kind of English publications that were established in Hong Kong contrasted sharply with the situation in China in the early twentieth century, a phenomenon which to a large extent reflects the different historical and cultural developments in the two societies in the early twentieth century. These research materials were incorporated in an essay, ‘Charles Dickens: Transnational Responses and Cultural Imaginaries’, to be published in the forthcoming Wiley-Blackwell Companion to World Literature. The CTWL is a five-volume project containing original essays on topics of world literature. My research into the everyday and the city has led to another research article that seeks to compare two novels: Lao She’s Mr Ma and Son and Charles Dickens’s The Old Curiosity Shop. Despite being written in different time and by writers coming from different cultural backgrounds, both novels explore the theme of alienation and highlight the ‘unmappable’ spaces in the city, especially for those who are seen as ‘outsiders’ or neglected subjects in society. It is through this investigation that the relationship between power and narrative of space in a cross-cultural context is explored. This investigation has resulted in a research essay titled ‘Against the City: A Comparative Study of Charles Dickens’s The Old Curiosity Shop and Lao She’s Mr Ma and Son’, to be published by Comparative Literature Studies. Overall, all the project objectives have been achieved, though there are also limitation and area for further study. Two major limitations can be identified: firstly, through archival research it can be established that Dickens has a ‘presence’ in Hong Kong. For example, his works were advertised in major English newspapers and some of his works were adapted for the theatre. His associations with Christmas were sometimes invoked by individuals and publications circulated among the expatriate community in Hong Kong during Christmas time. In most instances, however, these episodes were mentioned briefly in newspapers, nor were they significant enough to warrant further investigation. In few instances I intended to find out the adapted versions of Dickens’s texts in Hong Kong, though many of which are no longer available. Having said these, and as mentioned in preceding paragraphs, I discovered a Christmas edition of South China Weekly Post, which clearly invoked Dickens’s Christmas writings in order to establish an ‘imagined community’, in Benedict Anderson’s terms, in the city. In a nutshell, while this area of inquiry deserves attention, upon the conclusion of this project I can say that his presence in Hong Kong appears to be much less significant than his presence in China, the latter of which is the focus of attention in my monograph. Another area that can be further studied is the engagement with everyday studies in investigating cross-cultural interactions. As indicated earlier, while selected publications do engage with everyday studies, I think that this is an area that I can further develop, especially in relation to the city and the everyday, the topic of which has been explored in my forthcoming article on comparing Dickens and Lao She’s novels as discussed above.

21610515.label: Major findings and research outcome
21610515.value: The project has demonstrated Dicken’s ‘connections’ with China and Hong Kong. It critically explores the cross-cultural interactions, and the transfer of Dickens’s works from Britain to China in the early twentieth century. It shows that, while Dickens was amongst some of the major Western authors whose literary works (such as fiction) were brought to China by Chinese translators and adaptors for particular social and political purposes, in Hong Kong his presence was less prominent though his work has been promoted and used to invoke in particular the Christmas spirit that he came to embody in selected English literary journals and newspapers. For my publications that arise directly out of this project, and one which I have highlighted in Section 5.3, spatiality has emerged as a key theoretical lens through which various cross-cultural encounters are explored and highlighted. The relationship between space, the city and the everyday has also been one of the features that I explored when discussing the translation and adaptation of Dickensian texts in China, and when I carried out a comparative study between the novels by Lao She and Dickens in one of the research articles that I produced as part of this project. Overall, this project succeeds in exploring cross-cultural encounters from a perspective that goes beyond the usual Anglo-American criticisms pertaining to Victorian Studies. It also contributes to the emerging field of literary geographies.

21610515.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
21610515.value: The research on Dickens in Hong Kong can be used as a starting point for future research that seeks to investigate the publication and circulation of literary texts by authors not only from Britain but also from other parts of the world in early twentieth-century Hong Kong. This is in fact one of the key areas of investigation in my next project. During the ECS project, I uncovered some archival materials relating to some English and other expatriate writers in Hong Kong; while they are not of direct relevance to my ECS project, I have incorporated some of them into my GRF project (which I started working on in January) because I hope to investigate the publication scene and the literary and journalistic connections between Hong Kong, Britain and China in the early twentieth century. So in many ways, the ECS project not only helps me complete an author-specific study, but it also paves the ground for my next research.

21610515.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
21610515.value: This project addresses the current knowledge gap in Dickens studies by exploring his connections with China and Hong Kong in the early twentieth century. Combining theoretical explorations and archival research on Dickens’s works in both their original and translated or adapted forms, as well as related publications in literary magazines and newspapers, this research contributes to the recent ‘global turn’ in Dickens scholarship, and Victorian Studies more generally. Adopting theoretical perspectives that are drawn from both Western and Chinese sources and making use of different archival materials, this research leads to a deeper understanding of cross-cultural encounters from a perspective that goes beyond the usual Anglo-American criticisms. The study also contributes to the emerging field of literary studies by exploring the relationship between space, everyday and the city, especially in cross-cultural contexts.

21611115.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
21611115.value: With an estimated market volume of US$ 5.1 billion by 2020, 3D printing is predicted to radically change all manufacturing and design industries. Today the global impact of such innovation is hard to overestimate. 3D printing is increasingly becoming an affordable and common everyday process. Yet currently most of 3D prints are digital replicas of existing objects. There is little understanding of how 3D printing technologies can lead to a new design, new products, and new fields of work. The key to the future of 3D printing lies in the past. In the long history of applied arts, the innovation of technologies and design has been supported by craftsmanship. Precision, transparency, curiosity and discovery to innovate are the keywords of success. In the era of Rococo, all aspects of craftsmanship and design were geared together to create a total work of art. Open to different cultures, the architects and designer of Rococo have understood the value of combining technology and art into an interdisciplinary approach. With a role model like Chinoiserie, cultural diversity and globalization became part and essence of this style. Based on this interplay of forces and cultures of the Rococo, this research will examine the factors of design as well as transfer these methods and strategies to a digital craftsmanship. The form-finding process for 3D printing, as visualized in the role model of the Rococo, can be seen as an initial point, which opens up, hitherto undiscovered spaces of action and intervention in design and architecture. The result of this initial investigation will manifest in the design of prototypes for 3D printing and further material amalgamations. These objects will articulate the idea and qualities of digital craftsmanship into a total work of art. The analysis of the role model of Rococo, the development of the design as well as the process of the creation of these objects will be accompanied, evaluated and documented by periodic recorded meetings of an expert panel. The interdisciplinary members of this panel correspond to the idea of the interplay of art and technology, shown in the craftsmanship and design of the Rococo. The members are artist Jane Prophet (SCM), architect Marjan Colletti (TU Innsbruck), Turlif Villebrand, Norwegian computer scientist and pioneer in 3D printing, philosopher Sarah Schmidt (Humboldt University Berlin) and Harald Kraemer, media art/design historian (SCM). The results will be discussed in a symposium, published in a book, and exhibited. 市場估計三維打印技術的市場規模於二零二零年將達到51億美金，由此可見三維打印技術將於未來為製造和設計等行業帶來重大改革。現時三維打印技術的成本逐漸下降，應用廣泛程度也越趨普遍，但三維打印技術不應只簡單地以數碼形態呈現和複製實物，它應當用於展示如何推動這種科技在設計上的創新的潛質。過往造就今日，應用美術、創新科技和設計能發展至今，全賴手工藝的支持，希望三維打印技術的發展亦有鑑於此。精確，透明，好奇心和探索創新都是成功的關鍵。 在洛可可時代，基於主張多元文化及全球化，於工藝及設計過程中融合科技和藝術的跨領域實踐擔當著重要角色。本研究將透過考究相關的設計要素，以及轉化方法和策略，在如三維打印技術般的數碼技術，去探索跨領域實踐這個概念。三維打印技術的找形分析過程將被視為本研究的第一步。而整個研究可通過了解經三維打印完成的樣板的形態及更進一步的材料結合實驗來完成。 多位跨領域的專家會定期參與本研究的會議，會議過程將被記錄。參與成員包括國際藝術家、建築師、計算機科學家及三維打印技術先驅、哲學家和媒體藝術∕設計史學家。研究結果將一併在研討會上討論，並以書刊和展覽形式發佈。
