28608115.label: Major findings and research outcome
28608115.value: NSSLS makes a difference in fostering the sustainability consciousness (SCo) of Hong Kong students. It allows teachers to create unique pedagogical models that ignite quality learning experiences and foster SCo. The majority of the surveyed 4985 students reported self-perceived increase (“slightly more” or above) of sustainability-related knowledge, attitude and behavioural aspects of their SCo, but low participation in environmental groups and activities as fostered by NSSLS. Students reported an awareness increase (on average, “slightly more” and above) for the topics of climate change, air pollution, nature conservation, renewable energy, industrial pollution, water disposal; and renewable energy, water disposal (on average, “much more”). Students reported a high increase of behaviour for the areas of paper recycling and plastic disposal. 25% perceived that NSSLS made no change in their knowledge of biodiversity and ozone depletion. Over 40% answered that their behaviour of recycling metal products had not change. Over 80% answered that television and Internet were their major means of learning about sustainability (Part C12 Reports; C8 Savelyeva 2017, 2018). Furthermore, students perceived their low participation in sustainability-related civic groups and activities. Their reported increase of environmental knowledge, attitude and behaviour together with low environmental activism and participation phenomena is coined as “sustainability consciousness with nil activism” (Part C8, Savelyeva, 2018; 2019) Document analysis of the reflective students’ narratives (n=989) indicated that students apply critical, imaginative, reflexive, and forward-looking approaches to shape and project their sustainable reality in an action- and future-oriented way. The three resulting themes that described students’ SCo were intentionality to make a difference; engagement with the complex issues regarding identity, society, nature; and students’ eschatological perspectives. The action- and future-oriented imagery theme derived from the students' narratives provided evidence of their high sustainability consciousness (Part C8 Savelyeva, 2017; 2018; 2019). The data from teachers’ interviews (n=31) revealed four clusters that constitute a unique teaching model that fosters SCo: adaptation, socialisation, innovation/creativity, parents’ involvement. The quality of teachers was highly significant. Respondents had rich teaching experience, strong passion, hope, and ambitions to increase students’ SCo. The quality of teaching support—group teaching, peer-support, resources provided by the government, HKPTU, HKLSTA—was an important feature of successful fostering of SCo. Disconnection between the values taught in class and those practiced in some of the students’ families, low income family background, lack of parental connection with NSSLS, tensions between examination pressure and teaching aimed at SCo were found as major blocks to SCo.

28608115.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
28608115.value: IMPLICATIONS OF FINDINGS FINDING1: Sustainability consciousness (Sco) is complex and a composite of many meanings within NSSLS. A further longitudinal study will help to detect different aspects of long-term SCo and propose a comprehensive set of classroom activities. FINDING2: Family sustainability values, economic background, parenting style are important in fostering SCo through NSSLS. A longitudinal study of family-school relationships and family bound sustainability values will be beneficial for further NSSLS advancement. FINDING3: Imagination and creativity are crucial features in fostering SCO through NSSLS. This emphasizes the importance of developing of teaching materials which target imagination and creativity in NSSLSS lessons, as well as teacher training. FINDING4: Over 80 % of students gather environmental knowledge from the Internet and social media. The development of quality teaching materials that introduce Internet and media in NSSLS lessons is desirable. DEVELOPMENTS OF RESEARCH ANALYSIS The current survey instrument can be a useful tool in evaluating SCo development. Adding items that detect gaps in SCo will address possible limitations of the instrument. Continuing the study as longitudinal research will detect systemic developments and changes in the participants’ perceptions and monitor progress at each year of the study (S4-S6). Interviewing students will further detect the NSSLS transformative potential.

28608115.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
28608115.value: In light of the ongoing revision of the New Senior Secondary Liberal Studies (NSS LS) curriculum, the purpose of this study was twofold: 1) to identify and analyse sustainability consciousness of secondary school graduates who enter the tertiary institutions; and 2) to understand what NSS LS curricular features might have fostered it and how we may inform and align liberal education practices at all levels of the Hong Kong educational system. The study stressed the understanding and analysing of students’ self-perceptions of environmental sustainability and teachers’ discernments of NSS LS elements that might contribute to sustainability-related knowledge, awareness and the action of young Hong Kong students. This study was interdisciplinary between the fields of education and sustainability, and it relied on the use of two theoretical perspectives, namely Bateson’s transformative learning model and Hanvey’s conceptualizations of global awareness. Surveys of over 5000 Hong Kong students, analysis of nearly 1000 descriptive students’ narratives, and 31 teacher interviews showed that, sustainability-wise, NSS LS makes a difference. It fosters a high level of sustainability consciousness and creates unique pedagogical experience that benefits Hong Kong education

28608715.label: Project Objectives

rows: To examine whether beliefs about group malleability may predict positive or negative attitudes of Hong Kong locals towards immigrants and tourists from Mainland China.

To test, for the first time, whether different forms of historical narrative of the Chinese nation—a key component of China’s nation building programs—affect its Hong Kong audience’s beliefs about group malleability, and subsequently their attitudes towards immigrants and tourists from Mainland China.

28608715.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
28608715.value: This project explores how popular nation-building discourse may influence Hong Kong residents’ attitudes towards immigrants and tourists from Mainland China, particularly by shaping the former’s beliefs about group malleability. Group malleability refers to the extent to which the core character, morality, and competence of groups are shaped by context and can be changed and developed through effort, practice, and experience. Past literature in social psychology suggests that several practices can be applied to cultivate the belief that inter-group boundaries are malleable, and thus alleviate intergroup hostility. Extending this body of research to the fields of political science and public administration, this proposed project investigates the potential relationship between beliefs about group malleability and the ongoing state-led nation-building effort in Hong Kong, which emphasizes Chinese as a historically unified nation and understates the deep contradictions that have long existed between different ethnic groups. A key hypothesis is that such nation-building narrative will strengthen their audience’s perception that groups have a fixed inherent nature, and thus intensify rather than alleviate conflicts between Hong Kong locals and mainland Chinese. This proposed 24-month project adopts an experimental research design, supplemented by a telephone survey of Hong Kong citizens. The telephone survey, which targets to interview 1000 Hong Kong citizens, will examine if beliefs about group malleability and perceptions of heterogeneity of the Chinese nation predict positive attitudes towards Mainland Chinese. The causal relationship between the key variables will be tested by two separate experiments. Participants in the first experiment will be randomly assigned to read an article that portrays discourteous groups as having a fixed nature or a malleable nature; whereas participants in the second experiment will be randomly assigned to read an article that describe “Chinese” as a historically unified or divided entity. After the experiments, the participants’ attitudes towards Mainland Chinese will be measured by questionnaires. While numerous accounts regarding the impacts of nation-building on intergroup relations have been proposed by critical theorists and historians, to date none of them have been experimentally tested. The proposed study will bridge an important gap between political science and social psychology, and enhance our understanding of the relationship between nation building and intergroup relations.

28608715.label: Realisation of objectives
28608715.value: The project has fully achieved its two objectives: 1) “to examine whether beliefs about group malleability may predict positive or negative attitudes of Hong Kong locals towards immigrants and tourists from Mainland China”; and 2) “to test, for the first time, whether different forms of historical narrative of the Chinese nation—a key component of China’s nation building programs—affect its Hong Kong audience’s beliefs about group malleability, and subsequently their attitudes towards immigrants and tourists from Mainland China.” I find strong evidence that, first, beliefs about group malleability predict positive attitudes of Hong Kong locals towards immigrants and tourists from Mainland China. Second, narratives that describe the Chinese nation as a historically unified community undermine its Hong Kong audience’s beliefs about group malleability, and subsequently intensify their hostility towards immigrants and tourists from Mainland China. In addition to these two key findings, I also discover that beliefs about group malleability not only shape people’s immigration attitudes, but also their national identification. This was unexpected because national identification is usually considered more resilient than immigration attitudes. The technical details of the findings are reported in section 6.1 and the two manuscripts in Part C. These results have four notable theoretical and empirical implications. First, they directly contradict the prevailing optimistic assumptions in the literature and media about the cohesion building effects of nation building. Research in comparative politics has long shown that nation building may backfire, but did not offer any systematic explanation for it. This project fills the gap, by showing that nation building promotes not just a unified identity but also the belief that group characteristics and boundaries are fixed. Second, conceptually, my findings advance a previously unexplored psychological process through which nation building shapes national cohesion. Third, my study enhances the extant understanding of the domestic effects of China’s nation building program, which is arguably the most massive attempt at ideological reeducation in human history. The identity conflicts in Hong Kong are noteworthy because they take place amid increased state-led nation building effort. By explaining how nation building backfires in the city, the study enables a new evaluation of China’s current nation building policies. Forth, my study contributes to the burgeoning scholarship on the psychological determinants of public attitudes to immigrants. Under the “one country, two systems” arrangement, Hong Kong enjoys considerable autonomy in immigration control. To visit or settle in the city, mainland Chinese, like foreigners, need to apply for visas. This makes my findings directly relevant to the studies of immigration attitudes and intergroup relations. In particular, although psychologists have acknowledged the potential impacts of implicit beliefs on intergroup relations, the formation of those beliefs is rarely studied in the context of political manipulation. My study is the first to demonstrate experimentally that narratives of nation building could indeed shape people’s beliefs about group malleability. My findings affirm the political and social embeddedness of implicit beliefs. Given the significance of these findings, I report them in two journal manuscripts. The first one illustrates how nation building transmits its effects on immigration attitudes through implicit beliefs about group malleability. The manuscript has been submitted to the journal Political Psychology and is under review. The second manuscript, forthcoming in Ethnic and Racial Studies, a leading journal in the studies of race and immigration, presents evidence that beliefs about group malleability increase the likelihood for people to identify themselves as Chinese. In addition, as a part of preparation for this project, I re-examined survey data collected in 2016 to gain initial insights into the determinants of immigration attitudes in Hong Kong. The results of which are published in The Asian Pacific Migration Journal (title: “Explaining attitudes toward immigrants from Mainland China in Hong Kong”). I do not include the manuscript in Part C because its data was collected before the project commenced. To publicize the results and improve the quality of analysis, I presented preliminary findings in at least five international conferences and workshops (Part C), and received supportive comments from the participants. The principal investigator have also attended two media interviews (Part C), and will submit a 3000-word commentary in Chinese to Initium Media in May (invitation email attached in Part C). I have already uploaded the details of the project to my personal website. This project has achieved its education plan. Nearly five hundred local undergraduate students were recruited as participants and were debriefed on the logic of experimental research. I also trained at least 4 part-time student helpers to support the experiments. They acquired skills to communicate instructions effectively with the participants and learned the nuance of experimental methods in social sciences. The principal investigator shared his research design and findings in seminars and lectures at the Education University of Hong Kong (see lecture slides in Part C). Inspired by the project, two groups of undergraduate students under the supervision of the principal investigator designed their own experiments in their final year projects to examine people’s perceptions towards stray animals and media neutrality in Hong Kong. Finally, I have trained an MPhil student, who provided research assistance to the project. He has successfully completed his research on the political preferences of district councilors in Hong Kong using experimental methods (abstract attached in Part C). I experienced some difficulties in recruiting participants and retaining research assistants in the first year of this project. However with a four month extension I successfully tackled those problems. Overall, I believe that the study has successfully achieved its original objectives, and has made some unexpected contributions to the literature. I am grateful for the support from the RGC and the helpful comments from the reviewers.

28608715.label: Major findings and research outcome
28608715.value: The key hypothesis of this project is that by promoting beliefs that groups have fixed inherent characteristics, nation building narratives may intensify Hong Kong natives’ hostility towards immigrants from mainland China. I find strong support for this hypothesis in the project, and uncover unexpected effects of implicit beliefs on national identification. To be more specific, my telephone survey of the Hong Kong population (n=1032) confirms that perceived national homogeneity is negatively associated with beliefs about group malleability (β= -0.19, p<0.001). Meanwhile, respondents who have a stronger belief that group characteristics are malleable are more likely to welcome mainland Chinese migrants (β=0.30, p<0.001). Further analysis shows that beliefs about group malleability (β=-0.01, p<0.01) mediate the effects of perceptions towards the Chines nation on immigration attitudes. The laboratory experiments suggest that the aforementioned relationships are at least partially causal. In the first experiment, respondents who are exposed to narratives that emphasize the homogeneity of the Chinese nation report a higher level of fixed group perceptions than those who receive the opposite message (t = 5.01; p < 0.001). Furthermore, consistent with the findings from telephone survey, the mediation effect of beliefs about group malleability is negative and equal to –0.05 (p < 0.05). In other words, the fixed belief triggered by an exposure to nation building narratives undermined the participants’ support toward migrants. In the second experiment, respondents who are primed to believe that group characteristics are fixed report significantly more negative attitudes toward migrants from other parts of China (t = 3.04, p < 0.001), fewer stereotypes (t = -2.13, p < 0.01), and lower levels of perceived cultural (t = -3.24, p < 0.01) and economic threats (t = -2.13; p < 0.05). The results demonstrated that a fixed (malleable) belief about group characteristics undermines (improves) individuals’ attitudes toward migrants from other parts of the country. These findings are reported in the first manuscript in Part C (under review in Political Psychology). Finally, in testing the key hypothesis I discover that beliefs about group malleability not only shape people’s immigration attitudes, but also their national identification. Specifically, people who perceive the core character of groups as shaped by context (i.e. it is malleable) are more likely to have a higher level of Chinese identification (β=0.09, p<0.01). I report this finding in the second manuscript in Part C (forthcoming in Ethnic and Racial Studies).

28608715.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
28608715.value: Immigration is one of the most divisive issues in contemporary politics. This research suggests that nation building policies may be counterproductive in reducing hostility against immigrants. Policy makers must carefully evaluate if existing nation building strategies have spread beliefs that may harden intergroup boundaries. Future research may build upon this project, and identify policies that are more likely to reduce conflicts between natives and immigrants. Past research on immigration attitudes has tended to treat immigration policies as an outcome rather than a determinant of natives’ immigration attitudes. In particular, no research to date has distinguished between immigrants admitted under restrictive and liberal immigration policies, even though this distinction is a critical component in the theoretical story about natives’ responses to immigrants. Guided by untested assumptions, many countries impose tight restrictions on immigration, which in most cases not only undermines their ability to compete in the international labor market, but also intensifies the natives’ perception of threats from immigrants. To address this issue, in my latest proposal submitted to the RGC, I develop a plan to disentangle the complex relationships between immigration policy and natives’ attitudes toward skilled foreign workers by a survey experiment.

28608715.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
28608715.value: Political elites have long leveraged on their influence to promote a unified national identity, and are often baffled at the resistance and localism they encounter. Based on data collected in Hong Kong, an epicenter of subnational conflicts in China, my research suggests that nation building may intensify tension between subnational groups because it helps spread the belief that groups have fixed inherent characteristics. Specifically, in the face of deep intergroup cultural and political differences, people who see their nation as a historically unified entity are more likely to believe that those differences are unchangeable and, in turn, develop negative attitudes toward other subnational groups. We support these arguments with a representative survey of the population and two laboratory experiments. In the first experiment, respondents who are exposed to narratives that emphasize the homogeneity of the Chinese nation report a higher level of fixed group perceptions than those who receive the opposite message. In the second experiment, respondents who are primed to believe that group characteristics are fixed report significantly more negative attitudes toward migrants from other parts of China. My findings contribute substantively to the study of nation building, and shed new light on the formation of immigration attitudes.

28611215.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
28611215.value: This proposal argues for research that aims to better understand middle leadership in Hong Kong secondary schools and factors that influence how middle leadership is conceptualised and enacted. The premise of the study is that, following international trends of decentralisation, the responsibilities of principals have expanded, contributing to a further distribution of school principals’ leadership to other senior leaders, middle leaders (MLs), and key staff members. The proposed study builds on recent research which contends that just as effective principals must lead across a broad purview of responsibilities, so too must effective MLs in order to build successful schools. Conventionally, the work of secondary school MLs has focused on managerial tasks of subject area administration, but has not accounted for MLs’ potential in leading innovative practice, participating in school-wide leadership and engaging the professional and local communities beyond the school. This conception of middle leadership requires of senior leaders, teachers and MLs themselves a significant shift in understanding the nature of secondary school MLs’ work: a change in focus from managing to leading. However, the research base on secondary school middle leadership is very limited, typically focusing on MLs’ subject area responsibilities, issues of hierarchy and influence within schools, and formal job preparation. There is vast potential for MLs to contribute to their schools beyond subject area management, yet the research base yields limited insight on such work and on how MLs can be supported to accomplish it. In essence, the main purposes of this study are to examine how teachers and leaders in Hong Kong secondary schools understand middle leadership, what MLs do, and the factors shaping such understanding and actions. The analysis examines: (a) the opportunities that MLs have for school leadership at the subject area, school-wide and external levels; (b) the resulting benefits, challenges and tensions that MLs experience; (c) the skills sets and support structures needed to address (b) above; (d) how MLs are developed for their roles in the three leadership levels; and (e) organisational and cultural factors that influence how MLs’ roles are understood and enacted. This research employs multi-site qualitative case studies of MLs in six secondary schools in Hong Kong. Selection criteria target schools that aim to provide leadership opportunities to MLs that extend beyond subject area administration to uncover challenges and opportunities that result from such engagement. 是次提案旨在理解香港中學中層領導之定位及影響中層領導的概念化和制定之因素。 是次研究建基於國際發展趨勢下之權力下放、校長職責擴大繼而進一步將學校校長領導推向其他高層領導、中層領導（MLS）以及主要教職員。是次研究以最近的專題研究作延伸以 有效的校長必須跨越及引領廣泛範圍的責任以及有效的中層領導亦必須以同一手法建立成功的學校為基礎。 傳統上，中學中層領導的工作一直專注於學科的管理但沒有考慮中層領導在領導變革、參與學校層面及投入學校以外社區的領導潛能。此中層領導的概念需要高層領導，教師及中層領導者自身對理解中學中層領導本質上作出顯著的轉變─從管理層面轉移到領導層面。然而，現時專注於中學中層領導之研究有限，基本只集中於中層領導之學科上的職責，職級問題及其對學校之影響和正式工作的準備。事實上，中層領導者對學校學科以外之貢獻有顯著的潛在正面影響，唯現時此層面之研究缺乏前瞻性，對中層領導者支持不足令其目標難以實現。 是次研究的主要目的在於探討香港中學教師及領導者對中層領導，中層領導者職責理解及背後之因素。分析將探討一：中層領導對學校領導於學科層面、學校及外在層面之機遇；二：中層領導者面對的益處、困難及張力；三：滿足須求二所須之技能及支持；四：中層領導在三個領導層面之職位發展及五：組織及文化因素如何影響中層領導角色的理解和扮演。 本研究採用了多元定性個案研究中層領導在六間香港中學之概況。被選擇的學校都旨在提供領導機遇為中層領導者開拓超越學科領域的管理機會以迎合及揭示當中的困難和機遇。

28611215.label: Realisation of objectives
28611215.value: The research envisioned 6 schools in which individual and focus group interviews would be conducted, with the supplementary focused observation of leadership events. In the end, data were collected from 8 schools with a total of 114 participants (n= 21 Senior Leaders (SLs), 51 Middle Leaders (MLs), and 31 teachers in 11 focus groups) were interviewed. Each interview lasted between 40 to 60 minutes. Often school principals were unable to facilitate focused observations. Instead, ethnographic-like observations were recorded as field notes. Two schools provided the opportunity to trial time-use surveys and social network surveys, which yielded additional insight. Drawing on an analysis of pilot data and building on the ECS’s conceptual framework, a small grant was obtained from the International Baccalaureate (IB) to study middle leadership in an additional 4 IB curricula schools in East Asia (including one school located in Hong Kong; n= 16 SLs, 64 MLs, 25 Teachers). Although not part of the ECS research, and funded separately, the ECS provided the conceptual basis the analytical structure use in the IB Case Reports (See Report included in Other Outputs below). This facilitated the comparison of contextual and cultural features that impact on Middle Leadership. The piloting process suggested the importance of including both subject area leaders, and leaders with cross-school responsibilities as middle leaders. School principals also contended that Middle leaders with coordinating roles, such as Special Educational Needs or Information Technology Coordinators, should be sampled as middle leaders who influence the accomplishment of school priorities. Often the presence of these roles and the profile extended to them by principals reflected prioritisation in the school mission and resource planning (Bryant, 2018, Wong et al, under review). Accordingly, this sampling provided a more comprehensive understanding of how leadership is distributed across each school than a more limited emphasis on subject leaders alone could have. Objective 1: To theorize middle leadership by examining commonalities and variation in teacher, middle and senior leaders’ understanding of MLs’ roles in secondary schools. This was fully accomplished by assessing commonalities and variation across schools and leaders in participants’ understanding of middle leadership. Often, perceptions fractured around prioritising managerial versus leadership roles. Differences in perceptions among principals on ML roles considered issues of school needs or priorities. MLs were influenced by their own perceptions of professional autonomy, relevant experience, support from senior leaders, and collegial relationships. These influenced their role identification and their tendency to initiate innovative practices. The results clearly show how senior leaders (SLs) understand, frame and structure MLs’ work. The results have included typography of middle leadership practices at the instructional, school-wide, and external leadership and a closer analysis of the conditions that support or inhibit middle leaders from exercising leadership in these domains (Bryant, 2018). Objective 2: To analyze opportunities for middle leadership at the subject, school-wide and external leadership levels. This was fully accomplished by categorizing leadership activities in three levels and by differentiating them from management activities (summarised in Bryant, 2018). Additional data were obtained through the use of time-use studies in two schools and social network analysis in a second school (utilizing instruments for the IB research project to supplement observation data). These data found that predominantly MLs worked on instructional leadership in their departments. However, unique school contextual features such as school mission and its alignment with the design of organizational structures and opportunities to mediate external policies (Bryant, 2018; Bryant & Rao, 2019) in addition to SLs’ conceptualization of middle leadership, impacted on MLs’ roles in capacity building (L2) and external leadership (L3). Objective 3: To evaluate opportunities and challenges faced by ML in their role enactment. This was fully accomplished by coding, identifying and itemizing the impediments and supports to developing middle leadership capacity. In particular human resources, organizational design, and professional relationship (Bryant, 2018; Bryant & Rao, 2019; Wong et al., under review) . Differences were partially explained by variation in SLs’ resource allocation for professional learning, innovative practices, time allocation, and organizational restructuring. These impacted on MLs’ autonomy to innovate, develop teachers’ capacity and mediate government and school-based policies. Objective 4. To examine critical skills and support structures needed to help MLs optimize their leadership opportunities and mitigate challenges that they face. This was fully accomplished by identifying areas of development valued by MLs and organizational structures erected by SL (Bryant & Walker, in preparation). The progressive focusing of the research allowed for new themes or findings to be further interrogated in later data collection. A key critical skill identified by participants was the capacity to develop effective teams. MLs were effective when team structures (sometimes involving interlocking membership) were co-designed with senior leaders—typically around mission-critical agendas, and when MLs were empowered in the recruitment process and enabled to design structures within teams (Bryant, 2018; Wong et al., under review). The latter also entails MLs recognizing the capacity of individual team members to lead or contribute to team processes. Objective 5: To examine how MLs’ roles are developed for their roles within and outside their schools and postulate strategies to support and strengthen their preparation. This was fully accomplished by identifying opportunities for professional learning through formal education and in situ training that overlapped with objective 3 and 4. Structures that support the latter appear to account for differences in MLs’ development (Bryant & Walker, in preparation). Objective 6: To provide evidence of and explain the impact of organizational and cultural factors on intra- and inter-school variations in middle leadership. School type was a consideration in school selection. Four aided schools and four Direct Subsidy Scheme schools participated. The differences in autonomy around funding, curriculum and human resources impacted on resource allocation. This accounted for variation in capacity to develop MLs through in situ opportunities and on the development of middle leadership positions beyond conventional subject heads. Accordingly, the findings related to the above objectives were also categorized by school type and by sampling MLs leading in different areas. The number of schools sponsored by the same organization impacted on the opportunity for engagement beyond the school through networking. The capacity of aided school sponsors to resource mission-critical leadership positions was also a factor. Differing school development priorities and resourcing of MLs influenced MLs efficacy as leaders as opposed to managers partially accounted for variation within schools in terms breadth of leadership distribution (i.e. to a range of middle leaders and from middle leaders to team members), and as opposed to delegation. In order to operationalize the objectives, six interrelated research questions were investigated. The findings in section 6.1 are summarized against these questions: 1. What opportunities do MLs in secondary schools have to engage in L1 [instructional leadership], L2 [organizational leadership] and L3 [systems leadership] leadership? 2. Why do they engage (or decline to engage) in these opportunities? 3. What challenges do they face when engaging in these opportunities? 4. What critical skills and support structures do MLs need to navigate these opportunities, challenges and tensions? 5. How are MLs developed for L1, L2 and L3 leadership? 6. What organisational (e.g. school contexts and priorities) and cultural factors account for variance in how MLs’ roles are understood and enacted within and across schools?

28611215.label: Major findings and research outcome
28611215.value: RQ1. Leadership activities were categorised into the three levels, examples included: L1: Facilitating collaboration, improving curriculum, mentoring and coaching teachers, developing instructional resources, distributing leadership within departments. L2: Conducting professional learning activities, setting and operationalizing departmental vision, selling school mission, motivating innovation and improvement, collaborative strategic planning, negotiating resource allocation, building individual and team capacities, leading cross-curricular instruction. L3: Advocating for policy change, interpreting policies, promoting programmes to government and stakeholders, accounting for demographic change. Commonality in understanding was accomplished in light of strongly articulated and resourced school missions and clearly defined and agreed-upon roles. RQ2. MLs primarily engaged in L1 activities. Schools enhanced MLs' engagement in L2 and L3 by resourcing and implementing novel technologies, pedagogies or curriculum, or enacting unique missions. Schools established conditions that supported L2 & L3 middle leadership by recruiting specialist MLs, focusing MLs' work around school mission, investing in professional learning, empowering, mentoring by SLs, resourcing innovation, developing collegiality, establishing team structures, and aligning initiatives to systemic policies. RQ3. MLs reported tensions in balancing teaching and leading responsibilities, and in prioritising leadership and management responsibilities. Mediating factors enhanced MLs’ development included: SLs clarifying and communicating the scope of MLs' roles, defining strong school missions, aligning innovations to school mission; MLs being responsible for developing and engaging informal teacher leaders, overseeing financial and human resources, and establishing routines and organizational structures. RQ4. Participants prioritised critical skills regarding understanding and aligning work to vision and mission, the capacity to communicate and motivate, attentiveness to colleagues' social needs, and building effective team cultures and capacity. Effective support structures (in addition to RQ3 above) included the establishment of formal expectations, committees and teams, positions on organizational hierarchy, mission-driven specialisms. RQ5. Schools did not formally distinguish among leadership levels in terms of targeted ML development or professional learning. Leader development occurred through participation in formal university-based programmes, on-site ML development training, on-the-job shadowing, mentoring by senior leaders, inclusion in development planning and regular meetings with principals. RQ6. School autonomy (e.g. DSS or aided) shaped and impacted on MLs. This concerned differentiation of curriculum, and financial and human capital. Schools attentive to succession planning prioritised MLs’ development. Mission-critical resource allocation established specialised ML positions (SEN, ECA or curriculum coordinators) and layers of middle leadership roles (some reporting to others) and committee membership. School histories influenced role perception, commitment and activism, perceptions of hierarchy, and capacity to recruit and retain MLs.

28611215.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
28611215.value: MLs reported self-efficacy when they prioritized building team and individual capacity. Ongoing research is examining how MLs lead Professional Communities. This is being supervised by the PI though an EdD dissertation (to be completed by mid-June 2019). The PI is collaborating with colleagues to conduct school-based middle leadership training at three schools in Hong Kong (2019-20). The training includes an intervention study on MLs role in building team capacity and innovative practices. Pre- and post- intervention data will be collected on teaching, learning and pastoral care (L1), professional learning (L2), family and community partnerships (L3). This extends from the ECS and may inform a subsequent grant proposal. In two schools, the importance of MLs work to leadership succession was uncovered. A small-scale study on succession planning (2019-20) is being led by the PI and funded by an Asia Pacific Centre for Leadership and Change Regional Research Grant. It examines how SLs develop leadership capacity to meet succession challenges in Hong Kong schools. A comparative research agenda on Middle Leadership in Hong Kong, Shenzhen and Guangdong is progressing using data collected from this ECS, the IB study, and doctoral research supervised by the PI.

28611215.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
28611215.value: This study built on previous research findings that educational reforms had led to an increase in school principals’ work and that successful schools are marked by patterns of shared leadership. By the beginning of this study, very little research had been conducted on the work of middle leaders (MLs), with whom leadership is often shared or distributed. The significance and value of this research may be summarized in three propositions related to MLs' efficacy and development. Proposition 1: Senior leaders influence the direction of MLs’ work and their capacity development through school-based aims, structures and initiatives. These include focusing middle leadership activity around unique school missions, curriculum and pedagogical innovations; defining leadership roles; formally established routines; and through organizational restructuring. Proposition 2: The above can propel MLs' engagement in systems-level leadership by stimulating MLs to engage government and other stakeholders around issues concerning advocacy and policy implementation. Proposition 3: Where MLs perceive themselves, and are perceived by others, as most effective, they identify informal teacher leaders and build the capacity other teachers and teaching teams. This can be facilitated through modeling, mentoring, and coaching others. Moving forward, these findings can potentially inform middle leadership and teacher leadership professional learning programmes.

28611515.label: Project Objectives
28611515.value: To investigate (RH1) whether familial expressed emotion and experienced professional discrimination predict greater stereotype self-concurrence and stronger habitual self-stigma; To investigate (RH2) whether greater stereotype self-concurrence is related to stronger habitual self-stigma, and whether this relationship is strengthened by greater experiential avoidance; To investigate (RH3) whether stereotype self-concurrence and habitual self-stigma independently predict poorer objective and subjective outcomes.

To investigate (RH2) whether greater stereotype self-concurrence is related to stronger habitual self-stigma, and whether this relationship is strengthened by greater experiential avoidance;
To investigate (RH3) whether stereotype self-concurrence and habitual self-stigma independently predict poorer objective and subjective outcomes.

28611515.label: Realisation of objectives
28611515.value: Realization of Objective 1: The objective “to investigate whether familial expressed emotion and experienced professional discrimination predict greater stereotype self-concurrence and stronger habitual self-stigma” was well achieved as evidenced by the three new models that we have formulated in this project (Chan & Fung, 2019; Chan & Lam, 2018; Chan & Leung, under preparation). By validating the new models with structural equation modeling, we have demonstrated that experienced discrimination in general was a significant predictor of self-stigma content and self-stigma process (Chan & Fung, 2019). Moreover, we have demonstrated that familial expressed emotion (Chan & Lam, 2018) and professional stigma (Chan & Leung, under preparation) significantly predicted higher levels of self-stigma content and self-stigma process. Realization of Objective 2: The objective “to investigate whether greater stereotype self-concurrence is related to stronger habitual self-stigma, and whether this relationship is strengthened by greater experiential avoidance” was well achieved as evidenced by the four new models that we have formulated in this project (Chan & Fung, 2019; Chan & Lam, 2018; Chan, Lee, & Mak, 2018; Chan & Leung, under preparation). By validating the new models with structural equation modeling, we have shown that self-stigma content was positively related to self-stigma process (Chan & Fung, 2019; Chan & Lam, 2018; Chan, Lee, & Mak, 2018; Chan & Leung, under preparation). We have also shown that experiential avoidance (also known as psychological inflexibility) significantly predicted lower levels of stigma resistance and then higher levels of self-stigma content and self-stigma process (Chan, Lee, & Mak, 2018). Finally, we have shown that, after controlling for mindfulness and self-compassion, psychological flexibility significantly predicted higher levels of stigma resistance and then lower levels of self-stigma content and self-stigma process. Realization of Objective 3: The objective “to investigate whether stereotype self-concurrence and habitual self-stigma independently predict poorer objective and subjective outcomes” was well achieved as evidenced by the four new models that we have formulated in this project (Chan & Fung, 2019; Chan & Lam, 2018; Chan, Lee, & Mak, 2018; Chan & Leung, under preparation). By validating the new models with structural equation modeling, we have revealed that self-stigma content and self-stigma process were significant independent predictors of clinical recovery (as indicated by symptom remission and functional restoration) and personal recovery (as indicated by positive recovery perceptions and life satisfaction) (Chan & Lam, 2018; Chan, Lee, & Mak, 2018; Chan & Leung, under preparation). Moreover, we have revealed that the content and process of self-stigma were significant independent predictors of sleep disturbance, leading to impairments in physical and mental health-related quality of life (Chan & Fung, 2019). Our project has important theoretical contributions and practical implications. Theoretically, our work has supported a content-process distinction in studies of self-stigma. As self-stigma content and self-stigma process each explained unique variance in various recovery outcomes, they were two different dimensions of self-stigma. Given that individuals with mental illness may be affected by both the content and process of self-stigma, relying solely on traditional content-oriented measures may underestimate the associations of self-stigma with recovery. Future research should consider both self-stigma content and self-stigma process in order to capture a fuller picture of the impact of self-stigma on individuals with mental illness. Practically, our findings have important implications on the development of anti-self-stigma interventions for individuals with mental illness. Given the independent effects of self-stigma content and self-stigma process on recovery outcomes, anti-self-stigma strategies should be geared toward tackling self-stigma content as well as targeting self-stigma process. To reduce self-stigma content, practitioners may help individuals with mental illness build critical consciousness and develop cognitive restructuring skills that enable them to recognize the illegitimacy of discrimination and challenge their self-stigmatizing views. Also, to alleviate self-stigma process, practitioners may empower individuals with mental illness to extend their self-characterizations beyond their stigmatized identities, which may help them think about their self-stigmatizing thoughts less often.

28611515.label: Major findings and research outcome
28611515.value: Major findings: Self-stigma has long been assessed as a global, unidimensional construct among individuals with mental illness. Our research, however, has demonstrated that self-stigma is a more differentiated, multifaceted concept. In this project, we have formulated and validated four new conceptual models that offer an advanced understanding of the components, antecedents, and consequences of self-stigma (Chan & Fung, 2019; Chan & Lam, 2018; Chan, Lee, & Mak, 2018; Chan & Leung, under preparation). In terms of components, we have demonstrated that individuals with mental illness may vary in not only the extent to which they endorse their self-stigmatizing thoughts, referred to as self-stigma “content,” but also the extent to which they think about their self-stigmatizing thoughts repetitively and habitually, referred to as self-stigma "process” (Chan & Fung, 2019; Chan & Lam, 2018; Chan, Lee, & Mak, 2018; Chan & Leung, under preparation). In terms of antecedents, we have identified several risk factors (i.e., experienced discrimination, familial expressed emotion, and professional stigma) that increase the chances for individuals with mental illness to endorse self-stigma content and experience self-stigma process (Chan & Fung, 2019; Chan & Lam, 2018; Chan & Leung, under preparation). We have also identified several protective factors (i.e., mindfulness, self-compassion, and psychological flexibility) that reduce the chances for individuals with mental illness to suffer from the content and process of self-stigma (Chan, Lee, & Mak, 2018). In terms of consequences, we have demonstrated the adverse impact of self-stigma content and self-stigma process on a myriad of recovery outcomes, including symptom remission, functional restoration, sleep quality, recovery perceptions, life satisfaction, and physical and mental health-related quality of life (Chan & Fung, 2019; Chan & Lam, 2018; Chan, Lee, & Mak, 2018; Chan & Leung, under preparation). Research outcomes: This project has led to publications in internationally leading journals, including Mindfulness, Quality of Life Research, and American Journal of Orthopsychiatry. In addition, findings of the project have been presented at international conferences, including the Association for Psychological Science Annual Convention, the International Convention of Psychological Science, and the Asian Conference on Psychology and the Behavioral Sciences.

28611515.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
28611515.value: The practical utility of our project findings can be further enhanced by the development and implementation of a large-scale evidence-based intervention program that targets both self-stigma content and self-stigma process among individuals with mental illness. Specifically, given the protective effects of mindfulness, self-compassion, and psychological flexibility against self-stigma, an evidence-based program that combines the elements of mindfulness intervention, self-compassion training, and acceptance and commitment therapy that target self-stigma should be designed and developed. On the other hand, given the adverse impact of familial expressed emotion and professional stigma on self-stigma, anti-stigma interventions should be conducted for the individuals’ family members and healthcare service providers. Finally, future research can be expanded to test our newly proposed conceptualization of self-stigma, namely the content-process distinction in self-stigma, to other stigmatized populations, such as individuals with physical disabilities, sexual minorities, and students with special educational needs.

28611515.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
28611515.value: Self-stigma has long been assessed as a unidimensional construct, but our research suggests that self-stigma is multifaceted. Specifically, individuals with mental illness may vary in not only the extent to which they endorse their self-stigmatizing thoughts, referred to as self-stigma content, but also the extent to which they think about their self-stigmatizing thoughts repetitively and habitually, referred to as self-stigma process. In this project, we have identified the risk and protective factors for self-stigma content and self-stigma process. The risk factors include experienced discrimination from family members and healthcare professionals, whereas the protective factors include mindfulness, self-compassion, and psychological flexibility. In addition, we have demonstrated the independent adverse impact of self-stigma content and self-stigma process on functioning and well-being in physical and mental dimensions of health. Theoretically, our findings point to a content-process distinction in studies of self-stigma. Practically, our findings highlight the importance of designing multipronged intervention programs to reduce the potential harmful impact of both self-stigma content and self-stigma process on individuals with mental illness.
